# Constructible complexes on algebraic varieties

*AI-generated exposition by GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).*

A point of a singular space has two different kinds of local data. A stalk records what a sheaf assigns at the point. A costalk also records how that value attaches to the surrounding punctured space. We will calculate that attachment in three examples, then show how finite stratifications and duality organize the answers. The puncture contributes a monodromy operator, a node contributes a diagonal map between branch values, and a cone contributes the cochains of a circle bundle.

The classical setting is a complex algebraic variety with its classical topology and coefficients in a characteristic-zero field \(\Lambda\). The arithmetic setting is a separated finite-type scheme over a finite field or its algebraic closure, with coefficients \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), where \(\ell\) is invertible on the scheme. Finite torsion coefficients will be used to construct the arithmetic operations; the passage to normalized adic coefficients is treated explicitly in Section 3. A local system has finite rank, and an arithmetic local system means a lisse sheaf.

Our convention is \(H^m(K[a])=H^{m+a}(K)\). In particular, a vector space \(V[a]\) lies in degree \(-a\). The Tate coefficient \(\Lambda(1)\) has geometric Frobenius \(q^{-n}\) at an \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\)-point.

## 1. Compute the attaching map first

Let \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow X\) and \(j:X\setminus\{x\}\hookrightarrow X\). For a complex \(K\), name its point value and boundary value

\[
A=i^*K,\qquad B=i^*Rj_*j^*K.
\]

Restriction gives a map \(a:A\to B\). The supported restriction is its derived fibre:

\[
i^!K\simeq\operatorname{Fib}(a)
=\operatorname{Cone}(A\xrightarrow a B)[-1].
\tag{1.1}
\]

To see the map as well as the degrees, take an injective resolution. Sections supported on the closed set form the kernel of restriction to the open complement. Appendix B.2 constructs the resulting support triangle, and B.3 takes its point restriction to obtain (1.1). Appendix A.1 proves the exactness of stalk colimits and the resolution properties used here. Thus a punctured-neighbourhood computation must include its restriction maps and the attaching map; a list of cohomology dimensions alone does not determine the costalk.

### Proposition 1.1. The boundary stalk

For \(j:\mathbb C^\times\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), a local system with fibre \(V\) and positive monodromy \(T\) satisfies

\[
i^*Rj_*L\simeq[\,V\xrightarrow{T-1}V\,]_{[0,1]}.
\]

**Proof.** Appendix A.4 constructs transport, proves the winding-number classification by explicit angle lifts, and constructs the local system with prescribed monodromy as a quotient of the constant sheaf on the logarithmic covering. It proves that morphisms are exactly the intertwiners of the monodromy operators. We use those constructions with the fixed fibre \(V\) and positive-loop operator \(T\).

Cut a punctured disc along each of two different rays. The two resulting contractible angular regions overlap in two components. Trivialize along one overlap; transport on the other supplies \(T\). The two-cover section differential is

\[
(x,y)\longmapsto(y-x,Ty-x):V^2\longrightarrow V^2.
\]

Put \(u=y-x\). Subtracting the first target coordinate from the second changes this differential to \((u,y)\mapsto(u,(T-1)y)\). Its first summand is an acyclic identity complex; the second is the asserted complex. A.3 proves acyclicity of the angular regions, and A.4 proves the two-cover comparison with derived sheaf sections, so the calculation is a derived one. Shrinking the disc preserves the cover and its matrices under radial transport. Taking the exact colimit over these discs therefore computes the actual boundary stalk. Its groups are \(\ker(T-1)\) in degree zero and \(\operatorname{coker}(T-1)\) in degree one. \(\square\)

### Proposition 1.2. Stalks and costalks

Writing \(B=[V\xrightarrow{T-1}V]_{[0,1]}\), the extensions of \(L\) have the following boundary data:

| Complex | Point value \(A\) | Attaching map \(A\to B\) | Costalk |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(Rj_*L\) | \(B\) | identity | \(0\) |
| \(j_!L\) | \(0\) | zero | \(B[-1]\) |
| \(\Lambda_{\mathbb C}\) | \(\Lambda[0]\) | inclusion of constant cochains | \(\Lambda[-2]\) |

**Proof.** On an open direct image, the adjunction to restriction is the identity after restricting to that open; the injective model of B.2 gives the identity boundary map and zero supported kernel. Extension by zero has zero point stalk. Their fibres in (1.1) give the first two rows. In the last row \(T=1\). The fibre is represented in degrees \(0,1,2\) by \(\Lambda\xrightarrow1\Lambda\xrightarrow0\Lambda\); cancelling the identity gives the answer. Thus \(j_!L\) has costalk groups \(\ker(T-1)\) and \(\operatorname{coker}(T-1)\) in degrees one and two. \(\square\)

For the étale constant sheaf on \(\mathbb G_m\subset\mathbb A^1\), the boundary groups are \(\Lambda\) in degree zero and \(\Lambda(-1)\) in degree one; smooth purity places \(\Lambda(-1)\) in the line's degree-two costalk. Section 3 gives the finite-coefficient purity argument; Appendices BV–BX treat its coefficient comparisons. A general arithmetic local system requires the full inertia action. The single-operator description applies to tame local monodromy; it does not remove wild inertia.

### Proposition 1.3. A node separates two branch values

At an ordinary node \(p\) on a reduced complex algebraic curve, let \(N=\nu_*\Lambda_{\widetilde X}\) for the normalization. Then

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
K&i_p^*K&H^m(i_p^!K)\\\hline
\Lambda_X&\Lambda[0]&\Lambda\ (m=1),\quad\Lambda^2\ (m=2)\\
N&\Lambda^2[0]&\Lambda^2\ (m=2).
\end{array}
\]

All unlisted costalk groups are zero.

**Proof.** Appendix L derives the two smooth normalization branches and the local analytic equation \(uv=0\) from the completed-local node criterion. A small neighbourhood is two discs joined at their centres, with puncture the disjoint union of two punctured discs. By Proposition 1.1 and the compatible branch computation in B.4, its boundary value is \([\Lambda^2\xrightarrow0\Lambda^2]_{[0,1]}\). A constant value at the node restricts to the same value on each branch, so the attaching map is the diagonal. Formula (1.1) gives

\[
\Lambda\xrightarrow{\Delta}\Lambda^2\xrightarrow0\Lambda^2
\quad\text{in degrees }0,1,2.
\]

The diagonal is injective; its cokernel is one-dimensional. For \(N\), the two centre values are independent and the attaching map in degree zero is the identity of \(\Lambda^2\). Cancelling this identity leaves degree two alone. B.4 identifies the supported complex with local cohomology by its section resolution, and proves the branch description of \(N\). No identification of a costalk with an ordinary stalk has been made. \(\square\)

Taking the difference of the two branch values gives the exact sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow\Lambda_X\longrightarrow N
\longrightarrow i_{p*}\Lambda\longrightarrow0.
\tag{1.2}
\]

This is local at the chosen node; globally there is one quotient summand for each node. For the cubic \(y^2z=x^2(x+z)\), B.5 constructs the normalization as \(\mathbb P^1\), identifies the two points over \([0:0:1]\) as \(t=1,-1\), and checks that every other point is smooth. Consequently (1.2) is global for this particular cubic. At a smooth point both \(\Lambda_X\) and \(N\) have stalk \(\Lambda\) and degree-two costalk \(\Lambda\).

Over an algebraically closed field, the finite-coefficient étale calculation uses the same stalkwise sequence and purity on the normalization branches. Its costalk groups are \(\Lambda\) in degree one and \(\Lambda(-1)^2\) in degree two. Over a finite field these statements describe geometric vector spaces: Frobenius may permute the two branches, acting also on \(\Lambda^2/\Delta\Lambda\). They assert trivial branch action only for a split node. The passage to adic coefficients uses the operations and coefficient comparisons of Appendices BV–BX.

### Proposition 1.4. The circle bundle around a plane-curve cone

Let \(C\subset\mathbb P^2(\mathbb C)\) be smooth of degree \(n\geq1\), with genus \(g\), and let \(X\) be its affine cone. The link \(M=X\cap S^5_\epsilon\) is the oriented circle bundle of \(\mathcal O_C(-1)\), whose Euler class is \(-n\eta\), where \(\int_C\eta=1\). With our characteristic-zero field,

\[
H^k(M;\Lambda)=
\begin{cases}
\Lambda&k=0,3,\\
\Lambda^{2g}&k=1,2,\\
0&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad 2g=(n-1)(n-2).
\tag{1.3}
\]

**Proof.** A nonzero point of the cone is a line of \(C\) together with a nonzero vector on it. Normalizing the norm of that vector identifies the link with the unit vectors of the tautological line. C.3 verifies these maps, the cone topology, and the comparison of compatible punctured-neighbourhood sections with link cochains.

E.1–E.4 construct the connected compact curve and its finite oriented triangle decomposition. They give integral cohomology \(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z^{2g},\mathbb Z\) in degrees \(0,1,2\). Counting a hyperplane section gives degree \(n\) for \(\mathcal O_C(1)\), hence Euler class \(-n\eta\) for its dual. The integral Thom construction in Appendix D yields

\[
H^{k-2}(C)\xrightarrow{\smile(-n\eta)}H^k(C)
\longrightarrow H^k(M)\longrightarrow H^{k-1}(C)
\xrightarrow{\smile(-n\eta)}H^{k+1}(C).
\]

Over \(\Lambda\), the displayed map from degree zero to degree two is invertible. Exactness therefore identifies \(H^1(M)\) with \(H^1(C)\) and \(H^2(M)\) with another copy of \(H^1(C)\). The endpoints give \(H^0(M)=H^3(M)=\Lambda\), and the other terms vanish. E.5–E.6 prove the plane-curve genus formula by the tangent/normal sequences and a ramification count; specifically \(\omega_C\simeq\mathcal O_C(n-3)\), \(\chi(C)=3n-n^2\), and \(\deg\omega_C=n(n-3)=2g-2\). These supply the numerical value used above. \(\square\)

### Proposition 1.5. Recover the vertex costalk from the link

For the cone vertex \(v\), the only nonzero costalk groups of the constant sheaf are

\[
H^2(i_v^!\Lambda_X)=\Lambda^{2g},\qquad
H^3(i_v^!\Lambda_X)=\Lambda^{2g},\qquad
H^4(i_v^!\Lambda_X)=\Lambda.
\tag{1.4}
\]

**Proof.** The attaching map is \(\Lambda[0]\to C^\bullet(M;\Lambda)\), sending a scalar to its constant cochain. C.3 proves this statement for the actual shrinking cone neighbourhoods, using the cochain/sheaf comparison in C.2. Its fibre has \(H^k=\widetilde H^{k-1}(M;\Lambda)\). Connectedness removes the reduced degree-zero term; (1.3) gives precisely (1.4). For \(j:X\setminus\{v\}\hookrightarrow X\), the boundary value of \(Rj_*\Lambda\) is \(C^\bullet(M;\Lambda)\), with identity attaching map and zero costalk. \(\square\)

For a smooth plane cubic, \(g=1\). Thus the link dimensions are \(1,2,2,1\), the costalk dimensions are \(2,2,1\) in degrees \(2,3,4\), and \(i_v^*Rj_*\Lambda[2]\) lies in degrees \(-2,-1,0,1\). This last calculation is the input for the later intermediate-extension example.

The algebraic punctured cone is also \(\mathcal O_C(-1)^\times\). In the étale setting its global Gysin calculation gives \(H^1(C)\), \(H^1(C)(-1)\), and \(\Lambda(-2)\) in positive degrees \(1,2,3\), with \(\Lambda\) in degree zero. This global computation uses the étale Gysin formalism; it does not identify a strict-local vertex costalk. The proof of (1.4) is the classical cone argument just given.

## 2. Assemble local data and dualize it

A finite algebraic stratification partitions \(X\) into smooth locally closed subvarieties, with each closure a union of pieces. A sheaf is constructible when its restrictions to the pieces of some such partition are finite-rank local systems. For a fixed partition \(\mathcal S\), let \(D^b_{\mathcal S}(X)\) consist of bounded complexes whose cohomology sheaves have this property. Allowing the partition to vary gives \(D^b_c(X)\). The condition is on cohomology sheaves; resolution terms need not be constructible.

### Proposition 2.1. Closure under triangles and truncation

The category \(D^b_{\mathcal S}(X)\) is triangulated and stable under ordinary cohomological truncation. The same holds for \(D^b_c(X)\).

**Proof.** Kernels and cokernels of maps of local systems are local systems: on a common trivializing neighbourhood the map is a constant matrix. An extension is locally constant as well. Classically, shrink to a convex coordinate neighbourhood. The vanishing of \(H^1\) of the constant kernel, proved in A.3, lifts a basis of the constant quotient to sections of the middle sheaf and splits the extension there. Appendix N constructs the finite-monodromy correspondence and its strict lisse coefficient passage. In the global-lattice lisse category, kernels and cokernels correspond to the invariant kernel and quotient representations. Identifying extensions taken in the full constructible category with lisse extensions uses the normalized adic comparison specified in Section 3.

For a triangle \(A\to B\to C\to A[1]\), the long cohomology sequence expresses each \(H^m(C)\) as an extension of a cokernel by a kernel of maps between the cohomology of \(A,B\). Restricting to a stratum applies the preceding argument. Boundedness is preserved, and ordinary truncations retain a subset of the same cohomology sheaves. For finitely many constructible objects, take a common finite smooth refinement; K.6 proves the classical algebraic refinements used here. The same triangle argument then proves the assertion for \(D^b_c\). \(\square\)

### Proposition 2.2. Finite assembly from strata

Every object of \(D^b_c(X)\) is obtained by finitely many triangles from shifts of local systems extended by zero from strata.

**Proof.** Choose a constructibility stratification and remove its open strata, with inclusions \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\), \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\). The exact extension/restriction sequence of B.2 gives

\[
j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K\longrightarrow j_!j^*K[1].
\]

The closed term has fewer strata. Repeat until a single stratum is left. On that stratum, ordinary truncation triangles assemble the bounded restriction from its cohomology local systems. Both inductions are finite. This produces triangles, without asserting that their extension maps vanish. \(\square\)

For the structural map \(a:X\to\mathrm{pt}\), define

\[
\omega_X=a^!\Lambda,\qquad D_XK=R\mathcal Hom(K,\omega_X).
\]

Appendix F constructs the classical structural right adjoint and identifies its local pairing with the dual of compactly supported sections. H constructs the relative operations and their pre-bidual exchanges. I–J establish the normal-neighbourhood geometry and finite local cohomology needed to prove constructible biduality. K then verifies the algebraic constructibility hypotheses for general separated finite-type morphisms. Consequently, in the classical setting,

\[
K\xrightarrow{\sim}D_XD_XK,\qquad
D_YRf_*K\simeq Rf_!D_XK,\qquad
D_Xf^*A\simeq f^!D_YA.
\]

These are natural maps with the evaluation and adjunction counits described in those appendices. Applying internal Hom to a shift also gives \(D(K[a])=(DK)[-a]\). For a geometric closed point the two restriction formulas are

\[
H^m(i_x^*D_XK)=H^{-m}(i_x^!K)^\vee,\qquad
H^m(i_x^!D_XK)=H^{-m}(i_x^*K)^\vee.
\tag{2.1}
\]

F.6 proves the second formula from the closed-embedding adjunction; J.2 and J.5 prove the first using finite evaluation and biduality. M.5–M.7 give the separate singular finite-coefficient étale argument over fields. The arithmetic formulas use the finite-coefficient constructions of M and the complete-coefficient constructions of BV–BX, with their stated geometric hypotheses. Formula (2.1) concerns geometric closed points; a generic-point restriction has a dimension correction.

### Proposition 2.3. Smooth orientation fixes the shift

For a smooth complex variety of pure dimension \(d\) and finite-rank local system \(L\),

\[
\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X[2d],\qquad D_XL\simeq L^\vee[2d].
\]

The arithmetic counterpart is \(\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]\), \(D_XL\simeq L^\vee(d)[2d]\), subject to the coefficient foundations of Section 3.

**Proof.** C.4–C.5 compute the compact cohomology of a real \(m\)-ball and the sign of its orientation transitions. The local compact-support dual defining \(a^!\Lambda\) is therefore \(\mathrm{or}_X[m]\), as proved in F.5. A complex coordinate change has positive real determinant, so the orientation sheaf is canonically constant and \(m=2d\). Locally \(L\) is finite free; internal Hom gives \(L^\vee\otimes\omega_X\), and these identifications agree under its transition matrices.

For finite étale coefficients, Proposition 3.3 constructs the trace and proves the smooth formula with its Tate twist. The coefficient dual is exact over the self-injective ring \(\mathbb Z/n\), also for finite stalks that are not free. The derived-complete and rational forms need the additional normalized adic comparison; no single finite reduction proves them. \(\square\)

In particular, \(D(L[d])=L^\vee[d]\) classically and \(L^\vee(d)[d]\) arithmetically. Both the shift and the twist survive the calculation.

### Proposition 2.4. Constructibility of the dual

For a classical algebraic Whitney stratification \(\mathcal S\), duality preserves \(D^b_{\mathcal S}(X)\). For finite étale coefficients, a fixed constructibility system must also be compatible with boundary direct images of the dual local systems. Without that compatibility the assertion allows refinement.

**Proof.** For the given classical Whitney stratification, Appendix I constructs compatible normal products. J.1–J.3 prove the coefficient comparison and finite link cohomology. In a normal product the support and attaching complexes are constant along a small stratum box; J.4–J.5 combine them with its orientation to compute the dual there. Its bounded cohomology is consequently finite-rank and locally constant on that stratum. K.6 supplies a finite algebraic Whitney refinement when needed.

For finite étale coefficients, Proposition 2.2 reduces the assertion to \(b_!L\) for a stratum inclusion. The pre-bidual identity (M.12) gives \(D_Xb_!L=Rb_*D_SL\). Smooth duality, finite direct-image constructibility in M.4, and the stipulated compatibility make this constructible for the chosen system. M.5 supplies the field descent. The finite triangle construction finishes the argument. The complete and rational coefficient forms use the operation and duality comparisons of BV–BX at their stated hypotheses. The compatibility issue is also explained in the free BBD text, §2.2.10. \(\square\)

We can now dualize the concrete attaching calculations. For a puncture, G.3–G.4 prove

\[
D_{\mathbb C}j_!L\simeq Rj_*L^\vee[2],\qquad
D_{\mathbb C}Rj_*L\simeq j_!L^\vee[2].
\]

The dual transport operator is \((T^{-1})^\vee\). For the node, the complex orientations on the two normalization branches identify \(D_XN=N[2]\); G.4 verifies agreement on overlaps and under permutation of branches. Dualizing (1.2) therefore gives the actual triangle

\[
i_{p*}\Lambda\longrightarrow N[2]\longrightarrow D_X\Lambda_X
\longrightarrow i_{p*}\Lambda[1].
\tag{2.2}
\]

Thus the node's dual constant sheaf has stalk \(\Lambda^2\) in degree \(-2\) and \(\Lambda\) in degree \(-1\), with costalk \(\Lambda\) in degree zero. The triangle includes the attaching maps and does not specify a canonical splitting. The corresponding geometric étale triangle has \(N(1)[2]\); branch permutations must still be retained over a finite field.

For the cone, G.2–G.3 verify finite link cohomology with local coefficients and both dual exchanges for the actual radial model. Applying (2.1) to (1.4) places the dual constant sheaf's stalk groups in degrees \(-2,-3,-4\), with dimensions \(2g,2g,1\); its costalk is \(\Lambda\) in degree zero.

### Proposition 2.5. Euler functions discard extension data

The function \(\chi_K(x)=\sum_m(-1)^m\dim H^m(i_x^*K)\) is integer-valued and constructible. For every triangle \(A\to B\to C\to A[1]\), it satisfies \(\chi_B=\chi_A+\chi_C\).

**Proof.** Each stratum has constant cohomology ranks, and the sum is finite by boundedness. Stalk restriction preserves a triangle. In its finite long exact cohomology sequence, write the dimension of each term as the dimension of its incoming image plus that of its outgoing image. The alternating contributions of those images cancel, giving the asserted identity point by point. \(\square\)

For a puncture, \(T-1:V\to V\) has kernel and cokernel of equal dimension. Hence every \(Rj_*L\) has boundary Euler value zero, though its two boundary groups may be large. For the node, (1.2) says that the normalization's Euler function exceeds the constant function by the indicator of the node. These two examples show exactly what the Euler function retains from the attaching calculation.

## 3. Operations and the coefficient passage

For a separated finite-type algebraic morphism \(f:X\to Y\), the six-operation assertion is preservation of bounded constructibility by \(Rf_*\), \(Rf_!\), \(f^*\), \(f^!\), derived tensor product and internal \(R\mathcal Hom\). It allows compatible refinements of source and target stratifications. Appendices H–K supply the classical construction and proof. The finite-coefficient étale arguments are given below and in Appendices M and BF–BJ. Appendices BK–BX give the complete and rational coefficient comparisons at their stated hypotheses.

The adjunctions to be used are

\[
f^*\dashv Rf_*,\qquad Rf_!\dashv f^!,\qquad
(-\otimes^L A)\dashv R\mathcal Hom(A,-).
\]

In a Cartesian square, with \(g:Y'\to Y\), \(f':X'\to Y'\), and \(g':X'\to X\), the proper-support comparisons are

\[
g^*Rf_!K\simeq Rf'_!g'^*K,\qquad
Rf_!(K\otimes^L f^*A)\simeq Rf_!K\otimes^L A.
\]

For proper \(f\), \(Rf_!=Rf_*\), giving arbitrary base change for ordinary direct image in that case. Étale smooth base change gives another ordinary-image comparison when \(g\) is smooth and torsion coefficients are prime to the characteristic. For an open immersion, \(j^!=j^*\) and \(j_!\) is exact. Ordinary direct images of general analytic maps need not be algebraically constructible; K.8 uses algebraicity in its compactification and stratification argument.

The proper-comparison foundations and reductions used here are proved in AU–BE. These coefficient constructions do not themselves give constructibility or enlarge the geometric scope of smooth base change.

### Proposition 3.1. Smooth comparison after completion

Let \(\mathcal O\) be a complete discrete valuation ring of residue characteristic \(\ell\), invertible on \(Y\). Let \(f:X\to Y\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let \(g:Y'\to Y\) be smooth, or an affine inverse limit of smooth changes of base. Let \(K\) be derived complete with bounded-below finite reductions coming from the étale site. Write \(g^*_{\mathrm{comp}}\) for pullback followed by derived completion. Then the canonical map

\[
g^*_{\mathrm{comp}}Rf_*K\longrightarrow
Rf'_* (g')^*_{\mathrm{comp}}K
\tag{3.1}
\]

is an isomorphism.

**Proof.** Work with the constant coefficient sheaf \(\underline{\mathcal O}\) on the pro-étale site, and write \(C\) for derived completion. This is not an identification of the constant sheaf with its completed coefficient sheaf. Put \(K_n=K\otimes^L_{\mathcal O}\mathcal O/\pi^n\). BK.3 represents this by
\([\mathcal O\xrightarrow{\pi^n}\mathcal O]\otimes K\), in degrees \(-1,0\), with transition components \((\pi,1)\). BK.4 constructs \(C(K)=\operatorname{holim}_nK_n\) and proves that its unit induces an isomorphism on every derived reduction. Its proof supplies the actual cone maps and needs no uniform bound on the reductions.

BK.5 proves \(Rf_*K_n=(Rf_*K)_n\) by those finite free terms and their multiplication map. Since direct image is a right adjoint, it preserves the homotopy limit; hence \(Rf_*C=C Rf_*\) with its unit compatibility. Define (3.1) by applying \(C\) to the ordinary adjunction map \(g^*Rf_*K\to Rf'_*g'^*K\) and then using this last comparison on the target. BK.6 identifies its two objects and its arrow as
\[
\operatorname{holim}_n g^*Rf_*K_n
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{holim}_n\beta_{K_n}}
\operatorname{holim}_n Rf'_*g'^*K_n.
\]
The identification follows from the \(\mathcal O\)-linear adjunction units and counits applied to the specified two-term complexes. It respects transition maps and successive changes of base.

BK.1–BK.2 prove the site and coefficient comparisons needed to identify each \(\beta_{K_n}\) with its bounded-below étale torsion comparison. A power of \(\ell\) kills \(\mathcal O/\pi^n\), so the required torsion orders are invertible on the base. AS.1–AS.7 prove this smooth comparison over arbitrary bases for each such invertible modulus, including affine limits of smooth base changes. Each level map is then an isomorphism, and so is the displayed homotopy limit. The lower bound may vary with \(n\). The coefficient proof uses a uniformizer and its two-term resolutions, so it applies to every complete discrete valuation ring in the statement, without requiring a finite residue field or a finite extension of \(\mathbf Z_\ell\).

The general-base geometric proof uses the connected-neighbourhood and degree-zero arguments AM–AN, the normal Noetherian generic-cover extension AR, and the arithmetic-model normalization AG.5 inside AS.4–AS.6. Thus each required finite-level comparison is established at the stated qcqs and smooth-limit scope, and the preceding completion argument proves (3.1). No finiteness or bounded constructibility of \(Rf_*K\) is deduced from this comparison. The constructibility and normalized adic constructions are treated separately in BM–BX. \(\square\)

### Proposition 3.2. Finite coefficients and proper supports

Let \(k\) be a field, let \(\ell\) be invertible in \(k\), and let \(\Lambda\) be a finite ring killed by a power of \(\ell\). Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a separated morphism of finite type between separated finite-type \(k\)-schemes. If \(K\) is bounded with constructible \(\Lambda\)-cohomology, then \(Rf_!K\) is bounded constructible. For a constructible sheaf \(F\),

\[
(R^qf_!F)_{\bar y}=H^q_c(X_{\bar y},F|_{X_{\bar y}})
\tag{3.2}
\]

is finite and vanishes for \(q>2\dim X_{\bar y}\). In particular, compactly supported cohomology over a separably closed field is finite; for proper \(X\), ordinary cohomology is finite too. If the fibre dimensions are at most \(d\) and \(K\) has cohomology in \([a,b]\), then \(Rf_!K\) has cohomology in \([a,b+2d]\).

In this finite-coefficient statement, constructibility means finite local constancy on a finite partition into locally closed subschemes. Smoothness of these pieces over \(k\) is not required, so the statement includes imperfect fields. An empty fibre has zero cohomology.

**Proof.** We use the constructed proper-support functor, its composition, arbitrary base change, excision and Mayer–Vietoris from [Cohomology with compact support](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#7-definition-and-independence-of-compactification). Its proper cohomological-dimension proof gives the bound \(2\dim X_{\bar y}\) before a general finiteness theorem is used: compactify the fibre and extend by zero. Consequently all the spectral sequences below have finite contributing ranges. That companion's general constructibility assertion is not an input to this proof.

First take \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaves. Appendix P proves the curve input needed here: compactly supported cohomology of a constructible prime-to-characteristic sheaf on a separated curve over an algebraically closed field is finite and vanishes above degree two. It uses the programme construction of the curve's Picard scheme, proves finiteness and surjectivity of invertible multiplication on its points by infinitesimal lifting, and then gives the Kummer, finite-boundary and trace arguments. No formula for the degree of multiplication or the rank of Jacobian torsion is required for this deduction. AK.1–AK.5 prove the continuity, exact finite-curve pushforward and ordinary/compact finiteness assertions at the smooth-curve scope used in the pairing argument. The stronger curve computations in [Torsion sheaves on curves](course:ag-etale-cohomology/torsion-sheaves-on-curves#4-prime-to-characteristic-constants-and-the-actual-extension-map) retain their own stated scope. Over a separably closed field one may first pass to its algebraic closure, a purely inseparable extension which does not change the étale topos.

We will need proper smooth families of curves without assuming general constructibility. If \(h:C\to S\) is such a family, with \(S\) locally Noetherian, proper base change and the preceding curve theorem make every geometric stalk of \(R^qh_*\mathbf F_\ell\) finite. Every specialization map is an isomorphism by [Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Corollary 11.3](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#11-properness-makes-the-two-maps-inverse). That result uses smooth local acyclicity and proper base change, without a constructibility hypothesis.

Here is why these two facts imply finite local constancy. For any étale \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaf \(A\) with finite stalks and invertible specialization maps, choose a basis of \(A_{\bar s}\). Lift its finitely many elements to sections on an affine Noetherian étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\bar s\). They give \(\varphi:\underline{\mathbf F_\ell^r}\to A|_U\), an isomorphism at \(\bar s\). Naturality and the invertible specialization maps of both sheaves make the isomorphism locus stable under specialization and generization. Geometric lifts of these relations exist in strict localizations; changing a lift conjugates the maps and preserves invertibility. Delete the finitely many irreducible components of \(U\) not containing the distinguished point. Every remaining generic point is a generization of that point, so \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism there. Every other point specializes from one of these generic points, so \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism on all geometric stalks of the remaining neighbourhood. It is an isomorphism of sheaves. Thus \(R^qh_*\mathbf F_\ell\) is finite locally constant. No general direct-image constructibility theorem has entered this deduction.

A separated quasi-finite morphism has exact proper-support image and preserves constructibility. Indeed, Zariski's Main Theorem factors it as an open immersion followed by a finite morphism. [Pushforward, pullback and finite morphisms](course:ag-etale-cohomology/pushforward-pullback-and-finite-morphisms#4-finite-pushforward-is-a-finite-product-on-stalks) proves exact finite direct image and étale topological invariance. [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#6-extension-by-zero-and-finite-pushforward-preserve-constructibility) proves constructibility of extension by zero and finite direct image from finite presentations and generic finite-algebra splitting. These elementary results precede the theorem we are proving.

We next prove that \(Rf_!\mathbf F_\ell\) is constructible for a smooth affine family of curves \(f:X\to S\), by induction on \(\dim S\), working on an affine base. In dimension zero, its finitely many geometric stalks are finite by the curve calculation, and the étale topos is that of finitely many residue fields. A continuous action on a finite stalk is trivialized by a finite separable extension, which proves constructibility in this case.

For the induction step it suffices to prove the assertion near each generic point of \(S\); the closed complement has smaller dimension, and arbitrary proper-support base change permits induction there. The geometric curve-completion input has the following exact form. After shrinking to a neighbourhood \(U\) of a generic point and making a finite surjective radicial change \(V\to U\), there is a finite map

\[
\nu:\coprod_i Y_i\longrightarrow X_V,
\qquad Y_i\subset C_i\longrightarrow T_i\longrightarrow V.
\tag{3.3}
\]

Here \(T_i\to V\) is finite étale, \(C_i\to T_i\) is smooth proper with geometrically connected curve fibres, and \(Y_i\subset C_i\) is open. There is an open \(W\subset X_V\), dense in every fibre, for which \(\nu^{-1}W\to W\) is a nilpotent thickening; each \(\nu^{-1}W\cap Y_i\) is dense in its curve fibres. Appendix O constructs this diagram for the smooth affine family used here, with the stronger conclusions \(\coprod_iY_i=X_V\), \(\nu=\mathrm{id}\), \(W=X_V\), and finite boundary \(\coprod_i(C_i\setminus Y_i)\to V\). Zero-dimensional smooth generic components become finite étale after shrinking and need no curve argument. The construction supplies the geometric step in the finiteness argument of [AI Integrated Stacks].

The complement \(X_V\setminus W\) is quasi-finite over \(V\), since all its fibres have dimension zero. The complement of \(\nu^{-1}W\) in \(\coprod_i C_i\) is quasi-finite for the same reason. Étale topological invariance identifies \(W\)'s constant-sheaf image with that of \(\nu^{-1}W\). Apply excision first to \(W\subset X_V\) and then to \(\nu^{-1}W\subset\coprod_i C_i\). The two boundary terms are constructible by the quasi-finite case. The proper middle term is

\[
\bigoplus_i (T_i\to V)_*R(C_i\to T_i)_*\mathbf F_\ell,
\tag{3.4}
\]

which is constructible by the proper smooth curve result and exact finite direct image. The two triangles prove the assertion over \(V\). The finite surjective radicial map is a universal homeomorphism, so topological invariance descends it to \(U\). Induction completes the constant-coefficient case. A finite affine cover and the proper-support Mayer–Vietoris triangle extend this result to smooth separated families of curves whose source need not be affine; all affine intersections remain smooth families of curves.

Now let \(L\) be finite locally constant on an open \(U\subset\mathbf A^1_S\). On a connected component its monodromy has finite image \(G\), by N.2–N.3. We construct the subgroup needed for the reduction. Write \(|G|=\ell^a m\), with \(\ell\nmid m\), and let \(G\) act by left multiplication on its \(\ell^a\)-element subsets. Their number is prime to \(\ell\): the coefficient of \(t^{\ell^a}\) in
\[
(1+t)^{\ell^a m}=(1+t^{\ell^a})^m
\quad\text{in }\mathbf F_\ell[t]
\]
is \(m\). This identity follows by iterating the binomial formula in characteristic \(\ell\). At least one orbit therefore has size prime to \(\ell\). If \(P\) stabilizes a subset in that orbit, the orbit is in bijection with \(G/P\), so \(\ell^a\) divides \(|P|\). But left multiplication by \(P\) acts freely on that subset, partitioning its \(\ell^a\) elements into sets of size \(|P|\). Thus \(|P|=\ell^a\), as required. This proves the Sylow existence assertion used here.

Let \(g:U'\to U\) be the finite étale cover corresponding to the transitive \(G\)-set \(G/P\), constructed in N.3. Its degree \(e=[G:P]\) is prime to \(\ell\). Pulling back this cover gives a diagonal section, so \(\pi_1(U')\) fixes the chosen coset and the pulled-back representation factors through \(P\). On a nonzero finite \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-vector space, every nontrivial \(P\)-orbit has size divisible by \(\ell\). The number of fixed vectors is consequently divisible by \(\ell\); it includes zero, hence is at least \(\ell\). Choose a nonzero fixed vector and apply the same argument to the quotient by its line. Induction on dimension gives a filtration with trivial one-dimensional quotients.

Étale locally the cover is a disjoint union of \(e\) copies of the base. The diagonal map into those copies and their sum are invariant under permuting them, so they glue to unit and trace maps. Their composite is multiplication by \(e\) on every stalk. Thus

\[
L\longrightarrow g_*g^*L\longrightarrow L,
\qquad\text{composite }e\,\mathrm{id}_L.
\tag{3.5}
\]

Multiplying the trace by \(e^{-1}\) splits the unit. The smooth separated curve-family case, the filtration, composition of proper-support images and this retraction prove constructibility of \(R(U\to S)_!L\). There are only finitely many connected components, so the result holds without connectedness.

For arbitrary constructible \(F\) on \(\mathbf A^1_S\), induct again on \(\dim S\). Choose an open \(U\) on which \(F\) is locally constant and which contains all generic points of the fibres over the generic points of \(S\). After shrinking \(S\) to a dense open, its complement \(Z\) is quasi-finite over \(S\). To justify the shrinking, the non-quasi-finite locus of \(Z\to S\) is closed in \(Z\); its image is constructible and contains no generic point of \(S\). Its closure therefore misses those generic points and can be deleted. In the excision triangle

\[
R(U\to S)_!F|_U\longrightarrow
R(\mathbf A^1_S\to S)_!F\longrightarrow
R(Z\to S)_!F|_Z\longrightarrow,
\tag{3.6}
\]

the outer terms are constructible by the lisse and quasi-finite cases. The closed complement of the chosen dense base open is handled by induction and base change. This proves the result for the affine-line projection.

Finally work on an affine open of \(Y\), and take a finite affine cover of \(X\). Its intersections are affine because \(f\) is separated. Mayer–Vietoris reduces to an affine source. Embed that source as a closed subscheme of \(\mathbf A^n_Y\). Closed direct image is exact and constructible. Factor the projection of affine space into \(n\) affine-line projections, and apply the result just proved at each stage. The finite cohomological-dimension bound permits the ordinary cohomology spectral sequence, or finitely many truncation triangles, to pass from sheaves to bounded constructible complexes. This proves the assertion for \(\mathbf F_\ell\).

For a finite \(\ell\)-primary \(\Lambda\)-sheaf, filter its underlying abelian sheaf by powers of \(\ell\). The finitely many successive quotients are constructible \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaves. Exact sequences and the preceding result give finite constructible underlying cohomology sheaves of its proper-support image. They are constructible as \(\Lambda\)-sheaves too: on each finite locally constant piece, the actions of the finitely many elements of \(\Lambda\) are morphisms of local systems. Bounded truncation again handles \(K\). Formula (3.2) and the degree bound were established by proper-support base change and proper cohomological dimension. For a structural map to a separably closed field, a constructible output has finite groups; if the map is proper, \(Rf_!=Rf_*\). The amplitude bound follows from the same finite spectral sequence. \(\square\)

For \(\mathcal O\) the valuation ring of a finite extension of \(\mathbf Q_\ell\), this proposition applies to every \(\mathcal O/\pi^m\). It proves the finite-level proper finiteness used in the nearby-cycle argument. BM constructs proper support on complete complexes with bounded-below classical reductions, proves its choice-independent composition and arbitrary base change, and proves bounded constructibility defined by first derived reduction. BN proves uniform finite-level Tor bounds, closure under completed tensor and inverse image, and the completed proper-support projection formula with its coherent comparison maps. BO proves the finite-coefficient local finite-free theorem and constructs the actual compatible adic local model on each connected stratum. BP proves the equivalence of strict constructible systems with complete constructible sheaves in degree zero, including torsion and all their sheaf morphisms. BQ proves normalized constructible cohomology, bounded standard truncations, the strict-system heart, and t-exact completed inverse image and open extension. BR proves equivalence with the specified derived category of cartesian pro-étale coefficient diagrams, including all higher morphisms and their limit sequence. BS proves the corresponding étale-diagram comparison, including transitions and higher morphisms. BT proves bounded-derived realization at each finite coefficient ring, constructs the strict adic heart realization functor, and proves its low-degree comparisons and exact higher-effacement criterion. BU proves full adic heart realization in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields, including torsion coefficients. BV constructs the adic exceptional right adjoint on whole coefficient diagrams, proves ordinary-image and internal-Hom constructibility, and proves singular biduality with its operation exchanges. BW proves the equivalence with actual completed-ring module complexes and constructs central rationalization, its heart and operations. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves, including higher morphisms, integral models and ordinary-operation comparisons. BY proves integral and rational heart realization on curves. BZ–CB prove the finite-coefficient geometric fibre comparison (BY.26), including all geometric base points and the characteristic-two descent. BY.7 deduces higher-dimensional realization over finite or algebraically closed fields, allowing a finite extension of a finite ground field and using the coefficient hypotheses of BO–BY throughout. The proposition does not assert nonproper ordinary-direct-image finiteness.

### Proposition 3.3. Smooth trace from the affine line

Let \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\), with \(n\geq2\) invertible in \(k\), and let \(f:X\to S\) be separated and smooth of relative dimension \(d\), between finite-type \(k\)-schemes. For every coefficient complex \(A\), there is a canonical isomorphism

\[
f^!A=f^*A(d)[2d].
\tag{3.7}
\]

Its counit gives the smooth trace \(Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\to\Lambda\), compatible with base change and composition. This is the finite-coefficient formula; adic normalization is an additional coefficient passage.

**Proof.** BF.1–BF.6 construct the locally small unbounded derived categories of presheaves and sheaves, their triangles and coproducts, and exact derived sheafification with a fully faithful right adjoint. The resolution existence theorem used there is proved for general Grothendieck categories in [Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Theorem 7.2](course:derived-categories-and-sheaf-operations/sheaves-of-modules-and-their-derived-categories#7-k-injective-resolutions-of-unbounded-complexes). The explicit cone identities in B.1 supply the triangulated structure, without a boundedness restriction. BF.5 verifies the compact-generator hypotheses for the earlier programme representability theorem, and BF.6 deduces representability on the sheaf category. Hence every exact coproduct-preserving functor out of this category has an exact right adjoint. No bound on the cohomological dimension of the field is used.

BG.1–BG.6 construct the exact, coproduct-preserving proper-support functor on arbitrary ordinary complexes at the present field scope. The finite relative cohomological bound proves unbounded proper comparison and preservation of sums; the compactification and proper–open exchange arguments give independence and composition. Apply BF.6 to \(H_B(K)=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K,B)\). The representing objects define \(f^!B\); uniqueness of representing maps makes this a functor and gives the adjunction counit. Composition identifies right adjoints of composite maps. Étale upper shriek is ordinary inverse image, since étale lower shriek is its exact left adjoint. The resulting local Hom test is written in [Poincaré duality for smooth varieties, Section 8](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-smooth-varieties#8-exceptional-inverse-image-and-its-local-description), with the complete arbitrary-complex local and internal adjunction in BI.1. BH.1–BH.4 construct the unbounded tensor product on the actual étale site, its inverse-image compatibility and internal-Hom adjunction. BH.5–BH.7 prove the proper-support projection formula and its canonical comparisons, including the invertible-twist adjunction used below. We now construct the trace from the affine line.

For \(p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S\), the unit and the Kummer class of \(\mathcal O(1)\) give a map

\[
\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-2]\longrightarrow Rp_*\Lambda.
\]

It is an isomorphism on every geometric stalk by proper base change and the curve calculation: the class has degree \(+1\) and generates the degree-two group. It is therefore an isomorphism. Restriction to the infinity section is the identity on the first summand and zero on the second, because \(\mathcal O(1)\) restricts there to a trivial line bundle. Excision identifies, canonically,

\[
Rq_!\Lambda=\Lambda(-1)[-2],\qquad
q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S.
\]

BI.2 gives the geometric-fibre calculation and specifies this isomorphism as the composite (BI.6). Thus \(Rq_!\Lambda(1)[2]\to\Lambda\) has a specified trace, compatible with arbitrary base change: both the unit and the degree-one Kummer class pull back to their counterparts. For an étale \(u:U\to\mathbf A^1_S\), define its relative curve trace by composing the étale counit with this trace. Étale refinement preserves it. On geometric fibres it is the curve trace, because [Poincaré duality for curves](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-curves#2-the-trace-and-its-normalization) proves compatibility of the degree-normalized trace with open extension and finite maps; factor the quasi-finite étale map into these two kinds.

We next justify \(q^!A=q^*A(1)[2]\) for arbitrary \(A\), without a higher-dimensional trace. Use the dimension-one local argument of [Poincaré duality for smooth varieties](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-smooth-varieties#5-the-relative-curve-calculation). Its neighbourhoods of \(\mathbf A^1_S\) are precisely étale maps of the preceding form. AI.3–AI.4 give the uniform-refinement, derived-cone and descent details at this exact scope. Here are the geometric inputs and the resulting maps. AT.1–AT.4 prove that the filtered ordinary cohomology of the selected strict-local fibre is \(\Lambda\) in degree zero and zero in higher degrees, using the exact pointed pairs and selected base maps of (AT.9). The curve-duality argument, with its ramification and finite-counting inputs proved in AJ.1–AJ.4, identifies the finite compact groups with the duals of those ordinary groups. BI.3 proves that their actual étale trace transitions are the transposes of pullback. Killing finitely many ordinary generators makes the unwanted compact transition maps zero. In top degree the trace kernel is killed in the same way, while the trace is surjective.

Constructibility from Proposition 3.2 makes the zero-map loci of these finite sheaf systems open in the constructible topology. Compactness of that topology gives one refinement killing all stalk maps; the fixed cohomological range and the bounded-ghost lemma give a further refinement killing the derived cone map. The strict-local bases cause no change of hypotheses: every finite neighbourhood diagram descends to a finite-type étale base neighbourhood, and proper-support base change supplies its constructible sheaves on the strict base. AI.4 descends the zero cohomology maps by writing their constructible image supports as finitely many locally closed finite-presentation schemes, and then kills the derived maps by four successive ghost refinements.

BI.4 constructs the required zero cone map by a finite chain of triangle completions. It does not assume a functorial cone on the entire neighbourhood category. BI.5 then proves directly that precomposition by the trace induces an isomorphism of the filtered Hom groups in (AI.7), by lifting each morphism and killing its obstruction at a later neighbourhood. The two colimits are \(H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s}\) and \(H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}\). BI.1 and BI.5 identify this map with the stalk map adjoint to the specified trace and projection formula, for arbitrary unbounded \(A\). Its isomorphism on every stalk proves the affine-line formula. This uses the constructed affine-line trace, curve duality, the selected-neighbourhood calculation and Proposition 3.2; no higher-dimensional trace has been assumed.

Compose the affine-line traces to obtain the trace of an affine space. BJ.1 proves the exact top-cohomology composition and source-cover descent used for this construction. BJ.3 proves that the product trace is invariant under coordinate permutations: the geometric product class is a tensor of degree-two generators, whose exchanges have positive sign.

For an étale coordinate chart \(u:U\to\mathbf A^d_S\), compose its summation counit with this affine-space trace. BJ.4 proves independence of the chart directly on top cohomology. After geometric base change, the coordinate lemma of BJ.2 joins two charts, locally, by finitely many changes of one coordinate. Permute that coordinate to the last position. The common first \(d-1\) coordinates define a smooth relative curve, and its two traces agree by the relative-curve construction of BJ.3. The source-cover exact sequence and geometric stalks then give equality of the original top trace maps. This constructs a global, coordinate-independent \(t_f:R^{2d}f_!\Lambda(d)\to\Lambda\).

The bound \(Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\in D^{\leq0}\) makes this top trace specify a unique derived map \(T_f:Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\to\Lambda\), by (BJ.11). For arbitrary \(A\), transpose

\[
Rf_!\bigl(f^*A(d)[2d]\bigr)
\simeq A\otimes^LRf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]
\xrightarrow{1\otimes T_f}A.
\]

On each coordinate chart this map is the composite of the affine-line isomorphisms and exact étale inverse image, because its counit is the same composed trace. BI.1's local adjunction and exact stalks therefore prove that its transpose is the isomorphism (3.7). BJ.5 gives this argument for unbounded \(A\), using BH's arbitrary-complex projection formula.

BJ.6 checks composition by the explicit interchange of étale summation with affine-space trace, and checks base change on the actual counit mate. In particular, for \(X_1=X\times_S\mathbf A^1_S\), with projections \(q_X:X_1\to X\), \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\), and induced \(f_1:X_1\to\mathbf A^1_S\), it gives

\[
f_1^!q^*A=q_X^*f^!A.
\tag{3.8}
\]

For a parameter section \(s_t\), transitivity and the invertible-twist adjunction give \(s_t^!q^*B=B(-1)[-2]\). BJ.6 identifies its positive generator with the negative supported Kummer boundary \(-\lambda\kappa(t-t_0)\), whose trace is \(+1\) by AI.2 and BI.2. These parameter comparisons follow from the constructed coordinate-independent trace. Thus the trace, its smooth orientation and the base-change and composition maps are all specified. \(\square\)


If \(X\) is smooth of dimension \(d\) over a separably closed field, the result gives \(a^!\Lambda=\Lambda(d)[2d]\). If \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) is a closed immersion of smooth varieties of pure codimension \(c\), transitivity for their structural maps and the invertible twist gives

\[
i^!\Lambda_X=\Lambda_Z(-c)[-2c].
\tag{3.9}
\]

BJ.6 proves the same identity for arbitrary coefficients pulled back from a common smooth base and identifies its Gysin counit and composition. This proves purity for these smooth pairs. It does not assert the general absolute-purity theorem for arbitrary regular schemes or traits.

For a finite locally constant \(F\) on smooth \(X\) over an algebraically closed field, the internal-Hom adjunction proved in the same companion now gives

\[
R\Gamma\bigl(X,R\mathcal Hom(F,\Lambda(d)[2d])\bigr)
=R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(X,F),\Lambda).
\]

The coefficient ring \(\mathbf Z/n\) is self-injective, and finite-module evaluation is biduality, by the explicit extension and cardinality proof in M.6. Thus \(D_XF=F^\vee(d)[2d]\); Proposition 3.2 and the displayed comparison give finite mutually perfect pairings \(H^r_c(X,F)\times H^{2d-r}(X,F^\vee(d))\to\Lambda\), with evaluation followed by the constructed trace. This smooth local-system statement does not replace the full singular constructible Verdier-duality theorem.

The structural map \(a:X\to\mathrm{pt}\) gives \(Ra_*K=R\Gamma(X,K)\) and \(Ra_!K=R\Gamma_c(X,K)\). Proper-support base change identifies a geometric stalk of \(Rf_!K\) with compactly supported cohomology of the geometric fibre. For ordinary direct image the analogous fibre formula is asserted here when \(f\) is proper. These distinctions explain why the local computations in Section 1 retained their actual punctured-neighbourhood limits.

Appendix M extends the finite-coefficient construction over fields to ordinary direct-image finiteness, constructibility of the dual, singular biduality and the operation exchanges. It writes the finite-support and generic-restriction reductions explicitly. Its inputs include curve finiteness, cohomological continuity and the categorical exceptional adjunction identified in M.1.

The finite-coefficient operation statements occur in [SGA 4, XVI, Corollary 1.2] and [SGA 4, XVII, 5.2.6, 5.2.8, 5.2.9 and 5.3.6]. [SGA \(4\frac12\), *Théorèmes de finitude*, 1.1, 1.3 and 1.5–1.6] treat finiteness over a regular base of dimension at most one, including our fields; 4.3 requires finite Tor dimension for biduality, while 4.7 supplies the self-injective \(\mathbb Z/n\) variant. The field case is proved in Appendix M.

[Laszlo–Olsson, II] treats the adic theory: Theorem 3.20 and Remark 3.21 for bounded comparison and rational coefficients, Proposition 4.1 for internal Hom, Theorem 7.7 for duality, §§8–9 for operations, (9.6.1) for projection, and Theorem 12.1 with §12.3 for base change. BK–BN construct the completed operations, proper support, base change and projection specified there at the explicit reduction-defined scope used here. BO supplies the local finite-free and compatible adic model proofs. BP proves the strict-system comparison in degree zero, and BQ proves constructible cohomology, standard truncations and the resulting strict-system heart. BR proves the derived-cartesian pro-étale diagram comparison and its higher-morphism formula; BS identifies the corresponding whole étale diagrams and all their morphisms. BT supplies finite-coefficient realization and the adic heart realization functor, with degree-one comparison, degree-two injectivity and a necessary-and-sufficient effacement criterion. BU proves the full realization equivalence in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields. BV constructs the adic exceptional adjunction, proves its coefficient compatibility, and establishes singular biduality and the dual exchanges. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization, including the torsion kernel and the conservative map to actual rational sheaf complexes. BX supplies the full rational-sheaf comparison, its higher morphisms and its operation comparisons. BY proves integral and rational heart realization on curves. BZ–CB prove its geometric fibre comparison (BY.26) for finite coefficient fields of characteristic invertible in the ground field. BY.7 gives higher-dimensional realization with the complete integral and rational coefficients specified in BO–BY, over finite or algebraically closed ground fields; the construction permits a finite extension in the finite-field case. The intended scope remains bounded constructible coefficients on finite-type schemes with the stated dimension bounds, including all the coefficient comparisons needed by the later lessons.

## 4. Exercises and complete solutions

**Exercise 1 (easy).** For \(j:\mathbb C^\times\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), compute all stalks of \(Rj_*\Lambda\). Then compare the boundary stalks and costalks of \(Rj_*L\) and \(j_!L\) when \(T=J_2(1)\oplus(-1)\) on \(\Lambda^3\).

**Solution.** On the open stratum the constant direct image is \(\Lambda\) in degree zero. At zero, Proposition 1.1 has differential \(1-1=0\), so it gives \(\Lambda\) in both degrees zero and one and no other groups. For the specified rank-three system, choose a Jordan basis \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) with \((T-1)e_2=e_1\), \((T-1)e_1=0\), and \((T-1)e_3=-2e_3\). The kernel is spanned by \(e_1\); the cokernel is represented by \(e_2\). Thus the two boundary stalk groups of \(Rj_*L\) are one-dimensional in degrees zero and one. Its attaching map is the identity, so its costalk is zero. For \(j_!L\) the stalk is zero, and taking the fibre shifts those same boundary groups to costalk degrees one and two. All other boundary groups vanish. On the smooth open stratum both extensions restrict to \(L\); at any of its points their stalk is \(V\) in degree zero and their costalk is \(V\) in degree two, by the oriented disc calculation.

**Exercise 2 (easy).** Dualize \(j_!\Lambda\) on the punctured line. Specify the object, its boundary stalk and costalk, and the arithmetic twist.

**Solution.** The open-immersion exchange and the smooth orientation give \(D_{\mathbb C}j_!\Lambda=Rj_*\Lambda[2]\). Its stalk at zero is the complex \([\Lambda\xrightarrow0\Lambda]_{[-2,-1]}\), and its costalk is zero. This agrees with reversing and dualizing the two nonzero costalk degrees of \(j_!\Lambda\) in Proposition 1.2. Arithmetically the formula is \(Rj_*\Lambda(1)[2]\): the boundary groups are \(\Lambda(1)\) in degree \(-2\) and \(\Lambda\) in degree \(-1\). This arithmetic statement uses the purity and coefficient comparisons identified in Section 3; the shift alone does not account for Frobenius.

**Exercise 3 (medium).** Compute local cohomology at a node and compare it with normalization. Extend the calculation to an ordinary point with \(r\geq2\) smooth branches and distinct tangent lines.

**Solution.** L.5 identifies the actual separated smooth normalization branches, and B.4 proves the local section comparison. For \(r\) branches, the puncture has \(r\) circular components. The constant stalk-to-boundary map gives

\[
\Lambda\xrightarrow{\Delta}\Lambda^r\xrightarrow0\Lambda^r
\quad\text{in degrees }0,1,2.
\]

Therefore \(H^1_{\{p\}}(X,\Lambda)=\Lambda^r/\Delta\Lambda\), of dimension \(r-1\), and \(H^2_{\{p\}}(X,\Lambda)=\Lambda^r\); the other local groups vanish. For normalization the first map is \(1:\Lambda^r\to\Lambda^r\), leaving just \(\Lambda^r\) in degree two. At a node \(r=2\), so the constant local groups have dimensions one and two, whereas the normalization has only the two-dimensional degree-two group. This difference is the branch-value quotient in (1.2). Finite-coefficient étale purity places \((-1)\) on the degree-two term; over a nonclosed field the branch-permutation representation is retained. The complete and rational coefficient formulations use the purity and finite-map comparisons of BV–BX at their stated hypotheses.

**Exercise 4 (medium).** Show that the stalk Euler function defines a homomorphism from the Grothendieck group of \(D^b_c(X)\) to integer-valued constructible functions. Compute it for the constant and normalization sheaves of a nodal curve.

**Solution.** The Grothendieck group is the free abelian group on object classes modulo the triangle relations \([B]=[A]+[C]\). Proposition 2.5 proves that the corresponding function relation holds at every point, so the assignment factors through that quotient. Each function is constructible because its cohomology ranks are constant on a finite stratification. The constant sheaf has function one. The normalization sheaf has function one on the smooth locus and two at each node: its stalk counts the separate branches. Their difference is the sum of node indicators, exactly as the stalkwise quotient sequence predicts. The triangle \(K\to0\to K[1]\) also proves \([K[1]]=-[K]\); the same sign follows by reindexing the Euler sum.

**Exercise 5 (hard).** Describe the link of the affine cone over a smooth degree-\(n\) plane curve. Compute its field and integral cohomology and its constant-sheaf vertex costalk; include the plane cubic.

**Solution.** A link point is a unit vector of the tautological line, so the link is the circle bundle of Euler class \(-n\eta\). Put \(b=(n-1)(n-2)=2g\). Over our field, the Gysin map \(\Lambda\xrightarrow{-n}\Lambda\) is invertible. The link dimensions in degrees \(0,1,2,3\) are consequently \(1,b,b,1\). The attaching fibre removes the constant degree-zero class and raises each remaining degree by one, so the vertex costalk dimensions in degrees \(2,3,4\) are \(b,b,1\). For a cubic \(b=2\).

Over \(\mathbb Z\), that map remains injective but has cokernel \(\mathbb Z/n\). The same exact sequence gives \(H^0(M;\mathbb Z)=H^3(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\), \(H^1(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^b\), and

\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z/n\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^b\longrightarrow0.
\]

Choose a lift of each free basis vector to split this sequence as abelian groups. The result is \(H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\simeq\mathbb Z^b\oplus\mathbb Z/n\), without a preferred splitting. For \(n=1\), the cone is a complex plane and its link is \(S^3\), the Hopf bundle over \(\mathbb P^1\). For \(n=2\), \(b=0\) but \(H^2(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2\). For \(n=3\), it is \(\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z/3\). These checks also explain why characteristic zero was specified for the field formula.

## Appendix A. Derived sections on the punctured disc

This appendix proves the classical sheaf-cohomology input of Proposition 1.1. Coefficients are vector spaces over a field \(\Lambda\). The construction concerns open subsets of Euclidean space and spaces homeomorphic to them. In particular, it applies to the angular coordinate regions used below. It does not establish the étale or adic comparisons in Section 3.

### A.1. Resolutions and sections

Kernels of sheaves are computed on sections; cokernels are obtained by sheafifying the sectionwise cokernel. Both have the expected stalks. Indeed, equality or a lift of a germ is witnessed on a smaller neighbourhood. The same observation proves exactness of filtered colimits of vector spaces: a finite equation involving representatives can be tested at one common later index. Consequently stalks and filtered colimits commute with cohomology of complexes.

There are enough injective sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-vector spaces. For a point \(x\), let \(e_x\) denote its inclusion. The skyscraper \((e_x)_*V\) has sections \(V\) on an open containing \(x\), and zero otherwise. The identity

\[
\operatorname{Hom}(F,(e_x)_*V)=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(F_x,V)
\tag{A.1}
\]

follows by taking germs. Its right side is exact in \(F\): stalks are exact, and a linear map from a subspace extends after extending a basis. Thus every skyscraper here is injective. A product of injectives is injective, since maps into it are products of maps into its factors and each component extension can be chosen separately. The germ map

\[
F\longrightarrow G(F):=\prod_{x\in X}(e_x)_*F_x
\tag{A.2}
\]

is injective: a section with all zero germs is zero. Iterating (A.2) on the successive cokernels gives an injective resolution. We compute \(R\Gamma(X,F)\) by the sections of such a resolution. Two resolutions give the same derived object: extend a map degree by degree into the injective target, first on the image of the preceding differential; two extensions differ by a homotopy constructed by the same induction. The induction starts on the common copy of \(F\).

A sheaf is *flabby* if sections extend from any open subset to a larger one. Each \(G(F)\) is flabby, because its sections are arbitrary collections of stalk elements. Any injective is a direct summand of its own \(G(F)\), hence flabby.

We need two elementary consequences. In an exact sequence \(0\to F\to G\to H\to0\) with \(F\) flabby, a section of \(H\) lifts globally. Choose local lifts and well-order their domains. At a successor step, the old lift and the new one differ on the overlap by a section of \(F\). Extend that difference to the new domain, subtract it, and glue. At a limit step the compatible lifts glue by the sheaf axiom. If \(G\) is also flabby, this lifting assertion shows that \(H\) is flabby: lift on the smaller open, extend in \(G\), then project. Applied to successive cokernels in an injective resolution of a flabby sheaf, these assertions show that its higher derived sections vanish.

More generally a bounded-below flabby resolution computes derived sections. To see this without assuming a comparison theorem, map it into an injective resolution by the extension induction above. The cone is an exact bounded-below complex of flabby sheaves. Its cycles are flabby by induction from the first nonzero term, using the quotient assertion. Its sections are therefore exact by the lifting assertion. The comparison map on sections is a quasi-isomorphism.

For an open inclusion \(a:W\hookrightarrow X\), extension by zero \(a_!F\) consists of sections on \(O\cap W\) whose support is closed in \(O\), for each open \(O\subset X\). It has stalk \(F_x\) in \(W\) and zero outside. This proves its exactness. Extending a local morphism by zero proves \(a_!\dashv a^*\). Thus restriction to an open preserves injectives, since maps from a subobject extend after applying the exact functor \(a_!\).

### A.2. A flabby cochain resolution on Euclidean open sets

For \(O\subset\mathbb R^d\) open, let \(C_q(O)\) be the vector space freely generated by continuous singular simplices \(\Delta^q\to O\), with the alternating face boundary. Put \(C^q(O;V)=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(C_q(O),V)\), and let \(\mathscr C^q(V)\) be its sheafification. The cancellation of each codimension-two face twice with opposite signs gives \(\partial^2=0\), so the dual differentials give a complex of sheaves.

We first prove that every section of \(\mathscr C^q(V)\) on \(O\) is represented by one cochain on \(O\). A section has local representatives \(c_i\) on a cover \(W_i\). That cover admits a locally finite family of closed sets \(K_j\) covering \(O\), with \(K_j\subset W_{i(j)}\). Here is the needed construction. Choose compact sets

\[
E_m=\{x\in O:|x|\le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus O)\ge1/m\},
\]

with \(E_0=E_{-1}=\varnothing\); if the complement is empty, omit the distance condition. They exhaust \(O\) and \(E_m\subset\operatorname{int}E_{m+1}\). Cover the compact layer \(E_m\setminus\operatorname{int}E_{m-1}\) by finitely many open balls whose closures lie in members of the given cover and in \(\operatorname{int}E_{m+1}\setminus E_{m-2}\). Their closures are the \(K_j\). They cover \(O\). A neighbourhood lying inside some \(\operatorname{int}E_M\) meets only finitely many layers, hence only finitely many \(K_j\).

For a singular simplex \(\sigma\), set \(c(\sigma)=c_{i(j)}(\sigma)\) using the first index \(j\) for which its image meets \(K_j\) and lies in \(W_{i(j)}\); set it to zero if there is no such index. This defines a cochain. Fix \(x\). Local finiteness and closedness allow a neighbourhood of \(x\) to avoid every \(K_j\) in that neighbourhood which does not contain \(x\). Only finitely many remaining indices matter. Shrink again inside their \(W_{i(j)}\), and until their cochains agree there: they represent the same germ at \(x\). Every simplex in this final neighbourhood has an eligible index because the \(K_j\) cover, and every eligible representative gives the same value. Thus \(c\) represents the prescribed section near \(x\), proving surjectivity.

A cochain on a smaller open extends to a larger open by assigning zero to simplices not contained in the smaller one. Surjectivity just proved therefore makes every \(\mathscr C^q(V)\) flabby. This argument uses the Euclidean hypotheses; sheafification of an arbitrary flabby presheaf need not be flabby.

The augmentation

\[
0\longrightarrow V_O\longrightarrow\mathscr C^0(V)
\longrightarrow\mathscr C^1(V)\longrightarrow\cdots
\tag{A.3}
\]

is exact. To check a stalk, take the filtered system of convex balls about the point. On a convex set, coning a singular simplex to a fixed point \(b\) gives an operator \(p_b:C_q\to C_{q+1}\) on the augmented chain complex: in barycentric coordinates its value is

\[
(t_0,\ldots,t_{q+1})\longmapsto
t_0b+(1-t_0)\sigma\!\left(\frac{t_1}{1-t_0},\ldots,\frac{t_{q+1}}{1-t_0}\right),
\]

with value \(b\) at \(t_0=1\); in degree \(-1\), send \(1\) to the point \(b\). The face formula gives \(\partial p_b+p_b\partial=1\). Dualizing proves that cochains on the ball have cohomology \(V\) in degree zero and zero in positive degree. Taking the exact filtered colimit proves (A.3) on stalks. Its degree-zero kernel consists of functions constant on small path-connected balls, precisely \(V_O\).

### A.3. Constant sheaves on convex regions are acyclic

We must still compute the sections of (A.3); the stalk calculation alone does not compute them. For an open cover \(\mathcal U\) of \(O\), write \(C_q^{\mathcal U}(O)\) for chains generated by simplices contained in one member. Surjectivity in A.2 and the definition of a zero germ give

\[
\Gamma(O,\mathscr C^\bullet(V))
=\varinjlim_{\mathcal U}
\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(O),V),
\tag{A.4}
\]

where refinements induce restriction of cochains. Indeed a cochain represents zero exactly when it vanishes on every simplex in some open cover. Restriction onto the small-chain subspace is surjective by extension on the remaining basis simplices, so this describes both the quotient and the colimit.

Suppose now \(O\) is nonempty and convex. We prove that each augmented small-chain complex is exact. The subdivision operators needed for this have an explicit construction. For an affine simplex \(\lambda\), let \(b_\lambda\) be its barycenter and let \(b_\lambda*c\) mean prepend this vertex to each simplex of the affine chain \(c\). On augmented affine chains,

\[
\partial(b*c)=c-b*(\partial c).
\]

Define subdivision and a homotopy inductively by

\[
S\lambda=b_\lambda*(S\partial\lambda),\qquad
P\lambda=b_\lambda*(\lambda-P\partial\lambda),
\quad S_{-1}=1,\quad P_{-1}=0.
\tag{A.5}
\]

The cone identity first gives \(\partial S=S\partial\). For the second formula it gives
\(\partial P\lambda=\lambda-P\partial\lambda-b_\lambda*(S\partial\lambda)\), by induction on dimension. Hence \(\partial P+P\partial=1-S\). Apply these affine formulas on the standard simplex and compose with a singular simplex to define the same operators on singular chains. They preserve its image. Iteration gives

\[
P_N=\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}PS^r,\qquad
\partial P_N+P_N\partial=1-S^N.
\tag{A.6}
\]

The simplices occurring in a subdivision have vertices which are barycenters of nested faces. If those faces have \(a\le b\) vertices, their barycenters differ by \((b-a)/b\) times a difference of two points of the original simplex. Thus their distance is at most \(q/(q+1)\) times its diameter in dimension \(q>0\). The diameter of a convex hull is at most the largest distance between its vertices, by expanding the difference of two convex combinations. Repeated subdivision therefore makes the mesh tend to zero. For a continuous simplex, pull back the open cover to its compact standard simplex. A finite subcover by sufficiently small balls gives a positive number such that any subset of smaller diameter lies in one cover member: choose balls of radius \(2\epsilon_x\) inside cover members, cover by finitely many balls of radius \(\epsilon_x\), and take the minimum \(\epsilon_x\). Consequently every finite singular chain becomes \(\mathcal U\)-small after sufficiently many subdivisions.

Let \(z\) be an augmented small cycle of degree at least zero; in degree zero this means its coefficients sum to zero. Its cone \(p_bz\) is a finite chain with boundary \(z\), though it need not be small. Choose \(N\) so that \(S^Np_bz\) is small. Since \(P_N\) preserves each simplex's image, \(P_Nz\) is already small. Equations (A.5)–(A.6) give

\[
\partial\bigl(S^Np_bz+P_Nz\bigr)=S^Nz+(z-S^Nz)=z.
\tag{A.7}
\]

The augmentation onto \(\Lambda\) is surjective using any point of \(O\). This proves exactness in every degree. Over a field, choose a complement to the boundary subspace in each chain group; the differential identifies that complement with the next boundary subspace. This splits the augmented exact complex into two-term identity complexes. Its dual with values in any \(V\) is exact as well.

Thus each cochain complex in (A.4) has cohomology \(V\) in degree zero and zero otherwise, and refinement preserves that degree-zero identification. Exactness of filtered colimits and A.1 now prove

\[
R\Gamma(O,V_O)\simeq V[0]
\qquad(O\text{ nonempty, open and convex}).
\tag{A.8}
\]

The same holds on a space homeomorphic to such an \(O\): transporting sheaves across a homeomorphism is an exact equivalence preserving sections and injectives. A disjoint union of two such regions has degree-zero sections \(V\oplus V\) and no higher cohomology, by the same statement on its two components.

### A.4. The two angular regions and the differential

Let \(D_R^*=\{z:0<|z|<R\}\), allowing \(R=\infty\).

**Transport and monodromy.** Fix a base point in \(D_R^*\). A finite-rank local system is determined, including its morphisms, by its fibre \(V\) and an invertible operator \(T\) for one positive turn. We give the underlying topological and sheaf constructions.

Along a path, choose finitely many consecutive intervals mapped into trivializing opens and compose their fibre identifications. Refining intervals changes nothing. Two choices admit a common refinement; transition matrices are locally constant, so their values agree along each connected interval and cancel at its endpoints. For a homotopy, a sufficiently fine rectangular grid maps each rectangle into a trivializing open: compactness gives a Lebesgue number, by the finite-ball argument in A.3. Transport around each rectangle is the identity. Cancelling shared edges shows that endpoint-fixed homotopic paths have the same transport. Concatenation composes transport, and reversing a path inverts it. On a convex region, straight-line homotopies therefore trivialize a local system from any chosen fibre.

The covering map \((s,\theta)\mapsto e^{s+i\theta}\) has convex domain \(( -\infty,\log R)\times\mathbb R\), with \(\log R=\infty\) when needed. Local angle branches lift a path uniquely after its initial angle is fixed: subdivide into branch domains and adjust successive branches by integral multiples of \(2\pi\). The difference of two lifts is a continuous integer multiple of \(2\pi\), hence constant. The same construction works on a fine grid of a homotopy square, extending rectangle by rectangle; agreement at a corner forces agreement on each shared edge. A based loop's lifted endpoint thus differs from its starting angle by \(2\pi n\), with \(n\) invariant under based homotopy. Conversely two lifts with the same endpoints are joined by straight-line interpolation in the convex covering domain. Projecting gives a based homotopy. Concatenation adds \(n\), and the loop making \(n\) turns realizes every integer. This proves the loop classification used in Proposition 1.1.

To construct a local system from \((V,T)\), give \(V\) the discrete topology and impose on the product of the covering domain with \(V\) the identifications

\[
(s,\theta+2\pi n,v)\sim(s,\theta,T^n v).
\tag{A.11}
\]

Over an angular branch this quotient is the product with \(V\): every class has a unique representative in that branch. On overlaps, the coordinates differ by locally constant powers of \(T\); the powers add on triple overlaps. Continuous local sections therefore form a sheaf of vector spaces, locally the constant sheaf \(V\). Lifting one positive turn with constant coordinate \(v\) ends at the class of \((s,\theta+2\pi,v)\), which is the class of \((s,\theta,Tv)\). Its monodromy is exactly \(T\).

Conversely, pull any local system to the convex covering domain. Transport gives its constant trivialization. If \(\Phi_{s,\theta}:V\to L_{e^{s+i\theta}}\) denotes transport from the fixed base lift, the loop calculation and concatenation give \(\Phi_{s,\theta+2\pi n}=\Phi_{s,\theta}T^n\). Hence this trivialization factors through (A.11), providing an isomorphism with the original local system on every branch and thus globally. A sheaf morphism commutes with transport, so its base-fibre map satisfies \(bT=T'b\). Conversely that equation makes the constant map \(b\) respect (A.11), and it descends to a unique sheaf morphism. Fibre evaluation and the quotient construction are therefore inverse on objects and morphisms. This construction also identifies restrictions to smaller punctured discs using transport along a fixed radial ray.

For the covering calculation and its lifting proof, see Hatcher, Chapter 1, Theorem 1.7. The local-system quotient above includes the required transport compatibility.

Cover it by \(A\), with angle \(-\pi<\theta<\pi\), and \(B\), with angle \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Their intersection has upper and lower components. The coordinates \((\log|z|,\theta)\) identify each region and intersection component with an open convex rectangle. Transport trivializes \(L\) there. Choose the two trivializations to agree on the upper component. In the lower component the trivialization coming from \(B\) differs from that from \(A\) by \(T\): its continuation has made one extra positive turn.

For clarity, this cover computes **derived sheaf sections**. Resolve \(L\) by injectives \(I^\bullet\) on \(D_R^*\). In every degree the sequence

\[
0\to\Gamma(D_R^*,I^q)\to
\Gamma(A,I^q)\oplus\Gamma(B,I^q)\to
\Gamma(A\cap B,I^q)\to0
\tag{A.9}
\]

is exact: the kernel assertion is sheaf gluing, and a section on the intersection extends to \(B\) because \(I^q\) is flabby. The total complex of its last two columns is therefore quasi-isomorphic to \(\Gamma(D_R^*,I^\bullet)\). Restrictions remain injective by A.1; (A.8) shows each of these columns has only degree-zero cohomology, equal to the sections of \(L\). Replacing those columns by their degree-zero section complexes is a quasi-isomorphism on totals. To verify this last assertion, filter the cone of the comparison by its two columns; the two successive quotients are shifted acyclic column cones, so the total cone is acyclic.

Consequently the required derived sections are represented by

\[
V\oplus V\longrightarrow V\oplus V,\qquad
(x,y)\longmapsto(y-x,Ty-x).
\tag{A.10}
\]

Use domain coordinates \((z,y)=(y-x,y)\) and target coordinates \((s,t-s)\). The differential becomes

\[
(z,y)\longmapsto(z,(T-1)y).
\]

Discarding the contractible identity summand gives \([V\xrightarrow{T-1}V]\) in degrees \(0,1\). All maps commute with intertwiners \(bT=T'b\), so this is a functorial derived model. Shrinking \(R\) restricts the same angular cover and the same locally constant sections; identifying base fibres along one radial ray makes the resulting two-term maps identities. This proves the compatibility needed for the stalk colimit in Proposition 1.1, without an unproved homotopy-invariance assertion for sheaf cohomology.

The familiar cellular description agrees with this model. The augmented chains of the lifted one-vertex, one-edge circle are
\(0\to\Lambda[t,t^{-1}]\xrightarrow{t-1}\Lambda[t,t^{-1}]\xrightarrow{f\mapsto f(1)}\Lambda\to0\).
They are exact: multiplication by \(t-1\) is injective, and division after clearing negative powers identifies the augmentation kernel with its image. Applying equivariant \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,V)\) gives exactly the two-term complex already obtained from (A.9)–(A.10). The derived-sheaf justification is the preceding argument.

For cochain sheaves and their topological hypotheses, see Sella; for subdivision, see Hatcher; for flabby sheaves, see the Stacks Project references below.


## Appendix B. Classical localization and the local curve calculations

This appendix works with classical sheaves of vector spaces over a field. It constructs the bounded-below derived operations needed for the boundary, stalk and costalk calculations of this lesson. It also checks the local branch model and the explicit normalization of the displayed nodal cubic.
