The resulting \(C_{K'}\) is finite over the fixed projective scheme \(Z_{K'}\), and is therefore proper. Use the finite standard-smooth chart argument in O.2 to make \(C_{K'}\) smooth of relative dimension one. Every coefficient used belongs to one finite purely inseparable extension, so this process ends at such a \(K'\). In characteristic zero no extension is needed. AH.2 proves that the boundary of \(C_F\) is finite by pulling back the finite boundary of \(Z\) along the finite normalization map. The homeomorphism for \(F/K'\) then makes the reduced boundary of \(C_{K'}\) zero-dimensional, and the finite-algebra calculation there proves it finite over \(K'\).

### O.2. Why the smooth charts and their dimensions descend

Let \(R=\varinjlim R_\alpha\), and suppose a finitely presented \(R\)-scheme \(D\) is smooth of relative dimension one. Cover it by finitely many affine standard-smooth charts. Such a chart has a presentation
\[
\left(R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/(g_1,\ldots,g_c)\right)_h,
\qquad m-c=1,
\tag{O.2}
\]
with a chosen \(c\)-column Jacobian minor invertible. Record a polynomial expression for its inverse in the localized quotient. Coefficients of the \(g_j\), of \(h\), and of that expression form a finite list. The equation saying that the product is one holds at a sufficiently late stage. That same presentation is consequently standard smooth there, with the same relative dimension: the conormal calculation eliminates the selected \(c\) differentials and leaves \(m-c\) free differentials. The existence of the charts, their infinitesimal lifting and differential calculations are proved in [Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Theorems 4.1–5.1](course:AG-CA/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps#4-standard-smooth-presentations).

Descend each chart as an open of the already chosen model, using finite open descent and eventual affineness. Descend its isomorphism to (O.2), the inverse and the two identities. Finite open descent also makes these finitely many charts cover the model eventually. This proves the required smoothness and dimension assertions. It uses no assertion that an arbitrary geometric property descends. We apply it first to the system of finite subextensions of \(F/K\), and then to the localizations of an integral base ring.

### O.3. Extend the completion over a neighbourhood of the generic point

Return to \(S\) and \(\eta\). Remove the other irreducible components and pass to the reduction. The resulting affine base \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) is integral, with fraction field \(K=\kappa(\eta)\). The reduction map to the original base is finite, surjective and radicial; it will be included in \(V\to U\). Base change preserves smoothness and affineness of \(X\).

Choose an affine embedding of \(X\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), and apply O.1 to \(X_K\) using the generic fibre of this same embedding. In positive characteristic write its finite purely inseparable extension as \(K'=K(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_r)\), with one power \(q=p^e\) such that every \(\beta_j^q\) lies in \(K\). Localize \(A\) so these finitely many elements lie in \(A\), and put \(B=A[\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_r]\subset K'\). Monomials with each exponent less than \(q\) generate \(B\) over \(A\), so it is finite; its fraction field is \(K'\). Every \(b\in B\) satisfies \(b^q\in A\). Lying over makes \(\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) surjective. After extension to any algebraically closed residue field each \(\beta_j\) has a unique possible image, because \(T^q-a\) has one root. Thus every geometric fibre has one point and purely inseparable residue extension, proving radiciality. In characteristic zero take \(B=A\).

Let \(Z_B\) be the projective closure of the base-changed embedding of \(X_B\). AH.3 proves, using the homogeneous ideal and its saturation, that its generic fibre is exactly the closure used in O.1. Descend the finite map \(C_{K'}\to Z_{K'}\) to a finite map \(C\to Z_B\) after localizing \(B\). Descend the specified open, its isomorphism to \(X_{K'}\) and the inverse identities; this identifies the resulting open with all of \(X_B\). The finite map makes \(C\) proper over \(B\). Apply O.2 to make \(C\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) smooth of relative dimension one.

Choose the reduced closed structure on \(D=C\setminus X_B\). It is of finite presentation, and its generic fibre is finite by O.1. AH.4 checks the hypotheses of the finiteness proof in Theorem 4.2 of the limit lesson, which makes \(D\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) finite after another localization. In concrete terms, after making the source affine, finitely many generic module generators and the equations expressing their products by algebra generators descend; they then generate the whole algebra. This supplies finiteness of the boundary, not just its generic dimension.

All these base changes can be made over a smaller open of the original base while retaining a finite radicial map. For a localization \(B_b\), invert \(b^q\in A\): since \(b^{-1}=b^{q-1}/b^q\), one has \(B_b=B\otimes_A A_{b^q}\). In characteristic zero the same assertion uses \(q=1\). Finitely many such localizations can be combined. Write the final map as \(V\to U\).

### O.4. Separate the constants and verify every fibre

Write \(V=\operatorname{Spec}B\) and \(h:C\to V\). The finite map to the projective closure constructed in O.3 makes every \(H^i(C,\mathcal O_C)\) finite over \(B\), by AF.1 and W.4. AF.2 permits a further shrinking, still of the form allowed in O.3, after which these cohomology groups commute with every change of base. In particular \(E=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)\) is a finite \(B\)-algebra and
\[
E\otimes_BK'=\Gamma(C_{K'},\mathcal O_{C_{K'}}).
\tag{O.3}
\]
This is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of \(K'\). Indeed it is a finite-dimensional reduced algebra, since \(C_{K'}\) is smooth. The same equalizer commutes with field extension; smoothness makes its scalar extension to an algebraic closure reduced too. A finite field factor containing an inseparable element would contain a polynomial quotient with a repeated root after that extension, and hence a nonzero nilpotent. Tensoring the inclusion of the subfield generated by that element remains injective, a contradiction.

After shrinking \(V\), the algebra \(E\) itself is finite étale. Write each field factor of (O.3) as a finite tower of simple separable extensions. Descend the monic minimal polynomials and the Bezout equations that invert their derivatives, clearing their finite lists of denominators. They define a finite free étale tower over a localization of \(B\), by the square-zero root correction in AB.1. Let \(D\) be the product of these towers. The generic algebra isomorphism \(D\otimes_BK'\simeq E\otimes_BK'\) descends explicitly: \(D\) is finite free, and AF.2 has made \(E\) finite free, so write it and its inverse as matrices in those bases. Clear their denominators and the finitely many equations asserting mutual inverse, preservation of the unit, and preservation of products of basis elements. These matrices then define an algebra isomorphism \(D\simeq E\) over that localization. Thus \(E\) is finite étale. The \(b^q\) argument of O.3 makes this an additional shrinking of \(U\), preserving the finite radicial map \(V\to U\) and the base-change conclusion of AF.2.

Put \(T=\operatorname{Spec}E\). Restriction of global functions defines the factorization \(C\to T\to V\). AF.3 proves that its first map is proper, smooth of relative dimension one, and has geometrically connected nonempty fibres. It computes the global functions after each algebraically closed field extension by AF.2, and identifies each geometric fibre with the factor selected by one primitive idempotent of \(E\). Its global-function algebra is that field, so the fibre is nonempty and connected. Properness follows from the closed graph and base change; smoothness follows from the open graph and the smooth product projection. The diagonal calculation underlying the open-graph assertion is as follows.

Here the diagonal's openness has a direct algebraic check. For a finite étale \(B\)-algebra \(E\), the kernel \(I\) of \(E\otimes_BE\to E\) is finitely generated and satisfies \(I/I^2=\Omega_{E/B}=0\). Write generators as \(x_i=\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\), with \(a_{ij}\in I\). The adjugate identity makes \(d=\det(\delta_{ij}-a_{ij})\) annihilate \(I\), and \(d\equiv1\pmod I\). Put \(e=1-d\). Then \(e\in I\), every \(x\in I\) satisfies \(x=ex\), and \(e^2=e\). Thus \(I=(e)\), so its closed subscheme is also the open \(D(1-e)\). This proves the diagonal assertion used above.

The product idempotents in the descended algebra split \(T=\coprod_iT_i\) and \(C=\coprod_iC_i\). Put \(Y_i=X_V\cap C_i\). The boundary is finite over \(V\), so also has zero-dimensional fibres over \(T_i\). Every geometric fibre of \(C_i\to T_i\) is a connected smooth curve. Its irreducible components cannot meet, since its regular local rings are domains; with finitely many components they would therefore form a disjoint open-and-closed decomposition. Connectedness forces one component. Deleting the finite boundary leaves a dense nonempty open in each such fibre. Density and nonemptiness descend from a faithfully flat algebraic closure of the residue field. This proves every assertion of (O.1) and the stronger version of (3.3).

For a smooth zero-dimensional generic component, its affine algebra over the generic field is finite étale. Finite presentation descends finiteness and its finite standard étale charts over a smaller open, so that component is finite étale there. It can be separated by descending the generic open-and-closed decomposition. This accounts for the zero-dimensional case without adding a curve calculation.

AG.1–AG.4 prove the normalization and perfect-field smoothness steps in O.1. AF.1–AF.4 prove the finite-map cohomology, arbitrary base change on the chosen neighbourhood, and connected-fibre factorization in O.4. AH.1–AH.3 prove the purely inseparable density, finite-boundary and generic-closure assertions. AH.4 verifies the hypotheses and proof chain for the finite diagrams in O.1–O.3, using the exact proved assertions of the limits lesson linked above.

## Appendix P. The curve finiteness input

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed. We prove the curve assertion used in Proposition 3.2, keeping its geometric and cohomological inputs separate. Appendix Q supplies the Picard construction needed here, using the represented divisor charts of [The Picard functor and the Picard scheme of a curve, Sections 2 and 4–6](course:AG-HP/the-picard-functor-and-the-picard-scheme-of-a-curve#4-an-open-chart-and-its-translates), with explicit coherent-cohomology inputs and a degree-\(g\) properness argument. It proves the following precise input for a smooth connected projective curve \(C\):

\[
J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k},\qquad
J(k)=\ker(\deg:\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to\mathbb Z),
\tag{P.1}
\]

where \(J\) is a smooth proper connected commutative group scheme. The construction includes nonreduced parameter schemes. Q.1 proves the Euler-degree formula and the vanishing needed for the chart translations; Q.2 proves properness of the divisor parameter scheme; Q.3 supplies the finite cohomology complex for arbitrary parameters; and Q.4–Q.5 assemble the Picard scheme and prove properness. The high-degree Abel projective-bundle theorem and coherent Serre duality are not needed for this particular input. Their stronger statements elsewhere retain their own scope. The free comparison statements are [Stacks, Tags 0B9Z and 0BA0].

### P.1. Division by an invertible integer

For any smooth proper connected commutative group scheme \(G/k\) of finite type and any positive integer \(n\) invertible in \(k\), multiplication \([n]:G\to G\) is surjective and étale. Its kernel has finitely many \(k\)-points. We prove precisely these assertions.

First consider a square-zero thickening \(T_0\subset T\) with ideal \(I\). The kernel of \(G(T)\to G(T_0)\), interpreted locally on \(T\), is

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{T_0}}
       (e^*\Omega_{G/k}\otimes_k\mathcal O_{T_0},I).
\tag{P.2}
\]

Here \(e\) is the identity. Indeed a map reducing to the identity has the same underlying topological image and hence lies in an affine neighbourhood of it. Subtract the identity's map on functions from the given map. The difference takes values in \(I\), and the product identity says exactly that it is a derivation, since \(I^2=0\). Conversely adding such a derivation gives a map on functions. This is [Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Proposition 2.1](course:AG-CA/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps#2-uniqueness-is-measured-by-differentials), applied at the identity. The group operation on (P.2) is addition: its differential is linear on the two tangent factors, and its restrictions to either factor are the identity because multiplying by the identity does nothing. Consequently \([n]\) acts on (P.2) by the scalar \(n\).

Suppose \(x_0:T_0\to G\) and \(y:T\to G\) satisfy \([n]x_0=y|_{T_0}\). Smoothness of \(G/k\) supplies, locally on \(T\), a lift \(x\) of \(x_0\). The error \(\delta=[n]x-y\) lies in (P.2). Set

\[
x'=x-n^{-1}\delta.
\tag{P.3}
\]

Then \([n]x'=y\). If two such lifts exist, their difference belongs to (P.2) and is killed by \(n\), so is zero. This uniqueness glues the local lifts. We have proved the infinitesimal lifting test for formal étaleness. The morphism is of finite presentation, since it is a morphism between finite-type schemes over the Noetherian field \(k\); hence it is étale by the finite-presentation criterion proved in Section 4 of the same algebra lesson. Successive square-zero thickenings also give the test for every nilpotent ideal.

AE.1 proves flatness for these étale charts over the Noetherian target, from the split presentation and the fibre-regular quotient argument. AD.2 then proves their openness. The map \([n]\) is also proper: its graph is closed in \(G\times_kG\) by separatedness, and the projection to the target is a base change of the proper structure map of \(G\). The base-change and composition assertions are proved in AE.2. Its image is therefore both open and closed, and contains the identity. Connectedness of \(G\) makes the image all of \(G\).

Each geometric fibre is a finite-type étale scheme over an algebraically closed field. AB.1 proves that it is a finite disjoint union of points, using the finite-presentation lifting criterion and the field-algebra calculation. In particular the fibre over the identity has finitely many points. Surjectivity implies surjectivity on \(k\)-points: the fibre over each \(k\)-point is nonempty, and its points have residue field \(k\) by the same classification. Thus

\[
n:G(k)\twoheadrightarrow G(k),\qquad G(k)[n]\text{ is finite}.
\tag{P.4}
\]

For \(n=1\) the kernel is the trivial group, as required. This proof uses neither a polarization nor an intersection-number calculation. Applied to the constructed \(J\), it gives all the division and torsion finiteness needed below.

### P.2. Kummer on a proper smooth curve

AD.3 proves the degree-one identification by unit cocycles and line-bundle descent. Appendix R proves the higher vanishing by its function-field and valuation-sheaf calculation, as in [The multiplicative group on a curve, Theorem 4.2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-multiplicative-group-on-a-curve#4-higher-direct-images-of-rational-units). Together these give

\[
H^1(C,\mathbf G_m)=\operatorname{Pic}(C),\qquad
H^q(C,\mathbf G_m)=0\quad(q\geq2).
\tag{P.5}
\]

Appendix R gives the function-field and valuation-sheaf deduction used here. Its calculation on finite generic fibres proves the needed higher-direct-image vanishing without the strict-local cohomology continuity theorem. It uses no Picard input. The divisor argument of the linked lesson also gives

\[
0\longrightarrow J(k)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)
 \xrightarrow{\deg}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0.
\tag{P.6}
\]

X.2 constructs divisor representatives for every line bundle. X.3 proves finiteness of the morphism defined by a nonconstant rational function, and X.4 computes its fibre lengths, proving that principal divisors have degree zero. A point of \(C(k)\) has degree one. The kernel identification is (P.1).

X.1 proves that the global regular functions on \(C\) are \(k\), using finite-dimensional coherent sections and integrality. Thus \(\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)^\times=k^\times\), and the \(n\)-th-power map on this group is surjective. AD.4 proves the exact Kummer sequence by its explicit finite étale root cover. That sequence and (P.5) now give

\[
\begin{aligned}
H^0(C,\mu_n)&=\mu_n(k),\\
H^1(C,\mu_n)&=\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]=J(k)[n],\\
H^2(C,\mu_n)&=\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n,
\end{aligned}
\tag{P.7}
\]

and zero in degrees above two. The second equality in degree one follows because \(\mathbb Z\) has no torsion. The degree map identifies \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\) with \(\mathbb Z/n\): if \(\deg L=na\), choose \(M\) of degree \(a\). Then \(L\otimes M^{-n}\) lies in \(J(k)\), and (P.4) supplies an \(n\)-th root of it. This proves the kernel assertion; a degree-one bundle proves surjectivity. Every group in (P.7) is therefore finite. Choosing a primitive \(n\)-th root identifies \(\mu_n\) with the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Z/n\). The choice is unnecessary for finiteness; the canonical degree map itself has coefficients \(\mu_n\). For the Kummer calculation, see [Stacks, Tag 03RN]. Only finiteness of torsion is used here.

### P.3. The finite boundary and compact supports

Let \(U\) be a smooth connected affine curve. Over our algebraically closed field the normalization construction in O.1 gives an open immersion \(U\subset C\), with finite boundary \(D\), and a finite map from \(C\) to a projective curve. The completion \(C\) is projective as well as proper. To check this additional property, pull back the hyperplane bundle from that projective curve. Its coordinate-section opens pull back to affine opens because the map is finite; they cover \(C\). For a principal open \(D(b)\) inside one of these affine opens \(C_s\), the denominator-extension lemma gives \(a\geq0\) and a section \(u\) of the \(a\)-th tensor power with \(u/s^a=b\). The nonvanishing open of \(us\) is exactly \(D(b)\): its factor \(s\) excludes the complement of \(C_s\). Such principal opens form a basis, so the pulled-back bundle is ample by the affine-section-open definition. The denominator-clearing construction and affine-base very-ample-power theorem in [Ample invertible sheaves, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 4.2](course:AG-MO/ample-invertible-sheaves#4-relative-ampleness-and-very-ample-powers) embed a power into finite projective space. Properness makes this immersion closed. Since normalization preserves the connected smooth open and its closure is integral, \(C\) is a connected smooth projective curve.

The same completion construction applies to every smooth connected separated finite-type curve \(X\). Choose a nonempty affine open \(U\subset X\) and its smooth projective completion \(C\) just constructed. Y.6 and L.1 make the local ring at each closed point of \(X\) a DVR. The rational map \(X\dashrightarrow C\) extends over each such local spectrum by properness of \(C\). Finite presentation extends each local map to a neighbourhood, and separatedness of \(C\) makes these extensions agree on overlaps, since their maps on the common function field agree. They glue to a birational morphism \(X\to C\). Its closed fibres are proper closed subsets of the integral curve \(X\), hence finite; its generic fibre is one point. It is therefore quasi-finite and is separated because \(X\) is separated over the field. AW.4 identifies it with an open immersion into the integral closure of \(C\) in its unchanged function field. That integral closure is \(C\), since \(C\) is normal. Thus \(X\) is an open subscheme of \(C\) with finite boundary. If \(X\) is proper, the graph argument of AU.1 makes this open immersion proper, so its dense image is also closed and \(X=C\). Otherwise the boundary is nonempty, and X.4 makes its complement \(X\) affine. This proves both the projective and affine alternatives for a connected smooth curve.

Put \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z/n\), let \(j:U\hookrightarrow C\), and give \(D\) its reduced structure with inclusion \(i\). On geometric stalks the following sequence is either the identity sequence on \(U\) or the identity sequence on \(D\), so it is exact:

\[
0\longrightarrow j_!\Lambda_U\longrightarrow\Lambda_C
 \longrightarrow i_*\Lambda_D\longrightarrow0.
\tag{P.8}
\]

The definition of compact support and properness of \(C\) identify \(R\Gamma(C,j_!\Lambda)\) with \(R\Gamma_c(U,\Lambda)\). If \(r=|D|>0\), the cohomology sequence of (P.8) is

\[
\begin{gathered}
0\longrightarrow\Lambda\xrightarrow{\mathrm{diag}}\Lambda^r
 \longrightarrow H_c^1(U,\Lambda)
 \longrightarrow H^1(C,\Lambda)\longrightarrow0,\\
H_c^2(U,\Lambda)\simeq H^2(C,\Lambda).
\end{gathered}
\tag{P.9}
\]

Also \(H_c^0(U,\Lambda)=0\) and \(H_c^q(U,\Lambda)=0\) for \(q>2\). Here a finite union of algebraically closed points has no positive étale cohomology, and finite direct image is exact, as proved in the valuation-sheaf calculation cited in P.2. If the boundary is empty, compact-support cohomology is simply the proper-curve cohomology from P.2. In either case all groups are finite. The same conclusions hold for finitely many connected components by taking their finite direct sum.

### P.4. Constructible coefficients on any separated curve

Let \(X/k\) be separated of finite type and of dimension at most one, and let \(F\) be a constructible \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaf, with \(\ell\) invertible in \(k\). Passing to the reduction does not change its étale topos or its compact-support cohomology, by finite topological invariance and proper-support composition.

There is an open \(U\subset X\) which is a finite disjoint union of smooth affine curves, on which \(F\) is finite locally constant, and whose complement \(Z\) is finite. Indeed, at the generic point of each one-dimensional reduced component its function field is separably generated over the perfect field \(k\), so the smoothness criterion supplies a dense smooth open. Intersect it with the constructible sheaf's open lisse stratum, delete the intersections with other components, and choose a nonempty affine open inside it. Its complement in that component is zero-dimensional and closed, hence finite. There are finitely many components; any zero-dimensional components can be included in \(Z\). These choices give the stated disjoint open union. If there are no curve components, take \(U\) empty.

On a connected component of \(U\), the finite-monodromy construction N.2–N.3 and the elementary subgroup argument in Proposition 3.2 give a finite étale cover \(g:U'\to U\) of degree \(e\) prime to \(\ell\) for which \(g^*F\) has a finite filtration with constant \(\mathbf F_\ell\) quotients. This subgroup and invariant-vector argument uses only finite group theory, so its occurrence later in the proof of Proposition 3.2 creates no dependence on that proposition's finiteness conclusion. The cover is affine, smooth and of dimension one, since it is finite étale over \(U\). P.3 and successive cohomology sequences prove finiteness and vanishing above two for \(H_c^q(U',g^*F)\).

The unit and the sum over the finite étale fibres define

\[
F\longrightarrow g_*g^*F\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}}F,
\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\circ\operatorname{unit}=e\,\mathrm{id}.
\tag{P.10}
\]

This identity is checked after splitting the cover étale locally and hence on all geometric stalks. Multiplying the trace by \(e^{-1}\) gives a retraction. Finite direct image is exact and agrees with proper-support image; proper-support composition therefore makes \(H_c^q(U,F)\) a direct summand of \(H_c^q(U',g^*F)\). It too is finite and zero above two.

Finally apply compact-support excision to \(U\subset X\). The term on the finite complement \(Z\) is a finite group in degree zero and zero in higher degrees. The long exact sequence proves the claimed finiteness and vanishing for \(X\). Filtering a finite \(\ell\)-primary coefficient sheaf by powers of \(\ell\) proves the same assertion for it. Finite truncation triangles then give finite compact-support cohomology for every bounded complex with such constructible cohomology; a sheaf range \([a,b]\) gives the range \([a,b+2]\) on a curve. For a proper curve these are ordinary cohomology groups. Every reduction uses only the independently constructed compact-support operations and the explicit curve and group arguments above, before general direct-image constructibility is proved. At the smooth-curve scope, AK.4–AK.5 give a direct proof using finite normalization and a projective completion, without a general proper-support composition input.

## Appendix Q. Divisor charts and the Picard input

Fix an algebraically closed field \(k\), a smooth connected projective curve \(C/k\), and a point \(p\in C(k)\). Put \(g=\dim_k H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\). We construct the smooth proper connected group required in (P.1), retaining arbitrary parameter schemes. The argument uses the finite-algebra construction of the curve's divisor functor, not projectivity of a general Quot scheme.

### Q.1. Euler degree and vanishing at one point

Choose two hyperplanes in a projective embedding of \(C\) whose intersections with \(C\) are disjoint. To do this, choose the first not containing \(C\); its intersection is finite. Since \(k\) is infinite, choose the second avoiding those finitely many points and not containing \(C\). Their complements give a cover by two affine opens with affine intersection. W.1–W.2 prove that the ordered Čech complex computes quasi-coherent cohomology in degrees zero and one only. This remains true after any field extension \(K/k\), and after any change of parameter ring.

W.3–W.4 prove finite coherent cohomology by the projective-space monomial calculation, finite quotients by twists and descending induction, then a common affine-cover complex for a closed projective subscheme. They give finite-dimensional cohomology here and finite modules over any Noetherian parameter ring. No duality theorem enters it. Flat field extension tensors the affine-cover complex term by term, so preserves cohomology dimensions. In particular \(H^0(C_K,\mathcal O)=K\) and \(h^1(C_K,\mathcal O)=g\).

For a closed point \(x\) of \(C_K\) and a line bundle \(L\), the discrete valuation local ring gives

\[
0\longrightarrow L(-x)\longrightarrow L
 \longrightarrow i_{x,*}(L|_x)\longrightarrow0.
\tag{Q.1}
\]

The last sheaf has only degree-zero cohomology, of dimension \([K(x):K]\). Additivity of the finite Euler characteristic therefore gives \(\chi(L)-\chi(L(-x))=[K(x):K]\). X.2 proves that every line bundle has a rational section and is \(\mathcal O(D)\) for a finite divisor \(D\), including over the extension field \(K\). Iterating (Q.1) forward and backward over the positive and negative coefficients proves

\[
h^0(C_K,L)-h^1(C_K,L)=\deg L+1-g.
\tag{Q.2}
\]

Here degree is the divisor degree, with residue-field multiplicities. In particular this formula proves that the divisor and Euler-characteristic definitions agree. Since cohomology commutes with field extension, the degree does too. It also gives the inequality \(h^0(L)\geq\deg L+1-g\). We have proved the portion of curve Riemann–Roch needed in this appendix directly from point exact sequences; no identification of \(H^1\) with a dual space is required.

For \(m\geq g+1\), (Q.2) gives \(h^0(C,\mathcal O(mp))\geq2\). Choose a nonconstant element of that space. It is a rational function with its only pole at \(p\): having no pole would make it a constant regular function on the proper curve. It defines a morphism \(C\to\mathbf P^1\), since at a discrete valuation ring either the function or its inverse is regular. X.3 proves this map is finite by its projective graph and W.4 coherent finiteness; X.4 proves surjectivity and the exact fibre degrees. The inverse image of \(\mathbf A^1\) is exactly \(C\setminus\{p\}\), which is therefore affine. This argument works with any point of \(C(k)\). The same nonconstant finite map is surjective onto \(\mathbf P^1\); its fibres over the infinitely many \(k\)-points show that \(C(k)\) is infinite.

Let \(L\) now be any line bundle on \(C_K\). With \(U_K=C_K\setminus\{p_K\}\) and inclusion \(j\), pole orders give an equality of quasi-coherent sheaves

\[
\underset{m\geq0}{\operatorname{colim}}L(mp_K)=j_*(L|_{U_K}).
\tag{Q.3}
\]

Locally this is ordinary localization at an equation of \(p_K\): each fraction has a finite pole order. Compute both sides on the two-affine cover above. Filtered colimits commute with its finite products, kernels and cokernels; the intersections of these affine opens with \(U_K\) are affine as well. Thus the colimit of \(H^1(C_K,L(mp_K))\) is \(H^1(U_K,L|_{U_K})=0\). The transition maps on \(H^1\) are surjective by (Q.1). Their finite dimensions decrease and eventually stabilize; in the stable range the surjections are isomorphisms. Their zero colimit forces that stable dimension to be zero. Consequently

\[
H^1(C_K,L(mp_K))=0\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }m.
\tag{Q.4}
\]

This proves the twisting vanishing used below over every extension field, including imperfect extensions of \(k\).

### Q.2. The finite-divisor parameter scheme

Write \(H_d\) for the functor of closed subschemes of \(C_T\) finite locally free of degree \(d\) over \(T\). U.3 proves that these families are relative effective Cartier divisors over arbitrary parameter schemes, by lifting fibre generators and descending the finite algebra matrices. The finite-divisor charts are constructed in [Hilbert and Quot schemes, Sections 5 and 7](course:AG-HP/hilbert-and-quot-schemes#5-finite-points-on-affine-schemes).

For clarity, the representability used here is the elementary part of that lesson. Choose \(d+1\) distinct points of \(C(k)\). Any degree-\(d\) support misses one; Q.1 makes its complement affine. These finitely many affine opens suffice to cover the divisor functor, because the locus where a finite family lies inside a specified open is open: its complement is the finite image of the part of the family outside that open. On an affine curve with generators \(z_1,\ldots,z_s\), a rank-\(d\) quotient algebra is covered by the choices of a basis of monomials of degree at most \(d-1\), containing \(1\). These monomials span over every field: until their span is the whole algebra, multiplication by the generators increases its dimension. There can be at most \(d-1\) strict increases.

For a fixed monomial basis, multiplication by each \(z_i\) is a matrix. The equations that the matrices commute, satisfy the curve's relations, and send the vector of \(1\) to the chosen monomial basis vectors are finite polynomial equations. Conversely those equations make the resulting free module a cyclic quotient algebra: the kernel of evaluation at the vector of \(1\) is an ideal. Overlaps invert a change-of-basis determinant and conjugate the matrices. This is the full construction in Proposition 5.1 of the linked lesson, including finite presentation and the gluing maps. It gives a scheme \(H_d\) of finite type. For \(d=0\) it is \(\operatorname{Spec}k\).

We supply the separation and properness needed here. For two families \(D_1,D_2\) over \(T\), containment \(D_1\subset D_2\) means that the map

\[
(D_1\to T)_*(\mathcal I_{D_2}|_{D_1})
 \longrightarrow (D_1\to T)_*\mathcal O_{D_1}
\tag{Q.5}
\]

is zero. Both sheaves are finite locally free of rank \(d\): \(D_1/T\) is finite locally free, and the restricted ideal is invertible. They and their map commute with arbitrary base change. Locally the zero condition is exactly the vanishing of all entries of a matrix, so is represented by a closed subscheme of \(T\). On that subscheme the containment is equality: it gives a surjection between the two finite locally free rank-\(d\) algebras, whose determinant is invertible at every point. Thus the diagonal of \(H_d\) is closed, proving separation.

Adding the \(d\) graph divisors gives a morphism \(C^d\to H_d\); U.3–U.4 prove that their product ideal defines a finite locally free family of degree \(d\). On a geometric fibre every finite divisor is a sum of points with multiplicities, by the discrete valuation description, so the map is surjective after every base change. AE.2 proves properness of \(C^d\) from the projective embedding and the graded closed-image calculation. For any \(T\) and closed subset \(B\subset H_d\times T\), its inverse image in \(C^d\times T\) is closed. Its image in \(T\) is closed by that properness, and equals the image of \(B\) by surjectivity. Hence \(H_d\) is universally closed over \(k\). Finite type and separation make it proper. AE.3 proves that \(C^d\) remains integral after every field extension; the same surjection therefore proves geometric irreducibility of \(H_d\).

The explicit etale charts in V.1–V.3 prove smoothness without a characteristic restriction. V.4 also proves the following local coefficient description. At \(D=\sum_i d_i x_i\), choose formal parameters \(u_i\). Over a local Artinian test algebra \(R\) with residue field \(k\), idempotents split a finite flat deformation into its distinct support clusters. In the cluster of length \(d_i\), Nakayama makes \(1,u_i,\ldots,u_i^{d_i-1}\) a basis. It has one unique relation

\[
u_i^{d_i}+a_{i,1}u_i^{d_i-1}+\cdots+a_{i,d_i}=0,
\qquad a_{i,j}\in\mathfrak m_R.
\tag{Q.6}
\]

Conversely every such relation defines a free quotient with that basis. If \(\mathfrak m_R^N=0\), it implies \(u_i^{d_iN}=0\); hence formal series evaluate by finite sums, so the polynomial and formal descriptions agree. Therefore

\[
\widehat{\mathcal O}_{H_d,D}
 =k[[a_{i,j}:1\leq j\leq d_i]],
\tag{Q.7}
\]

with \(d\) variables. V.4 constructs the inverse maps giving this power-series description, including its separate support clusters. Smoothness and dimension \(d\) follow independently from V.3: a neighbourhood of every closed point has an etale coefficient map to \(\mathbf A^d_k\), and those neighbourhoods cover \(H_d\). Thus \(H_d\) is smooth, proper and geometrically integral. Only these properties of divisors are used below; no division by \(d!\) has occurred.

### Q.3. Cohomology over arbitrary parameter rings

For a line bundle \(L\) on \(C_A\), with \(A\) any \(k\)-algebra, there is locally on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) a complex of finite free modules

\[
K^0\xrightarrow{d}K^1
\tag{Q.8}
\]

which computes the cohomology of \(L_B\) after every \(A\)-algebra change \(B\).

Here is a proof specialized to this fixed curve. Write \(A\) as the filtered union of its finitely generated \(k\)-subalgebras \(A_i\). The invertible sheaf descends to an invertible sheaf \(L_i\) on \(C_{A_i}\). On the fixed finite affine cover, descend its finite module presentations, its dual, the evaluation isomorphisms, the gluing maps and their inverses. Each involves finitely many coefficients. The equations for the inverse maps and triple-overlap identities hold at a sufficiently late stage. These explicit finite data give the descent; the finite-diagram arguments are also proved in O.2–O.3's limit provider. Because the curve is fixed over a field, \(C_{A_i}\) is \(A_i\)-flat, and the descended sheaf is invertible, so it is automatically \(A_i\)-flat. No descent of flatness for a general coherent sheaf is needed.

Over Noetherian \(A_i\), the two-affine Čech complex has flat \(A_i\)-modules in degrees zero and one. Flatness follows by tensoring an injection and using exact affine sections; it does not require those section modules to be finite over \(A_i\). W.4 proves both the stated flatness and finite cohomology over \(A_i\), using the affine comparison in W.2. U.1 constructs a finite replacement for precisely this two-term flat complex: adjoin finitely many representatives of its degree-one cohomology and take the kernel of the resulting surjection. That kernel is finite and flat, hence locally finite free, and the comparison remains a quasi-isomorphism after every tensor product. Tensor that comparison with \(A\), and then with any \(B\). The affine cover and all its section modules base change term by term, proving (Q.8). The finite model is taken on the free neighbourhoods supplied by U.1.

Two consequences now follow by finite matrices. First, \(\chi(L_t)=\operatorname{rank}K^0-\operatorname{rank}K^1\) is locally constant. Second, if \(h^0(L_t)=1\) and \(h^1(L_t)=0\) at a point, a full-size minor of \(d\) is invertible nearby. The map is surjective there and splits; its kernel is a line bundle \(N\). The complex is the direct sum of \(N[0]\) and a two-term identity complex. This decomposition survives every base change. Thus the condition

\[
h^0(L_t)=1,\qquad h^1(L_t)=0
\tag{Q.9}
\]

defines an open subfunctor, and on it \(f_*L=N\) with arbitrary-base-change compatibility. These are statements about actual parameter schemes, including nilpotents, not just their field-valued points.

### Q.4. A represented chart and its translates

For every \(T/k\), the affine-cover calculation and exact tensoring over \(k\) give \((C_T\to T)_*\mathcal O_{C_T}=\mathcal O_T\). Hence every automorphism of a line bundle comes from a unique base unit. Normalize a line bundle by tensoring with the inverse pullback of its restriction to \(p_T\), and retain its canonical trivialization there. An automorphism respecting that trivialization is the identity.

Rigidified bundles form an fppf sheaf by AD.1–AD.2 and AD.4. The argument descends finite presentation and rank one over arbitrary rings, constructs finite affine refinements of fppf covers over every parameter scheme, and descends both the bundle and its trivialization. Uniqueness of rigidified overlap isomorphisms gives the cocycle. Thus the relative Picard sheaf is the functor of rigidified bundles on every \(T\), with the normalization and quotient identification proved in AD.4.

Let \(F\) be the open subfunctor (Q.9). Its elements have degree \(g\) by (Q.2). Q.3 makes its inclusion representable by open immersions. It is represented by

\[
W=\{D\in H_g:H^1(C,\mathcal O(D))=0\}.
\tag{Q.10}
\]

The functorial inverse is worth specifying. For \(L\in F(T)\), evaluate the line bundle \(N=f_*L\) to obtain \(f^*N\to L\). It is nonzero on every curve fibre. U.4 proves that its zero scheme is a relative effective Cartier divisor, finite locally free of degree \(g\) over \(T\), including non-Noetherian parameter schemes. Its associated bundle is \(L\otimes f^*N^{-1}\). Normalizing at \(p_T\) cancels this base factor and recovers the original rigidified bundle. In the reverse direction, the canonical section of \(\mathcal O(D)\) spans its one-dimensional space of sections on every fibre. Q.3 makes \(\mathcal O_T\to f_*\mathcal O(D)\) an isomorphism, and evaluation recovers exactly \(D\). These constructions commute with all base changes, proving (Q.10) as an isomorphism of functors.

Every field-valued Picard point can be translated into this chart by a bundle defined over \(k\). For \(L\) on \(C_K\), choose \(m\) so large that (Q.4) kills its first cohomology and (Q.2) makes \(h^0\geq1\). If \(h^0>1\), take a nonzero section and choose \(x\in C(k)\) outside its finite zero divisor on \(C_K\); infinitely many such \(k\)-points are available. The evaluation in (Q.1) is surjective, so twisting by \(-x_K\) reduces \(h^0\) by one and leaves \(h^1=0\). Repeat until \(h^0=1\). All twists are the pullback of

\[
\mathcal O_C(mp-x_1-\cdots-x_s),
\tag{Q.11}
\]

a bundle defined on \(C\).

Translate the represented open \(W\) by all elements of \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\). Pairwise intersections are represented opens in both charts and identify the same subfunctor, so their identifications satisfy the cocycle identity. Glue them. They cover the Picard functor on every parameter scheme: at each parameter point apply (Q.11) to its residue field, and then take the inverse image of the resulting open chart. This is the proof of the represented-open gluing criterion in Section 4 of the Picard provider. We obtain a smooth group scheme \(P\), locally of finite type and of dimension \(g\), representing all rigidified bundles. The universal rigidified line bundle is the one corresponding to the identity map of \(P\).

### Q.5. Proper degree pieces from degree \(g\) divisors

The group scheme \(P\) is separated. Its rational identity has no proper specialization: in an affine neighbourhood of a proposed specialization, the identity point corresponds to a maximal ideal, since evaluation is a surjective \(k\)-algebra map to \(k\). Thus the point is closed. Evaluation also identifies its inclusion with a closed immersion on that affine neighbourhood; the complement of the point supplies the empty closed immersion on the remaining target open. Its pullback under \((a,b)\mapsto a-b\) is exactly the diagonal as a functor on schemes, so the diagonal is a closed immersion.

By Q.3 and (Q.2), degree is locally constant in a family. Apply this to the universal bundle to decompose

\[
P=\coprod_{d\in\mathbb Z}P^d.
\tag{Q.12}
\]

Each piece is open and closed. Tensoring by \(\mathcal O_C(rp)\) gives an isomorphism \(P^d\to P^{d+r}\), and tensor product adds degrees. The universal divisor gives the Abel map \(H_g\to P^g\). It is universally surjective: over any extension field, (Q.2) gives at least one section of every degree-\(g\) bundle. Its zero divisor has degree \(g\) and maps to that bundle. Checking geometric points proves surjectivity after every base change.

The image of the quasi-compact scheme \(H_g\) is all of \(P^g\), so \(P^g\) is quasi-compact. It is locally of finite type, hence of finite type. For any base \(T\) and closed subset of \(P^g\times T\), its inverse image in \(H_g\times T\) is closed and has closed image in \(T\), because \(H_g\) is proper. Universal surjectivity identifies that image with the original closed subset's image. Thus \(P^g\) is universally closed, and its separation and finite type make it proper. The same surjection makes it geometrically irreducible; its smoothness makes it geometrically reduced. Translations give these properties for every \(P^d\).

In particular \(J=P^0\) is smooth, proper and geometrically connected. It is the identity component, because it is connected, open and closed, and all degree pieces are disjoint opens. Its group of \(k\)-points consists exactly of degree-zero line bundles, proving (P.1). The argument includes \(g=0\): then \(H_g\) is a point and the degree-zero piece is a point. No high-degree Abel-fibre formula, coherent Serre duality, or projectivity theorem for a general Quot scheme is needed for this construction. The stronger versions of those results are unaffected; only the precise Picard input for curve finiteness has been proved here.

## Appendix R. Function fields and rational units

For Appendix P we need the vanishing of positive-degree unit cohomology over function fields, followed by a calculation on a smooth curve. The finite stages themselves suffice for the second step. Throughout this appendix, \(k\) is algebraically closed and \(F/k\) has transcendence degree one; finite generation of \(F\) is not assumed.

### R.1. A polynomial count over the constant field

We first recall precisely the elementary dimension input. Fewer homogeneous equations of positive degree than variables have a common nonzero zero over \(k\). Indeed, if \(r<N\) equations had only the origin as zero, the strong Nullstellensatz proved in Y.5 would make the radical of their ideal equal to \((Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)\). The height bound (Y.7) makes this prime have height at most \(r\), whereas the chain of coordinate primes has length \(N\). Zero equations can be discarded.

Let \(f\) be a homogeneous form of degree \(d>0\) in \(n>d\) variables over \(F\). Choose a transcendental \(t\in F\). The field \(F_0\) generated over \(k\) by \(t\) and the finitely many coefficients of \(f\) is finite over \(k(t)\), say of degree \(e\). Choose a \(k(t)\)-basis \(w_1,\ldots,w_e\) of \(F_0\). This argument allows inseparability. For an integer \(m\geq0\), substitute

\[
x_j=\sum_{i=1}^e w_i\sum_{a=0}^m z_{jia}t^a,
\qquad z_{jia}\in k.
\tag{R.1}
\]

Expand the finitely many products consisting of a coefficient of \(f\) and \(d\) basis elements in that basis. Their rational coordinates admit a common nonzero polynomial denominator \(D(t)\). Let \(B\) bound the degrees of the resulting polynomial numerators. Both \(D\) and \(B\) are fixed before choosing \(m\). Consequently

\[
D(t)f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^e w_i
             \sum_{b=0}^{dm+B} h_{ib}(z)t^b,
\tag{R.2}
\]

where the \(h_{ib}\) are homogeneous of degree \(d\), or zero. Thus there are at most \(e(dm+B+1)\) equations in \(ne(m+1)\) scalar variables. Choose \(m\) so that

\[
(n-d)m+n-B-1>0.
\tag{R.3}
\]

The preceding dimension argument gives a nonzero solution \(z\). Transcendence of \(t\) and linear independence of the \(w_i\) imply that the resulting tuple \(x\) is nonzero. Equation (R.2) gives \(f(x)=0\). This proves that \(F\) is \(C_1\). It also proves the same assertion for every algebraic extension of \(F\), since that extension still has transcendence degree one over \(k\). No passage of Brauer groups or cohomology through a field limit is used. This is the finite-coefficient form of the proof in [Brauer groups and Tsen's theorem, Section 5](course:ag-etale-cohomology/brauer-groups-and-tsen-s-theorem#5-tsen-s-theorem-by-bounded-polynomials); see also [Stacks, function fields].

### R.2. From forms to degree-two cohomology

Z.1 proves the finite-dimensional simple-algebra classification and scalar extension used here. Z.2 constructs a finite separable splitting field over the infinite fields in this appendix, using a trace Gram determinant to choose an element with distinct eigenvalues. Passing to its finite normal closure gives a Galois splitting field, including in positive characteristic over imperfect fields.

For a central division algebra \(A/F\) of degree \(a\), Z.2 constructs its reduced norm as a degree-\(a\) homogeneous polynomial over \(F\) in \(a^2\) coordinates, and proves that it is nonzero exactly on invertible elements. If \(a>1\), R.1 produces a nonzero element of norm zero, contradicting division. Thus \(A=F\), and Z.1 makes every central simple algebra a matrix algebra. In particular \(\operatorname{Br}(F)=0\).

Z.3 proves the finite-dimensional semilinear descent needed next. Z.4 associates a descended matrix algebra to each finite scalar two-cocycle. Once that algebra is split, its invariant matrix units make the semilinear operators scalar, and their multiplication identity explicitly expresses the cocycle as a coboundary. The full identification with the Brauer group is [Brauer groups and Tsen's theorem, Theorem 3.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/brauer-groups-and-tsen-s-theorem#3-the-boundary-and-the-cohomological-brauer-group). The local scalar calculation and the division-algebra argument already prove, for every field \(L\) algebraic over \(F\),

\[
H^2(G_L,(L^s)^\times)=\operatorname{Br}(L)=0.
\tag{R.4}
\]

Here \(L^s\) denotes a separable closure. The sign convention for the scalar boundary has no effect on this vanishing statement.

### R.3. Additive contraction and the Sylow test

We use continuous group cohomology. AA.2 constructs enough injective discrete modules and proves that continuous homogeneous cochains compute the derived functors of invariants. It also proves the finite-quotient comparison (AA.4) and compatibility with filtered colimits of coefficients. AB.1–AB.2 supply the field-site classification and the exact equivalence identifying these groups with étale cohomology, including the additive and multiplicative coefficient modules.

Here is a direct additive calculation valid for every field \(L\). If \(E/L\) is finite Galois with group \(Q\), the map \(\operatorname{Tr}(b)=\sum_{g\in Q}g(b)\) is nonzero: otherwise it would be a nontrivial linear relation between distinct field automorphisms. The minimal-relation proof of their independence is given in Z.3 and works over every field. Its values lie in \(L\), so scaling a value which is nonzero supplies \(a\in E\) with \(\operatorname{Tr}(a)=1\).

For an equivariant homogeneous cochain \(c:Q^{r+1}\to E\), with omission differential \(d\), define, for \(r\geq1\),

\[
(s c)(g_0,\ldots,g_{r-1})
 =\sum_{u\in Q}u(a)c(u,g_0,\ldots,g_{r-1}).
\tag{R.5}
\]

This is equivariant: substitute \(u=hv\) when translating every argument by \(h\), and use both \(u(a)=h(v(a))\) and equivariance of \(c\). In \(ds+sd\), all terms omitting one of the original arguments cancel in opposite pairs. The terms omitting the newly inserted argument sum to \(\sum_u u(a)c=c\). Therefore \(ds+sd=1\) in positive degrees, and \(H^r(Q,E)=0\) there. Finite-quotient comparison, with \((L^s)^U=E\), now gives

\[
H^r(G_L,(L^s,+))=0\qquad(r>0).
\tag{R.6}
\]

This supplies additive acyclicity directly, without a normal-basis existence theorem. In characteristic \(p\), the polynomial \(T^p-T-b\) has derivative \(-1\) and splits over a separably closed field. Thus

\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbf F_p\longrightarrow L^s
 \xrightarrow{\,b\mapsto b^p-b\,}L^s\longrightarrow0
\tag{R.7}
\]

is exact. Equation (R.6) and its long exact sequence give \(H^r(G_L,\mathbf F_p)=0\) for \(r\geq2\).

Now put \(G=G_F\), take the Sylow pro-\(\ell\) subgroup \(P\) constructed in AA.3, and let \(L=(F^s)^P\). AA.1 proves that \(F^s\) is a separable closure of \(L\) and \(G_L=P\) with its induced topology. The field \(L/k\) still has transcendence degree one. If \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\), the action of \(P\) on \(\mu_\ell\) is trivial: its finite image has \(\ell\)-power order dividing \(\ell-1\). Scalar Hilbert 90, proved in Z.3, makes the Kummer long exact sequence inject \(H^2(L,\mu_\ell)\) into \(H^2(G_L,(L^s)^\times)\), which vanishes by Z.4. Hence

\[
H^2(P,\mathbf F_\ell)
 \simeq H^2(L,\mu_\ell)=0.
\tag{R.8}
\]

A choice of primitive root supplies the first isomorphism. For \(\ell=p=\operatorname{char}k\), (R.7) gives the same vanishing. In particular this reasoning never needs to identify \(H^2(L,\mu_\ell)\) with a limit of cohomology groups of smaller fields.

AA.5 proves the passage from this single coefficient to all torsion coefficients. A finite nonzero \(\ell\)-primary \(P\)-module has a filtration by trivial \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-lines, by orbit counting on its \(\ell\)-torsion and iteration on quotients. Long exact sequences and filtered unions give degree-two vanishing for every discrete \(\ell\)-primary module. The acyclic continuous-function module (AA.3) and its successive quotients give all higher degrees. Restriction from \(G\) to \(P\) is injective on \(\ell\)-primary cohomology by (AA.10): a cocycle and a primitive of its restriction descend to one finite quotient, where the explicit prism and coset-sum formulas (AA.7)–(AA.9) multiply the cocycle by the prime-to-\(\ell\) index. Consequently

\[
H^r(G_F,T)=0\quad(r>1)
\quad\text{for every discrete torsion module }T.
\tag{R.9}
\]

For general torsion \(T\), take its primary parts and their finite direct sums; filtered-cochain comparison justifies the union.

### R.4. The multiplicative module is not torsion

Write \(M=(F^s)^\times\) additively for this paragraph. Let \(T\subset M\) be its torsion subgroup, \(N=M/T\), and \(V=N\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q\). The group \(N\) is torsion free: if a multiple of a class is torsion in \(M\), another multiple annihilates its representative. Thus

\[
\begin{gathered}
0\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow0,\\
0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow V\longrightarrow V/N\longrightarrow0
\end{gathered}
\tag{R.10}
\]

are exact sequences of discrete continuous modules, with \(V/N\) torsion. Discreteness of the rationalization follows by intersecting the open stabilizers of the finitely many numerators in a representative. Positive-degree cohomology of \(V\) vanishes by AA.5: the finite homogeneous insertion sum annihilates finite-group cohomology by the group order, and (AA.4) therefore makes each positive profinite class torsion. With rational coefficients the same cohomology is a rational vector space, so it is zero.

The second sequence of (R.10), followed by (R.9), gives \(H^r(G_F,N)=H^{r-1}(G_F,V/N)=0\) for \(r\geq3\). The first then gives \(H^r(G_F,M)=0\) for \(r\geq3\). Degree two is (R.4), and degree one is scalar Hilbert 90, whose finite-value proof works for arbitrary fields. The field-topos comparison (AB.5) therefore proves

\[
H^r(\operatorname{Spec}F,\mathbf G_m)=0
\qquad(r\geq1).
\tag{R.11}
\]

The separate degree-two argument is necessary: torsion cohomological dimension alone would not give that degree for \(M\).

### R.5. Calculate before taking a strict-local limit

Let \(X/k\) be a smooth connected separated curve, \(K=k(X)\), and \(j:\operatorname{Spec}K\to X\). A quasi-compact étale scheme \(U\to X\) of finite presentation has generic fibre

\[
U_K=\coprod_{i=1}^v\operatorname{Spec}E_i,
\tag{R.12}
\]

where the \(E_i/K\) are finite separable extensions; the empty fibre is allowed. AB.1 proves this finite étale algebra description over a field. The restriction of \(\mathbf G_{m,K}\) to the étale slice is its units sheaf, since AB.3 identifies the slice with the small étale site of \(U_K\). Each \(E_i/k\) has transcendence degree one. Equation (R.11) and exactness of finite products therefore give \(H^r(U_K,\mathbf G_m)=0\) for \(r>0\).

The slice-resolution formula (AB.8) identifies \(R^rj_*\mathbf G_{m,K}\) with the sheafification of \(U\mapsto H^r(U_K,\mathbf G_m)\). The presheaf is zero on the quasi-compact finite-presentation basis, so its associated sheaf is zero. AB.3 also proves that inverse image is exact and direct image preserves injectives. An injective resolution on \(\operatorname{Spec}K\) therefore becomes an injective resolution of \(j_*\mathbf G_{m,K}\). Taking sections and using (R.11) yields

\[
H^r(X,j_*\mathbf G_{m,K})=0\qquad(r>0).
\tag{R.13}
\]

It remains to compare rational units with regular units. AB.4 proves preservation of a local parameter on étale curve neighbourhoods. AB.5 uses those parameters to lift every divisor section locally and proves the kernel calculation, giving the valuation sequence also proved in [The multiplicative group on a curve, Sections 1–2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-multiplicative-group-on-a-curve#2-the-valuation-sequence):

\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbf G_{m,X}
 \longrightarrow j_*\mathbf G_{m,K}
 \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{x\in X_{\rm cl}}i_{x*}\mathbb Z
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{R.14}
\]

AB.4 also proves the degree-zero strict-local description: the pointed local-ring colimit is a discrete valuation ring with the common uniformizer, and the quotient of its fraction-field units by its ring units is \(\mathbb Z\). The local-lift proof in AB.5 establishes (R.14) directly on neighbourhoods. Neither argument uses a higher-cohomology limit comparison.

For a single closed point \(x\), the stalk of \(i_{x*}A\) is \(A\) at \(x\) and zero elsewhere. A quasi-compact étale neighbourhood has finite fibre over \(x\); select the pointed component and remove the other fibre points. Away from \(x\) one can exclude \(x\). For exactness and cohomology, AB.5 gives the section formula \((i_{x*}A)(U)=A^{U_x}\), so direct image is exact. AB.3 makes it preserve injectives, and AB.2 identifies the étale topos of algebraically closed \(k\) with sets. Thus \(H^r(X,i_{x*}\mathbb Z)=H^r(k,\mathbb Z)=0\) for \(r>0\).

Appendix S proves directly that the infinite point sum in (R.14) has zero positive-degree cohomology. Its finite-cover contractions preserve support in the base points; the signed total-complex argument supplies the comparison with derived sections. In particular this deduction requires neither general hypercover comparison nor a theorem interchanging arbitrary filtered coefficient colimits with cohomology. The long exact sequence of (R.14), constructed in T.4, uses that vanishing and (R.13) to prove

\[
H^r(X,\mathbf G_m)=0\qquad(r\geq2),
\tag{R.15}
\]

which is the higher-degree assertion required in (P.5). Line-bundle descent supplies its degree-one Picard identification. The construction retains the algebra, continuous-cochain and sheaf foundations explicitly; neither a strict-local higher-continuity assertion nor a normal-basis theorem is an additional input to this deduction.

## Appendix S. Finite covers and the infinite divisor sheaf

The sum of all closed-point valuation sheaves in (R.14) is infinite. Its acyclicity does not follow merely by adding the separate point calculations: derived sections need not commute with an arbitrary infinite sum. We prove the required assertion using finite families of étale covering maps, with explicit contractions and a finite elimination argument for the comparison with derived sections.

### S.1. The finite-cover basis and the sections to be calculated

Let \(X\) be as in R.5. Use the basis \(\mathcal B\) of quasi-compact separated étale schemes of finite presentation over \(X\). AC.4 proves that it is a basis, that finite fibre products over its objects stay in it, and that every cover refines to a finite covering family in it. The proof uses the open-diagonal and cancellation calculation of AB.3, the local parameter calculation of AB.4, and the Noetherian image and flat-openness arguments of AC.1–AC.3. It also proves the same finite-cover assertion after base change to any basis object. Thus these finite covers generate the restricted site. T.1 identifies its sheaves and cohomology with those on the full small étale site.

For each closed point \(x\) of \(X\), let \(A_x\) be an abelian group, and put

\[
\mathscr D_A=\bigoplus_{x\in X_{\rm cl}}i_{x*}A_x.
\tag{S.1}
\]

Every closed point of a finite-type \(k\)-scheme has residue field \(k\), by the Nullstellensatz, since \(k\) is algebraically closed. For \(U\in\mathcal B\), its fibre \(U_x\) is a finite discrete set of such points. The direct image of \(A_x\) has sections \(A_x^{U_x}\). We claim that the sheaf sum in (S.1) has the exact section formula

\[
\mathscr D_A(U)
 =\bigoplus_{x\in X_{\rm cl}}A_x^{U_x}
 =\bigoplus_{y\in U_{\rm cl}}A_{f(y)},
\tag{S.2}
\]

where \(f:U\to X\). Closed points of \(U\) map to closed points of \(X\): their residue field is \(k\), and the image of a \(k\)-point in a finite-type \(k\)-scheme is closed. Thus the second indexing is precisely the disjoint union of the finite fibres in the first one.

To prove the first equality, take a finite cover of \(U\). A matching family in the presheaf sum uses finitely many \(x\)'s on each member, hence finitely many in total. It therefore belongs to a fixed finite sum of the sheaves \(i_{x*}A_x\), where the sheaf axiom gives a unique glue. Equality can be checked in the same finite sum. Hence the presheaf sum already satisfies the sheaf axiom for the finite-cover topology on \(\mathcal B\). That topology generates the basis site, so its sheafification has exactly these sections. This is only a degree-zero argument; no higher-cohomology colimit assertion has been used.

### S.2. A signed comparison using finitely many diagonal terms

We record the sheaf-cohomology tools needed to pass from a finite-cover calculation to derived groups. T.1–T.4 supply their abelian-sheaf, injective-resolution and comparison foundations explicitly. Choose a resolution \(F\to I^\bullet\) in nonnegative degrees. The exact slice adjunction (AB.7) proves that restriction preserves injectives: its left adjoint sheafifies the direct sum over arrows into the slice, and finite sums of local lifts can be lifted on a common refinement. Thus \(H^n(U,F)\) is the cohomology of \(I^\bullet(U)\) and agrees with cohomology on the slice over \(U\).

For a finite cover \(\mathcal V=\{V_i\to U\}_{i=1}^m\), form the full Čech complex, retaining repeated indices:

\[
\check C^p(\mathcal V,F)
 =\prod_{i_0,\ldots,i_p}F(V_{i_0}\times_U\cdots\times_U V_{i_p}).
\tag{S.3}
\]

The differential \(d_h\) is the alternating sum of restrictions obtained by omitting an index. Its square is zero: the two orders of omitting any pair give opposite signs.

The augmented Čech complex of an injective sheaf is exact. Here is the local chain argument behind that assertion. Write \(P_V\) for the free abelian sheaf on the representable \(V\), so \(\operatorname{Hom}(P_V,I)=I(V)\). Form the augmented chain complex of the \(P_{V_{i_0\ldots i_p}}\), ending in \(P_U\). A sheaf cycle is locally a finite sum of arrows into these products. After a common covering refinement, every arrow into \(U\) occurring in that sum has a chosen lift to some \(V_i\). Inserting this lift first in each tuple defines a chain contraction: the face deleting the inserted lift is the original tuple, and all other faces cancel against insertion after taking the boundary. It respects each arrow into \(U\), hence each of the finitely many supports. Equalities introduced by sheafification hold after a further cover. The chain complex is therefore exact as a sheaf complex. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,I)\) is exact for injective \(I\), proving the assertion, including the augmentation. This is the free-chain proof in Section 3, Lemma 3.1 of the cohomology lesson.

Now use the double complex

\[
D^{p,q}=\check C^p(\mathcal V,I^q),\qquad
d_{\rm Tot}=d_h+(-1)^p d_v,
\qquad p,q\geq0.
\tag{S.4}
\]

Here \(d_v\) is the resolution differential, which commutes with restrictions. The sign makes \(d_{\rm Tot}^2=0\). The total group in degree \(n\) has exactly the \(n+1\) diagonal summands \(D^{p,n-p}\). The restriction augmentation

\[
I^\bullet(U)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tot}D
\tag{S.5}
\]

is a quasi-isomorphism, as the following direct elimination proves.

For surjectivity on cohomology, let \(z\) be a total cocycle of degree \(n\). If its highest nonzero horizontal column is \(r>0\), with component \(z^{r,n-r}\), the cocycle equation in column \(r+1\) says \(d_hz^{r,n-r}=0\). The augmented row is exact, so write this component as \(d_hb^{r-1,n-r}\). Subtracting \(d_{\rm Tot}b\) removes column \(r\) and changes only column \(r-1\). Repeating leaves a representative in column zero. Its horizontal differential is zero, so row exactness makes it the restriction of a unique \(a\in I^n(U)\). Its vertical differential is zero, and injectivity of the row augmentation gives \(d_va=0\). This is a preimage under (S.5).

For injectivity, suppose a restricted global cocycle is \(d_{\rm Tot}b\). If \(b\) has highest column \(r>0\), its horizontal differential there is zero, since \(d_{\rm Tot}b\) has only column zero. Write that component as \(d_hc^{r-1,q}\) and replace \(b\) by \(b-d_{\rm Tot}c\); the total differential is unchanged and the highest column decreases. At the end, \(b\) lies in column zero and has zero horizontal differential. It is the restriction of some \(v\in I^{n-1}(U)\), and the original global cocycle equals \(d_vv\), by injectivity of restriction into the Čech row. In degree zero, there are no boundaries and the augmentation is already injective. These finite procedures prove (S.5) in every degree, without a spectral-sequence convergence or hypercover theorem.

### S.3. When these Čech contractions imply derived vanishing

Suppose an abelian sheaf \(F\) has \(\check H^p(\mathcal V,F)=0\) for \(p>0\), for every finite basis cover of every \(U\in\mathcal B\). Then

\[
H^n(U,F)=0\qquad(n>0,\ U\in\mathcal B).
\tag{S.6}
\]

We prove this simultaneously over all basis objects by induction on \(n\). Represent a class by a global resolution cycle \(a\in I^n(U)\). Exactness of the resolution as a sheaf complex means that it is locally a boundary. Choose a finite basis cover and sections \(b_i\in I^{n-1}(V_i)\) with \(d_vb_i=a|_{V_i}\). This is permitted by S.1's cofinality. Under (S.5), the class has initial representative in bidegree \((0,n)\). Subtracting the total differential of \((b_i)\in D^{0,n-1}\) removes that component.

Suppose the current lowest nonzero column is \(p\), with \(0<p<n\). Its component has vertical degree \(q=n-p\), strictly between zero and \(n\). The total cocycle identity makes it a vertical cycle. Every intersection in (S.3) is a basis object, and its degree-\(q\) cohomology is zero by induction. The product in (S.3) is finite, so choose primitives component by component. Multiplying by \((-1)^p\) gives \(b^{p,q-1}\) with \((-1)^p d_vb^{p,q-1}=z^{p,q}\). Subtract \(d_{\rm Tot}b\); this removes column \(p\) and changes only column \(p+1\). After finitely many steps the representative lies in \((n,0)\).

The vertical cycle condition now puts it in \(\check C^n(\mathcal V,F)\), because \(F\) is the kernel of \(I^0\to I^1\). Its horizontal differential is zero. The assumed Čech vanishing writes it as \(d_hc\), for \(c\in\check C^{n-1}(\mathcal V,F)\). Such a \(c\) has vertical differential zero, so its total differential is also \(d_hc\). The original total class is zero, and (S.5) makes its global class zero. For \(n=1\) there are no intermediate positive vertical degrees, so the same argument starts the induction. This proves (S.6). It is the finite-cover criterion of [Cohomology on sites, Theorem 4.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-on-sites#4-a-practical-vanishing-criterion), here with its finite total-complex calculation made explicit; compare [Stacks, finite-cover acyclicity].

### S.4. Pointwise contractions preserve finite support

Apply this criterion to \(F=\mathscr D_A\). Fix a finite cover \(\mathcal V\) of a basis object \(U\). For each closed point \(y\in U\), let

\[
E_y=\coprod_{i=1}^m (V_i)_y.
\tag{S.7}
\]

This is a nonempty finite set: the cover is surjective and étale, and the residue field of \(y\) is algebraically closed. Choose one element \(e_y\in E_y\). These choices are set-theoretic; they need not form a section of the scheme covering.

Using (S.2) on every intersection, finite products commute with the point sums and give

\[
\check C^p(\mathcal V,\mathscr D_A)
 =\bigoplus_{y\in U_{\rm cl}}
       \operatorname{Maps}(E_y^{p+1},A_{f(y)}).
\tag{S.8}
\]

Indeed the points in a fibre of \(V_{i_0}\times_U\cdots\times_U V_{i_p}\) are precisely the tuples of points in those chosen fibres over the same \(y\). The alternating restriction differential becomes omission of the entries of a tuple, independently for each \(y\). The augmentation is the constant-function map from \(\bigoplus_yA_{f(y)}\).

For \(p\geq1\) define

\[
(h c)_y(v_0,\ldots,v_{p-1})
     =c_y(e_y,v_0,\ldots,v_{p-1}),
\tag{S.9}
\]

and in degree zero put \((hc)_y=c_y(e_y)\) in the augmented term. If \(c\) is supported on finitely many \(y\)'s, so is \(hc\), with no new base point introduced. Thus (S.9) is an actual operator on the direct sum (S.8), not merely on the larger product over all points.

Expanding the omission differential proves \(d_hh+hd_h=1\): the term deleting the inserted \(e_y\) is \(c_y\), and every other term has an equal term of opposite sign in the other composition. In augmented degree \(-1\), evaluation of a constant function is the original coefficient, so the identity holds there too. The augmented Čech complex is contracted. Therefore its positive Čech groups vanish for every finite basis cover. Applying S.3 gives

\[
H^n(U,\mathscr D_A)=0
\qquad(n>0,\ U\in\mathcal B).
\tag{S.10}
\]

Taking \(U=X\) and every \(A_x=\mathbb Z\) proves the divisor-sheaf assertion in R.5. This proof does not claim that all infinite sums are acyclic or that Čech cochains on one fixed cover compute arbitrary sheaf cohomology. The essential extra fact is that the support-preserving contraction works on every finite basis cover; S.3 then supplies precisely the needed derived conclusion.

## Appendix T. From local lifts to the cohomology exact sequence

The curve argument uses cohomology of abelian sheaves, including the non-torsion sheaves of rational units and divisors. We supply the ordinary resolution foundations at that scope. Work on a small site with fibre products and covering families, using the axiom of choice. For the curve, a small basis as in S.1 suffices; the equivalence with the full small étale site is proved below. These constructions concern resolutions of sheaves in nonnegative degrees.

### T.1. Local representatives, exactness and the choice of basis

For an abelian presheaf \(M\), let \(M^+(U)\) consist of matching families of sections on covers of \(U\), identifying two families when they agree on a common refinement. Such a refinement exists by taking pairwise fibre products. Two choices of refinement arrows have the same effect on a matching family: the two arrows from one member factor together through an overlap, where the matching equality applies. Taking a further common refinement proves transitivity of the equivalence relation. Addition is componentwise after taking a common refinement. Pulling back a cover defines restrictions, and the associativity of fibre products proves that restrictions compose. The identity cover defines \(M\to M^+\).

A class represented by \((m_i)\) becomes the image of \(m_i\) on its covering member. Two original sections have the same image precisely when they agree locally. These facts also show that \(M^+\) is separated: if two classes agree on a cover, refine their representatives to that cover, then refine once more to witness each equality in \(M\). Composing covers witnesses equality of the original classes.

If \(M\) is separated, \(M\to M^+\) is injective on sections. Given a matching family of plus-classes, represent each locally in \(M\). On every overlap their images in \(M^+\) agree; injectivity makes the representatives themselves agree there. The composite cover therefore carries one matching family in \(M\). Its class glues the original plus-classes, and separation proves uniqueness. Thus

\[
aM=M^{++}
\tag{T.1}
\]

is a sheaf. Every section of \(aM\) is locally represented in \(M\), and equality of two such representatives is witnessed locally in \(M\). A map from \(M\) to a sheaf extends by gluing matching families twice. Local representation and separation make the extension unique. This proves the associated-sheaf universal property, including its naturality.

Here are its exactness consequences. For a presheaf map \(u:M\to N\), a section of \(aM\) in the kernel of \(au\) can locally be represented by \(m\in M\); its image is locally zero in \(N\). After refining, the representative lies in \(\ker u\). Local equality proves injectivity of the resulting kernel comparison. For the cokernel, representatives are locally classes in \(N/uM\); its universal property follows by factoring maps which kill \(uM\). Consequently

\[
a(\ker u)=\ker(au),\qquad
a(\operatorname{coker}u)=\operatorname{coker}(au).
\tag{T.2}
\]

Kernels of sheaf maps are computed on sections, since compatible kernel sections glue to a section still killed by the map. Cokernels are sheafified presheaf cokernels. Sectionwise, the map from the quotient by the kernel to the image sends the class of \(m\) to \(u(m)\); it is well-defined, injective and surjective by the definitions. Sheafifying this isomorphism proves the coimage-to-image axiom. Finite sums are biproducts, so these constructions form an abelian category. A sheaf map is an epimorphism exactly when every target section lifts on a cover, by the local-zero description of its cokernel. It need not be surjective on sections over the original object. A monomorphism is sectionwise injective, by the kernel description.

Arbitrary sums and colimits are obtained by sheafifying their presheaf versions: a map from that associated sheaf is exactly a compatible family of maps from the summands or diagram objects. Filtered colimits are exact. At the presheaf level, a representative and any finite equation involving representatives occur at one common later index; an equation which becomes zero is zero at some later index. This proves preservation of kernels and finite sums for filtered diagrams of abelian groups. Apply this objectwise. For a diagram exact as sheaves, each remaining failure of presheaf surjectivity is locally zero; any element of its filtered colimit comes from one such stage and is still locally zero. Applying (T.2) proves exactness in sheaves. The same finite-support argument proves that a sum of monomorphisms is monic. In particular, an increasing union of subobjects is a subobject, and filtered unions commute with pullbacks, since a pullback is the kernel of a map from a finite direct sum.

To justify using the basis \(\mathcal B\) of S.1, restrict a sheaf to its basis objects. In the other direction, for a basis sheaf \(F\), assign to an arbitrary étale object \(U\) the group of families

\[
(s_b),\qquad s_b\in F(W)
\quad\text{for every }b:W\to U,\ W\in\mathcal B,
\tag{T.3}
\]

compatible under arrows between basis objects over \(U\). If \(U\) itself is a basis object, evaluation at its identity and restriction from that value are inverse, so (T.3) gives \(F(U)\). It is a sheaf on the full site. Indeed, for a matching family on a cover of \(U\), pull the cover back to any \(W\to U\), refine by basis objects, and glue in \(F\). A common refinement proves independence of the choices, compatibility with further arrows, and uniqueness. On basis objects the chosen refinements may be reduced to finite covers by S.1. Every full-site sheaf is recovered in this manner: cover \(U\) by basis objects and glue its compatible sections; overlaps can again be covered by basis objects. These two constructions are inverse on maps as well as objects. The local-lifting criterion proves their exactness. An exact equivalence preserves injectives by transporting the defining extension problem, and preserves resolutions and sections on \(X\). Thus it preserves the cohomology used here. The general sheafification construction is also proved in [Sites and sheaves, Sections 2–4](course:ag-etale-cohomology/sites-and-sheaves#2-refining-a-description); compare [Stacks, abelian sheaf foundations].

### T.2. An injective target for every abelian sheaf

For each basis object \(U\), sheafify the free abelian presheaf on arrows into \(U\), and denote the result by \(P_U\). A map \(P_U\to F\) is determined by the image of the identity arrow. Conversely a section \(s\in F(U)\) sends a generator \([b:V\to U]\) to \(b^*s\). Linearity, restriction and (T.1) give inverse constructions. Hence

\[
\operatorname{Hom}(P_U,F)=F(U),\qquad P=\bigoplus_U P_U.
\tag{T.4}
\]

The object \(P\) detects nonzero maps: a section on which a map is nonzero gives a map from one summand of \(P\); set all other summands to zero. Subobjects of \(P\) form a set, since they are specified by compatible subgroups of its section groups on a small set of objects.

We first prove an extension test. Suppose every map \(K\to J\), for every subobject \(K\subset P\), extends to \(P\). For an arbitrary inclusion \(A\subset B\) and map \(A\to J\), order its extensions to intermediate subobjects of \(B\) by extension. A chain has a union by T.1, with a compatible map to \(J\). Zorn's lemma supplies a maximal extension \(C\to J\). If \(C\ne B\), (T.4) detects the nonzero quotient map: there is \(h:P\to B\) with image not contained in \(C\). Put \(K=h^{-1}C\), and extend the induced \(K\to J\) to \(v:P\to J\). The map \(C\oplus P\to J\) which adds the old map and \(v\) kills every pair \((-h(k),k)\). Those pairs are exactly the kernel of \((c,p)\mapsto c+h(p)\). It descends to \(C+\operatorname{im}h\), contradicting maximality. Thus the extension exists on \(B\), which says that \(J\) is injective.

For a sheaf \(M\), take all pairs \((K,v)\) with \(K\subset P\) and \(v:K\to M\), and form

\[
T(M)=\left(M\oplus\bigoplus_{(K,v)}P\right)
 \big/\left\langle(v(k),-k)\right\rangle.
\tag{T.5}
\]

The quotient is a sheaf quotient. The map \(M\to T(M)\) is monic: locally, a relation whose \(P\)-coordinates vanish has every \(k\)-coordinate zero, because each \(K\to P\) is monic; its \(M\)-coordinate is therefore zero too. For every specified pair the corresponding copy of \(P\) supplies the desired extension into \(T(M)\).

Starting with \(M_0=M\), use (T.5) at successor stages and filtered union at limit stages. All maps remain monic. We recall the cardinal bound used to stop this construction. For every infinite cardinal \(\kappa\), \(|\kappa\times\kappa|=\kappa\). Induct over infinite cardinals and order pairs first by their maximum, then lexicographically within that maximum. At \(\kappa=\aleph_0\) each initial segment is finite. At a later cardinal, an initial segment lies inside \((\gamma+1)^2\) for some \(\gamma<\kappa\), so by the induction hypothesis it has cardinality less than \(\kappa\). The ordering therefore has order type at most \(\kappa\): a larger order type would have an initial segment of order type \(\kappa\). The diagonal gives the reverse inequality. This proves the bound.

Now take an infinite \(\kappa\) at least the size of the set of subobjects of \(P\), and let \(\beta\) be the least ordinal of cardinality greater than \(\kappa\). It is a limit ordinal, since adding one point to an infinite well-ordered set does not increase its cardinality, as also follows from the preceding bound. Its cofinality is greater than \(\kappa\): otherwise it would be the union of at most \(\kappa\) smaller ordinals, each of cardinality at most \(\kappa\), hence itself of cardinality at most \(\kappa\), a contradiction.

Given \(v:K\to M_\beta\), form the increasing subobjects \(K_\alpha=v^{-1}M_\alpha\). Their union is \(K\), by the pullback assertion in T.1. There are at most \(\kappa\) distinct such subobjects. Choose an index for each; the cofinality bound puts all these indices below one \(\alpha<\beta\). Thus \(K_\alpha=K\), so \(v\) factors through \(M_\alpha\). At the next stage it extends to \(P\), with values in \(M_\beta\). The extension test proves that \(M_\beta\) is injective. We have proved enough injectives without assuming that the site has enough points. The programme construction is [Cohomology on sites, Proposition 1.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-on-sites#1-why-injective-resolutions-exist).

### T.3. Maps and homotopies between ordinary resolutions

Embed \(F\) into an injective \(I^0\), embed its cokernel into \(I^1\), and continue. The quotient followed by the next embedding defines the differential. Its kernel is the preceding image, giving an exact augmented complex \(0\to F\to I^\bullet\).

A map \(f:F\to G\) extends to a chain map between any chosen injective resolutions \(I^\bullet,J^\bullet\). Extend first from \(F\subset I^0\) into \(J^0\). Having defined the map through degree \(n\), the composite \(d_J^nf^n\) kills \(\ker d_I^n\): in degree zero this kernel is \(F\), and later it is \(\operatorname{im}d_I^{n-1}\), where the assertion follows from the previous chain-map identity. It therefore defines a map on \(\operatorname{im}d_I^n\subset I^{n+1}\). Injectivity of \(J^{n+1}\) extends it to \(f^{n+1}\). This proves the induction.

If \(f^\bullet,g^\bullet\) extend the same sheaf map, write \(w=f-g\). Construct maps \(h^{n+1}:I^{n+1}\to J^n\) so that

\[
w^n=d_J^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d_I^n,
\qquad h^0=0.
\tag{T.6}
\]

For \(n=0\), \(w^0\) vanishes on \(F\), so it factors through \(\operatorname{im}d_I^0\); injectivity of \(J^0\) extends this factor to \(h^1\). Inductively, set \(r^n=w^n-d_J^{n-1}h^n\). On the preceding image, the chain-map identity and the already proved equation give

\[
r^nd_I^{n-1}
 =d_J^{n-1}w^{n-1}-d_J^{n-1}h^nd_I^{n-1}=0.
\tag{T.7}
\]
