We use that map to prove the cohomological statements needed in O.4, including base change to every geometric fibre after one further shrinking. All cohomology below is ordinary Zariski cohomology, as constructed in T and computed in W.

### AF.1. Finite maps and the projective cohomology calculation

First, finite morphisms are proper. Here is the algebraic closed-image argument in the finite case. For a finite algebra \(R\to D\) and an ideal \(J\subset D\), put \(R'=R/(J\cap R)\) and \(D'=D/J\). The induced map \(R'\to D'\) is injective and finite. At any prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(R'\), its localization is still injective, so \(D'_{\mathfrak p}\ne0\). If its residue algebra were zero, Nakayama would make this finite module zero. Thus the residue algebra is nonzero and has a maximal ideal. Its inverse image is a prime of \(D'\) over \(\mathfrak p\). This proves

\[
\operatorname{image}(V(J)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}R)
=V(J\cap R).
\tag{AF.1}
\]

Tensoring a finite list of module generators proves that every base change remains finite, so the same argument proves universal closedness. The multiplication map \(D\otimes_R D\to D\) is surjective, giving a closed diagonal on affine charts. Module generators also generate the algebra, proving finite type. Hence the morphism is proper. Composition of finite maps is finite, by taking products of module generators. This is the finite-case argument in [Affine, integral and finite morphisms, Sections 4–5](course:AG-MO/affine-integral-and-finite-morphisms#5-closed-images-and-fibres), with the needed lying-over assertion proved above by Nakayama.

Let \(B\) be Noetherian and suppose

\[
q:C\longrightarrow\mathbf P^N_B
\quad\text{is finite}.
\tag{AF.2}
\]

For a coherent sheaf \(F\) on \(C\), the sheaf \(q_*F\) is coherent. On a standard affine chart with coordinate ring \(R\), its inverse image is \(\operatorname{Spec}D\), where \(D\) is finite over \(R\). A finite \(D\)-module is finite over \(R\), by multiplying the two finite generating lists. Restriction to a principal open localizes that module, by W.1, so these descriptions give a coherent sheaf on the projective space. This also proves the pushforward description directly, without a higher-direct-image theorem.

The standard affine cover of \(\mathbf P^N_B\) and its inverse-image cover of \(C\) have identical ordered section complexes for \(q_*F\) and \(F\). All intersections in both covers are affine. W.2 therefore gives

\[
H^i(C,F)=H^i(\mathbf P^N_B,q_*F).
\tag{AF.3}
\]

W.4 makes these modules finite over \(B\), and W.2 makes them zero for \(i>N\). The finite map of O.3, composed with the closed projective embedding of its target, has form (AF.2). Thus (AF.3) proves precisely the coherent finiteness needed for that family.

### AF.2. A bounded flat complex after shrinking an integral base

Let \(B\) now be a domain, with fraction field \(K\). Every finite \(B\)-module \(M\) becomes finite free after inverting one nonzero element. Choose elements of \(M\) whose images form a \(K\)-basis of \(M\otimes_B K\); clearing denominators of a chosen basis supplies such elements. The resulting map \(B^r\to M\) is injective, since its kernel becomes zero over \(K\) and \(B^r\) is torsion-free. Its finite cokernel becomes zero over \(K\). Each member of a finite generating list for that cokernel is killed by a nonzero element of \(B\). Inverting their product kills the cokernel. This includes rank zero. For finitely many modules, multiply their finitely many choices of denominator.

We will also use the following tensor calculation. Suppose \(D^\bullet\) is a bounded complex of flat modules over a ring \(A\), and every \(H^i(D)\) is flat. Write \(Z^i\) for its cycles and \(B^i_D\) for its boundaries. If \(b\) is its last degree, \(Z^b=D^b\) is flat. The two sequences

\[
\begin{aligned}
0\longrightarrow B^i_D\longrightarrow Z^i
\longrightarrow H^i(D)\longrightarrow0,\\
0\longrightarrow Z^{i-1}\longrightarrow D^{i-1}
\longrightarrow B^i_D\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{AF.4}
\]

and U.1 show successively that \(B^b_D,Z^{b-1},B^{b-1}_D,\ldots\) are flat and that all these sequences remain exact under every tensor product. The differential factors through its boundary module. The tensorized sequences identify its kernel and image with \(Z^i\otimes_A M\) and \(B^i_D\otimes_A M\). Consequently

\[
H^i(D^\bullet\otimes_A M)=H^i(D^\bullet)\otimes_A M
\quad\text{for every }A\text{-module }M.
\tag{AF.5}
\]

This argument uses boundedness and flatness of the cohomology as well as flatness of the terms. It is the cycle calculation underlying [Base change and the Grothendieck complex, Lemma 3.1](course:AG-QC/base-change-and-the-grothendieck-complex#3-a-finite-projective-replacement); no assertion that arbitrary cohomology always commutes with tensoring is being made.

Apply it to the inverse-image affine cover in AF.1 with \(F=\mathcal O_C\), for the smooth family over the integral Noetherian ring \(B\) in O.3. AE.1 makes each affine coordinate module flat over \(B\). The ordered complex is bounded, its cohomology modules are finite by (AF.3), and only finitely many degrees occur. Localize \(B\) once so that every one of those modules is free, using the preceding denominator argument. Localization commutes with the complex and its cohomology by W.1.

After this localization, every \(B\)-algebra \(A\) gives the base-changed affine cover with section complex \(D^\bullet\otimes_B A\), by W.1. W.2 and (AF.5) prove

\[
H^i(C,\mathcal O_C)\otimes_B A
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
H^i(C_A,\mathcal O_{C_A})
\qquad\text{for every }B\text{-algebra }A.
\tag{AF.6}
\]

The comparison sends a section or cocycle to its scalar extension, so the degree-zero isomorphism is an isomorphism of algebras. Further localizations preserve it. The affine-cover comparison is also described in [Stacks, curve constants]; here W.1–W.2 supply its cohomology proof and (AF.4) supplies the additional arbitrary-tensor step on this open neighbourhood.

### AF.3. The finite algebra separates exactly the geometric components

Put \(E=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)\). It is finite by AF.1. The generic algebra \(E\otimes_B K\) is a product of finite separable fields, as proved in O.4: its formation commutes with field extension, and smoothness makes its scalar extension to an algebraic closure reduced. The finite-dimensional algebra and Chinese remainder argument is the one in AB.1. O.4 descends the monic separable polynomials, derivative inverses and algebra isomorphisms, so after another localization \(E\) is finite étale over \(B\). This extra localization retains (AF.6).

Let \(T=\operatorname{Spec}E\). Global sections define a canonical morphism \(g:C\to T\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}B\): on each affine open of \(C\), use restriction of functions to define its ring map; those maps agree on overlaps. The graph of \(g\) is a closed immersion into \(C\times_B T\), since it is the pullback of the closed diagonal of the finite morphism \(T\to\operatorname{Spec}B\). The projection of that product to \(T\) is a base change of the proper map \(C\to\operatorname{Spec}B\), proved by AF.1 and AE.2. Thus \(g\) is proper by AE.2. Its graph is also open, by the étale diagonal calculation in O.4. Composing this open immersion with the smooth product projection proves that \(g\) is smooth of relative dimension one.

Take any algebraically closed field \(\Omega\) with a map \(B\to\Omega\). The field calculation in AB.1 and (AF.6) give an isomorphism of algebras

\[
\Gamma(C_\Omega,\mathcal O_{C_\Omega})
=E\otimes_B\Omega\simeq\Omega^r.
\tag{AF.7}
\]

The \(r\) primitive idempotents decompose \(C_\Omega\) into the inverse images of the \(r\) points of \(T_\Omega\). A section of a product decomposition is a tuple of sections, so the algebra of global functions on each such inverse image is the corresponding factor \(\Omega\). It is nonzero, making that inverse image nonempty. A decomposition into two nonempty open-and-closed subsets would glue the constants zero and one to an idempotent other than zero or one. A field has no such idempotent. Every inverse image is therefore connected.

Every geometric point of \(T\) is included in this calculation: compose its map \(E\to\Omega\) with \(B\to E\), and take the factor selected by that point. Its inverse image is exactly the geometric fibre of \(g\). Hence \(g\) has geometrically connected nonempty fibres, as required in O.1. Their smoothness and Y.6 make them geometrically integral by the component argument of AE.3.

### AF.4. Compatibility with the original neighbourhood

All extra changes above invert finitely many nonzero elements of the integral ring \(B\) from O.3. For their product \(b\), O.3 has a power \(q\) with \(b^q\in A\), where \(A\) is the original reduced base ring, and

\[
B_b=B\otimes_A A_{b^q}.
\tag{AF.8}
\]

Thus the changes shrink the original open neighbourhood and retain its finite surjective radicial cover. The finite boundary remains finite by base change. The smoothness and relative dimensions remain unchanged. Splitting by the idempotents of \(E\) now gives every factor in (O.1), with the connectedness, nonemptiness and properness proved in AF.3. This proves the needed constant-field factorization for the family already constructed in O.3; the general Stein-factorization and formal-functions theorems are not needed for this step.

## Appendix AG. Finite normalization and smoothness of normal curves

The completion in O.1 requires normalization over a perfect field that may have positive characteristic. This appendix supplies the field-independent algebra and the finite separable residue-field step. The normal-local-ring argument already proved in L.1 applies in every characteristic.

### AG.1. Polynomial normalization and a separable trace bound

Let \(A\) be a finite-type domain over a field \(k\), and let \(L\) be a finite extension of its fraction field. Y.5 extends K.1's weighted-generator argument to every field. It gives a finite integral inclusion

\[
P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\subset A,
\qquad K=\operatorname{Frac}P\subset L.
\tag{AG.1}
\]

The extension \(L/K\) is finite: tensor the finite \(P\)-module \(A\) with \(K\); the resulting finite-dimensional domain over \(K\) is a field, because multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective. It is the fraction field of \(A\). If \(d=0\), this already makes \(L\) finite over \(k\), and its integral closure over \(A\) is a subspace of this finite-dimensional space. Thus this case is finite. Suppose \(d>0\).

The content and reduced-fraction proofs in K.1 use only that coefficients form a field, so \(P\) is a unique-factorization domain and is integrally closed over arbitrary \(k\). Its Noetherianity is proved in W.4. Suppose first that \(L/K\) is separable. The field \(K\) is infinite. The primitive-element argument in K.1 therefore applies: choose a linear combination of generators that takes distinct values under all embeddings in a splitting field. A choice exists by avoiding the finitely many nonzero linear equations; substituting powers of one parameter reduces this to avoiding finitely many roots in the infinite field \(K\). Its distinct conjugate values show that it generates \(L\).

Scale this primitive element by a nonzero member of \(P\) so that it is integral over \(P\). Explicitly, for a monic equation with coefficients \(a_i\in K\), choose \(s\ne0\) clearing their denominators; the equation for \(s\theta\) has coefficients \(s^i a_i\in P\). Denote the scaled element by \(z\). Its powers \(e_i=z^i\), \(0\leq i<n=[L:K]\), form a basis. L.3's multiplication-matrix and Vandermonde calculation now works without any characteristic-zero assumption: separability makes the conjugate values distinct. For the trace matrix and its determinant it gives

\[
G_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}_{L/K}(e_i e_j)\in P,
\qquad 0\ne\Delta=\det G\in P.
\tag{AG.2}
\]

Here integrality of conjugates, closure under sums and products, and normality of \(P\) put the traces in \(P\), exactly as in L.3. If \(c\) is integral over \(P\), every \(\operatorname{Tr}(ce_j)\) is in \(P\). The adjugate of \(G\) bounds its coordinates in the power basis. Thus the integral closure \(D\) of \(P\) in \(L\) satisfies

\[
D\subseteq\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}\Delta^{-1}P e_i.
\tag{AG.3}
\]

It is a submodule of a finite module over the Noetherian ring \(P\), hence finite. The trace comparison is [Normalization, Theorem 4.1](course:AG-MO/normalization#4-a-trace-lattice-proves-separable-finiteness); L.3 supplies the actual nondegeneracy calculation used here.

### AG.2. Coefficient roots handle inseparability

In characteristic zero every finite extension is separable, because an irreducible polynomial is relatively prime to its nonzero derivative. Now suppose \(\operatorname{char}k=p>0\). Choose finitely many generators \(\alpha_j\) of \(L/K\). Their irreducible minimal polynomials have the form

\[
f_j(T)=h_j(T^{q_j}),\qquad q_j=p^{e_j},
\tag{AG.4}
\]

where \(h_j\) is separable. Indeed, a zero derivative means every exponent is divisible by \(p\); remove such powers until the derivative is nonzero. The remaining polynomial is still irreducible, and is therefore relatively prime to its derivative.

Choose a common \(q=p^e\) divisible by all \(q_j\). Only finitely many elements of \(k\) occur in the numerators and denominators of the coefficients of the \(h_j\). In an algebraic closure, adjoin their \(q\)-th roots to obtain a finite extension \(k'/k\), and put

\[
P'=k'[t_1^{1/q},\ldots,t_d^{1/q}],
\qquad K'=\operatorname{Frac}P',\qquad L'=LK'.
\tag{AG.5}
\]

The root variables are algebraically independent: raising a proposed relation to the \(q\)-th power would give a relation among the original parameters. Thus \(P'\) is again a polynomial ring. A basis of \(k'/k\), multiplied by the monomials in the root variables with exponents less than \(q\), generates it over \(P\), so it is finite over \(P\).

Every coefficient of \(h_j\) has a \(q_j\)-th root in \(K'\): take the indicated roots term by term in a numerator and denominator. Replace the coefficients of \(h_j\) by these roots, obtaining a polynomial \(g_j\). In characteristic \(p\) the power of a sum is the sum of the powers, and hence
\(g_j(T)^{q_j}=h_j(T^{q_j})=f_j(T)\).
The roots of \(g_j\) are the unique \(q_j\)-th roots of the distinct roots of \(h_j\), so they are distinct. Since \(\alpha_j\) is a root of \(g_j\), it is separable over \(K'\). Adjoining these generators successively shows that \(L'/K'\) is finite separable: at each step the minimal polynomial divides a separable polynomial.

AG.1 makes the integral closure \(D'\) of \(P'\) in \(L'\) finite over \(P'\), hence over \(P\). The closure \(D\) of \(P\) in \(L\) embeds in \(D'\), since its monic equations remain equations over \(P'\). It is a \(P\)-submodule and therefore finite. Finally, integral closure over \(A\) and over \(P\) agree: one implication uses \(P\subset A\), the other uses the integrality of \(A/P\) and transitivity from K.1. Its finite \(P\)-generators also generate it over \(A\). This proves finiteness in every characteristic and over imperfect fields. The coefficient-root construction is the proof in [Normalization, Theorem 5.1](course:AG-MO/normalization#5-finiteness-over-fields-including-inseparability).

### AG.3. Componentwise gluing and the normal local rings

Let \(A\) be reduced and of finite type over \(k\), with minimal primes \(\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_r\). There are finitely many by K.1. The total-fraction calculation in L.3 works over any field; explicitly choose
\(a_i\in\bigcap_{j\ne i}\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i\)
by multiplying one element from each \(\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i\). For one prime use \(a_1=1\). Reducedness makes \(A\to\prod_i A/\mathfrak p_i\) injective. An element outside every minimal prime is consequently a nonzerodivisor. The sum \(s=\sum_i a_i\) is such an element, and \(a_i/s\) are the component idempotents. If \(b\notin\mathfrak p_i\), the element \(a_i b+\sum_{j\ne i}a_j\) is again a nonzerodivisor and supplies the inverse of \(b\) in the selected component. Conversely an element of \(\mathfrak p_i\) annihilates the nonzero \(a_i\). These statements prove

\[
Q(A)=\prod_i\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p_i),
\qquad
\overline A=\prod_i\overline{A/\mathfrak p_i}.
\tag{AG.6}
\]

For the second equality, the component idempotents are integral, and adjoining them gives the product of the component rings. Integral closure commutes with this finite integral extension by transitivity; integrality over a product is tested componentwise. AG.1–AG.2 make each factor finite, hence make \(\overline A\) finite over \(A\). Each factor is integrally closed: an element integral over that factor is integral over the original component ring and already belongs to the closure.

Integral closure commutes with localization. For clarity, if an element satisfies a monic equation after localization, choose one denominator \(v\) clearing its coefficients and its representation as a localized element. Multiplication by \(v\) turns it into an element \(c\) of the original ambient algebra with a monic equation \(P(c)=0\) in the localization. Some further allowed denominator \(h\) kills \(P(c)\) before localization. Multiplying the degree-\(n\) equation by \(h^n\) gives a monic equation for \(hc\) in the original algebra. This proves the reverse inclusion; the forward inclusion follows by localizing a monic equation. This is the full denominator argument of [Integral extensions, Theorem 2.1](course:AG-CA/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down#2-integral-closure-survives-localization).

The affine normalizations therefore agree on principal opens and glue, with compatible identifications on overlaps, to a finite normalization of every reduced finite-type \(k\)-scheme. Their local rings are normal domains by (AG.6) and localization. The finite lying-over proof in AF.1 makes the normalization surjective, and its generic fields are unchanged by (AG.6). On a normal open it is an isomorphism, since integral closure there adds no functions.

For a curve, its normal local rings at closed points have dimension one. On each component, Noether normalization is finite over \(k[t]\). The closed point has finite residue field over \(k\), by Y.5, so its contraction contains a nonzero polynomial in \(t\). It is not the generic point. Incomparability for integral extensions, proved in K.1, bounds every prime chain by a chain in \(k[t]\); the chain from the zero prime to this maximal prime has length one. Localization gives dimension one. L.1 now applies exactly as written: the fraction acting on the maximal ideal forces a single generator, and Krull separation gives the valuation by its powers. Thus these rings are DVRs. This uses neither complex analysis nor a characteristic-zero assumption.

### AG.4. A separable residue field gives a smooth curve chart

Let \(S\) be a finite-type \(k\)-algebra and \(x\) a closed point whose local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\) is regular of dimension one. Suppose its finite residue field \(\kappa/k\) is separable. The square-zero root-lifting proof in AB.1 makes \(\kappa\) formally étale over \(k\). It therefore supplies a \(k\)-algebra section of \(R/\mathfrak m^2\to\kappa\).

A derivation from \(R\) to a \(\kappa\)-vector space kills \(\mathfrak m^2\). In the splitting \(R/\mathfrak m^2=\kappa\oplus\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\), it vanishes on \(\kappa\): differentiating a separable minimal polynomial, whose derivative is invertible, kills the derivative of each algebraic generator. On the square-zero summand it is exactly a \(\kappa\)-linear map. The universal property of differentials consequently gives

\[
\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa\simeq\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,
\qquad\dim_\kappa(\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa)=1.
\tag{AG.7}
\]

Present \(S=k[X_1,\ldots,X_N]/I\), and let \(\mathfrak Q\) be the polynomial prime over \(x\). The polynomial differential presentation and (AG.7) say that the gradients of the equations span a space of dimension \(N-1\). Choose \(N-1\) equations with an invertible minor at \(x\). Their classes in the maximal ideal of \(k[X]_{\mathfrak Q}\), modulo its square, are independent: a relation modulo the square would differentiate to a relation among those gradients. Y.5 makes this ambient local ring regular of dimension \(N\), since its residue field is finite over \(k\). Y.4 makes the quotient by the chosen equations a regular local domain of dimension one.

That quotient surjects onto \(R\). A nonzero kernel would contain a nonzero nonunit; the dimension-drop formula (Y.8) would make its quotient zero-dimensional, contradicting \(\dim R=1\). Thus the kernel is zero. The remaining equation ideal is finitely generated. Clear denominators annihilating its generators in this local quotient, and invert the selected minor. On the resulting neighbourhood the chosen equations generate the entire ideal and retain that invertible minor. Their square-zero lifting calculation solves for corrections in the selected variables, exactly as in Y.6, giving a standard smooth chart of relative dimension one. This proves the needed case of [Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion, Theorem 3.2](course:AG-CA/smooth-algebras-over-a-field-and-the-jacobian-criterion#3-cotangent-spaces-and-separable-residue-fields).

Over a perfect field every finite residue extension is separable. In positive characteristic, an irreducible polynomial with zero derivative would have all exponents divisible by \(p\), and taking \(p\)-th roots of its coefficients would make it a proper \(p\)-th power, a contradiction. In characteristic zero its derivative is nonzero. Y.5 supplies finiteness of the residue extension. Hence every closed point of a normal finite-type curve over a perfect field has the smooth neighbourhood just proved.

Those neighbourhoods cover the curve. Indeed, a nonempty closed complement has a nonempty affine open and a maximal ideal, giving a point with finite residue field over the ground field. Such a point is closed in the whole scheme: in an affine neighbourhood of any specialization, its coordinate-ring image in that finite field is itself a field, so the corresponding prime is maximal and has no proper specialization. This contradicts the choice of complement. The normalization over \(K^{\mathrm{perf}}\) in O.1 is therefore smooth. Its unchanged normal open contains the original smooth curve by Y.6 and L.1, completing the normalization and smoothness steps used there.

### AG.5. Finite normalization of integer models

Let \(A\) be a domain of finite type over \(\mathbf Z\), let \(K=\operatorname{Frac}A\), and let \(L/K\) be finite. Its integral closure \(C\subset L\) is a finite \(A\)-module. We prove this locally on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), using the separated quasi-finite factorization proved in AW.1–AW.5. That factorization uses integral elements but does not assume finite normalization.

First recall the trace argument in a form which does not require a field as the coefficient ring. If \(P\) is a normal Noetherian domain with infinite fraction field \(E\), and \(L/E\) is finite separable, choose an integral primitive element by the scaling argument of AG.1. Its power basis and the distinct-conjugate calculation of L.3 give the nonzero trace determinant \(\Delta\). Normality of \(P\) puts every trace of a product of integral elements in \(P\). The adjugate calculation (AG.3) therefore places the whole integral closure in a free fractional \(P\)-module of finite rank. A submodule of that module is finite, by Noetherianity. In particular this applies to
\[
P=\mathbf Z[t_1,\ldots,t_d],\qquad
E=\mathbf Q(t_1,\ldots,t_d).
\tag{AG.8}
\]
Here \(P\) is Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem, starting with the principal ideals of \(\mathbf Z\). For normality, the content argument in K.1 applies to a polynomial over any unique-factorization domain: reduction modulo a prime factor shows that a product of primitive polynomials is primitive; factoring in the fraction-field polynomial ring and clearing contents proves unique factorization in the original polynomial ring. Induction starts with prime factorization of integers. The reduced-fraction argument then proves integral closedness: a monic equation for a fraction in lowest terms forces its denominator to divide a power of its relatively prime numerator. The same proof applies to a localization of \(P\). Every finite extension of \(E\) is separable, because characteristic zero makes the derivative of an irreducible polynomial relatively prime to that polynomial.

If \(A\) has positive characteristic, its characteristic is a prime \(p\), and AG.1–AG.2 already prove the assertion over \(\mathbf F_p\). Suppose therefore that \(\mathbf Z\hookrightarrow A\). At a prime of \(A\) contracting to zero, first apply AG.1–AG.2 to \(A\otimes\mathbf Q\). The finitely many parameters and monic equations in its polynomial normalization descend after inverting one nonzero integer \(m\). They make \(A[1/m]\) finite over \(\mathbf Z[1/m][t_1,\ldots,t_d]\). Algebraic independence over \(\mathbf Q\) makes this inclusion injective. The trace argument just given proves finite normalization there, since \(L\) is finite over \(\mathbf Q(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). Thus the generic-fibre points have the required open neighborhoods.

Now fix a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset A\) containing a rational prime \(p\). The nonzero algebra \(A/pA\) is of finite type over \(\mathbf F_p\); it may be reducible or nonreduced. The weighted-variable proof of Noether normalization still applies in precisely this situation. To see this directly, present a nonzero finite-type field algebra on \(N\) generators. If their relation ideal is zero, they are independent. Otherwise choose a nonzero relation. The separated integer weights of K.1 make its highest power in the last variable unique, with nonzero scalar coefficient. The resulting monic equation makes the algebra finite over the subalgebra on \(N-1\) new generators. This subalgebra is nonzero; repeat the induction there and compose the finite inclusions. No step assumes a domain. This is also [Krull dimension and Noether normalization, Corollary 3.2](course:AG-CA/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization#3-normalization-that-respects-ideals).

Choose its polynomial parameters and lift them to \(t_i\in A\). They give
\[
\mathbf F_p[\bar t_1,\ldots,\bar t_d]\hookrightarrow A/pA
\quad\hbox{finite},\qquad
P=\mathbf Z[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\hookrightarrow A.
\tag{AG.9}
\]
For the second injectivity assertion, a nonzero integer-coefficient relation can be divided by the largest common power of \(p\) in its coefficients. Its evaluation remains zero because \(A\) is a characteristic-zero domain. Reduction modulo \(p\) would then be a nonzero polynomial relation among the independent \(\bar t_i\), a contradiction.

The morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}P\) is of finite type. Its fibre at the image of \(\mathfrak q\) is finite, because its restriction over \(p\) is the finite map in (AG.9). Thus it is quasi-finite at \(\mathfrak q\). Its quasi-finite locus is open by the algebraic neighborhood in AW.1: the identity \(B_c=D_c\) there, with \(D\) a finite intermediate algebra, identifies a neighborhood with a principal open of a finite scheme. Such an open has finite discrete fibres. The finite intermediate algebra exists by choosing the finitely many integral numerators used to express a finite list of generators of \(B_c\). This is the in-course proof of [Zariski's Main Theorem, Theorem 3.1](course:AG-MO/zariskis-main-theorem#3-from-local-equalities-to-finite-affine-completions).

Choose a nonempty principal open \(U\subset\operatorname{Spec}A\) containing \(\mathfrak q\) in this locus. It is quasi-finite and separated over \(\operatorname{Spec}P\). AW.5 gives an open immersion into a finite \(P\)-scheme. Replace that finite scheme by the reduced closure of \(U\). This replacement is integral, is still finite over \(P\), and contains \(U\) as an open: restricting the closure ideal to the reduced open \(U\) gives zero. Write it as \(\operatorname{Spec}D\). The inclusion in (AG.9) makes \(U\) dominant over \(\operatorname{Spec}P\), and its dense open immersion gives
\[
P\hookrightarrow D\subset K,\qquad
D\text{ finite over }P,\qquad \operatorname{Frac}D=K.
\tag{AG.10}
\]
Indeed a function on the integral affine closure restricts injectively to the rational functions of its nonempty open. Since \(D\) is finite, tensoring with \(E=\operatorname{Frac}P\) gives a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field; it is \(K\). Therefore \(L/E\) is finite and separable. The trace argument for (AG.8) makes the integral closure of \(P\) in \(L\) finite. It is also the closure of \(D\), by transitivity of integrality. Its finite \(P\)-generators generate over \(D\) as well.

Restrict this finite normalization to \(U\). Integral closure commutes with localization by AG.3, so its restriction is precisely the normalization of \(U\) in \(L\). We have proved finiteness on a neighborhood of every point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). Quasi-compactness gives a finite principal cover \(D(f_i)\) with \(C_{f_i}\) finite over \(A_{f_i}\). Lift its finitely many generators, clearing their powers of \(f_i\), to elements of \(C\), and let \(M\) be their finite \(A\)-span. Then \((C/M)_{f_i}=0\) for every \(i\). For an individual element of \(C/M\), some power of each \(f_i\) kills it. These powers generate the unit ideal: otherwise a prime containing that ideal would miss the cover. Hence the element is zero. Thus \(M=C\), proving the theorem.

For a reduced finite-type integer algebra, apply this theorem to each of its finitely many component domains. The product description (AG.6) makes its normalization finite. These finite algebras glue by the localization proof of AG.3. More generally an integral finite-type integer scheme has finite normalization in every finite extension of its function field; the same affine argument and localization give the gluing. A nonreduced scheme is first replaced by its finite reduced closed subscheme. All these conclusions also apply over \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\), whose finite-type algebras are still finite type over \(\mathbf Z\).

The free primary comparisons are [Noether normalization, Tag 00OY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00OY), [the separable trace bound, Tag 032L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032L), and [the open quasi-finite locus, Tag 01TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01TI). The proof above obtains the integer case from local polynomial charts and AW.5; it does not use general Nagata stability as an unproved premise.

## Appendix AH. The boundary and the finite diagram of a curve completion

The field extension and the localizations in Appendix O have specific algebraic forms. We use them to check that the completed curve keeps its dense open, that its boundary is finite, and that its chosen projective model has the correct generic fibre.

### AH.1. Purely inseparable extension preserves the underlying space

Let \(F/K\) be an algebraic purely inseparable extension in characteristic \(p>0\), without a finiteness assumption. For a \(K\)-algebra \(A\), the map \(A\to A\otimes_KF\) is injective: extend \(1\) to a \(K\)-basis of \(F\), or tensor the injection \(K\to F\) with the \(K\)-vector space \(A\). Every element \(b=\sum_{i=1}^r a_i\otimes f_i\) has a power \(q=p^e\) for which all \(f_i^q\) belong to \(K\). Consequently

\[
b^q=\sum_{i=1}^r a_i^q\otimes f_i^q\in A.
\tag{AH.1}
\]

The extension is integral, so lying over, proved in K.1, supplies a prime over every prime \(\mathfrak p\subset A\). That prime is unique: for a prime \(\mathfrak q\) over \(\mathfrak p\), equation (AH.1) gives \(b\in\mathfrak q\) if and only if \(b^q\in\mathfrak p\). The resulting bijection of spectra is a homeomorphism. Indeed, the basic open \(D(b)\) corresponds exactly to \(D(b^q)\), so its image is open; the spectrum map is already continuous. These calculations commute with restriction to affine opens and prove

\[
|T_F|\simeq |T|
\quad\text{for every }K\text{-scheme }T.
\tag{AH.2}
\]

Passing to the reduction also leaves the underlying space unchanged, since every prime contains the nilradical. Thus \((Z_F)_{\mathrm{red}}\) in O.1 has exactly the same component and specialization structure as \(Z\), and \(X_F\) remains dense in every component. The characteristic-zero case of O.1 uses the identity extension and needs no change of space.

### AH.2. A zero-dimensional boundary is a finite scheme over the field

First consider any zero-dimensional finite-type scheme \(D\) over a field \(k\). It is Noetherian by the polynomial-ring argument of W.4. Its finitely many irreducible components are single closed points: all primes are maximal, so each component contains only its generic point. Thus its space is a finite discrete set. Each singleton has an affine neighbourhood equal to that singleton. To see this inside an affine chart, choose, for each of the other maximal ideals, an element in that ideal but outside the selected maximal ideal, and multiply these elements. Its principal open contains just the selected point.

Write the ring of such a neighbourhood as \(R\). Its unique prime \(\mathfrak m\) is its nilradical and is nilpotent. In fact Noetherianity gives finitely many generators \(u_j\), each killed by a power; every monomial of sufficiently large total degree then vanishes. Y.5 proves that \(R/\mathfrak m\) is a finite field extension of \(k\). Each quotient \(\mathfrak m^i/\mathfrak m^{i+1}\) is a finite module over this field, since its ideal is finitely generated and \(\mathfrak m\) acts by zero. The finite filtration by these powers therefore makes \(R\) a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector space. The finitely many singleton affines are disjoint, so their union is the spectrum of the product of these finite algebras. This proves that \(D\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is finite, including when \(D\) is nonreduced.

Apply this to the complement of \(X\) in its reduced projective closure \(Z\) over \(K\). The components of \(Z\) are curves. They have the function fields of the components of \(X\), of transcendence degree one; Y.5 gives finite Noether normalization of each affine component chart over \(K[t]\), and the integral-extension dimension argument of K.1 bounds its prime chains by dimension one. A closed subset which misses the generic point of every component consequently has dimension zero. The reduced boundary \(E=Z\setminus X\) is therefore finite over \(K\).

After the extension \(F/K\), the scheme \(E_F\) is still finite, by tensoring its finite-dimensional algebra. Its underlying space is the complement of \(X_F\) in \(Z_F\). For the finite normalization \(\nu:C_F\to Z_F\), the inverse image \(\nu^{-1}(E_F)\) is finite over \(F\): finite morphisms remain finite under base change and composition, by AF.1. It has precisely the boundary as its support. Its reduction is a closed subscheme and is finite as well, by taking a quotient of the finite algebra. This proves the finite-boundary assertion before descent.

Now descend the specified open immersion to \(X_{K'}\subset C_{K'}\), as in O.1. Since \(F/K'\) is still purely inseparable, (AH.2) identifies its complement with the finite closed boundary just found. The reduced complement in \(C_{K'}\) is a zero-dimensional finite-type scheme, so the first paragraph proves it finite over \(K'\). This argument proves the boundary assertion for the descended curve itself; it does not infer it merely from the word “dense”.

### AH.3. The chosen projective closure has the prescribed generic fibre

Let an affine scheme \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I)\) be embedded in the standard affine chart of \(\mathbf P_A^n\). Write \(X_0\) for the extra homogeneous coordinate. Choose generators of \(I\), homogenize them to form a homogeneous ideal \(J\), and set

\[
H=J:X_0^\infty=\bigcup_{m\geq0}(J:X_0^m).
\tag{AH.3}
\]

Then \(\operatorname{Proj}(A[X_0,\ldots,X_n]/H)\) is the scheme-theoretic closure of \(X\). Indeed a homogeneous polynomial restricts to zero on \(X\) exactly when its dehomogenization belongs to \(I\). Homogenizing an expression in the chosen generators, and multiplying by a sufficiently large power of \(X_0\) to equalize degrees, puts that polynomial in the saturation. Conversely such membership becomes an expression in \(I\) on setting \(X_0=1\). Hence \(H\) is exactly the homogeneous ideal of equations vanishing on \(X\), which proves the closure assertion on the projective affine charts.

For any multiplicative set \(S\subset A\), localization commutes with each colon ideal in (AH.3). If \(X_0^m g/s\) belongs to \(S^{-1}J\), some \(t\in S\) makes \(tX_0^m g\) belong to \(J\); thus \(tg\in J:X_0^m\). The converse follows by localizing an equation. Localization also commutes with the displayed increasing union. Homogenizing the generators to their fixed chosen degrees commutes with localization of their coefficients, even if some leading coefficients become zero. Therefore the whole closure construction commutes with \(A\to S^{-1}A\). In particular, the generic fibre of the projective closure over \(B\) in O.3 is the closure of its fixed generic embedding. That generic affine scheme is smooth and reduced, so the closure ideal, as the ideal of functions vanishing on that open, is radical; this is the reduced closure used in O.1.

There is also an elementary test for an empty generic fibre. For an integral base \(A\) and an affine family \(\operatorname{Spec}R\), the equality \(R\otimes_A\operatorname{Frac}A=0\) says that \(1\) becomes zero after localization. Some nonzero \(a\in A\) therefore kills \(1\), and \(R_a=0\). This gives the empty family on an actual open neighbourhood of the generic point.

### AH.4. Apply the finite-diagram proofs with their hypotheses

The stages used in O.1 are fields \(K'\) finite and purely inseparable over \(K\). Those in O.3 are localizations \(B_b\) of a finite algebra over an integral finite-type base. All these rings are Noetherian. Their affine spectra have affine transition maps. The schemes in the completion diagram are of finite type over these rings; their finite affine covers and finite generation of the defining ideals make them of finite presentation. All their opens are quasi-compact. Thus the following exact proofs in [Limits of schemes and Noetherian approximation](course:AG-MO/limits-and-noetherian-approximation#2-opens-sections-and-affine-charts-at-finite-stages) apply.

Lemma 2.1 descends the chosen opens, their equality and their finite covering property. Its proof tests failure of a covering by the complement and uses the finite-affine-cover nonemptiness proof of Theorem 1.1. Lemma 2.2 descends finitely many sections and equations by the sheaf equalizer on finite affine covers and finite covers of their intersections. This uses the affine section and localization calculation of W.1. Filtered colimits preserve that finite equalizer because finitely many representatives and equations can be put at one stage. Lemma 2.3 then proves eventual affineness by descending principal opens and a unit-ideal equation; it does not assume that an arbitrarily chosen model of an affine scheme is affine.

Lemma 3.1 writes an algebra map as the images of finitely many generators satisfying finitely many relations. Theorem 3.2 glues these maps and proves eventual equality. Theorem 4.1 uses the same equality assertion for inverse maps and triple-overlap identities, giving the objects and commuting finite diagrams needed here. Over our Noetherian stages, every overlap is a quasi-compact open in a finite-type scheme, so these finite-cover arguments apply to the overlaps as well.

Finally Theorem 4.2 first makes a morphism affine and then proves finiteness with a finite multiplication table. On a chart \(A_i\to R_i\), choose algebra generators \(t_\ell\). They exist in the present setting because the source algebra is finite type over the common Noetherian affine base, and the same generators generate over the target algebra. Lift module generators from the limit \(b_j\), an expression for \(1\), and expressions for every \(t_\ell b_j\). At a common stage their span contains \(1\) and is stable under each \(t_\ell\); hence it contains every polynomial in the algebra generators and equals \(R_i\). This is the finiteness assertion used for both the normalization map and the boundary in O.3. The closed boundary is itself of finite presentation by Noetherianity, and AH.2 verifies its finite generic fibre. Smoothness and relative dimension descend by the explicit presentations and inverse Jacobian minors in O.2. Thus all the descent steps in O.1–O.3 use proved assertions with the required finiteness hypotheses.

## Appendix AI. Point orientations and the derived trace comparison

The curve trace is normalized by degree: the Kummer class of a degree-one line bundle has trace \(+1\). We first identify the supported class with that normalization, then give the finite refinement argument used for the affine line in Proposition 3.3.

### AI.1. Constant coefficients at a strict smooth trait

Let \(C\) be a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), let \(s\) be a closed point, and let \(R=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{C,s}\). Write \(L=\operatorname{Frac}R\), \(i:s\to\operatorname{Spec}R\), and \(j:\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}R\). Fix \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\), with \(n\) invertible in \(k\).

The ring \(R\) is a discrete valuation ring with the same uniformizer \(t\) as \(\mathcal O_{C,s}\). Here is the direct limit check. In the pointed affine étale neighbourhoods one can restrict to the normal component containing the point, by Y.6 and AG.3. Their local rings are DVRs. The étale local differential calculation makes the image of \(t\) a parameter: modulo \(t\) the chosen local factor is the separable residue field, so the maximal ideal is generated by \(t\). Transition maps are injective, because they are flat local maps between domains. Every nonzero element at every stage is consequently \(t^a u\), for a unit \(u\); a unit remains a unit in the local limit. The same description holds in \(R\). A nonzero ideal has a least occurring exponent \(a\) and equals \((t^a)\), proving the DVR assertion for the limit itself.

Each stage fraction field is algebraic over \(k(C)\). Hence \(L/k\) has transcendence degree one. The full field statement (R.9), which allows non-finitely-generated fields, and the field-site comparison AB.2 give

\[
H^q(L,\Lambda)=H^q(L,\mu_n)=0\qquad(q>1).
\tag{AI.1}
\]

Kummer gives \(H^1(L,\mu_n)=L^\times/L^{\times n}\). The Picard group of a field vanishes because every one-dimensional vector space has a basis, so no additional term occurs. Every unit of \(R\) has an \(n\)-th root: the standard étale algebra defined by \(z^n-u\), whose derivative is a unit at a residue root, has a section over the strictly henselian ring. Thus valuation induces

\[
L^\times/L^{\times n}\simeq\mathbf Z/n,
\qquad [t]\longmapsto1.
\tag{AI.2}
\]

Sections of a sheaf on a strictly henselian local scheme equal its closed stalk. At the strict smooth-curve trait used here, AK.4 proves the section assertion by finite free coordinates, including the rank-one algebra over the trait itself. A stalk section and an equality are represented on a pointed étale neighbourhood, which has a section back over the strict local scheme; pulling back proves surjectivity and injectivity of this identification. The stalk functor is exact, so these schemes have no higher sheaf cohomology. The localization triangle therefore identifies the supported cohomology with the difference between the strict trait and its generic point. Its degree-zero restriction map for \(\mu_n\) is an isomorphism: all roots of unity lie in \(R\), and they are the same roots in \(L\). Equations (AI.1)–(AI.2) show that supported cohomology is zero except in degree two, where the boundary
\(\lambda:H^1(L,\mu_n)\to H^2_s(\operatorname{Spec}R,\mu_n)\)
is an isomorphism. This proves the constant-coefficient local purity calculation, before choosing its sign.

### AI.2. The positive point class is the negative boundary

Use the degree-one convention of AD.3: a cocycle \(g_{ab}\) glues frames by \(e_b=e_a g_{ab}\). For a divisor \(D\) with local rational equations \(f_a\), the connecting cocycle of its valuation sequence is \(f_b/f_a\). These are the transition ratios of the frames \(f_a\) of \(\mathcal O(-D)\). Hence the divisor connecting homomorphism sends \(D\) to \(\mathcal O(-D)\). This agrees with the explicit calculation in [The multiplicative group on a curve, Section 5](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-multiplicative-group-on-a-curve#5-divisors-line-bundles-and-the-connecting-sign).

We keep the two connecting signs explicit. On a two-open cover \(C=U\cup V\), let the Mayer–Vietoris quotient be \(q(a,b)=b|_{U\cap V}-a|_{U\cap V}\), and write \(m\) for its connecting map. If \(\delta\) is a coefficient connecting map, lifting a cocycle through the two exact sequences gives

\[
\delta m=-m\delta.
\tag{AI.3}
\]

The full lift-and-differentiate calculation is [Poincaré duality for curves, Lemma 4.3](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-curves#4-inertia-and-the-valuation-calculation): for compatible lifts it produces \(qv=a+du\); replacing \(v\) by \(v-dw\), with \(qw=u\), gives a lift of \(a\) whose differential is the negative of the other connecting representative. T.4 supplies the compatible resolutions and the rule for their connecting maps. This is a sign in the actual maps, including over \(\mathbf Z/n\) with odd \(n\).

Take \(V=C\setminus\{s\}\) and choose \(t\) on \(U\) with divisor \([s]\). If \(e\) forgets supports, then \(e\lambda=-m\): a lift \(\widetilde a\) on \(U\) of a cocycle \(a\) on \(U\cap V\) has supported differential, whereas its lift under \(q\) is \((-\widetilde a,0)\). The divisor boundary, using local lifts \(t\) on \(U\) and \(1\) on \(V\), is \(m_{\mathbf G_m}(t)=[\mathcal O(-s)]\). Combining these two signs with (AI.3) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
e\lambda\kappa(t)
 &=-m_{\mu_n}\kappa(t)
  =\kappa_C m_{\mathbf G_m}(t)\\
 &=c_1^{(n)}\mathcal O_C(-s),\\
e\epsilon_s&=c_1^{(n)}\mathcal O_C(s),
\qquad \epsilon_s=-\lambda\kappa(t).
\end{aligned}
\tag{AI.4}
\]

By the degree trace, \(\epsilon_s\) has trace \(+1\). A change of uniformizer multiplies \(t\) by a unit whose Kummer class vanishes on the strict trait, so \(\epsilon_s\) is independent of that choice. Étale pullback preserves these connecting maps and the chosen parameter. The trace-normalized purity identifications are therefore

\[
Ri^!\mu_n\simeq\Lambda[-2],
\qquad Ri^!\Lambda\simeq\Lambda(-1)[-2],
\qquad \epsilon_s\longmapsto1.
\tag{AI.5}
\]

For the parameter section \(s_{t_0}:S\to\mathbf A^1_S\), the corresponding relative supported class is \(-\lambda\kappa(t-t_0)\). Its map \(s_{t_0,*}\Lambda\to\mu_n[2]\), followed by the already constructed affine-line trace, is the identity of \(\Lambda_S\): compact-support base change reduces that endomorphism on every geometric stalk to (AI.4). Once the affine-line upper-shriek formula is established, adjunction and \(q s_{t_0}=1\) identify this map with the section orientation in Proposition 3.3. Thus its endpoint argument uses this negative boundary. For \(n=3\), the raw boundary has trace \(2\), and its negative has trace \(1\); a check modulo two alone would miss the distinction.

### AI.3. Uniform refinements kill the derived cone

Fix a pointed base neighbourhood \(V_0\to S\) and its strict localization \(B\) at the selected point. Use pointed affine étale pairs \(V\to V_0\), \(U\to\mathbf A^1_V\), and set \(U_B=U\times_VB\) through the selected map \(B\to V\). Equation (AT.9) and AT.4 prove that these are cofinal among pointed affine étale neighbourhoods of the chosen point of \(\mathbf A^1_B\). The entire product \(U\times_{V_0}B\) is not substituted for this selected pullback. Each \(g_U:U_B\to B\) is a smooth separated affine curve map whose image contains the closed point. Smooth openness from AE.1 and AC.3 makes that image all of the local base, so every geometric fibre is nonempty.

For each relative curve trace choose a triangle with cone

\[
C_U=\operatorname{Cone}
 \bigl(Rg_{U,!}\Lambda(1)\longrightarrow\Lambda[-2]\bigr).
\tag{AI.6}
\]

The source has degrees zero through two. Thus every cone has degrees in the same interval \([-1,2]\). Refinement gives commuting squares between the trace arrows. BI.4 shows that any completion to a triangle map induces the prescribed maps on the cone cohomology, and uses only finite chains of such completions. Compact base change and Proposition 3.2 make all its cohomology sheaves constructible: the finite neighbourhood diagram is defined over a Noetherian finite-type base neighbourhood, and exact pullback gives its cohomology sheaves on \(B\). Kernels, images and cokernels remain constructible by the local constant-module calculation in [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, Section 3](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#3-constructible-pieces-and-basic-permanence).

Here is how the two geometric inputs give pointwise pro-zero. For the selected pairs just specified, (AT.10) identifies the colimit of ordinary fibre cohomology with \(\Lambda\) in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. The curve-duality proof located in AJ.4 identifies the finite compact groups with the exact \(\Lambda\)-duals of the ordinary groups in complementary degree, with trace transitions dual to restriction. AK.5 supplies the required finiteness of the ordinary and compact groups. A finite set of ordinary generators dies at one later neighbourhood in positive degree. In degree zero apply the same argument to the finite quotient by the injective constant-section map \(\Lambda\to H^0(U_{\bar t},\Lambda)\). Its dual is the kernel of the surjective top trace. Exact duality is the coefficient calculation of M.6. Thus the canonically identified cone cohomology systems in (BI.9) are pro-zero at every stalk. AT.1–AT.4 give the complete field-scope local-fibre and cofinality deduction corresponding to [Smooth base change, Section 9](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#9-local-fibres-and-universal-local-acyclicity). The compact-cone calculation also uses the proper-support and categorical constructions of BG–BI.

For a fixed target cohomology sheaf, the support of the image from a refinement is constructible. Its complement is open in the constructible topology. These complements cover \(B\) by the stalkwise conclusion. Lemma 5.2 of [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#5-filtered-approximation-not-always-a-union) proves compactness of that topology: on an affine an ultrafilter determines the prime \(\{a:V(a)\text{ belongs to the ultrafilter}\}\), which satisfies all its basic conditions. Hence finitely many complements cover \(B\). A common refinement has zero map to the fixed target at every stalk, therefore as a sheaf map. There are only four possible cohomology degrees in (AI.6), so one refinement kills them all.

To pass to derived maps, call a map a ghost when it kills every cohomology sheaf. If \(u:A\to D\) is a ghost and both objects lie in \(D^{[a,b]}\), its composite with \(D\to H^b(D)[-b]\) is zero: maps from \(A\in D^{\leq b}\) into that one-degree object are determined by \(H^b(A)\), by the truncation triangle. Hence \(u\) factors through \(\tau_{\leq b-1}D\). The next ghost, restricted to that truncation, factors through degree at most \(b-2\) of its target. Repeat. A composite of \(b-a+1\) ghosts factors through \(\tau_{\leq a-1}\) of the final target and is zero. Four successive refinements therefore kill a cone map in (AI.6) in the derived category itself.

### AI.4. Descend the zero maps and test arbitrary complexes

The vanishing just obtained can be achieved on actual base neighbourhoods. Each of the finitely many source neighbourhoods and refinement maps used in a four-step chain descends from \(B\) to a common pointed affine étale \(V\to V_0\), by the finite-diagram proofs checked in AH.4. Consider one cohomology map of their relative cones at that stage. Its image is constructible on the Noetherian scheme \(V\), and its pullback to \(B\) is zero. Its support is a finite union of locally closed subsets, each represented on a finite affine cover by finitely many equations and inequations. Regard each piece as a finite-presentation locally closed scheme. Its base change to \(B\) is empty. The finite-affine-cover limit argument in AH.4 makes it empty after some further pointed base neighbourhood. Taking a common refinement for all the pieces and cohomology degrees makes the descended sheaf maps zero.

Repeat this for the four maps and use the ghost calculation on that final neighbourhood. If \(v:V\to V_0\), the resulting relative cone map into \(v^*C_{U_0}\) is zero. Its adjoint \(v_!C_U\to C_{U_0}\) is zero as well. Exact extension by zero along \(V_0\to S\) then gives the required zero transition on \(S\). This verifies the derived pro-zero assertion including the transitions between different base neighbourhoods.

Untwist (AI.6). Write \(K_{U,V}=R(qj_U)_!\Lambda\) and \(T_{U,V}=j_{V,!}\Lambda(-1)[-2]\). BI.4 completes a finite chain of trace squares to triangle maps and proves that their composite cone map is zero, after the finite descent just described. BI.5 applies exact Hom sequences to that finite comparison: a morphism out of \(K\) extends over \(T\) once its boundary obstruction is killed, and a morphism out of \(T\) restricting to zero on \(K\) factors through the cone and vanishes at a later stage. These two arguments prove, for every complex \(A\), bounded or unbounded,
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_{(U,V)}
 \operatorname{Hom}(T_{U,V},A[r])
\simeq
\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_{(U,V)}
 \operatorname{Hom}(K_{U,V},A[r]).
\tag{AI.7}
\]

The projections of the diagram category to its pointed source and base neighbourhoods are cofinal: any finite list is refined by taking fibre products and a pointed affine chart. Adjunction identifies the left side with \(H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s}\), and the right side with \(H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}\). The stalk assertion for an unbounded complex follows directly from a K-injective representative: exact filtered colimits commute with its degreewise sections over pointed neighbourhoods, giving its stalk complex and then its cohomology. No boundedness of \(A\) is used in this argument. Formula (AI.7) is the map adjoint to the affine-line trace and the projection formula, so it proves the stated local comparison, with its specified orientation, from the curve-duality, local-acyclicity and proper-support inputs of Proposition 3.3.

## Appendix AJ. Ramified coefficients in the curve pairing

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed, let \(p\) be its characteristic exponent, and let \(R\) be the strict local ring of a smooth \(k\)-curve at a closed geometric point. Put \(L=\operatorname{Frac}R\), and fix a uniformizer \(t\). AI.1 proves that \(R\) is a discrete valuation ring with residue field \(k\). We prove the ramification calculation needed for finite coefficients \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\), where \(n\) is prime to \(p\). In characteristic zero, “prime to \(p\)” imposes no restriction.

### AJ.1. Finite extensions of this strict local field

We first spell out the finite-algebra consequence of strict locality. A square system of polynomial equations with invertible Jacobian at a specified residue solution has a solution in \(R\). Indeed, its finitely many coefficients belong to one pointed étale neighbourhood defining \(R\). Descend the equations and invert their Jacobian determinant. After clearing the finitely many localization denominators, this defines another pointed étale neighbourhood: AB.1 proves the unique square-zero lifting property and AE.1 proves flatness on these Noetherian charts. Composition makes it an object of the same neighbourhood system. Its structure map to the colimit \(R\) supplies the solution with the specified residue.

In particular, a coprime monic factorization \(\bar f=\bar g\bar h\) lifts to a monic factorization over \(R\). Use the nonleading coefficients of \(g,h\) as unknowns. If their degrees are \(a,b\), the Jacobian is

\[
k[T]_{<a}\oplus k[T]_{<b}\longrightarrow k[T]_{<a+b},
\qquad(u,v)\longmapsto\bar h u+\bar g v.
\tag{AJ.1}
\]

Its kernel is zero: coprimality forces \(\bar g\mid u\), and the degree bound then gives \(u=v=0\). Equal dimensions make it invertible.

Every finite \(R\)-algebra \(B\) is a product of local rings. Here are the algebraic steps, also proved in [Henselian local rings and henselization, Sections 2–3](course:AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization#2-factorization-and-the-finite-algebra-criterion). All maximal ideals of \(B\) contract to the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) of \(R\), by integrality and K.1. The finite-dimensional algebra \(B/\mathfrak mB\) is a product of Artinian local rings, by the Artinian decomposition used in AH.2. Lift an idempotent \(e_0\) of this quotient to \(b\in B\), and choose a monic \(f\) annihilating \(b\), using the finite-module determinant argument. For \(e_0\neq0,1\), its residue polynomial vanishes at both 0 and 1: evaluate on the two nonzero orthogonal summands \(1-e_0,e_0\). Separate the full power of \(T-1\) from \(\bar f\), and lift this coprime factorization by (AJ.1). The lifted factors are comaximal, since their finite quotient has zero reduction and Nakayama kills it. The Chinese remainder idempotent in \(R[T]/(f)\), equal to one on the factor at 1 and zero on the other factor, maps to a lift of \(e_0\) in \(B\).

Such a lift is unique. If two idempotents agree modulo an ideal in the Jacobson radical, their products with each other's complement are idempotents in that radical and hence zero: \(z(1-z)=0\) and \(1-z\) is a unit. The lifted primitive idempotents are therefore orthogonal and sum to one. Each resulting factor has a single maximal ideal, detected modulo \(\mathfrak m\). This proves the product assertion. It also proves that any finite local \(R\)-algebra \(B\) is henselian. For a monic polynomial with a simple residue root, decompose its finite free algebra over \(B\) into local factors, applying the assertion over \(R\). The factor at that root is a finite projective \(B\)-module of residue dimension one, hence free of rank one. Its unit is a basis by Nakayama, so that factor is \(B\) itself and gives the root. To justify the module assertion, lift a residue basis of any finite projective module, split the resulting surjection from a finite free module, and apply Nakayama to its kernel.

Now let \(E/L\) be finite separable of degree \(d\). Its integral closure \(B\) over \(R\) is finite. The trace proof AG.1 works directly over this integrally closed Noetherian ring: choose a primitive element, scale it to an integral element \(\theta\), and use \(1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{d-1}\) as a field basis. Scaling is possible by multiplying by a common denominator of the minimal-polynomial coefficients. The nonzero trace determinant \(\Delta\) of L.3 bounds the coordinates of every integral element inside \(\Delta^{-1}R^d\). Indeed, its traces against the basis are integral and belong to \(L\), hence belong to \(R\); the inverse trace matrix gives the bound. The integral closure is an \(R\)-submodule of that finite module, so is finite by Noetherianity.

The ring \(B\) is a domain and a product of local rings, so is local. Its residue field is finite over \(k\) and therefore equals \(k\). Integral incomparability in K.1 gives dimension one; L.1 makes this Noetherian normal local domain a discrete valuation ring. It is henselian by the preceding argument. As an \(R\)-module it is finite torsion free, hence free by X.4, of rank \(d\), since its generic fibre is \(E\). If \(\pi\) is a uniformizer of \(B\), write \(t=u\pi^e\), with \(u\) a unit. The \(e\) successive quotients in \(B/\pi^eB\) are copies of \(k\). Reducing the free module modulo \(t\) consequently gives

\[
[E:L]=\dim_k(B/tB)=e.
\tag{AJ.2}
\]

This proves the degree and ramification equality here, rather than assuming a theorem about complete valued fields. The argument does not require \(R\) to be complete.

### AJ.2. The wild kernel and the tame quotient

Suppose first that \(E/L\) is finite Galois, with group \(G\). It acts on the local integral closure \(B\), fixes the embedded coefficient field \(k\), and acts trivially on its residue field. The rule

\[
\chi(g)=\overline{g(\pi)/\pi}\in k^\times
\tag{AJ.3}
\]

is a homomorphism: apply \(g\) to the unit \(h(\pi)/\pi\) and reduce. Replacing \(\pi\) by \(v\pi\) changes this unit by \(g(v)/v\), whose residue is one, so \(\chi\) is independent of the parameter. A finite subgroup of \(k^\times\) is cyclic: select commuting elements realizing the maximal prime-power factors of its exponent, multiply them, and compare the number of elements with the number of roots of the corresponding polynomial. Its order is prime to \(p\), since in characteristic \(p\) the only \(p\)-power root of unity is one.

For \(r\geq1\), set

\[
\begin{gathered}
G_r=\{g:g(\pi)-\pi\in\pi^{r+1}B\},\\
G_r/G_{r+1}\longrightarrow(k,+),\qquad
g\longmapsto\overline{(g(\pi)-\pi)/\pi^{r+1}}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AJ.4}
\]

Here \(G_1=\ker\chi\). Substitution in \(gh(\pi)-\pi\) proves that the displayed map is additive with kernel \(G_{r+1}\): both automorphisms fix residues, and \(g(\pi)^{r+1}\equiv\pi^{r+1}\pmod{\pi^{r+2}}\). This also verifies that the sets are subgroups. Their intersection is trivial. An element in it fixes \(\pi\) by Krull separation in L.1. Every \(b\in B\) has, modulo \(\pi^N\), a polynomial expansion of degree less than \(N\) in \(\pi\) with coefficients in \(k\), obtained by repeatedly taking its residue and dividing the remainder by \(\pi\). Such an automorphism fixes every expansion, hence fixes \(b\), again by separation.

Since \(G\) is finite, the filtration reaches the identity. Each additive quotient in (AJ.4) is a finite \(p\)-group in positive characteristic, and is zero in characteristic zero. Thus \(P_E=G_1\) is a \(p\)-group, trivial in characteristic zero, and \(G/P_E\) is cyclic of order prime to \(p\). In positive characteristic \(P_E\) is the unique Sylow \(p\)-subgroup.

Every finite separable extension of degree \(m\) prime to \(p\) has a particularly simple form. By (AJ.2), \(t=u\pi^m\). The residue of \(u\) has an \(m\)-th root in \(k\), and henselianity of \(B\) lifts it to \(v\in B^\times\). Thus \(\alpha=v\pi\) satisfies \(\alpha^m=t\). Conversely, if \(\alpha^m=t\), the extension \(L(\alpha)/L\) is separable. Its ramification index equals its degree \(d\) by (AJ.2), while
\(d=v_{L(\alpha)}(t)=m v_{L(\alpha)}(\alpha)\). Hence \(m\mid d\), and the polynomial degree gives \(d\leq m\). Thus \(d=m\), and the original extension is exactly \(L(t^{1/m})\). All roots of unity lie in \(k\), so this is a cyclic Galois extension.

Take the union \(L^t\) of these root extensions in a fixed separable closure. Compatible roots can be chosen by the finite inverse-limit argument AA.1. Their automorphisms identify
\(\operatorname{Gal}(L^t/L)=\varprojlim_{(m,p)=1}\mu_m(k)\).
Changing \(t\) by a unit does not change this identification: its prime-to-\(p\) roots already lie in \(R\) by henselianity and are fixed by every automorphism. For finite Galois \(E/L\), the fixed field \(E^{P_E}\) has prime-to-\(p\) degree and thus lies in \(L^t\). Conversely any finite subextension of \(E\cap L^t\) has prime-to-\(p\) cyclic Galois group, so the normal \(p\)-group \(P_E\) acts trivially on it. Therefore \(E\cap L^t=E^{P_E}\). Passing to finite quotients, with the surjective Sylow transitions proved in AA.3, yields

\[
1\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow I=\operatorname{Gal}(L^{\mathrm{sep}}/L)
\longrightarrow T=\widehat{\mathbf Z}^{(p')}(1)\longrightarrow1,
\qquad P=\varprojlim_E P_E.
\tag{AJ.5}
\]

Exactness at the inverse limit follows from compactness as in AA.1: a prescribed compatible quotient element has nonempty finite sets of lifts satisfying every finite collection of compatibility equations. Thus \(P\) is pro-\(p\), with \(P=1\) in characteristic zero.

### AJ.3. Cohomology and the actual restriction pairing

Let \(M\) be a finite continuous \(\Lambda[I]\)-module and put \(N=M^P\). Taking \(P\)-invariants is exact, including on arbitrary discrete \(\Lambda\)-modules: a lift of an invariant element has finite \(P\)-orbit, so average it over a finite \(p\)-group quotient, whose order is invertible in \(\Lambda\). Moreover \((-)^P\), as a functor to \(T\)-modules, is right adjoint to the exact inflation functor, so preserves injectives. Apply it to an injective resolution, using AA.2's existence and continuous-cochain comparison. Exactness makes the result an injective resolution of \(N\); taking \(T\)-invariants is the same as taking \(I\)-invariants. Consequently \(H^q(I,M)=H^q(T,N)\).

Choose a topological generator \(\tau\) of \(T\). Its finite quotients have orders prime to \(p\). The alternating cyclic resolution with differentials \(\tau-1\) and \(1+\tau+\cdots+\tau^{a-1}\), and its inflation maps, are proved explicitly in [Galois cohomology and the étale cohomology of a field, Section 6](course:ag-etale-cohomology/galois-cohomology-and-the-etale-cohomology-of-a-field#6-procyclic-groups-and-finite-fields). The same calculation applies to these prime-to-\(p\) quotients: their orders can be multiplied by the exponent of \(N\), still prime to \(p\). The norm then vanishes on \(N\); inflation is the identity on degree-one representatives and multiplication by \(b^{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\) in degree \(q\) when the quotient order is multiplied by \(b\). Every degree at least two is therefore killed in the filtered colimit. AA.2 proves that this is continuous cohomology. We obtain

\[
H^0(I,M)=M^I,\qquad
H^1(I,M)=N_T(-1),\qquad H^q(I,M)=0\quad(q>1).
\tag{AJ.6}
\]

The twist records the generator dependence, not an extra choice in the result. Projecting a cocycle to \(N_T\) gives a continuous homomorphism \(T\to N_T\). Evaluation at \(\tau\) is the preceding cyclic identification; replacing \(\tau\) by \(\tau^u\) multiplies that value by \(u\). Thus the canonical group is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(T,N_T)=N_T(-1)\).

For \(M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(M,\Lambda)\), averaging identifies \((M^\vee)^P\) with \((M^P)^\vee\). Restriction of functionals gives a surjection \(N^\vee\to(N^T)^\vee\), by exact duality M.6. Its kernel is \((\tau-1)N^\vee\): dualize the kernel sequence of \(\tau-1:N\to N\); the dual operator has the same image as \(\tau-1\) on \(N^\vee\). Therefore the canonical map induced by restriction and evaluation is an isomorphism

\[
H^1(I,M^\vee)\longrightarrow(M^I)^\vee(-1).
\tag{AJ.7}
\]

No semisimplicity of tame monodromy, or freeness of \(M\) over \(\Lambda\), has entered the proof. This is the precise input to [Poincaré duality for curves, Theorem 5.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-curves#5-the-local-calculation-for-a-ramified-extension). In its dual of \(0\to j_!L\to j_*L\to i_*M^I\to0\), the boundary is **minus** (AJ.7), by the constant evaluation and the sign calculation AI.2. It is still invertible. The adjacent degree-one and degree-two terms vanish, giving \(R\mathcal Hom(j_*L,\Lambda)=j_*L^\vee\). Thus a ramified extension requires both the coinvariant computation and the identification of the boundary map.

### AJ.4. The finite counting input to Artin's argument

For a connected smooth projective curve \(C/k\), choose a primitive \(n\)-th root in \(k\). It gives an isomorphism of coefficient sheaves \(\Lambda\simeq\mu_n\), hence an isomorphism of their degree-one cohomology groups. Kummer and divisibility of \(k^\times\) identify the latter with \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]\); P.1 proves its finiteness. Finite coefficient duality M.6 therefore gives

\[
\bigl|H^1(C,\Lambda)\bigr|
=\bigl|H^1(C,\mu_n)\bigr|
=\bigl|H^1(C,\mu_n)^\vee\bigr|.
\tag{AJ.8}
\]

This is the counting assertion needed in [Poincaré duality for curves, Lemma 8.2 and Section 10](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-curves#8-artin-s-comparison-functors-on-the-projective-line). Use (AJ.8) in that lemma. It requires neither the stronger formula \(n^{2g}\) for these orders nor a previously perfect degree-one pairing.

The argument there works with \(T^r(F)=H^{-r}(C,D_CF)^\vee\) and the evaluation comparisons \(\eta_F^r:H^r(C,F)\to T^r(F)\). Its finite-support reduction and vanishing outside degrees 0–2 are proved in Sections 6 and 8. Section 9 embeds the remaining sheaf \(G\) into a finite constant direct image \(I\), with the maps \(H^r(G)\to H^r(I)\) zero for \(r>0\). For the finite monodromy module \(M\), take the evaluation map \(h:M\to\Lambda^{M^\vee}\), given by \(h(m)=(\lambda(m))_{\lambda\in M^\vee}\). Its target is finite free and it is injective by M.6. If the monodromy factors through \(\Gamma\), the embedding \(m\mapsto(\gamma\mapsto h(\gamma m))\) is injective by evaluation at the identity and equivariant for \((g\phi)(\gamma)=\phi(\gamma g)\). This constructs the embedding for every finite \(\Lambda\)-module without a decomposition theorem. Its cover extends by finite normalization and smoothness from AG.1–AG.4. To kill degree one, take the product of the finitely many torsors supplied by the finite group in (AJ.8). To kill degree two, adjoin an \(n\)-th root of a rational uniformizer and normalize. Its degree is \(n\): after extension to the strict local field, the valuation proof following (AJ.4) shows that its polynomial is irreducible, so it was already irreducible over the original function field. Pullback on degree two is multiplication by \(n\), by the divisor-degree calculation X.4, hence zero.

For \(0\to G\to I\to Q\to0\), Section 10 compares the two long exact sequences in the following order. First the degree-zero comparison for \(I\) gives degree-zero injectivity for all sheaves; this gives degree-zero surjectivity. Effacement and those isomorphisms give degree-one injectivity for every sheaf, including \(I\). Formula (AJ.8) then upgrades injectivity for \(I\) to an isomorphism. The next diagram chase gives degree-one surjectivity for all sheaves. Finally effacement and the established degree-one isomorphisms give degree-two injectivity; the degree-two comparison for \(I\) then gives degree-two surjectivity. Each chase is written there with its lifts and boundaries. This order avoids using the sought pairing on a covering curve to prove itself.

The finite-map evaluation and trace comparisons in Section 7 transfer the full constructible theorem on \(\mathbf P^1\) to a smooth projective curve; subsection AJ.5 proves the required norm and degree compatibility. For the required map, take a rational function that is a uniformizer at a closed point. Its differential is a local basis by AB.4, so its map to the affine line is étale near that point by the standard smooth presentation in AG.4 with this parameter as coordinate. It is therefore generically étale; X.4 proves that its extension to the projective line is finite. Section 11 applies the proper pairing to \(j_!F\) in a smooth completion and then to truncation triangles. These are the curve-pairing arguments used in Proposition 3.3 and AI.3, with (AJ.5)–(AJ.8) supplying their ramification and finite-counting inputs. AK.1–AK.5 supply the needed stalk continuity, exact finite-curve transport and ordinary/compact finiteness. AT.1–AT.4 supply the strict-local acyclicity and selected-neighbourhood comparison over a field. The categorical and general proper-comparison constructions are separate inputs; the curve pairing alone does not imply them.

### AJ.5. The norm and the finite-map trace

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be finite and generically étale between smooth connected curves over the algebraically closed field \(k\). It is surjective and finite locally free of degree \(d\), by X.4. Multiplication by a section \(b\) of \(f_*\mathcal O_X\) is an endomorphism \(m_b\) of this rank-\(d\) bundle. Define

\[
N_f(b)=\det(m_b).
\tag{AJ.9}
\]

A change of basis conjugates the matrix and leaves its determinant unchanged, so these expressions glue. Multiplication gives \(N_f(bc)=N_f(b)N_f(c)\), and \(N_f(a)=a^d\) for a scalar from \(Y\). Units map to units and \(n\)-th powers to \(n\)-th powers. The same matrix after base change computes the new norm. Thus (AJ.9) defines a map of Kummer sequences after exact finite pushforward, whose exactness is AL.2.

We compute its valuation. At a closed point \(y\), put \(A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}\) and \(B=(f_*\mathcal O_X)_y\). Then \(B\) is free over the DVR \(A\). For \(0\ne b\in B\), multiplication by \(b\) is injective with finite-length cokernel. A square matrix over a DVR with nonzero determinant can be diagonalized as follows. Move an entry of least valuation into its first position; it divides every entry. Subtract row and column multiples to clear that column and row, then repeat on the remaining block. These invertible operations give diagonal entries \(u_j\pi_y^{r_j}\), with \(u_j\) units and \(r_j\geq0\). The cokernel length and determinant valuation are both \(\sum_jr_j\). Hence \(v_yN_f(b)=\operatorname{length}_A(B/bB)\).

The finite-length algebra \(B/bB\) decomposes into its local factors at points over \(y\), as in X.4. In the DVR \(B_x=\mathcal O_{X,x}\), its parameter filtration has length \(v_x(b)\). Each residue factor is \(k\), of length one over \(A\). Therefore

\[
v_yN_f(b)=\sum_{x\mid y}v_x(b).
\tag{AJ.10}
\]

For a nonzero rational function \(b\), multiply by \(\pi_y^N\) to put it in \(B\); this is possible because \(B\otimes_Ak(Y)=k(X)\). The extra contribution on the left is \(Nd\), and on the right it is \(N\sum_{x\mid y}e_x=Nd\), by (X.8). Subtraction proves (AJ.10) for rational functions. Thus \(\operatorname{div}(N_f(b))=f_*\operatorname{div}(b)\), where \(f_*[x]=[f(x)]\). This divisor pushforward has no ramification factor.

A line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) is trivial on inverse images of a Zariski open cover of \(Y\). Indeed, over the semilocal ring \(B\), the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a section nonzero in every residue fibre of its rank-one module. Nakayama makes it a basis at every maximal ideal, hence over \(B\); its finite presentation descends this basis to a neighbourhood of \(y\). Apply the norm to the resulting transition units. Multiplicativity preserves their cocycle identities and changes of frames, giving the line bundle \(N_f(L)\). This is the map on \(H^1(\mathbf G_m)\) induced by the sheaf norm, with the frame convention of AD.3; it is also \(\det(f_*L)\otimes\det(f_*\mathcal O_X)^{-1}\). Applying (AJ.10) to the local rational coefficients of a section gives

\[
N_f\mathcal O_X(D)=\mathcal O_Y(f_*D),
\qquad \deg(f_*D)=\deg D.
\tag{AJ.11}
\]

When both curves are projective, X.4 makes degree well-defined on line bundles, so (AJ.11) also gives \(\deg N_f(L)=\deg L\).

On \(\mu_n\), the norm is the finite trace. On a split étale chart it is the product of sheet values, or their sum in additive root-of-unity notation. At a closed geometric point, AL.2 identifies a section with its values \((a_x)_{x\mid y}\). After strict localization the finite algebra splits into local factors. The residue algebra of the factor at \(x\) has dimension \(e_x\), by (X.8), so multiplication by its constant root of unity has determinant that root to the power \(e_x\). Base-change compatibility of (AJ.9) gives the stalk formula \((a_x)\mapsto\sum_{x\mid y}e_xa_x\). This is the extension of generic summation used in the finite-map pairing.

Naturality of the Kummer connecting map identifies the map on \(H^2(\mu_n)\) with the norm on \(\operatorname{Pic}/n\). For projective curves, (AJ.11) and P.2 give \(\operatorname{Tr}_Y H^2(N_f)=\operatorname{Tr}_X\). Pullback instead multiplies degree by \(d\), as in (X.9).

For open curves, the map extends to their smooth projective completions. At a missing point of the source, write its generic map in homogeneous coordinates of a projective embedding of the target completion. Scale these coordinates so that their valuations are nonnegative and at least one is zero. They then define a map on that DVR; the target equations still hold because they hold in its fraction field. The maps extend to neighbourhoods and glue by separatedness. X.3 makes the extended nonconstant map finite. Its inverse image of \(Y\) is exactly \(X\): over an affine open of \(Y\), the finite normal algebra defining \(X\) is the integral closure in \(k(X)\). A valuation ring of a point above that open contains this algebra, since its elements are integral over the target ring and the valuation ring is integrally closed. The resulting centre in \(X\) agrees with the point in the completion by separatedness. Exact finite base change in this cartesian open square and extension by zero carry the projective identity to \(\operatorname{Tr}_Y H^2_c(N_f)=\operatorname{Tr}_X\). Finite disjoint unions use products of norms and sums of traces.

For the determinant construction, see [Stacks, Lemma 31.18.6, Tag 0BD2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BD2).

## Appendix AK. Finite data in curve cohomology

The curve pairing uses three different assertions: cohomology passes to a strict-local limit; finite direct image is exact; and constructible curve cohomology is finite. A statement about sections alone proves neither the first assertion in positive degree nor the third. We give the finite-data argument for the first, then prove the finite-map and finiteness assertions at the smooth-curve scope used in AI–AJ.

### AK.1. Descending objects, covers and sections

Let \((A_i)_{i\geq0}\) be a directed system of Noetherian rings with a chosen initial stage, let \(A=\operatorname{colim}_iA_i\), and let \(T_0\) be separated and of finite presentation over \(A_0\). Put \(T_i=T_0\times_{A_0}A_i\) and \(T=T_0\times_{A_0}A\). The limit ring need not be Noetherian. We work with quasi-compact separated étale objects of finite presentation over these schemes. They form a basis, include the final object, and are closed under finite fibre products and equalizers. For the last assertion, the diagonal of a separated étale object is an open and closed immersion of finite presentation; its pullbacks are the required equalizers. Quasi-compactness then persists. A finite covering refinement by affine objects exists because étale maps are open and these objects are quasi-compact.

Every finite diagram of such objects, maps and identities descends to some stage. Use the finite-presentation and gluing proof AH.4; étaleness descends with the finitely many standard Jacobian presentations, and separatedness descends with the diagonal. A finite covering family also descends as a covering. After the objects and maps have descended, their image at a Noetherian stage is a quasi-compact open. Its closed complement is of finite presentation. If the family covers the limit, that complement has empty limit. Cover it at its original stage by finitely many affine charts. In each chart the assertion that its limiting ring is zero is the finite equality \(1=0\), so holds at a later stage. A common stage makes every chart empty. This is exactly the empty-limit argument of AH.4. No assertion about the surjectivity of all individual transition maps is needed.
