Suppose \(F_i\) are abelian étale sheaves with compatible transition maps \(f_{ji}^{-1}F_i\to F_j\), and put \(F=\operatorname{colim}_i p_i^{-1}F_i\) on \(T\). If \(V_i\) is one of these basis objects and \(V_j,V\) its base changes, then

\[
\operatorname{colim}_{j\geq i}F_j(V_j)=F(V).
\tag{AK.1}
\]

Here is the sheaf argument. A section of a pullback or associated colimit sheaf is locally represented by a section at a stage, by the inverse-image colimit and sheafification construction of [Pushforward, pullback and finite morphisms, Sections 1–2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/pushforward-pullback-and-finite-morphisms#1-pullback-transports-the-selected-geometric-point). Choose finitely many representing basis charts covering \(V\). Their overlaps are quasi-compact; choose finite charts there too. Equality of two representatives is locally an equality at a later stage, allowing a further finite covering refinement when sheafification introduced the equality. There are only finitely many sections, restrictions and equalities. The diagram and covering assertions just proved place them at one stage, where the sheaf axiom glues them. This proves surjectivity of (AK.1). Apply the same finite selection to the local equality of two sections to obtain their equality at a later stage, proving injectivity. This proof works for sets as well as abelian groups.

For a constant scheme diagram the argument also proves that filtered colimits of sheaves have sectionwise colimits on this basis. Equivalently, the matching equalizer for a finite cover involves only finite products and kernels, which commute with filtered colimits. The new issue in positive cohomological degree is to make the entire representing cochain diagram finite.

### AK.2. Finite families suffice in each hypercover degree

A hypercover has a family \(K_r\) of étale objects in each degree, together with faces and degeneracies, and a covering map from \(K_r\) to its matching object \(M_rK\). The latter records all compatible boundaries of an \(r\)-simplex; \(M_0K=T\). These matching objects are finite limits. Use the definitions and proofs in [Hypercoverings, Sections 1–7](course:ag-etale-cohomology/hypercoverings#1-families-and-finite-limits). We may restrict that argument to hypercovers for which **each degree is a finite family** of the basis objects in AK.1. There is no bound on the number of degrees.

We verify this restriction in the constructions, rather than assume that an arbitrary infinite hypercover descends. Finite limits and products of finite families remain finite families of basis objects. The constant hypercover exists. Products of hypercovers provide common refinements. In Section 5's degree-refinement construction, a chosen section of a quotient sheaf on \(K_r\) lifts on a cover of each component. Select a finite basis subcover on each of the finitely many components. Its family \(Z\) is finite, and the construction

\[
(Q_rZ)_m=\prod_{\alpha:[r]\to[m]}Z,
\qquad L=K\times_{Q_rK_r}Q_rZ
\tag{AK.2}
\]

still has finite families in every degree. The proof there identifies its relative matching maps as finite products of the chosen covering maps, so \(L\) is a hypercover and gives the required lift. Section 6's path object uses \(\Delta[m]\times\Delta[1]\), a simplicial set with finitely many nondegenerate simplices; its defining limits are finite as well. Hence two maps become homotopic after a refinement still inside this finite-family class. The resulting category modulo homotopy is cofiltered.

For clarity, the cohomological comparison requires more than this filteredness. The augmented free-sheaf chain complex of a hypercover is exact: Section 3 fills the finite support of any cycle by a cone after a cover, with the contraction \(\partial c+c\partial=1\). Applying Hom into an injective sheaf makes its augmented cochain complex exact. Thus injectives have no positive hypercover cohomology. For a short exact sequence of coefficient sheaves, (AK.2) lifts a representing cochain after refinement; differentiating that lift defines the connecting class. Section 7 verifies independence of the lift, independence under homotopy and refinement, and all three exactness conditions. Its argument uses only finitely many such refinements at a time and therefore stays in our class.

Consequently the filtered cohomology functors just constructed are an effaceable delta-functor, with degree zero equal to sections. To compare with derived cohomology, embed \(F\) in an injective \(I\) and put \(C=I/F\). Both long exact sequences identify degree one with the cokernel of \(\Gamma(I)\to\Gamma(C)\), and identify degree \(q\geq2\) for \(F\) with degree \(q-1\) for \(C\). Induction, using the compatible resolution maps of T.4, gives the natural comparison in all degrees. Section 7 checks that it is the map obtained from the injective double complex, including the signs of connecting maps. We have proved, for any abelian sheaf,

\[
H^q(T,F)=\operatorname{colim}_K
 H^q\!\left(\prod_{V\in K_\bullet}F(V),
                 \sum_a(-1)^a d_a^*\right),
\tag{AK.3}
\]

with \(K\) ranging over these finite-family hypercovers. A class is represented by a cocycle on one such hypercover; a zero class becomes the boundary of a cochain after a refinement. This comparison does not claim that a fixed hypercover's zero-row complex always computes derived cohomology.

### AK.3. Descend a cocycle and its vanishing witness

For degree \(q\), only degrees through \(q+1\) of the cochain complex enter the cocycle condition. All those degrees together contain finitely many objects, maps and simplicial identities. AK.1 descends that truncated hypercover to a stage and makes each of its finitely many matching maps a covering there. It extends to a full hypercover by coskeleton: in degree \(m\) take the finite limit indexed by the maps \([r]\to[m]\) with \(r\leq q+1\). Above the chosen truncation a compatible boundary specifies exactly those same lower simplices, so the matching map is an isomorphism. This is the coskeleton construction and matching verification of the earlier hypercover lesson.

Let a cocycle in (AK.3) represent a class on \(T\). Its finitely many degree-\(q\) sections descend by (AK.1). The finitely many equations saying their alternating restriction sum is zero in degree \(q+1\) hold at a common later stage. We obtain a cohomology class there. The natural comparison of (AK.3) sends it to the original class: replacing a hypercover by the coskeleton of this truncation leaves the terms and differentials computing \(H^q\) unchanged, and the natural map to that coskeleton respects the comparison. This proves surjectivity below.

For injectivity, represent a class at a stage by a finite-family hypercover. If its image is zero at the limit, (AK.3) supplies a refinement and a cochain whose differential is its pullback. Descend the refinement's truncated diagram, its map to the original truncated hypercover, and that cochain. Equation (AK.1) makes the equality between its differential and the pulled-back cocycle hold at a later stage. Taking coskeleton of both truncated hypercovers extends the map; their degree-\(q\) cohomology is unchanged. Hence the original derived class vanishes at that stage. For \(q=0\), use the equality of sections in (AK.1), without a degree-minus-one cochain. We have proved the natural isomorphism

\[
\operatorname{colim}_i H^q(T_i,F_i)
 \xrightarrow{\sim} H^q(T,F),\qquad q\geq0.
\tag{AK.4}
\]

This proves the continuity needed here for the stated Noetherian models and their possibly non-Noetherian limit. BA.5 supplies the finite-cover descent argument over arbitrary rings and extends this proof to every qcqs affine inverse system and compatible abelian coefficient system. It includes fixed-scheme filtered coefficient systems and the affine pointed étale systems defining a strict localization of a finite-type scheme. In the latter case, the presheaf formula for higher direct image follows from the injective slice calculation AB.3. Exactness of stalk colimits and (AK.4) give

\[
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar y}
 =H^q\!\left(X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{Y,\bar y},F\right)
\tag{AK.5}
\]

for the separated finite-type morphisms used here. This is cohomology over the **strict local base**, not an identification with cohomology of the closed geometric fibre. Proper base change is a separate assertion.

### AK.4. Exact finite direct image for the curve covers

Let \(h:Y\to X\) be finite and generically étale between smooth curves over algebraically closed \(k\). It is finite flat: on a target discrete valuation ring its finite module is torsion free, hence free, by X.4. At a closed geometric point of \(X\), let \(R\) be its strict local ring. The algebra of \(Y_R\) is finite free over \(R\), and AJ.1 splits it into local factors \(B_a\). Each factor is finite projective over the local \(R\), hence finite free. Its residue field is \(k\). AL.1–AL.2 extend the section and finite-image arguments to arbitrary finite maps of locally Noetherian schemes, including nonflat maps.

Every pointed étale neighbourhood of the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec}B_a\) has a section. We can prove this directly with finite free coordinates. Choose an affine neighbourhood of the selected point and a standard square Jacobian presentation over the Noetherian ring \(B_a\), using AB.1 and the standard smooth presentations already used in AE.1. Any localization can be written with an extra variable for an inverse. The closed-point solution lifts to \(B_a/\mathfrak m_RB_a\): this is an Artinian local ring, and the invertible Jacobian lifts a solution successively across its nilpotent maximal ideal. This is the square-zero correction of AB.1 iterated a finite number of times.

Now choose an \(R\)-basis of \(B_a\), and express every unknown as a vector in that basis. The square polynomial system over \(B_a\) becomes a square polynomial system over \(R\). Modulo \(\mathfrak m_R\), its derivative is the underlying \(k\)-linear map of the invertible \(B_a/\mathfrak m_RB_a\)-linear Jacobian, so is invertible. AJ.1's pointed-neighbourhood lifting gives a solution over \(R\), equivalently a solution of the original system in \(B_a\). The inverted element remains a unit because it is a unit modulo the maximal ideal. This proves the section assertion without a general standard-univariate-neighbourhood or Zariski's Main Theorem input.

For any sheaf on \(\operatorname{Spec}B_a\), sections consequently equal the closed-point stalk. Every germ is represented on a pointed neighbourhood and its section pulls that representative back globally. If two global sections have the same germ, their equality holds on such a neighbourhood; its section makes them equal globally. At the generic geometric point, the finite generically étale algebra splits over the separably closed field, by AB.1. The degree-zero limit formula (AK.1) therefore gives, at every geometric point of \(X\),

\[
(h_*F)_{\bar x}=\bigoplus_{\bar y\mid\bar x}F_{\bar y}.
\tag{AK.6}
\]

All maps are the actual restriction maps. Finite sums and stalks are exact, so \(h_*\) is exact on abelian sheaves. It preserves injectives as the right adjoint of exact inverse image; applying it to an injective resolution proves \(H^q(X,h_*F)=H^q(Y,F)\). The canonical finite base-change maps for restriction to an open or extension of the algebraically closed ground field are isomorphisms: (AK.6) identifies them with the same maps on the same geometric lifts. Thus these comparisons preserve the unit and the sum-over-sheets trace.

A closed finite set of points has the analogous exact pushforward, independently of flatness. At one of those points a pointed étale neighbourhood can be shrunk to exclude the other points of its finite fibre, giving its one point-module stalk; away from the set the stalk is zero. Exactness follows on stalks. Its global cohomology is the finite direct sum of its point modules in degree zero, with no positive groups, since an algebraically closed field has the exact section functor of AB.1–AB.2.

### AK.5. Ordinary and compact cohomology on a smooth curve

Let \(X/k\) be smooth, separated and of finite type, and let \(F\) be a constructible \(\mathbf Z/n\)-sheaf with \(n\) invertible in \(k\). Then its ordinary and compactly supported cohomology groups are finite and vanish above degree two. Its ordinary groups vanish above degree one if \(X\) is affine. Here is the proof using the precise earlier inputs.

For constant coefficients on a connected projective curve, P.1–P.2 give finiteness and the degree-two bound, without a torsion-rank formula. For an affine smooth curve \(X=C-D\), the divisor calculation X.1–X.4 gives
\(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}(C)/\langle\mathcal O_C(d):d\in D\rangle\).
Since \(D\neq\varnothing\), its point bundles remove the degree part, and P.1 makes this quotient divisible by \(n\). R.5 and the Kummer sequence therefore give vanishing in degrees at least two. Finiteness in degree one follows from the actual boundary sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow H^1(C,\mu_n)\longrightarrow H^1(X,\mu_n)
\longrightarrow
\ker\!\left((\mathbf Z/n)^D\xrightarrow{\sum}\mathbf Z/n\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{AK.7}
\]

The full normalized-line-bundle proof is [The multiplicative group on a curve, Proposition 7.2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-multiplicative-group-on-a-curve#7-affine-curves-and-their-boundary). Its ingredients are divisor extension, twisting by boundary divisors, and division of a degree-zero bundle; X.1–X.4 and P.1 supply exactly these. It requires no assertion about the rank of Jacobian torsion. The right group in (AK.7) is finite, and P.2 proves finiteness of the left group. A primitive root identifies \(\mu_n\) with the constant coefficient sheaf. A connected smooth curve is projective or such an affine open by the completion and boundary arguments O.1, P.3 and X.4.

To pass to constructible coefficients, first use primary decomposition and the exact sequences with submodule \(F[\ell]\) to reduce to a constructible \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaf. Choose a dense open \(j:U\to X\) where it is locally constant. Its complement is finite, and
\(0\to j_!F|_U\to F\to i_*F|_{X-U}\to0\)
shows that finiteness and the stated degree bounds are unchanged by this reduction: the boundary has only finite degree-zero cohomology, by AK.4. The same sequence reduces constant sheaves extended from any dense open to the already proved constant case.

On a connected component of \(U\), N.2–N.3 supply the finite monodromy cover. Choose an \(\ell\)-Sylow subgroup of its finite group. The resulting finite étale map \(V\to U\) has degree \(d\) prime to \(\ell\), and its pulled-back sheaf has a flag of constant \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-quotients: orbit counting gives a nonzero invariant vector for an \(\ell\)-group acting on an \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-space, then induction applies to the quotient. Normalize \(X\) in the function field of each component of \(V\). By AG.1–AG.4 this produces a finite map \(h:Y\to X\) with \(Y\) smooth and generically étale. Its inverse image of \(U\) is exactly \(V\): a finite normal algebra with that fraction field is the integral closure, since every element integral over the base is integral over it and belongs to it. This proves the required extension of the cover directly.

If \(X\) is affine, \(Y\) is affine. If \(X\) is projective, \(Y\) is proper; its dense open immersion in the projective completion of P.3 is also proper, hence closed and therefore the whole completion. On \(Y\), apply exact extension by zero to the flag. The constant case and long exact sequences prove finiteness and the same degree bounds for that extension. Formula (AK.6) identifies
\(j_!f_*G=h_*j'_!G\): both sides have the same restriction on \(U\) and zero stalks off \(U\). Exact finite pushforward therefore transfers the cohomology conclusions to \(X\). Finally the unit followed by trace is multiplication by \(d\). Multiply trace by the inverse of \(d\) in \(\mathbf F_\ell\); this exhibits \(j_!F|_U\) as a direct summand, in every degree at once. This proves the ordinary-cohomology assertions.

Choose a smooth projective completion \(a:X\hookrightarrow\overline X\). Its finite boundary makes \(a_!F\) constructible, and the definition
\(R\Gamma_c(X,F)=R\Gamma(\overline X,a_!F)\)
now gives compact finiteness and the degree-two bound from the proper ordinary case. For arbitrary \(\mathbf Z/n\)-sheaves, the same degree bounds follow by (AK.4) for a constant scheme diagram and the filtered constructible approximation proved in [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, Sections 4–5 and 7](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#4-finite-data-the-generators). The generator proof there uses finite sections and relations; on our Noetherian schemes its images are constructible. No finiteness assertion is made for the resulting infinite colimit. AL.3 also proves the canonical comparison under an algebraically closed field extension. These arguments supply the curve finiteness and stalk-continuity inputs of AJ.4 and AI.3. AT.1–AT.4 supply the smooth-local-acyclicity comparison over a fixed field. BE.1–BE.8 prove general proper base change; the arbitrary-complex operation constructions retain their separate requirements.

## Appendix AL. Finite maps and the inputs to smooth comparison

The induction for smooth base change makes finite replacements of its source and base. Those finite maps can be ramified and nonflat, so AK.4's smooth-curve case does not suffice. We first extend the finite-map argument. We then check the actual field-extension maps on curve cohomology and distinguish étale limits from the smooth comparison theorem.

### AL.1. Lift through a finite free algebra before taking a quotient

Let \(R\) be the strict localization of a locally Noetherian scheme at a geometric point, with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) and separably closed residue field \(k\). We use the square-Jacobian lifting argument in the first paragraph of AJ.1. That argument does not use dimension one or perfection of the residue field: a finite system, its coefficients, a selected residue solution and the inverse of its Jacobian determinant descend to a pointed étale neighbourhood. The associated square Jacobian chart is another such neighbourhood by AB.1 and AE.1. Its map to the defining colimit gives a solution in \(R\).

Let \(C\) be a finite free \(R\)-algebra. The idempotent proof in AJ.1 applies over this \(R\): its inputs are the square-system lifting just recalled, the finite-module determinant argument, Artinian decomposition, integrality and Nakayama. It gives

\[
C=\prod_a C_a,
\tag{AL.1}
\]

where each \(C_a\) is local. As a direct summand of the finite free module, each factor is finite projective over \(R\), hence free. To recall the last step, lift a residue basis, split the resulting finite free surjection, and apply Nakayama to its finite kernel. The ring \(C_a/\mathfrak m C_a\) is Artinian local; its residue field \(k_a\) is finite over \(k\), therefore purely inseparable and separably closed. In characteristic zero \(k_a=k\). In positive characteristic, raising a separable polynomial over \(k_a\) and its roots to a sufficiently large characteristic power gives a separable polynomial over \(k\); its roots lie in \(k\), so the original roots, being both separable and purely inseparable over \(k_a\), lie in \(k_a\).

A square polynomial system over \(C_a\), with a specified simple solution in \(k_a\), has a solution in \(C_a\). First lift across the nilpotent maximal ideal of \(C_a/\mathfrak m C_a\), using the successive square-zero Jacobian corrections of AB.1. Choose an \(R\)-basis of \(C_a\), of rank \(r\). Expressing each of the \(m\) unknowns in this basis turns the system into \(mr\) equations in \(mr\) variables over \(R\). Its residual derivative is the underlying \(k\)-linear map of an invertible \(C_a/\mathfrak m C_a\)-linear map; it is invertible. The lifting property of \(R\) solves this coordinate system. Recombining coordinates gives the desired solution over \(C_a\). This is AK.4's coordinate argument, now allowing the possibly imperfect separably closed \(k\).

Now let \(B\) be any finite \(R\)-algebra. Choose algebra generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\) and monic annihilating polynomials \(p_i\). There is a surjection

\[
C=R[T_1,\ldots,T_s]/(p_1(T_1),\ldots,p_s(T_s))
 \twoheadrightarrow B.
\tag{AL.2}
\]

Successive monic division makes \(C\) finite free, with basis the monomials whose \(T_i\)-exponent is smaller than \(\deg p_i\). Decompose it by (AL.1). Every ideal in this finite product is the product of its factor ideals, so \(B\) is the product of the nonzero quotients \(B_a=C_a/J_a\). Each \(B_a\) is local and has residue field \(k_a\).

Consider a pointed étale neighbourhood of the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec}B_a\). On an affine neighbourhood of the selected point, use a standard square Jacobian presentation, with an extra inverse variable for a localization. These presentations are the ones proved in AB.1 and AE.1. They also apply here without assuming in advance that the strict localization is Noetherian: the finitely presented étale neighbourhood descends to a Noetherian ring model by AH.4. Choose the standard chart there at the image of the selected point, and pull it back. Lift the finitely many polynomial coefficients from \(B_a\) to \(C_a\). The specified residue solution, including its invertible determinant, is unchanged. The preceding coordinate argument solves the lifted system in \(C_a\), hence the original system in \(B_a\). This gives a section through the chosen point.

For every étale sheaf \(A\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}B_a\), restriction is consequently a bijection

\[
\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}B_a,A)=A_{\bar b_a}.
\tag{AL.3}
\]

A germ has a representative on a pointed neighbourhood; pulling back by its section represents it globally. Equality of germs has the same argument. This proves both directions. The abelian section functor is exact because stalks are exact. In particular these local factors have zero higher sheaf cohomology. Taking \(B=R\) also proves that assertion for the original strict localization.

### AL.2. Exact finite pushforward and its actual base-change map

Let \(h:Y\to X\) be finite, with \(X\) locally Noetherian. On an affine neighbourhood of a geometric point \(\bar x\), base change to its strict localization \(R\). The resulting scheme is \(\operatorname{Spec}B\), with \(B\) finite over \(R\). The degree-zero continuity proof (AK.1), followed by (AL.1)–(AL.3), gives

\[
(h_*A)_{\bar x}=\prod_{\bar y\mid\bar x} A_{\bar y}.
\tag{AL.4}
\]

The factors correspond to the geometric lifts in the finite fibre. For abelian sheaves this finite product is also the finite direct sum. Thus \(h_*\) is exact. No flatness, smoothness or reducedness of \(h\) was used. Since its left adjoint \(h^{-1}\) is exact, \(h_*\) also preserves injectives. Applying it to an injective resolution yields

\[
R^qh_*A=0\ (q>0),\qquad
H^q(X,h_*A)=H^q(Y,A).
\tag{AL.5}
\]

For a base-change square with \(X'\to X\), \(Y'=Y\times_X X'\), projections \(h':Y'\to X'\) and \(g':Y'\to Y\), and \(X'\) locally Noetherian, the canonical map is

\[
g^{-1}h_*A\longrightarrow h'_*g'^{-1}A.
\tag{AL.6}
\]

At a geometric point \(\bar x'\), the cartesian square gives a bijection between its geometric lifts in \(Y'\) and the lifts of its composite geometric point in \(Y\). Inverse-image stalks are the corresponding original stalks. Formula (AL.4) therefore identifies (AL.6) with the identity on those same factors. It is an isomorphism, and this calculation proves that it respects adjunction units and all coefficient maps. In particular the derived composition and finite-replacement identities in [Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Lemma 5.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#5-make-a-generic-class-vanish) hold for its Noetherian finite models. This conclusion includes a finite surjection and a closed immersion; a finite flat hypothesis is unnecessary.

### AL.3. Curve cohomology under an algebraically closed extension

Let \(k'/k\) be an extension of algebraically closed fields, \(X/k\) a smooth separated finite-type curve, and \(F\) a constructible \(\mathbf Z/n\)-sheaf, with \(n\) invertible in \(k\). Pullback gives isomorphisms

\[
H^q(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(X_{k'},F|_{X_{k'}}),
\qquad
H^q_c(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q_c(X_{k'},F|_{X_{k'}}).
\tag{AL.7}
\]

We check the maps, rather than compare group cardinalities. For a connected projective curve \(C\), P.2 computes its constant cohomology using \(\mu_n\). The Picard functor constructed in Q and AD is defined on all base schemes, so restricting that represented functor to \(k'\)-schemes is represented by \(J_{k'}\). Degree-zero bundles and their rigidifications have the same meaning there. Hence the degree-one map is exactly \(J[n](k)\to J[n](k')\). By P.1, \(J[n]\) is a finite-type étale scheme over \(k\), and AB.1 makes it a finite disjoint union of \(k\)-points. It has no new points after extension. This proves the degree-one isomorphism without a formula for the number of these points.

Degree zero identifies the same roots of unity. In degree two, the bundle of a \(k\)-point pulls back to the bundle of the corresponding \(k'\)-point, still of degree one. Naturality of Kummer makes the map the identity on the degree group \(\mathbf Z/n\) of P.2. Higher groups vanish. The same chosen primitive root identifies the constant coefficient sheaf with \(\mu_n\) before and after extension.

For an affine \(X=C-D\), use (AK.7). A base-field uniformizer remains a uniformizer after extension, because its smooth local coordinate remains étale. Thus the normalized-line-bundle residue map retains each labelled boundary coordinate. The outside maps in (AK.7) are isomorphisms; exactness proves this for the middle map. Degree zero and vanishing in higher degrees follow as in AK.5. Connected components stay connected under the field extension by the geometric integrality argument AE.3, so finite disjoint unions cause no change.

All reductions in AK.5 respect these canonical maps. For the finite boundary, the point modules and their pullback maps are unchanged. The natural long exact sequence then passes the assertion between a sheaf and its extension from the dense open. On a finite normalization \(h:Y\to X\) extending a monodromy cover, (AL.6) identifies the comparison for \(h_*G\) with the comparison for \(G\); its unit and trace remain the same maps. Base change of this particular \(Y\) is still smooth and finite over \(X_{k'}\). There is no need to identify it with a separately chosen normalization. The constant flag on the Sylow cover retains its exact sequences after pullback. The five-lemma argument passes comparison through that flag, and the trace splitting passes it to the required direct summand. Primary devissage proves it for \(\mathbf Z/n\)-coefficients. This establishes ordinary comparison for \(F\).

For compact support, use the same smooth projective completion before and after extension; extension by zero commutes with pullback on stalks. Ordinary comparison on the completion proves the second assertion of (AL.7). Filtered constructible approximation and AK.4 extend the comparison and degree bounds to arbitrary \(\mathbf Z/n\)-sheaves, without asserting their groups finite. The constant-coefficient case is the field-invariance input of [Smooth base change, Lemma 3.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#3-a-class-on-an-affine-curve-can-be-killed); its proof can use algebraic closures and finite extensions throughout, so this input does not itself assume smooth base change.

### AL.4. Étale limits require only continuity

Some parameter changes used in Appendix M are affine inverse limits of étale morphisms. For these, the comparison needs no smooth-local-acyclicity theorem. At a single étale stage it is localization of the site: the slice and injective calculation AB.3 identifies restriction of a higher direct image with the higher direct image on the restricted site.

Suppose the schemes at the stages are Noetherian, the morphism whose image is taken is separated of finite presentation, and the coefficient sheaf is pulled back from the initial stage. To pass to an affine inverse limit of étale parameter changes, take an affine étale test object at the limit. Its finite presentation descends to a stage by AH.4. Apply (AK.4) to its inverse images under the given morphism. This identifies the colimit of their cohomology groups with the group on the limiting inverse image. Sheafification gives the sheaf comparison, since sections and their equalities are local and the finite charts and equalities descend as in AK.1. All maps are restriction maps. For a bounded-below coefficient complex, the cohomology-sheaf spectral sequence has only finitely many terms in each total degree, so the same comparison holds in the derived category.

This applies to a separable algebraic field extension, expressed as a limit of finite étale field extensions. It also applies to the separable geometric generic points of coordinate lines in M.4–M.5: a finite separable extension of the function field spreads to a finite étale cover of a nonempty open, by its separable polynomial and inversion of its discriminant. These opens and covers are étale over the line. Purely inseparable algebraic extensions are handled by the separate equivalence of étale topoi. Thus the particular algebraic-closure and generic-point comparisons in Appendix M do not require the full smooth comparison theorem.

### AL.5. The remaining geometric input to smooth comparison

The degree and dimension inductions are written in [Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Sections 4–6](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#4-reduce-the-theorem-to-injectives-over-finite-models). AL.1–AL.3 supply its finite replacements and canonical curve-invariance input. The geometric assertion required in its Section 5, proved here in AR.1–AR.5, is the following: for a smooth family with geometrically connected fibres over an integral normal Noetherian base, a finite étale Galois cover of the generic fibre, of group order invertible on the base and split at the generic point of a section, extends to a finite étale cover of the family. Finite normalization alone does not prove that extension étale over the special fibres.

AM.1–AM.6 prove the local connected-fibre neighbourhood construction in Section 2 for schemes over a fixed field, and AN.1 supplies its degree-zero sheaf comparison. AN.2–AN.6 prove the completed-section and punctured formal-neighbourhood inputs. AO.1–AO.6 prove the finite coherent cover-algebra extension, its flat-base-change compatibility and relative purity in smooth families over Noetherian bases. AP.1–AP.7 prove regular local purity and tame root base change for the relevant Galois DVR extensions. AQ.1–AQ.5 prove codimension-one gluing and descent at the split section, completing the DVR-base case. AR.1–AR.5 complete the generic-cover theorem over an arbitrary integral normal Noetherian base. AS.1–AS.7 complete the positive-degree cohomological induction over a fixed field. AT.1–AT.4 prove the strict-local geometric-fibre and selected-neighbourhood assertions used in Proposition 3.3 and AI.3. AM.7 states the equal-characteristic finite-model scope of the connected-fibre construction; the mixed-characteristic normalization and component arguments use AG.5 and the general-base construction in AM–AN. The étale-limit argument of AL.4 does not imply these assertions. Proper base change for a general proper morphism remains a separate theorem as well.

## Appendix AM. Connected fibres in étale neighbourhoods

We prove that a smooth morphism over an arbitrary base has an étale covering by affine schemes which, after an étale change of the base, have geometrically connected fibres and a section. The fibre arguments work over any residue field. The specialization step uses a discrete valuation witness proved in AM.4 from a one-dimensional length bound; finite normalization is not required. Finite-presentation descent then removes the Noetherian restriction on the base.

### AM.1. A component containing a rational point

First suppose \(C\) is a connected smooth finite-type scheme over a field \(K\), and \(c\in C(K)\). Then \(C\) is geometrically integral.

Indeed, every local ring of a smooth scheme over a field is a regular local domain by Y.4–Y.6. Its finitely many irreducible components are therefore disjoint: an intersection would give two minimal primes in a local domain. The components are open and closed. Over a separable closure \(K^{\mathrm s}\), the component containing \(c\) is fixed by every element of \(\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm s}/K)\). On a finite affine covering of \(C\), its open-and-closed indicator is an idempotent. These finitely many idempotents, their equations and their agreements on finite covers of overlaps descend to one finite Galois extension \(L/K\), by the finite-presentation argument AH.4. Their Galois invariance already holds there: extension from \(L\) to \(K^{\mathrm s}\) is injective on every coordinate module. The equalizer calculation AD.1, or its Galois form under

\[
L\otimes_KL\simeq\prod_{\gamma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)}L,
\tag{AM.1}
\]

descends each invariant idempotent to the corresponding affine chart over \(K\). The algebra decomposition (AM.1) follows from the primitive-element proof in AM.5 and the Chinese remainder calculation AB.2 applied to its distinct conjugate roots. They glue to a nonempty open-and-closed part of \(C\). Connectedness makes it all of \(C\), so \(C_{K^{\mathrm s}}\) is connected. The purely inseparable extension to an algebraic closure is a homeomorphism on underlying spaces by AH.1. Thus \(C_{\overline K}\) is connected, smooth and integral.

Here is why this also controls arbitrary field extensions, not just algebraic ones. If \(A\) is a domain over an algebraically closed field \(E\), then \(A\otimes_E L\) is a domain for every extension field \(L/E\). Suppose nonzero elements \(u,v\) have product zero. Express each in a finite \(E\)-linearly independent list of elements of \(A\). Let \(B\subset L\) be the finitely generated \(E\)-algebra containing their scalar coefficients. The inclusion \(A\otimes_EB\to A\otimes_EL\) is injective, so the product is already zero there. Choose nonzero coefficients \(b\) of \(u\) and \(b'\) of \(v\). A maximal quotient of the nonzero finite-type algebra \(B[1/(bb')]\) is \(E\), by Y.5. Specializing its coefficients to \(E\) leaves both \(u\) and \(v\) nonzero, by the chosen linear independence, and gives a zero product in \(A\), a contradiction.

Consequently an integral scheme over an algebraically closed field stays integral after extension: its affine charts stay domains, and intersections of nonempty charts stay nonempty by faithful flatness. For an arbitrary \(L/K\), choose an algebraically closed overfield containing both \(L\) and a compatible \(\overline K\). The preceding argument makes \(C\) integral over that overfield. Surjectivity on spectra and injection on affine coordinate rings then imply that \(C_L\) is irreducible and reduced. This proves the assertion.

Now let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth of finite presentation, with a section \(\sigma\), and let \(X^0\) be the union, fibre by fibre, of the connected components containing \(\sigma(s)\). Each such component has a \(\kappa(s)\)-point, and is geometrically integral by the result just proved. Its open-and-closed complement cannot join it under extension. Therefore, as subsets of a changed family,

\[
(X_T)^0=X^0\times_S T
\tag{AM.2}
\]

for every base change \(T\to S\). We have not yet asserted that this subset is open.

### AM.2. Spreading a geometrically integral smooth fibre

Suppose \(S\) is integral and Noetherian, with function field \(K\), and \(X\to S\) is smooth of finite presentation with nonempty geometrically integral generic fibre of dimension \(d\). There is a nonempty open \(S'\subset S\) over which all fibres are geometrically integral.

We give the specialization argument. Work over an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) of \(S\). The relative dimension of a smooth chart is the number of free coordinates in its standard presentation, equivalently the locally constant rank of \(\Omega_{X/S}\). The finitely many dimension pieces different from \(d\) have empty generic fibre. Their images are constructible by AC.2 and miss the generic point, so their closures are proper. Removing those closures makes every fibre smooth of pure dimension \(d\). Here the dimension statement follows on each geometric chart from Y.5–Y.6.

Choose an étale coordinate chart of the generic fibre. It gives a finite separable function-field extension

\[
K(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\subset F=K(X_K).
\tag{AM.3}
\]

If \(d=0\), the geometrically integral smooth zero-dimensional generic fibre is \(\operatorname{Spec}K\), by AB.1, and we may take \(P=T\) in the argument below. If \(d>0\), the field \(K(t)\) is infinite. The finite separable primitive-element argument in Z.3 writes \(F=K(t)[\theta]\). Clearing denominators and removing content in its minimal polynomial gives a primitive irreducible \(P(t,T)\in K[t,T]\). The content and factorization argument is proved in [Integral extensions, Proposition 2.3](course:AG-CA/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down#2-integral-closure-survives-localization): reduction modulo a prime factor proves that products of primitive polynomials are primitive, and Euclidean factorization over the fraction field gives factorization over the polynomial ring. It applies in any number of variables by induction.

The injection \(K[t,T]/(P)\hookrightarrow F\) stays injective after extending the field to \(\overline K\). The ring \(F\otimes_K\overline K\) is a domain: \(F\) is a localization of an affine coordinate ring of the geometrically integral \(X_K\). Thus \(\overline K[t,T]/(P)\) is a domain too, proving that \(P\) is absolutely irreducible. Its homogenization \(H\), of total degree \(D\), is absolutely irreducible too: dehomogenization of any factorization would factor \(P\), and a factor dehomogenizing to a constant would be a power of the homogenizing variable, which does not divide \(H\).

After inverting finitely many elements of \(A\), all coefficients belong to \(A\), and some degree-\(D\) coefficient is a unit. For each \(1\le a<D\), multiply homogeneous forms of degrees \(a\) and \(D-a\). This defines a morphism between their projective coefficient spaces

\[
\mathbf P^{N_a}_A\times_A\mathbf P^{N_{D-a}}_A
\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{N_D}_A.
\tag{AM.4}
\]

Here \(N_b\) is one less than the number of degree-\(b\) monomials in the homogenized variables. The map is defined everywhere because a product of two nonzero forms over a field is nonzero. Its image is closed: the source is proper over \(A\) by AE.2; its graph in the product with the separated target is closed, and projection from that product is proper by base change. This factorization also proves the asserted properness of the multiplication map. The finite union of these images is precisely the locus of forms reducible over an algebraic closure of the residue field. Membership is unchanged upon field extension, since a nonempty fibre of a scheme of finite type over a field has a geometric point. The coefficient section of \(H\) avoids this closed locus at the generic point. Shrinking \(S\) makes it avoid the locus everywhere. Thus every \(P_s\) is absolutely irreducible.

The hypersurface \(P=0\) and \(X_K\) have the same function field. They have isomorphic dense affine opens: express finite generating sets for either affine coordinate algebra as fractions in the other, and invert the finitely many denominators on both sides. Localizing further makes both opens principal in their respective affine charts. Descend that open and the inverse coordinate maps to a sufficiently small open of \(S\), using AH.4. We obtain an open \(W\subset X\) isomorphic to a principal open of the hypersurface family. Since \(W\to S\) is smooth, its image is open by AE.1 and AC.3. Restrict to this image. Every geometric fibre of \(W\) is then nonempty and integral.

It remains to exclude extra components in \(X_s\setminus W_s\). Put \(Z=X\setminus W\). Its generic fibre has dimension at most \(d-1\); when \(d=0\) it is empty and AC.2 lets us remove its image. For \(d>0\), remove the images of the finitely many irreducible components of \(Z\) which do not dominate \(S\). Cover the reduced remaining components by finitely many affines. For each affine domain \(B\), its generic fibre has some dimension \(m\le d-1\). The relative normalization calculation AC.1, after a further base localization, makes \(B\) finite over \(A[z_1,\ldots,z_m]\). Every geometric fibre of this affine therefore has dimension at most \(m\). Indeed the fibre ring is integral over the image of the polynomial ring. A strict chain of its primes contracts strictly: after quotienting the smaller prime and localizing its contraction, a domain integral over a field is a field, which proves incomparability. Hence such a chain has length at most the dimension \(m\) of the polynomial ring.

After the finitely many localizations, \(Z_{\bar s}\) has dimension at most \(d-1\) in every fibre. It contains no component of the smooth pure-\(d\)-dimensional \(X_{\bar s}\). Thus the integral open \(W_{\bar s}\) meets every component. Those components are disjoint open-and-closed sets by Y.4–Y.6, so there can be only one. Smoothness gives reducedness. This proves geometric integrality of every fibre over the resulting \(S'\).

### AM.3. Constructibility of the component along a section

Assume first that \(S\) is Noetherian, and \(f:X\to S\) is smooth of finite presentation with section \(\sigma\). On an integral reduced locally closed part of \(S\), let \(\eta\) be the generic point. Write
\(X_\eta=C_\eta\amalg D_\eta\), where \(C_\eta\) contains \(\sigma(\eta)\). Take their closures in \(X\). The intersection of the closures and the complement of their union both have empty generic fibre. Their constructible images miss a nonempty base open, by AC.2. Over that open the two closures give an open-and-closed decomposition of \(X\). Shrink again so that \(\sigma\) lies in the first part. That part is smooth with geometrically integral generic fibre by AM.1. Applying AM.2 makes all its fibres geometrically integral, so it equals \(X^0\) over a nonempty base open.

Apply this argument on each irreducible component of the reduced base, first outside the other components, and then repeat on the remaining proper closed subset. Noetherian induction gives a finite locally closed stratification on which \(X^0\) is open and closed. Thus \(X^0\) is constructible in \(X\). Nilpotents in the base cause no change to the underlying sets or to their fibres.

### AM.4. Specializations and openness

We prove generization stability over an arbitrary Noetherian base. The required discrete valuation witness does not require finite normalization. We give its algebraic construction first.

**The length bound.** Let \((R,\mathfrak m)\) be a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain, let \(K=\operatorname{Frac}R\), and let \(0\ne x\in R\). For every submodule \(M\subset K^r\), even one which is not finitely generated,
\[
\operatorname{length}_R(M/xM)
\le r\operatorname{length}_R(R/xR)<\infty.
\tag{AM.4a}
\]
If \(x\) is a unit both sides vanish. Otherwise \(R/xR\) is Noetherian of dimension zero, and therefore has finite length by [Noetherian and Artinian rings, Theorem 4.2](course:AG-CA/noetherian-and-artinian-rings#4-what-an-artinian-ring-looks-like). That lesson's Theorems 3.2–3.3 prove length and its additivity by composition series.

First let \(M=N\) be finite, and choose a \(K\)-basis of its span from elements of \(N\). Their \(R\)-span \(N_0\) is free of rank \(d\le r\). The quotient \(T=N/N_0\) is finite torsion: clearing the finitely many coordinates of generators kills it by a nonzero element of \(R\). Thus it is a finite module over a zero-dimensional Noetherian quotient of \(R\), and has finite length. Multiplication by \(x\) is injective on \(N_0\) and \(N\). Taking kernels and cokernels in their inclusion gives
\[
0\longrightarrow T[x]\longrightarrow N_0/xN_0
\longrightarrow N/xN\longrightarrow T/xT\longrightarrow0,
\tag{AM.4b}
\]
where \(T[x]=\ker(x:T\to T)\). The kernel and cokernel of multiplication on the finite-length module \(T\) have equal length, by additivity applied to its image. Equation (AM.4b) therefore gives
\(\operatorname{length}_R(N/xN)=d\operatorname{length}_R(R/xR)\).

For arbitrary \(M\), any finite strict chain of submodules of \(M/xM\) is witnessed by finitely many elements: select an element at each strict step and lift it to \(M\). Let \(N\) be the finite submodule generated by those lifts. Inverse images under \(N/xN\to M/xM\) retain every strict step. Their number is bounded by the finite-case formula. Consequently every chain has at most the bound in (AM.4a). A strict chain of maximal possible length must have simple successive quotients, since otherwise it could be refined. It is a composition series. This proves the bound, including finiteness of length for the possibly infinite module quotient.

As a consequence, if \(L/K\) is finite and \(R\subset B\subset L\) is any intermediate ring, then \(B\) is Noetherian. Indeed for a nonzero ideal \(J\subset B\), choose \(0\ne z\in J\). A polynomial equation for \(z\) over \(K\), with denominators cleared and nonzero constant coefficient, expresses a nonzero \(a\in R\) as a multiple of \(z\) in \(B\). Thus \(a\in J\). Regard \(B\) as an \(R\)-submodule of \(L\simeq K^{[L:K]}\). By (AM.4a), \(B/aB\), and hence its submodule \(J/aB\), has finite length over \(R\). Lifts of finitely many \(R\)-generators of this quotient, together with \(a\), generate \(J\) as a \(B\)-ideal. The zero ideal is already finite. This proves the local one-dimensional Krull–Akizuki assertion needed here. It does not assert that \(B\) is finite as an \(R\)-module.

**A discrete valuation witness.** Let \((A,\mathfrak n)\) be any Noetherian local domain which is not a field, with fraction field \(F\). [Valuation rings and separatedness, Theorem 2.1](course:AG-MO/valuation-rings-and-separatedness#2-a-valuation-ring-over-every-local-subring) constructs a valuation ring \(V\subset F\) dominating \(A\). In a finite nonzero generating list of \(\mathfrak n\), choose \(a\) of least value. The ring \(S=A[\mathfrak n/a]\) lies in \(V\), and \(\mathfrak nS=aS\ne S\). For a prime \(\mathfrak q\) minimal over \(aS\), the principal height theorem Y.3 gives height one. Its contraction contains \(\mathfrak n\), hence equals \(\mathfrak n\). Thus \(R=S_{\mathfrak q}\subset F\) is a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain dominating \(A\), with fraction field \(F\).

Take the integral closure \(B\) of \(R\) in \(F\). The preceding length argument makes \(B\) Noetherian. Integral transitivity makes it integrally closed. Lying over gives a prime \(\mathfrak p\) above the maximal ideal of \(R\). Its height is one: primes contract along the integral map, strict inclusions have strict contractions by incomparability, and localization at all nonzero elements of \(R\) is the field \(F\). The normal Noetherian local domain \(B_{\mathfrak p}\) is therefore a DVR by L.1. It dominates \(A\) and has fraction field \(F\). None of these steps presumes that the integral closure is a finite \(R\)-module.

For a strict specialization \(x_1\leadsto x_0\) in a locally Noetherian scheme, apply this construction to
\(A=\mathcal O_{\overline{\{x_1\}}_{\mathrm{red}},x_0}\).
It is a local domain with nonzero maximal ideal and fraction field \(\kappa(x_1)\). We obtain
\[
\operatorname{Spec}R\longrightarrow X,\qquad
\eta_R\longmapsto x_1,\quad 0_R\longmapsto x_0,
\tag{AM.5}
\]
where \(R\) is a DVR and \(\operatorname{Frac}R=\kappa(x_1)\). No restriction on the characteristic or on the residue-field extension at the closed point is needed. For the trivial specialization one may use \(\kappa(x_0)[t]_{(t)}\).

Apply this to \(x_0\in X^0\) and a generization \(x_1\) in the smooth family. Base change \(X\to S\) along the composite \(\operatorname{Spec}R\to X\to S\). Besides \(\sigma_R\), the resulting family \(X_R\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) has the section \(\tau\) given by (AM.5).

The total scheme \(X_R\) is regular. To see this using the proved local algebra, Y.5 shows that polynomial rings over the regular Noetherian ring \(R\) have regular local rings. The standard smooth presentation AE.1 realizes a local ring of \(X_R\) as the quotient of such a regular local ring by relations with an invertible Jacobian minor. Differentiation over \(R\) kills products of maximal-ideal elements modulo that ideal, so the minor makes the classes of these relations independent in the cotangent space. Y.4 proves that the quotient is regular. This argument applies at every prime, including those on the generic fibre.

Consequently the finitely many components of \(X_R\) are disjoint, open, closed and integral. By (AM.2), the closed points of \(\sigma_R\) and \(\tau\) lie in the same connected component of the special fibre. They therefore lie in the same component \(E\) of the total scheme. Each section has connected image, so both entire sections lie in \(E\). Its generic fibre is a nonempty open of the integral scheme \(E\), hence is integral and connected. Their generic points therefore lie in the same connected component of the generic fibre. Equation (AM.2) gives \(x_1\in X^0\).

Thus \(X^0\) is constructible and stable under generization. The criterion (AC.4) makes it open. It is retrocompact, meaning that its intersection with any quasi-compact open of \(X\) is quasi-compact, since \(X\) is Noetherian.

For later use take \(X\to S\) affine and smooth of finite presentation over an arbitrary affine scheme \(S=\operatorname{Spec}A\), with a section. Write \(A\) as the filtered union of its finitely generated \(\mathbf Z\)-subalgebras. These are Noetherian by [Noetherian and Artinian rings, Theorem 2.1](course:AG-CA/noetherian-and-artinian-rings#2-polynomial-rings-and-finite-geometric-descriptions). AH.4 descends the presentation, section and its identities to one stage. Smoothness descends as follows. The conormal splitting and local generator argument at the start of AE.1 use only finite presentation, finite projective modules and Nakayama; they give standard Jacobian charts over an arbitrary ring as well. Choose finitely many such charts. Descend their equations, inverse determinants and presentation isomorphisms, together with the finite identities saying that they cover. The square-Jacobian lifting calculation makes the stage smooth. Pull back its open component, proved above over a Noetherian base. Equation (AM.2) identifies that pullback with \(X^0\). It is quasi-compact, because the stage open is a finite union of principal opens in the affine stage of \(X\). The same description shows retrocompactness after arbitrary base change.

This argument also supplies the flatness and openness needed below over a non-Noetherian base. A standard chart descends to a smooth chart over one of those Noetherian rings, where AE.1 and AC.3 prove flatness and openness. Flatness survives base change by associativity of tensor products. The image of a base-changed morphism is the inverse image of its image: a nonempty scheme over a residue field stays nonempty after extending that field, since an affine coordinate algebra tensors faithfully with a field extension. Therefore the descended open image remains open after base change. Apply this to the principal opens of each chart and take unions. Smooth morphisms, including étale morphisms, are consequently open over every base used here.

### AM.5. Producing the section at a separable point

Separable closed points are dense in a smooth finite-type \(K\)-scheme. In any nonempty open choose a standard étale coordinate chart to affine space; AE.1 and AC.3 show that its image is open. Over \(K^{\mathrm s}\) this image contains a rational point. Here \(K^{\mathrm s}\) is infinite: a finite field with \(q\) elements is not separably closed, since \(T^q-T-1\) is separable and has no root there. Over an infinite field a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish at every tuple, by induction on the number of variables and the root bound in one variable. Applying this to a principal open inside the image supplies the point. Its nonempty étale fibre has a \(K^{\mathrm s}\)-point by the finite separable field description AB.1. The coordinates of that point lie in a finite separable extension of \(K\). Its image is a closed point with finite separable residue extension, by Y.5. This proves density in every open and every connected component.

Suppose \(y\in X_s\) is such a point, with \(L=\kappa(y)\). A pointed étale change of base gives a section through it, as follows. Choose a primitive element for \(L/\kappa(s)\). Over an infinite base field the embedding-separation argument Z.3 proves its existence. Over a finite base, \(L\) is finite and its multiplicative group is cyclic: for each prime choose an element whose order has the largest possible power of that prime, take its primary part, and multiply these commuting elements. The product has order the exponent \(m\) of the group. Every element is a root of \(T^m-1\), so the root bound forces the group to have at most \(m\) elements, hence exactly \(m\). A generator then generates \(L\) as a field. Lift the primitive element's monic separable polynomial to functions near \(s\), clearing finitely many denominators. Inverting its derivative gives an affine étale \(S'\to S\) with a point \(t\) of residue field \(L\). In \(X_{S'}\) the selected point is \(L\)-rational over \(t\).

Choose a standard étale chart \(W\to\mathbf A^d_{S'}\) near this point. Such a chart uses the free variables in the square-Jacobian presentation AE.1; it needs no assertion about an arbitrary choice of coordinates. Lift their values at the selected point to functions on an affine neighbourhood of \(t\). The resulting map \(a:S'\to\mathbf A^d_{S'}\) defines

\[
T=W\times_{\mathbf A^d_{S'},\,a}S'.
\tag{AM.6}
\]

It is affine and étale over \(S'\), with a selected point of residue field \(L\). The projection \(T\to X\) gives, by its graph, a section of \(X_T\to T\). This is the explicit construction in [Smooth morphisms, Theorem 5.2](course:AG-FSE/smooth-morphisms#5-slicing-and-étale-local-sections), with the standard-coordinate and separable-point inputs proved above. It asserts a section through a separable closed fibre point; it does not assert one through every point with an arbitrary residue field.

### AM.6. Covering every point of the family

Let \(x\) be any point of a smooth morphism \(X\to S\) over an arbitrary base. Restrict first to affine neighbourhoods of \(x\) and \(s=f(x)\). The restricted smooth morphism is of finite presentation. Let \(C\) be the connected component of \(X_s\) containing \(x\), and choose a separable closed point \(y\in C\) by AM.5. Construct the affine étale \(T\to S\), selected \(t\in T\) with residue \(L=\kappa(y)\), and section of \(X_T\to T\) just described.

The component \(C'\) of \(C_L\) containing that \(L\)-rational point is geometrically integral by AM.1. Its map to \(C\) is finite and flat: \(C_L\to C\) is finite free, and an open-and-closed component cuts out a direct summand of its finite locally free algebra. Its image is closed by finiteness and open by AE.1 for the étale map \(C_L\to C\), restricted to this open component. The image is nonempty, so connectedness of \(C\) makes it all of \(C\). Choose a lift \(\widetilde x\in C'\) of the original \(x\).

The affine scheme \(X_T\) has the open component \(X_T^0\) of AM.4. It contains both \(\widetilde x\) and the section point over \(t\). There is a principal open \(D(b)\subset X_T^0\) containing both points. Indeed, the ideal of the closed complement is contained in neither of their prime ideals. For two primes one can choose an element outside both: if elements chosen outside the respective primes each lie in the other, their sum lies in neither. This gives the required \(b\).

Choose an affine open \(V\subset T\) containing \(t\) and contained in \(\sigma^{-1}D(b)\). Set \(U=D(b)\times_TV\), an affine fibre product. Then \(U\to V\) is smooth with a section. Each geometric fibre is a nonempty open subset of the corresponding geometrically integral fibre of \(X_T^0\), and is therefore geometrically integral and connected. Also \(U\to X\) and \(V\to S\) are étale, and the image of \(U\to X\) contains the original \(x\). Applying this construction at every \(x\) proves:

**Connected-fibre neighbourhood theorem.** A smooth morphism of schemes over an arbitrary base has an étale covering \(\{U_i\to X\}\) with factorizations \(U_i\to V_i\to S\), where \(U_i,V_i\) are affine, \(V_i\to S\) is étale, and \(U_i\to V_i\) is smooth, has a section, and has geometrically connected fibres.

### AM.7. Use in the comparison argument

AM.6 supplies the connected-fibre neighbourhoods for [Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Section 2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#2-degree-zero-and-the-geometric-inputs) over arbitrary bases, including mixed characteristic. AN.1 consequently proves degree-zero smooth comparison in this same generality. The proof is local on the source and imposes no quasi-compactness condition on the morphism whose ordinary direct image occurs in degree zero.

The generic-cover extension is a different input. AN.2–AN.6 supply formal neighbourhoods, AO.1–AO.6 coherent algebra extension and relative purity, AP.1–AP.7 regular local purity and tame DVR extensions, and AQ.1–AQ.5 their split-section descent. AR.1–AR.5 then prove the generic-cover extension over integral normal Noetherian bases, including mixed characteristic. These assertions retain their stated hypotheses.

For the positive-degree induction, finite affine models must also have finite normalization in finite function-field extensions. AG.1–AG.3 prove this over fields; AG.5 proves it for finite-type integer models by local polynomial charts, AW.5 and the separable trace lattice. AS.4 therefore descends the diagram to finite-type \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\)-models, retaining the inverse of the coefficient modulus. AS.5 uses AG.5 for every finite replacement, and AS.6 completes the dimension and cohomological inductions. The one-dimensional Noetherianity argument of AM.4 is distinct from this module-finiteness proof. Together these inputs establish the general-base torsion comparison at the coefficient scope specified in AS, which is also the scope used in AT and Proposition 3.1.

## Appendix AN. Sections and formal neighbourhoods in smooth comparison

There are two different extension problems in the smooth-comparison argument. A section of a pulled-back sheaf descends along the connected-fibre charts of AM.6. A finite étale cover near a section of a smooth family can be compared with its restriction to a punctured zero section in a power-series ring. We prove these assertions and the formal algebra they require.

### AN.1. A section gives degree-zero comparison

Let \(a:U\to V\) be smooth, with geometrically connected fibres and a section \(\sigma\). For an étale sheaf of sets \(A\) on \(V\), pullback is a bijection

\[
\Gamma(V,A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Gamma(U,a^{-1}A),
\qquad b\longmapsto a^{-1}b.
\tag{AN.1}
\]

Its proposed inverse is restriction along \(\sigma\). One composite is the identity because \(a\sigma=1\). To check the other, fix a geometric point \(\bar v\) of \(V\). On \(U_{\bar v}\) the coefficient sheaf is constant with value \(A_{\bar v}\): the étale topos of the separably closed point is the category of sets, by AB.1–AB.2, and inverse images compose. A section of a constant sheaf on a connected scheme has one value. In this situation that statement can be checked directly. Represent the section on an étale covering by constant labels. The images of the labelled pieces are open, by AE.1 and AC.3 on the smooth geometric fibre. Pieces with different labels have disjoint images, since a point in both images gives a geometric point of their fibre product, where the sheaf compatibility equates the labels. These images partition the fibre into open-and-closed subsets. Connectedness makes exactly one label occur.

The value of a section upstairs is therefore its value at \(\sigma(\bar v)\). Its restriction to every geometric fibre agrees with the pullback of its restriction along \(\sigma\). Equality on geometric stalks proves equality of sheaf sections, and proves (AN.1). No finiteness of the set of labels was assumed.

Now consider a cartesian square of schemes over an arbitrary base as in (1.1) of [Smooth base change and local acyclicity](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#1-which-morphism-is-smooth), with \(f:X\to S\) smooth and \(g:T\to S\) any morphism. Write \(Y=X\times_ST\), with projections \(h:Y\to X\) and \(e:Y\to T\). For every étale sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(T\), the canonical map

\[
f^{-1}g_*F\longrightarrow h_*e^{-1}F
\tag{AN.2}
\]

is an isomorphism. Indeed, apply AM.6 to each affine étale test object over \(X\). It gives a covering by \(U\)'s with \(U\xrightarrow a V\to S\), where \(V\to S\) is étale and \(a\) has geometrically connected fibres and a section. Its change of base along \(V\times_ST\to V\) has the same properties. Formula (AN.1) on these two families gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma(U,f^{-1}g_*F)
&=\Gamma(V,g_*F)\\
&=\Gamma(V\times_ST,F)\\
&=\Gamma(U\times_ST,e^{-1}F)\\
&=\Gamma(U,h_*e^{-1}F).
\end{aligned}
\tag{AN.3}
\]

Restriction to the étale \(V\) is the localization of the site, as in AB.3. Each displayed map is pullback of sections, so the composite is exactly (AN.2). A morphism of sheaves which is a bijection on this covering basis is an isomorphism: local lifts glue by local injectivity, and equality is detected on the same covers. This proves degree-zero smooth comparison over an arbitrary base, without a separate faithfully flat descent theorem for arbitrary étale sheaves. It makes no positive-degree comparison claim.

### AN.2. Completion along a smooth section

Let \(A\) be Noetherian local, let \(B\) be a smooth \(A\)-algebra, and let \(\sigma:B\to A\) split the structure map. Put \(I=\ker\sigma\). The module \(I/I^2\) is finite free over \(A\). In fact, writing \(b=\sigma(b)+(b-\sigma(b))\) identifies derivations from \(B\) to an \(A\)-module, on which \(B\) acts through \(\sigma\), with linear maps from \(I/I^2\). Thus
\(I/I^2=\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_{B,\sigma}A\). The conormal splitting AE.1 makes \(\Omega_{B/A}\) finite projective, and U.1 makes its pullback free over local \(A\).

Choose lifts \(f_1,\ldots,f_d\in I\) of a basis and put \(P=A[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\), \(J=(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). The map \(t_i\mapsto f_i\) induces

\[
\Psi_n:P/J^n\longrightarrow B/I^n.
\tag{AN.4}
\]

It is surjective: the basis generates \(I/I^2\), its degree-\(r\) products generate \(I^r/I^{r+1}\), and induction lifts through the finite filtration. It is an isomorphism for \(n=2\), since both algebras are \(A\) plus the same square-zero module.

Suppose an inverse has been constructed at level \(n-1\), where \(n\ge3\). Formal smoothness lifts the corresponding map \(B\to P/J^{n-1}\) to \(B\to P/J^n\). The lift sends \(I\) into \(J/J^n\), hence factors through \(B/I^n\). Composed with \(\Psi_n\), it sends \(t_i\) to \(t_i+\delta_i\), with \(\delta_i\in J^{n-1}/J^n\). This is an automorphism: the substitutions \(t_i-\delta_i\) are inverse, because changing a monomial of degree at least \(n-1\) by these corrections changes it only in degree at least \(n\). Hence \(\Psi_n\) is injective as well as surjective. Its inverses are uniquely compatible. Taking limits proves

\[
\widehat B^{\,I}\simeq A[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]].
\tag{AN.5}
\]

We will use flatness of this completion. For a Noetherian ring \(R\) and any ideal \(K\), L.1 proves exactness of completion on finite modules and \(\widehat M=M\otimes_R\widehat R\). This already proves flatness on arbitrary modules. Given \(N\subset M\), express \(M\) as the filtered union of its finite submodules \(M_\lambda\). Each \(N\cap M_\lambda\) is finite. Their tensorized injections into \(M_\lambda\otimes_R\widehat R\) are injective by L.1; filtered colimits preserve these injections and identify their source and target with \(N\otimes_R\widehat R\) and \(M\otimes_R\widehat R\). Thus \(R\to\widehat R\) is flat.

L.1 also proves that \(\widehat R\) is Noetherian and that its ideal-power quotients are the original quotients. In particular \(A[[t]]\) is Noetherian and flat over \(A\), by applying completion to \(A[t]\). It is local with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_A A[[t]]+(t)\): a series with unit constant term has an inverse by recursive coefficient multiplication, and reduction modulo \((t)\) identifies the remaining maximal ideals with those of \(A\).

### AN.3. Two depth calculations

We use depth at least two in its regular-sequence meaning: in a Noetherian local ring \((A,\mathfrak m)\), there are \(a,b\in\mathfrak m\) with \(a\) injective on \(A\), \(b\) injective on \(A/aA\), and \(A/(a,b)\ne0\).

Such a pair gives the algebraic Hartogs identity

\[
A=\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\},\mathcal O).
\tag{AN.6}
\]

First \(b\) is injective on \(A\). Its finite kernel \(K\) satisfies \(K=aK\): reduce an element of \(K\) modulo \(a\), then cancel \(a\). Nakayama gives \(K=0\). The filtration of \(A/a^nA\) by powers of \(a\) has factors \(A/aA\), so \(b\), and then every positive power of \(b\), acts injectively on \(A/a^nA\).

Put \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\). Restriction of a section on \(U\) to \(D(a)\) is injective. On each affine principal open contained in \(U\), a section zero after inverting \(a\) is killed by a power of the nonzerodivisor \(a\), hence is zero. Its values on \(D(a)\) and \(D(b)\) agree in \(A_{ab}\). Write them as \(u/a^n\) and \(v/b^r\). Equality implies \(b^ru=a^nv\), because \(ab\) is a nonzerodivisor. Injectivity of \(b^r\) on \(A/a^nA\) gives \(u\in a^nA\). Thus the section on \(D(a)\), and consequently on \(U\), comes from \(A\). This proves (AN.6).

A second calculation concerns associated primes. If a finite nonzero module \(M\) over a Noetherian local ring \(R\) has a regular list of length \(r\), then

\[
r\le\dim(R/\mathfrak p)
\quad\text{for every }\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}(M).
\tag{AN.7}
\]

The required associated-prime facts—existence, localization, submodule inclusion and minimal support—are proved in [Associated primes and primary decomposition, Sections 1–3](course:AG-CA/associated-primes-and-primary-decomposition#1-annihilators-that-are-prime). Here is a proof of the bound which uses regular lists directly. Induct on \(r\). For first entry \(x\), an associated copy \(N=R/\mathfrak p\subset M\) has \(x\notin\mathfrak p\). The one-equation dimension calculation Y.3 gives a prime \(\mathfrak q\) minimal over \(\mathfrak p+(x)\) with
\(\dim R/\mathfrak q=\dim R/\mathfrak p-1\).
Artin–Rees supplies \(n\) with \(N\cap x^nM\subset xN\). The image
\(L=N/(N\cap x^nM)\subset M/x^nM\) maps onto \(N/xN\). Thus \(\mathfrak q\) is a minimal point of its support and is associated to \(L\), hence to \(M/x^nM\).

The remaining \(r-1\) entries are regular on \(M/x^nM\). To verify this, filter that module by the powers of \(x\); its factors are \(M/xM\). An element injective on the two ends of a short exact sequence is injective in the middle, and the sequence of its quotients is still exact. Apply this successively to the remaining entries. The final filtered quotient is nonzero since its factors are the nonzero final quotient for the original list. Induction at \(\mathfrak q\) gives (AN.7). The power-filtration step is also proved in [Regular sequences, Proposition 1.3](course:AG-CA/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules#1-equations-that-act-injectively). This gives the associated-point depth bound directly from regular lists, without requiring an Ext characterization of depth.

For the normal local bases in AL.5, the regular pair exists whenever the dimension is at least two. Indeed, an associated prime of \(A/aA\), with \(a\ne0\), localizes to a normal local domain \(R\) in which a fraction \(u\notin R\) satisfies \(u\mathfrak m_R\subset R\). If it preserved \(\mathfrak m_R\), the determinant trick would make \(u\) integral. Otherwise \(u\mathfrak m_R=R\), so the maximal ideal is principal and has height one by Y.3. Thus every associated prime of \(A/aA\) has height one. Finiteness and prime avoidance choose \(b\in\mathfrak m_A\) outside their union when \(\dim A\ge2\), giving the pair. This is [Normal rings, Proposition 3.4](course:AG-CA/discrete-valuation-rings-normal-rings-and-serres-criterion#3-normal-domains-and-codimension-one-detection); its determinant argument is the same one used in L.1.

### AN.4. Functions on a punctured formal neighbourhood

Let \(A\) be Noetherian local of depth at least two, let
\(B=A[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]\), \(d\ge1\), and put \(I=(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). Let \(V\subset\operatorname{Spec}B\) be any open whose intersection \(V_0\) with \(V(I)=\operatorname{Spec}A\) is the puncture \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m_A\}\). Set \(V_n=V\cap\operatorname{Spec}(B/I^n)\). We claim

\[
B=\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\varprojlim_n\Gamma(V_n,\mathcal O_{V_n}).
\tag{AN.8}
\]

Each \(V_n\) is the truncated polynomial thickening of \(U\). Its coordinate sheaf, viewed on \(U\), is a finite direct sum of copies of \(\mathcal O_U\), indexed by the monomials of total degree less than \(n\). Formula (AN.6) identifies its sections with \(A[t]/(t)^n\), and their limit with \(B\). The composite from \(B\) through the two maps in (AN.8) is therefore the identity. We must still check that restriction from \(\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)\) to that limit is injective.

The list \(t_1,\ldots,t_d,a,b\) is regular in \(B\), with \(a,b\) a regular pair in \(A\). Consequently (AN.7) gives
\(\dim B/\mathfrak p\ge d+2\) for every \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}(B)\).
There is a nonmaximal prime \(\mathfrak q\) containing \(\mathfrak p+I\). Otherwise the maximal ideal of \(B/\mathfrak p\) would be the radical of an ideal generated by the \(d\) variables, contradicting the height bound Y.3. Such \(\mathfrak q\) lies in \(V_0\), and its generization \(\mathfrak p\) lies in \(V\).

If a section on \(V\) vanishes at every finite formal level, its germ at \(\mathfrak q\) belongs to every \(I^nB_{\mathfrak q}\), and is zero by the Krull-intersection proof in L.1. Its germ at \(\mathfrak p\) is therefore zero. This applies to every associated prime of \(B\). It forces the section itself to be zero: on a principal affine covering of \(V\), a nonzero section has a nonzero cyclic submodule with an associated element; localization of associated primes identifies it with an associated prime of \(B\) at which that section survives. This contradicts what we just proved. Thus restriction is injective, and its split identity with \(B\) proves both equalities in (AN.8).

### AN.5. From functions to maps of vector bundles

For every finite locally free sheaf \(E\) on this \(V\), (AN.8) extends to

\[
\Gamma(V,E)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\varprojlim_n\Gamma(V_n,E|_{V_n}).
\tag{AN.9}
\]

We give the finite generation argument needed to pass from functions to \(E\). A vector bundle on a quasi-compact open of an affine scheme is generated by finitely many global sections. Choose a finite covering by principal opens on which it is free. For a principal \(D(f)\subset V\), the map
\(\Gamma(V,E)_f\to\Gamma(D(f),E)\) is an isomorphism: compute sections by the equalizer for a finite principal affine covering of \(V\), and localize that equalizer. Localization is exact and commutes with finite products; on each affine chart it is the usual localization formula for a quasi-coherent module, proved in W.1. Clearing the finitely many denominators in the local bases gives global generators.

Apply this to \(E^\vee\) and dualize a finite free surjection onto it. We get an injection \(E\to\mathcal O_V^r\) with locally free cokernel \(C\), because that surjection splits on trivializing opens. Applying the same construction to \(C\) gives a sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow\mathcal O_V^r
\longrightarrow\mathcal O_V^s
\tag{AN.10}
\]

which stays exact after every base change. Sections of \(E\) are the kernel of the indicated map on functions. The same holds at every \(V_n\). Inverse limits preserve kernels, so (AN.8) proves (AN.9). Applying (AN.9) to \(E^\vee\otimes F\) shows that every compatible system of bundle maps on the \(V_n\) comes from exactly one bundle map on \(V\). This proves the quasi-affine case of [Formal geometry, Proposition 2.1](course:AG-LCL/formal-geometry#2-what-comparison-of-sections-proves) directly, without an ample-generation prerequisite.

### AN.6. Finite étale covers and the punctured zero section

Restriction is fully faithful:

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{FÉt}(V_0).
\tag{AN.11}
\]

Let \(P,Q\) be finite étale over \(V\), with algebras \(E_P,E_Q\), finite locally free over \(\mathcal O_V\). A map \(P|_{V_0}\to Q|_{V_0}\) lifts uniquely to every \(V_n\). The required infinitesimal assertion follows from the square-Jacobian equations for an étale map. Across a square-zero ideal, lift the coordinates arbitrarily, then cancel the error in the equations by multiplying it by the inverse Jacobian. Taylor expansion has no higher terms in that ideal. The same invertible matrix makes the correction unique. Iterate through the powers of a nilpotent ideal. Local lifts glue by uniqueness, so this proves the assertion for the schemes \(P|_{V_n}\), not only for an affine chart.

The lifts give compatible algebra maps \(E_Q|_{V_n}\to E_P|_{V_n}\). Formula (AN.9), applied to their Hom bundle, gives a unique module map on \(V\). It is an algebra map: the difference of its two multiplication maps, and the difference of its unit map from the required unit, vanish after every restriction. Faithfulness of (AN.9) on the relevant tensor and Hom bundles makes those differences zero. Conversely two algebra maps agreeing on \(V_0\) agree at every finite level by the same unique lifting, and hence agree on \(V\). This proves (AN.11), including the uniqueness of an extended isomorphism and its inverse.

In the specific case \(V=U\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\operatorname{Spec}B\), projection gives a map \(V\to U=V_0\). For a finite étale \(W\to V\), its restriction \(W_0\to U\) and the cover \(W_0\times_UV\) have the same restriction at the zero section. Full faithfulness extends that identity and its inverse to give

\[
W\simeq W_0\times_UV.
\tag{AN.12}
\]

In particular, if \(W_0\) is a disjoint union of copies of \(U\), then \(W\) is the corresponding disjoint union of copies of \(V\). This is the precise punctured power-series comparison used in the formal calculation of the generic-cover extension.

### AN.7. From formal comparison to extension

AN.2 constructs the completed smooth section and its flat completion map. AN.3 supplies the regular pair on a normal local base of dimension at least two, and AN.4–AN.6 prove full faithfulness on the punctured formal neighbourhood, including (AN.12). These results justify that formal comparison once the finite cover is present there.

The passage from this formal comparison to actual extension of the cover is proved in AO.1–AO.6: coherent extension of its algebra, flat-base-change compatibility, essential extension over the power-series neighbourhood and purity in a smooth family over a Noetherian base. AP.1–AP.7 add absolute regular local purity and the tame root-base-change calculation over a DVR. AQ.1–AQ.5 supply codimension-one gluing and descent at the section and prove the discrete-valuation-base case of AL.5. AR.1–AR.5 assemble the full generic-cover theorem over an integral normal Noetherian base. AN.1 proves degree-zero smooth comparison over arbitrary bases. For a quasi-compact, quasi-separated direct-image morphism, AS.1–AS.7 prove the positive-degree comparison for torsion sheaves with invertible annihilators and the stated filtered unions. The argument uses the connected-fibre neighbourhoods of AM.6 and the finite normalization of integer models in AG.5. AT.1–AT.5 give strict-local acyclicity, the selected-neighbourhood colimit and the ordinary nearby-cycle unit for the same allowed torsion orders.

## Appendix AO. Extending the cover algebra and removing a fibrewise branch locus

The formal comparison in AN.6 concerns a cover already defined on an open set. We now construct its finite algebra across the complement. Two regular elements recover functions, and a presentation by vector bundles recovers the algebra. This construction then lets us use the formal comparison to extend the cover itself.

### AO.1. Hartogs across a depth-two complement

Let \(R\) be Noetherian, let \(U=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus V(J)\), and suppose that \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) has depth at least two for every \(\mathfrak p\supset J\). Then

\[
R\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U).
\tag{AO.1}
\]

The case \(J=R\) is immediate. Otherwise we first find \(a,b\in J\) such that both are nonzerodivisors on \(R\) and \(b\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(R/aR\). We use the finiteness, zero-divisor detection and localization of associated primes proved in [Associated primes, Sections 1–3](course:AG-CA/associated-primes-and-primary-decomposition#1-annihilators-that-are-prime), and its Solution 8.5 on finite prime avoidance. No associated prime of \(R\) contains \(J\): at such a prime the local maximal ideal annihilates a nonzero element, contradicting the existence of even one regular element. Avoiding the finitely many associated primes therefore gives \(a\in J\) regular on \(R\).

No associated prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(R/aR\) contains \(J\) either. If it did, put \(T=R_{\mathfrak p}\). There would be \(u\notin aT\) with \(\mathfrak m_Tu\subset aT\). In \(T[1/a]\), the fraction \(u/a\) belongs to \(T_r\) for every \(r\in\mathfrak m_T\): write \(ru=av\), so that the fraction is \(v/r\). These values agree on intersections because multiplication by \(a\) is injective in every localization. They give a section on the punctured spectrum of \(T\). AN.3 identifies that section with an element of \(T\), forcing \(u\in aT\), a contradiction. Prime avoidance, now for \(\operatorname{Ass}(R)\cup\operatorname{Ass}(R/aR)\), supplies \(b\).

The power filtration makes \(b^r\) injective on \(R/a^nR\) for all positive \(n,r\), exactly as in AN.3. A section on \(U\) has values \(u/a^n\) and \(v/b^r\) on \(D(a)\) and \(D(b)\). Equality on \(D(ab)\), and cancellation of the nonzerodivisor \(ab\), give \(b^ru=a^nv\). Thus \(u\in a^nR\). Restriction from \(U\) to \(D(a)\) is injective: on every principal affine chart of \(U\), vanishing after inverting \(a\) means annihilation by a power of a nonzerodivisor. This proves (AO.1), including injectivity.

The same statement holds locally on a locally Noetherian scheme \(X\): if \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) has depth at least two at every missing point, then

\[
\mathcal O_X=j_*\mathcal O_U.
\tag{AO.2}
\]

Trivializing a vector bundle on affine opens proves the corresponding assertion for every finite locally free sheaf on \(X\), including its Hom and tensor bundles.
