Consequently restriction of finite étale covers from \(X\) to \(U\) is fully faithful. Indeed the underlying algebra map extends as a bundle map; its unit and multiplication identities are equalities of bundle maps and are detected on \(U\).

### AO.2. A finite presentation of the extended bundle

Keep \(X=\operatorname{Spec}R\) and \(U\) as above, and let \(E\) be finite locally free on \(U\). AN.5 supplies a sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow\mathcal O_U^r
\xrightarrow{\ D\ }\mathcal O_U^s
\tag{AO.3}
\]

which remains exact after every base change. Its proof uses only a finite principal covering of the quasi-compact open \(U\), localization of its section equalizer, and finite global generators of the dual bundles. In particular it applies to this \(U\). Each matrix coefficient of \(D\) belongs to \(\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)=R\). Therefore

\[
M:=\Gamma(U,E)=\ker(R^r\xrightarrow D R^s)
\tag{AO.4}
\]

is a finite \(R\)-module. Localizing the finite section equalizer shows that \(M_f=\Gamma(U\cap D(f),E)\). Thus \(\widetilde M=j_*E\); in particular its restriction to \(U\) is \(E\). These intrinsic descriptions glue over affine opens of any locally Noetherian \(X\).

The extension is reflexive, even when \(R\) is not a domain. A section of \(E^\vee\) gives a map \(M\to R\) by taking sections of its evaluation map and using (AO.1). Conversely a map \(M\to R\) restricts to a section of \(E^\vee\). These operations are inverse: their restrictions agree on \(U\), and a map to \(R\) whose restriction is zero kills every element of \(M\) by injectivity in (AO.1). Hence

\[
M^*=\Gamma(U,E^\vee),\qquad
M^{**}=\Gamma(U,E^{\vee\vee})=M.
\tag{AO.5}
\]

There is also a direct depth check. At a missing point put \(T=R_{\mathfrak p}\), and choose a regular pair \(a,b\) in its maximal ideal. The module \(M_{\mathfrak p}\) is a kernel between finite free \(T\)-modules. Multiplication by \(a\) is injective on this kernel. If \(bm=an\) in it, regularity of \(b\) modulo \(a\) in the ambient free module gives \(m=av\). Applying \(D\) gives \(aD(v)=0\), hence \(D(v)=0\), so \(v\) belongs to the kernel. Thus \(b\) is injective modulo \(aM_{\mathfrak p}\). If the kernel is nonzero, its final quotient by \((a,b)\) is nonzero by Nakayama. It has depth at least two.

For a flat map \(R\to R'\), use a finite principal covering of \(U\) in the section equalizer. Its terms and pairwise intersections are affine. Flat tensoring preserves the kernel and the finite products in that equalizer, and quasi-coherent sections on each chart commute with affine base change. It follows that the natural map

\[
M\otimes_R R'\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\Gamma(U\times_R R',E\otimes_R R')
\tag{AO.6}
\]

is an isomorphism. This argument proves the degree-zero flat base change needed here directly. It does not require a theorem on higher direct images.

### AO.3. The finite algebra and the test for étaleness

If \(E=\pi_*\mathcal O_W\) for a finite étale \(\pi:W\to U\), multiplication and unit on sections turn (AO.4) into a finite \(R\)-algebra \(C\). Its spectrum restricts to \(W\). At a point \(y\) over a missing point \(\mathfrak p\), the regular pair just constructed on \(C_{\mathfrak p}\) remains regular after localizing at \(y\). Its entries lie in the maximal ideal of \(C_y\), so Nakayama gives a nonzero final quotient there. Thus \(C_y\) has depth at least two.

This characterizes the finite extension uniquely. For any other finite extension \(\operatorname{Spec}D\) with depth at least two at every point outside \(W\), apply (AO.1) on \(\operatorname{Spec}D\) itself, with open \(W\). It gives \(D=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)=C\), compatibly with the given restriction. This avoids any separate theorem transferring depth through a finite map. All algebra maps are recovered by taking sections. The construction commutes with flat base change by (AO.6).

It also commutes with enlarging the open on which the cover is étale. If \(U\subset U'\subset X\) and a finite étale cover on \(U'\) extends the given cover on \(U\), apply (AO.2) to its algebra bundle on \(U'\). Its direct image to \(X\) is the same algebra \(j_*E\). In particular the restriction of the canonical finite extension to \(U'\) is precisely that cover.

For this extension we have the useful global criterion

\[
\operatorname{Spec}_X(j_*E)\longrightarrow X
\text{ is finite étale}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j_*E\text{ is locally free}.
\tag{AO.7}
\]

We give the algebra behind this criterion. Over a Noetherian ring \(R\), a finite locally free commutative algebra \(C\) is étale if its module \(\Omega_{C/R}\) vanishes. To see this from local equations, first pass a fibre to an algebraic closure \(L\) of its residue field. Differentials commute with base change by their universal property. The finite \(L\)-algebra in the fibre is a product of local Artinian algebras. Indeed its primes are finitely many maximal ideals, its nilradical is nilpotent (take a common power for finitely many nilpotent generators), and sufficiently large powers of those comaximal maximal ideals have zero product; the Chinese remainder argument gives the factors. In each factor with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak n\), its cotangent space is
\(\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2=\Omega\otimes L\), since its residue field and the coefficient field are both \(L\). Nakayama makes \(\mathfrak n=0\). The fibre is therefore a product of copies of \(L\); the descent argument in AB.1 makes each original fibre a product of finite separable residue fields.

Now present \(C=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/K\). At a prime of \(C\), the vanishing of differentials says that the gradients of relations generate the free module with basis \(dx_1,\ldots,dx_n\). Choose \(n\) relations whose square Jacobian determinant is invertible there. The resulting algebra \(D\), localized at that determinant, is étale by the square-Jacobian lifting in AB.1. There is a surjection from its local ring at the chosen point onto the corresponding local ring of \(C\). Both closed fibres over the local base are the same finite separable field: the source is an étale local fibre and the residue-field map of this surjection is an isomorphism. If \(L_0\) is the kernel of this local surjection, flatness of \(C\) over the base makes reduction of
\(0\to L_0\to D\to C\to0\) injective on the left. Thus \(L_0/\mathfrak m_RL_0=0\). This kernel is finite over the Noetherian local ring \(D\), so Nakayama makes it zero. Clearing denominators in its finite generators gives an étale neighbourhood of the original point. This proves the criterion. The converse follows either from the same square-Jacobian equations or from the uniqueness of infinitesimal lifts.

The equivalent trace criterion is particularly convenient. For finite locally free \(C\), let

\[
\theta_C:C\longrightarrow C^*,\qquad
c\longmapsto\bigl(d\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{C/R}(cd)\bigr).
\tag{AO.8}
\]

It is an isomorphism exactly when \(C\) is étale. Indeed trace matrices commute with base change. Over an algebraically closed field, a nilpotent element pairs to zero with every element, since all those multiplication matrices are nilpotent. A perfect trace pairing therefore forces a finite algebra to be reduced, hence to be a product of copies of the field by AB.1's finite-prime and Chinese-remainder argument. Its differentials vanish. Nakayama in every local ring then gives \(\Omega_{C/R}=0\), and the preceding criterion applies. Conversely the trace pairing of a product of copies of a field is the identity matrix. Testing the determinant after extension to algebraic closures of the residue fields proves perfection for every finite étale algebra.

If our extended algebra is locally free on \(X\), the inverse of (AO.8) on \(U\) extends to \(X\) by (AO.2) for the appropriate Hom bundle. Its two inverse identities are detected on \(U\), so it is an inverse everywhere. This proves (AO.7). The reverse implication includes the local freeness of finite flat algebras, proved by the residue-basis and Nakayama argument in N.1 and AD.1.

We will also use faithfully flat descent of this test. If \(R\to R'\) is faithfully flat and \(C\otimes_RR'\) is finite étale, flatness of \(C\) descends by the tensor-injection argument of AD.1. Since \(C\) is already finite over Noetherian \(R\), it is locally free by N.1. Moreover \(\Omega_{C/R}\otimes_RR'=0\), so faithfulness makes \(\Omega_{C/R}=0\). The proved criterion gives finite étaleness over \(R\).

### AO.4. Essential extension over a power-series base

Let \((A,\mathfrak m)\) be Noetherian local of depth at least two, put \(B=A[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]\) with \(d\ge1\), and write \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}B\). Suppose an open \(V\subset Y\) contains every point whose contraction to \(A\) differs from \(\mathfrak m\), and also contains the prime \(\mathfrak mB\). Then

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(Y)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{FÉt}(V).
\tag{AO.9}
\]

If \(V=Y\) there is nothing to prove. Otherwise its intersection with the zero section is precisely \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\): it contains that puncture and cannot contain the closed point of the local scheme \(Y\). At every missing point, \(A\to B_{\mathfrak q}\) is flat and local by AN.2. A regular pair on \(A\) remains regular after this flat map; its final quotient is nonzero because its ideal lies in the local maximal ideal. Hence the missing local rings have depth at least two. AO.1 gives full faithfulness, and AO.3 constructs the finite algebra
\(C=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)\) of a given finite étale \(W\to V\).

Set \(V'=U\times_A Y\), and let \(W_0\to U\) be the restriction to the zero section. AN.6 gives an isomorphism between \(W|_{V'}\) and \(W_0\times_A Y\) over \(V'\). Its algebra \(C_0=\Gamma(W_0,\mathcal O_{W_0})\) is finite over \(A\) by AO.3. At points of \(V\setminus V'\) the same flat-local regular-pair argument gives depth at least two. Applying (AO.2) on \(V\) to the algebra bundle of \(W\), and then (AO.6), gives canonical algebra isomorphisms

\[
C=\Gamma(W|_{V'},\mathcal O)
\simeq C_0\otimes_A B.
\tag{AO.10}
\]

At \(\mathfrak q=\mathfrak mB\), the left side is finite étale over \(B_{\mathfrak q}\), since \(\mathfrak q\in V\). The map \(A\to B_{\mathfrak q}\) is faithfully flat: it is flat and local, and AC.3 proves faithfulness by tensoring a nonzero cyclic submodule. Thus AO.3's descent test makes \(C_0\) finite étale over \(A\). Its base change \(C\) is finite étale over \(B\), giving the extension. Full faithfulness already proved its uniqueness and all assertions about maps.

### AO.5. Making a closed fibre point into a section

We need two local preparations for applying (AO.9). First, for a Noetherian local \((A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)\) and a finite extension \(L/\kappa\), there is a finite free local \(A\)-algebra \(A'\) with

\[
\mathfrak mA'=\mathfrak m_{A'},\qquad A'/\mathfrak mA'=L.
\tag{AO.11}
\]

Choose a finite tower of simple field extensions ending at \(L\). At each step lift the coefficients of its monic minimal polynomial to the current local algebra and take the monic polynomial quotient. The powers below its degree give a free basis. Its reduction modulo the previous maximal ideal is the desired field, so it has just one maximal ideal: every maximal ideal contracts to the maximal ideal under this finite integral extension. For completeness, contraction is maximal because a domain integral over a field is a field, and, conversely, if an integral extension is a field, the monic equation of an inverse shows the base domain is a field. Thus each quotient is local with exactly the claimed maximal ideal. Compose the finite free maps. No separability of \(L/\kappa\) is required.

Second, suppose \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is smooth and \(z\) in its closed fibre has residue field \(\kappa\). Choose an étale coordinate chart \(X_1\to\mathbf A^d_A\) around \(z\), supplied by the local equations of AE.1. Lift the coordinates of \(z\) to elements of \(A\). Their graph gives \(\operatorname{Spec}A\to\mathbf A^d_A\). Pulling the chart back along this graph gives an étale neighbourhood of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) with a point above \(z\) and residue field \(\kappa\). Localize there, obtaining a faithfully flat local étale \(A\)-algebra \(A''\). The morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}A''\to X\) yields a section of \(X_{A''}\to\operatorname{Spec}A''\), with closed value \(z\) after base change. Both (AO.11) and this local étale change preserve a regular pair by flatness.

These constructions also preserve density of an open subset of a fibre after the residue-field extension. Indeed the map from a base-changed fibre to the original fibre is flat. AC.3's prime lifting shows that a minimal prime upstairs contracts to a minimal prime downstairs: a strictly smaller prime downstairs would lift to a strictly smaller one upstairs. A dense open contains all the generic points, and therefore so does its inverse image. This proves the required density without assuming the original residue extension separable.

### AO.6. Purity in a smooth family

Let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth with \(S\) Noetherian, and let \(U\subset X\) be open. Assume

\[
\begin{gathered}
U_s\text{ is dense in }X_s\text{ for every }s\in S,\\
U_s=X_s\text{ whenever }\operatorname{depth}\mathcal O_{S,s}\le1.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AO.12}
\]

Then restriction \(\operatorname{FÉt}(X)\to\operatorname{FÉt}(U)\) is an equivalence. At a missing point \(x\), its image \(s\) has depth at least two. Smooth flatness from AE.1 carries a regular pair from \(\mathcal O_{S,s}\) to \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\); the map is local, so the quotient is nonzero. Thus AO.1 gives full faithfulness and AO.3 constructs the canonical coherent algebra \(\mathcal C\) of any finite étale cover of \(U\).

It remains to prove that \(\mathcal C\) is locally free. This is local on \(X\) and \(S\), so take affine charts with \(X\) of finite type over the Noetherian affine base. Its nonfree locus \(Z\) is closed. To see openness of freeness directly, lift a basis at a point to a map from a finite free module. The cokernel vanishes on a neighbourhood; its now finite kernel vanishes on a smaller neighbourhood because its localization at the point is zero. Finite generation permits both shrinkings. By (AO.7), the complement of \(Z\) is precisely the open on which the canonical extension is finite étale. It contains the original \(U\), and AO.3 identifies its cover with the original extension construction. Enlarge \(U\) to this complement.

Suppose \(Z\ne\varnothing\). Its image in \(S\) is constructible by AC.2. A nonempty constructible set in a Noetherian scheme has a point with no strict generalization in that set: express it as finitely many locally closed pieces, take the generic points of the irreducible components of their closures, which lie in their respective pieces, and choose a minimal point under specialization in this finite list. Every point of every piece specializes from one of these generic points. This proves the assertion about the chosen point \(s\).

After localizing the base at \(s\), all of \(Z\) lies in the closed fibre, whose intersection with \(Z\) is nowhere dense. Put \(A=\mathcal O_{S,s}\). It has depth at least two by (AO.12). The nonempty closed subset \(Z\) of the finite-type closed fibre contains a closed point \(z\) with finite residue extension of \(\kappa(s)\), by the Nullstellensatz proved in Y.5. Apply (AO.11) to this extension and take the point over \(z\) with that residue field. Then apply the étale preparation in AO.5. We have reduced to a local base \(A\) of depth at least two and a section through a point \(z\) of \(Z\). The reductions are faithfully flat at the chosen points, so freeness and étaleness descend there by AD.1 and AO.3. AO.6 uses no normality assumption on these new bases.

Choose an affine neighbourhood \(\operatorname{Spec}B\subset X\) of \(z\). The section factors through it, since its inverse image is an open containing the closed point of the local base, hence the whole base. Write \(I\) for the section ideal. AN.2 gives a flat map

\[
B\longrightarrow\widehat B^{\,I}
\simeq A[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]].
\tag{AO.13}
\]

Here \(d>0\). If \(d=0\), the smooth closed fibre is zero-dimensional at \(z\); its point \(z\) would be a generic point and hence would belong to the dense open \(U_s\). More explicitly, smooth fibre local rings are regular by Y.6, and their dimension is the number of local smooth coordinates; the zero-dimensional local ring is a field.

Let \(V\) be the inverse image of \(U\) in the completed spectrum. It contains every point not over \(\mathfrak m_A\), since all the missing points before completion lie in the closed fibre. It also contains the prime \(\mathfrak m_A\widehat B\). Indeed the closed-fibre map near \(z\) is the flat completion map from its regular local ring into \(\kappa(s)[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]\). The zero prime of the latter contracts to a minimal prime by flat prime lifting. The former local ring is a domain by Y.4–Y.6, so that contraction is zero. Thus this prime maps to the generic point of the closed-fibre component through \(z\), which belongs to \(U_s\). The identifications of the closed-fibre completion and its quotients follow from L.1 and (AN.5).

AO.4 now extends the pulled-back cover to a finite étale cover of the whole completed spectrum. By (AO.6) and uniqueness in AO.3, its algebra is the completion pullback of \(\mathcal C\). At the completed closed point, (AO.13) gives a flat local map from \(B_z\), hence a faithfully flat map by AC.3. The finite module \(\mathcal C_z\) therefore becomes free after a faithfully flat extension and is itself free by AD.1. This contradicts \(z\in Z\). Thus \(Z\) is empty, proving essential extension. Full faithfulness was already proved, so the claimed equivalence follows.

### AO.7. From purity to generic-cover extension

AO.1–AO.3 give the coherent cover algebra, its depth property, uniqueness, compatibility with flat base change and enlargement of the open, and the global locally-free test for étaleness. AO.4 proves essential extension over the stated power-series neighbourhood; AO.5–AO.6 remove the branch locus under (AO.12), for arbitrary Noetherian bases. These arguments include the inseparable residue-field preparation and the faithfully flat descent at the completed point.

AP.1–AP.7 prove the regular local purity and tame root-base-change inputs to AL.5. AQ.1–AQ.5 add codimension-one gluing and split-section descent, proving the DVR-base case. AR.1–AR.5 assemble the generic-cover theorem over an arbitrary integral normal Noetherian base. AS.1–AS.7 combine this cover extension with degree-zero comparison from AN.1, connected-fibre neighbourhoods from AM.6 and finite normalization of integer models from AG.5. They prove smooth comparison over arbitrary bases for a quasi-compact, quasi-separated direct-image morphism and the specified torsion coefficients of invertible orders. AT.1–AT.5 deduce strict-local acyclicity and the ordinary smooth-locus nearby-cycle unit at that coefficient scope. Proper base change has its separate proof in BE.

## Appendix AP. Regular local purity and the tame DVR calculation

The DVR case of the generic-cover theorem uses two kinds of local algebra. A cover unramified in codimension one must extend across higher codimension, and a root of the uniformizer must remove tame ramification. We prove the regular-local extension theorem first, using the coherent algebra of AO.2. We then make the required valuation calculation over an arbitrary DVR, without assuming an algebraically closed residue field or a coefficient field.

### AP.1. Completion detects extension

Let \((A,\mathfrak m)\) be Noetherian local of depth at least two, put \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\), and let \(W\to U\) be finite étale. AO.2–AO.3 construct the finite algebra \(C=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)\). It is an extension algebra, and it is the only one whose local rings at the missing points have depth at least two. The cover extends finite étale over \(A\) exactly when \(C\) is finite étale: apply (AO.2) to the algebra bundle of any proposed étale extension.

Write \(\widehat A\) for the maximal-ideal completion. It is Noetherian local, has maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\widehat A\), and is flat over \(A\), by L.1 and AN.2. A flat local map is faithfully flat by AC.3. Its inverse image of \(U\) is exactly the punctured spectrum \(\widehat U\). A regular pair on \(A\) remains regular on \(\widehat A\), and (AO.6) gives

\[
C\otimes_A\widehat A
=\Gamma(W\times_U\widehat U,\mathcal O).
\tag{AP.1}
\]

If the pulled-back cover extends finite étale over \(\widehat A\), Hartogs identifies that extension with (AP.1). Faithfully flat descent in AO.3 then makes \(C\) finite étale. The converse is base change. Thus completion detects extendability in this depth range; no formal-gluing theorem is needed.

If \(A\) is regular local of dimension \(d\), then so is \(\widehat A\), with the same dimension. Indeed (L.2) identifies all maximal-ideal quotients and their associated graded rings. Y.4 identifies the latter with a polynomial ring on \(d\) generators. The length-growth calculation Y.1–Y.3 gives dimension \(d\) for the completion, and its cotangent space also has dimension \(d\). This proves the assertion including its Noetherian hypothesis.

### AP.2. The surface case from the kernel presentation

Suppose \(A\) is regular local of dimension two, and choose its regular parameters \(x,y\), as in Y.4. The module underlying the extension algebra \(C\) has a presentation

\[
0\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow A^r\longrightarrow A^s.
\tag{AP.2}
\]

The kernel argument in AO.2 shows that this particular pair \(x,y\) is regular on \(C\) when \(C\ne0\). In particular \(C/xC\) is torsion free over the DVR \(A/xA\): its uniformizer is the image of \(y\), and every nonzero element is a unit times a power of that uniformizer by L.1. A finite torsion-free module over a DVR is free by the basis argument in X.4.

Lift a basis to a map \(A^n\to C\). Its cokernel is zero by Nakayama, since its reduction modulo \(x\) is zero. Let \(K\) be its finite kernel. The injectivity of \(x\) on \(C\) shows that \(K\cap xA^n=xK\): if \(xv\) belongs to \(K\), the image of \(v\) is killed by \(x\), hence is zero. Reducing the exact sequence modulo \(x\) therefore gives
\(K/xK=0\), since the reduced map is the chosen basis isomorphism. Nakayama makes \(K=0\). Thus \(C\) is free over \(A\). Criterion (AO.7) makes it finite étale. The zero algebra gives the empty cover. This proves purity in dimension two without a separate miracle-flatness or normalization theorem.

### AP.3. Formal restriction through a regular parameter

Let \(A\) now be complete regular local of dimension \(d\ge3\), choose one regular parameter \(x\), and put

\[
U_n=\operatorname{Spec}(A/x^nA)\setminus\{\mathfrak m\},
\qquad U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}.
\tag{AP.3}
\]

The remaining parameters include a pair \(y,z\) regular on \(A/x^nA\). For \(n=1\) this is Y.4. For general \(n\), the filtration by powers of \(x\) has factors \(A/xA\); the successive-injection and quotient argument in AN.3 carries the regular pair through this filtration. Hartogs AN.3 therefore gives

\[
\Gamma(U,\mathcal O)=A,\qquad
\Gamma(U_n,\mathcal O)=A/x^nA.
\tag{AP.4}
\]

The ring \(A\) is also \(x\)-adically complete. A compatible sequence modulo \(x^n\) can be represented by elements whose successive differences lie in \(x^nA\subset\mathfrak m^n\). Their maximal-ideal-adic limit has the prescribed residues because every ideal \(x^nA\) is closed by L.1. Uniqueness follows from Krull intersection. Consequently (AP.4) identifies sections on \(U\) with the inverse limit of sections on \(U_n\).

For a vector bundle \(E\) on \(U\), use AN.5's universally exact presentation by two finite free bundles. Taking sections and then the inverse limit of the restricted kernels gives

\[
\Gamma(U,E)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\varprojlim_n\Gamma(U_n,E|_{U_n}).
\tag{AP.5}
\]

Applying this to Hom bundles recovers all compatible formal bundle maps. A map of finite étale covers on \(U_1\) lifts uniquely to each \(U_n\) by the square-Jacobian lifting and gluing in AN.6. Formula (AP.5) extends the resulting module map; faithfulness detects its multiplication and unit equations. It follows that

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(U)\longrightarrow\operatorname{FÉt}(U_1)
\quad\text{is fully faithful}.
\tag{AP.6}
\]

Only maps of covers already defined on \(U\) have been lifted here. Essential extension will follow from induction and a finite change of the residue field.

### AP.4. Purity in every regular local dimension

For every regular local \(A\) of dimension \(d\ge2\), restriction

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(\operatorname{Spec}A)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\operatorname{FÉt}(U)
\tag{AP.7}
\]

is an equivalence. Full faithfulness is AO.1. We prove essential extension by induction on \(d\); AP.2 is the base. By AP.1 it suffices at each stage to treat complete \(A\). For \(d\ge3\), restrict a finite étale \(W\to U\) to \(U_1\) in AP.3. The regular local ring \(A/xA\) has dimension \(d-1\), so induction extends that restriction to a finite étale algebra \(C_0\) over \(A/xA\).

Let \(\kappa=A/\mathfrak m\). The closed fibre of \(C_0\) is a product of finite separable extensions of \(\kappa\), by AB.1. Choose a finite Galois extension \(\kappa'/\kappa\) splitting all of them. Finite normal closures and a common compositum give such an extension by the finite Galois theory in AA.1. Choose a primitive element, using Z.3 and AM.5 for infinite and finite fields respectively. Lift the coefficients of its separable monic polynomial to \(A\), obtaining \(p(T)\), and set

\[
A'=A[T]/(p(T)).
\tag{AP.8}
\]

This algebra is finite free. Its reduction is the field \(\kappa'\), so it is local with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak mA'\), by the finite-integral argument of AO.5. The derivative \(p'\) is invertible in it, making (AP.8) étale by AB.1. It is faithfully flat by AC.3, and it is complete by the finite-module completion in L.1. The regular parameters of \(A\) remain regular on \(A'\) by flatness and generate its maximal ideal. Their length \(d\) gives \(\dim A'\ge d\) by (AN.7), while the bound by the number of maximal-ideal generators gives \(\dim A'\le d\). Thus \(A'\) is complete regular local of dimension \(d\).

The algebra
\(C'_0=C_0\otimes_A A'\) over \(A'/xA'\) is split. Here is the precise completeness argument. Its reduction modulo \(\mathfrak mA'\) is \((\kappa')^n\), where \(n\) is its rank. Each primitive idempotent lifts to \(C'_0\). Starting with a lift \(e\), the correction

\[
e\longmapsto e-(e^2-e)(2e-1)^{-1}
\tag{AP.9}
\]

squares the order of the error in the maximal-ideal filtration. The inverse exists because \((2e-1)^2=1+4(e^2-e)\) is a unit. The algebra is complete as a finite module over the complete local ring \(A'/xA'\), so the corrections converge to an idempotent. Uniqueness is the Jacobson-radical argument of AJ.1. The lifted primitive idempotents are consequently orthogonal and sum to one. Each resulting algebra factor is a finite projective module of residue dimension one, hence free of rank one by N.1. Its unit is a basis by Nakayama. Therefore

\[
C'_0\simeq(A'/xA')^n.
\tag{AP.10}
\]

Put \(U'=\operatorname{Spec}A'\setminus\{\mathfrak mA'\}\). The pullback of \(W\) to \(U'\) and the disjoint union of \(n\) copies of \(U'\) have isomorphic restrictions modulo \(x\), by (AP.10). Full faithfulness (AP.6) for \(A'\) lifts the isomorphism and its inverse, so the covers themselves are isomorphic. AO.6 and Hartogs identify their section algebras as

\[
C\otimes_A A'\simeq(A')^n.
\tag{AP.11}
\]

Faithfully flat descent in AO.3 makes \(C\) finite étale over \(A\). This proves the induction and (AP.7). In particular the argument does not presume that a finite étale algebra over \(A/xA\) has already been lifted over \(A\); the finite residue extension and the split algebra (AP.10) supplied the comparison actually used.

### AP.5. Extension across regular points of higher codimension

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be an open immersion with \(X\) locally Noetherian. Suppose every \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\), for \(x\notin U\), is regular local of dimension at least two. Then

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{FÉt}(U).
\tag{AP.12}
\]

AO.1 proves full faithfulness, and AO.2–AO.3 construct the finite algebra \(\mathcal C\) of a cover on \(U\). Work on an affine Noetherian chart. The nonfree locus \(Z\) of \(\mathcal C\) is closed by the finite-presentation argument in AO.6; by (AO.7) its complement is exactly the locus of finite étaleness. If \(Z\) were nonempty, choose a generic point \(z\) of one of its irreducible components. Over the local ring \(A=\mathcal O_{X,z}\), the algebra \(\mathcal C_z\) is finite étale on the puncture, because every strict generalization of \(z\) lies outside \(Z\). The ring \(A\) is regular of dimension at least two by the hypothesis on missing points.

By (AP.7) this punctured cover has a finite étale extension. Its sections recover \(\mathcal C_z\): localize AO.2's matrix-kernel presentation and apply Hartogs to the two finite free modules on the puncture. Thus \(\mathcal C_z\) is the finite étale extension algebra and is free over \(A\), contradicting \(z\in Z\). The nonfree locus is empty. This proves essential extension on each chart; the intrinsic algebra \(j_*E\) and full faithfulness already glue the answers. No finiteness assumption on the number of affine charts is required.

### AP.6. Ramification indices over an arbitrary DVR

Let \(R\) be a DVR, \(K\) its fraction field, \(\pi\) a uniformizer, and \(L/K\) a finite separable field extension. Its integral closure \(T\) over \(R\) is finite: the integral-basis and inverse-trace-matrix argument in AJ.1 works over every integrally closed Noetherian ring, independently of strict locality. The ring \(T\) is a normal Noetherian domain of dimension one by integral incomparability and going up in K.1. Its finitely many maximal ideals \(\mathfrak n_i\) lie over \((\pi)\), and their localizations are DVRs by L.1. Let

\[
e_i=v_{T_{\mathfrak n_i}}(\pi),\qquad
f_i=[\kappa(\mathfrak n_i):\kappa(R)].
\tag{AP.13}
\]

As an \(R\)-module, \(T\) is finite torsion free and therefore free by X.4, of rank \([L:K]\). The Artinian algebra \(T/\pi T\) is the product of its localizations at the \(\mathfrak n_i\), by the finite-prime and nilpotent-radical Chinese remainder argument in AO.3. The uniformizer filtration of the \(i\)-th factor has \(e_i\) factors equal to \(\kappa(\mathfrak n_i)\). Taking dimensions gives

\[
[L:K]=\sum_i e_i f_i.
\tag{AP.14}
\]

If \(L/K\) is Galois with group \(G\), its action on \(T\) is transitive on the maximal ideals. Otherwise the Chinese remainder theorem supplies \(b\in T\) whose residues are zero on one orbit and one on another. Its product \(\prod_{g\in G}g(b)\) lies in \(T^G=R\), since \(K\cap T=R\). Its residues would be zero on the first orbit and one on the second, impossible for an element of \(R\), since every maximal ideal lies over the same maximal ideal of \(R\). Transitivity makes all \(e_i\) equal to \(e\) and all \(f_i\) equal to \(f\), so

\[
[L:K]=r e f,
\tag{AP.15}
\]

where \(r\) is the number of maximal ideals. If \(|G|\) is invertible in \(R\), then \(e\) is prime to the residue characteristic and every residue extension is separable. In positive characteristic \(p\), an inseparable element has a minimal polynomial whose degree is divisible by \(p\); that degree divides \(f\), contradicting (AP.15). In characteristic zero all finite residue extensions are separable. This proves the tame assertion needed for the generic Galois cover.

### AP.7. Removing this tame ramification by a root

For any positive integer \(n\), the algebra

\[
R_n=R[t]/(t^n-\pi)
\tag{AP.16}
\]

is a DVR with uniformizer \(t\), fraction-field degree \(n\) over \(K\), and the same residue field as \(R\). Indeed it is finite free on the powers below \(n\); multiplication by \(\pi\), and consequently by \(t\), is injective. Every maximal ideal contains \(t\), and its quotient by \((t)\) is the residue field. L.1 therefore makes it a DVR. It is its own integral closure in its fraction field. For \(n\) invertible in \(R\), the field extension is separable, since the derivative \(nt^{n-1}\) is nonzero in the fraction field.

Suppose \(L/K\) is as in AP.6, Galois of order invertible in \(R\), with common ramification index \(e\). Put \(K_e=\operatorname{Frac}R_e\), and let \(D\) be the integral closure of \(R_e\) in the finite product of fields \(L\otimes_KK_e\). It is finite by the same trace bound on each field factor. We claim it is finite étale.

Fix one localization \(B=T_{\mathfrak n_i}\), with uniformizer \(s\), and write \(\pi=u s^e\) for a unit \(u\). The algebra

\[
E=B[v]/(v^e-u)
\tag{AP.17}
\]

is finite étale over \(B\): \(v\) and \(ev^{e-1}\) are units. Its total fraction algebra is \(L\otimes_KK_e\), by \(t=sv\). Each local ring over the closed point of \(B\) has maximal ideal generated by \(s\), because its fibre is a finite separable field; multiplication by \(s\) is injective by flatness. It is a DVR by L.1. The generic local rings are fields, since the generic polynomial is separable. Thus \(E\) is integrally closed in its total fraction algebra: integrality can be checked in these localizations, and an element whose class vanishes in every maximal localization of the quotient module \((L\otimes_KK_e)/E\) already belongs to \(E\). Consequently \(E\) is the integral closure of \(B\) in that algebra.

Integral closure commutes with localization, by the denominator-clearing proof in AG.1. Moreover the integral closure of \(R\), of \(T\), and of \(R_e\) in \(L\otimes_KK_e\) is the same ring: each of the latter two rings is integral over \(R\), so transitivity of integrality gives one inclusion and their containing \(R\) gives the other. Hence (AP.17) describes the localization of \(D\) over \(\mathfrak n_i\). At every one of its closed points, \(t=sv\) is a uniformizer. Its residue field is separable over \(\kappa(R)\), since it is separable over \(\kappa(\mathfrak n_i)\) and AP.6 made the latter extension separable. We have proved that every closed branch of \(D/R_e\) has ramification index one and separable residue field.

The finite torsion-free \(R_e\)-module \(D\) is free. Its closed fibre is the product of those separable residue fields, with no nonreduced factor, because \(t\) is a uniformizer in every closed localization. Its generic fibre is also a product of finite separable fields. Thus its differential module vanishes after reduction to either fibre, and Nakayama at every point gives \(\Omega_{D/R_e}=0\). The proved finite-flat criterion in AO.3 makes \(D\) finite étale.

More generally, let \(n\) be an invertible multiple of \(e\), with compatible roots so that \(R_e\to R_n\) sends \(t\) to the \(n/e\)-th power of the new uniformizer. Then \(D\otimes_{R_e}R_n\) is finite étale over \(R_n\). The DVR argument just given makes it integrally closed in its generic product of fields, so it is exactly the integral closure in \(L\otimes_K\operatorname{Frac}R_n\). Therefore adjoining an \(n\)-th root of \(\pi\) removes all ramification in this Galois situation. In particular \(n=|G|\) works by (AP.15).

### AP.8. From the DVR calculation to the family

AP.1–AP.5 prove absolute purity at regular missing points of codimension at least two. AP.6 proves the common ramification index and separable residue fields for a Galois extension of DVR fraction fields of invertible degree. AP.7 proves the root base change that removes that ramification, including the normalization calculation on every branch.

AQ.1–AQ.5 assemble these results with extension over the missing codimension-one points and descent at the split section, proving the DVR-base case of AL.5. The section makes the root action trivial on the closed cover, and the weight decomposition then supplies the descended finite étale algebra. AR.1–AR.5 combine this DVR case with AO's coherent algebra and relative purity, AN's completed-section comparison and a trace proof of generic splitting, proving the full generic-cover theorem over integral normal Noetherian bases. AS.4–AS.6 supply the cohomological-degree and dimension inductions, using the finite integer models and normalization of AG.5; AS.7 passes to bounded-below complexes and affine limits of smooth base changes.

## Appendix AQ. Divisor gluing and descent at a split section

We now prove the DVR case of the generic-cover assertion in AL.5. The descent calculation keeps track of the action on the cover after the root base change in AP.7. In particular, removing ramification after that base change will not by itself be treated as descent.

### AQ.1. Spreading an algebra and extending its maps

Here is the finite gluing argument needed below. Let \(A\) be Noetherian, let \(\mathfrak p\) be a prime, and let \(V\subset\operatorname{Spec}A\) be open. A finite étale algebra over \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) is free as a module, since the base is local. Choose a basis. Its multiplication constants and unit coordinates belong to some \(A_f\), with \(f\notin\mathfrak p\). Associativity, commutativity and the unit laws are finitely many equalities between these constants. Each equality valid in \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) becomes valid after inverting another element outside \(\mathfrak p\). The determinant of the trace pairing is a unit in \(A_{\mathfrak p}\); invert its numerator too. The resulting free algebra \(C\) over \(A_f\) is finite étale by AO.3's trace criterion. Thus

\[
C\otimes_{A_f}A_{\mathfrak p}\simeq C_{\mathfrak p}
\tag{AQ.1}
\]

is an actual algebra with the desired étale property on a neighbourhood, not just a list of equations at the point.

Suppose a finite étale algebra \(E\) is already given on \(V\), with an isomorphism between \(E\) and \(C_{\mathfrak p}\) over \(V\times_A\operatorname{Spec}A_{\mathfrak p}\). Cover \(V\cap D(f)\) by finitely many principal opens \(D(g_i)\) in \(\operatorname{Spec}A_f\). Such a cover exists because this open is quasi-compact. On each chart both algebras are finitely presented. An algebra map after localization at \(A\setminus\mathfrak p\) is specified by finitely many generator images and finitely many relations. Clear denominators to obtain it after inverting one element outside \(\mathfrak p\). Do this for the inverse map, the two inverse identities and the agreements on every \(D(g_i g_j)\). Only finitely many elements and equations occur. Their common product gives \(h\notin\mathfrak p\) such that the isomorphism exists on \(V\cap D(fh)\). Charts with zero limiting ring cause no problem: the equality \(1=0\) also holds after one such localization. Gluing the algebra sheaves \(E\) and \(C|_{D(fh)}\) gives a finite étale algebra on \(V\cup D(fh)\). The same argument spreads a map or an equality of maps. This proves the particular gluing and limit statements used here directly.

We also need uniqueness and extension of maps. Let \(U\subset X\) be dense and open in a locally Noetherian scheme, with every local ring at a missing point regular. Then restriction is fully faithful:

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{FÉt}(U).
\tag{AQ.2}
\]

First it is faithful. On an affine chart no associated prime of its ring lies in the complement: a missing point has positive local dimension, whereas a regular local ring of positive dimension has a nonzerodivisor in its maximal ideal by Y.4 and hence cannot have that maximal ideal associated. The associated-prime detection used in AO.1 therefore shows that a section of a finite free module vanishing on \(U\) is zero. Apply this after trivializing the Hom bundle of the two finite étale algebras. Thus any extended map is unique, and maps defined on different neighbourhoods agree on their intersections.

For existence, take the union \(W\) of the opens where a given map on \(U\) extends. Uniqueness glues the extensions. If a Noetherian affine chart has a nonempty complement of \(W\), choose a generic point \(x\) of that complement and put \(B=\mathcal O_{X,x}\). The map is defined on the punctured spectrum of \(B\). If \(\dim B\geq2\), Y.4 and AN.3 give the Hartogs equality for \(B\). The two algebra modules are free, so every matrix entry extends to \(B\), and the multiplication and unit identities are detected on the puncture.

If \(\dim B=1\), then \(B\) is a DVR. Every finite étale \(B\)-algebra \(T\) is its own integral closure in \(T\otimes_B\operatorname{Frac}B\). Indeed its closed local rings have maximal ideal generated by the uniformizer, which remains a nonzerodivisor by flatness; L.1 makes them DVRs. Its generic local rings are separable fields by AB.1. An integral element belongs to every maximal localization and hence to \(T\), by applying localization detection to the quotient of the total fraction algebra by \(T\). A map of generic algebras preserves integral elements and therefore extends between the two finite étale \(B\)-algebras. Finally spread the resulting local map and its agreement with the given one on \(W\), using the finite-chart argument above. This enlarges \(W\) through \(x\), a contradiction. This proves (AQ.2), including its assertion for isomorphisms and all identities between maps.

### AQ.2. Adding the codimension-one points

Under the hypotheses of AQ.1 on \(U\subset X\), let \(Z\to U\) be finite étale. Suppose that at every missing point \(\xi\) with \(\dim\mathcal O_{X,\xi}=1\), its generic algebra is the generic fibre of a finite étale algebra over the DVR \(\mathcal O_{X,\xi}\). Then there is a unique extension, up to its specified unique isomorphism,

\[
Y\longrightarrow X\quad\text{finite étale},\qquad Y|_U\simeq Z.
\tag{AQ.3}
\]

Work first on a Noetherian affine chart. There are only finitely many missing height-one points: each is a generic point of a component of the closed complement, since a strict generalization in that complement would have height zero, contrary to density of \(U\). At each of these points the inverse image of \(U\) in the local spectrum is its generic point. The spreading and gluing calculation in AQ.1 adds a neighbourhood of the point while preserving the given cover. Repeat for the finitely many points. Any point still missing now has regular local ring of dimension at least two, so AP.5 extends the cover across the rest. On overlapping affine charts the extensions agree uniquely by (AQ.2). Those identifications satisfy the cocycle identity by the same uniqueness and glue the extensions on all of \(X\).

In particular this applies when \(X\setminus U=D\) is a regular effective Cartier divisor and the cover is unramified in codimension one. At a missing point its equation \(f\) is a nonzerodivisor and the local quotient by \(f\) is regular. The converse lifting step in Y.4 makes the local ring of \(X\) regular. At each generic point of \(D\) it is a DVR with uniformizer \(f\). Here “unramified in codimension one” means precisely that the integral closure of this DVR in the generic finite separable algebra is finite étale. The trace bound and localization calculation of AP.6–AP.7 give the normalization meant by this definition. Thus the regular-divisor extension assertion, including its gluing, is now proved.

### AQ.3. Geometry and a test for the identity on a finite cover

We record the elementary geometry used in the descent. A scheme smooth over a field has regular local rings by Y.6. A scheme smooth over a DVR \(R\), with uniformizer \(\pi\), also has regular local rings: points over its fraction field are covered by Y.6; at a point of the closed fibre, flatness makes \(\pi\) a nonzerodivisor and the quotient local ring is regular by Y.6, so Y.4 applies. The same statements hold for a finite étale cover of such a scheme, since finite étale followed by smooth is smooth. On standard presentations this is obtained by adjoining the two lists of equations: the relevant Jacobian block matrix is triangular with the product of the two invertible minors. This also verifies the assertion after every field extension.

A locally Noetherian scheme with regular local rings is reduced and its irreducible components are disjoint and open. Here are the local details. Each local ring is a domain by Y.4. On a Noetherian affine neighbourhood there are finitely many minimal primes, and a point lying on two distinct components would give two distinct minimal primes in its local ring. Thus the components there are disjoint closed subsets and therefore open. Removing the other components gives an irreducible neighbourhood of each point; these neighbourhoods show that the global components are open too. A connected such scheme is consequently integral. A smooth family over a DVR with connected nonempty generic fibre is connected whenever all its components meet that fibre. They do: smooth maps are open by AC.3, whereas a nonempty component contained in the closed fibre would have image the nonopen singleton consisting of the closed point. In particular, a smooth family with geometrically connected fibres is integral, and both its fibres are geometrically integral.

For a finite étale algebra \(B/A\), the diagonal in \(\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A B)\) is open and closed. To see this algebraically, let \(I\) be the kernel of multiplication \(B\otimes_A B\to B\). The differential identification \(I/I^2=\Omega_{B/A}=0\) gives \(I=I^2\). The ideal is finitely generated. Write its generators as an \(I\)-valued matrix times the same generators. The adjugate matrix then shows that \(1-e\) annihilates \(I\) for some \(e\in I\). It follows that \(I=e(B\otimes_A B)\) and \(e^2=e\). A quotient by this idempotent ideal is both an open and a closed subscheme. Pulling the diagonal back proves that the equalizer of two maps into a finite étale cover is open and closed.

Let \(V\) be smooth and connected over an algebraically closed field and let \(W\to V\) be finite étale. Every connected component of \(W\) is open and closed by the preceding regularity argument. Its image is closed because the map is finite, and open because it is étale, so the image is all of \(V\). Thus every component meets the fibre at any chosen point \(v\in V\). An automorphism \(a\) of \(W/V\) which fixes every point of that fibre is the identity: its open-and-closed equalizer with the identity meets every connected component, hence contains every component. We have proved

\[
a|_{W_v}=\mathrm{id}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=\mathrm{id}_W.
\tag{AQ.4}
\]

Finally, a finite étale algebra over a DVR whose generic algebra is \(K^r\) is \(R^r\). This follows from the integral-closure argument in AQ.1, since the elements integral over \(R\) in \(K^r\) are exactly the coordinatewise elements of \(R^r\). The identification is unique when its generic identification is specified.

### AQ.4. The graded descent calculation

Let \(A\) be a Noetherian \(R\)-algebra on which \(\pi\) is a nonzerodivisor, let \(n\) be invertible in \(R\), and put

\[
A'=A[t]/(t^n-\pi),\qquad
\mu_n=\operatorname{Spec}R[z]/(z^n-1).
\tag{AQ.5}
\]

The group law on \(\mu_n\) has \(z\mapsto z\otimes z\), and its action on \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\) is dual to \(t\mapsto t\otimes z\). Suppose \(D\) is a finite étale \(A'\)-algebra with a compatible \(\mu_n\)-action over \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). Suppose also that the induced action on \(D/tD\) is trivial. We prove that \(D\) descends to a finite étale \(A\)-algebra.

Write the coaction uniquely as

\[
\rho(d)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}p_i(d)\otimes z^i.
\tag{AQ.6}
\]

Comparison of the coefficients of \(z^i\otimes z^j\) in the coassociativity identity gives \(p_i p_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\) and \(p_i^2=p_i\). The identity element of the group gives \(\sum_i p_i=1\). Since \(\rho\) is an algebra map, with indices modulo \(n\),

\[
D=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}D_i,\qquad
D_iD_j\subset D_{i+j},\qquad
tD_i\subset D_{i+1},\qquad D_i=p_i(D).
\tag{AQ.7}
\]

This coefficient computation works over \(R\); no roots of unity in \(R\) are assumed. The \(A\)-algebra of invariant elements is \(C=D_0\). Multiplication by \(t\) is injective, because \(t^n=\pi\) and \(D\) is flat over the \(A\)-free algebra \(A'\). The ideal \(tD\) is graded. Triviality of the action on the quotient says that its nonzero weight pieces vanish. Taking the homogeneous part of a preimage under multiplication by \(t\) therefore gives

\[
D_i=tD_{i-1}=t^iC\qquad(1\leq i<n).
\tag{AQ.8}
\]

The \(A\)-linear map \(C\otimes_A A'\to D\) sends the \(i\)-th basis summand to \(t^iC=D_i\). It is surjective by (AQ.7)–(AQ.8), and injective because the sum in (AQ.7) is direct and multiplication by \(t^i\) is injective. It is an algebra map, hence

\[
C\otimes_A A'\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D.
\tag{AQ.9}
\]

For \(n=1\) this is simply \(A'=A\) and \(C=D\). In general \(D\) is finite projective over \(A\), since it is finite projective over the finite free \(A\)-algebra \(A'\). Its direct summand \(C\) is therefore finite projective over \(A\). Alternatively its flatness follows directly from the faithfully flat map \(A\to A'\). The differential module of \(C/A\) becomes zero after tensoring with \(A'\), by (AQ.9) and étaleness of \(D/A'\). Faithful flatness makes it zero already. AO.3's finite-flat criterion proves that \(C/A\) is finite étale. The construction commutes with localization in \(A\), since each \(p_i\) is \(A\)-linear. Consequently these invariant algebras glue.

### AQ.5. Extending a generic Galois cover over a DVR

Let \(R\) be a DVR with fraction field \(K\) and residue field \(k\). Let \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) be smooth with geometrically connected fibres and section \(\sigma\). Let \(Z\to X_K\) be a finite étale Galois cover with group \(G\), where \(n=|G|\) is invertible in \(R\). Assume that the fibre of \(Z\) at \(\sigma_K\) has a \(K\)-point. The torsor action then makes that fibre the disjoint union of \(n\) copies of \(\operatorname{Spec}K\). We claim that

\[
\begin{gathered}
Y\longrightarrow X\quad\text{finite étale Galois with group }G,\\
Y|_{X_K}\simeq Z.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AQ.10}
\]

Put \(R'=R[t]/(t^n-\pi)\), a DVR by AP.7, and \(X'=X\times_R R'\). Its closed fibre is \(X_k\), a regular geometrically integral divisor by AQ.3. At its generic point, the local ring before base change is a DVR \(B\) with uniformizer \(\pi\). The function field extension defined by \(Z\) is Galois of degree \(n\): both \(X_K\) and the connected cover \(Z\) are integral by AQ.3, and the generic fibre of the torsor has the given simply transitive \(G\)-action. AP.6–AP.7 applied to \(B\) say that the normalization after adjoining \(t\) is finite étale over \(B[t]/(t^n-\pi)\). This is exactly the local ring of \(X'\) at the generic point of its closed fibre. Thus the base-changed generic cover is unramified at that codimension-one point. AQ.2 now produces a finite étale cover

\[
W\longrightarrow X',\qquad
W|_{X'_{K'}}=Z\times_K K',\qquad K'=\operatorname{Frac}R'.
\tag{AQ.11}
\]

The group scheme \(\mu_n\) acts on \(X'/X\) by multiplying \(t\). Over \(K\), the cover on the right of (AQ.11) already has the compatible action which fixes the \(Z\)-factor. This action extends uniquely to \(W\). Indeed on \(X'\times_R\mu_n\) its two pullbacks are finite étale covers, isomorphic over the generic fibre. This base is smooth over \(R'\): \(\mu_n/R\) is finite étale because \(nz^{n-1}\) is a unit. Its missing closed-fibre points are regular by AQ.3. Full faithfulness (AQ.2) therefore extends the isomorphism. On \(X'\times_R\mu_n\times_R\mu_n\), the same full faithfulness extends its action identity; the identity element is handled likewise. This constructs an actual compatible group action on \(W\).

Pull (AQ.11) back along \(\sigma_{R'}\). Its generic algebra is \((K')^n\), with each factor labelled by the original \(K\)-point of the split fibre. AQ.3 identifies the whole pullback with \((R')^n\). The \(\mu_n\)-action preserves every label: this holds generically, and equality of the corresponding maps is detected there by (AQ.2), also after the finite étale base \(\mu_n\) is added. Hence every geometric point over the closed point of the section is fixed.

Pass to an algebraic closure \(\overline k\) of \(k\). The group \(\mu_n\) is now the disjoint union of the \(n\) distinct roots of \(z^n-1\). Each of its elements is an automorphism of the finite étale cover \(W_{\overline k}\to X_{\overline k}\) and fixes every point above \(\sigma_{\overline k}\). The base is smooth and connected. Equation (AQ.4) makes each automorphism the identity on the whole cover. Thus the group-scheme action on the closed fibre is trivial over \(\overline k\), and therefore over \(k\), since equality of maps of \(k\)-modules is detected by the faithfully flat field extension \(k\to\overline k\).

On any affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X\), the inverse image in \(X'\) has algebra \(A'\) from (AQ.5), and the inverse image in \(W\) has a finite étale algebra \(D/A'\). The action just proved is trivial modulo \(t\). AQ.4 produces the finite étale algebra \(C=D_0\) over \(A\). These algebras agree on overlaps and define \(Y\to X\). Its generic restriction is \(Z\): on that open \(D\) is the algebra of \(Z\) tensored with \(K'\), whose coaction fixes the first factor and assigns weight \(i\) to \(t^i\). Its weight-zero part is precisely the original algebra. This also proves compatibility of the constructed extension with the specified generic identification.

Finally extend each element of the \(G\)-action using (AQ.2). Its group identities extend by faithfulness. The generic torsor isomorphism extends with its inverse between the finite étale covers

\[
G\times Y\longrightarrow Y\times_XY,\qquad (g,y)\longmapsto(gy,y).
\tag{AQ.12}
\]

The scheme \(Y\) is smooth over \(R\), so its components are open by AQ.3, and each component meets the generic fibre by openness of the smooth map. Since that generic fibre is the connected scheme \(Z\), there is only one component. Thus \(Y\) is connected, and (AQ.12) makes it the required Galois cover. The argument did not require \(R\) to be complete, henselian, of equal characteristic, or to contain roots of unity. Nor did it require a finite affine cover of \(X\): the finite-chart gluing in AQ.1 was applied on Noetherian affine neighbourhoods and the resulting algebras agree uniquely.

### AQ.6. From the DVR case to a normal base

Equation (AQ.10) proves the DVR-base case of AL.5, including codimension-one gluing, descent from the root base change and the Galois assertion. AR.1–AR.5 assemble the local extensions over an arbitrary integral normal Noetherian base, including finite base gluing, trace splitting, the completed-section calculation and relative purity. The arbitrary-base connected-fibre neighbourhoods of AM.6 and finite normalization of integer models in AG.5 provide the remaining geometric inputs to AS.1–AS.7. That induction proves smooth comparison for quasi-compact, quasi-separated direct images and torsion coefficients with invertible annihilators, including the stated filtered unions and bounded-below complexes. AT.1–AT.5 deduce strict-local acyclicity and the ordinary smooth-locus nearby-cycle unit for the same allowed torsion orders. The normality and Noetherian hypotheses on the intermediate cover-extension theorem are retained when it is applied to the finite models.

## Appendix AR. Generic covers over a normal base

The DVR theorem (AQ.10), the formal comparison (AN.12) and relative purity (AO.12) now give the generic-cover extension needed in AL.5. We first supply the splitting and gluing arguments that connect those results.

### AR.1. A split generic algebra over a normal domain

Let \(A\) be an integrally closed domain with fraction field \(K\), and let \(C\) be a finite étale \(A\)-algebra with a specified identification \(C\otimes_AK=K^n\). Flatness embeds \(C\) into this product. Every element of \(C\) is integral over \(A\), by the finite-module determinant argument, so each of its coordinates lies in \(A\). Hence

\[
C\subset A^n\subset K^n.
\tag{AR.1}
\]

Each coordinate projection is an \(A\)-linear functional on \(C\). The perfect trace pairing (AO.8) supplies \(e_i\in C\) representing the \(i\)-th projection. After tensoring with \(K\), the trace pairing is the ordinary dot product on \(K^n\). Its representing element is the standard vector with a single coordinate equal to one. Thus all those vectors belong to \(C\); their \(A\)-span gives the reverse inclusion in (AR.1). We have proved

\[
C=A^n
\quad\text{with the specified generic identification.}
\tag{AR.2}
\]

This applies on every affine open of a normal integral scheme. Its coordinate domain is integrally closed: an element integral over it belongs to all its normal local rings, and membership in the ring is detected by localizing the quotient of its fraction field by the ring at maximal ideals. The identifications (AR.2) agree on overlaps because they agree generically and the algebra bundles are torsion free. Consequently a finite étale cover of a normal integral scheme which is generically split is split everywhere. This proof uses trace duality, and does not presume that the covering scheme has already been proved normal.

### AR.2. Finite data over a localized base

Let \(A\) be Noetherian and \(T\) a quasi-compact scheme locally of finite presentation over \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). Then \(T\) is Noetherian: it is locally Noetherian and has a finite affine cover. All opens and finite intersections of opens used below are consequently quasi-compact. For a multiplicative subset \(M\subset A\), finite étale algebras on
\(T_M=T\times_A\operatorname{Spec}M^{-1}A\), their maps, inverse maps and finitely many identities descend after inverting finitely many elements of \(M\).

Here is the algebra behind that assertion. Cover \(T\) by finitely many affine opens \(\operatorname{Spec}B_i\). On their base changes a finite étale algebra has a finite projective underlying module, say the image of an idempotent matrix \(e\) on \((M^{-1}B_i)^r\). Multiplication, unit and the inverse of its trace pairing are maps between these summands and their tensor products and duals. They are represented by finitely many matrices. Their entries have denominators in \(M\). The idempotent identity, the conditions that the maps take values in the chosen summands, the algebra identities, and the two trace-inverse identities are finitely many matrix equalities. After clearing a common finite set of denominators all hold over the localized \(B_i\). Trace here also commutes with this descent: extend an endomorphism of the summand by zero on its complementary summand and take the usual matrix trace. Thus the descended projective algebra has perfect trace pairing and is finite étale by AO.3.

On overlaps, cover by finitely many affine opens again. Algebra maps are determined by finitely many generator images and relations. Clearing denominators descends the overlap isomorphisms, their inverses and their triple-overlap identities. Gluing yields the algebra on the localized \(T\). The same matrix and generator calculation descends any given finite diagram of maps and equations. For equations that hold only after localization, multiply by a further element of \(M\) that kills their finitely many differences.

Two cases will be used. If \(A\) is a domain and \(M=A\setminus\{0\}\), data over its fraction field descend over \(D(a)\) for some \(a\ne0\). If \(M=A\setminus\mathfrak p\), they descend over a neighbourhood \(D(a)\) of \(\mathfrak p\). In the second case suppose a cover is also given on \(T_U\) for an open \(U\subset\operatorname{Spec}A\), together with an identification on \(T_U\times_A\operatorname{Spec}A_{\mathfrak p}\). Choose a finite principal cover of \(U\), and use the same finite affine covers over it. The isomorphism and its inverse descend on \(T_U\cap T_{D(a)}\) after shrinking this neighbourhood. They then glue the two covers on

\[
T_{\,U\cup D(a)}.
\tag{AR.3}
\]

Finite group actions and torsor isomorphisms can be included in these finite diagrams. This proves the precise base-local gluing needed below, including its finiteness hypotheses.

### AR.3. Full faithfulness at the generic fibre

Let \(S\) be normal, integral and Noetherian with generic point \(\eta\), and let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth. Then

\[
\operatorname{FÉt}(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{FÉt}(X_\eta)
\quad\text{is fully faithful.}
\tag{AR.4}
\]

We first prove this when \(S=\operatorname{Spec}A\) is affine and \(X\) is quasi-compact. Faithfulness follows directly from flatness. On every affine chart of \(X\), a nonzero element of \(A\) acts injectively on the coordinate ring, and hence on every finite locally free module. A bundle map whose generic restriction is zero is therefore zero. In particular two algebra maps agreeing generically agree everywhere.

Given a map between the generic restrictions of two finite étale covers, AR.2 spreads it over some nonempty base open. Uniqueness glues all its extensions over base opens. Let \(U\subset S\) be the union of those opens. If its complement is nonempty, choose a generic point \(s\) of a component of that complement. Every strict generalization of \(s\) lies in \(U\). With \(B=\mathcal O_{S,s}\), the inverse image of \(U\) is the punctured spectrum of \(B\).

If \(\dim B=1\), normality makes \(B\) a DVR by L.1. The scheme \(X_B\) is regular by AQ.3, and its generic fibre is dense by flatness. Equation (AQ.2) extends the map across the closed fibre. If \(\dim B\geq2\), AN.3 gives a regular pair on \(B\). Flatness carries it to the local ring at every point of \(X_B\) over the closed point; the quotient is nonzero because the map is local. Thus the missing local rings have depth at least two, and AO.1 extends the algebra map and its identities. In either case AR.2 glues this local extension to the map over \(X_U\) on a strictly larger base open. This contradicts the definition of \(U\), proving fullness.

For arbitrary \(S\), apply this argument on affine opens of \(S\) and glue by faithfulness. For arbitrary smooth \(X\), cover it by quasi-compact opens, each a finite union of affine opens. Such opens are Noetherian, as are their open intersections; the argument just proved applies to them and to those intersections. The unique maps therefore glue. This removes the quasi-compactness condition from (AR.4). No assertion about normality of \(X\) was used.

### AR.4. Extension across the closed fibre of a local normal base

Let \((A,\mathfrak m)\) be a normal Noetherian local domain of dimension at least two, set \(S=\operatorname{Spec}A\) and \(U=S\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\), and let \(X\to S\) be smooth with geometrically connected fibres and section \(\sigma\). Suppose a finite étale cover \(Y_U\to X_U\) has generically split pullback along \(\sigma_U\). We prove that it extends to a finite étale cover of \(X\).

At every point of the closed fibre, a regular pair from \(A\), supplied by AN.3, stays regular in the local ring of \(X\) by flatness. For \(j:X_U\hookrightarrow X\) and \(E\) the algebra bundle of the given cover, AO.2–AO.3 construct the finite algebra

\[
\mathcal C=j_*E.
\tag{AR.5}
\]

Choose an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}B\subset X\) containing \(\sigma(\mathfrak m)\). The section factors through this open: its inverse image in the local scheme \(S\) is an open containing the closed point, hence all of \(S\). With \(I\) its ideal, AN.2 gives the flat completion map

\[
B\longrightarrow D=\widehat B^{\,I}
 \simeq A[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]
\qquad(d\geq0).
\tag{AR.6}
\]

Let \(V=\operatorname{Spec}D\times_S U\) and let \(W\to V\) be the pulled-back cover. Its restriction \(W_0\) to the punctured zero section is the pullback of \(Y_U\) along \(\sigma_U\). By AR.1 this is the split cover of degree \(n\), where \(n\) is its generic degree. If \(d>0\), (AN.12) therefore gives \(W\simeq\coprod_1^n V\). For \(d=0\) the same assertion is immediate because \(V=U\). The regular pair on \(A\) remains regular at every missing point of \(\operatorname{Spec}D\), so AO.1 gives \(\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)=D\). Flat base change (AO.6) now identifies the algebra in (AR.5) on this completed chart:

\[
\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}B,\mathcal C)\otimes_B D
 \simeq D^n.
\tag{AR.7}
\]

This is an isomorphism of algebras, since all the base-change and section identifications preserve multiplication and unit.

We explain exactly where étaleness descends from (AR.7). The prime \(\mathfrak mD\) has quotient \(k[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]\), with \(k=A/\mathfrak m\). The induced map
\(B/\mathfrak mB\to k[[t_1,\ldots,t_d]]\) is flat, by base change in (AR.6). The contraction of the zero prime of the target is a minimal prime of the source: if there were a strict generalization of that contraction, flat prime lifting from AC.3 would lift it to a prime strictly below zero. The closed fibre \(X_k\) is geometrically integral by smoothness and geometric connectedness, as proved in AQ.3. Thus \(B/\mathfrak mB\) is a domain, and that contraction is zero. The prime \(\mathfrak mD\) therefore maps to the unique generic point \(\xi\) of \(X_k\). The local map

\[
B_{\mathfrak mB}\longrightarrow D_{\mathfrak mD}
\tag{AR.8}
\]

is flat and local, hence faithfully flat by AC.3. Equation (AR.7) and AO.3's descent criterion show that \(\mathcal C_\xi\) is finite étale.

The locus \(X^\circ\) where \(\mathcal C\) is locally free is open by AO.6's finite-presentation argument, and it is exactly its finite étale locus by (AO.7). It contains \(X_U\) and \(\xi\). Hence its intersection with every fibre is dense; on each fibre away from the closed point it is the whole fibre. Every base point of depth at most one is away from that closed point, since \(A\) has depth at least two. These are precisely the hypotheses (AO.12). Relative purity extends the cover from \(X^\circ\) to all of \(X\). Its algebra is \(\mathcal C\): applying AO.1 to its algebra bundle recovers its sections from \(X_U\), and those sections are (AR.5). This proves the local extension assertion. Maps and identities on \(X_U\) extend uniquely by the same AO.1 full faithfulness.

### AR.5. The generic Galois cover theorem

Let \(S\) be an integral normal Noetherian scheme, with generic point \(\eta\). Let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth with geometrically connected fibres and section \(\sigma:S\to X\). Suppose \(Z\to X_\eta\) is a finite étale Galois cover with group \(G\), the order of \(G\) is invertible on \(S\), and \(Z\) has a \(\kappa(\eta)\)-point over \(\sigma(\eta)\). Then

\[
\begin{gathered}
Y\longrightarrow X\quad\text{is a finite étale Galois cover with group }G,\\
Y|_{X_\eta}\simeq Z,
\end{gathered}
\tag{AR.9}
\]

for an extension unique up to its specified unique isomorphism. Uniqueness and extension of its maps follow from (AR.4).

First suppose \(S\) is affine and \(X\) quasi-compact. By AR.2 the finite algebra of \(Z\), its \(G\)-action and its torsor isomorphism descend to \(X_U\) for some nonempty open \(U\subset S\). The resulting cover is connected. Indeed a nontrivial open-and-closed decomposition would, by openness of its smooth map to \(S\), give a nontrivial decomposition of the generic fibre \(Z\). Every nonempty open of the integral base contains \(\eta\). The same observation shows that any finite étale extension of \(Z\) over a base open is connected.

Equation (AR.4) glues the extensions over all possible base opens, with their \(G\)-actions and specified generic identifications. Denote their union again by \(U\). Suppose it is not all of \(S\). Choose a generic point \(s\) of a component of the complement. Over \(A=\mathcal O_{S,s}\), the current cover is defined over the punctured base. If \(\dim A=1\), use the DVR theorem (AQ.10). If \(\dim A\geq2\), its pullback along the punctured section is generically split: the given generic rational point and the torsor action give all \(|G|\) rational points of that fibre. The local extension proved in Section AR.4 supplies a cover over \(X_A\). Full faithfulness on the puncture extends the \(G\)-action, all group identities and the inverse of the torsor map. The extension is connected by the generic-fibre argument just given.

The finite-diagram gluing (AR.3) now enlarges the base open through \(s\), including the group action and its torsor isomorphism. This contradicts maximality of \(U\). Thus the extension exists over all of the affine base. Over a general \(S\), apply this result on affine base opens and glue by (AR.4).

Finally allow \(X\) to be non-quasi-compact. Each fibre is geometrically integral, by AQ.3 applied after every field extension. Since \(S\) is Noetherian it is quasi-compact, as is the section image \(\sigma(S)\). For each \(x\in X\), choose a finite union \(T_x\) of affine opens of \(X\) containing \(x\) and the whole section image. It is a quasi-compact smooth \(S\)-scheme. Every geometric fibre is a nonempty open in the corresponding integral geometric fibre of \(X\), so is integral and connected. The restriction of \(Z\) to \((T_x)_\eta\) is still a connected Galois cover: \(Z\) itself is integral by AQ.3 over the field \(\kappa(\eta)\), and this restriction is a nonempty open in \(Z\). The quasi-compact case applies to \(T_x\).

On intersections \(T_x\cap T_y\), the resulting finite covers have the same generic restriction. Formula (AR.4), which was proved for arbitrary smooth schemes, supplies their unique isomorphism. Its faithfulness gives the triple-overlap identities, so the covers and their \(G\)-actions glue on \(X\). Finiteness and étaleness are local on \(X\), and the torsor identity is preserved by this gluing. The resulting cover is connected: two nonempty clopen pieces would both meet the generic fibre by smooth openness and would disconnect \(Z\). This proves (AR.9) in the full stated generality.

### AR.6. What the extension theorem supplies

Equation (AR.9) is the generic-cover input used in AL.5 and in the positive-degree argument of the linked smooth-base-change lesson. It includes normal bases of mixed characteristic and does not require the smooth family to be quasi-compact. The finite-chart restrictions in the proof are removed by the final gluing argument.

AS.1–AS.7 complete the positive-degree cohomological induction over arbitrary bases at each invertible modulus, using this theorem, the AL finite-map and curve calculations, and the integer-model normalization AG.5. AM–AN give connected neighbourhoods and degree-zero comparison at that generality. AT.1–AT.5 give the resulting local-acyclicity and selected-neighbourhood conclusions, including mixed characteristic. Complete coefficients and their operation comparisons are treated in BK–BX.

## Appendix AS. Smooth comparison by effacing a class

Let \(X,S,T\) be schemes, let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth, and let \(g:T\to S\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Set \(Y=X\times_ST\), with projections \(h:Y\to X\) and \(e:Y\to T\). Fix an integer \(n>0\) invertible on \(S\). For every étale \(\mathbf Z/n\)-module sheaf \(F\), the canonical comparison is an isomorphism:

\[
f^{-1}R^qg_*F\longrightarrow R^qh_*e^{-1}F
\qquad(q\geq0).
\tag{AS.1}
\]

The same conclusion holds for filtered unions of such coefficient sheaves, with varying invertible annihilators. In particular it retains the full assertion for torsion orders prime to the characteristic over an arbitrary fixed field, including arbitrary torsion in characteristic zero. The schemes need not be Noetherian. AG.5 supplies the finite normalization of integer models which permits the general-base proof.
The proof has two different induction parameters. Lower cohomological degrees control restriction to an open subset of \(T\). Lower dimension controls the complementary closed subset. Before using either induction we establish how a generic curve class can be killed and why finite replacements preserve the vanishing problem.

### AS.1. Finite data and the cohomological reductions

We use étale \(\Lambda\)-module sheaves, where \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\) and \(n\) is invertible on \(S\). The case \(n=1\) is zero throughout; assume \(n>1\) in the argument. T.1–T.4 provide injectives and connecting maps. Their cohomology agrees with the underlying abelian-sheaf cohomology: in AK.2–AK.3 replace the augmented free abelian sheaves of a hypercover by free \(\Lambda\)-module sheaves. The local cone contraction remains valid over \(\Lambda\). Applying Hom into a module injective makes that augmented complex exact, so the same effaceable-functor comparison identifies derived cohomology with the cochains of the underlying sheaf. In particular module injectives are acyclic for the underlying section functor and its localized direct-image calculations. This does not assert that their underlying abelian sheaves are injective.

For any quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme, cohomology commutes with filtered coefficient colimits. The fixed-scheme proof in AK.1–AK.3 needs no Noetherian hypothesis: affine étale objects and finite covers of their quasi-compact overlaps give the same finite-family hypercovers. A cocycle and a cochain witnessing its vanishing involve only finitely many sections and equalities. They occur at one coefficient stage. The comparison with derived cohomology therefore gives the assertion. Apply it on affine étale test objects and their quasi-compact, quasi-separated inverse images to obtain the analogous assertion for \(R^qg_*\).

We will also use continuity when both the scheme and coefficients vary. For affine schemes expressed as limits of Noetherian affine models, AK.1–AK.3 apply to every affine étale test object and its inverse image. Descend the object, the finite truncated hypercover, its cocycle and any vanishing cochain. This proves both surjectivity and injectivity after sheafification. Consequently, for compatible affine diagrams \(Y_i\to X_i\) of finite presentation over Noetherian models, with affine limit \(Y\to X\), and compatible coefficients \(L_i\),

\[
R^qh_*\!\left(\operatorname{colim}_i v_i^{-1}L_i\right)
 =\operatorname{colim}_i u_i^{-1}R^qh_{i*}L_i.
\tag{AS.2}
\]

Here \(u_i:X\to X_i\) and \(v_i:Y\to Y_i\) are the projections. In the application below, each \(Y_i\) is the base change of one fixed smooth affine scheme by its affine base ring \(B_i\); hence it is precisely the finite-presentation situation of AK.4. For a fixed morphism between possibly non-Noetherian affine schemes the same argument works: finite presentations, maps and the equalities witnessing an empty complement descend by AH.4. The finite-family cochain proof is unchanged. Finite affine covers and their overlap covers extend these assertions to the quasi-compact, quasi-separated restrictions used below.

The canonical comparison in (AS.1) is obtained from the section adjunction and resolutions. It respects coefficient connecting maps, restriction to étale objects, and successive changes of base. These facts can be checked before passing to cohomology: restriction and the adjunction unit commute, and the composite of two adjunction pullbacks is the pullback for the composite. AB.3 identifies étale localization of resolutions with the corresponding slice-site resolutions.

We recall the precise open-cover reduction. If \(T=W\cup W'\), the two-open-cover resolution sequence gives the relative Mayer–Vietoris sequence, with restriction difference on \(W\cap W'\). For an injective sheaf the required restriction surjections follow by applying Hom to the inclusion of the extension-by-zero free module of an open into that of the larger open. Thus this sequence computes derived direct images; no acyclicity of an arbitrary coefficient sheaf is presumed. In degree \(q\), use its five terms with middle term \(R^qg_*F\): the other four have degrees \(q-1\) or \(q\) on \(W,W'\) and their intersection. Comparison on these schemes proves comparison on \(T\). A quasi-compact open of an affine scheme has a finite principal cover with affine intersections, so induction first treats those opens. For a finite affine cover of a general quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme, the intersection of the last affine with the preceding union is such a quasi-compact open. A second induction gives the reduction to affine \(T\).

### AS.2. A pointed cover kills a generic curve class

Let \(K/L\) be fields with \(n\) invertible in \(L\), let \(C/L\) be a geometrically connected smooth affine curve with \(x\in C(L)\), and let \(M\) be a \(\Lambda\)-sheaf on \(\operatorname{Spec}K\). For every \(q>0\) and
\(\xi\in H^q(C_K,M|_{C_K})\), there are compatible finite extensions \(L'/L\), \(K'/K\), with \(L'\subset K'\), and a connected finite étale Galois cover

\[
D\longrightarrow C_{L'}
\tag{AS.3}
\]

whose group has order dividing a power of \(n\), whose fibre over \(x_{L'}\) is split, and on whose base change to \(K'\) the class \(\xi\) vanishes.

Choose compatible algebraic closures \(\overline L\subset\overline K\). Over \(\overline K\) the coefficient sheaf is constant. It is a filtered union of finite subgroups, since it is killed by \(n\). AK.5 and filtered continuity imply that its cohomology on the smooth affine curve vanishes above degree one. Thus for \(q>1\), \(\xi\) vanishes over \(\overline K\). AK.4 descends this vanishing to a finite extension \(K'/K\); take \(L'=L\) and the identity cover.

For \(q=1\), AB.2 describes \(M\) as a discrete continuous Galois module. The orbit of each element is finite: its stabilizer is open and the Galois group is compact. Finitely many orbits generate a finite subgroup because the module is killed by \(n\). Filtered continuity therefore represents \(\xi\) with a finite stable coefficient subgroup. Its action becomes trivial after a finite separable extension of \(K\), since the kernel of its action on this finite set is open. We may now use a finite constant abelian group \(M_0\), with \(nM_0=0\).

By AL.3, the class on \(C_{\overline K}\) comes from the constant-coefficient group \(H^1(C_{\overline L},M_0)\). To construct its torsor directly, embed \(M_0\) in an injective sheaf \(J\) and put \(Q=J/M_0\). The coefficient exact sequence represents the class by a global section of \(Q\). Its sheaf of lifts to \(J\) is locally nonempty and addition by \(M_0\) is simply transitive on those lifts. It has a section exactly when that cohomology class is zero. A finite trivializing cover and its translation permutations descend the finite free algebras by N.1, representing this torsor by a finite étale scheme.

Choose a connected component \(D_0\) of that torsor. It maps onto the connected base, because its finite image is closed and its étale image is open. Translation by \(M_0\) acts transitively on the components: each component meets a fixed geometric fibre, on which the action is transitive. The stabilizer \(G\subset M_0\) acts simply transitively on the fibre of \(D_0\), since any translation carrying one of its points to another carries its component to itself. Hence \(D_0\) is a connected Galois cover with group \(G\). Its order divides \(|M_0|\), which divides a power of \(n\). The torsor restricted to \(D_0\) has its tautological section, so the class is zero there. This treats the finite abelian coefficient group at once, without a choice of cyclic decomposition.

The finite algebra, action, torsor identity and inclusion in the original torsor descend by AR.2 to a finite extension \(L'/L\) inside \(\overline L\). Enlarge \(L'\) so that a point above \(x\) descends as well. Its translates give all points of the split fibre. The descended cover is geometrically connected, since its base change to \(\overline L\) is \(D_0\). Over \(\overline K\) the original class is zero on this cover.
