AK.4 descends the zero cochain to a finite extension \(K'/K\) containing \(L'\) and the finite extension already used to make the coefficient action trivial. This proves (AS.3), including the specified coefficient map. All field extensions here are finite algebraic extensions when finiteness is claimed; none is assumed separable merely from being finite.

### AS.3. Two finite replacements preserve injective effacement

Suppose for the moment that \(S,T\) are affine of finite type over \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\), \(X\to S\) is a smooth affine relative curve, and \(I\) is an injective \(\Lambda\)-sheaf on \(T\). Our vanishing problem is

\[
R^qh_*e^{-1}I=0.
\tag{AS.4}
\]

For a finite surjection \(\pi:T'\to T\), embed \(\pi^{-1}I\) in an injective \(I'\). The unit followed by that embedding gives a monomorphism \(I\to\pi_*I'\). Indeed its pullback to the stalk at any geometric lift of a point of \(T\) has the original stalk injection as a component, and every point has a lift. Since \(I\) is injective this monomorphism splits. Exact finite pushforward and its canonical base change in AL.2 give

\[
R\pi'_*e'^{-1}I'=e^{-1}\pi_*I',
\qquad \pi':Y\times_TT'\to Y.
\tag{AS.5}
\]

The left side is concentrated in degree zero. Finite direct image preserves injectives, being right adjoint to exact inverse image. Applying the composite direct image to resolutions therefore identifies the cohomology after this finite replacement with the cohomology of the right side. The split injection makes (AS.4) a direct summand of the replacement vanishing problem, as sheaves on \(X\). This is compatible with every étale localization on \(X\).

If instead \(T\to S\) factors through a finite \(S'\to S\), put \(X'=X\times_SS'\). Then \(h\) factors as \(Y\xrightarrow{h'}X'\xrightarrow b X\), with \(b\) finite. AL.2 gives

\[
R^qh_*e^{-1}I=b_*R^qh'_*e^{-1}I.
\tag{AS.6}
\]

Thus proving the sheaf on \(X'\) zero proves the desired vanishing on \(X\). This is a sheaf statement; it does not require an étale cover of \(X'\) to be an étale cover of \(X\). Smoothness, relative dimension, the section and geometric connectedness survive the base change when present.

These models have finite dimension: they are quotients of localizations of \(\mathbf Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]\), whose prime local rings have dimension at most \(N+1\) by the polynomial induction of Y.5, starting with the dimension-zero or dimension-one local rings of \(\mathbf Z\). Neither replacement increases \(\dim T\). More generally a finite map or an étale map between these finite-dimensional schemes has zero-dimensional fibres, so a strictly increasing chain of primes has a strictly increasing chain of contractions: if two nested primes contracted to the same prime, localization and quotient would give nested distinct primes of its zero-dimensional fibre. Localization cannot identify them, by primeness. This proves the required dimension bound. For a closed proper subset of an integral finite-dimensional \(T\), dimension decreases strictly: any chain in that subset can be preceded by the generic point of \(T\).

### AS.4. From arbitrary affine coefficients to finite models

We prove (AS.1) by induction on \(q\), for all the stated diagrams. The case \(q=0\) is AN.1. Assume comparison is proved in every lower degree. If \(0\to F\to I\to Q\to0\) is an injective embedding, the coefficient exact sequences identify the two degree-\(q\) groups in (AS.1) as the cokernels of the respective degree-\(q-1\) maps for \(I\to Q\), provided (AS.4) holds. Those degree-\(q-1\) maps are identified by induction. It is therefore enough to prove (AS.4).

We first work with \(\Lambda\)-coefficients. Smooth coordinates and étale localization reduce the change of base to a smooth affine relative curve over an affine \(S\): an étale chart over \(\mathbf A^r_S\) factors through the successive affine-space projections, each of relative dimension one. Pasting the canonical comparisons proves comparison for their composite, followed by the étale chart. The case \(r=0\) is already étale localization. The open-cover argument of AS.1 reduces \(T\) to affine; then \(Y\) is affine too.

Write \(S=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(T=\operatorname{Spec}B\). Choose a directed system of finite-type \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\)-subalgebras \(A_i\subset A\), \(B_i\subset B\), with the image of \(A_i\) contained in \(B_i\), whose unions are \(A,B\). Every finite collection of coefficients is included at some stage. AH.4 descends the smooth affine curve and its finitely many standard smooth charts to \(X_i\to S_i\); the dimension-one Jacobian presentations descend at the same stage. With \(T_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i\) and \(Y_i=X_i\times_{S_i}T_i\), all schemes at these stages are of finite type over \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\). The inverse of \(n\) is retained at every stage. A finite list of generators of the two coefficient subalgebras, the finitely many equations and Jacobian inverse identities, and the identity expressing the finite chart cover all belong to a common later stage. Thus smoothness and relative dimension descend with the diagram, rather than being inferred from its limit.

Let \(\pi_i:T\to T_i\), and put \(I_i=\pi_{i*}I\). It is injective because its left adjoint \(\pi_i^{-1}\) is exact. The counits induce

\[
\operatorname{colim}_i\pi_i^{-1}I_i\xrightarrow{\sim} I.
\tag{AS.7}
\]

Here is the point that permits arbitrary injectives. Each affine étale object of finite presentation over \(T\) descends to a stage; a section of \(I\) on its pullback is, by definition, a section of \(\pi_{i*}I\) on the descended object. This proves local surjectivity in (AS.7). A local equality of representatives is witnessed on an étale covering; choose finitely many charts and overlap charts and descend them. At a common stage their restrictions are exactly the given sections of \(I\) on the pullbacks, where the equality already holds. Sheafification gives local injectivity. Equivalently the same construction applies to the filtered basis of pointed objects at each geometric stalk. It does not assume \(I\) constructible.

After exact inverse image, (AS.2) now gives

\[
R^qh_*e^{-1}I
 =\operatorname{colim}_i u_i^{-1}R^qh_{i*}e_i^{-1}I_i.
\tag{AS.8}
\]

Thus it remains to prove injective effacement for finite-type \(\mathbf Z[1/n]\)-models. AG.5 proves the finite-normalization input for these models and their finite function-field extensions.

### AS.5. Killing the class on a dense open

Fix such a finite model and induct on \(d=\dim T\), with the empty scheme as the starting case. The assertion in each dimension includes every smooth affine relative curve and every injective coefficient sheaf. A section of \(R^qh_*e^{-1}I\) is locally represented by a class \(\xi\in H^q(Y,e^{-1}I)\), by the resolution and sheafification calculation in AK.3. It suffices to kill these representatives étale-locally on \(X\).

AM.6 permits an étale localization of \(X\) and an étale change of \(S\) so that the affine relative curve has geometrically connected fibres and a section. The induced change of \(T\) does not increase dimension by AS.3. Restriction of \(I\) to an étale object remains injective: the slice restriction has the exact extension-by-zero left adjoint of AB.3. We may again work with affine neighbourhoods. These changes preserve the local vanishing problem.

Replace \(T\) by the disjoint union of the finite normalizations of the irreducible components of \(T_{\mathrm{red}}\). This is finite and surjective by AG.3 and AG.5. AS.3 permits the replacement and an injective coefficient embedding. Treat each component separately. Its image has an integral reduced closure \(S_0\) in \(S\), and the map factors through \(S_0\), since a function vanishing at its generic image vanishes in the domain defining \(T\). Normalize \(S_0\) in its own function field. That normalization \(S_1\) is finite by AG.5; normality of \(T\) makes the map factor through it. On coordinate rings, every element integral over \(\mathcal O(S_0)\) lies in \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathcal O(T)\), is integral over \(\mathcal O(T)\), and hence belongs to \(\mathcal O(T)\). Formula (AS.6) permits this finite base replacement. We are reduced to a dominant map of normal integral affine schemes. We have not taken normalization in a possibly transcendental function-field extension.

Write \(s,t\) for their generic points. Apply AS.2 to \(X_s\), its section point, the extension \(\kappa(t)/\kappa(s)\), and the coefficient \(I|_t\). Normalize \(S,T\) in the two finite field extensions supplied there. Both maps are finite by AG.5. The inclusion of the new base field in the new source field gives a map between the normalizations: integrality over the base again implies integrality over the source ring, so its elements belong to the source normalization. AS.3 permits both finite replacements. If the injective coefficient embedding changes the class, its image still vanishes wherever the original class vanished.

We now have a finite étale connected Galois cover \(D\to X_s\), split along the generic section, with group order dividing a power of \(n\), such that the class vanishes on \(D_t\). Its group order is invertible everywhere on \(S\), since it divides a power of the fixed invertible integer \(n\). Thus the normal-base hypotheses of AR.5 hold also when the residue characteristics vary. AR.5 extends it to a finite étale Galois cover \(U\to X\). This cover is surjective: its finite locally constant rank equals its positive generic rank on every component, and every component meets the generic fibre by smooth openness. Replace \(X\) by \(U\) and pull back the class. This is an allowed étale localization; the new curve is still affine and smooth of relative dimension one. Connected fibres and a section are no longer needed. The class is now zero on \(Y_t\).

The generic point \(t\) is the affine inverse limit of the nonempty principal opens of the integral affine \(T\). AK.4 applied to the smooth affine family \(Y\to T\) gives a nonempty principal open \(V\subset T\) such that

\[
\xi|_{Y_V}=0.
\tag{AS.9}
\]

Throughout these reductions, finite base changes use (AS.6) on the sheaf of higher direct images. Only the explicitly étale changes are used as coverings of \(X\). This distinction ensures that a local vanishing conclusion descends through each finite replacement.

### AS.6. The open and closed parts finish the induction

Let \(Z=T\setminus V\) with its reduced closed structure, and write \(j:V\hookrightarrow T\), \(i:Z\hookrightarrow T\), with pullbacks \(j',i'\) to \(Y\). Embed \(i^{-1}I\) in an injective \(J\) on \(Z\). On stalks the adjunction map

\[
I\longrightarrow j_*I|_V\oplus i_*J
\tag{AS.10}
\]

is injective: on \(V\) use its first component, and on \(Z\) use the chosen second-component embedding and AL.2. Injectivity of \(I\) splits (AS.10). It suffices to kill the two images of \(\xi\).

Since \(e:Y\to T\) is smooth, degree-zero comparison AN.1 and finite base change AL.2 identify their coefficient sheaves as

\[
e^{-1}j_*I|_V=j'_*e_V^{-1}I|_V,
\qquad e^{-1}i_*J=i'_*e_Z^{-1}J.
\tag{AS.11}
\]

The restriction \(I|_V\) is injective because open extension by zero is exact. The induction on cohomological degree, applied to the smooth base change \(e\) and the direct image \(j_*\), therefore gives

\[
R^aj'_*e_V^{-1}I|_V
 =e^{-1}R^aj_*I|_V=0
\quad (1\leq a<q).
\tag{AS.12}
\]

It follows that the natural edge map

\[
H^q(Y,j'_*e_V^{-1}I|_V)
 \longrightarrow H^q(Y_V,e_V^{-1}I|_V)
\tag{AS.13}
\]

is injective. To verify precisely the vanishing needed here, resolve the sheaf on \(Y_V\), apply \(j'_*\), and take a resolution double complex for sections on \(Y\). Direct image of an injective is injective, and the first-quadrant filtration gives terms \(H^a(Y,R^bj'_*e_V^{-1}I|_V)\). A differential entering position \((q,0)\) has source \((q-r,r-1)\). If \(2\leq r\leq q\), its second coordinate is covered by (AS.12); if \(r>q\), its first coordinate is negative. No differential leaves \((q,0)\). The resulting term is the last filtration piece of degree-\(q\) cohomology, proving injectivity, including \(q=1\), when the vanishing range is empty. This argument uses only finitely many terms in the given total degree.

Naturality of adjunction sends the first image of \(\xi\) under (AS.13) to its restriction in (AS.9). It is zero, so the first image vanishes already. For the other image, exact finite pushforward identifies

\[
H^q(Y,i'_*e_Z^{-1}J)=H^q(Y_Z,e_Z^{-1}J).
\tag{AS.14}
\]

The scheme \(Z\) has dimension strictly less than \(d\), by AS.3. The induction on dimension says that the corresponding \(R^q\) on \(X\) is zero. The class on the right of (AS.14) consequently vanishes on an étale covering of \(X\). The split injection (AS.10) kills \(\xi\) on that covering. This proves (AS.4) in dimension \(d\), and completes the dimension induction.

Formula (AS.8) removes the finite-model assumption. The injective cokernel argument proves degree \(q\); induction on \(q\) proves the theorem for \(\Lambda\)-sheaves. Finally suppose \(F\) is a filtered union of its subsheaves \(F[n]\) with \(n\) invertible on \(S\). Order these integers by divisibility; their least common multiples are again invertible, so this is a filtered system. The filtered-colimit assertion in AS.1 and exact inverse image prove (AS.1) for \(F\). Over a field every torsion group of orders prime to its characteristic is exactly such a union, recovering all the earlier coefficient cases. All identifications were made with the adjunction comparison, so this proves the canonical map, with its localization and composition compatibilities.

### AS.7. Bounded-below complexes and smooth limits

If \(E\in D^+(T_{\mathrm{ét}})\) has cohomology sheaves of these torsion orders, then

\[
f^{-1}Rg_*E\xrightarrow{\sim}Rh_*e^{-1}E.
\tag{AS.15}
\]

Filter the bounded-below resolution by its cohomological truncations. The resulting spectral sequences have terms \(R^ag_*H^b(E)\) and their base-changed counterparts. Exact inverse image preserves cohomology sheaves, and (AS.1) identifies these terms by the canonical maps. For a fixed total degree, \(a\geq0\) and the fixed lower bound on \(b\) allow only finitely many terms. Comparison of the finite filtrations proves (AS.15). There is no assertion here about convergence for an unbounded coefficient complex.

The same conclusion holds when the change of base is an affine inverse limit of smooth changes of base over \(S\). On affine test objects use the finite-presentation and cochain continuity argument of AS.1 to pass the sheaf comparisons to the limit; quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness of \(g\) give the required finite covers of inverse images. Then use the same bounded-below argument. Thus the general-base comparison includes those limiting changes of base, with the same invertible coefficient moduli.

This completes the positive-degree smooth-comparison induction over arbitrary bases for each invertible modulus and for the stated filtered unions, including bounded-below complexes and affine limits of smooth base changes. The actual coefficient and adjunction maps were retained throughout. AT.1–AT.5 deduce the strict-local geometric-fibre assertions, the selected-neighbourhood comparison used in Proposition 3.3 and AI.3, and the ordinary smooth-locus nearby-cycle unit. General proper comparison is proved separately in BE, and BF–BH construct the stated unbounded ordinary operations. The complete-coefficient constructions in BK–BX require, in addition, completion, constructibility and coefficient-compatibility arguments; (AS.15) alone does not imply these assertions.

## Appendix AT. The selected strict-local fibre

Let \(a:X\to S\) be smooth. Fix a set of primes invertible on \(S\), and allow torsion coefficients whose element orders involve only these primes. This includes coefficients killed by a fixed invertible integer and all the previous prime-to-characteristic cases over a field. Choose a geometric point \(\bar x\) of \(X\), with image \(\bar s\), and put

\[
B=S_{(\bar s)}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,\bar s},
\qquad X_{(\bar x)}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X,\bar x}.
\tag{AT.1}
\]

For a geometric point \(\bar t\to B\), the local fibre is

\[
F_{\bar x,\bar t}=X_{(\bar x)}\times_B\bar t.
\tag{AT.2}
\]

The chosen map to \(B\) in this formula is part of the construction. We prove its cohomological acyclicity from AS, and identify the neighbourhood system that occurs in AI.3. Throughout, torsion orders have the just specified invertibility property; no finiteness or common annihilator is assumed unless stated.

### AT.1. Strict localization and the actual stalk map

We recall the facts about strict localization needed here, including their limit justification. On an affine neighbourhood of a geometric point, take the filtered system of pointed affine étale neighbourhoods, allowing principal shrinking around the selected point. Its ring colimit is local: every element not vanishing at the selected point becomes invertible after such a shrinking. Its residue field is the separable closure of the residue field inside the chosen geometric field. Every finite separable residue extension occurs by a monic separable polynomial with its derivative inverted, as in AB.1–AB.2.

Every pointed étale neighbourhood of the closed point of this local colimit has a section. Choose an affine chart of finite presentation through its selected point. Its equations, maps and étale presentations descend to a stage by the finite-data argument of AH.4 and AS.1. Composing that chart with the original pointed neighbourhood gives another object of the system defining the colimit. Its structural map to the colimit ring gives the section, with the prescribed geometric point. The same argument works when the starting scheme is not Noetherian: only a finite presentation is being descended.

For any sheaf \(L\) on this strict local scheme \(R\), the section map

\[
\Gamma(R,L)\xrightarrow{\sim}L_{\bar r}
\tag{AT.3}
\]

is a bijection. A stalk element is represented on a pointed neighbourhood; pull it back by its section to obtain a global representative. An equality of germs is represented on such a neighbourhood as well, and its section proves the global equality. For abelian sheaves this is an exact functor, since stalks are exact. Thus, for bounded-below complexes, derived sections on \(R\) are the stalk complex. No statement about acyclicity of a general local scheme is used.

The canonical lift \(\widetilde x\) of \(\bar x\) to \(\widetilde X=X\times_SB\) satisfies

\[
\widetilde X_{(\widetilde x)}=X_{(\bar x)}
\quad\text{as schemes over the selected }B.
\tag{AT.4}
\]

To check this identity, express \(B\) as the limit of pointed affine étale \(V\to S\). An affine étale neighbourhood of \(\widetilde x\), with a map or equality between finitely many such neighbourhoods, descends to \(X\times_SV\) at one stage. Its composite to \(X\) is a pointed étale neighbourhood. Conversely a pointed neighbourhood of \(\bar x\) pulls back to a neighbourhood of \(\widetilde x\). Refining by fibre products and a pointed affine open compares the two constructions and their maps. They therefore give the same filtered ring colimit. This argument retains the selected geometric lift; it does not identify the entire product \(X_{(\bar x)}\times_SB\) with \(X_{(\bar x)}\).

For an affine map \(u:Z\to W\), the higher-direct-image stalk formula is

\[
(R^qu_*L)_{\bar w}
 =\operatorname{colim}_{(U,\bar w)}H^q(Z\times_WU,L)
 =H^q(Z\times_WW_{(\bar w)},L).
\tag{AT.5}
\]

The first equality is sheafification of the cohomology presheaf, using the slice resolution calculation AB.3. Restrict to pointed affine étale \(U\)'s in an affine neighbourhood of \(\bar w\). Their inverse images are affine and have affine transition maps. The finite cocycle and vanishing-witness argument AK.1–AK.3, in the general finite-data form of AS.1, gives the second equality. For the geometric-fibre maps used below, these inverse images are of finite type over the geometric field, so their rings are Noetherian even if the strict local base is not. All maps in (AT.5) are restrictions, and hence agree with the adjunction comparison. The bounded-below complex version follows by the same finite-diagonal resolution argument as AS.7.

### AT.2. Smooth comparison computes the local fibre

Replace \(S\) by \(B\) and \(X\) by \(\widetilde X\). Equation (AT.4) identifies the desired local fibre with the one after this replacement. Write
\(g:\bar t\to B\), \(u:\widetilde X_{\bar t}\to\widetilde X\), and \(e:\widetilde X_{\bar t}\to\bar t\). The map \(g\) is affine, since it is a map between affine schemes; in particular it is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The map \(\widetilde X\to B\) remains smooth and the allowed integers remain invertible after this base change.

Let \(M\) be any abelian torsion group of the allowed orders, regarded as a constant sheaf on \(\bar t\). Smooth comparison (AS.1), followed by the stalk at \(\widetilde x\), gives

\[
(R^qg_*\underline M)_{\bar s}
 \xrightarrow{\sim}(R^qu_*\underline M)_{\widetilde x}.
\tag{AT.6}
\]

On the left, strict localization of \(B\) at its closed geometric point is \(B\) itself. This follows from the section property in AT.1: every pointed neighbourhood receives that section, and equalities are checked after refinement. Thus (AT.5) makes the left side \(H^q(\bar t,\underline M)\). On the right, (AT.4)–(AT.5) make it \(H^q(F_{\bar x,\bar t},\underline M)\). AB.2 identifies the étale topos of the separably closed field of \(\bar t\) with sets, whose abelian section functor is exact. We conclude that the constant-section map gives

\[
M\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0(F_{\bar x,\bar t},\underline M),
\qquad H^q(F_{\bar x,\bar t},\underline M)=0\quad(q>0).
\tag{AT.7}
\]

The first isomorphism is the indicated map, not a comparison of abstract groups. It is compatible with every coefficient homomorphism and every refinement used in (AT.5), because (AS.1) is the canonical adjunction comparison. We applied the arbitrary-torsion form of AS directly, so no classification of finite abelian groups is needed here.

### AT.3. Locally constant coefficients and universality

Let \(L\) be locally constant on \(X\) with allowed torsion stalks. Its restriction to \(X_{(\bar x)}\) is constant with group \(M=L_{\bar x}\): choose a pointed trivializing étale neighbourhood and pull the trivialization back by the section of AT.1. Equations (AT.3) and (AT.7) identify the canonical restriction map as an isomorphism

\[
L_{\bar x}\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(F_{\bar x,\bar t},L).
\tag{AT.8}
\]

The assertion is independent of the chosen trivialization, since (AT.7) commutes with its coefficient automorphisms.

More generally, (AT.8) holds with \(E\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{ét}})\) in place of \(L\), if each \(H^b(E)\) is locally constant with allowed torsion stalks. Apply (AT.7) to each restricted cohomology sheaf. In the hypercohomology filtration for the right side, all terms \(H^p(F,H^b(E))\) with \(p>0\) vanish; the \(p=0\) terms are the corresponding stalks. The lower bound on \(E\) makes each total-degree comparison finite, as in AS.7. Its edge maps are restriction from (AT.3), proving the claimed canonical isomorphism.

These assertions are universal under base change. For any \(S'\to S\), the pulled-back morphism is smooth, every allowed integer stays invertible, and the coefficient cohomology sheaves remain locally constant with the same torsion orders. The proof just given applies to that new morphism and its own strict localizations. Hence smooth morphisms are universally locally acyclic for these sheaves and bounded-below complexes. This includes non-Noetherian and mixed-characteristic changes of base, using the general-base comparison now proved in AS.

### AT.4. Which neighbourhoods occur in the affine-line argument?

We now give the exact colimit needed in AI.3. Fix \(V_0\to S\) pointed étale, set \(B=(V_0)_{(\bar s)}\), and choose the point \(\bar x\) of \(\mathbf A^1_B\). Use pairs consisting of a pointed affine étale refinement \(V\to V_0\) and a pointed affine étale
\(U\to\mathbf A^1_V\). Form

\[
U_B=U\times_V B
\quad\text{using the selected map }B\to V.
\tag{AT.9}
\]

The pointed map \(B\to V\) is the one from the defining strict-local system. It is unique with that geometric lift: two such maps have an open equalizer, since \(V\to V_0\) is étale; it contains the closed point of the local scheme \(B\), hence all of \(B\).

The schemes in (AT.9), with their selected points and refinements, are cofinal among pointed affine étale neighbourhoods of \(\bar x\) in \(\mathbf A^1_B\). Indeed an affine étale object of finite presentation over \(\mathbf A^1_B\) descends along the affine system defining \(B\), as do its selected geometric point, finitely many maps and equalities. It is then an \(U\) over some \(V\), and its pullback along the selected \(B\to V\) is the given object. Fibre products and pointed affine shrinking provide common refinements; descending the finitely many maps gives the same comparison for morphisms. Thus these pairs compute the strict localization of \(\mathbf A^1_B\) at \(\bar x\).

For every geometric \(\bar t\to B\), (AT.5), (AT.7) and continuity yield

\[
\operatorname{colim}_{(U,V)}H^q(U_B\times_B\bar t,\Lambda)
 =\begin{cases}\Lambda,&q=0,\\0,&q>0,\end{cases}
\qquad \Lambda=\mathbf Z/n.
\tag{AT.10}
\]

Each \(U_B\to B\) is a smooth affine relative curve whose image contains the closed point. Smooth openness from AC.3 and AE.1 makes that image all of the local base, so every geometric fibre is nonempty. The constant-section map into its degree-zero group is consequently injective. Formula (AT.10) applies also to its cokernel: exact filtered colimits and the identity constant maps give zero colimit of those cokernels. When their groups are finite, as established in AK.5 at this curve scope, finitely many representatives have a common vanishing refinement. This is precisely the ordinary-cohomology input to the dual compact transition calculation in AI.3.

The selection in (AT.9) matters even for constant field extensions. For example let \(V_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_3\), \(V=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_9\), and \(B=\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbf F}_3\). The polynomial \(z^2+1\) has no root in \(\mathbf F_3\), and has two distinct roots over its algebraic closure. The Chinese remainder formula therefore makes \(V\times_{V_0}B\) a disjoint union of two copies of \(B\). Pulling back through the specified embedding \(\mathbf F_9\to\overline{\mathbf F}_3\) selects one. The full product has two constant-section summands and cannot be substituted for that selected copy. The same distinction is essential in the varying pairs \((U,V)\).

### AT.5. The nearby-cycle unit on the smooth locus

Over the strict local base \(B\), let \(v:\widetilde X_{\bar s}\to\widetilde X\) be the closed geometric fibre map and let \(u:\widetilde X_{\bar t}\to\widetilde X\) be as in AT.2. For \(E\) as in AT.3, the adjunction unit restricts to an isomorphism

\[
v^{-1}E\xrightarrow{\sim}
 v^{-1}Ru_*(E|_{\widetilde X_{\bar t}}).
\tag{AT.11}
\]

At each geometric point of the closed fibre, (AT.5) identifies its target stalk with derived cohomology of the local fibre (AT.2). The unit on that stalk is (AT.8), because both are restriction through the same pointed neighbourhoods. It is an isomorphism by AT.3. Exact stalks detect isomorphisms of cohomology sheaves, proving (AT.11).

In particular, for a strict trait on which the coefficient orders are invertible, take \(\bar t\) to be its geometric generic point. The right side is the ordinary nearby-cycle complex. Formula (AT.11) identifies it with the restriction of \(E\), and its ordinary vanishing-cycle cone is zero on the smooth locus with locally constant cohomology. These identifications respect the generic-field automorphisms: pullback by such an automorphism commutes with the adjunction unit, while the source of (AT.11) comes from the total scheme and has the trivial resulting inertia action. Thus that action is trivial under the canonical identification. This statement is about the indicated ordinary torsion complexes; it does not silently pass to normalized adic complexes.

### AT.6. Use and remaining foundations

Equations (AT.7)–(AT.10) supply the strict-local acyclicity and selected-neighbourhood colimit used in Proposition 3.3 and AI.3. Equation (AT.11) supplies the ordinary smooth-locus nearby-cycle comparison for the stated invertible torsion coefficients. Properness was not used in these deductions. AU–BE separately prove the proper-comparison foundations and the actual general proper base-change map. The field-scope finite-coefficient duality and proper-support constructions use their stated finiteness and trace hypotheses. Complete coefficients and rationalization are treated in BK–BX.

## Appendix AU. Proper geometry behind the comparison theorem

The degree-zero argument for proper comparison needs control of connected fibres. We prove the Noetherian geometric input here, starting with the projective cohomology calculation of W. We also prove the proper quasi-finite consequence used in the projective-space reduction. Throughout AU.1–AU.6, a proper morphism has locally Noetherian target; neither flatness nor reducedness is assumed. Cohomology in this appendix is Zariski cohomology of quasi-coherent sheaves. It is not the étale comparison theorem we are trying to establish.

### AU.1. Functions, affine covers and projective coordinates

For a quasi-compact separated scheme over an affine ring, intersections in a finite affine cover are affine, by the closed-diagonal argument in W.2. The ordered section complex of that cover computes quasi-coherent cohomology. Localizing a base ring localizes this finite complex, and tensoring by a flat base algebra tensors it exactly. In particular, for any flat algebra \(A\to A'\),

\[
H^q(X,F)\otimes_A A'
\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(X_{A'},F_{A'}).
\tag{AU.1}
\]

These are the canonical restriction and pullback maps: on each intersection they are the affine module maps of W.1. The same calculation on principal base opens proves that \(R^qf_*F\) is quasi-coherent. In degree zero it also gives

\[
\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)_b
=\Gamma(X_b,\mathcal O_X),\qquad
X_b=\{x\mid b_x\text{ is a unit}\},
\tag{AU.2}
\]

for a global function \(b\), even when \(b\) is not pulled back from the base: localize the finite affine-cover equalizer by its compatible restrictions. Its principal intersections cover \(X_b\).

Two elementary scheme facts will be used. A morphism from a proper \(S\)-scheme to a separated \(S\)-scheme is proper: its graph is a closed immersion and the subsequent projection is a proper base change. An immersion which is proper is a closed immersion. To check the latter locally, write it as a closed immersion into an open subset of the target. Its image is closed in the whole target by properness. Adjoin the open complement of that image to the original open; on this target cover the morphism is a closed immersion, with empty inverse image on the complement. The defining ideals glue.

For completeness, finite products of projective spaces embed in a single projective space. For two factors the coordinates are \(z_{ij}=x_i y_j\), subject to the equations

\[
z_{ij}z_{ab}-z_{ib}z_{aj}=0.
\tag{AU.3}
\]

On the open where \(z_{ij}\) is invertible, these equations express every coordinate ratio as the product of the ratios in its row and column. Thus this affine chart of their zero scheme is the corresponding product chart, with inverse coordinates \(x_a/x_i=z_{aj}/z_{ij}\) and \(y_b/y_j=z_{ib}/z_{ij}\). These charts cover that projective zero scheme and the product. They prove the closed immersion, over every ring, and iteration handles finitely many factors. Properness of the projective spaces is proved in AE.2; finiteness of coherent cohomology on their closed subschemes over Noetherian rings is W.4.

### AU.2. A projective modification over an affine Noetherian base

Let \(X\) be separated and of finite type over a Noetherian ring \(A\). We construct a proper surjection \(\pi:T\to X\), an immersion \(T\to\mathbf P^N_A\), and a dense open \(U\subset X\) over which \(\pi\) is an isomorphism. When \(X\) is proper over \(A\), both \(T\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) and \(T\to X\) are projective.

There are finitely many irreducible components of \(X\). An affine neighbourhood of a point can be chosen to avoid the components not containing it, by first taking their open complement. It contains the generic point of every component through the point. For each remaining component, choose an affine neighbourhood of its generic point avoiding all other components. These added neighbourhoods are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the first one. Their finite disjoint union is affine and contains all component generic points. A finite subcover therefore gives affine opens \(U_1,\ldots,U_r\), each containing all those generic points. Their intersection \(U\) is dense.

For a quasi-compact immersion \(j:V\to Y\) between the Noetherian separated schemes in this construction, its schematic closure is defined by

\[
\ker(\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow j_*\mathcal O_V).
\tag{AU.4}
\]

This ideal is quasi-coherent: on an affine chart compute sections by a finite affine cover of \(V\), and use the localization equalizer in AU.1. The quotient embeds in \(j_*\mathcal O_V\); its underlying space is the closure of \(V\), and \(V\) is open in it, as is checked on an open where the immersion is closed. Thus \(V\) is schematically dense in the closure. A map from this closure to a separated target is determined by its restriction to \(V\): the ideal of the closed equalizer of two such maps vanishes on \(V\), hence vanishes by that embedding. This remains true after restriction to any open containing part of \(V\).

Replace \(X\), if necessary, by the schematic closure of \(U\) in \(X\). This is a surjective closed immersion, unchanged on \(U\), and its intersections with the \(U_i\) are still affine. It suffices to make the construction for this new scheme and compose its map to the old one. Hence assume \(U\) schematically dense in \(X\).

Each \(U_i\) has a closed embedding into some \(\mathbf A_A^{n_i}\), by finite algebra generators, and hence an immersion into \(\mathbf P_A^{n_i}\). Let \(Z_i\) be its schematic closure there. Let \(Z\) be the schematic closure of the simultaneous immersion of \(U\) into the product of these projective spaces. This simultaneous map is an immersion: one component is an immersion and the other components give a closed graph. The projections of \(Z\) factor through the \(Z_i\), since their defining ideals vanish on the schematically dense \(U\). Write them as \(p_i:Z\to Z_i\). They are proper by AU.1.

Set \(V_i=p_i^{-1}(U_i)\) and \(T=\bigcup_iV_i\). The maps \(V_i\to U_i\to X\) agree on the schematically dense common open \(U\), so the equalizer argument glues them to \(\pi:T\to X\). The open immersion

\[
V_i\longrightarrow\pi^{-1}(U_i)
\tag{AU.5}
\]

is proper over \(U_i\): its source is proper there and its target is separated there. Consequently its image is closed. It contains \(U\), which is dense in the target, so it is surjective and is an isomorphism of these open subschemes. Thus \(\pi\) is proper on a target cover, and hence proper. Its closed image contains \(U\), so it is surjective. Applying the same proper-open-immersion argument to \(U\to\pi^{-1}(U)\) proves \(\pi^{-1}(U)=U\).

The scheme \(T\) is an open of \(Z\), and (AU.3) embeds the ambient product in \(\mathbf P^N_A\). This gives the promised immersion. If \(X\) is proper, then \(T\) is proper over \(A\), so that immersion is closed. Finally \((\pi,h):T\to X\times_A\mathbf P^N_A\) is a closed immersion: factor through the closed graph in \(X\times_A T\), followed by the base change of the closed immersion \(h\). This proves that \(\pi\) itself is projective. The construction includes nonreduced and reducible \(X\); schematic density, rather than only topological density, is what permits the gluing.

### AU.3. Finiteness for all proper coherent cohomology

We now prove that for proper \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\), with \(A\) Noetherian, and coherent \(F\),

\[
H^q(X,F)\text{ is a finite }A\text{-module for every }q\geq0.
\tag{AU.6}
\]

Use Noetherian induction on the closed support. The induction assertion for a closed subset \(Z\) includes every coherent sheaf supported on \(Z\), not just its structure sheaf. If \(J\) defines the reduced closed scheme \(Z\), some power of \(J\) annihilates such a sheaf: on each of finitely many affine charts, its finite generators are killed by powers of the finitely many generators of \(J\), and one common power works. The filtration by \(J^aF\) reduces to coherent sheaves on the reduced scheme \(Z\). Closed pushforward gives the same cohomology, by the affine section complexes. We may therefore work with a coherent \(F\) on the proper reduced scheme \(Z\).

Apply AU.2 to \(Z\), obtaining a projective \(\pi:T\to Z\) which is an isomorphism over a dense open \(U\), with \(T\) projective over \(A\). Put \(G=\pi^*F\). The sheaves \(R^b\pi_*G\) are coherent: on every affine open of \(Z\), W.4 gives finite cohomology for its projective inverse image, and the localization calculation in AU.1 identifies these finite modules with the direct-image sheaves. For \(b>0\) they are supported on \(Z\setminus U\). The kernel and cokernel of \(F\to\pi_*G\) are coherent and supported there as well. The induction hypothesis gives finite cohomology in every degree for all these sheaves on the smaller closed set.

Consider the first-quadrant Leray sequence

\[
E_2^{a,b}=H^a(Z,R^b\pi_*G)
\ \Longrightarrow\ H^{a+b}(T,G).
\tag{AU.7}
\]

It can be constructed from injective resolutions of underlying abelian sheaves as in T and S; the induced scalar maps make its differentials \(A\)-linear. The bottom term \(E_2^{q,0}\) has no outgoing differential. Its possible incoming differentials have sources \(E_r^{q-r,r-1}\), for \(2\leq r\leq q\), which are subquotients of finite modules by the support induction. The limiting bottom term is a subquotient of the finite \(H^q(T,G)\), finite by W.4. There are only finitely many incoming terms on this diagonal. Successive extensions therefore show that \(H^q(Z,\pi_*G)\) is finite. The two short exact sequences through the image of \(F\to\pi_*G\), and their long exact cohomology sequences, prove (AU.6) for \(F\). Submodules of finite modules are finite because \(A\) is Noetherian. This completes the support induction.

For a locally Noetherian target, apply (AU.6) on affine target opens. AU.1 supplies the compatible localization maps, proving coherence of every \(R^qf_*F\). In particular \(f_*\mathcal O_X\) is a finite quasi-coherent algebra. This proof uses projective cohomology and the preceding modification; neither Stein factorization nor étale proper comparison is an input.

### AU.4. Completion and the disappearing kernels

Let \(I\subset A\), with \(A,X,F\) as in AU.3, and put \(M^q=H^q(X,F)\). The graded ring \(R=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nT^n\) is Noetherian: a finite list of generators of \(I\) gives a polynomial-algebra surjection onto it. On \(X_R\), the graded quotient

\[
F\otimes_A R\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nF
\tag{AU.8}
\]

defines a coherent sheaf, since its finitely many degree-zero local generators generate it over \(\mathcal O_X\otimes_A R\). Its cohomology is \(Q^q=\bigoplus_nH^q(X,I^nF)\): use the inverse images of a finite affine cover of \(X\), whose section complex is the direct sum of the corresponding complexes. Direct sums commute with kernels and images. AU.3 applied to the proper map \(X_R\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) shows that \(Q^q\) is a finite graded \(R\)-module.

Write \(J_n^q\) and \(K_n^q\) for the image and kernel of \(H^q(X,I^nF)\to M^q\). Their graded sums are respectively an image of and a submodule of \(Q^q\), so are finite. Finite homogeneous generating lists give constants \(c_J,c_K\) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
I^nM^q&\subset J_n^q\subset I^{n-c_J}M^q
&& (n\geq c_J),\\
\operatorname{im}(K_m^q\longrightarrow K_n^q)&=0
&& (m\geq n+c_K).
\end{aligned}
\tag{AU.9}
\]

The kernel groups may be nonzero even when these transition maps vanish. For the first inclusion multiply a class by an element of \(I^n\), using the factorization through \(I^nF\). The second follows by expressing an image class using generators of degrees at most \(c_J\). For the transition assertion, take a kernel generator \(k\) of degree \(d\leq c_K\). A coefficient in \(I^{m-d}\) is a sum of products \(ba\), with \(b\in I^n\), when \(m\geq n+c_K\). After transition, \(ba k\) is obtained by first mapping \(k\) into \(H^q(X,F)\), then multiplying by \(a\) and by \(b:F\to I^nF\). The first map kills \(k\). This proves the bound without assuming that any finite-level comparison is an isomorphism.

The quotient sequence gives exact inverse systems

\[
0\longrightarrow M^q/J_n^q
\longrightarrow H^q(X,F/I^nF)
\longrightarrow K_n^{q+1}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{AU.10}
\]

A compatible family in the middle has zero image on the right, since each right coordinate is the image of a sufficiently distant zero transition. It therefore has unique compatible preimages on the left. The two filtrations \(J_n^q\) and \(I^nM^q\) are cofinal by (AU.9). Consequently the actual quotient maps induce

\[
\widehat{H^q(X,F)}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\varprojlim_n H^q(X,F/I^nF).
\tag{AU.11}
\]

In degree zero for \(F=\mathcal O_X\) this is an isomorphism of algebras. L.1 proves exactness of completion of finite modules and \(\widehat M/I\widehat M=M/IM\). Localization in AU.1 applies (AU.11) over any local ring of a locally Noetherian target. These facts supply the formal-functions input with its actual finite-module and transition-map hypotheses.

### AU.5. Fibre idempotents and the finite intermediate scheme

Let \(f:X\to S\) be proper with \(S\) locally Noetherian. Every idempotent on \(X_s\) comes from a function in \((f_*\mathcal O_X)_s\). To prove this, localize to \((A,\mathfrak m)=\mathcal O_{S,s}\). An idempotent is exactly a partition into two open-and-closed pieces: its value in each local ring is zero or one, since one of \(e,1-e\) is a unit. Each thickening \(X_n=X\times_A A/\mathfrak m^n\) has the same underlying space as the closed fibre. Putting zero and one on these two pieces gives compatible idempotents \(e_n\). Formula (AU.11) gives their compatible lift in the completion of the finite module \(M=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\). Reducing modulo \(\mathfrak m\) and using \(\widehat M/\mathfrak m\widehat M=M/\mathfrak mM\) gives a representative in \(M\) with the required fibre restriction. That representative need not itself be idempotent.

Suppose now that the unit \(\mathcal O_S\to f_*\mathcal O_X\) is an isomorphism. The closed image of \(f\) is all of \(S\): on its open complement the unit would map a nonzero local ring to zero. Thus fibres are nonempty. The preceding lift sends every fibre idempotent into the image of \(A\), and that image factors through \(\kappa(s)\). A field embeds in the nonzero function algebra of a nonempty fibre, so an idempotent in this image is zero or one. Every fibre is connected.

We verify geometric connectedness. Let \(L/\kappa(s)\) be a finite extension and choose a finite list of algebraic generators. Lift the coefficients of their monic minimal polynomials over \(\kappa(s)\) to \(A\), and form the algebra defined by these separate monic polynomials. Monic division makes it finite free over \(A\). Evaluation in \(L\) defines a residue-field quotient; localize at its kernel. The resulting Noetherian local ring \(C\) is flat over \(A\) and has residue field \(L\). AU.1 preserves the unit isomorphism after this flat base change. The connectedness argument therefore proves that \(X_s\) stays connected after every finite field extension, including inseparable ones.

Here is why that suffices in the present proper setting. For a proper connected \(T/k\), its function algebra \(B\) is finite-dimensional by AU.3 and has no nontrivial idempotents. A finite-dimensional commutative algebra is a product of local algebras: it has finitely many maximal ideals by the Chinese remainder theorem and a nilpotent radical, and the Chinese remainder theorem applied to sufficiently high powers of those ideals gives the product. The radical is nilpotent because it has finitely many nilpotent generators. Thus \(B\) has just one local factor and its reduced quotient is a finite field extension \(K/k\). The same reasoning over an algebraic closure shows that if \(K/k\) is not purely inseparable, \(K\otimes_k\overline k\) has more than one prime, from the distinct roots of a separable subextension, and hence a nontrivial idempotent. To see the subextension directly in characteristic \(p\), raise each algebraic generator to a sufficiently high \(p\)-power until its minimal polynomial has nonzero derivative; these powers generate a separable subextension, over which \(K\) is purely inseparable. In characteristic zero no power is needed. Idempotents lift across the nilpotent kernel from \(B\) to \(K\): the zero-and-one decomposition of spectra gives this as above. Their finitely many coefficients in \(\overline k\) lie in one finite extension of \(k\). By (AU.1), such an idempotent contradicts the connectedness just proved after all finite extensions. Therefore \(K/k\) is purely inseparable. Over any algebraically closed extension it has just one prime, since the equations \(z^{p^a}=c\) have unique roots. Faithful scalar extension detects a nontrivial idempotent, so \(B\otimes_k k'\) has none for any field extension \(k'/k\). Formula (AU.1) identifies this with the functions of \(T_{k'}\). This proves geometric connectedness.

Put \(\mathcal B=f_*\mathcal O_X\). On an affine target open it is a finite algebra by AU.3. Localizations in AU.1 glue the affine schemes \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal B\) into a finite \(S\)-scheme \(S'\), and their evaluation maps give

\[
X\xrightarrow{h}S'\xrightarrow{\pi}S,
\qquad h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{S'}.
\tag{AU.12}
\]

Indeed on \(\operatorname{Spec}B\subset S'\), the inverse images of its principal opens have function rings \(B_b\) by (AU.2), proving the asserted unit isomorphism. The graph argument of AU.1 proves that \(h\) is proper. Its target is locally Noetherian because it is finite over \(S\). The connectedness result now proves that \(h\) is surjective with geometrically connected fibres. The construction and both maps commute with flat base change by (AU.1). Thus (AU.12) proves Stein factorization in the locally Noetherian case with all the geometric and coherent prerequisites supplied above.

### AU.6. Proper maps with finite fibres are finite

Let \(f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) be proper with finite fibres and \(A\) Noetherian. For any coherent \(F\), every positive \(H^q(X,F)\) vanishes. Localize at a prime of \(A\) and apply (AU.11) for its maximal ideal. A finite-type scheme over a field with finitely many points has dimension zero: an affine positive-dimensional component has, by AC.1's Noether normalization, an integral surjection onto a positive-dimensional affine space, which has infinitely many points. Thus the fibre is a finite discrete space, and its thickenings have that same space. Their affine chart rings are Noetherian of dimension zero. Such a ring has finitely many minimal primes, all maximal. Its nilradical is nilpotent, because it is generated by finitely many nilpotent elements. The Chinese remainder theorem makes the reduced quotient a finite product of fields. The successive quotients of powers of the nilradical are finite modules over that product, hence have finite length; so the ring is Artinian. Its local factors make each singleton open affine. The finite disjoint union of these opens is affine, proving affineness of every thickening. W.2 makes all their positive coherent cohomology zero. Thus the completion of the localized finite \(H^q(X,F)\) is zero. Reduction modulo the maximal ideal and Nakayama, with the determinant proof of U.1, make that localized module zero. This holds at every prime, proving the vanishing.

We give the needed affineness consequence. If a Noetherian separated scheme \(X\) has \(H^1(X,G)=0\) for every coherent \(G\), take a closed point \(x\) in an affine open \(V\), and let \(Z=X\setminus V\) with its reduced closed structure. The disjoint closed union \(Z\amalg\{x\}\) has a coherent defining ideal. Its quotient sequence and the vanishing of \(H^1\) lift the function zero on \(Z\), one at \(x\), to a global function \(b\) on \(X\). Then \(x\in X_b\subset V\) and \(X_b\) is affine, a principal open of \(V\). These opens cover every closed point, hence all of \(X\): a nonempty closed complement in a Noetherian scheme has a closed point. Choose a finite subcover \(X_{b_1},\ldots,X_{b_r}\). The kernel of \(\mathcal O_X^r\to\mathcal O_X\), with coefficients \(b_i\), is coherent; its \(H^1\) vanishes, so

\[
1=\sum_i a_i b_i,\qquad a_i\in B=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X).
\tag{AU.13}
\]

Equation (AU.2) identifies the affine \(X_{b_i}\) with \(\operatorname{Spec}B_{b_i}\). Equation (AU.13) says that the corresponding principal opens cover \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). The identifications agree on intersections by localization, proving \(X=\operatorname{Spec}B\). In our proper case AU.3 makes \(B\) finite over \(A\). Therefore \(f\) is finite. Target localization proves the assertion for every locally Noetherian target. No form of Zariski's Main Theorem is used in this deduction.

### AU.7. The remaining proper-comparison inputs

AU.2 proves the projective modification used in proper comparison over an affine Noetherian base. AU.3–AU.5 prove coherent finiteness, formal functions and the locally Noetherian Stein factorization; AU.6 proves the proper finite-fibre consequence. These arguments apply in particular to finite-type schemes over any field, with no perfection assumption. They also apply to Noetherian mixed-characteristic bases.

AV.1–AV.6 prove the arbitrary-base Stein and Chow statements through the finite-type ambient construction, proper finitely presented thickenings and finite-data limits. The finite étale lifting theorem for a proper scheme over a henselian local ring needs more than (AU.11): BC.1–BC.6 prove coherent algebraization and finite-cover lifting over complete Noetherian pairs; BD.3–BD.6 supply the approximation and exact G-ring inputs for arbitrary henselian local bases. AW.1–AW.6 supply the general separated quasi-finite factorization and finite-cover refinement, including their nonaffine gluing and finite-presentation arguments. AX.1–AX.7 supply the henselian-pair, arbitrary-sheaf extension and finite-cover full-faithfulness arguments. Essential surjectivity is not implied just by these assertions or by the proper finite-fibre consequence. AY.1–AY.6 prove general proper comparison in degree zero for every sheaf of sets. AZ.1–AZ.6 supply the constructible-coefficient embedding and its normal-generic, compactness and finite-stage prerequisites. BA.1–BA.7 supply affine closed-subscheme torsion effacement and arbitrary-base higher continuity. BB.1–BB.4 prove affine henselian comparison and the restricted-injective bound. BD.6 proves the degree-one projective-line comparison from proper finite-torsor lifting. BE.1–BE.8 then prove general higher proper base change and the geometric-fibre formula. Unbounded derived operations and complete coefficients are treated in BF–BX; specialization assertions require their own geometric hypotheses.

## Appendix AV. Proper approximation and connected fibres over any base

A proper morphism is of finite type; over a non-Noetherian ring it need not be of finite presentation. We therefore use two distinct operations: embed its source in a finitely presented ambient scheme, then approximate the closed defining ideal. Only the finitely presented terms are descended to Noetherian bases. This also supplies the general Chow modification needed in proper comparison.

### AV.1. The finite-data limit tools

We use the written proofs in [Limits of schemes and Noetherian approximation](course:AG-MO/limits-and-noetherian-approximation): Theorem 1.1 constructs limits with affine transitions; Lemmas 2.1–2.3 descend quasi-compact opens, sections and affine charts; Theorems 3.2 and 4.1 descend finitely presented maps, objects and their equalities; Theorem 4.2 descends affineness, finiteness, closed immersions and separatedness. Its Theorem 5.1 gives the system of finitely generated integer subalgebras of a ring. Its [Theorem 5.2](course:AG-MO/limits-and-noetherian-approximation#absolute-noetherian-approximation) proves absolute approximation, including the directed system of compatible gluings and the affineness of its transitions. Thus a qcqs scheme, with a prescribed finite affine cover, has an approximation

\[
S=\varprojlim_i S_i
\tag{AV.1}
\]

by finite-type integer schemes with affine transitions and eventual affine models of that cover.

Here is how the two kinds of finite data fit together. On an affine chart, a finite presentation uses finitely many generators, coefficients and equations. An equality between maps is equality on that finite list of generators. For a qcqs scheme there are finitely many chart and overlap choices; the section equalizer uses finite products of modules. Filtered colimits commute with this equalizer, because any finite list of agreement equations holds at a common stage. If affine charts are first chosen at the limit, eventual affineness is essential: represent a finite principal cover subordinate to old stage charts, represent a unit relation among its defining functions, and make their containments true at a common stage. The resulting principal affines identify that stage with its spectrum of global functions. This is the proof of Lemma 2.3, rather than an assumption that every chosen affine at the limit already came from an affine.

Absolute approximation also retains compatibility of the overlaps. In the induction step of Theorem 5.2, write a scheme as \(V\cup\operatorname{Spec}B\), set \(W=V\cap\operatorname{Spec}B\), and descend this quasi-compact open to \(W_i\subset V_i\), using its exact inverse images at subsequent stages. With \(R_i=\Gamma(W_i,\mathcal O)\) and \(R=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)\), its intermediate rings are

\[
Q_i=B\times_R R_i,\qquad \varinjlim_iQ_i=B.
\tag{AV.2}
\]

The limit identity follows by representing the restriction of each \(b\in B\), and then killing any second component with zero image in \(R\). The proof makes \(W_i\) an open in \(\operatorname{Spec}Q_i\). Choose a finite principal cover \(W=\bigcup_\nu D_B(g_\nu)\), and represent the restricted functions by compatible \(g_{\nu,i}\in R_i\). Their nonvanishing opens in \(W_i\) eventually are affine and cover. For \(h_{\nu,i}=(g_\nu,g_{\nu,i})\), the crucial calculation is

\[
(Q_i)_{h_{\nu,i}}
 =B_{g_\nu}\times_{R_{g_\nu}}(R_i)_{g_{\nu,i}}
 \simeq(R_i)_{g_{\nu,i}}.
\tag{AV.2a}
\]

For the first equality, localize the kernel of the \(Q_i\)-linear map \(B\oplus R_i\to R\), \((b,r)\mapsto b|_W-r\). Localization is exact, and the actions of \(h_{\nu,i}\) on its three terms are respectively those of \(g_\nu,g_{\nu,i},g_\nu|_W\). The second equality uses \(B_{g_\nu}=R_{g_\nu}\). No map to \(R\) has been assumed injective. The identifications agree after further localization, so give the required open immersion of \(W_i\). Choose finitely generated integer subrings \(A\subset Q_i\) containing all \(h_{\nu,i}\) and numerators of algebra generators for their localizations. Then \(A_{h_{\nu,i}}=(Q_i)_{h_{\nu,i}}\): surjectivity follows from those generators, and injectivity follows because \(A\) is an actual subring.

Index the glued schemes \(V_i\cup_{W_i}\operatorname{Spec}A\) by pairs \((i,A)\), ordered by increasing \(i\) and containment of the image of \(A\) in the next subring. This index set is directed: choose a common later \(i\) and include the images of the finitely many subring generators. It is cofinal over the original indices. The same elements \(h_{\nu,i}\) define the overlap at every stage. Therefore the inverse images of the two gluing opens are exactly the corresponding two opens at the next stage; on each the transition is affine. The transitions are consequently affine. Every element of \(B\) is represented in some \(Q_i\) and then in such an \(A\), and an element mapping to zero in \(B\) vanishes at a later stage. Thus the limit of the affine pieces is \(\operatorname{Spec}B\); the other pieces and their overlaps limit to \(V\) and \(W\). This proves the required compatibility of the gluing, including for nonseparated \(S\).

**Finite diagrams and covering conditions.** Let \(S=\varprojlim S_i\), with qcqs stages and affine transitions. A finite diagram of schemes of finite presentation over \(S\), together with finitely many specified composition equalities, is defined over some \(S_i\). Specified isomorphisms, Cartesian squares, étale arrows and finite jointly surjective families can all be retained at a common later stage. Here “finite” includes the number of required equalities, not just the number of objects.

The object, map and equality assertions follow from Theorems 3.2 and 4.1 of the limits lesson. To retain an isomorphism, descend its inverse and both inverse identities. For a Cartesian square, form the fibre product of the descended objects and descend the inverse to the comparison map, with its two inverse identities. These fibre products remain of finite presentation. The remaining two assertions require conditions beyond equations defining the objects themselves.

For étaleness, fix an affine presentation

\[
C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I,\qquad
I=(F_1,\ldots,F_m),\qquad P=A[t_1,\ldots,t_n].
\tag{AV.2b}
\]

The conormal map \(d:I/I^2\to C^n\) sends \([F]\) to its vector of partial derivatives. If \(C\) is étale, this map is an isomorphism. Here is the square-zero argument, also proved in [Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Theorem 3.1 and Section 4](course:AG-CA/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps#3-existence-is-measured-by-the-conormal-sequence). Formal lifting supplies a section \(s:C\to P/I^2\). The difference between the quotient \(P\to P/I^2\) and \(s\) composed with \(P\to C\) is a derivation into \(I/I^2\), restricting on \(I\) to the class map. Its values on the variables define a left inverse of \(d\). Formal uniqueness makes \(\Omega_{C/A}=0\): the two maps \(c\mapsto(c,0)\) and \(c\mapsto(c,dc)\) to the square-zero algebra \(C\oplus\Omega_{C/A}\) must coincide. The presentation of differentials by the \(dt_j\) modulo the \(dF_\ell\) says that this module is the cokernel of \(d\). Thus \(d\) is also surjective.

Choose \(U_j\in I\) representing \(d^{-1}(e_j)\). There are polynomials \(a_{j\ell},v_{\ell ab},w_{jk\ell}\) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
U_j&=\sum_\ell a_{j\ell}F_\ell,\\
F_\ell-\sum_j\frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial t_j}U_j
 &=\sum_{a,b}v_{\ell ab}F_aF_b,\\
\frac{\partial U_j}{\partial t_k}-\delta_{jk}
 &=\sum_\ell w_{jk\ell}F_\ell.
\end{aligned}
\tag{AV.2c}
\]

These are finitely many polynomial identities. For \(A=\varinjlim A_i\), represent their coefficients and make the identities true at one stage. If a model of \(C\) was already specified, use its fixed defining polynomials and descend only the additional coefficients, so the resulting algebra is that model's base change. At this stage \(e_j\mapsto[U_j]\) is inverse to the conormal map: the second line checks the composite on the generators \([F_\ell]\), and the third checks the opposite composite on the free basis. No finite presentation of the module of relations among the \([F_\ell]\) is needed.

The identities also verify formal étaleness directly at that stage. Given a square-zero ideal \(J\subset D\) and a map \(C\to D/J\), lift the variables to \(x_j\in D\). Then \(F_\ell(x)\in J\) and \(U_j(x)\in J\). Replace \(x_j\) by \(x_j-U_j(x)\). The first-order polynomial expansion and the second line of (AV.2c) make every \(F_\ell\) vanish, since products of two elements of \(J\) vanish. If two lifts differ by \(z_j\in J\), the same expansion gives \(\sum_j(\partial F_\ell/\partial t_j)(x)z_j=0\). Differentiate the first line of (AV.2c) and use its third line, reducing coefficients modulo \(J\); these identities force every \(z_j=0\). The lift is therefore unique. Together with the fixed finite presentation, this is étaleness.

For a scheme arrow, take finite affine charts in its source and target. If the useful source charts were chosen only at the limit, Lemmas 2.1–2.3 descend them, their affine structures, their covering condition and their containments in the chosen inverse images of target charts. The arrow between each such pair has a finite presentation. Apply (AV.2c) to these finitely many presentations at a common stage. This proves étaleness of the entire descended arrow.

For the covering assertion we can work with any finite family of finitely presented arrows \(U_\alpha\to T\) in the diagram. At a stage where these arrows are defined, restrict to an affine target chart \(\operatorname{Spec}A_i\). Their image \(E_i\) is a finite Boolean combination of principal opens. The constructible-image proof in Theorem 4.3 of the limits lesson establishes this over arbitrary rings: descend the finitely many chart equations to a finite type integer ring, prove the image constructible there by Noether normalization, lying over and Noetherian induction, and pull its finite description back. Formation of this image commutes with every base change. Indeed a nonzero affine fibre algebra remains nonzero after extending its residue field, by faithful tensoring of vector spaces; the converse follows by mapping a point of the new fibre to the old one.

Write the complement of \(E_i\) as a finite union of pieces \(D(a)\cap V(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\). If the family covers the limit, each limiting piece is empty. Equivalently,

\[
(A/(b_1,\ldots,b_r))[1/a]=0,
\qquad
a^N=\sum_{\nu=1}^r c_\nu b_\nu
\quad\text{for some }N\geq0,\ c_\nu\in A.
\tag{AV.2d}
\]

The equivalence is the definition of zero in a localization: \(1/1=0\) exactly when some power of \(a\) is zero in the quotient. The coefficients of the displayed identity and its equality descend at one later stage. That stage's corresponding piece is empty. Finitely many pieces on finitely many target charts give one stage where the family covers. This includes an empty chart or an empty family: the necessary assertion is then the finite equation \(1=0\). No surjectivity of transition maps, radical-ideal finiteness, flatness descent or openness assertion is used in this covering argument.

All the retained conditions survive base change to later stages. Pointings already given by geometric points of the limit diagram are retained simply by composing with its projections; no descent of their algebraically closed residue fields is required. These assertions apply to finite refinement and overlap diagrams, and to any fixed finite collection of simplicial levels and their identities. They do not assert that an infinite diagram or an arbitrary sheaf is defined at a single stage; the sheaf and cohomology continuity arguments still require their own local representation and gluing steps.

We also use the proved finite-submodule assertion, [Zariski connectedness and Stein factorization, Lemma A.3.1](course:AG-QC/zariski-connectedness-and-stein-factorization#appendix-a-approximation-and-connectedness-over-an-arbitrary-base). To recall its extension argument, on an affine scheme a finite-type submodule over a quasi-compact open \(j:W\hookrightarrow T\) first extends inside \(F\) as the kernel of \(F\to j_*(F|_W/G)\). The finite-cover localization equalizer makes this kernel quasi-coherent. Finitely many numerators of local generators give a finite-type submodule with the exact restriction \(G\). Adding finitely many affine opens and gluing the equal restrictions proves the assertion on a qcqs scheme. In particular every quasi-coherent ideal is a directed union of finite-type quasi-coherent ideals.

### AV.2. A separated ambient scheme over a nonaffine base

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated and of finite type, with \(S\) qcqs. We prove that there is a closed immersion

\[
X\hookrightarrow Y,\qquad Y\to S\text{ separated and finitely presented}.
\tag{AV.3}
\]

Choose finite affine covers \(V_j\) of \(S\) and \(U_a\) of \(X\), with each \(U_a\) mapping into a chosen \(V_{j(a)}\). Approximate \(S\) by (AV.1), retaining affine models \(V_{j,i}\), and fix one stage \(i\). Approximate \(X\) absolutely by \(T_l\), retaining the \(U_a\). Since \(S_i\) is finitely presented over \(\mathbf Z\), the map \(X\to S_i\) descends to some \(T_l\to S_i\). Eventual containment of quasi-compact opens makes each \(U_{a,l}\) map into \(V_{j(a),i}\). Choose finitely many \(\Gamma(V_{j(a)},\mathcal O)\)-algebra generators of \(\Gamma(U_a,\mathcal O)\) and represent them on the affine stages \(U_{a,l}\), increasing \(l\) once for the finite list.

Put \(Y_0=T_l\times_{S_i}S\). Its indicated chart over \(U_{a,l}\) is

\[
U_{a,l}\times_{V_{j(a),i}}V_{j(a)}.
\tag{AV.4}
\]

It is affine, its inverse image in \(X\) is exactly \(U_a\), and its ring maps onto \(\Gamma(U_a,\mathcal O)\) by the chosen generators. These charts cover \(Y_0\); hence \(X\to Y_0\) is a closed immersion. The morphism \(T_l\to S_i\) is of finite presentation: both schemes are of finite type over \(\mathbf Z\), and finite affine presentations with the finitely many images of target generators give finite presentations for the chart maps. All their open preimages are quasi-compact because the schemes are Noetherian. Consequently \(Y_0\) is finitely presented over \(S\).

Write its defining ideal as \(J=\bigcup J_\alpha\) with the finite-type ideals of AV.1. Then \(Y_\alpha=V(J_\alpha)\) is finitely presented over \(S\), its transitions are closed immersions, and its limit is \(X\). Some \(Y_\alpha\) is separated over \(S\). To see this, work over the finite affine cover \(V_j\) and choose finite affine covers of a stage there. Pairwise chart intersections at the limit are affine, since \(X\) is separated. Eventual affineness makes all these intersections affine at a common stage. Their separatedness tests are the maps

\[
R_\alpha\otimes_A R'_\alpha\longrightarrow C_\alpha,
\qquad V_j=\operatorname{Spec}A.
\tag{AV.5}
\]

The intersection ring \(C_\alpha\) is of finite type over \(A\): it is an affine quasi-compact open in a finitely presented scheme. Fix its finite algebra generators. Subsequent intersection rings are quotients, because all transitions are closed immersions, so the images of those generators continue to generate. The limit of (AV.5) is surjective by separatedness of \(X\). Represent preimages of the chosen generators and make their equality equations true at a common later stage. The stage map is then surjective. There are finitely many chart pairs and base charts, so one stage satisfies every diagonal test. Taking that stage as \(Y\) proves (AV.3). No finite generation of the original ideal \(J\) was assumed.

### AV.3. Chow modification over a qcqs base

We first supply the projective coordinates needed when the Noetherian base is nonaffine. If \(U=\operatorname{Spec}B\to S\) is of finite type and \(S\) is qcqs, choose finitely many principal opens \(D(g_l)\) covering \(U\), each mapping into an affine \(V_j=\operatorname{Spec}A_j\subset S\). Such a finite choice follows from quasi-compactness and the principal-open basis. Each \(B_{g_l}\) is a finite-type \(A_j\)-algebra. Express generators as fractions of elements of \(B\); include their numerators and all the \(g_l\) in a finite tuple of global functions. This gives a map \(U\to\mathbf A^N_S\). On the target open over \(V_j\) where the coordinate corresponding to \(g_l\) is invertible, the inverse image is exactly \(D(g_l)\), and the chart ring map is surjective by construction. The target opens in question contain the image and cover \(U\) by their inverse images. Closed immersions are local on the target, so the map is a closed immersion into their union. Thus

\[
U\longrightarrow\mathbf A^N_S\longrightarrow\mathbf P^N_S
\tag{AV.6}
\]

is an immersion.

For Noetherian \(S\) and separated finite-type \(X/S\), the finite affine cover containing every component generic point used in AU.2 is still available: its construction only uses the Noetherian space \(X\). Give these affines the immersions (AV.6). Every subsequent step of AU.2 is over \(S\): take the schematic closure of their common dense open in the product of projective spaces, use separated equalizers to glue maps on the inverse images of the affine opens, and use the proper open immersions (AU.5) to identify the exact inverse images. Projective spaces remain proper and separated over \(S\), their Segre charts are (AU.3), and all schemes here are Noetherian. These are precisely the ingredients of that proof; thus it produces a proper surjection \(T\to X\) and an immersion \(T\to\mathbf P^N_S\) over this nonaffine Noetherian base as well.

For general qcqs \(S\), choose (AV.3). Descend \(Y\) along (AV.1), retaining finite presentation and separatedness by AV.1. Apply the preceding Noetherian construction to \(Y_i/S_i\), and pull it back first to \(S\), then along \(X\hookrightarrow Y\). We obtain

\[
T\xrightarrow{\pi}X\longrightarrow S,
\qquad T\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_S
\tag{AV.7}
\]

with \(\pi\) proper, surjective and of finite presentation, and the second map an immersion. Surjectivity survives every base change: a nonempty fibre remains nonempty after field extension, since tensoring a nonzero affine fibre ring with a field extension is faithful. Finite presentation of \(\pi\) holds in the Noetherian construction and survives the two base changes. If \(X/S\) is proper, so is \(T/S\); its immersion is closed by AU.1. The graph then embeds \(T\) closedly in \(X\times_S\mathbf P^N_S\), so \(\pi\) is projective. We have not asserted that \(T/S\) is finitely presented when \(X/S\) is only of finite type.

### AV.4. Proper thickenings and Noetherian models

Let \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) be proper. Embed it closedly in the separated finitely presented \(Y\) of (AV.3), and write \(X_\alpha=V(J_\alpha)\subset Y\) as above. We prove that a cofinal tail of these schemes is proper over \(A\).

Choose the Chow map \(Y'\to Y\) by descending the finitely presented \(Y\) to a finitely generated integer subalgebra of \(A\), applying AU.2, and pulling back. Thus \(Y'\to Y\) is proper, surjective and finitely presented, and \(Y'\) is immersed in \(\mathbf P^N_A\). Put \(X'_\alpha=Y'\times_YX_\alpha\) and \(X'=Y'\times_YX\). The latter is proper over \(A\), so its immersion in projective space is closed. The inverse images of a finite affine cover of projective space become affine at a common stage, by eventual affineness. On each resulting chart we have \(R\to C_\alpha\), whose colimit is surjective. The maps between the \(C_\alpha\) are surjective, and a fixed stage algebra is of finite type over \(R\). Lift from \(R\) the limit images of its finite list of generators and make those equations hold at a later stage. The chart map is then surjective there. This proves that \(X'_\alpha\to\mathbf P^N_A\) is a closed immersion eventually.

For such an \(\alpha\), the proper surjection \(X'_\alpha\to X_\alpha\) proves universal closedness of \(X_\alpha/A\): after any base change, a closed subset of \(X_\alpha\) has the same image as its closed inverse image in \(X'_\alpha\). That image is closed because \(X'_\alpha/A\) is proper. Separatedness and finite presentation were already known. We have proved

\[
X=\varprojlim_\alpha X_\alpha,
\quad X_\alpha/A\text{ proper and finitely presented},
\tag{AV.8}
\]

with closed transitions and closed maps \(X\to X_\alpha\).

A proper finitely presented \(Z/A\) in turn has a proper Noetherian model. First descend it and separatedness to a finitely generated integer subalgebra \(A_i\). Apply AU.2 to this model, obtaining \(Z'_i\to Z_i\) proper surjective and \(Z'_i\to\mathbf P^N_{A_i}\) an immersion. Over \(A\) this immersion is closed, since \(Z'_A\) is proper. The eventual closed-immersion theorem of AV.1 makes \(Z'_j\to\mathbf P^N_{A_j}\) closed at a later stage. Hence \(Z'_j\) is proper, and its proper surjection onto the separated finitely presented \(Z_j\) makes \(Z_j\) proper by the same closed-subset argument. This proves the required model assertion without assuming a separate descent theorem for properness. It does not turn the original possibly infinitely related \(X\) into the base change of one Noetherian model.

### AV.5. Integral functions and lifting a fibre idempotent

For proper \(X/A\), every \(b\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\) is integral over \(A\). Sections in (AV.8) represent it by \(b_\alpha\). Descend the proper finitely presented \(X_\alpha\) to a proper Noetherian model as in AV.4, then descend \(b_\alpha\) by the section limit theorem. AU.3 makes the resulting function algebra a finite module over its Noetherian base ring. Multiplication by the descended function on finite module generators, followed by the adjugate identity, supplies a monic annihilating polynomial. Pulling back that equation proves

\[
A\longrightarrow\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\text{ is integral}.
\tag{AV.9}
\]

Next let \(f:X\to S\) be proper, \(s\in S\), and \(e\in\Gamma(X_s,\mathcal O_{X_s})\) satisfy \(e^2=e\). We prove that \(e\) is the restriction of an element of \((f_*\mathcal O_X)_s\). Work over an affine neighbourhood \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) of \(s\). The fibres in (AV.8) form a closed-transition limit. Descend the section \(e\), then its equation \(e^2-e=0\), to the fibre of one \(X_\alpha\). Properly descend that term to a finitely generated integer subalgebra \(A_i\) as in AV.4. If \(s\) corresponds to \(\mathfrak p\), the fields of its images satisfy

\[
\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\varinjlim_{j\ge i}\kappa(\mathfrak p\cap A_j).
\tag{AV.10}
\]

Indeed their residue domains are subrings with union \(A/\mathfrak p\), and each fraction has its numerator and nonzero denominator at a common stage. The model fibres therefore have the required affine-transition limit. Descend the idempotent and its equation once more to one Noetherian model fibre. AU.5 lifts that idempotent as a function near its base point. Pullback and restriction to \(X\) give the promised stalk element. Its restriction is \(e\); the function itself need not be an idempotent.

The flat comparison (AU.1) in degree zero needs no Noetherian hypothesis: a proper scheme over an affine base has a finite affine cover with affine overlaps, and flat tensor product preserves its section equalizer. Consequently formation of \(f_*\mathcal O_X\) commutes with every flat base change over any base scheme. The same calculation proves quasi-coherence and principal localization.

### AV.6. Connectedness and the general Stein factorization

Suppose first that \(f:X\to S\) is proper and \(\mathcal O_S\to f_*\mathcal O_X\) is an isomorphism. The image is closed; on a nonempty complementary open the direct image would be zero, contradicting the unit isomorphism at a point there. Thus every fibre is nonempty. By AV.5 a fibre idempotent comes from \(\mathcal O_{S,s}\). Its image factors through the embedded field \(\kappa(s)\), so it is zero or one. Hence every fibre is connected.

To check geometric connectedness, localize to \(A=\mathcal O_{S,s}\) by flat comparison. Any finite extension \(k'/\kappa(s)\) can be realized as the residue field of a flat local \(A\)-algebra. Choose algebraic generators, lift their monic minimal polynomials individually to \(P_r\in A[z_r]\), and form

\[
C_0=A[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/(P_1,\ldots,P_m).
\tag{AV.11}
\]

Successive monic division makes it a finite free \(A\)-module. Evaluation of the residue variables in \(k'\) is surjective; localize \(C_0\) at its kernel to obtain a flat local algebra with residue field \(k'\). Flat comparison preserves the unit isomorphism. Applying the connectedness argument over this new local ring shows that the fibre remains connected over \(k'\). AU.5 proves the field criterion: the finite function algebra of a proper connected field scheme is local Artinian, and connectedness after all finite extensions forces its residue field to be purely inseparable over the ground field; its scalar extensions then have no nontrivial idempotents. Thus our fibres are geometrically connected over every field extension.

For a general proper \(f\), set \(\mathcal B=f_*\mathcal O_X\) and form its relative spectrum, by gluing the affine spectra using the localization calculation of AV.5. The canonical factorization is

\[
X\xrightarrow{h}S'=\operatorname{Spec}_S\mathcal B
\xrightarrow{p}S.
\tag{AV.12}
\]

Equation (AV.9) makes \(p\) integral. Since \(S'/S\) is affine and separated, the closed graph of \(h\), followed by the base change of the proper \(f\), makes \(h\) proper. Over an affine \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S\), write \(B=\Gamma(X_A,\mathcal O)\). The inverse image of \(D(b)\subset\operatorname{Spec}B\) is \((X_A)_b\), whose functions are \(B_b\) by (AU.2). On this affine basis the unit \(\mathcal O_{S'}\to h_*\mathcal O_X\) is therefore an isomorphism. The preceding connectedness theorem applies to \(h\).

This proves Stein factorization over any base: \(h\) is proper with nonempty geometrically connected fibres and \(h_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{S'}\), while \(p\) is integral. It is finite when the base is locally Noetherian by AU.3, but that stronger conclusion has not been assumed over arbitrary rings. The relative spectrum is also the normalization of \(S\) in \(X\), in the precise sense of the spectrum of the integral closure of \(\mathcal O_S\) inside \(f_*\mathcal O_X\): (AV.9) says that this integral closure is all of \(\mathcal B\). Flat comparison of \(\mathcal B\) shows that (AV.12) commutes with flat base change, including its unit map and canonical first arrow.

### AV.7. What is still needed for proper comparison

AV.1–AV.6 supply the arbitrary-base ambient, Chow, proper-approximation and connectedness arguments. They do not give essential surjectivity for finite étale covers over a proper henselian base. BC.1–BC.6 supply the complete Noetherian algebraization and lifting argument; BD.1–BD.6 prove pointed approximation and pass to arbitrary henselian local bases. AX.1–AX.7 supply the henselian-pair inputs, degree-zero restriction for arbitrary sheaves and full faithfulness for finite étale covers. AW.1–AW.6 prove that separated quasi-finite factorization and the finite, finitely presented refinement of an étale covering over a qcqs base. AY.1–AY.6 complete general proper comparison in degree zero for every sheaf of sets. AZ.1–AZ.6 prove the constructible-coefficient embedding over arbitrary qcqs bases. BA.1–BA.7 prove affine closed-subscheme effacement and the exact arbitrary-base higher-continuity theorem. BB.1–BB.4 prove affine henselian comparison and restricted-injective vanishing above the affine-covering bound. For the projective line this gives degrees above one; BD.6 supplies the degree-one torsor-lifting input and proves comparison in all degrees over a henselian local base. BE.1–BE.8 supply the field-extension and reduction arguments for general higher proper comparison. The categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are treated in BF–BX.

## Appendix AW. Finite neighborhoods and finite refinements
