A quasi-finite map can lose points under specialization. For proper comparison we need to put back those points: a separated quasi-finite scheme must be an open part of a finite scheme. We also need a finite cover which, on a Zariski cover of its source, lifts to a given étale covering. We prove both statements over a quasi-compact, quasi-separated base. No Noetherian hypothesis is imposed on that base.

### AW.1. The algebra used at one point

The algebraic input is [Zariski's Main Theorem](course:AG-MO/zariskis-main-theorem#1-the-algebraic-neighbourhood), Theorem 1.1 and its proof in Sections 1–2. For a finite-type map of rings \(A\to B\), let \(C\subset B\) be the elements integral over \(A\). If \(q\in\operatorname{Spec}B\) is isolated in its fibre, that proof gives

\[
c\in C\setminus q,\qquad C_c=B_c.
\tag{AW.1}
\]

Here integral closure is inside the specified algebra, not inside a fraction field; nilpotents and noninjective base maps are allowed. The proof first handles one generator by successively reducing the degree of a polynomial relation at \(q\). Its finite-over-one-generator step uses the conductor to replace an algebra by its polynomial subalgebra near \(q\). The induction then selects a finite intermediate algebra containing the finitely many numerators needed for the localization, rather than assuming that an entire integral closure is finite.

The conductor argument is written in [The theorem on formal functions](course:AG-QC/the-theorem-on-formal-functions#appendix-z-conductor-coefficients-and-strong-transcendence), Appendix Z.1–Z.12. In particular Z.3 clears a monic denominator, Z.4–Z.7 turn the conductor quotient into a strongly transcendental algebra, and Z.8–Z.12 show that such a quotient has no quasi-finite points. The four-ring argument of Z.8 is needed when changing an intermediate base: it splits off the Artinian factor in a fibre, tensors it and passes to a quotient. Merely comparing sets of fibres would not prove this assertion.

The normal-domain step in Z.10 uses the going-down proof in [Integral extensions, lying over, going up and going down](course:AG-CA/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down#4-going-down-why-the-normal-base-matters), Section 4. Its earlier Sections 1–3 prove transitivity of integrality, the localization identity for integral closure, lying over, and closedness of integral maps. The polynomial-normality argument preceding Appendix Z uses the valuation-domination construction in [Valuation rings and separatedness](course:AG-MO/valuation-rings-and-separatedness#2-a-valuation-ring-over-every-local-subring): a maximal dominating local overring is a valuation ring, and the minimum of the coefficient valuations is multiplicative for polynomials. These are the written algebraic prerequisites of (AW.1). The isolated-fibre test itself is proved in [Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley's theorem](course:AG-MO/quasi-finite-morphisms-and-chevalley#1-an-isolated-point-of-a-fibre), Theorem 1.1; its field-algebra and Artinian decompositions also appear in AB.1 and AU.5.

We need the local form of an étale algebra and its consequences over an arbitrary ring. Here étale means finitely presented and formally étale, as in AB.1 and AV.1. We first give the formal quotient argument that will be used in constructing the local form.

Suppose \(A\to D\) and \(A\to C=D/J\) are formally étale and \(J\) is finitely generated. Then \(D\to C\) is formally étale. Indeed, in a square-zero lifting problem over \(D\), formal étaleness of \(C/A\) supplies an \(A\)-algebra lift. Its restriction to \(D\) and the prescribed structure map from \(D\) have the same reduction. Formal uniqueness for \(D/A\) makes them equal, so the lift is \(D\)-linear; its uniqueness already holds among \(A\)-algebra lifts. Apply this to \(D/J^2\to D/J\). A \(D\)-algebra section must kill the image of every element of \(J\), so \(J/J^2=0\).

For any finitely generated ideal \(J=J^2\), write a generating column \(x\) as \(x=Mx\), with all entries of \(M\) in \(J\). The adjugate identity gives \(\det(1-M)J=0\). Write this determinant as \(1-e\), where \(e\in J\). Since \((1-e)e=0\), the element \(e\) is idempotent; since \(a=ea\) for all \(a\in J\), it generates \(J\). Thus

\[
J=eD,\qquad e^2=e,\qquad
D/J\simeq D_{1-e}.
\tag{AW.1a}
\]

This is a localization assertion obtained directly from square-zero lifting and finite generation.

**Changing the base of a quasi-finite point.** The passage to an intermediate ring in the algebraic theorem uses the following statement. Consider a commutative square

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
A&\longrightarrow&B\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
A'&\longrightarrow&B'
\end{array}
\qquad
B\otimes_A A'\twoheadrightarrow B'.
\tag{AW.1b}
\]

Suppose \(B\) is of finite type over \(A\). Let \(q'\subset B'\) contract to \(q\subset B\), and write \(p'=q'\cap A'\), \(p=q\cap A\). If \(q\) is isolated in its fibre over \(A\), then \(q'\) is isolated in its fibre over \(A'\). No flatness of \(A'\) over \(A\), injectivity of the vertical maps, or reducedness is assumed.

We first prove the finite-dimensional calculation that will survive this change of base. Let \(F\) be a finite-type algebra over a field \(k\), and let \(q\) be an isolated point of its spectrum. A principal open \(D(h)\) containing \(q\) can be chosen inside \(\{q\}\), so \(D(h)=\{q\}\). Set \(E=F_h\). This is still of finite type over \(k\), since adjoining \(h^{-1}\) requires one generator and the relation \(h h^{-1}=1\). It is Noetherian by [Hilbert's basis theorem, Theorem 2.1](course:AG-CA/noetherian-and-artinian-rings#2-polynomial-rings-and-finite-geometric-descriptions). Its unique prime \(\mathfrak m\) is both its maximal ideal and its nilradical, by the prime correspondence for localization and [the intersection-of-primes theorem](course:AG-CA/spectra-of-rings#1-points-as-consistent-tests).

Choose ideal generators \(z_1,\ldots,z_r\) of \(\mathfrak m\), with \(z_i^{e_i}=0\). If \(r=0\), put \(N=1\); otherwise put \(N=1+\sum_i(e_i-1)\). Every product of \(N\) generators contains a vanishing power, so \(\mathfrak m^N=0\). The field \(L=E/\mathfrak m\) is of finite type over \(k\), hence finite over \(k\) by [Zariski's lemma, Theorem 1.3](course:AG-CA/the-nullstellensatz-and-jacobson-rings#1-why-an-algebra-generated-field-is-finite). Each \(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}\) is a finite \(L\)-module: the ideal \(\mathfrak m^j\) is finitely generated and multiplication by \(\mathfrak m\) vanishes in this quotient. The finite filtration therefore gives

\[
\dim_k F_h
 =\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\dim_k
       \bigl(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}\bigr)<\infty,
\qquad \mathfrak m^0=E.
\tag{AW.1c}
\]

This argument proves the needed finite-dimensional neighbourhood directly; it does not require the isolated point to have been split off as a global factor beforehand.

Apply it to \(F=B\otimes_A k\), where \(k=\kappa(p)\). Contraction gives a field inclusion \(k\hookrightarrow k'=\kappa(p')\). Put \(F'=B'\otimes_{A'}k'\), and let \(h'\) be the image in \(F'\) of the chosen \(h\in F\). Tensoring the surjection in (AW.1b), then localizing, gives

\[
F_h\otimes_k k'\ \twoheadrightarrow\ F'_{h'}.
\tag{AW.1d}
\]

Indeed \(F\otimes_k k'=B\otimes_A k'\), which maps onto \(F'\); inverting \(h\) commutes with this tensor product and with the quotient. Thus \(F'_{h'}\) is finite-dimensional over \(k'\). The point corresponding to \(q'\) lies in \(D(h')\): the composite \(F\to F'\to\kappa(q')\) has kernel equal to the fibre prime corresponding to \(q\), and \(h\) avoids that prime.

For completeness, a finite-dimensional algebra \(H\) over a field has a finite discrete spectrum. Every prime quotient is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field: multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism and therefore surjective. Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal. For any \(n\) of them, the Chinese remainder map onto their \(n\) nonzero residue fields is surjective. One can construct the needed elements explicitly: for the \(i\)-th ideal, multiply elements that are \(1\) modulo that ideal and \(0\) modulo each of the other ideals; then sum their multiples to prescribe the residues. Consequently \(n\leq\dim H\), so there are only finitely many primes. They are all closed, and the complement of a point is a finite union of closed points. Every point is therefore open. Applying this to \(F'_{h'}\) isolates \(q'\) in the open \(D(h')\) of its fibre. Also \(B'\) is of finite type over \(A'\), being a quotient of \(B\otimes_A A'\). This proves the assertion.

In particular, for an intermediate ring \(A\to D\to B\), take \(A'=D\), \(B'=B\), and the multiplication map \(B\otimes_A D\twoheadrightarrow B\). A quasi-finite point over \(A\) remains quasi-finite over \(D\). For quotients \(A'=A/I\), \(B'=B/J\) with \(IB\subset J\), the required surjection is \(B/IB\twoheadrightarrow B/J\), giving the quotient step in the conductor argument. The same calculation applies to its normalization square \(B\otimes_A A'\twoheadrightarrow B[A']\). Thus all three uses preserve the actual isolated point, including when the intermediate integral closure is not finite over the original base. The general statement is also [Stacks, Lemma 10.122.7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00PN).

The local form we require is that every point of an étale affine scheme over \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) has a principal affine neighbourhood with algebra

\[
D=(A[t]/(P))_h,\qquad P\text{ monic},\quad P'(t)\in D^\times.
\tag{AW.2}
\]

Here is the construction, using the algebraic theorem (AW.1). The corresponding programme proof is [Étale morphisms and their local structure, Theorem 3.1](course:AG-FSE/etale-morphisms-and-their-local-structure#3-why-one-monic-polynomial-is-enough); the formal quotient argument above supplies its final localization step directly.

First obtain a square Jacobian chart without using flatness. In the finite presentation (AV.2b), the conormal map is an isomorphism by AV.1. At the selected prime choose \(n\) of the \(F_\ell\) whose gradient rows form a basis over its residue field. Their determinant is nonzero there. If \(J_0\) is the ideal they generate in \(P\), their classes generate \(I/I^2\) locally. Nakayama applied to the finite \(P_{\mathfrak Q}\)-module \(I_{\mathfrak Q}/(J_0)_{\mathfrak Q}\), where \(\mathfrak Q\) lies over the selected prime, gives \(I_{\mathfrak Q}=(J_0)_{\mathfrak Q}\). The finitely many generators of \(I/J_0\) vanish after one principal localization avoiding \(\mathfrak Q\). Localize further by the determinant. The resulting presentation is square with invertible Jacobian. Conversely such a presentation is formally étale: for tentative variable lifts across a square-zero ideal, subtract the inverse Jacobian applied to their equation errors; first-order expansion proves existence and uniqueness. This also proves the square-system assertion of [Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Theorem 4.1](course:AG-CA/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps#4-standard-smooth-presentations).

Its finitely many coefficients and inverted polynomials lie in a finitely generated integer subring \(A_0\subset A\). Using the same equations and inverses defines a square Jacobian algebra over \(A_0\), hence an étale model by the same lifting calculation. A standard monic neighbourhood of the contracted prime base changes to the desired neighbourhood. We may therefore work over Noetherian \(A\).

Let \(B\) be the resulting étale algebra and \(q\) the selected prime. By AB.1 its fibre at \(p=q\cap A\) has an isolated separable point. Equation (AW.1) gives a localization agreeing with that of an integral subalgebra of \(B\). Choose a finite \(A\)-subalgebra containing the localization element and the finitely many integral numerators for the algebra generators of \(B\). Its localization agrees with \(B\) near \(q\). We may consequently replace \(B\) by this finite algebra, retaining formal étaleness on a principal neighbourhood of the selected point.

Write \(k=\kappa(p)\). The finite-dimensional fibre algebra has an Artinian product decomposition

\[
B\otimes_A k=L\times R_2\times\cdots\times R_s,
\qquad L=\kappa(q),
\tag{AW.2a}
\]

with \(L/k\) finite separable. The finite-dimensional decomposition is proved in AU.5–AU.6, and AB.1 identifies the selected local factor as a separable field. Choose a nonzero primitive element \(\alpha\) of \(L/k\). For infinite \(k\), Z.3 proves its existence by separating the finitely many embeddings. For finite \(k\), the field \(L\) is finite and \(L^\times\) is cyclic, as follows. Let \(e\) be the least common multiple of its element orders. For each maximal prime-power divisor of \(e\), take a suitable power of an element whose order contains that prime power. Multiplying these elements of coprime orders gives an element of order \(e\). Every element of \(L^\times\) is a root of \(X^e-1\), so the polynomial root bound gives \(|L^\times|\leq e\); the element of order \(e\) gives the reverse inequality. A generator of \(L^\times\) generates \(L\) over \(k\), proving the assertion also in this case.

Clearing a denominator from \(A\setminus p\) lets a nonzero scalar multiple of \((\alpha,0,\ldots,0)\) lift to \(t\in B\); rename its first coordinate \(\alpha\), which remains primitive. Put \(C=A[t]\subset B\) and \(r=C\cap q\). Every prime of \(B\) over \(r\) lies over \(p\). In (AW.2a), all factors except the first send \(t\) to zero, whereas the selected factor sends it to the nonzero \(\alpha\); hence \(q\) is the only such prime. Since \(B\) is finite over \(C\), \(B\otimes_C C_r\) is local and equals \(B_q\). The map \(C_r\to B_q\) is finite and injective.

Moreover \(pB_q=qB_q\), and \(\kappa(r)=\kappa(q)\), since \(t\) generates the selected residue extension. Thus \(C_r/rC_r\to B_q/rB_q\) is an isomorphism. The finite \(C_r\)-module \(B_q/C_r\) is zero by Nakayama. The finite \(C\)-module \(B/C\) therefore vanishes after one localization \(C_h\), with \(h\notin r\). This makes \(C_h=B_h\), so a neighbourhood of the selected point is monogenic.

Write \(C=A[T]/I_0\). The image ideal of \(I_0\) in \(k[T]\) is principal. Choose \(u\in I_0\) reducing to a nonzero scalar multiple of its generator, clearing a denominator in \(A\setminus p\). Its selected local fibre factor is the separable field \(L\), so this generator has a simple factor at \(\alpha\); hence \(\overline u'(\alpha)\ne0\). Since \(t\) is integral, \(I_0\) contains a monic polynomial \(m\). For an integer \(N\geq2\) with \(N\deg m>\deg u\), the polynomial

\[
P=m^N+u\in I_0
\quad\text{is monic and satisfies}\quad
\overline P'(\alpha)=\overline u'(\alpha)\ne0.
\tag{AW.2b}
\]

Consequently \((A[T]/(P))_{P'}\to C_{P'}\) is surjective and retains the selected point. Further invert a lift of a function restricting the target to its already given formally étale neighbourhood. The source is formally étale by the one-variable square-zero correction; the target is formally étale by construction. Its kernel is finitely generated, since these are Noetherian rings. Equation (AW.1a) makes this quotient a principal localization of the source. Principal localizations of a monic standard étale algebra again have form (AW.2), by multiplying the localization polynomial by a numerator for the additional element. Restoring the neighbourhoods and base changing from \(A_0\) proves (AW.2). This construction has used the already proved algebraic (AW.1), not the later scheme factorization or flatness of an étale quotient.

**Flatness over arbitrary rings.** For monic \(P\) of degree \(d\), put \(E=A[T]/(P)\). Polynomial division gives the free basis \(1,T,\ldots,T^{d-1}\). As an \(A\)-module, \(E_h\) is the filtered colimit of \(E\xrightarrow{h}E\xrightarrow{h}\cdots\), with the \(n\)-th copy mapping by \(b\mapsto b/h^n\). Each copy is free over \(A\). Tensoring an injection of \(A\)-modules with each copy preserves injectivity; exactness of filtered module colimits proves the same for \(E_h\). Thus every chart (AW.2) is flat over \(A\). For any étale \(A\)-algebra, the kernel of a tensorized injection vanishes on these principal charts covering its spectrum, hence is zero: a nonzero module element has a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal, where it remains nonzero. This proves flatness on all affine charts, with no Noetherian assumption on \(A\).

**Images of principal opens.** We can also prove openness directly. For \(h\in E\), let \(M_h\) be its multiplication matrix in the free basis and write

\[
\chi_h(Z)=\det(ZI-M_h)
 =Z^d+c_{d-1}Z^{d-1}+\cdots+c_0.
\tag{AW.2c}
\]

At \(p\in\operatorname{Spec}A\), the fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec}E_h\) is empty exactly when \(h\) is nilpotent in \(E\otimes_A\kappa(p)\). Indeed, its localization is zero exactly when a power of \(h\) kills \(1\). This is equivalent to nilpotence of the multiplication matrix. Over a field a nilpotent matrix has characteristic polynomial \(Z^d\): a basis adapted to its increasing kernel filtration makes it strictly triangular. Conversely the Cayley–Hamilton identity makes a matrix with characteristic polynomial \(Z^d\) nilpotent. For completeness, that identity follows over any commutative ring by expanding
\((ZI-M)\operatorname{adj}(ZI-M)=\det(ZI-M)I\).
The top adjugate coefficient is \(I\); successive coefficient equations express each next coefficient as \(M\) times the preceding one plus a scalar coefficient of the determinant. The constant equation is then exactly \(\chi_M(M)=0\).

Determinants commute with base change, so the fibre test gives the explicit formula

\[
\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}E_h\to\operatorname{Spec}A)
 =\bigcup_{j=0}^{d-1}D(c_j).
\tag{AW.2d}
\]

The zero-rank algebra has empty spectrum and the formula uses an empty union. Any principal open in \(\operatorname{Spec}E_h\) is obtained by also inverting a numerator from \(E\), so the same calculation applies to it. These opens form a basis; hence the map of every chart (AW.2) is open. The charts cover an arbitrary étale morphism locally over each affine target open, proving that the morphism is open. Their monic presentations and formula (AW.2d) persist after arbitrary base change, so it is universally open. This supplies the arbitrary-ring assertion independently of the field-base argument in AD.2.

**The diagonal.** On an affine chart \(B/A\), the kernel \(K\) of \(B\otimes_A B\to B\) is generated by the finitely many differences \(b_j\otimes1-1\otimes b_j\) for algebra generators \(b_j\). Its quotient \(K/K^2\) identifies with \(\Omega_{B/A}\): the differences give the universal derivation, with the product rule obtained modulo \(K^2\). This module is zero by formal uniqueness, as in AV.1. Thus \(K=K^2\), and the determinant argument of (AW.1a) makes \(K\) generated by an idempotent. The affine diagonal is therefore an open immersion. The products of the same source affine chart with itself are open subsets of the global fibre product and cover the diagonal's image. The affine identifications glue, proving that the global diagonal is an open immersion without a separatedness hypothesis. The same calculation applies after every base change.

### AW.2. Integral closure after an étale base change

We first prove a coefficient identity which avoids any separability assumption on an auxiliary polynomial. Let \(P\in A[t]\) be monic of degree \(d>0\), and let \(v\in B[t]/(P)\) be integral over \(A\). Then every coefficient of the unique representative of degree less than \(d\) of \(P'v\) is integral over \(A\).

Adjoin roots successively: adjoining a root of a monic polynomial is finite free with basis its powers; dividing by the corresponding monic linear factor leaves a monic polynomial of smaller degree. Iteration gives an injective finite free extension \(B\subset E\) in which \(P=\prod_{i=1}^d(t-a_i)\). Each \(a_i\) is integral over \(A\). Write \(v\) using its representative of degree less than \(d\). In \(E[t]/(P)\) one has

\[
P'(t)v(t)=
\sum_{i=1}^d v(a_i)\prod_{j\ne i}(t-a_j).
\tag{AW.3}
\]

To prove the identity even with repeated roots or zero divisors, first regard the \(a_i\) and the coefficients of \(v\) as independent variables over \(\mathbb Z\). Reduce the left side by the monic polynomial \(P\). Over the fraction field, the two polynomials of degree less than \(d\) agree at the \(d\) distinct roots, so their difference is zero. Their coefficients are polynomials with integer coefficients, so the identity holds before passing to that fraction field. Specializing the variables proves (AW.3) in every ring.

The monic equation for \(v\) remains true after evaluation at each \(a_i\); thus \(v(a_i)\) is integral over \(A\). All coefficients on the right of (AW.3) are consequently integral. The coefficients on the left lie in \(B\). Injectivity of \(B\to E\) makes their monic equations true already in \(B\), proving the assertion.

Now let \(C\) be the integral closure of \(A\) in an arbitrary \(A\)-algebra \(B\), and let \(A\to D\) be étale. Flatness makes \(D\otimes_A C\) a subalgebra of \(D\otimes_A B\). We claim that

\[
\overline D^{\,D\otimes_A B}=D\otimes_A C.
\tag{AW.4}
\]

Both sides commute with localization on \(D\). For the integral closure this follows by multiplying the coefficients of a monic equation by powers of the denominator; if the equation holds only in the localization, multiply once more by a power annihilating its error. This is the localization proof identified in AW.1, and works in rings with zero divisors. Hence (AW.2) reduces the claim to \(D=(A[t]/(P))_h\). Before inverting \(h\), an element integral over \(A[t]/(P)\) is integral over \(A\), since the latter extension is finite. Equation (AW.3) puts its product with \(P'\) in \(C[t]/(P)\). After localization \(P'\) is a unit, proving its membership in \(D\otimes_A C\). Localizing this assertion proves the desired inclusion for every element of the closure. The reverse inclusion follows from preservation of integrality under base change and finite sums and products. This proves (AW.4).

### AW.3. Isolating a finite piece

Suppose \(A\to B\) is finite type and \(q\in\operatorname{Spec}B\) is isolated over \(p=q\cap A\). We construct an étale neighborhood \((\operatorname{Spec}A',p')\) with \(\kappa(p')=\kappa(p)\) such that

\[
B\otimes_A A'=B_1\times B_2,
\qquad B_1\text{ finite over }A',
\tag{AW.5}
\]

and the fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec}B_1\) at \(p'\) consists of the point over \(q\). No point of the other factor over \(p'\) maps to \(q\).

First we need to lift a coprime factorization of a monic polynomial \(Q\). Suppose \(\overline Q=\overline G\,\overline H\) in \(\kappa(p)[t]\), with monic coprime factors of degrees \(r,s\). Introduce variables for their nonleading coefficients and impose the \(r+s\) equations saying \(GH=Q\). At the specified residue point, the differential of these equations is

\[
(\delta G,\delta H)\longmapsto
\overline H\delta G+\overline G\delta H,
\qquad \deg\delta G<r,\quad\deg\delta H<s.
\tag{AW.6}
\]

Its kernel is zero: coprimality forces \(\overline G\mid\delta G\), then both variations vanish. Source and target have dimension \(r+s\), so the determinant is nonzero. Invert it in the coefficient algebra. The square Jacobian criterion of AW.1 makes this algebra étale over \(A\). Its map to \(\kappa(p)\) has a prime kernel with residue field exactly \(\kappa(p)\): its image contains \(A/p\), whose fraction field is that field. The same matrix, now invertible over the new algebra, expresses the constant polynomial one as \(H u+G v\) with the corresponding degree bounds. Thus the lifted factors are comaximal. The cases of a constant factor give the same statement with the empty coefficient block.

Apply (AW.1) to \(C\subset B\), and denote its localization element by \(g\). In \(F=C\otimes_A\kappa(p)\), the point corresponding to \(q\) is isolated, because localization at \(g\) agrees with the corresponding localization of \(B\). It is closed because \(F\) is integral over a field.

Here is the idempotent construction for this possibly non-Noetherian fibre. For any ring \(R\) and clopen subset \(U\subset\operatorname{Spec}R\), both \(U\) and its complement are quasi-compact, being closed in an affine spectrum. Choose finite principal covers \(U=\bigcup_iD(a_i)\) and \(U^c=\bigcup_jD(b_j)\). Since \(D(a_ib_j)\) is empty, each \(a_ib_j\) is nilpotent: its localization is the zero ring, so a power of it kills \(1\). A common exponent \(N\geq1\) gives \(a_i^Nb_j^N=0\) for every pair. The ideals \(I=(a_i^N)\) and \(J=(b_j^N)\) satisfy \(IJ=0\) and \(I+J=R\); the latter follows because their principal opens still cover the spectrum, so no maximal ideal contains their sum. Choose \(e\in I\), \(f\in J\) with \(e+f=1\). Then

\[
ef=0,\qquad e^2=e,\qquad f^2=f,\qquad
R\simeq eR\times fR,\qquad U=D(e).
\tag{AW.6a}
\]

Indeed \(e(1-e)=ef=0\), and multiplication by \(e,f\) gives the displayed product and its inverse by addition. On each \(D(a_i)\) one has \(f=0\), while on each \(D(b_j)\) one has \(e=0\); thus \(e\) is the required characteristic idempotent. Empty sides use \(e=0\) or \(e=1\). Apply this to the selected singleton in \(\operatorname{Spec}F\). Lift a nonzero scalar multiple of its characteristic idempotent to \(c\in C\), clearing the denominator from \(A\setminus p\). Its image is \((a,0)\) in the two factors, with \(a\in\kappa(p)^\times\).

Choose a monic equation \(Q(c)=0\). Write \(\overline Q=t^e\overline H\), where \(\overline H(0)\ne0\), multiplying \(Q\) by \(t\) if necessary to arrange \(e\ge1\). Lift this coprime factorization by the preceding construction to \(Q=GH\), with \(\overline G=t^e\). The elements \(G(c)\) and \(H(c)\) have product zero and generate the unit ideal. They split both \(C'=A'\otimes_A C\) and \(B'=A'\otimes_A B\) into two direct factors. Choose as the first factor the localization at \(G(c)\). On the selected fibre \(G(c)=(a^e,0)\), so this factor selects exactly the original point, with no point over it in the other factor.

Write \(C_1\to B_1\) for the first factors. The algebra \(C_1\) is integral over \(A'\), because it is a quotient, as well as a localization, of the integral algebra \(C'\). Its fibre at \(p'\) has just the selected prime, where \(g\) is nonzero. Thus \(g\) is a unit on that entire fibre. The image of \(V(g)\subset\operatorname{Spec}C_1\) is closed by integrality and misses \(p'\). Invert one base element outside \(p'\) to remove this image. Then \(g\) is a unit in \(C_1\), and \((C_1)_g=(B_1)_g\) makes \(C_1=B_1\). This algebra is integral and finite type over the new base, hence finite. All base localizations preserve étaleness and the residue field. This proves (AW.5).

For a separated morphism \(X\to S\) locally of finite type, apply this construction in affine neighborhoods of any isolated fibre point \(x\). It gives an open neighborhood \(V\subset X_T\) finite over an elementary étale neighborhood \((T,t)\to(S,s)\). It is also closed: the map \(V\to X_T\) factors as its closed graph into \(V\times_T X_T\), followed by the finite, hence closed, projection to \(X_T\). Consequently

\[
X_T=V\amalg W,
\qquad V\to T\text{ finite},\quad V_t=\{x\}.
\tag{AW.7}
\]

The residue field at that point is unchanged, because \(\kappa(t)=\kappa(s)\). Several distinct selected points can be treated successively. Finite pieces remain finite after the successive base changes; their pairwise intersections are closed in a finite scheme and have images missing \(t\). Removing those finitely many images makes the pieces disjoint. We shall only need the one-point assertion.

### AW.4. The open part of the integral completion

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated and of finite type. The algebra \(f_*\mathcal O_X\) is quasi-coherent. On an affine base, take a finite affine cover of \(X\); its pairwise intersections are affine by separatedness. Sections are the kernel of the two finite products of sections on charts and intersections. Localization commutes with this kernel, proving quasi-coherence. Tensoring by a flat base algebra also commutes with that kernel. This proves flat comparison for this degree-zero algebra without a properness hypothesis.

Let \(\mathcal C\subset f_*\mathcal O_X\) be the integral closure of \(\mathcal O_S\), and set

\[
S'=\operatorname{Spec}_S\mathcal C,\qquad
X\xrightarrow{f'}S'\xrightarrow\nu S.
\tag{AW.8}
\]

Localization of integral closure shows that \(\mathcal C\) is quasi-coherent; \(\nu\) is integral. The evaluation of sections defines \(f'\). The flat comparison just proved and (AW.4) show that (AW.8) commutes with étale base change.

Take a quasi-finite point \(x\), and make the base change (AW.7). Since \(V\) is finite over \(T\), every element of its algebra is integral. The integral closure for \(V\amalg W\) is therefore the product of the algebra of \(V\) and the integral-closure algebra for \(W\). One can check this on affine opens of \(T\): both coordinate idempotents are integral, and two monic equations combine by multiplying their polynomials. Thus \(S'_T=V\amalg W'\), and the inverse image of its open part \(V\) under \(f'_T\) maps isomorphically to \(V\).

We will descend this local inverse. We first prove the exact scheme-morphism assertion needed, including its open-set step.

**Étale descent for morphisms.** If \(p:U\to T\) is surjective étale and \(Z\) is any scheme, pullback gives a bijection

\[
\operatorname{Mor}(T,Z)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\
\operatorname{Eq}\bigl(
\operatorname{Mor}(U,Z)\rightrightarrows
\operatorname{Mor}(U\times_TU,Z)\bigr).
\tag{AW.8a}
\]

No quasi-compactness or separatedness hypothesis on \(T,U,Z\) is imposed. The same assertion for a covering family follows by taking its disjoint union.

First consider an affine open \(Q=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset T\). Affine opens in \(p^{-1}(Q)\) have open images by AW.1, and these images cover \(Q\). Choose finitely many of them, \(U_a=\operatorname{Spec}B_a\), whose images cover \(Q\). Their disjoint union is \(\operatorname{Spec}B\), where \(B=\prod_a B_a\), and \(A\to B\) is flat and surjective on spectra. It is faithfully flat: for a nonzero \(A\)-module \(M\), choose a nonzero cyclic submodule \(A/I\subset M\). Choose a maximal ideal containing \(I\), and then a prime of \(B\) above it. Thus \(B/IB\ne0\); flatness preserves its injection into \(B\otimes_A M\), which is therefore nonzero.

For this faithfully flat algebra the sequence

\[
0\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow B
 \xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }B\otimes_A B,\qquad
\delta(b)=b\otimes1-1\otimes b
\tag{AW.8b}
\]

is exact at \(A\) and \(B\). Here is the algebraic verification. Tensor the sequence with \(B\) on the left. Its first nonzero map sends \(b\) to \(b\otimes1\) and is split by multiplication. If \(z\in B\otimes_A B\) maps to zero under \(1\otimes\delta\), multiply the first two factors of that equality in \(B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B\). The result is \(\mu(z)\otimes1-z=0\), so \(z\) lies in the image of the first map. Hence the tensorized sequence is exact. Flatness commutes with its kernels and quotients, and faithfulness detects their vanishing, proving (AW.8b). Its kernel identification respects multiplication and the unit, so it is also an equalizer of rings.

This already proves that equality of two morphisms \(T\to Z\) can be tested after \(p\). Surjectivity first makes their maps on points equal. Near each point of \(T\), choose a common affine target neighbourhood and an affine source neighbourhood \(Q\) whose two images lie in it. The two ring homomorphisms agree after the injection \(A\to B\) of (AW.8b), so agree on \(Q\). These neighbourhoods cover \(T\). This uniqueness argument applies to every surjective étale morphism and to all its base changes.

Now suppose \(g:U\to Z\) has equal pullbacks to \(U\times_T U\). For an affine open \(W\subset Z\), set \(U_W=g^{-1}(W)\). This open is saturated over \(T\). To see this, let \(u,u'\) lie over the same \(t\), with \(u\in U_W\). The tensor product \(\kappa(u)\otimes_{\kappa(t)}\kappa(u')\) is nonzero, since tensoring nonzero vector spaces over a field is nonzero; a prime of this ring gives a point of \(U\times_T U\) over both \(u\) and \(u'\). Equality of the two composites with \(g\) gives \(g(u)=g(u')\), so \(u'\in U_W\). Therefore

\[
T_W=p(U_W)\text{ is open},\qquad p^{-1}(T_W)=U_W.
\tag{AW.8c}
\]

Openness uses the arbitrary-base openness of \(p\) proved in AW.1. The sets \(T_W\), as \(W\) runs through affine opens of \(Z\), cover \(T\).

Take an affine \(Q=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset T_W\) and choose the finite affine cover above \(Q\) as before. Its pieces lie in \(U_W\), so the restrictions of \(g\) give a ring map \(\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)\to B\). Compatibility on their pairwise fibre products says that its image lies in the equalizer (AW.8b); hence it factors uniquely through \(A\). This constructs a morphism \(g_Q:Q\to W\). Its pullback agrees with \(g\) on all of \(p^{-1}(Q)\), not just on the selected pieces: test the equality on the surjective étale base change
\(\operatorname{Spec}B\times_Qp^{-1}(Q)\to p^{-1}(Q)\).
There the two maps agree by the original overlap condition and the defining equality on \(\operatorname{Spec}B\); the uniqueness result just proved descends that equality. On overlaps of different \(Q\)'s, the constructed maps likewise agree after the surjective étale pullback, and thus agree. Ordinary open gluing of the underlying maps and their structure-sheaf homomorphisms gives \(T\to Z\), whose pullback is \(g\). Uniqueness proves (AW.8a). This is the étale case of [descent for representable functors](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/023P).

Return to \(V\subset S'_T\). Its image \(O\subset S'\) is open by AW.1, and \(V\to O\) is a surjective étale morphism. Put \(X_O=f'^{-1}(O)\). The base change \(X_O\times_O V\to V\) is the isomorphism already constructed from the product \(V\amalg W'\). Its inverse has equal pullbacks on \(V\times_O V\), because both are inverses to the same base-changed morphism. Compose with the projection to \(X_O\) and apply (AW.8a) to obtain a morphism \(O\to X_O\). The condition of being a morphism over \(O\), and both inverse identities, hold after the cover \(V\to O\); the uniqueness part of (AW.8a), also applied to its base change over \(X_O\), proves them downstairs. Thus the actual map \(X_O\to O\) is an isomorphism.

Every point of \(f'^{-1}(O)\) is quasi-finite over \(S\). Indeed, it is identified with a point of the open \(O\subset S'\), whose residue field is algebraic over that of its image because \(\nu\) is integral. A fibre is locally of finite type over its residue field and has dimension zero: its points have algebraic residue fields, so each is closed, and a Noetherian affine neighborhood has finitely many irreducible components, all points. It is therefore locally discrete. The isolated-fibre criterion of AW.1 applies. Taking the union of the opens \(O\) proves that the entire quasi-finite locus of \(X\) is the inverse image of an open of \(S'\) and maps isomorphically onto it. In particular, when \(f\) is quasi-finite, \(f'\) is an open immersion.

### AW.5. A finite scheme containing the quasi-finite scheme

Assume now that \(S\) is qcqs and that \(X\to S\) is quasi-finite and separated. Then \(X\) is qcqs. By AW.4 it is a quasi-compact open in \(S'\).

Write \(\mathcal C\) as a directed union of finite quasi-coherent \(\mathcal O_S\)-algebras \(\mathcal C_i\). To justify the finiteness here, AV.1 proves that a quasi-coherent module on a qcqs scheme is the union of its finite-type quasi-coherent submodules. For each such submodule of \(\mathcal C\), take the subalgebra it generates together with one. On an affine chart it is generated by finitely many integral elements, so their monic equations bound the powers needed to span it as a module. It is finite there, hence finite on \(S\). Sums of the chosen submodules give a directed family of these algebras and exhaust \(\mathcal C\). Put \(T_i=\operatorname{Spec}_S\mathcal C_i\). These are finite over \(S\) and have affine transitions, with limit \(S'\).

The finite-data open and affine-chart lemmas of AV.1 descend the quasi-compact open \(X\subset S'\) to an open \(U_i\subset T_i\). Its inverse images \(U_j\) have limit \(X\). We claim that \(X\to U_j\) is a closed immersion for sufficiently large \(j\). Cover \(U_i\) by finitely many affines lying over affine opens \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S\). Their inverse images at every stage, including the limit, are affine. On one of these charts write \(B=\varinjlim B_j\). The algebra \(B\) is finite type over \(A\), because the affine chart of \(X\) is quasi-compact and locally of finite type over \(A\). Choose finitely many \(A\)-algebra generators of \(B\) and represent them in some \(B_j\). The map \(B_j\to B\) is then surjective. This works at one stage for all charts and proves the claim.

Take the schematic closure \(T\) of \(X\) inside that \(T_j\). Explicitly its ideal is the kernel of \(\mathcal O_{T_j}\to i_*\mathcal O_X\), where \(i:X\to T_j\) is the quasi-compact immersion just obtained. That kernel is quasi-coherent by the localization equalizer for a qcqs morphism. On \(U_j\) it is exactly the ideal of the closed subscheme \(X\), so \(T\cap U_j=X\). Hence

\[
X\hookrightarrow T\longrightarrow S,
\qquad T\to S\text{ finite}.
\tag{AW.9}
\]

The first arrow is a quasi-compact open immersion and the second is finite. This proves the required nonaffine finite factorization. As a consequence, a proper quasi-finite map is finite over any base. Work over an affine base open and apply (AW.9). The open immersion into \(T\) is proper: its graph is closed and its projection is a base change of the original proper map. Its image is therefore also closed, making it an open-and-closed immersion, hence finite. Compose with \(T\to S\) and use that finiteness is local on the target. The arbitrary-base assertion follows without reducing the original map to one Noetherian model.

### AW.6. Refining an étale covering by a finite cover

Let \(X\) be qcqs and \(U\to X\) a surjective étale morphism. We prove the existence of a finite surjective morphism of finite presentation \(T\to X\) and a Zariski open covering \(T=\bigcup T_a\) with maps \(T_a\to U\) over \(X\).

Replace \(U\) by the disjoint union of finitely many affine neighborhoods whose images cover \(X\), each mapping to an affine open of \(X\). They may be chosen with presentations (AW.2); quasi-compactness of \(X\) makes a finite choice possible since the images are open. This new \(U\to X\) is quasi-compact, separated and étale, and retains a map to the original covering. The sum of the degrees of its monic polynomials bounds its geometric fibre cardinalities by an integer \(d\).

For a quasi-compact separated étale map, the locus where the geometric fibre has at least \(r\) points is open. In its \(r\)-fold fibre power, remove all pairwise diagonals. The remaining open has an étale, hence open, map to the base; its image is exactly that locus, since its geometric points are ordered lists of distinct fibre points. The diagonals are closed by separatedness. Thus the geometric fibre cardinality is lower semicontinuous.

First construct the refinement without the finite-presentation requirement, by induction on \(d\). If \(d=1\), the covering is an isomorphism: its diagonal is an open immersion and is surjective on geometric points, hence is an isomorphism. The covering is therefore a monomorphism, and its inverse descends along itself as in AW.4. Take \(T=X\).

For \(d>1\), (AW.9) embeds \(U\) in a finite \(Y\to X\). Replace \(Y\) by the schematic closure of \(U\), so that \(U\) is dense and \(Y\to X\) is still surjective. In \(U\times_XY\) the graph of \(U\to Y\) is open and closed: over the open U in Y it is a section of the étale projection to Y, giving openness; it is also the graph of a map to the separated X-scheme Y, giving closedness. Let \(V\) be its complement, and let \(W\subset Y\) be the image of \(V\to Y\). This is a quasi-compact open, and

\[
Y\setminus U\subset W,\qquad
\#V_{\bar y}\leq d-1\quad(\bar y\text{ geometric over }Y).
\tag{AW.10}
\]

For the first assertion, over \(Y\setminus U\) the removed graph is empty while the pullback of \(U\to X\) is surjective. Over \(U\) exactly one point was removed, so the second assertion holds on the dense open \(U\). If it failed somewhere on \(Y\), lower semicontinuity would give a nonempty open disjoint from that dense open. This proves (AW.10).

Apply induction to the covering \(V\to W\). Obtain a finite surjection \(T_W\to W\) which locally maps to \(V\), hence to \(U\). Its composite to \(Y\) is separated and quasi-finite. Embed it as an open in a finite \(T_Y\to Y\) using (AW.9), and again take its schematic closure. Its restriction over \(W\) is exactly \(T_W\): that open is also closed over \(W\), since \(T_W\to W\) is finite, and taking the closure commutes with restriction to the open \(W\).

Adjoin the reduced closed subscheme with support \(Y\setminus W\). The finite map

\[
T_Y\amalg(Y\setminus W)_{\mathrm{red}}\longrightarrow X
\tag{AW.11}
\]

is surjective, because its map to \(Y\) covers \(W\) and its complement. It locally lifts to \(U\). Above \(W\) use the induction. Every remaining point lies above \(Y\setminus W\subset U\), where the structural map to \(Y\) already factors through the open \(U\). These two kinds of open neighborhoods cover (AW.11). This proves the finite version.

Finally we show carefully that finite presentation can be imposed. Any finite map \(T\to X\), with \(X\) qcqs, is a limit of finite maps of finite presentation with closed transition maps. Indeed, AV.2 embeds \(T\) as a closed subscheme of a separated finitely presented \(X\)-scheme. Express its defining ideal as the union of finite-type quasi-coherent ideals, using AV.1, to get finitely presented closed thickenings \(T_i\). Over each member of a finite affine cover of \(X\), their limit is affine, so the affine-limit lemma of AV.1 makes the thickenings affine eventually. Fix finite algebra generators at that stage. Their images in the finite limit algebra satisfy monic equations over the base. Those finitely many equations hold at a later stage; the transition maps are closed immersions, so the images of the fixed generators still generate. Thus that later algebra is finite. A common stage works on the finite cover of \(X\), giving the assertion.

Choose finitely many quasi-compact opens covering the finite refinement just constructed, on each of which a lift to \(U\) is defined. The opens and their covering condition descend to one of the finite thickenings. Each map to \(U\) descends too, since \(U\to X\) is locally of finite presentation: this is the finite-generator, finite-relation and overlap argument of AV.1. No agreement between the different local lifts is required. The resulting finite, finitely presented stage is surjective over \(X\), because the original surjective limit scheme maps to it over \(X\). It and its descended open cover prove the assertion.

### AW.7. The next proper-comparison inputs

AW.1–AW.6 prove the separated quasi-finite factorization, including its nonaffine gluing, the arbitrary-base proper quasi-finite consequence, and the finite refinement used in Lemma 4.2 of [The proper base change theorem](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#4-proper-henselian-schemes-and-the-degree-zero-theorem). AX.1–AX.7 prove the henselian-pair inputs, degree-zero restriction for arbitrary sheaves, arbitrary-base finite direct image and full faithfulness for finite étale covers. BC.1–BC.6 prove essential surjectivity for complete Noetherian pairs; BD.3–BD.6 supply approximation and G-ring reduction for arbitrary henselian local bases. AY.1–AY.6 prove the general proper degree-zero stalk and base-change formulas. AZ.1–AZ.6 establish the constructible-coefficient embedding with its finite-stage descent and normal-generic prerequisites. BA.1–BA.7 prove affine closed-subscheme torsion effacement and arbitrary-base higher continuity. BB.1–BB.4 prove the affine henselian and restricted-injective steps. BD.6 supplies the proper finite-torsor lifting input of BB.5 and proves henselian projective-line comparison. BE.1–BE.8 pass to general higher proper comparison and the geometric-fibre formula; broader specialization assertions retain their exact hypotheses. The categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are treated in BF–BX at their stated geometric scopes.

## Appendix AX. Sections over a proper henselian base

We prove the degree-zero comparison for an arbitrary sheaf of sets on a scheme proper over a henselian pair. This requires no torsion assumption on the sheaf and no Noetherian assumption on the base. The proof uses finite refinements from AW.6 and connected fibres from AV.6. We first establish the ring-theoretic and topological assertions which turn those geometric results into extension of sections.

### AX.1. Henselian pairs and integral algebras

A pair \((A,I)\) is henselian if \(I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(A)\) and every factorization of a monic polynomial modulo \(I\) into two coprime monic polynomials lifts to monic factors over \(A\) of the prescribed degrees. A henselian local ring with its maximal ideal is a special case. The equivalence with the simple-root convention follows from the coefficient-Jacobian argument (AW.3) and the section criterion in [Henselian local rings and henselization](course:AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization#1-roots-and-maps-with-a-prescribed-residue), Theorem 1.2 and Proposition 2.1. That section criterion uses exactly the local standard form (AW.2).

For every integral \(A\)-algebra \(B\), reduction induces a bijection

\[
\operatorname{Idem}(B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Idem}(B/IB).
\tag{AX.1}
\]

Here is the proof, including the finite-module step. First suppose \(B\) is finite. Given \(\bar e^2=\bar e\) in \(B/IB\), choose generators of its two summands and lift them to elements of \(B\). They generate \(B\) by Nakayama, since \(I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(A)\). Choose a lift \(b\) of \(\bar e\). Multiplication by \(b\) on this generating list has a matrix \(M\) reducing to a diagonal matrix with \(r\) entries one and \(s\) entries zero: each error is in \(IB\) and hence can be expressed in the same list with coefficients in \(I\). The determinant trick gives

\[
P(b)=0,\qquad P(t)=\det(t-M),\qquad
\overline P=(t-1)^r t^s.
\tag{AX.2}
\]

The list need not be a free basis. The adjugate identity annihilates every member of the list, hence annihilates the unit of \(B\), proving \(P(b)=0\).

Lift the factorization in (AX.2) by henselianity, writing \(P=GH\) with the indicated reductions. The coefficient matrix \((u,v)\mapsto Hu+Gv\), with \(\deg u<r\), \(\deg v<s\), is invertible modulo \(I\): for the coprime polynomials \((t-1)^r,t^s\), repeated division, or the finite geometric expansion of the inverse of \((t-1)^r\) modulo \(t^s\), gives its inverse. Its determinant therefore is a unit over \(A\), because \(I\) is in the Jacobson radical. Thus \(G,H\) generate the unit ideal. The decomposition of \(A[t]/(P)\) into its \(G\)- and \(H\)-factors gives an idempotent taking values one and zero respectively. Sending \(t\) to \(b\) produces a lift of \(\bar e\). Constant factors are included, with the corresponding summand zero.

If \(B\) is only integral, write \(b^2-b=\sum i_jb_j\), with \(i_j\in I\). The subalgebra generated by \(b\) and the finitely many \(b_j\) is finite over \(A\). Apply the finite case there. Finally \(IB\subset\operatorname{Jac}(B)\): every maximal ideal of an integral algebra contracts to a maximal ideal. If two lifts \(e,f\) exist, the idempotents \(e(1-f)\) and \(f(1-e)\) belong to this radical, hence vanish. Therefore \(e=ef=f\). This proves (AX.1), the integral-algebra assertion of Lemma 5.3 in [Étale neighborhoods, henselization and quasi-finite morphisms](course:AG-FSE/etale-neighbourhoods-henselization-and-quasi-finite-morphisms#5-splitting-unramified-schemes-and-étale-coverings), with the generating-list and determinant arguments made explicit.

Conversely, suppose \(I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(A)\) and idempotents lift in every finite \(A\)-algebra. For monic \(P\) and a coprime monic factorization \(\overline P=G_0H_0\), lift the corresponding idempotent of \((A/I)[t]/(\overline P)\) to \(A[t]/(P)\). Its two summands are finite projective \(A\)-modules, since the whole algebra is finite free. Their ranks equal \(\deg G_0\) and \(\deg H_0\) at every maximal ideal, all of which contain \(I\), and hence everywhere. The characteristic polynomials of multiplication by \(t\) on these summands are defined in local bases and agree on overlaps by invariance of determinant under conjugation. Their product is \(P\), the characteristic polynomial of the companion endomorphism on \(A[t]/(P)\). After reduction they are \(G_0,H_0\). This proves the factorization criterion.

In particular, if \(B\) is integral over a henselian pair \((A,I)\), then \((B,IB)\) is henselian. Indeed, every algebra integral over \(B\) is integral over \(A\), so (AX.1) and the converse criterion apply. If \(B\) is a nonzero domain, then

\[
\operatorname{Spec}(B/IB)\text{ is nonempty and connected}.
\tag{AX.3}
\]

It is nonempty because \(IB\) is contained in every maximal ideal of \(B\). Its only idempotents are zero and one by (AX.1) and the domain property; the correspondence between idempotents and clopen decompositions proves connectedness.

### AX.2. Extending a partition from a closed subset

Let \(W\) be a spectral space and \(Z\subset W\) closed. Suppose that

\[
\overline{\{w\}}\cap Z\text{ is nonempty and connected for every }w\in W.
\tag{AX.4}
\]

Recall the two precise topological inputs. The topology generated by quasi-compact opens and their complements, called the patch topology, is compact Hausdorff. A patch-closed subset stable under specialization is Zariski closed. Both proofs are written in [Spectral spaces and affine realization](course:AG-CA/spectral-spaces-and-affine-realization#1-keeping-track-of-both-membership-and-nonmembership), Lemmas 1.1–1.2. For the first, an ultrafilter specifies which quasi-compact opens meet a nonempty irreducible closed set; its generic point is the patch limit. For the second, compactness finds a point of the subset in every quasi-compact neighborhood of a point in its Zariski closure, and specialization stability then includes that point.

These inputs apply to a qcqs scheme. Affine spectra are sober by the prime-ideal description of irreducible closed sets. Every irreducible closed subset of a scheme has a generic point by finding it in a nonempty affine open; that open is dense in the irreducible set, so its generic point is also generic in the whole set. Uniqueness follows from the affine \(T_0\) property. Quasi-separatedness makes intersections of quasi-compact opens quasi-compact, giving the required basis. A closed subspace of a spectral space is again spectral: its intersections with the quasi-compact open basis remain quasi-compact, and its irreducible closed sets are closed irreducible subsets of the original space.

Write a clopen partition of \(Z\) as \(Z_1\amalg Z_2\). For each \(i\), let \(W_i\) consist of points specializing to some point of \(Z_i\). Condition (AX.4) says that these sets partition \(W\). They are patch-closed. In fact the specialization relation is closed in the product of the patch topologies: a pair \((w,z)\) violates \(w\leadsto z\) precisely when some quasi-compact open contains \(z\) but not \(w\). Each such condition defines an open rectangle. The relation with second coordinate in the patch-closed, compact set \(Z_i\) is therefore compact, and its projection is closed in the Hausdorff patch space \(W\).

Each \(W_i\) is stable under specialization. If \(w\leadsto v\), any further specialization of \(v\) in \(Z\) also belongs to \(\overline{\{w\}}\cap Z\). Connectedness in (AX.4) forces it into the same part \(Z_i\) as every specialization of \(w\) in \(Z\). The second patch-topology fact now makes both \(W_i\) Zariski closed. They are complementary, hence clopen. This is the unique extension: a clopen subset puts a point and all its specializations on the same side. Repetition handles finite partitions. Equivalently, for every finite set \(E\), restriction gives

\[
\Gamma(W,\underline E)\simeq\Gamma(Z,\underline E).
\tag{AX.5}
\]

### AX.3. Finite descriptions of arbitrary Zariski sheaves

We now justify why (AX.5) suffices for every sheaf of sets, including sheaves with infinite stalks. For a quasi-compact open \(U\subset W\), let \(h_U\) be the subterminal sheaf represented by \(U\): its sections on \(V\) are a singleton if \(V\subset U\), and empty otherwise. A map \(h_U\to F\) is a section of \(F\) on \(U\). These sheaves generate all sheaves, because every germ has such a representative.

Sections on a quasi-compact open commute with filtered colimits of sheaves. A section of the sheafified colimit has local representatives at stages; take finitely many quasi-compact representatives covering the open. Their pairwise intersections are quasi-compact, so their local equalities have finite witnesses on a finite refinement. A common stage contains all representatives and witnesses, and the sheaf axiom glues them there. The same argument for equality proves injectivity. It works also on the closed spectral subspace \(Z\).

It follows that every sheaf is a filtered colimit of sheaves with a presentation

\[
\coprod_{b=1}^m h_{V_b}\ \rightrightarrows\
\coprod_{a=1}^n h_{U_a}\ \longrightarrow F_0,
\tag{AX.6}
\]

where all opens are quasi-compact and the last arrow is a coequalizer in sheaves. To see this explicitly, use all local sections as generators of an epimorphism onto \(F\), and all local sections of its relation sheaf as relations. A relation over a quasi-compact open uses only finitely many summands of the generator coproduct: its locally specified summand labels have a finite cover. All finite selections of generators and relations form a filtered system of presentations (AX.6). Every germ is represented in this system; every equality of germs has a local relation and hence a finite witness in it. The resulting colimit is \(F\), as can be tested on stalks.

Each \(F_0\) in (AX.6) comes by inverse image from a sheaf with finite stalks on a finite \(T_0\) space. Here is a direct construction. A section of the finite coproduct in (AX.6) on \(V_b\) specifies a locally constant choice of summand, with its chosen part lying in the corresponding \(U_a\). The finitely many parts are clopen in \(V_b\), hence quasi-compact opens in \(W\). Form the finite distributive lattice \(L\) generated under unions and intersections by all these parts and the opens in (AX.6). Map each point of \(W\) to its membership pattern in \(L\). Let \(P\) be the finite set of patterns which actually occur, ordered by coordinatewise inclusion and endowed with its upward-open topology. The map \(r:W\to P\) is continuous: inverse images of minimal neighborhoods are finite intersections of members of \(L\). The opens, their partitions and their inclusions in (AX.6) all descend to \(P\), since a relation between these sets holds on \(W\) exactly when it holds on the occurring patterns. The two maps and their coequalizer therefore descend. Inverse image preserves coproducts and coequalizers, so \(F_0=r^{-1}G\). The stalks of \(G\) are finite, being quotients of stalks of a finite coproduct of subterminal sheaves.

For each point \(p\in P\), the germ map gives \(G\to(i_p)_*G_p\), where \(i_p\) is the inclusion of that point. Their finite product is a monomorphism: at a point \(p\), its own factor induces the identity on \(G_p\). The sheaf \((i_p)_*G_p\) is the pushforward of the constant sheaf on the closed set \(\overline{\{p\}}\). Indeed every nonempty open in this irreducible space contains its generic point, so every locally constant map on that open is constant. Pulling back gives an embedding

\[
F_0\hookrightarrow\prod_{p\in P}(j_p)_*\underline{G_p},
\qquad j_p:r^{-1}(\overline{\{p\}})\hookrightarrow W.
\tag{AX.7}
\]

For this base-change assertion, a closed inclusion has stalk equal to the original stalk on the closed set and terminal stalk outside it. Thus inverse image of a closed pushforward of a constant sheaf is the corresponding closed pushforward of that constant sheaf; check the asserted natural map on stalks. Inverse image also preserves finite products and monomorphisms, as required in (AX.7).

Condition (AX.4) is inherited by every closed subset of \(W\). Hence (AX.5) and (AX.7) prove that restriction on sections is a bijection for the product on the right. It is then surjective for \(F_0\): extend a section from \(Z\) to that product, and observe that its germ lies in \(F_0\) everywhere. Indeed any point \(w\) specializes to a point \(z\in Z\); the map of stalks from \(z\) to \(w\) carries the subsheaf into itself. Membership in a subsheaf is local. Injectivity holds for every sheaf by the same specialization maps. Finally pass through the filtered presentation (AX.6), using commutation of sections with filtered colimits on both \(W\) and \(Z\). We have proved

\[
\Gamma(W,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(Z,F|_Z)
\quad\text{for every Zariski sheaf of sets }F.
\tag{AX.8}
\]

### AX.4. Connected intersection with the closed fibre

Let \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) be proper, where \((A,I)\) is henselian, and put \(Z=X\times_A A/I\). For any point \(x\in X\), give its closure \(C\) the reduced structure. This is a nonempty integral scheme proper over \(A\). Its ring of functions \(B=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)\) is a domain: restriction to the generic point embeds its sections in the function field. By AV.5 it is integral over \(A\).

The general Stein factorization in AV.6 gives a proper surjection \(C\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) with geometrically connected fibres. Its base change induces a closed surjection with connected fibres

\[
C\times_A A/I\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(B/IB).
\tag{AX.9}
\]

The target is nonempty and connected by (AX.3). A closed surjection with connected fibres over a connected target has connected source. For if the source had a separation into two nonempty clopen parts, their images would be closed, disjoint by fibre connectedness, and cover the target, contradicting connectedness. Thus \(C\cap Z\) is nonempty and connected. This proves (AX.4) for \(W=|X|\).

It also proves (AX.4) on every finite \(T\to X\), with closed subset \(Z_T=T\times_XZ\), since \(T\) is proper over \(A\). Properness makes these schemes qcqs, so AX.2–AX.3 apply. Consequently (AX.8) holds on \(X\) and on every such finite \(T\). No assertion that the integral Stein algebra is finite has been used.

### AX.5. Finite direct image over arbitrary schemes

We need finite-surjective descent for sheaf sections at the same arbitrary-base scope. We first remove the locally Noetherian restriction from the finite-map argument of AL.1–AL.2.

The degree-zero continuity proof of AK.1 applies to a filtered system of arbitrary rings \(B_i\), with affine schemes \(T_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i\) and limit \(T=\operatorname{Spec}(\varinjlim B_i)\). Use affine étale objects of finite presentation and their finite covering families. The finite-diagram assertion in AV.1 descends the objects, maps, fibre products, composition equalities and étaleness together. In particular (AV.2c) gives finite polynomial witnesses for étaleness in the specified models, including all relations needed for existence and uniqueness of square-zero lifts.

For the covering condition, use the constructible image and the explicit empty-complement identities (AV.2d), on each affine target in the finite diagram. These identities put all covering and refinement conditions at one stage. This proof does not require the stage rings to be Noetherian, the transition maps to be surjective, or a radical ideal to be finitely generated.

A section, or an equality of sections, of a pulled-back sheaf is locally represented at a stage. Choose finitely many representing affine étale charts; their pairwise fibre products are affine. Choose finite refinements for the finitely many equality witnesses. The preceding finite-data argument puts all of these at one stage, and the sheaf axiom glues them. Thus, for compatible sheaves of sets, the section colimit formula (AK.1) holds for this affine system as well. In particular it applies to an affine scheme finite over a base and then pulled to the strict localization of that base.

For clarity, the strict localization at a chosen geometric point is strictly henselian without a Noetherian hypothesis. The construction and proof are [Henselian local rings and henselization](course:AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization#5-strict-henselization-and-the-choice-of-an-embedding), Theorem 5.1. Pointed étale algebras form a filtered category by tensor products and the étale diagonal. In their colimit, an element with nonzero selected residue becomes a unit by localization; the residue field is the chosen separable closure. A monic polynomial and a selected simple residue root descend to one pointed neighborhood, after enlarging it to represent the root. Adjoining that root and inverting its derivative gives another neighborhood and supplies the root in the colimit. This proves precisely the strictly henselian property used below. Localizing the original base ring before taking this colimit has the same effect as allowing affine étale neighborhoods of the original geometric point; the finite equations and inverted base elements descend in both descriptions.

Let \(R\) be this strict local ring and \(B\) a finite \(R\)-algebra. The finite-algebra criterion in Sections 2–3 of that henselian lesson, or (AX.1) applied to the component idempotents of \(B/\mathfrak m_RB\), gives a finite product of local rings

\[
B=\prod_a B_a.
\tag{AX.10}
\]

Each \(B_a\) is henselian: every finite \(B_a\)-algebra is finite over \(R\), so is a product of local rings; the converse finite-algebra criterion gives henselianity of \(B_a\). Its residue field is finite over the separably closed residue field of \(R\), hence is purely inseparable and separably closed, as proved in AL.1. Thus \(B_a\) is strictly henselian. Every pointed étale neighborhood of its closed geometric point has a section, by (AW.2) and the simple-root property. A germ of any sheaf of sets therefore extends globally by that section. Applying the same argument to equality proves

\[
\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}B_a,F)=F_{\bar b_a}.
\tag{AX.11}
\]

Let \(p:T\to X\) now be any finite morphism, with no restriction on \(X\). Work in an affine neighborhood of a geometric point \(\bar x\). The affine continuity argument, followed by (AX.10)–(AX.11), gives

\[
(p_*F)_{\bar x}=\prod_{\bar t\mid\bar x}F_{\bar t}.
\tag{AX.12}
\]

There are finitely many factors, corresponding to the geometric points of the fibre. Extension of a geometric field does not alter them: finite algebras over a separably closed field are products of Artinian local algebras with purely inseparable residue extensions, each having exactly one geometric point. This also identifies their selected stalks after that extension.

Formula (AX.12) proves that finite direct image of abelian sheaves is exact over any base. Its left adjoint is exact, so it preserves injectives, proving the cohomology comparison (AL.5) at this generality. It also proves arbitrary base change for finite direct image of sets or abelian groups: the two sides of the canonical map have precisely the same factors at a geometric point of the new base. The map is restriction on those factors, by its adjunction construction. This proves the actual canonical comparison, not just an abstract equality of products.

If \(p\) is finite and surjective, the finite set of lifts in (AX.12) is nonempty. The two projections from \(T\times_XT\) give all ordered pairs of lifts. Their equalizer is the diagonal copy of the original stalk. Enough geometric points therefore proves the equalizer identity

\[
F\simeq\operatorname{Eq}\bigl(
p_*p^{-1}F\rightrightarrows q_*q^{-1}F\bigr),
\qquad q:T\times_XT\to X.
\tag{AX.13}
\]

Taking sections gives effective descent of sections through this finite surjection. Flatness of the cover is not required.

### AX.6. From Zariski extension to étale extension

Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) be a closed immersion, with \(X\) qcqs. Suppose (AX.8) holds on \(X\) and on every finite \(T\to X\), with the inverse-image closed set. We show that

\[
\Gamma(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(Z,i^{-1}F)
\quad\text{for every étale sheaf of sets }F.
\tag{AX.14}
\]

There is a natural monomorphism from the Zariski inverse image of \(F\)'s Zariski restriction into the Zariski restriction of its étale inverse image. To verify injectivity, represent two germs by sections on one Zariski neighborhood of a point of \(Z\). If their pulled germs agree, they agree after an étale neighborhood of that point in \(X\). Its image is open, and it is a covering of that image; the sheaf axiom makes the original sections agree there. This proves the asserted monomorphism on stalks. Applying the Zariski comparison shows injectivity in (AX.14), also on every finite \(T\).

Take \(t\in\Gamma(Z,i^{-1}F)\). By the construction of inverse image and sheafification, there is an étale cover \(V_j\to Z\), an étale \(U_j\to X\), a section \(s_j\in F(U_j)\), and a map \(V_j\to U_j\times_XZ\) on which \(s_j\) and \(t\) agree. That last map is étale, hence has open image. Since \(U_j\times_XZ\) is closed in \(U_j\), extend its open image to an open of \(U_j\) and replace \(U_j\) by that open. Then \(V_j\) covers the entire \(U_j\times_XZ\), and the sheaf axiom gives equality there.

The images of these \(U_j\) cover \(X\). They cover \(Z\); any nonempty closed complement would contradict the assumed Zariski comparison, applied to the pushforward of a two-element constant sheaf on that complement. More explicitly its sections on the complement include the two distinct constant sections, while its restriction to the empty intersection with \(Z\) has just one section. Thus their restrictions could not be injective.

Apply AW.6 to this étale covering. It yields a finite surjection \(p:T\to X\) and a Zariski covering of \(T\) with maps to the \(U_j\). Pull back the sections \(s_j\) to that covering. Their restrictions to \(Z_T\) are the common pullback \(t_T\). The monomorphism of Zariski sheaves just proved shows that the corresponding sections on \(Z_T\) glue in the Zariski inverse-image subsheaf: their images agree, so they themselves agree. Hence \(t_T\) belongs globally to that subsheaf. The assumed Zariski comparison on \(T\) extends it to a section \(s_T\) on \(T\).

On \(T\times_XT\), its two pullbacks agree on the inverse image of \(Z\). The injectivity already proved, applied to this finite scheme over \(X\), makes them equal globally. Equation (AX.13) descends \(s_T\) to a section \(s\) on \(X\). Its restriction equals \(t\), because equality of sections is detected by the finite surjection \(Z_T\to Z\), again by (AX.13). This proves surjectivity and finishes (AX.14).

Combining this with AX.4 proves the henselian degree-zero theorem: for \(X\) proper over any henselian pair \((A,I)\), every étale sheaf of sets has exactly the same sections on \(X\) and on \(X_{A/I}\). In particular this applies to the closed fibre over any henselian local ring. Neither a finite étale lifting theorem for a proper scheme nor any higher-cohomology comparison was used.

### AX.7. Full faithfulness of restriction of finite étale covers

Let \(X\) be proper over a henselian pair \((A,I)\), and let \(Z=X_{A/I}\). If \(U,V\) are finite étale over \(X\), any map \(U_Z\to V_Z\) over \(Z\) has a unique lift to an \(X\)-map \(U\to V\).

Apply (AX.14) on the proper \(A\)-scheme \(U\) to the étale sheaf represented by \(V\times_XU\). Its sections on \(U\) are precisely the \(X\)-maps \(U\to V\). Its inverse image on \(U_Z\) is represented by \(V\times_XU_Z\), whose sections are the \(Z\)-maps \(U_Z\to V_Z\). Thus (AX.14) gives the required bijection, including over a nonlocal henselian pair.

Here the two sheaf assertions have direct checks. A map into a scheme glues uniquely through an étale cover: on affine target charts, its ring map descends through the faithfully flat equalizer proved in N.1, and equality on overlaps then glues the resulting local maps. For an étale representing scheme, inverse image represents its base change. This can be checked on geometric stalks: both stalks are its geometric fibre, since a point of an étale scheme gives a pointed étale neighborhood and hence a germ, and equality of such germs is exactly equality after a common neighborhood. Enough geometric points identifies the natural map. These checks use neither essential surjectivity for covers of \(Z\) nor a higher-cohomology comparison.

Essential surjectivity is a different assertion: it must construct a cover of \(X\) from an arbitrary finite étale cover of \(Z\). BC.1–BC.6 prove that construction for proper schemes over complete Noetherian pairs, including coherent algebraization and recovery of the finite étale algebra. BD.3 proves pointed approximation on local integer models from the regular-completion and smooth-factorization theorems, and BD.5 proves cover lifting over every henselian local ring. AY.1–AY.6 prove the geometric field-extension and strict-local section comparisons, and hence the general proper degree-zero base-change formula, using AX.6 for henselian restriction. AZ.1–AZ.6 prove the constructible-coefficient embedding. BA.1–BA.7 supply cohomological effacement on affine closed subschemes and the exact arbitrary-base higher-continuity theorem. BB.1–BB.4 prove affine henselian comparison and restricted-injective vanishing above the affine-covering bound. BB.5 identifies proper finite-torsor lifting as the degree-one input to projective-line acyclicity. BC.6 supplies it for complete Noetherian bases; BD.1–BD.6 prove finite-cover descent, arbitrary proper henselian-local cover and torsor lifting, and projective-line comparison. The higher proper-comparison argument is in BE, and the categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are in BF–BX.

## Appendix AY. Geometric fibres and proper direct image in degree zero

We complete the degree-zero proper comparison for an arbitrary sheaf of sets. The henselian restriction theorem AX.6 already identifies sections with sections on a closed fibre. Two further steps are needed: sections must commute with the strict-local limit, and extending a separably closed residue field must preserve them. We prove both, including the faithfully flat descent of sheaf sections used in the second step. No higher-cohomology or finite-cover essential-surjectivity theorem is used.

### AY.1. Descent of open subsets through a flat cover

Let \(p:T\to S\) be flat, quasi-compact and surjective. Suppose \(W\subset T\) is open and its inverse images under the two projections from \(T\times_ST\) agree. There is a unique open \(V\subset S\) with

\[
W=p^{-1}V.
\tag{AY.1}
\]

First, membership in \(W\) is constant on a fibre. For two points over \(s\), the tensor product of their residue fields over \(\kappa(s)\) is a nonzero ring: tensoring two nonzero vector spaces over a field is nonzero. A prime in that ring gives a point of \(T\times_ST\) projecting to the chosen pair. The hypothesis therefore puts both points on the same side of \(W\). Thus the only possible subset is \(V=p(W)\), and its inverse image is \(W\).

It remains to show that \(V\) is open; no finite-presentation hypothesis on \(p\) is available. Work over an affine open of \(S\). Quasi-compactness gives a finite affine covering \(T_1,\ldots,T_r\) of its inverse image. Put \(F=T\setminus W\). Each \(F\cap T_i\) is closed in the affine spectrum \(T_i\), hence compact for the patch topology of AX.2. An affine spectrum map is continuous for patch topologies: the inverse image of a principal open is principal, and every quasi-compact open is a finite union of principal opens. Therefore each image \(p(F\cap T_i)\) is patch-compact and closed in the Hausdorff patch topology of \(S\). Their finite union \(p(F)\) is patch-closed.

This union is stable under specialization. If \(s\in p(F)\) specializes to \(s'\), choose \(t'\) over \(s'\). The flat prime-lifting argument of AC.3 gives a generization \(t\) of \(t'\) over \(s\). Saturation of \(F\) puts \(t\) in \(F\); closedness puts \(t'\) there too. Hence \(s'\in p(F)\). The patch specialization criterion from AX.2 makes \(p(F)\) Zariski closed. Its complement is \(V\), proving (AY.1). This argument works on every affine open of the base, so proves the assertion for arbitrary \(S\). The construction is unique and commutes with base change, since the inverse-image equation and the two-projection condition do.

### AY.2. Faithfully flat descent for sections of an étale sheaf

For any étale sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(S\), write \(F_T=p^{-1}F\). We prove

\[
\Gamma(S,F)=\operatorname{Eq}\left(
\Gamma(T,F_T)\rightrightarrows
\Gamma(T\times_ST,F_{T\times_ST})\right).
\tag{AY.2}
\]

An equality of two sections has an open locus. Indeed, equality at a geometric stalk is witnessed on a pointed étale neighborhood. The image of that neighborhood is open by AW.1, and it covers its image. The sheaf axiom makes the original sections equal on this image. Taking the union gives precisely the equality locus. Inverse image of sheaves preserves the selected geometric stalk, so this open locus pulls back to the equality locus after any change of base. This is also a direct proof of the equality-locus statement for arbitrary sheaves, including infinite sets of germs.

Surjective pullback detects equality of sections: choose a geometric point above each base point and a common separably closed extension of the relevant residue fields, then use the pullback stalk identity and enough geometric points. In particular the arrow on the left of (AY.2) is injective.

Let \(a\in\Gamma(T,F_T)\) have equal pullbacks to \(T\times_ST\). For an étale \(U\to S\) and \(b\in F(U)\), consider the equality locus of the two pulled sections \(a\) and \(b\) on \(T\times_SU\). Its two inverse images over \(T\times_ST\times_SU\) agree, by the hypothesis on \(a\). AY.1 descends it to an open \(V_{U,b}\subset U\). On \(T\times_SV_{U,b}\), the section \(b\) pulls back to \(a\).

These opens form an étale covering of \(S\). To verify covering, use the definition of the inverse-image sheaf: étale locally on \(T\), the section \(a\) is represented by some \(b\in F(U)\) and a map from that local chart to \(U\) over \(S\). Every point of that chart maps into the equality locus in \(T\times_SU\), hence into \(V_{U,b}\). Such charts cover \(T\), which surjects onto \(S\).

The sections \(b|_{V_{U,b}}\) agree on overlaps. Their pullbacks to the surjective base change by \(T\) both equal \(a\), and equality is detected by that pullback. The étale sheaf axiom now glues them to a unique section on \(S\). Its pullback is \(a\), proving (AY.2). We have used descent of opens and the original étale sheaf axiom; descent of arbitrary étale sheaves has not been assumed as an extra theorem.

### AY.3. Sections along geometrically connected fibres

Suppose, in addition, that every geometric fibre of \(p\) is nonempty and connected. Then

\[
\Gamma(S,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(T,p^{-1}F)
\tag{AY.3}
\]

for every étale sheaf of sets \(F\). To prove surjectivity, take a section on the right. On a geometric fibre \(T_{\bar s}\), its coefficient sheaf is the constant sheaf with value \(F_{\bar s}\), by the separably closed field calculation AB.1–AB.2 and composition of inverse images. A section of a constant étale sheaf on a nonempty connected scheme has one value. The argument in AN.1 needs no smoothness once étale openness is available: locally represent the section by labels; images of pieces with different labels are disjoint open sets, because a point in their intersection gives a geometric point of the fibre product where the labels must agree. Those open sets partition the scheme, so connectedness permits exactly one nonempty part. This argument allows infinitely many possible labels.

Consequently the two pullbacks of the given section to

\[
T_{\bar s}\times_{\bar s}T_{\bar s}
\tag{AY.4}
\]

both have that same value. Every geometric point of \(T\times_ST\) lies in such a geometric fibre, after enlarging its field if necessary. Thus the two pullbacks agree on every stalk. AY.2 descends the section, proving (AY.3). The product in (AY.4) need not itself be proved connected: both sections are already the same constant section.

### AY.4. Extending a separably closed field

Let \(k\) be separably closed, \(K/k\) an arbitrary field extension, and \(S\) any \(k\)-scheme. For \(p:S_K\to S\), we prove

\[
\Gamma(S,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(S_K,p^{-1}F)
\tag{AY.5}
\]

for every étale sheaf of sets \(F\). The map \(p\) is affine, faithfully flat and hence quasi-compact. We check geometric connectedness without assuming that \(K/k\) is algebraic or finitely generated.

First let \(k\) be algebraically closed and let \(R,B\) be nonzero \(k\)-domains. Then \(R\otimes_kB\) is a domain. For a direct proof, suppose two nonzero tensors have product zero. Write each with a linearly independent list of coefficients in \(R\), and let \(B_0\subset B\) be the finite-type \(k\)-subalgebra containing all their coefficients in \(B\). Tensoring \(B_0\hookrightarrow B\) with the \(k\)-vector space \(R\) is injective, so the product is already zero over \(B_0\). Choose one nonzero coefficient from each tensor. Their product \(c\) is nonzero in \(B_0\). The nonzero finite-type algebra \(B_0[1/c]\) has a maximal quotient equal to \(k\), by the weak Nullstellensatz proved over arbitrary fields in Y.5. Evaluation through this quotient sends both tensors to nonzero elements of \(R\): linear independence of their \(R\)-coefficients and the selected nonzero evaluated coefficient guarantee this. Their product cannot be zero in the domain \(R\), a contradiction.

Now choose an algebraic closure \(\bar k\) of our separably closed \(k\). This is purely inseparable: for an algebraic element, its irreducible polynomial is a separable irreducible polynomial in a power \(T^{p^e}\), and separable closedness makes that polynomial linear. In characteristic zero the extension is the identity. AH.1 shows that tensoring any \(k\)-algebra with \(\bar k\) preserves its spectrum homeomorphically.

It follows that the tensor product of two \(k\)-domains has irreducible spectrum. After the purely inseparable extension, each factor has irreducible spectrum and its reduction is a domain. The tensor product of those reductions is a domain by the preceding algebraically closed calculation. The ideal removed from the tensor product by reducing the two factors is nil: each of its elements is a finite sum of multiples of nilpotent elements, hence is nilpotent. The tensor product therefore has a unique minimal prime after extension, and has a unique minimal prime before extension by AH.1.

In particular, for a geometric point \(\bar s=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\) of \(S\), its fibre is

\[
(S_K)_{\bar s}=\operatorname{Spec}(K\otimes_k\Omega),
\tag{AY.6}
\]

a nonempty irreducible, hence connected, scheme. AY.3 proves (AY.5). This supplies both the field-connectedness and the sheaf-descent steps in Corollary 4.5 of [The proper base change theorem](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#4-proper-henselian-schemes-and-the-degree-zero-theorem).
