### AY.5. Nonaffine section continuity and strict localization

Let \(A=\operatorname{colim}_i A_i\) be a filtered colimit of arbitrary rings with a chosen initial stage. Let \(X_0\) be a qcqs scheme over \(A_0\), and write \(X_i=X_0\times_{A_0}A_i\), \(X=X_0\times_{A_0}A\). If \(F_i\) are étale sheaves of sets with compatible transition maps and \(F=\operatorname{colim}_i q_i^{-1}F_i\), then

\[
\operatorname{colim}_i\Gamma(X_i,F_i)
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X,F).
\tag{AY.7}
\]

Choose a finite affine cover \(U_a\) of \(X_0\). Every overlap \(U_a\cap U_b\) is quasi-compact by quasi-separatedness, so choose a finite affine cover of each overlap too. The affine section-continuity proof AX.5 applies on every one of these charts: their stage rings are their original rings tensored with \(A_i\). It uses finite étale presentations and the finite equation for the covering ideal, not Noetherianity or finite presentation of the chart over \(A_0\).

A section on \(X\) restricts to sections on the finitely many limiting \(U_a\). Affine continuity represents each at a stage. Choose a common stage. Their equalities on each overlap hold on its finitely many affine charts, and the injectivity part of affine continuity puts these equalities at a later common stage. The sheaf axiom glues the sections there. The same argument applied to the equality of two sections proves injectivity in (AY.7). Filtered categories, rather than a directed partially ordered index, cause no change: every finite diagram and finite list of equalities has a common object. No assertion about positive-degree continuity is being deduced from this section argument.

**A directed index for every filtered category.** For use with higher continuity, we now construct the change of index, including its effect on the comparison maps. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a small filtered category. Thus it is nonempty, every pair of objects has a common target, and every parallel pair of arrows is equalized by an arrow out of its target. These conditions give a cocone on every finite diagram: first map its finitely many objects to a common target; for each arrow of the diagram, equalize the two resulting maps from its source to that target. Postcomposition preserves equalities already obtained, so finitely many such operations give the required cocone.

We construct posets \(P_0\subset P_1\subset\cdots\), functors \(u_n:P_n\to\mathcal C\), and eventually \(P=\bigcup_nP_n\), \(u:P\to\mathcal C\). Start with one incomparable element \(p_c\) for each object \(c\) of \(\mathcal C\), and set \(u_0(p_c)=c\). At every stage, the set of predecessors of each element, including the element itself, will be finite.

Suppose \(P_n,u_n\) have been constructed. For every finite downward-closed subset \(D\subset P_n\), every object \(c\) of \(\mathcal C\), and every cocone

\[
\lambda_d:u_n(d)\longrightarrow c,\qquad
\lambda_e\,u_n(d\leq e)=\lambda_d
\quad(d\leq e\text{ in }D),
\tag{AY.7a}
\]

adjoin a new element \(q=(n+1,D,c,\lambda)\). Put \(d<q\) exactly when \(d\in D\), and keep distinct new elements incomparable. This is a partial order: downward closure of \(D\) gives transitivity with the old order, and the new level has no arrows back to an old level. The predecessors of \(q\) are exactly \(D\cup\{q\}\), so the finiteness condition persists. Extend the functor by

\[
u_{n+1}(q)=c,\qquad
u_{n+1}(d\leq q)=\lambda_d.
\tag{AY.7b}
\]

Equation (AY.7a) is precisely the required composition law. Smallness of \(\mathcal C\) makes the new objects a set, and a countable union of these sets is a set. The levels are tags on the new elements, so the construction also works when \(\mathcal C\) has only one object and has nonidentity endomorphisms.

The union \(P\) is directed. A finite set of its elements is contained in some \(P_n\); the union of their predecessor sets is a finite downward-closed \(D\subset P_n\). The finite diagram \(u_n|_D\) has a cocone. Its element \(q\) at the next stage is an upper bound. Nonemptiness comes from \(P_0\).

We need a stronger property than upper bounds alone. For every \(c\in\mathcal C\), consider the category with objects

\[
(p,\alpha),\qquad p\in P,\quad \alpha:c\to u(p),
\tag{AY.7c}
\]

and a morphism \((p,\alpha)\to(q,\beta)\) when \(p\leq q\) and \(u(p\leq q)\alpha=\beta\). This category is nonempty, since it contains \((p_c,1_c)\). For two of its objects, take a finite downward-closed \(D\) containing their underlying elements at some stage. Adjoin to the finite diagram \(u|_D\) one more vertex with value \(c\) and the two arrows \(\alpha,\alpha'\) to the selected vertices. A cocone gives maps \(\lambda_d:u(d)\to b\) and \(\gamma:c\to b\), with \(\lambda_p\alpha=\gamma=\lambda_{p'}\alpha'\). The construction includes the element \(q=(n+1,D,b,\lambda)\). Then \((q,\gamma)\) receives arrows from both original objects. Between two fixed objects of (AY.7c) there is at most one arrow, because \(P\) is a poset; hence the parallel-arrow condition is automatic. This proves that every category (AY.7c) is filtered.

Here is the universal-property consequence, without an additional cofinality theorem. For any diagram \(M : \mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) and target \(N\in\mathcal D\), let \(\psi_p:M(u(p))\to N\) be a cocone on its restriction to \(P\). Define \(\psi_c=\psi_{p_c}\). For an arrow \(a:c\to c'\), use a common target of \((p_c,1_c)\) and \((p_{c'},a)\) in (AY.7c). If its underlying element is \(q\), then
\(u(p_c\leq q)=u(p_{c'}\leq q)a\). The two cocone identities for \(\psi_q\) give \(\psi_c=\psi_{c'}M(a)\), as required. For an arbitrary \(p\), put \(c=u(p)\) and compare \((p,1_c)\) with \((p_c,1_c)\). Their common target shows that \(\psi_p=\psi_{p_c}\). Thus this extension and restriction of cocones are inverse, naturally in \(N\). In particular, existence of either colimit implies existence of the other, with canonical isomorphism

\[
\operatorname{colim}_{p\in P}M(u(p))
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\operatorname{colim}_{c\in\mathcal C}M(c).
\tag{AY.7d}
\]

Apply the same cocone argument in the opposite of the target category to a diagram \(L : \mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal D\). It gives existence of both limits when either exists, and the canonical restriction isomorphism

\[
\varprojlim_{\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}L
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\varprojlim_{P^{\mathrm{op}}}L\circ u^{\mathrm{op}}.
\tag{AY.7e}
\]

These are natural in the diagrams: every component of each comparison is the original diagram map. Consequently the construction preserves ring colimits, limits of schemes, colimits of sheaves on a fixed site, and colimits of section or cohomology groups. It does not discard distinct parallel arrows of the original category; those arrows enter the cocone equations. This is the directed-index assertion of [Stacks, Lemma 4.21.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0032), here constructed by adjoining all finite cocones level by level.

Let \(f:X\to S\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, \(\bar s\) a geometric point, and \(R=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,\bar s}\). Work over an affine neighborhood \(S_0\) of its image. Then \(X_0=f^{-1}S_0\) is qcqs. The pointed affine étale neighborhoods \(S_i\) of \(\bar s\) have filtered coordinate-ring colimit \(R\), by AX.5's strict-local construction. By definition the stalk of \(f_*F\) is the colimit of the sections on \(X_0\times_{S_0}S_i\). Equation (AY.7) therefore gives the canonical bijection

\[
(f_*F)_{\bar s}\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Gamma(X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}R,F_R).
\tag{AY.8}
\]

Every arrow here pulls back a representative section. Thus the identification is compatible with inverse images and with restriction to a geometric fibre. In particular, (AY.8) does not silently replace the chosen geometric residue field by the residue field of \(R\).

### AY.6. The proper stalk formula and base-change morphism

Assume now that \(f\) is proper, and write \(\bar s=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\). The residue field \(k\) of \(R\) is the separable algebraic closure of \(\kappa(s)\) selected inside \(\Omega\). It need not equal \(\Omega\). Apply the henselian restriction theorem AX.6 to the proper \(R\)-scheme \(X_R\), and then (AY.5) to \(\Omega/k\). Combined with (AY.8), these give

\[
(f_*F)_{\bar s}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X_R,F_R)
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X_k,F_k)
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X_{\bar s},F_{\bar s}).
\tag{AY.9}
\]

All three maps are pullbacks of sections. Their composite is exactly the usual map from a stalk representative to its restriction on the geometric fibre. Equation (AY.9) holds for every sheaf of sets and every proper morphism, without Noetherianity, finite-presentation or coefficient restrictions beyond those in the stated properness assumption.

Finally let \(g:S'\to S\), put \(X'=X\times_SS'\), and denote its projections by \(f':X'\to S'\) and \(g':X'\to X\). The canonical comparison is

\[
g^{-1}f_*F\longrightarrow f'_*g'^{-1}F.
\tag{AY.10}
\]

It is adjoint to applying \(f_*\) to the unit \(F\to g'_*g'^{-1}F\). At a geometric point \(\bar s'\) of \(S'\), use its very same geometric field for the composite point \(\bar s\) of \(S\). Formula (AY.9) identifies both stalks in (AY.10) with sections of the same sheaf on the same fibre: \(X'_{\bar s'}=X_{\bar s}\). The adjunction map sends a neighborhood representative to its pulled section, so on these identifications it is the identity. Enough geometric points proves that (AY.10) is an isomorphism. For abelian sheaves the bijections respect their group operations.

This establishes the full degree-zero proper comparison. It does not assert that higher direct images vanish after an arbitrary change of base on an injective resolution. That remaining step still requires the torsion-sheaf effacement and projective-line comparison arguments. Nor does degree-zero comparison construct an arbitrary finite étale cover of a closed fibre on a proper henselian scheme; that essential-surjectivity assertion retains its algebraization and approximation requirements.

## Appendix AZ. Constructible coefficients and finite direct images

The next step in proper comparison concerns the coefficient sheaf itself. We prove that, on a qcqs scheme, every constructible abelian sheaf embeds in a finite sum of constant sheaves pushed forward along finite, finitely presented maps. The maps need not be étale. We also prove the version for constructible modules over a Noetherian coefficient ring \(\Lambda\), where constructible means locally constant with finitely generated values on a finite constructible partition. The ring of the scheme need not be Noetherian.

### AZ.1. Finite generators on the étale site

For a qcqs étale morphism \(a:V\to X\) of finite presentation, set

\[
P_V=a_!\underline\Lambda_V,
\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(P_V,F)=\Gamma(V,a^{-1}F).
\tag{AZ.1}
\]

Here \(a_!\) is extension by zero for an étale map, including a map which is not an open immersion. Its construction in [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, §1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#1-extension-by-zero-for-an-étale-morphism) is the sheafification of the direct sum, over maps \(W\to V\) above \(X\), of the sections on \((W\to V)\). Mapping out of this sum gives the adjunction in (AZ.1). At a geometric point, its stalk is the direct sum over lifts of that point to \(V\): equal lifts agree after a pointed refinement because the étale diagonal is open, and a finite list of zero germs vanishes on a common refinement. This proves the stalk formula, exactness and arbitrary base change for \(a_!\). The geometric stalks and localized-site identifications are those of AB.1–AB.3.

We spell out why \(P_V\) is constructible at the stated base scope. For an affine étale morphism over a Noetherian integral ring \(A\), its generic algebra is a finite product of finite separable field extensions. Flatness embeds the algebra in its generic algebra. Choose a generic vector-space basis from elements of the algebra. The multiplication table, the identity and a finite set of algebra generators involve finitely many denominators in \(A\). Inverting their product makes the span of the basis an algebra containing the generators. Thus the map becomes finite étale on a nonempty open. For a general Noetherian base, separate its finitely many generic components by removing their intersections and perform this argument on their reductions. Nilpotents cause no additional finiteness problem: if \(J^e=0\) and a lifted monic equation has value in \(JB\), its \(e\)-th power is a monic equation with value zero. A finitely generated algebra integral over the base is finite, by the finite monomial spanning argument. Noetherian induction on the complementary closed subsets now gives a finite locally closed partition on which the map is finite étale.

Over an arbitrary affine base, descend the finitely presented algebra and its finite étale Jacobian charts to a finitely generated integer subalgebra. The finite-equation and covering-ideal arguments in AV.1 and AX.5 descend both the charts and their covering condition. Pull back the Noetherian partition. For a qcqs, possibly nonseparated, étale source, use a finite affine cover and finite affine covers of its pairwise overlaps. Take a common partition for all these affine maps. Over each part, an overlap chart is both open in a finite étale chart and finite over the base. It is closed there as well: a map between finite schemes over the base is finite, since the same finite base-module generators generate over the intermediate algebra. The overlaps are finite unions of clopen subsets. Add the charts one at a time, retaining from each new chart its clopen complement to the previous charts. This writes the glued source as a finite disjoint union of clopen pieces of the finite charts. It is finite étale over the part. A finite affine cover of \(X\) completes the argument.

A finite étale cover splits after an étale cover of its base. Explicitly, on a constant degree-\(d\) locus, the complement of the diagonals in its \(d\)-fold fibre product is the finite étale, surjective scheme of orderings of the geometric fibre. Its tautological sections split the cover. The diagonals are clopen, and the resulting map from \(d\) copies of the ordering scheme is an isomorphism on geometric fibres; for finite locally free algebras its kernel and cokernel vanish by the local Nakayama argument of AD.1. Consequently, on each stratum, \(P_V\) is locally a finite direct sum of copies of \(\Lambda\). This proves constructibility. The identical argument applies to \(a_!\underline M\) for any finitely generated \(\Lambda\)-module \(M\), or any finite abelian group \(M\).

We shall use two further elementary consequences. Maps between finitely generated locally constant modules become constant module maps after an étale refinement: trivialize both modules and then the images of finitely many source generators. Kernels and cokernels are the corresponding constant modules, and the kernel is finitely generated because \(\Lambda\) is Noetherian. Taking a common finite constructible partition therefore shows that kernels, images and cokernels of maps between constructible modules are constructible. Pullback preserves these partitions and local systems and is exact on stalks. A constructible module's nonzero-stalk locus is constructible: on a stratum its zero and nonzero loci are complementary opens, hence clopen, and the stratum is quasi-compact. Such supports are closed in the compact constructible topology from AX.2. These assertions also apply to finite abelian sheaves by using a common finite annihilator.

### AZ.2. Presentations, compactness and torsion approximation

On a qcqs étale object, sections commute with filtered colimits of sheaves. Indeed any covering has a finite refinement by qcqs basis objects, using étale openness and quasi-compactness. Their overlaps are qcqs. The sheaf condition is a finite equalizer of finite products, which commutes with a filtered colimit. Thus the pointwise presheaf colimit on this basis is already a sheaf. In particular,

\[
\operatorname{Hom}(P_V,\operatorname{colim}_\alpha F_\alpha)
=\operatorname{colim}_\alpha\operatorname{Hom}(P_V,F_\alpha).
\tag{AZ.2}
\]

The \(P_V\)'s generate all module sheaves: a geometric germ is represented by a section on an affine étale neighborhood, and (AZ.1) gives a map realizing that section. For a constructible module \(C\), take the surjection onto \(C\) from the sum of all these maps. For each finite partial sum, its cokernel is constructible by AZ.1. The supports of these cokernels form a decreasing family of closed subsets in the compact constructible topology. Their intersection is empty, because the stalk of \(C\) is finitely generated and the whole sum surjects onto it. The finite-intersection property makes one of these supports empty. Thus a finite partial sum surjects onto \(C\). Its kernel is constructible, so the same argument gives

\[
\bigoplus_{b=1}^{s}P_{V_b}\longrightarrow
\bigoplus_{a=1}^{r}P_{U_a}\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow0.
\tag{AZ.3}
\]

Hom from this cokernel is the kernel of the map between the two finite products of Hom groups. Equation (AZ.2) therefore proves

\[
\operatorname{Hom}(C,\operatorname{colim}_\alpha F_\alpha)
=\operatorname{colim}_\alpha\operatorname{Hom}(C,F_\alpha).
\tag{AZ.4}
\]

For a constructible abelian sheaf, choose an integer \(N>0\) killing all the finitely many finite values in a constructible partition. Apply (AZ.3) with \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). It proves compactness even among arbitrary abelian sheaves: Hom from \(a_!\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\) to \(F\) is \(\Gamma(V,F)[N]\), and taking this kernel of multiplication by \(N\) also commutes with filtered colimits.

Every module sheaf is a filtered colimit of constructible modules. Present it by an arbitrary sum of generators and another arbitrary sum mapping onto the kernel. Each individual relation factors through a finite partial sum of generators by (AZ.2). Finite choices of generators and relations, enlarged to contain the finitely many generators used by the selected relations, form a directed system. Their cokernels are constructible by AZ.1 and their colimit is the original sheaf. Exactness here follows on stalks from exactness of filtered colimits of modules.

Every torsion abelian sheaf \(F\) is likewise a filtered colimit of constructible abelian sheaves. One can first apply the preceding result to \(F[N]\). To combine these approximations without assuming their transition maps injective, use the category of constructible abelian sheaves mapping to \(F\). It is filtered: direct sums receive two objects, and a cokernel equalizes two parallel arrows. Its colimit maps onto \(F\) on stalks, since a torsion germ is represented after shrinking by an \(N\)-torsion section. If a germ from a constructible source maps to zero, represent it on an affine étale neighborhood where its image is zero. The source has a finite annihilator \(N\), so this section defines a map \(a_!\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\) into it. Its constructible cokernel still maps to \(F\) and kills the germ. This proves injectivity on stalks. There is no assertion here that \(F\) is a union of constructible subsheaves; that strengthening fails over general non-Noetherian bases.

### AZ.3. Descent of constructible coefficients to a finite stage

Let \(X=\varprojlim_i X_i\), where all \(X_i\) are qcqs and the transition morphisms are affine. For compatible étale sheaves \(F_i\), put \(F=\operatorname{colim}_i q_i^{-1}F_i\). The section-continuity statement extends from AY.5's base-change systems to this system:

\[
\operatorname{colim}_i\Gamma(X_i,F_i)\simeq\Gamma(X,F).
\tag{AZ.5}
\]

To prove it, choose a stage \(i_0\), a finite affine cover there, and finite affine covers of its overlaps. At every later stage their inverse images are affine, because the transition morphisms are affine. Their rings form the filtered systems to which AX.5 applies. A section on \(X\) is represented at a stage on each of the finitely many charts. Equalities on overlaps hold on their finite affine covers and hence hold at a later common stage. Gluing proves surjectivity in (AZ.5); the same equality argument proves injectivity. Passing to the cofinal indices after \(i_0\) changes none of the colimits. No positive-degree continuity is used in this proof.

Every constructible module \(C\) on \(X\) descends to a constructible module at some stage. Choose (AZ.3). Its finitely many étale objects of finite presentation descend by AV.1; their étale charts and covering conditions descend by AX.5. Thus all its generators are pullbacks of generators \(P_{U_a,i}\) and \(P_{V_b,i}\). Here base change for extension by zero is exactly the stalkwise comparison proved in AZ.1. The map from each relation generator is a section of the finite sum of the target generators on \(V_b\). Apply (AZ.5) to the inverse system of the descended \(V_{b,i}\)'s. A common stage represents all these sections, and hence the entire relation map. Its cokernel \(C_i\) is constructible and pulls back to \(C\), since inverse image preserves cokernels.

This argument also descends morphisms and their equalities. For constructible \(C_{i_0},D_{i_0}\), use a finite presentation of \(C_{i_0}\). At each later stage and at the limit, Hom into the pullback of \(D_{i_0}\) is the same finite kernel of section groups. Apply (AZ.5) and commute the filtered colimit with that finite kernel. The resulting formula is

\[
\operatorname{colim}_{i\geq i_0}
\operatorname{Hom}(C_i,D_i)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(C,D).
\tag{AZ.6}
\]

Thus every morphism exists at a stage, and an equality at the limit holds at a later stage. For constructible abelian sheaves choose one annihilator for the objects involved and use \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\) throughout. The descended sheaf is then genuinely finite on every stratum. In particular the absolute Noetherian approximation of AV.1 permits a constructible abelian sheaf on any qcqs scheme to descend to one on a finite-type integer scheme.

### AZ.4. Constant sheaves at a normal generic point

Let \(T\) be a normal integral scheme with function field \(L\), and let \(j:\operatorname{Spec}L\to T\). For any set \(M\), the natural map is an isomorphism

\[
\underline M_T\xrightarrow{\sim}j_*\underline M_L.
\tag{AZ.7}
\]

We prove the component assertion needed here without a Noetherian hypothesis on \(T\). Take a normal affine domain \(A\) in \(T\), with fraction field \(K\), and an affine étale chart \(\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) of finite presentation. Flatness gives \(B\subset B\otimes_AK\). The latter is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of \(K\), by AB.1. Apply the integral-closure base-change identity (AW.4) to \(A\subset K\). Since \(A\) is integrally closed, it says that \(B\) is integrally closed in that product.

Every primitive idempotent of the product is integral, by \(e^2-e=0\), and consequently belongs to \(B\). Hence \(B=\prod B_c\), where each \(B_c\) is a domain in the corresponding field \(L_c\), and \(S^{-1}B_c=L_c\) for \(S=A\setminus\{0\}\). Its fraction field is therefore \(L_c\). It is integrally closed there: if \(z\in L_c\) is integral over \(B_c\), regard it as the tuple having value zero in the other factors. Lift its monic equation to coefficients of \(B\) and multiply that polynomial by \(t\). The tuple is then integral over \(B\), so is in \(B\), and its component lies in \(B_c\). Thus the chart is a finite disjoint union of normal integral schemes, each with exactly one generic component over \(\operatorname{Spec}K\).

Sections of a constant étale sheaf on a connected scheme are single constant values, as proved by the open partition into labels in AN.1 and AY.3. The preceding chart therefore has exactly the same constant-sheaf sections as its generic fibre, one value for each \(B_c\). The restriction bijections commute with maps between charts. Such charts cover the étale site, proving (AZ.7). Group and module operations are preserved, so (AZ.7) holds for constant abelian groups and modules as well.

We shall also need a consequence for locally constant modules with finitely generated values. A map between two such sheaves on a normal integral scheme which is an isomorphism at the generic point is an isomorphism everywhere. Trivialize both sheaves and the images of finitely many source generators on affine étale charts. The map is constant there, by AZ.1. Each nonempty component of such a chart meets the generic fibre by the preceding algebra calculation. Its constant map is an isomorphism because it is an isomorphism at that generic point. Geometric stalks now prove the assertion on the entire scheme.

Here is the finite-cover consequence, including modules whose underlying sets are infinite. Let \(\Lambda\) be a ring and let \(E\) be a locally constant \(\Lambda\)-module sheaf with finitely generated values on the normal integral \(T\). Write \(\eta=\operatorname{Spec}L\). Restriction of morphisms between such sheaves is fully faithful:

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_T(E_1,E_2)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}
\operatorname{Hom}_\eta(E_1|_\eta,E_2|_\eta).
\tag{AZ.7a}
\]

Indeed, cover \(T\) by normal integral affine étale charts trivializing both sheaves; the component calculation above allows this refinement. On such a chart a generic morphism between the two constant modules is a single \(\Lambda\)-linear map, by the field-site equivalence AB.2. Apply this map to the constant sheaves on the whole chart. These extensions are unique: a section of a constant target module is determined by its generic value by (AZ.7), so equality can be tested on the constant source elements. On overlaps, use the same normal integral affine refinement. Every nonempty component dominates \(\eta\), and the generic maps agree there. Uniqueness glues the maps and proves (AZ.7a).

Choose a geometric generic point \(\bar\eta\) and put \(M=E_{\bar\eta}\). AB.2 gives a continuous action of \(G_L=\operatorname{Gal}(L^s/L)\) on this discrete module. The intersection of the open stabilizers of finitely many \(\Lambda\)-generators fixes every element of \(M\), since the action is \(\Lambda\)-linear. This intersection is the kernel of the action; it is open and normal, and has finite index by compactness. Let \(G\subset\operatorname{Aut}_\Lambda(M)\) be its finite image.

Regard \(M\) also as a constant module on \(\eta\). Inside the sheaf of isomorphisms from that constant module to \(E|_\eta\), take the orbit \(\Omega\) of the identity frame at \(\bar\eta\). On the geometric fibre this is the set \(G\), with its left \(G_L\)-action and commuting right \(G\)-action. The field-site equivalence makes \(\Omega\) a finite locally constant sheaf on \(\eta\).

We extend this particular finite set of frames over \(T\). Take a normal integral affine étale chart \(V\to T\) trivializing \(E\). Every value in that trivialization is isomorphic to \(M\), by restriction to a geometric generic point of \(V\). Over the function field \(L(V)\), the Galois action on \(E\)'s value is trivial. It follows that the pullback of \(\Omega\) is a finite constant subset of the set of frames of this trivial module. Extend each frame and its inverse by (AZ.7a); faithfulness makes their compositions the identities. They define a finite constant subsheaf \(P_V\) of the frame sheaf over \(V\), of cardinality \(|G|\).

On every normal integral affine chart in \(V\times_T V'\), the two such subsheaves have the same generic frames. The uniqueness just proved makes them identical on that chart. Thus the \(P_V\) glue to a finite locally constant sheaf \(P\) on \(T\), with its actual inclusion in the frame sheaf. Right composition by \(G\) preserves it: this holds for the generic frames and therefore for their unique extensions. It acts freely and transitively on every geometric fibre.

For completeness, represent each \(P_V\) by the disjoint union of its finitely many copies of \(V\). The overlap permutations act on the corresponding product algebras. On an affine base open choose a finite affine subcover and use (N.1)–(N.4) to descend these algebras and their maps. The arbitrary-ring verification in BA.3 descends their duals, evaluation and coevaluation, proving finite projectivity, and descends the unique square-zero lifts, proving étaleness. Uniqueness makes these affine answers agree on base overlaps. Hence \(P\) is represented by a finite étale surjection \(p:T'\to T\) of degree \(|G|\). Its tautological frame and its right action give

\[
p^{-1}E\simeq\underline M_{T'},\qquad
T'\times G\xrightarrow{\sim}T'\times_TT',
\quad (z,g)\longmapsto(z,zg).
\tag{AZ.7b}
\]

The second map is an isomorphism because it is one on each trivializing chart. This constructs the finite monodromy cover without requiring the whole, possibly infinite, frame sheaf to be finite. The argument permits arbitrary normal integral bases and arbitrary coefficient rings; finite generation is used to make the generic image finite. The general fundamental-group formulation is [Stacks, Lemma 59.65.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GIY); the finite-sheaf representability statement is [Lemma 59.64.4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RV).

Suppose now that \(\Lambda\) is Noetherian and \(\ell^bM=0\). Choose an \(\ell\)-Sylow subgroup \(H\subset G\), using AA.3. The finite locally constant quotient \(P/H\), formed on the same trivializing charts, is represented by a finite étale cover \(q:V\to T\) of degree \(d=[G:H]\), prime to \(\ell\). On this cover the transition matrices of \(q^{-1}E\) belong to \(H\): locally lift a coset frame to a frame in \(P\), and two such lifts differ by an element of \(H\).

Let \(J\) be the augmentation ideal of \(R=(\mathbf Z/\ell^b)[H]\). It is nilpotent. To check this, first work over \(\mathbf F_\ell\) and induct on \(|H|\). The conjugation class equation makes the centre of a nontrivial \(\ell\)-group have order divisible by \(\ell\); taking a suitable power of a nonidentity central element gives a central \(z\) of order \(\ell\). The quotient of \(\mathbf F_\ell[H]\) by \((z-1)\) is \(\mathbf F_\ell[H/\langle z\rangle]\). If the augmentation ideal of that quotient has \(N\)-th power zero, then the original ideal has \(N\)-th power in \((z-1)\), and its \(N\ell\)-th power is zero because \((z-1)^\ell=z^\ell-1=0\). The trivial group starts the induction. Lifting to \(R\) gives \(J^a\subset\ell R\) for some \(a\), and therefore \(J^{ab}=0\).

The finite filtration by \(J^iM\) is \(\Lambda\)-stable. Its terms and quotients are finitely generated by Noetherianity, and \(H\) acts trivially on each quotient. It consequently descends to a filtration of \(q^{-1}E\) by locally constant subsheaves with constant finitely generated quotients, including when these modules are infinite as sets. Finally the unit and sum-over-sheets trace of the finite étale map satisfy

\[
E\longrightarrow q_*q^{-1}E
 \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}}E,
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}\circ\operatorname{unit}=d\,1_E.
\tag{AZ.7c}
\]

Choose an integer \(a\) with \(ad\equiv1\pmod{\ell^b}\). Then \(a\operatorname{Tr}\) is a retraction. Pullback preserves the filtration and these maps, as is seen on their finite constant charts. Exact open extension by zero preserves them too. This supplies the monodromy, constant-filtration and summand steps for the Noetherian module coefficients in [Torsion sheaves on curves, Section 10](course:ag-etale-cohomology/torsion-sheaves-on-curves#10-finitely-generated-noetherian-coefficients), on its normal smooth dense opens.

### AZ.5. Constructing the embedding on a Noetherian scheme

Let \(X\) be Noetherian and \(C\) constructible, in either the finite-abelian or the Noetherian-coefficient module sense. Refine its partition into finitely many reduced irreducible locally closed strata on which it is locally constant. This refinement is finite: in each Noetherian locally closed part, separate the finitely many irreducible components on dense opens, then repeat on the strictly smaller closed remainder. Fix a stratum \(S\), write \(Z=\overline S_{\mathrm{red}}\), and let \(\eta\) be its generic point. The stratum is a nonempty open of \(Z\).

A locally constant sheaf at \(\eta\) becomes constant over a finite separable extension \(L/\kappa(\eta)\). Indeed take a trivializing étale neighborhood of a geometric point of the field; an affine piece has a finite étale algebra, and one of its field factors supplies such an extension. In the module case this respects the module operations, since local constancy was stipulated in that category. Denote the constant value by \(M\).

Normalize \(Z\) in \(L\), obtaining \(p:T\to Z\to X\). On an affine domain \(A\subset\kappa(\eta)\), use its integral closure in \(L\). Integral closure commutes with localization by AW.1, so these algebras glue. They are normal domains: an element of their fraction field integral over the closure is integral over \(A\) by transitivity of integrality. Their fraction field is \(L\), because for every algebraic element of \(L\), clearing the finitely many denominators in its monic equation makes a nonzero \(A\)-multiple integral. Lying over proves that \(T\to Z\) is surjective. The map is integral, but we do not assume it finite.

Adjunction from the chosen generic trivialization, followed by (AZ.7), gives

\[
p^{-1}C\longrightarrow j_*\underline M_L
=\underline M_T,
\qquad C\longrightarrow p_*\underline M_T.
\tag{AZ.8}
\]

On \(T_S\), both sheaves in the first map are locally constant with finitely generated values, and the map is a generic isomorphism. The open \(T_S\) is normal and integral, so AZ.4 proves that it is an isomorphism there. For a geometric point \(\bar s\) of \(S\), choose a geometric lift to \(T_S\), enlarging the algebraically closed field if needed. Under the inverse-image stalk identity, evaluating the second map of (AZ.8) at this lift is the first map. It is an isomorphism. The second map is therefore injective at \(\bar s\).

It remains to replace the integral map by a finite one. Its quasi-coherent algebra is the directed union of its finite-type quasi-coherent subalgebras. To see this globally, apply AV.1's finite-submodule extension assertion to any finite set of local sections of that algebra, and take the subalgebra generated by the resulting finite-type module. Every such subalgebra is integral and of finite type, hence finite. Taking relative spectra gives \(T=\varprojlim_i T_i\), with finite maps \(p_i:T_i\to X\) and affine transitions.

For every qcqs étale object \(V\to X\), equation (AZ.5), applied to \(T_i\times_X V\), identifies the sections of \(p_*\underline M\) with the colimit of the sections of \((p_i)_*\underline M\). Pullback of a constant sheaf remains constant. Filtered sheaf colimits on this basis are computed on sections by AZ.2. Consequently

\[
p_*\underline M=\operatorname{colim}_i(p_i)_*\underline M.
\tag{AZ.9}
\]

Compactness (AZ.4) factors the second map in (AZ.8) through one \((p_i)_*\underline M\). Its factor is still injective on every geometric stalk of \(S\), since its composite is injective there. Repeat this construction for the finitely many strata, and take the direct sum of the resulting maps. At each geometric point, the summand for its stratum detects its stalk. We obtain an embedding

\[
C\hookrightarrow
\bigoplus_{a=1}^{r}(p_a)_*\underline{M_a},
\qquad p_a:T_a\to X\text{ finite}.
\tag{AZ.10}
\]

Every \(p_a\) is of finite presentation, since \(X\) is Noetherian: locally its algebra is finite, hence finitely generated, and the kernel of a polynomial-algebra presentation is finitely generated. The proof used a finite stratification, not a descending-chain assertion inferred from an ascending-chain condition.

### AZ.6. Arbitrary bases and the remaining cohomological step

Now let \(X\) be any qcqs scheme. By AV.1 and AZ.3 there are a finite-type integer scheme \(X_i\) and a constructible sheaf \(C_i\) whose pullback is \(C\). Apply (AZ.10) on \(X_i\). Inverse image is exact, and AX.5 identifies the pullback of each finite direct image with the direct image on the fibre product. Pulling back (AZ.10) therefore gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
C&\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_{a=1}^{r}(q_a)_*\underline{M_a},\\
q_a&:T_a\times_{X_i}X\longrightarrow X.
\end{aligned}
\tag{AZ.11}
\]

Each \(q_a\) is finite and of finite presentation, since these properties are preserved by base change. The \(M_a\)'s are finite abelian groups when \(C\) is a constructible abelian sheaf, and finitely generated \(\Lambda\)-modules in the module version. In particular a constructible \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaf has such an embedding by \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-linear maps with finite-dimensional coefficient spaces. This proves the coefficient embedding in [The proper base change theorem, Lemma 5.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#5-embedding-constructible-coefficients-into-finite-direct-images), including its finite-presentation requirement over an arbitrary base.

Equations (AZ.4)–(AZ.6) concern finite data and degree-zero sections. They do not prove higher cohomological continuity or vanishing. BA.1–BA.7 prove the higher-continuity theorem, kill constant-coefficient classes by finite covers, and extend this effacement through (AZ.11) to arbitrary torsion sheaves on affine closed subschemes. BB.1–BB.4 prove the affine henselian comparison and restricted-injective bound. BC.1–BC.6 prove proper finite-torsor lifting over complete Noetherian pairs and the complete-local projective-line comparison. The arbitrary henselian degree-one step uses the approximation and G-ring reduction of BD.3–BD.6. Finite étale essential surjectivity, proper specialization and derived operations are distinct assertions with their own hypotheses.

## Appendix BA. Finite effacement on closed affine schemes

We now prove the cohomological step for which AZ's embedding was needed. If \(X\) is affine, \(Z\subset X\) is closed, \(F\) is a torsion abelian étale sheaf on \(X\), and \(q>0\), every class in \(H^q(Z,F|_Z)\) is killed by a monomorphism \(F\to F'\) of torsion sheaves on \(X\). We shall first kill classes with finite constant coefficients by a finite surjection. No Noetherian hypothesis is imposed on \(X\) or on the defining ideal of \(Z\).

### BA.1. Lifting one affine étale algebra

Let \(A\to\overline A=A/J\) be any quotient and \(\overline B\) an étale \(\overline A\)-algebra. We need an affine étale lift of the entire algebra, rather than only separate lifts of its charts. Here is the global presentation argument of [Infinitesimal lifting and invariance under thickenings, Lemma 6.1](course:AG-FSE/infinitesimal-lifting-and-invariance-under-thickenings#6-keeping-the-lift-finite), with its conormal input made explicit.

First, an étale algebra is formally étale. On a standard chart from AW.1, a root of its defining polynomial lifts uniquely across a square-zero ideal: correct a tentative root by minus its polynomial value divided by the invertible derivative. The square-zero Taylor formula proves existence and uniqueness. The inverted chart elements remain units. For a general étale algebra, use its standard-chart covering. The inverse images of this covering cover the square-zero test scheme, and its topology is unchanged by that thickening. The unique local lifts agree on overlaps and glue. On an affine test, this is precisely a unique algebra homomorphism. This proof also shows that all relative derivations vanish: two lifts to a split square-zero algebra differ by a derivation, and every derivation supplies such a difference. Thus the module of relative differentials is zero.

Temporarily write an étale algebra as \(B=P/I\), with \(P=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and \(I\) finitely generated. Formal étaleness gives an \(A\)-algebra section \(s:B\to P/I^2\) of the quotient map. The difference between \(P\to P/I^2\) and its composite \(P\to B\xrightarrow{s}P/I^2\) is a derivation with values in \(I/I^2\). Its restriction to \(I\) sends \(f\) to its own class. It is therefore a left inverse to the conormal differential. The usual differential presentation gives surjectivity, because \(\Omega_{B/A}=0\). Hence

\[
I/I^2\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}B\,dx_j
\quad\text{is an isomorphism}.
\tag{BA.1}
\]

Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\in I\) lifting a basis of \(I/I^2\), and put \(L=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\). The finite \(P\)-module \(I/L\) equals \(I(I/L)\). If \(m\) is a finite column of generators, write \(m=Em\) with the entries of \(E\) in \(I\). Multiplication by the adjugate shows that \(d=\det(1-E)\in1+I\) annihilates \(I/L\). Therefore \(I_d=L_d\). If \(\Delta=\det(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)\), equation (BA.1) says that its image in \(B\) is a unit. We have obtained

\[
B\simeq\bigl(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\bigr)_{d\Delta}.
\tag{BA.2}
\]

Apply this presentation to \(\overline B/\overline A\). Lift its finitely many coefficients and the element \(\overline d\) to \(A\), obtaining polynomials \(F_i\) and \(D\). Set

\[
\widetilde B=
\bigl(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(F_1,\ldots,F_n)\bigr)_{D\det(\partial F_i/\partial x_j)}.
\tag{BA.3}
\]

The square-zero correction for an invertible square Jacobian, whose algebraic proof is identified in AW.1, makes this algebra formally étale. Its finite presentation is explicit, so it is étale. Its reduction modulo \(J\) is exactly \(\overline B\), by (BA.2). No nilpotence assumption on \(J\) has been used. Nor is the lift claimed to be finite when \(\overline B\) is finite: for the next argument it is its étaleness and affineness that matter.

### BA.2. Étale branches over a normal separably closed generic field

Let \(R\) be a normal domain with separably closed fraction field \(K\). For an affine étale \(R\)-algebra \(B\), AZ.4 splits its generic algebra into field factors and puts the primitive idempotents in \(B\). Here every generic factor is \(K\). Each corresponding factor \(C\) of \(B\) is flat over \(R\), embeds in \(K\), and satisfies \(C\otimes_RK=K\). Flatness of \(C\otimes_RC\) over \(R\) gives an injection into its generic localization \(K\). Thus multiplication is an isomorphism

\[
C\otimes_RC\xrightarrow{\sim}C.
\tag{BA.4}
\]

Indeed it is surjective, and its generic localization is the identity, so that injection makes its kernel zero. Equation (BA.4) identifies the diagonal of \(V=\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) with an isomorphism. Its image \(W\) is open by AW.1, and the corestriction \(p:V\to W\) is surjective étale. Since \(W\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) is an open immersion, the fibre products \(V\times_WV\) and \(V\times_RV\) agree. Their diagonal from \(V\) is an isomorphism by (BA.4), so the two projections to \(V\) are equal: both are its inverse.

Apply the scheme-morphism descent bijection (AW.8a) to the cover \(p:V\to W\), with target \(V\). The identity map of \(V\) satisfies its overlap condition by the preceding equality of projections. It therefore descends to \(g:W\to V\) with \(gp=1_V\). The maps \(pg\) and \(1_W\) have equal pullbacks along \(p\), since \((pg)p=p\). The uniqueness part of (AW.8a), now with target \(W\), gives

\[
gp=1_V,\qquad pg=1_W.
\tag{BA.4a}
\]

Thus \(V\to W\) is an isomorphism, proving the asserted open immersion. The descent input here is the morphism theorem (AW.8a), whose proof includes descent of inverse images of affine target opens as well as the affine ring equalizer. For the general open-immersion criterion, see [Stacks, Theorem 41.14.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/025G).

Consequently every affine étale scheme over \(\operatorname{Spec}R\) is a finite disjoint union of opens. More generally a separated étale scheme over a normal integral scheme with separably closed function field is a possibly infinite disjoint union of opens. To check the gluing, label each affine branch by its generic point. Branches with the same label give inverse sections on intersecting base opens. Those sections agree at the generic point, and their equalizer is a closed subscheme by separatedness. On an affine open of the integral intersection, its defining ideal maps to zero in the function field. The coordinate domain injects into that field, so the ideal is zero. The sections therefore agree as scheme morphisms on the entire intersection. Branches with different labels are disjoint on every affine chart. The labeled pieces glue to disjoint open subschemes, each isomorphic to the union of its base opens. Their complements are unions of the other pieces, so the pieces are also closed in the étale source. This argument does not assume finitely many global branches.

All local rings of \(R\) are strictly henselian as well. Apply the affine description to a localization \(R_{\mathfrak p}\), still a normal domain with fraction field \(K\). A pointed étale neighborhood of its closed point has a branch which is an open of this local spectrum containing the closed point. That open is the whole spectrum and supplies a section. In particular every chosen simple residue root lifts by applying this assertion to its derivative-inverted polynomial algebra. Its residue field is separably closed: any finite separable extension is represented by a separable polynomial, which lifts to such an étale algebra; the branch over the closed point has residue field that of the base, forcing the extension to be trivial. These are exactly the henselian and residue-field conditions.

### BA.3. Closed subschemes and their finite constant torsors

Let \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(R/J)\) with \(R\) as in BA.2. An affine étale scheme over \(Z\) lifts by BA.1 to an affine étale scheme over \(R\). Splitting the lift by BA.2 and then reducing modulo \(J\) shows that the original scheme is a finite disjoint union of open subschemes of \(Z\).

This also compares the two sites directly. Every étale object is covered by affine étale objects, and these are unions of opens of \(Z\). Maps between opens over \(Z\) are the usual inclusions, and the covering condition among them is precisely the Zariski covering condition. A sheaf on these opens therefore extends uniquely to the étale site by taking compatible sections on such a covering of each object; refining two coverings gives the same result, by the sheaf axiom on opens. Restriction and this construction are inverse exact equivalences, preserving global sections. They consequently preserve injective resolutions and give

\[
H^q(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}},G)
=H^q(Z_{\mathrm{Zar}},G|_{\mathrm{Zar}})
\quad(q\geq0).
\tag{BA.5}
\]

The same statement holds on each open of \(Z\), by restricting this basis. This proof has not appealed to higher-cohomological continuity.

If \(V\to Z\) is finite étale and surjective, write its affine source as a finite disjoint union of opens of \(Z\) by the preceding argument. Each of these opens is also closed, since its map to \(Z\) is finite. Partition \(Z\) by the finite Boolean partition of these clopen images. Every nonempty part lies in at least one image, by surjectivity. Choose one such branch on each part and glue their inverse open immersions. The result is a section of \(V\to Z\).

It follows that

\[
H^1(Z,\underline M)=0
\quad\text{for every finite abelian group }M.
\tag{BA.6}
\]

Here is the needed relation with torsors, without assuming the cohomology claim. Embed \(\underline M\) in an injective abelian sheaf \(I\), and write \(Q=I/\underline M\). By the long exact sequence, a class in \(H^1(Z,\underline M)\) is represented by a global section \(s\) of \(Q\). The sheaf of its local lifts to \(I\) is locally nonempty, and addition of \(\underline M\) acts simply transitively. It is therefore finite locally constant as a sheaf of sets. It is represented by a finite étale surjection: trivialize it, represent the finite constant sets by disjoint copies of the base, and descend their finite locally free algebras using the unique overlap permutations. The construction is that of [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, Theorem 2.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#2-finite-local-systems-and-monodromy). We check its finite descent over our possibly non-Noetherian base in the next paragraph. The section just constructed for every such surjection is then a global lift of \(s\) to \(I\). Its connecting class is zero, proving (BA.6). Only this direction of the torsor correspondence is needed.

For that check, take a finite affine trivializing étale cover of the affine base, and combine it into one faithfully flat affine cover \(A\to B\). The module-and-algebra equalizer calculation (N.1)–(N.4) has no Noetherian assumption. Apply it both to the finite locally free algebra on the cover and to its module dual, with the dual descent isomorphism. Evaluation and coevaluation descend as well, since tensor products commute with the equalizer descent isomorphism after faithfully flat base change. Their two duality identities can be checked after that base change. A descended coevaluation is a finite sum \(\sum n_i\otimes d_i\); its identity says \(n=\sum_i n_i d_i(n)\). Thus the descended module is a direct summand of a finite free module, so is finite projective over \(A\). It is also finitely presented as an algebra: use a finite module presentation, a finite list of products of its module generators, and a relation expressing its unit. These relations reduce every polynomial to a linear combination of the generators, and the module relations identify exactly the zero combinations. Finally formal étaleness descends. For a square-zero test \(D\to D/L\), base change to the faithfully flat algebra \(B\otimes_A D\), lift uniquely there, and compare the two lifts over \(B\otimes_A B\otimes_A D\). Uniqueness makes them agree under the given descent data. The equalizer (N.4) descends the map to \(D\), and also proves its uniqueness. Finite presentation and formal étaleness make the descended algebra étale. This proves the required finite étale descent without inferring finite presentation merely from finite generation.

### BA.4. Vanishing in every positive degree

For \(B=R/J\) as above, every principal localization \(B_h\) is a quotient of \(R_f\), where \(f\) is any lift of \(h\). Thus (BA.5)–(BA.6) apply on every principal open of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). We prove simultaneously for all such opens that

\[
H^q(D(h),\underline M)=0\qquad(q>0).
\tag{BA.7}
\]

Degree one was proved in BA.3. Suppose that all smaller positive degrees vanish on every principal open. Replace \(B\) by \(B_h\), and let \(\xi\in H^q(\operatorname{Spec}B,\underline M)\). By (BA.5) this is Zariski sheaf cohomology. Positive-degree classes are locally zero: represent one by a cocycle in an injective resolution; exactness of the resolution as a sequence of sheaves gives local preimages. Hence the principal opens on which \(\xi\) vanishes cover the spectrum.

Let \(I_\xi\) consist of all \(b\in B\) with \(\xi|_{D(b)}=0\). It contains zero and is stable under negatives and multiplication by arbitrary elements, by restriction. If \(u,v\in I_\xi\), cover \(D(u+v)\) by \(D(u(u+v))\) and \(D(v(u+v))\). Their intersection is \(D(uv(u+v))\). The degree-\(q\) Mayer–Vietoris sequence and the inductive vanishing in degree \(q-1\) give \(u+v\in I_\xi\).

The Mayer–Vietoris sequence here follows directly from injectives. A Zariski injective sheaf is flasque: restriction surjectivity follows by extending a map from the free sheaf on the smaller open to that on the larger open. Restriction of injectives to an open remains injective, because its left adjoint, extension by zero, is exact on stalks. The two-open section sequence of each injective is therefore exact, including surjectivity onto the overlap. Its short exact sequence of resolution complexes gives the asserted long exact sequence. Thus no acyclicity theorem for our particular coefficients has been assumed in using it.

We have proved that \(I_\xi\) is an ideal. Its principal opens cover the spectrum, so it is contained in no prime ideal and must be the unit ideal. Thus \(1\in I_\xi\) and \(\xi=0\). This completes the induction and proves (BA.7) for every finite abelian \(M\), every closed subscheme of \(\operatorname{Spec}R\), and every positive degree.

### BA.5. Higher continuity for arbitrary qcqs affine limits

The finite-stage step below requires higher continuity beyond AK.1's Noetherian models. Let \(X=\varprojlim_i X_i\) be a directed inverse system of qcqs schemes with affine transitions \(p_{ji}:X_j\to X_i\), and write \(q_i:X\to X_i\). Compatibility of abelian étale sheaves \(F_i\) means that there are maps \(p_{ji}^{-1}F_i\to F_j\) satisfying the identity and composition laws. These maps need not be isomorphisms, and the sheaves need not be constructible or torsion. Put \(F=\operatorname{colim}_i q_i^{-1}F_i\). We prove

\[
\operatorname{colim}_i H^q(X_i,F_i)
\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(X,F),\qquad q\geq0.
\tag{BA.8}
\]

Use the basis \(\mathcal B(S)\) of separated étale objects of finite presentation over a qcqs scheme \(S\). These objects are qcqs, and the final object \(S\to S\) belongs to the basis even when \(S\) is nonaffine or nonseparated. Finite fibre products and equalizers stay in the basis: the diagonal of a separated étale morphism is a clopen immersion of finite presentation. Every étale object is covered by affine charts over affine opens of \(S\). Those charts belong to \(\mathcal B(S)\), since affine opens in a quasi-separated scheme are quasi-compact open immersions. Any covering of a basis object admits a finite refinement of this form, by quasi-compactness and openness of étale maps. The matching-section construction of T.1 gives an exact equivalence between sheaves on this finite-cover basis and sheaves on the full étale site. It preserves injectives and sections at the final object, hence also their derived functors.

AV.1 descends finite diagrams of basis objects and maps, including separatedness. The étale presentations and covering conditions descend by AX.5's arbitrary-ring argument: on finitely many affine charts, images are finite unions of principal opens, and the equation expressing that these opens cover holds at a stage. Thus a finite cover of an object over \(X\) descends to a finite cover over some \(X_i\). All its iterated intersections are then obtained by base change from that one cover. For any compatible system \(M_i\), any \(U_i\in\mathcal B(X_i)\), and \(U_j=U_i\times_{X_i}X_j\), \(U=U_i\times_{X_i}X\), (AZ.5) gives

\[
M(U)\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{j\geq i}M_j(U_j),
\qquad M=\operatorname{colim}_j q_j^{-1}M_j.
\tag{BA.8a}
\]

Indeed apply (AZ.5) to the qcqs schemes \(U_j\) and their restricted sheaves. Restriction is the inverse image for an étale object by AB.3, so it commutes with the colimit in this formula. In particular (BA.8a) applies to arbitrary auxiliary coefficient systems, not only to the given \(F_i\).

To construct a useful auxiliary system, choose a monomorphism \(e_i:F_i\hookrightarrow A_i\) with \(A_i\) injective, using T.2. For every \(i\), set

\[
G_i=\prod_{k\geq i}(p_{ki})_*A_k,\qquad
u_i:F_i\longrightarrow G_i.
\tag{BA.8b}
\]

The \(k\)-component of \(u_i\) is adjoint to \(p_{ki}^{-1}F_i\to F_k\xrightarrow{e_k}A_k\). Its \(k=i\) component is \(e_i\), so \(u_i\) is monic. For \(j\geq i\), projection onto the factors indexed by \(k\geq j\), followed by composition of pushforwards, gives

\[
G_i\longrightarrow
\prod_{k\geq j}(p_{ki})_*A_k
\simeq(p_{ji})_*G_j.
\tag{BA.8c}
\]

Take its adjoint as the transition map \(p_{ji}^{-1}G_i\to G_j\). For \(l\geq j\geq i\), either composite in the required compatibility law is adjoint to the projection onto the factors \(k\geq l\); they agree. On each such factor the compatibility of \(u_i\) is precisely the original composition law for \(F_i\to(p_{ji})_*F_j\to(p_{ki})_*F_k\), followed by \(e_k\). Thus the \(u_i\) form a monomorphism of systems. This construction does not require compatible choices of the individual embeddings \(e_i\).

Every factor \((p_{ki})_*A_k\) is injective, because \(p_{ki}^{-1}\) is exact by AB.3: the adjunction turns extension across a monomorphism into the injective extension problem for \(A_k\). A product of injectives is injective, since each component of a map across a monomorphism can be extended and the extensions assembled into a product map. Consequently \(G_i\) is injective. Write \(G=\operatorname{colim}_i q_i^{-1}G_i\).

We next prove that \(G\) has no positive cohomology on any basis object. Let \(\mathcal V=\{V_a\to U\}_{a=1}^m\) be a finite basis cover over \(X\), descended to a cover \(\mathcal V_i\) over \(X_i\). Denote its base change over \(X_j\) by \(\mathcal V_j\). Formula (BA.8a) on the iterated intersections identifies the Čech complexes:

\[
\check C^\bullet(\mathcal V,G)
\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{j\geq i}
       \check C^\bullet(\mathcal V_j,G_j).
\tag{BA.8d}
\]

In degree \(r\) there are \(m^{r+1}\) factors, so filtered colimit commutes with that finite product. The identification respects every face restriction, hence the alternating differential. No simultaneous choice of infinitely many descent stages is involved: all the intersections in every degree come from the single descended family. The right-hand complexes are acyclic in positive degrees by the injective Čech contraction in S.2. Filtered colimits of abelian groups preserve kernels and cokernels, so the left-hand complex is also acyclic in positive degrees.

For completeness, the passage from this assertion to derived vanishing uses S.3 on the whole basis, not one selected cover. Induct on \(n>0\), simultaneously for all \(U\in\mathcal B(X)\). A class in \(H^n(U,G)\), represented by an injective-resolution cycle, is locally a boundary; choose a finite basis cover on which it is a boundary. In the total complex of S.2, subtract those local primitives to remove the component in bidegree \((0,n)\). Each subsequent component in \((p,n-p)\), with \(0<p<n\), is a vertical cycle on finite intersections. The induction hypothesis supplies primitives there; subtract their signed total differentials. The resulting class is a Čech cocycle in bidegree \((n,0)\), where (BA.8d) makes it a boundary. S.2's augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism, so the original class is zero. At \(n=1\) there are no intermediate components, which starts the induction. This proves

\[
H^n(U,G)=0\quad
(n>0,\ U\in\mathcal B(X)).
\tag{BA.8e}
\]

In particular it holds for \(U=X\). This argument asserts acyclicity of \(G\), without requiring that a colimit of the pulled-back injectives be injective.

Finally let \(Q_i=\operatorname{coker}(u_i)\). Exact inverse image makes the \(Q_i\) a compatible system, and T.1's exact filtered-colimit construction gives \(0\to F\to G\to Q\to0\), where \(Q=\operatorname{colim}_i q_i^{-1}Q_i\). Compare its cohomology sequence with the filtered colimit of the stage sequences for \(0\to F_i\to G_i\to Q_i\to0\). In degree zero the comparison is (BA.8a). Since the \(G_i\) and \(G\) have zero positive cohomology, in degree one both groups for \(F\) are the cokernels of the corresponding section maps from \(G\) to \(Q\). They agree. For \(n>1\), the connecting maps identify degree \(n\) for \(F_i\), respectively \(F\), with degree \(n-1\) for \(Q_i\), respectively \(Q\). Induction over all compatible systems proves (BA.8).

The comparison maps here are the canonical pullback maps: apply exact inverse image to a resolution and compare with a target injective resolution as in T.3. That construction requires injectivity only in the target; exactness of the pulled-back source resolution suffices. The comparison homotopies and the connecting-map construction T.4 show that these maps commute with the two long exact sequences. Thus dimension shifting proves the asserted natural isomorphism, not merely equality of abstract groups. The same compatible-embedding argument is given in [Pushforward, pullback and finite morphisms, §2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/pushforward-pullback-and-finite-morphisms#proof-of-continuity-for-arbitrary-compatible-sheaves); see also [Stacks, compatible injective systems](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EXZ) and [cohomology of limit sites](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09YP). The geometric continuity statement is [Stacks, Theorem 59.51.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09YQ).

The same theorem holds when the inverse system of schemes is indexed by an arbitrary small cofiltered category. Apply AY.5's directed-index construction to its opposite category. Formula (AY.7e) identifies the scheme limits. Apply (AY.7d) on the fixed étale site of that limit to identify the coefficient sheaf colimits, and apply it to the diagram of cohomology groups to identify the left side of (BA.8). Every transition in the replacement is an original scheme map, so remains affine; all schemes remain qcqs. The directed-set case just proved therefore gives the full comparison. Its canonical maps agree with the original ones by the componentwise description in (AY.7d)–(AY.7e). In particular fixed-scheme filtered coefficients commute with every \(H^q\) on a qcqs scheme.

Using the injective slice calculation AB.3 and a strict localization as in AX.5 also gives, for every qcqs morphism \(f:X\to S\),

\[
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar s}
\simeq H^q\bigl(X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,\bar s},F\bigr).
\tag{BA.9}
\]

Indeed, the affine étale neighborhoods with their selected geometric points form a small cofiltered category after choosing finite presentations. Over an affine neighborhood of \(s\), their pullbacks to \(X\) are qcqs and have affine transition maps. Their limit is the strict-local base change, since its coordinate-ring limit on every affine chart is the pointed-ring colimit in AX.5; the finite chart and overlap gluing is the same as in AY.5. Apply the cofiltered-category form of (BA.8). The presheaf defining the higher direct image has exactly these cohomology groups by (AB.8), and sheafification leaves its stalk unchanged. Equations (AY.7d)–(AY.7e) ensure that the resulting isomorphism is the original restriction map from neighborhood cohomology. Formula (BA.9) compares with the strict local base; it does not yet replace that base by its closed geometric fibre.

### BA.6. Finite covers killing a constant-coefficient class

Let \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\). Choose a surjection from the polynomial domain \(P=\mathbb Z[x_i]_{i\in I}\) onto \(A\), with kernel \(J\); an arbitrary set of variables is allowed. Let \(\Omega\) be an algebraic closure of \(\operatorname{Frac}P\), and let \(R\) be the integral closure of \(P\) in \(\Omega\). Transitivity of integrality makes \(R\) normal. Clearing denominators in a monic equation over \(\operatorname{Frac}P\) makes a nonzero \(P\)-multiple of each element of \(\Omega\) integral, so \(\operatorname{Frac}R=\Omega\). Thus BA.4 applies to all closed subschemes of \(\operatorname{Spec}R\).

Put \(A'=R/JR\). Its map from \(A\) is integral and its spectrum maps surjectively onto \(X\): for a prime containing \(J\), choose a prime of \(R\) lying over it, which then contains \(JR\). A closed subscheme of \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\) is also closed in \(\operatorname{Spec}R\), so has the vanishing (BA.7). Hence any \(\xi\in H^q(Z,\underline M)\), with \(Z\subset X\) closed, \(q>0\) and \(M\) finite abelian, becomes zero after pullback to \(Z\times_X\operatorname{Spec}A'\).

We require finite stages which are also finitely presented over \(A\), even though \(A\) may be non-Noetherian. Here is an explicit system for an arbitrary integral \(A\)-algebra \(A'\). For a finite set of its elements, choose monic equations for each. The algebra given by these finitely many monic equations is finite free over \(A\), with the bounded monomials as a basis, and maps to \(A'\). Quotient further by any finite set of relations holding among the chosen elements. The resulting algebra is finite and finitely presented over \(A\). Enlarge the element set, retain the chosen monic equations and add relations as needed. These choices form a directed system: unions receive two sets of choices, and adding finitely many relation equations equalizes any finite set of identifications. Every element of \(A'\) is represented and every polynomial relation is eventually imposed. Thus

\[
A'=\operatorname{colim}_i A_i',
\qquad A_i'\text{ finite and finitely presented over }A.
\tag{BA.10}
\]

Equivalently one may index by the finite generator and relation choices in the single polynomial algebra whose variables are indexed by elements of \(A'\), choosing once a monic equation for each variable. All transition maps and their maps to \(A'\) are then specified by the inclusions and quotients. Each \(\operatorname{Spec}A_i'\to X\) is surjective, since the already surjective map from \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\) factors through it.

Apply (BA.8) to \(Z\times_X\operatorname{Spec}A_i'\), with its pulled-back constant sheaf. The vanishing of the limiting class means that it vanishes at some finite stage. We have proved

\[
\begin{gathered}
\xi\in H^q(Z,\underline M),\quad q>0,\quad |M|<\infty\\
\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\ p:X'\to X\text{ finite, surjective and finitely presented},\\
\xi|_{Z\times_XX'}=0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{BA.11}
\]

The finite stage may have additional relations or additional components; no claim that it is a finite subalgebra of \(A'\) is needed.

### BA.7. Effacement for arbitrary torsion coefficients

Let \(F\) be a torsion abelian sheaf on affine \(X\), with \(Z\subset X\) closed, and let \(\xi\in H^q(Z,F|_Z)\), \(q>0\). AZ.2 writes \(F\) as a filtered colimit of constructible abelian sheaves \(C\) mapping to it. Restriction commutes with this colimit, and (BA.8) for the constant scheme diagram on the affine scheme \(Z\) commutes it with cohomology. Choose one \(u:C\to F\) and a class \(\eta\in H^q(Z,C|_Z)\) mapping to \(\xi\).

By (AZ.11) embed \(C\) in \(\bigoplus_a(p_a)_*\underline{M_a}\), where the \(p_a:T_a\to X\) are finite and finitely presented and the \(M_a\) are finite abelian. Each \(T_a\) is affine. AX.5 proves finite direct-image base change, its exactness and its cohomology comparison. Thus the image of \(\eta\) has components in \(H^q(T_a\times_XZ,\underline{M_a})\). Apply (BA.11) to each of these finitely many components, producing a finite surjection \(r_a:T'_a\to T_a\) which kills it.

The unit map \(\underline{M_a}\to(r_a)_*\underline{M_a}\) is injective: at a geometric point it is the diagonal into the product indexed by the nonempty finite set of lifts, by (AX.12). Exact finite direct image preserves this injection. Consequently we obtain a monomorphism

\[
v:C\hookrightarrow C',
\qquad C'=\bigoplus_a(p_ar_a)_*\underline{M_a},
\tag{BA.12}
\]

and \(\eta\) becomes zero with coefficients \(C'|_Z\). The cohomology comparison uses the actual adjunction unit, so these images are precisely the pullbacks killed in (BA.11). The sheaf \(C'\) is torsion, since the finite list of groups \(M_a\) has a common annihilator.

Form the pushout

\[
F'=(F\oplus C')/\operatorname{im}(u,-v).
\tag{BA.13}
\]

The induced map \(F\to F'\) is injective: on stalks, if \((f,0)=(u(c),-v(c))\), then \(v(c)=0\), hence \(c=0\) and \(f=0\). Its stalks are torsion as quotients of torsion groups. Exact inverse image preserves this pushout on \(Z\). The two maps from \(C|_Z\) to \(F'|_Z\) agree, so the image of \(\xi=u_*(\eta)\) equals the image of the zero class through \(C'|_Z\). This proves the effacement assertion at the start of the appendix.

If the original sheaf is a sheaf of \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-vector spaces, use its constructible module approximation, the linear embedding in AZ.6, and the same finite-cover construction. The entire pushout is then \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-linear. This supplies both coefficient versions used in [The proper base change theorem, §6](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#6-killing-constant-coefficient-classes-on-closed-affine-schemes).

The argument establishes affine closed-subscheme effacement and the arbitrary-base continuity needed for it. BB.1–BB.4 pass from this effacement to affine henselian comparison and the restricted-injective bound. BC.1–BC.6 supply that lifting and the projective-line comparison over complete Noetherian local rings. BD.3–BD.6 supply the arbitrary henselian degree-one input through pointed approximation and proper finite-torsor lifting. BE.1–BE.8 prove general higher proper comparison and the geometric-fibre formula. Further specialization assertions require their own hypotheses; categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are treated in BF–BX.

## Appendix BB. Cohomology near a henselian closed subscheme

For a henselian pair, the degree-zero comparison (AX.14) and the torsion effacement of BA.7 determine all higher cohomology on the affine scheme. To apply this to a closed subscheme of an arbitrary affine scheme, we first construct its henselian neighbourhood. We also verify the coefficient-category assertion needed when an injective sheaf of vector spaces is used to compute abelian-sheaf cohomology.

### BB.1. Constructing the henselian neighbourhood of an arbitrary ideal

Let \(A\) be any ring and \(I\subset A\) any ideal. No finite-generation assumption on \(I\) is imposed. Consider the category \(\mathcal N_I\) of étale \(A\)-algebras \(B\) for which the structural map \(A/I\to B/IB\) is an isomorphism, with all \(A\)-algebra maps between them. Throughout this construction an étale algebra is finitely presented.

This category is filtered. It contains \(A\), and \(B\otimes_A C\) receives maps from any two of its objects and has the same closed quotient. To equalize two maps \(u,v:B\to C\), take the equalizer of their corresponding morphisms \(\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}B\). It is the inverse image of the diagonal of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). That diagonal is open because the morphism is étale and closed because it is affine. Its inverse image is therefore a clopen subscheme of \(\operatorname{Spec}C\), hence the spectrum of an idempotent factor \(D\) of \(C\). Both maps reduce to the structural identification on the closed quotient, so \(D/ID=A/I\). Thus \(D\) is another object and \(C\to D\) equalizes \(u,v\). The diagonal facts are the étale local criteria proved in AW.1; the idempotent description of clopen subsets was used in AX.1.

Set

\[
H=\operatorname{colim}_{B\in\mathcal N_I}B,
\qquad J=IH.
\tag{BB.1}
\]

Quotients commute with this filtered colimit, giving \(H/J=A/I\). Moreover \(J\subset\operatorname{Jac}(H)\). Indeed, write any \(x\in J\) as a finite sum of elements of \(I\) times elements of \(H\). At a common stage it is represented by \(b\in IB\). The algebra \(B_{1-b}\) is still an object of \(\mathcal N_I\), so \(1-x\) becomes a unit in \(H\). Applying this also to every multiple of \(x\) proves the Jacobson-radical assertion: if a maximal ideal omitted \(x\), a suitable multiple of \(x\) would be one in the residue field, contradicting invertibility of its complement.

We prove henselianity directly by lifting polynomial factors. Suppose \(P\in H[t]\) is monic and \(\overline P=g_0h_0\) in \((A/I)[t]\), where the monic polynomials \(g_0,h_0\) have degrees \(r,s\) and generate the unit ideal. Choose a stage \(B\) containing the coefficients of \(P\). Introduce \(r+s\) variables for the coefficients below the leading terms of monic polynomials \(g,h\), and impose the \(r+s\) coefficient equations of \(gh=P\). Their differential in the coefficient directions is

\[
(a,b)\longmapsto h a+g b,
\qquad \deg a<r,\quad \deg b<s.
\tag{BB.2}
\]

At \((g_0,h_0)\), this is an isomorphism. To see this over the possibly nonreduced ring \(A/I\), multiplication by \(h_0\) is invertible on \((A/I)[t]/(g_0)\), using a Bézout identity. For any polynomial \(c\) of degree below \(r+s\), choose the unique representative \(a\) of degree below \(r\) solving \(h_0a=c\pmod {g_0}\), then put \(b=(c-h_0a)/g_0\). Monic division gives \(\deg b<s\), and the same argument proves uniqueness. Thus the square Jacobian determinant is a unit at the selected factorization.

Invert that determinant in the coefficient algebra. The resulting algebra \(D\) is étale over \(B\) by the square-Jacobian criterion (AW.3), and its reduction has the section specified by \((g_0,h_0)\). A section of an affine étale morphism has clopen image: it is a base change of its open and closed diagonal. Consequently

\[
D/ID\cong (A/I)\times E,
\tag{BB.3}
\]

where the projection to the first factor is the selected section on rings. Lift \((1,0)\) to \(d\in D\). The algebra \(D_d\) is étale over \(A\), and its quotient by \(I\) is exactly \(A/I\); hence it occurs in \(\mathcal N_I\). Mapping its coefficients to \(H\) supplies the required factorization \(P=gh\) with the prescribed reductions and degrees. Constant factors cause no difficulty and may instead be lifted immediately. We have proved that \((H,J)\) is henselian in the definition of AX.1.

The ring \(H\) has the expected universal property. For a map \((A,I)\to(R,K)\) with \((R,K)\) henselian and \(B\in\mathcal N_I\), the étale \(R\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A R)\) has exactly one section over \(R/K\): its closed quotient is \(R/K\). Formula (AX.14), applied to the identity proper scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}R\) and this representable étale sheaf, lifts that section uniquely to \(R\). Uniqueness makes these maps compatible for all \(B\), producing the unique factorization \(H\to R\). Its image sends \(J\) into \(K\). Thus \(H\) is the henselization \(A_I^h\) of the pair, with

\[
A_I^h/IA_I^h=A/I.
\tag{BB.4}
\]

The construction is flat over \(A\), since its étale stages are flat and a filtered colimit preserves exactness of module sequences. It also gives \(A_I^h/I^m A_I^h=A/I^m\) for every \(m\geq1\). For each stage \(B\), the map \(B\to A/I\) lifts uniquely to \(A/I^m\) by formal étaleness, proved in BA.1. Its composite with \(A/I^m\to B/I^mB\) is the identity on the latter algebra: the two maps from \(B\) to \(B/I^mB\) have the same reduction and formal uniqueness applies across the nilpotent ideal \(IB/I^mB\). This gives the inverse isomorphism at every stage and hence at the colimit. These statements also include \(I=A\), when \(H\) is the zero ring and the closed scheme is empty.

### BB.2. Affine henselian comparison in every degree

Let \((A,I)\) now be henselian, write \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\), and let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\). For every torsion abelian étale sheaf \(F\), restriction induces an isomorphism

\[
r_F^q:H^q(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(Z,i^{-1}F)
\qquad(q\geq0).
\tag{BB.5}
\]

Here and below cohomology is on the small étale site. The case \(q=0\) is (AX.14), with the identity scheme proper over \(A\). We prove each higher degree simultaneously for all torsion sheaves. Suppose the assertion is known in degrees below \(q>0\). For a monomorphism \(F\hookrightarrow E\) of torsion sheaves put \(Q=E/F\), also torsion. Exact inverse image and the natural long exact sequences give a commutative comparison between the segments

\[
H^{q-1}(E)\longrightarrow H^{q-1}(Q)
\xrightarrow{\partial}H^q(F)\longrightarrow H^q(E)
\tag{BB.6}
\]

on \(X\) and \(Z\). These are the connecting maps constructed from injective resolutions in T.4.

First let \(\alpha\in H^q(X,F)\) restrict to zero. Apply BA.7 with closed subscheme \(X\) itself to choose \(F\hookrightarrow E\) killing \(\alpha\). Exactness gives \(\beta\in H^{q-1}(X,Q)\) with \(\partial\beta=\alpha\). Since \(\partial r_Q^{q-1}(\beta)=0\), choose \(\gamma_Z\in H^{q-1}(Z,i^{-1}E)\) mapping to \(r_Q^{q-1}(\beta)\). The induction hypothesis lifts \(\gamma_Z\) to \(\gamma\in H^{q-1}(X,E)\). Subtracting its image from \(\beta\) yields a class whose restriction is zero. Injectivity for \(Q\) in degree \(q-1\) makes that class zero. Hence \(\alpha=\partial\beta=0\).

Conversely, given \(\alpha_Z\in H^q(Z,i^{-1}F)\), apply BA.7 with the actual closed subscheme \(Z\) to choose a monomorphism \(F\hookrightarrow E\) killing this class on \(Z\). It is the boundary of some \(\beta_Z\in H^{q-1}(Z,i^{-1}Q)\). Surjectivity in degree \(q-1\) lifts \(\beta_Z\) to \(X\); its boundary restricts to \(\alpha_Z\). This completes the induction. The maps are the actual restrictions, so (BB.5) is natural in the sheaf and in maps of pairs. No higher proper comparison is used in the proof.

### BB.3. Module injectives and underlying abelian cohomology

Let \(\Lambda\) be a constant ring. On a qcqs scheme \(Y\), an injective sheaf \(J\) of left \(\Lambda\)-modules has

\[
H^q(Y,J)=0\quad(q>0)
\tag{BB.7}
\]

also when these groups are derived in abelian sheaves. This requires an argument: the forgetful functor is exact but that alone does not say it preserves injectives.

Take any finite-family hypercover \(K_\bullet\) of the basis used in AK.2 and BA.5. Its augmented chain complex of free \(\Lambda\)-module sheaves is exact. The local cone filling in AK.2 proves this directly with \(\Lambda\)-coefficients: for each finite-support cycle the same contraction satisfies \(\partial c+c\partial=1\), so the cycle is locally a boundary. It is not necessary to assert that tensoring every exact complex with \(\Lambda\) is exact. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,J)\) to this exact augmented complex gives an exact augmented cochain complex, since \(J\) is injective. Its term in degree \(a\) is precisely

\[
\prod_{V\in K_a}\Gamma(V,J),
\tag{BB.8}
\]

with the alternating face differential. For example exactness follows by factoring a cocycle through the appropriate image sheaf and extending the resulting map across its inclusion into the preceding chain term. Formula (AK.3), whose arbitrary-base finite-cover justification is BA.5, computes abelian cohomology as the filtered hypercover cohomology. Every positive group in this filtered system is zero, proving (BB.7).

Consequently an injective resolution in \(\Lambda\)-module sheaves computes the same cohomology as an abelian-sheaf resolution. Its underlying complex is still exact and its terms are acyclic by (BB.7). The acyclic-resolution comparison follows by successive cokernels and their long exact sequences, as in T.4; it agrees with the identity in degree zero and is therefore compatible with restriction and connecting maps. Enough module injectives exist for every constant ring: BF.5 verifies the Grothendieck axioms using exact sheafification and the sheafified free representables, and the generator-extension construction recalled in BF.1 constructs injectives before any derived category is used. For a prime \(\ell\) and \(\Lambda=\mathbb F_\ell\), the geometric-point product construction of T.4 also applies directly, since every vector space is injective: maps extend after extending a basis.

For an étale object \(a:U\to Y\), restriction of a module injective to \(U\) is again injective. Its left adjoint \(a_!\) has at a geometric point \(\bar y\) the direct sum of the stalks over all lifts of \(\bar y\) to \(U\), with their natural \(\Lambda\)-actions. The sheaf construction and adjunction are those of AZ.1 and the slice calculation AB.3. Direct sums of exact sequences are exact, and geometric stalks detect exactness, so \(a_!\) is exact. The adjunction then extends maps into \(a^{-1}J\) across every monomorphism. This includes restriction to open subschemes. When \(U\) is qcqs, (BB.7) applies to this restricted injective as well.

The same comparison holds for higher direct images under a qcqs morphism \(f:X\to Y\). Work on the basis of qcqs étale objects \(V\to Y\). The pullback \(X_V\) is qcqs and étale over \(X\), so the restriction of a module injective \(J\) is still module injective. The preceding argument gives \(H^q(X_V,J)=0\) in abelian sheaves for \(q>0\).
