Higher abelian direct images are the sheafifications of these cohomology presheaves: restrict an abelian injective resolution to \(X_V\), using the same exact étale left adjoint, and take sections. Thus the underlying abelian sheaf of \(J\) is \(f_*\)-acyclic. An injective resolution in module sheaves is consequently an acyclic resolution for abelian direct image. Comparing the two resolutions gives the natural identification of their higher direct images, compatible with restriction and connecting maps. No flatness, finite global dimension or field hypothesis on \(\Lambda\) is used. In particular the comparison applies to every constant commutative ring killed by an integer, as required for the cohomological bounds in BG.

### BB.4. Closed restrictions and a finite affine covering

Let \(X\) have affine diagonal and a covering by \(n+1\) affine opens, let \(Z\subset X\) be closed, and let \(J\) be an injective \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-module sheaf on \(X\). Then

\[
H^q(Z,J|_Z)=0\qquad(q>n).
\tag{BB.9}
\]

Begin with \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\). Apply BB.1 to this arbitrary pair, writing \(H=A_I^h\), and pull \(J\) back to \(\operatorname{Spec}H\). This sheaf is torsion. Comparison (BB.5) for the henselian pair \((H,IH)\), followed by (BA.8) for its affine étale-neighbourhood system, gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
H^q(Z,J|_Z)
&\cong H^q(\operatorname{Spec}H,J|_H)\\
&\cong\operatorname{colim}_{B\in\mathcal N_I}
 H^q(\operatorname{Spec}B,J|_B)=0
\qquad(q>0).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BB.10}
\]

Every stage is étale over \(X\); BB.3 makes its restricted sheaf injective and acyclic. The maps in (BB.10) are induced by restriction, so the two comparisons concern exactly the original closed restriction of \(J\). In particular we have not assumed that restriction to an arbitrary closed subscheme preserves injectives.

For the induction, let \(X=U\cup V\), with \(U\) the union of \(n\) members of the affine covering and \(V\) its last member. The intersection of two affine opens is affine: it is the base change of the affine diagonal to their affine product. Thus \(U\cap V\) is a union of \(n\) affine opens; these open subschemes inherit the affine-diagonal property. Restriction of \(J\) to them preserves injectivity by BB.3. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the cover \(Z=(Z\cap U)\cup(Z\cap V)\) contains

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{q-1}(Z\cap U\cap V,J)\longrightarrow H^q(Z,J)\\
\longrightarrow H^q(Z\cap U,J)\oplus H^q(Z\cap V,J).
\end{gathered}
\tag{BB.11}
\]

For \(q>n\), the left term vanishes by the induction hypothesis because \(q-1>n-1\); the right terms vanish by that hypothesis and the affine case. The exact sequence therefore proves (BB.9). Its sheaf-theoretic derivation is the two-open resolution argument in BA.4, so it applies to these étale coefficients.

In particular, for \(X=\mathbb P^1_A\) and any closed subscheme \(Z\), its two standard affine charts give

\[
H^q(Z,J|_Z)=0\qquad(q>1).
\tag{BB.12}
\]

This proves the restricted-injective bound used in [The proper base change theorem, §7](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#7-the-affine-henselian-comparison-and-restricted-injectives), including the henselization and coefficient-category inputs.

### BB.5. The degree-one step on the projective line

For a henselian local ring \(A\), write \(X=\mathbb P^1_A\) and \(X_0\) for its closed fibre. To obtain comparison in every degree from an injective resolution, we need \(H^1(X_0,J|_{X_0})=0\) for every injective \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaf \(J\). Formula (BB.12) handles degrees at least two; BD.6 supplies degree one using the finite-torsor lifting proved in BD.5.

The precise remaining input in [The proper base change theorem, §8](course:ag-etale-cohomology/the-proper-base-change-theorem#8-acyclic-resolutions-on-the-projective-line-fibre) is the following lifting assertion: if \(T\) is finite over \(X\), then every class of \(H^1(T_0,\underline M)\), for finite \(M\), must lift to \(H^1(T,\underline M)\). AZ.2 and (BA.8) first represent a fibre class using a constructible sheaf \(C\to J\); (AZ.11) embeds \(C\) into a finite sum of the sheaves \(p_*\underline M\), where \(p:T\to X\) is finite. Injectivity extends \(C\to J\) across that embedding. If the stated degree-one lifting is available, finite-map cohomology in AX.5 lifts the resulting sum to \(H^1(X,\bigoplus p_*\underline M)\). Its image in \(H^1(X,J)\) is zero by BB.3, and restriction kills the original fibre class. BD.5–BD.6 prove its degree-one lifting hypothesis over an arbitrary henselian local ring.

That hypothesis concerns torsors on proper \(A\)-schemes \(T\). AX.7 supplies full faithfulness, BC.1–BC.6 construct covers by coherent algebraization over complete Noetherian pairs, and BD.1–BD.5 pass to arbitrary henselian local rings by descent and pointed approximation. BD.6 then completes this projective-line argument. BE.1–BE.8 prove general higher proper comparison. The categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are treated in BF–BX.

## Appendix BC. Lifting finite covers over a complete base

We prove the complete Noetherian case of the cover-lifting input isolated in BB.5. The base may be complete along an arbitrary ideal; it need not be local. The argument first recovers coherent modules, then their algebra structures, and finally verifies étaleness. Approximation from a completion to a henselian ring is a subsequent requirement.

### BC.1. Formal coherent modules and completion

Let \(A\) be Noetherian and complete for an ideal \(I\), let \(X\) be proper over \(A\), and put \(X_n=X\times_A A/I^n\), for \(n\geq1\). A formal coherent module is a system \(\mathfrak F=(F_n)\) of coherent modules on \(X_n\) with specified compatible isomorphisms

\[
F_{n+1}/I^nF_{n+1}\cong F_n.
\tag{BC.1}
\]

The convention includes the structure maps, so an algebraization must recover those maps as well as the individual sheaves.

We use the affine description and formal kernels proved in [Grothendieck's existence theorem, §§1–2](course:AG-QC/grothendiecks-existence-theorem#1-compatible-coherent-systems). Here are their constructions and the relevant algebraic prerequisites. On \(V=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset X\), take \(M=\varprojlim M_n\), where \(M_n=\Gamma(V,F_n)\). Lift a finite generating list of \(M_1\) through the surjective transitions. The resulting maps \((R/I^nR)^r\to M_n\) are surjective, by the nilpotent form of Nakayama. Their kernels have surjective transitions: lift a kernel vector to the next free module and subtract a vector in \(I^n(R/I^{n+1}R)^r\) with the same image in \(I^nM_{n+1}\). The inverse-limit lifting argument in L.1 gives a surjection \(\widehat R^r\to M\), and reducing its kernel gives

\[
M/I^nM=M_n.
\tag{BC.2}
\]

Conversely every finite \(\widehat R\)-module is complete and is recovered from these quotients. The ring \(\widehat R\) is Noetherian by the initial-ideal construction in L.1. Completion is flat: for each ideal \(K\subset R\), L.1 identifies \(K\otimes_R\widehat R\to\widehat R\) with the injective completed inclusion. The ideal criterion proved in U.2 then applies. Thus completion is exact on finite modules and agrees with tensoring. These are precisely the inputs of [Completion, Theorems 3.1–3.3](course:AG-CA/completion#3-noetherian-exactness-tensoring-and-flatness), already proved here in L.1 and U.2.

For completeness, finite-level kernels need not themselves form a system satisfying (BC.1). If a formal map is represented on this affine by \(u:M\to N\), with kernel \(K\) and image \(H\), Artin–Rees for \(H\subset N\) gives

\[
u^{-1}(I^lN)\subset K+I^{l-c}M
\quad(l\geq c).
\tag{BC.3}
\]

Hence the image in \(M/I^mM\) of the kernel at a sufficiently late level is \(K/(K\cap I^mM)\). Applying Artin–Rees to \(K\subset M\), and then quotienting this stabilized image by \(I^n\) for sufficiently large \(m\), recovers \(K/I^nK\). These image and quotient constructions commute with restriction of the coherent sheaves. Finite affine covers give common bounds when needed, so the formal kernels glue. Cokernels are the levelwise cokernels. The affine descriptions prove that this is an abelian category and that coherent completion \(F\mapsto\widehat F\) is exact. Surjectivity of a formal map is detected at level one, by Nakayama on its finite completed cokernel; \(I\widehat R\) is in the Jacobson radical since geometric series invert \(1-a\) for \(a\in I\widehat R\).

### BC.2. Recovering morphisms and extensions

For coherent modules \(F,G\) on proper \(X\), put \(E^q=\mathcal Ext_X^q(F,G)\), in particular \(E^0=\mathcal Hom_X(F,G)\). Finite free resolutions on affine charts, taken only as far as the degree in question, show that \(E^q\) is coherent: the syzygies, kernels and images are finite over Noetherian rings. Localization commutes with these finite computations. Flat completion also preserves them, giving the corresponding formal sheaves \(\widehat{E^q}\).

We first check their cohomology. On a formal affine, the finite-principal-cover section complex of a coherent formal module is the inverse limit of the usual complexes of its coherent quotients. Those complexes are acyclic in positive degree by W.1–W.2. All their terms and their degree-zero cohomology have surjective transitions, so their inverse limit remains acyclic. One direct verification uses the exact sequence of complexes with last map

\[
\prod_n C_n^\bullet\longrightarrow\prod_n C_n^\bullet,
\qquad (c_n)\longmapsto(c_n-u_{n+1}c_{n+1}).
\tag{BC.4}
\]

This map is onto termwise, by recursive lifting; its kernel is the inverse limit. Its long exact cohomology sequence gives the assertion. The finite-principal-basis acyclicity argument of W.2 then computes formal coherent cohomology by any finite affine cover and its affine intersections.

For an algebraic coherent \(E\) on proper \(X\), that formal cover complex is the inverse limit of the complexes for \(E/I^nE\). The cohomology systems are Mittag–Leffler. Indeed (AU.10) expresses them as an extension of the surjective system \(H^p(X,E)/J_n^p\) by a system with eventually zero transition maps, by (AU.9). For fixed \(n\), every sufficiently late image in the middle term is exactly the embedded left term: it contains that term by surjectivity on the left and is contained in it by the zero transition on the right. Stabilized images permit recursive compatible lifts. Applied to (BC.4), this proves that its map on the products of degree-\((p-1)\) cohomology is onto. Formal functions (AU.11) and completeness of finite \(A\)-modules therefore give

\[
H^p(\widehat X,\widehat E)
\cong\varprojlim_n H^p(X,E/I^nE)
\cong H^p(X,E).
\tag{BC.5}
\]

The product-map assertion for a Mittag–Leffler system can be checked explicitly. Replace each term by its stabilized image; the resulting transition maps are surjective, and the quotient system has eventually zero maps into every fixed term. In that quotient, a preimage of \((a_n)\) under (BC.4) is the sum of all later images of the \(a_m\), a finite sum at each coordinate. Lift these preimages arbitrarily to the original groups. The remaining error lies in the stabilized-image system, where recursive lifting solves the same equation because its transitions are onto. This proves the surjectivity used above.

Here \(\widehat X\) denotes the ringed space on \(|X_1|\) with the completed affine rings and completed restriction maps; coherent modules on it are the systems of BC.1. The construction above also defines the cohomology on the left through its acyclic affine basis.

For \(E=E^0\), local finite presentations identify completed Hom with Hom of completed modules. Formula (BC.5) in degree zero thus proves full faithfulness:

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_X(F,G)
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat X}(\widehat F,\widehat G).
\tag{BC.6}
\]

We need the analogous assertion for short exact sequences. It can be proved using only the first two local Ext degrees. The affine-cover description of extensions gives an exact sequence

\[
\begin{gathered}
0\longrightarrow H^1(X,E^0)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Ext}^1_X(F,G)\longrightarrow H^0(X,E^1)\\
\longrightarrow H^2(X,E^0).
\end{gathered}
\tag{BC.7}
\]

In this formula Ext means short exact sequences with specified ends, modulo isomorphism. To verify it, choose extensions on the affine opens representing a section of \(E^1\). Equality of the classes on an affine intersection means there is an isomorphism of extensions there. On a triple intersection the failure of the chosen isomorphisms to compose is an automorphism inducing the identity on both ends. Such an automorphism is uniquely \(1+\iota h\pi\), with \(h:F\to G\); the square of \(\iota h\pi\) is zero. Their failures form a Čech 2-cocycle in \(E^0\). Its class vanishes exactly when adjusting the isomorphisms by a 1-cochain makes them a gluing datum. Locally split extensions are similarly classified by Čech 1-cocycles in \(E^0\), modulo changes of splitting. This proves the displayed exactness. On affines the required identification of extension classes with module Ext follows by choosing a finite free presentation of \(F\), lifting that free module to the middle term, and recording the resulting map from its relation module to \(G\), modulo maps from the free module. Thus no global locally free resolution is assumed.

The same construction over the completed affine rings gives (BC.7) for formal modules. Completion preserves its classes, gluing maps and obstruction cocycles. Formula (BC.5) for \(E^0,E^1\) identifies the first, third and fourth terms. A diagram chase, first on the obstruction and then on the 1-cocycle of a locally split difference, proves

\[
\operatorname{Ext}^1_X(F,G)
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\widehat X}(\widehat F,\widehat G).
\tag{BC.8}
\]

This supplies the extension comparison of [Grothendieck's existence theorem, Proposition 3.3](course:AG-QC/grothendiecks-existence-theorem#3-full-faithfulness-from-formal-functions) at the proper scope needed here, without importing an unbounded derived-category comparison.

### BC.3. Algebraizing a formal coherent module

First suppose \(X\) is projective over \(A\), and let \(L\) be the line bundle of a fixed projective embedding. For \(\mathfrak F=(F_n)\) put \(F_0=0\) and \(D_n=\ker(F_{n+1}\to F_n)\), for \(n\geq0\). The graded sheaf \(\bigoplus D_n\) is finite over \(\mathcal O_X\otimes_A B\), where

\[
B=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^n/I^{n+1}.
\tag{BC.9}
\]

Indeed its affine description is \(\bigoplus I^nM/I^{n+1}M\), generated in degree zero over the associated graded completed ring; the pullback of \(B\) surjects onto that ring. The graded algebra \(B\) is Noetherian by the polynomial-ring argument of L.1. Affine sheaf correspondence realizes this graded sheaf as the direct image of a coherent module on the projective scheme \(X_B\). W.4's Serre vanishing, applied once on \(X_B\), gives a single \(d\) for which

\[
H^1(X,D_n\otimes L^d)=0\quad\text{for every }n\geq0.
\tag{BC.10}
\]

The cohomology identification here is the finite affine-cover complex: direct sums commute with its kernels and images, and the affine projection has the same section modules. Increasing \(d\) makes \(F_1\otimes L^d\) globally generated, again by W.4. The quotient sequences and (BC.10) lift finitely many chosen generating sections compatibly through all \(F_n\otimes L^d\). They give a formal surjection \(\widehat P\to\mathfrak F\), with \(P=(L^{-d})^r\). Repeat this construction for its coherent formal kernel, obtaining

\[
\widehat Q\longrightarrow\widehat P\longrightarrow
\mathfrak F\longrightarrow0,
\tag{BC.11}
\]

where \(Q\) is another finite sum of one line-bundle twist. By (BC.6) the first map algebraizes; its coherent cokernel algebraizes \(\mathfrak F\) because completion is exact. This is the projective existence argument of [Grothendieck's existence theorem, §§4–5](course:AG-QC/grothendiecks-existence-theorem#4-one-twist-for-every-thickening), with the uniform bound supplied by one graded module.

For proper \(X\), use Noetherian induction on closed subschemes, including their scheme structures. Coherent ideal sheaves satisfy the ascending chain condition, as a finite affine cover reduces this to Noetherian rings. If existence failed, choose a maximal ideal defining a closed subscheme on which it fails, and replace \(X\) by that proper subscheme. Existence is then known on \(V(K)\) for every nonzero coherent ideal \(K\).

The schematic Chow construction in [Projective morphisms and Chow's lemma, Theorem 4.1](course:AG-MO/projective-morphisms-and-chows-lemma#4-chow-s-lemma-over-a-noetherian-base) gives a projective proper surjection \(p:Y\to X\), an isomorphism over an open \(U\) containing all generic points, with \(Y\) projective over \(A\). This includes nonreduced \(X\). The construction takes the scheme-theoretic closure of the common dense affine open in a product of projective spaces. Its maps on overlaps agree because their closed equalizers have ideals vanishing on that schematically dense open. Their proper open inclusions over the original affine charts are closed and contain the dense open, so give the whole inverse images; this proves properness and surjectivity. Taking the schematic closure of \(U\) in \(X\) first retains its scheme structure on \(U\) and gives a surjective closed immersion to \(X\). Thus no reduced replacement of the given formal module occurs. Here the base is affine: every chosen affine chart has finite affine coordinates over A, so embeds in an affine space and hence in a projective space. Since X is proper over A, the resulting Y is proper over A; its immersion into projective space is therefore closed. Also p is projective, by its closed graph in X times that projective space. The projective-space, graph and Segre inputs are AU.1, and this is the nonreduced version of the construction used in AU.2.

Algebraize \(p^*\mathfrak F\) on \(Y\) by the projective case, obtaining \(E\), and set \(H=p_*E\), coherent by AU.3. The actual adjunction maps at finite levels, together with formal functions for \(p\), give

\[
\alpha:\mathfrak F\longrightarrow\widehat H.
\tag{BC.12}
\]

Both its kernel and cokernel are killed by one power of the coherent ideal \(K\) of \(X\setminus U\). Here is the required uniformity argument. On \(V=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset X\), represent \(\mathfrak F\) by a finite \(\widehat R\)-module \(M\). The pullback of \(E\) to the projective scheme \(Y_{\widehat R}\) and \(p^*\widetilde M\) have the same specified completion. Projective full faithfulness (BC.6) makes them isomorphic. Flat base change (AU.1) identifies \(\alpha\) on this affine with the completed-ring adjunction

\[
M\longrightarrow\Gamma(Y_{\widehat R},p^*\widetilde M).
\tag{BC.13}
\]

It is an isomorphism off \(V(K\widehat R)\). Its two defects are finite \(\widehat R\)-modules, by proper coherence; a finite module supported on \(V(K\widehat R)\) is annihilated by a power of that ideal. To check this last statement, each generator of the ideal has some power killing each member of a finite module-generating list, and a sufficiently long monomial in the ideal generators contains one of those powers. A finite affine cover of \(X\) now gives one exponent for both defects. Thus they are coherent formal modules on \(V(K^c)\). The ideal \(K^c\) is nonzero, since it is the unit ideal at every generic point in \(U\).

Induction algebraizes these defects to \(C,D\). Full faithfulness algebraizes the quotient \(\widehat H\to\widehat D\) to \(H\to D\). It is onto: its coherent cokernel has zero completion, and (BC.6) detects a zero object by its identity map. For \(Q=\ker(H\to D)\), exact completion identifies \(\widehat Q\) with the image of \(\alpha\). The remaining sequence is

\[
0\longrightarrow\widehat C\longrightarrow\mathfrak F
\longrightarrow\widehat Q\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BC.14}
\]

By (BC.8) it is the completion of a coherent extension on \(X\). Its middle term algebraizes \(\mathfrak F\), contradicting the counterexample. We have proved coherent existence for every proper \(X/A\), with no dimension bound or assumption that \(X\) is reduced. Together with (BC.6) it is an equivalence of the coherent and formal coherent categories. This verifies the proper part of [Grothendieck's existence theorem, Theorem 6.1](course:AG-QC/grothendiecks-existence-theorem#6-proper-schemes-and-proper-supports); the more general proper-support statement on a nonproper scheme is not needed in this argument.

### BC.4. Compatible finite covers on nilpotent thickenings

Let \(R\to R/J\) have nilpotent kernel. Every finite étale \(R/J\)-algebra \(C\) lifts to a finite étale \(R\)-algebra. BA.1 gives an étale lift \(D\) with \(D/JD=C\). Choose finitely many lifts of an \(R/J\)-module-generating list of \(C\), and let \(N\) be their \(R\)-span in \(D\). Then \(D=N+JD\), so \(D/N=J(D/N)\). Iterating through a power with \(J^a=0\) gives \(D/N=0\). Thus \(D\) is finite; this reasoning does not assume in advance that its underlying module is finite.

Maps between two lifts are unique lifts of their quotient maps, by formal étaleness across the nilpotent ideal in the target algebra (BA.1). The same holds for isomorphisms, since lifting both inverses makes their composites identities by uniqueness. On an arbitrary scheme with a nilpotent ideal, construct these finite covers over affine opens. On intersections, their isomorphisms lift locally by the affine assertion, agree by uniqueness and glue. The lifted isomorphisms satisfy the cocycle identities for the same reason. Gluing the affine covers therefore proves an equivalence of finite étale categories across the thickening.

Starting with \(T_1\to X_1\) finite étale, this supplies compatible finite étale covers \(T_n\to X_n\). Their coherent finite locally free algebras \(B_n\) have specified quotient identifications

\[
B_{n+1}/I^nB_{n+1}=B_n.
\tag{BC.15}
\]

Every later transition and compatibility identity is obtained from these by composition, and uniqueness makes all the prescribed identifications agree.

### BC.5. Recovering the algebra and proving it is étale

By BC.3 algebraize the coherent system \((B_n)\) to a coherent \(\mathcal O_X\)-module \(B\). Its unit and multiplication algebraize by (BC.6): completion of \(B\otimes B\) is the system \(B_n\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X_n}}B_n\), as is checked by taking quotients of tensor products on affines. Faithfulness applied to the two sides of each identity proves associativity, commutativity and the unit identities. Thus \(B\) is a coherent algebra, and

\[
T=\operatorname{Spec}_X B\longrightarrow X
\tag{BC.16}
\]

is finite, with the specified reductions \(T_n\). The relative spectrum glues the ordinary affine spectra using the algebra restrictions, so its finite property is precisely the finite-module assertion.

We check local freeness at every \(x\in X_1\), rather than infer flatness from the first closed fibre. Put \(R=\mathcal O_{X,x}\), \(M=B_x\). Each \(M/I^nM\) is finite projective over the local ring \(R/I^nR\), hence free by AD.1. Lift a basis at \(n=1\) to \(M\). It generates \(M\) by Nakayama, giving \(R^r\twoheadrightarrow M\). At every level the induced surjection between free modules of the same rank is an isomorphism: its determinant is a unit modulo the maximal ideal. Therefore its kernel lies in \(I^nR^r\) for every \(n\); it is zero by the separation theorem of L.1, since \(IR\) lies in the maximal ideal. We have proved that \(M\) is free.

Furthermore \(\Omega_{B_x/R}\) is finite and its reduction modulo \(I\) is zero, because \(B_1\) is étale. As a finite \(R\)-module it is zero by Nakayama. Finite presentation, flatness and this vanishing give étaleness by the criterion in AW.1. These properties hold in a neighbourhood: a basis and its inverse maps spread from the local ring because all the modules are finitely presented, and the support of the finite differential module is closed. Thus the non-étale locus of \(T\to X\) is a closed subset disjoint from \(T_1\).

This locus is empty. The scheme \(T\) is proper over \(A\), so its closed locus has closed image in \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). Any nonempty closed subset of that spectrum contains a maximal ideal, and every maximal ideal contains \(I\): geometric series show \(I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(A)\). Such an image would meet \(V(I)\), contrary to the absence of points of the locus on \(T_1\). We conclude that (BC.16) is finite étale everywhere.

Finally \((A,I)\) is henselian. Given coprime monic factors modulo \(I\), the coefficient algebra and invertible differential (BB.2) lift those factors uniquely through each nilpotent quotient \(A/I^n\); taking the coefficientwise limit gives their factorization over the complete ring \(A\). Together with the Jacobson assertion this is exactly AX.1's definition. Full faithfulness of finite étale restriction is therefore AX.7. Combined with the existence just proved, it gives

\[
\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X)
\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X_1)
\quad\text{for proper }X/A,
\tag{BC.17}
\]

whenever \(A\) is Noetherian and \(I\)-adically complete. No approximation theorem has been used to obtain this case.

### BC.6. Finite torsors and the complete-local projective line

For a finite abelian group \(M\), (BC.17) also identifies \(M\)-torsors. Lift the finite étale cover underlying a torsor on \(X_1\), then lift its finitely many action maps by full faithfulness. The group identities lift by faithfulness. The torsor isomorphism \(M\times T\to T\times_XT\) is an isomorphism because its inverse on the closed fibre lifts and both composite identities lift. A cover obtained this way is surjective: its finite locally free rank is positive on \(X_1\), while any nonempty rank-zero clopen subset of proper \(X\) would have closed image meeting \(V(I)\). Thus it is a torsor in the étale topology, not just an algebra with an action.

The degree-one classification used here has a direct check. For an abelian sheaf, a class is the boundary of a quotient section after an embedding into an injective; its local lifts form a torsor. Conversely choose local sections of a torsor and subtract them on overlaps to obtain a 1-cocycle. Changes of sections give coboundaries, and refinement preserves the class in (AK.3). After embedding the coefficient sheaf into an injective, this cocycle becomes a coboundary on the same covering: its augmented free-sheaf Čech complex is exact, so injective Hom has no positive cohomology, by AK.2. The chosen local primitives have differences in the coefficient subsheaf and therefore glue to a section of the quotient. Its boundary recovers the cocycle, and its torsor of lifts recovers the original torsor. This proves that the two constructions invert one another. For constant finite \(M\), that locally constant torsor is represented by a finite étale scheme by the arbitrary-base descent argument in BA.3. Contracted products add the cocycles, so the equivalence respects the abelian group law. Hence

\[
H^1(X,\underline M)\xrightarrow{\sim}
H^1(X_1,\underline M)
\tag{BC.18}
\]

at the complete Noetherian scope of (BC.17).

In particular let \(A\) be complete Noetherian local, \(X=\mathbb P^1_A\), and \(X_1\) its closed fibre. Every scheme finite over \(X\) is proper over \(A\), so (BC.18) supplies exactly the degree-one lifting required in BB.5. That deduction gives \(H^1(X_1,J|_{X_1})=0\) for injective \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaves \(J\); (BB.12) gives all higher degrees. For an arbitrary \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaf \(F\), restrict an injective resolution to \(X_1\). It remains exact and now has acyclic terms. Degree-zero comparison (AX.14) identifies its two section complexes term by term. Their cohomology maps are the restriction maps, proving

\[
H^q(\mathbb P^1_A,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}
H^q(\mathbb P^1_{A/\mathfrak m},F|_{X_1})
\qquad(q\geq0).
\tag{BC.19}
\]

The prime \(\ell\) may equal the residue characteristic. Formula (BC.19) is the complete Noetherian local case. BD.1–BD.6 use finite-cover descent and pointed approximation on integer models to prove the same comparison over every henselian local ring. BE.1–BE.8 give the further field-extension and reduction arguments and prove general proper comparison. The categorical and complete-coefficient constructions are treated in BF–BX.

## Appendix BD. Finite coefficients and the henselian lifting reduction

The passage from BC's complete bases to arbitrary henselian local bases has two distinct parts. Finite covers and their identifications must descend through limits; a finite polynomial system solved in a completion must then acquire a solution on a pointed étale neighbourhood. We prove the descent statements, obtain pointed approximation from the earlier desingularization and regular-completion proofs, and deduce finite-cover and torsor lifting over every henselian local base. The last step gives projective-line cohomology comparison.

### BD.1. Finite étale algebras as finite systems of equations

Let \(R\) be any ring. A finite étale \(R\)-algebra \(B\) is a finite projective \(R\)-module. Here is the finite-presentation detail in this assertion. Choose finitely many algebra generators and a monic equation for each, using finiteness and the determinant argument. The algebra obtained by imposing just these monic equations is finite free over \(R\) and maps onto \(B\). Since \(B\) is finitely presented as an algebra, the kernel of that map is finitely generated as an ideal: adjoining its finite presentation and eliminating the chosen generators proves this by finitely many substitution equations. Multiplying those ideal generators by a finite module-generating list of the monic algebra gives a finite module presentation of \(B\). Flatness and AD.1 now make it projective.

Choose an idempotent matrix \(E\in M_r(R)\) identifying \(B\) with \(\operatorname{im}E\subset R^r\). Multiplication is a matrix \(m:R^{r^2}\to R^r\) with

\[
E^2=E,\qquad Em=m,\qquad m(E\otimes E)=m.
\tag{BD.1}
\]

The unit is a vector \(u\) with \(Eu=u\). Associativity, commutativity and the two unit identities are equalities of maps on finite free modules, hence finitely many polynomial equations in the entries of \(E,m,u\).

Étaleness also has a finite certificate. Write \(J=\ker(\mu:B\otimes_R B\to B)\). The ideal \(J\) is generated by the finitely many differences \(b_i\otimes1-1\otimes b_i\) for algebra generators \(b_i\). The universal derivation identifies \(J/J^2\) with \(\Omega_{B/R}\): send \(db\) to the class of \(1\otimes b-b\otimes1\), and use the product rule to construct the inverse. If \(B\) is étale, this quotient is zero. Choose ideal generators \(v_i\) of \(J=J^2\), and write \(v_i=\sum a_{ij}v_j\) with \(a_{ij}\in J\). The adjugate identity shows that \(e=\det(1-(a_{ij}))\) annihilates \(J\), and \(e\equiv1\pmod J\). Consequently

\[
\mu(e)=1,\qquad
(b\otimes1-1\otimes b)e=0\quad(b\in B),\qquad e^2=e.
\tag{BD.2}
\]

Conversely, suppose a commutative algebra on a finite projective module has an element satisfying the first two identities of (BD.2). The differences generate \(J\), so \(Je=0\); also \(1-e\in J\). Hence \(J=(1-e)(B\otimes_R B)=J^2\), proving \(\Omega_{B/R}=0\). The algebra is finitely presented: if \(b_i=Ee_i\) are its module generators, use their finitely many module relations, their multiplication table, and the equation expressing the unit. These present the algebra, since every polynomial reduces to a linear combination of the \(b_i\), with exactly their module relations. Flatness and the finite-presentation criterion of AW.1 now give étaleness. It is therefore enough to record the coordinates of \(e\) in \(\operatorname{im}(E\otimes E)\) and check (BD.2) on the finitely many \(b_i\).

Let \(R=\varinjlim_i R_i\) be a filtered colimit of arbitrary rings. Represent all the coordinates in (BD.1)–(BD.2) at one stage. The finite list of equations becomes true at some later stage, where it defines a finite étale algebra whose base change is the given \(B\). There is no Noetherian hypothesis in this construction.

Maps and their equalities descend as well. A linear map between two image modules is a rectangular matrix \(P\) with \(FP=P=PE\), for their two projectors. Preserving the unit and multiplication is again a finite list of equations. Equality is equality of the finitely many matrix entries. Inverse maps, group actions by a fixed finite group, and prescribed commuting finite diagrams descend by including their maps and equations. We have proved

\[
\mathop{\operatorname{colim}}_i\operatorname{F\acute Et}(R_i)
\simeq\operatorname{F\acute Et}(R),
\tag{BD.3}
\]

where the category on the left identifies two arrows precisely when they agree at a later stage. This statement includes the specified isomorphism with the limiting algebra, not merely the existence of an algebra of the same rank.

### BD.2. Gluing along an inverse system of schemes

Let \((X_i)\) be a directed inverse system of qcqs schemes with affine transition maps, and let \(X=\varprojlim X_i\), constructed in AV.1. Fix one index and a finite affine cover of its scheme. Its inverse images at every later stage and at the limit remain affine. Apply (BD.3) on those limit affines.

The overlap data can be retained at one common stage. Each pairwise overlap at the fixed starting stage is quasi-compact, so choose a finite affine cover of it. A gluing isomorphism on the limit descends on these affines by the arrow assertion of BD.1. Cover their pairwise overlaps by finitely many affines as well; quasi-separatedness supplies the required quasi-compactness. Equality of the two restricted maps then holds at a sufficiently late stage. The same construction on finite affine covers of the triple overlaps makes the cocycle equations true. There are only finitely many charts and equations under consideration, so filteredness gives a single stage for all of them.

The resulting finite locally free algebras glue as sheaves of algebras. Their relative spectra give a finite étale scheme on that stage. Applying the identical finite-cover argument to arrows and their equality proves

\[
\mathop{\operatorname{colim}}_i\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X_i)
\simeq\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X).
\tag{BD.4}
\]

In particular the diagrams need not be cartesian over their bases. This is the special case of the relative-object argument in [Limits of schemes and Noetherian approximation, §§3–4](course:AG-MO/limits-and-noetherian-approximation) that the cover proof needs, now with explicit algebra certificates for the finite étale property.

If surjectivity is required, it also descends. On an affine chart the rank of \(\operatorname{im}E\) is positive at every prime exactly when the matrix entries of \(E\) generate the unit ideal. Over a residue field an idempotent has zero image exactly when all its entries vanish. The absence of such a prime is equivalent to a finite equation expressing one in that ideal. Descend that equation on each chart. A finite-group torsor is a surjective finite étale map with an action for which \(M\times T\to T\times_XT\) is an isomorphism. Descend the action, the inverse to this map, and the finitely many identities. Thus (BD.4) also descends finite-group torsors with their action and identifying isomorphisms.

### BD.3. Pointed approximation for integer models

Let \((R,\mathfrak m,k)\) be local and essentially of finite type over \(\mathbf Z\). Then the following pointed approximation theorem holds:

> **Pointed approximation.** For every finitely presented \(R\)-algebra \(S\) and map \(a:S\to\widehat R\), there are a finitely presented étale \(R\)-algebra \(R'\), a residue map \(r:R'\to k\), and \(b:S\to R'\) such that

\[
r\circ b=(\widehat R\to k)\circ a.
\tag{BD.5}
\]

Only equality on the closed fibre is required. The map \(R'\to\widehat R\) associated to \(r\), when used, is the unique compatible lift through \(R/\mathfrak m^n\), obtained from formal étaleness. It is not asserted to be an embedding of \(R'\).

**Proof.** Such an \(R\) is Noetherian, since the integers are Noetherian and adjoining finitely many variables, taking a quotient and localizing preserve that property. Its completion is Noetherian as well, by [Completion, Theorem 3.3](course:AG-CA/completion#3-noetherian-exactness-tensoring-and-flatness). Two algebraic results now apply with their Noetherian hypotheses intact. [Artin approximation for polynomial equations, Proposition F.135](course:AG-RG/AG-RG-S05#more-algebra-proposition-ubiquity-G-ring) proves that \(R\) is a G-ring; thus \(R\to\widehat R\) is flat with geometrically regular fibres. [Theorem D.38 of that lesson](course:AG-RG/AG-RG-S05#smoothing-theorem-popescu) expresses this regular map as a filtered colimit of smooth finitely presented \(R\)-algebras.

Here the regular-completion theorem includes imperfect residue fields: F.132–F.135 use coefficient rings, the derivation argument F.110 in positive characteristic, and the faithful flatness of completed local maps F.99A. The smooth-factorization proof uses D.19–D.22 for lifting, D.26 for reduction to a field, and D.33 and D.37 for the two characteristic cases. Its local target remains Noetherian throughout; in the dimension-zero case of D.30 it is therefore Artinian, and all ideals whose generators are cleared are finite. This is the Noetherian version needed here.

For orthogonal idempotents \(e_i\) lifting a product decomposition modulo a nil ideal, put \(E=\sum_i e_i\). Then \(E^2=E\) and \(1-E\) is nilpotent; hence \(E\) is a unit and \(E=1\). Equivalently, the nilpotent idempotent is \(1-E\). This gives the product decomposition used in F.73. In the local flatness calculation F.13, put \(T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)\) and write \(S'=U^{-1}(S\otimes_R R')\). The surjection after localization has source \(U^{-1}(T\otimes_R R')\). Exact localization preserves the kernel calculation establishing that surjection. The assumed zero map from \(T\) extends to the zero map from this localized source, so the target Tor group vanishes. With the stated finite \(S'\)-module and Noetherian local hypotheses, the proper-ideal flatness criterion applies. These observations supply the product and localization steps used below.

Choose a finite presentation of \(S\). The images of its finitely many generators under \(a\) belong to one smooth algebra in the filtered system. Each of its finitely many defining relations becomes zero at some later stage; a common later stage handles all of them. We therefore obtain a factorization of the original map

\[
S\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow\widehat R,
\qquad B/R\text{ smooth and finitely presented}.
\tag{BD.6}
\]

Compose the second map with \(\widehat R\to k\). At the resulting point, the split-conormal construction in [Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Theorem 5.1 and Solution 8.5](course:AG-CA/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps#5-from-a-split-sequence-to-local-coordinates) gives a chart with equations \(h_1,\ldots,h_c\) in variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), and an invertible Jacobian minor in the first \(c\) variables. Include any localization variable and its equation in this chart. For \(j>c\), lift the residue value of \(x_j\) to an element \(t_j\in R\). Substitute those \(t_j\) into the equations, retain the first \(c\) variables, and invert the resulting determinant and chart denominators. Call the resulting algebra \(R'\).

There are now \(c\) equations in \(c\) variables. Across a square-zero ideal, lift a proposed solution arbitrarily, evaluate the equation error, and subtract the inverse Jacobian times that error. Taylor expansion has no higher terms in the square-zero ideal, so this produces a solution. The same invertible matrix makes two lifts equal. Thus \(R'\) is formally étale; its finite presentation makes it étale. The original residue coordinates define \(r:R'\to k\), since every inverted element has nonzero residue. Substitution gives \(B\to R'\), and its composite with \(S\to B\) is the required \(b\). It has exactly the residue map in (BD.5). The map \(r\) is surjective because its restriction to \(R\) already surjects onto \(k\); its kernel is the selected maximal ideal with residue field \(k\). This proves pointed approximation.

In particular the theorem requires neither regularity of the local ring \(R\) itself nor a perfect residue field. The smooth intermediate algebra is supplied by regularity of the map to its completion. The argument just given uses only the residue-order conclusion needed for the finite-cover construction.

### BD.4. Descending a cover from a completion

Let \(R\) be local and essentially of finite type over \(\mathbf Z\), and let \(Y/R\) be proper. A finite étale cover \(T_0\to Y_k\) lifts to \(Y_{R'}\) for some pointed étale neighbourhood \((R',r)\) of \(R\), with the prescribed cover on its selected closed fibre.

Indeed BC.1–BC.5 lift it to a finite étale cover \(\widehat T\to Y_{\widehat R}\), since \(\widehat R\) is complete Noetherian. Write \(\widehat R\) as the filtered union of its finitely generated \(R\)-subalgebras \(S_i\). The ring \(R\) embeds in its completion by L.1's separation theorem, so these are subalgebras over that fixed copy of \(R\). They are finitely presented because \(R\) is Noetherian. The system \(Y_{S_i}\) has affine transitions and qcqs terms. By (BD.4), for some \(i\) there are a finite étale cover \(T_i\to Y_{S_i}\) and a specified isomorphism

\[
T_i\times_{S_i}\widehat R\simeq\widehat T.
\tag{BD.7}
\]

Apply (BD.5) to \(S_i\to\widehat R\). Pulling \(T_i\) back along \(S_i\to R'\) gives the desired cover. Its selected closed fibre is \(T_0\): both maps \(S_i\to k\) are exactly equal by (BD.5), so the identifying isomorphism is the reduction of (BD.7), followed by the specified identification for \(\widehat T\). Merely choosing a nearby coefficient tuple without its equations would not give this conclusion.

### BD.5. Reduction over an arbitrary henselian local base

Restriction is an equivalence

\[
\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{F\acute Et}(X_k)
\tag{BD.8}
\]

for every proper scheme \(X\) over an arbitrary henselian local ring \((A,\mathfrak m,k)\). The base is not assumed Noetherian and the proper morphism is not assumed finitely presented.

Let \(T_0\to X_k\) be finite étale. First use the proper finitely presented thickenings of (AV.8):

\[
X=\varprojlim_\alpha X_\alpha,
\qquad X_\alpha/A\text{ proper and finitely presented}.
\tag{BD.9}
\]

Their closed fibres have limit \(X_k\), since the affine-chart ring colimits commute with quotienting by \(\mathfrak m\). By (BD.4) the cover, with its identifying isomorphism, descends to a finite étale cover on \((X_\alpha)_k\) for some \(\alpha\). No assumption that the original \(X/A\) is finitely presented has been made.

By AV.4 choose a proper model \(Z_i/A_i\) of this \(X_\alpha\), where \(A_i\subset A\) is a finitely generated integer subalgebra. Enlarge \(A_i\) within the directed collection of all such subalgebras, and put

\[
\mathfrak m_i=A_i\cap\mathfrak m,\qquad
R_i=(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_i},\qquad
k_i=\operatorname{Frac}(A_i/\mathfrak m_i).
\tag{BD.10}
\]

These local rings map locally to \(A\), and their residue fields embed in \(k\). They have colimits \(A\) and \(k\), respectively. For the first assertion, any element of \(A\) belongs to a finite subalgebra, and every denominator outside \(\mathfrak m_i\) is already a unit of \(A\). For the second, every residue has a representative in \(A\), and inverses of nonzero residues are present in the indicated fraction fields. These descriptions also show injectivity of the maps into \(A\) and \(k\), so no additional equalities are lost.

Apply (BD.4) to \(Z_i\) after extension to these residue fields. At a sufficiently late index \(j\), the cover on \((X_\alpha)_k\) descends to a finite étale cover of \((Z_j)_{k_j}\), with its given base-change isomorphism. Put \(Y_j=Z_j\times_{A_j}R_j\). It is proper over the Noetherian local ring \(R_j\). By BD.3–BD.4, the descended closed-fibre cover lifts to \((Y_j)_{R'_j}\) for a pointed étale \(R_j\)-algebra \(R'_j\).

The étale \(A\)-algebra \(R'_j\otimes_{R_j}A\) has the selected \(k\)-point obtained from \(R'_j\to k_j\to k\). Henselianity supplies an \(A\)-section with that point. Explicitly the standard monic étale neighbourhood of AW.2 reduces this to a chosen simple root; the henselian root property lifts it, and all chart denominators remain units. Equivalently it is AX.14 applied to the represented étale sheaf on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). We obtain \(R'_j\to A\) compatible with the selected residue maps. Pull back the lifted cover first to \(X_\alpha=Z_j\times_{A_j}A\), then along the closed map \(X\to X_\alpha\). It is finite étale and its closed fibre is the original \(T_0\), by the retained identifications at every step. This proves essential surjectivity. Full faithfulness is the already proved AX.7, giving (BD.8).

The construction applies the theorem BD.3 to \(R_j\) before henselization. The resulting pointed étale neighbourhood acquires its section only after base change to \(A\). Thus (BD.8) holds for every henselian local base, while the approximation theorem was needed only on Noetherian local integer models.

### BD.6. Torsors and projective-line comparison over a henselian local ring

Let \(X\) be proper over any henselian local ring \(A\), with closed fibre \(X_0\), and let \(M\) be a finite abelian group. The equivalence (BD.8) lifts the finite étale scheme representing an \(M\)-torsor on \(X_0\). Full faithfulness lifts its action maps and the inverse of its torsor map; faithfulness lifts all their identities. Surjectivity also holds. The locus on \(X\) where the rank of the lifted finite locally free algebra is zero is clopen. If nonempty, this closed subset of proper \(X\) would have nonempty closed image in the local spectrum \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). That image contains its closed point, contradicting the positive rank on \(X_0\). The lifted cover is therefore an \(M\)-torsor. The same full faithfulness identifies its isomorphisms with those on the closed fibre. The cocycle and injective-resolution constructions in BC.6 identify these torsors with degree-one cohomology and respect contracted products. Consequently

\[
H^1(X,\underline M)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^1(X_0,\underline M).
\tag{BD.11}
\]

We now prove the projective-line comparison for every \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaf \(F\):

\[
H^q(\mathbb P^1_A,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}
H^q(\mathbb P^1_k,F|_{\mathbb P^1_k})
\quad(q\geq0),\qquad k=A/\mathfrak m.
\tag{BD.12}
\]

First let \(J\) be injective in the category of \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-sheaves on \(X=\mathbb P^1_A\). Given a class in \(H^1(X_0,J|_{X_0})\), compactness and continuity (AZ.2 and BA.8) represent it by a class with constructible coefficients \(C|_{X_0}\) and a map \(C\to J\). Embed \(C\) in the finite direct sum \(D=\bigoplus_a(p_a)_*\underline{M_a}\) supplied by AZ.6, where \(p_a:T_a\to X\) are finite and each \(M_a\) is a finite \(\mathbb F_\ell\)-vector space. Injectivity extends \(C\to J\) to \(D\to J\). Each \(T_a\) is proper over \(A\), so (BD.11), together with the finite-map cohomology and base-change identification AX.5, lifts the image of the class in \(H^1(X_0,D|_{X_0})\) to \(H^1(X,D)\). Its image in \(H^1(X,J)\) is zero. Restriction then kills the original class, proving \(H^1(X_0,J|_{X_0})=0\). The module-to-abelian cohomology comparison used here is BB.3.

For \(q\ge2\), the two standard affine charts of \(\mathbb P^1_A\) and the restricted-injective bound (BB.12) give \(H^q(X_0,J|_{X_0})=0\). Restrict an injective resolution of \(F\) to \(X_0\). Exact inverse image leaves it exact, and the vanishing just proved makes its terms acyclic for sections on \(X_0\). The proper henselian degree-zero comparison (AX.14) identifies the two section complexes term by term. Their cohomology comparison is exactly restriction, proving (BD.12). There is no restriction on the residue characteristic relative to \(\ell\).

## Appendix BE. From the projective line to proper base change

The henselian comparison (BD.12) concerns the closed fibre over a local ring. A geometric stalk also involves extending that fibre's field. We first prove the required field comparison, including coefficients in the residue characteristic, and then pass from projective lines to arbitrary proper morphisms. All inverse images below are the exact inverse images of étale sheaves.

### BE.1. Coherent coefficients on the étale site

For an affine scheme \(T=\operatorname{Spec}A\) and an \(A\)-module \(M\), the quasi-coherent étale sheaf has value \(M\otimes_A B\) on an affine étale object \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). We verify that

\[
H^q(T_{\rm ét},\widetilde M)=0\quad(q>0).
\tag{BE.1}
\]

Every étale covering of an affine scheme refines to finitely many affine étale maps: their images are open, by AW.1, and quasi-compactness selects finitely many. Their disjoint union is \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) for a faithfully flat \(A\)-algebra \(B\). Flatness is local on those finitely many pieces; faithfulness follows because a nonzero module has a nonzero localization at some prime and the covering has a point above that prime. Equivalently, tensoring and then taking such a faithfully flat local factor detects a nonzero element, by the flat local criterion proved in U.1 and AE.1.

The augmented section complex of this cover is the Amitsur complex

\[
0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M\otimes_A B
 \longrightarrow M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B\longrightarrow\cdots,
\tag{BE.2}
\]

whose differential inserts a unit with alternating signs. After tensoring once more with \(B\), multiplication of the extra first factor with the first original \(B\)-factor is a contraction. The term inserting a unit in that first position gives the identity; the other insertion terms cancel in adjacent pairs. This also checks the augmented degree. Faithful flatness detects kernels modulo images, so (BE.2) is exact before tensoring. In degree zero it proves the sheaf gluing assertion for these affine covers.

Here is the passage from this covering calculation to derived cohomology. A positive-degree class is locally zero: in an injective resolution a cycle locally lifts through the preceding differential, because the resolution is exact as a sheaf complex. Induct on its degree \(q\), simultaneously over all affine schemes and modules. Choose a finite affine étale covering killing the class. All its iterated fibre products are affine. In the covering double complex of an injective resolution, taking cohomology in the resolution direction gives the groups on those fibre products; taking it in the covering direction gives the original section complex, since injectives are Čech-acyclic. This is the construction in S.3 and [Cohomology on sites, Sections 2–4](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-on-sites#2-sections-slices-and-local-vanishing). The rows with \(0<r<q\) vanish by induction, and the positive-degree part of row zero vanishes by (BE.2). In total degree \(q\) the edge map into the matching families in degree \(q\) is therefore injective. The chosen class maps to zero there and is zero. This proves (BE.1).

For a separated quasi-compact scheme, take a finite affine open cover. Its intersections are affine, so (BE.1) computes étale cohomology of a quasi-coherent sheaf by the same affine section complex that computes Zariski cohomology in W.2. The comparison is induced by restriction of sections, and hence is natural. Tensoring this complex by a field extension is exact. Thus the coherent base-change maps in (AU.1) also compute the étale groups, with their actual pullback maps. Cohomology here means abelian-sheaf cohomology; BB.3 justifies its agreement with computation in module sheaves.

### BE.2. Frobenius fixed vectors and the proper curve calculation

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed of characteristic \(p>0\), and let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(k\)-space with an additive map \(F\) satisfying \(F(av)=a^pF(v)\). Then \(F-1\) is surjective, has finite kernel, and the canonical map

\[
\ker(F-1:V\to V)\longrightarrow
\ker(F-1:V\otimes_k k'\to V\otimes_k k')
\tag{BE.3}
\]

is bijective for every algebraically closed extension \(k'/k\). On the tensor product, \(F(v\otimes a)=F(v)\otimes a^p\).

To prove this, use perfection of \(k\) to regard every image \(F^nV\) as a vector subspace. Their dimensions stabilize. For a sufficiently large \(n\), put \(W=F^nV\); then \(F\) is bijective on \(W\) and nilpotent on \(V/W\). On the latter quotient, \(F-1\) has inverse \(-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}F^i\). On \(W\), choose coordinates so that \(F(x)=A x^{[p]}\), with \(A\) invertible. The equation \(F(x)-x=y\) is

\[
x_i^p-\sum_j(A^{-1})_{ij}x_j=(A^{-1}y)_i.
\tag{BE.4}
\]

Its coordinate algebra has basis the monomials \(x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_r^{e_r}\), \(0\leq e_i<p\), where \(r=\dim W\). One can check independence as well as spanning by polynomial reduction. Replace every factor \(x_i^p\) by the linear expression plus constant in (BE.4). Each replacement lowers total degree. Two possible replacements in one monomial either use the same variable and give the same expression, or use different variables; in the latter case, performing both gives the same product of the two replacement expressions. Any further choices involve smaller degrees. Induction on degree therefore proves uniqueness of the reduced linear combination. Reduction kills every monomial multiple of a defining relation, and fixes the displayed monomials. Thus it descends to an inverse for their spanning map into the quotient algebra, proving the basis assertion.

The Jacobian matrix of (BE.4) is \(-A^{-1}\). The square-zero correction of AB.1 makes this finite algebra étale. Its dimension is \(p^r>0\), so over algebraically closed \(k\) it is a product of \(p^r\) copies of \(k\), by AB.1. Every \(y\) therefore has a preimage. The zero fibre is a finite étale scheme and acquires no additional points over \(k'\). Matrix ranks show that the stabilized image after field extension is \(W\otimes_k k'\), and the quotient remains nilpotent. Every fixed vector belongs to that stabilized image. Surjectivity on the quotient followed by surjectivity on \(W\) proves surjectivity on \(V\); the zero-fibre calculation proves (BE.3).

On any scheme in characteristic \(p\), there is an exact sequence of étale abelian sheaves

\[
0\longrightarrow\underline{\mathbf F_p}\longrightarrow\mathcal O
 \xrightarrow{\ F-1\ }\mathcal O\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BE.5}
\]

For its kernel, the factors of \(T^p-T=\prod_{a\in\mathbf F_p}(T-a)\) are pairwise comaximal. A root partitions the scheme into open-and-closed pieces on which it equals the respective \(a\); this is exactly a locally constant \(\mathbf F_p\)-section. For surjectivity, a section \(b\) acquires a preimage on the algebra \(A[T]/(T^p-T-b)\). Monic division makes it free of rank \(p\); its derivative is \(-1\), so it is étale and its nonzero geometric fibres make it a covering. This proves exactness without a reducedness assumption.

Let \(C/k\) be a smooth connected proper curve. We first construct a finite surjection \(f:C\to\mathbf P^1_k\). By Y.6 its local rings are regular domains; its finitely many irreducible components are therefore disjoint, so connectedness makes \(C\) integral. Its closed-point local rings are DVRs by Y.6 and L.1. Noether normalization on a nonempty affine chart, as in AC.1, gives a transcendental \(t\in k(C)\) with \(k(C)/k(t)\) finite. At each closed point either \(t\) or \(t^{-1}\) lies in the DVR, and hence is regular on a neighbourhood. These local maps to the two standard charts of \(\mathbf P^1_k\) agree on overlaps: their rational coordinate is the same \(t\), and equality of regular functions is detected in the function field of the integral scheme. Together with the generic point they define \(f\).

The graph argument of AU.1 makes \(f\) proper. It is dominant, so its closed image is all of \(\mathbf P^1_k\). Each closed fibre is a proper closed subset of a Noetherian integral curve, hence consists of finitely many zero-dimensional points. Closed points of \(C\) map to closed points, while the generic fibre is \(\operatorname{Spec}k(C)\) over \(k(t)\), a finite field extension. Thus every fibre is zero-dimensional and finite, so \(f\) is quasi-finite. AW.5 makes it finite. In particular

\[
U_0=f^{-1}(\mathbf P^1_k\setminus\{\infty\}),\qquad
U_1=f^{-1}(\mathbf P^1_k\setminus\{0\})
\]

are affine opens covering \(C\), and their intersection is the affine inverse image of \(\mathbf G_{m,k}\).

This also proves that \(C\) is projective. Put \(L=f^*\mathcal O(1)\), and let \(s_i\) be the pulled-back coordinate section with \(C_{s_i}=U_i\). For a principal open \(D(b)\subset U_i\), [Coherent sheaves on projective schemes, Lemma 1.1](course:AG-QC/serres-theorems-on-projective-schemes#1-clearing-denominators-in-a-line-bundle) gives \(a\geq0\) and \(u\in H^0(C,L^a)\) with \(u/s_i^a=b\) on \(U_i\). The section \(us_i\) of \(L^{a+1}\) has nonvanishing open exactly \(D(b)\): outside \(U_i\) its factor \(s_i\) vanishes, and inside it is invertible precisely when \(b\) is. These affine opens form a basis, proving ampleness of \(L\). Lemma 1.3 of the same programme lesson now gives a closed projective embedding. Surjectivity of \(f\) supplies closed \(k\)-points over every point of \(\mathbf P^1(k)\), in particular distinct points over \(0\) and \(\infty\); X.4 also makes the complements of either of these points affine.

The ordered affine section complex for \(U_0,U_1\) has length one. Consequently BE.1 gives \(H^q(C_{\rm ét},\mathcal O_C)=0\) for \(q>1\). The two remaining groups are finite-dimensional by AU.3. Also \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k\): this finite-dimensional algebra embeds in the function field of the integral curve, so is a finite field extension of the algebraically closed field.

Apply (BE.5), BE.1 and the semilinear calculation to this two-term cohomology. They give the canonical identifications

\[
\begin{aligned}
H^0(C,\mathbf F_p)&=\mathbf F_p,\\
H^1(C,\mathbf F_p)&=\ker(F-1:H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\to H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)),\\
H^q(C,\mathbf F_p)&=0\qquad(q\geq2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BE.6}
\]

The same affine cover after scalar extension computes the coherent groups by tensoring, and Frobenius tensors with the stated semilinear rule. Thus (BE.3) proves field-extension invariance of all the groups in (BE.6). Connectedness persists: (AU.1) identifies the new global function algebra with \(k'\), excluding a nontrivial component idempotent. The argument applies to each component of a smooth proper curve. It uses no proper base-change theorem for étale cohomology.

### BE.3. Arbitrary torsion coefficients on a smooth proper curve

For an extension of algebraically closed fields \(k'/k\), a smooth proper curve \(C/k\), and any torsion abelian sheaf \(F\), pullback induces

\[
H^q(C,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(C_{k'},F|_{C_{k'}}),\qquad q\geq0.
\tag{BE.7}
\]

First take a constructible \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaf. For constants, AL.3 proves the result when \(\ell\) is invertible in \(k\), and (BE.6) proves the remaining case. A sheaf supported on finitely many closed points has the same finite list of stalks after extension and has no positive cohomology, by AX.5 and AB.1. Hence, for a dense open \(j:U\hookrightarrow C\), the exact sequence
\(0\to j_!j^{-1}F\to F\to i_*i^{-1}F\to0\)
and its natural long exact sequence reduce comparison to \(j_!j^{-1}F\). The same argument proves comparison for the extension by zero of a constant sheaf on any dense open of a smooth proper curve.

Choose \(U\) where \(F\) is locally constant. On each connected component, the finite monodromy construction N.2–N.3 and the Sylow existence proof AA.3 give a finite étale cover \(V\to U\) of degree prime to \(\ell\) on which the pulled-back representation has a flag with constant \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-quotients. Here is the representation argument: an \(\ell\)-group acting on a nonzero finite \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-space has a number of fixed vectors divisible by \(\ell\), since every nontrivial orbit has size divisible by \(\ell\). Zero is fixed, so there is a nonzero fixed vector. Its line is invariant and trivial; repeat on the quotient.

Normalize \(C\) in each component field of \(V\). AG.1–AG.4 give a finite smooth proper curve \(h:D\to C\), with inverse image of \(U\) exactly \(V\). The inverse-image assertion follows from uniqueness of the integral closure, as in AK.5. Extend the flag by zero to \(D\). The constant case just proved, the flag's exact sequences, and the long exact cohomology sequences prove comparison on \(D\). Finite direct image is exact and satisfies arbitrary base change by AX.5, so
\(h_*j'_!G=j_!(V\to U)_*G\)
identifies this comparison with the corresponding one on \(C\). Both sides have that restriction over \(U\) and zero stalks outside it. The unit and the sum-over-sheets trace compose to multiplication by the degree. Its inverse in \(\mathbf F_\ell\) splits the unit, so comparison passes to \(j_!j^{-1}F\). These are compatible maps of the actual long exact sequences and retractions: no equality of dimensions is being substituted for the pullback map.

The finite normalization chosen over \(k\) remains smooth and proper after extension, and its inverse image of \(U_{k'}\) remains the chosen étale cover. Thus the same flag and trace work on both sides; a new normalization need not be chosen. Primary decomposition and the sequence with kernel \(F[\ell]\) and quotient killed by \(\ell^{a-1}\) prove the result for constructible sheaves killed by \(\ell^a\), then by any integer. On the Noetherian curve every sheaf with bounded torsion is a filtered colimit of constructible sheaves by the finite-section construction in AK.5 and AZ.2. BA.5 gives continuity of cohomology on these qcqs schemes. Finally a torsion sheaf is the filtered union of its \(F[n]\), ordered by divisibility. A germ has a finite order and a representative killed by that order after restriction, so this union is the whole sheaf. Another application of BA.5 proves (BE.7).

### BE.4. Separably closed fields and geometric fibres

We first prove topological invariance for an arbitrary integral, surjective, universally injective morphism \(p:T\to X\). These hypotheses are stable under every base change. Integrality makes the base-changed map closed, and the other two hypotheses make it bijective, so \(p\) is a universal homeomorphism. No finiteness, finite-presentation or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed. We will prove that the actual adjoint functors
\[
 p^{-1}:\operatorname{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})
 \ \rightleftarrows\
 \operatorname{Sh}(T_{\mathrm{\acute et}}):p_*
 \tag{BE.7a}
\]
are inverse equivalences, first for sheaves of sets and then for abelian sheaves and sheaves of modules over any fixed coefficient ring.

**The ring over a strict localization.** Choose an algebraically closed geometric point \(\bar x\) of \(X\), and put \(R=\mathcal O^{\rm sh}_{X,\bar x}\). The strict-local construction is recalled in AX.5; its full ring proof is [Henselian local rings and henselization, Theorem 5.1](course:AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization#5-strict-henselization-and-the-choice-of-an-embedding). Since \(p\) is affine, \(T_R=\operatorname{Spec}B\) for an integral \(R\)-algebra \(B\). Write \(B\) as the filtered union of the subalgebras \(C\) generated over the image of \(R\) by finitely many elements. Monic equations for those generators show that each \(C\) is a finite \(R\)-module. This construction does not assume that \(R\to B\) is injective.

Every intermediate \(\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) is again surjective and universally injective. Indeed \(C\subset B\) is integral, so its spectrum map is surjective by lying over and remains surjective after base change. For any base change of \(R\), two points of \(\operatorname{Spec}C\) over the same base point lift to points of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). Universal injectivity of the latter map makes the lifts, and hence their images, coincide. Surjectivity follows from the composite map. The closed fibre of \(C/R\) therefore has exactly one point.

The finite-algebra argument (AX.10) makes \(C\) a product of strictly henselian local rings; the singleton closed fibre leaves one factor. Its inputs are the idempotent and finite-algebra criteria proved in [Henselian local rings and henselization, Sections 2–3](course:AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization#2-factorization-and-the-finite-algebra-criterion). For \(C\subset D\), the maximal ideal of \(D\) contracts to that of \(C\), by integrality. These transition maps are local. Consequently \(B\) is local, its maximal ideal is the union of their maximal ideals, and its residue field is the union of their residue fields. A nonunit cannot become a unit at a later stage under a local map.

If a monic polynomial over \(B\) has a simple root in its residue field, its coefficients and a representative of that root occur at one stage \(C\). Contraction of the maximal ideal says that its value lies in the maximal ideal of \(C\), while its derivative is a unit there. The henselian property of \(C\) supplies the desired root in \(B\). A separable polynomial over the residue-field union has its coefficients at a stage; its discriminant is nonzero there because the residue-field transition maps are injective. It splits over that separably closed stage. Thus \(B\) is strictly henselian, including when \(B/R\) is not finite.

**The sheaf maps on stalks.** For a sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(T\), the degree-zero affine continuity argument of AX.5 gives
\[
 (p_*F)_{\bar x}
 =\varinjlim_{(U,\bar u)}\Gamma(T\times_XU,F|_{T\times_XU})
 \xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(T_R,F|_{T_R})
 \xrightarrow{\sim}F_{\bar t}.
 \tag{BE.7b}
\]
Here \(U\) runs through affine pointed étale neighbourhoods of \(\bar x\), and \(\bar t\) is its unique geometric lift to \(T\). The compatible sheaves in the middle system are the pullbacks of the single sheaf \(F\); no descent of \(F\) to a finite intermediate \(C\) is asserted. The schemes \(T\times_XU\) are affine. AX.5 applies to their affine limit because its section argument descends the finitely presented étale charts, finite covers and equality witnesses, without requiring their rings to be finite over the base. The final arrow is (AX.11): a germ on the strictly henselian local scheme extends along a section of its pointed étale neighbourhood, and the same argument detects equality. The purely inseparable algebraic residue extension has a unique compatible embedding in the chosen algebraically closed geometric field, which specifies \(\bar t\).

Under (BE.7b) and the inverse-image stalk formula, the unit \(G\to p_*p^{-1}G\) at \(\bar x\) is the identity of \(G_{\bar x}\). At every geometric point \(\bar t\) of \(T\), the counit \(p^{-1}p_*F\to F\) is the identity of \(F_{\bar t}\): (BE.7b) is restriction of a section to precisely that germ. Enough geometric points makes both maps isomorphisms, proving (BE.7a). Their constructions respect addition and scalar multiplication, proving the coefficient versions. Equivalences of abelian categories are exact and preserve injectives. The equality \(\Gamma_Xp_*=\Gamma_T\) therefore identifies the injective section complexes and gives the canonical cohomology comparison
\[
 H^q(X,G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(T,p^{-1}G)
 \qquad(q\geq0).
 \tag{BE.7c}
\]
The same argument applies after any change of base. The identities of units and counits just checked also show that these comparisons are compatible with composition and pullback. This proves the topological-invariance theorem used in [Finite morphisms, Section 6, Theorem 6.2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/pushforward-pullback-and-finite-morphisms#6-topological-invariance-including-nonfinite-morphisms) from the arbitrary-base continuity and finite-algebra arguments above; [Stacks, Section 59.45](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04DY) gives the free primary comparison.

Two cases will be used below. A closed immersion defined by a nil ideal satisfies the hypotheses: after base change every element of the extended ideal is a finite sum of multiples of nilpotents and is nilpotent, so the spectrum map is still bijective. This includes reduction by a nilradical with no uniform nilpotence exponent. If \(L/k\) is algebraic purely inseparable, AH.1 proves the hypotheses for \(X_L\to X\), and (BE.7a)–(BE.7c) give its étale and cohomological invariance. Thus (BE.7) passes to separably closed fields as follows.

For separably closed \(k\subset k'\), choose compatible algebraic closures \(\bar k\subset\bar k'\). Both vertical extensions are purely inseparable. Apply the equivalence just proved to the vertical arrows, and (BE.7) to \(\bar k\subset\bar k'\). Naturality of pullback proves (BE.7) for \(k\subset k'\) as well, for the given smooth proper curve and pulled-back sheaf.

Let \(f:\mathbb P^1_S\to S\), let \(F\) be an arbitrary \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaf, and choose a geometric point \(\bar s=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S\). Put \(R=\mathcal O^{\rm sh}_{S,\bar s}\), and write \(k\) for its separably closed residue field inside \(\Omega\). The arbitrary-base continuity BA.5, slice formula AB.3 and henselian theorem (BD.12) give

\[
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar s}
 =H^q(\mathbb P^1_R,F_R)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(\mathbb P^1_k,F_k)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(\mathbb P^1_\Omega,F_\Omega).
\tag{BE.8}
\]

The last arrow is (BE.7) in the separably closed case. All maps are restriction or pullback. For any \(g:S'\to S\), use the very same \(\Omega\) for a geometric point of \(S'\) and its composite point of \(S\). Both stalks of the base-change map identify by (BE.8) with cohomology of the same projective line and the same pulled-back sheaf. The map is the identity on those identifications. Thus projective-line projection satisfies base change for all \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaves, every \(\ell\), every base and every change of base.

### BE.5. An injective criterion and two descent steps

Fix a prime \(\ell\). Say that a proper morphism has property \(P_\ell\) when its higher direct images of all \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-sheaves commute with every base change. For a square with horizontal maps \(a:X'\to X\), \(b:Y'\to Y\) and vertical maps \(f',f\), this is equivalent to

\[
R^q f'_*a^{-1}I=0\quad(q>0)
\quad\text{for every injective }\mathbf F_\ell\text{-sheaf }I\text{ on }X.
\tag{BE.9}
\]

Indeed, necessity follows by applying base change to \(I\); BB.3 permits computation in \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-modules. Conversely resolve a sheaf by injective \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-modules. Its pullback remains an exact resolution. Condition (BE.9) makes the pulled-back terms acyclic for \(f'_*\). Proper degree-zero base change AY.6 identifies its pushed complex term by term with the pullback of the original pushed complex. The acyclic-resolution comparison, proved by successive cokernels and dimension shifting in T.4, gives precisely the higher base-change map. It is the map induced by the counit, since the degree-zero identifications are those counit maps and comparison of resolutions respects them. This proves the criterion.

Property \(P_\ell\) is local on the target for the étale topology, by the slice calculation AB.3 and enough geometric points. Finite morphisms have it by AX.5. It is also preserved by composition. To check the latter, let \(X\xrightarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{v}Z\) have both properties and take an injective \(I\) on \(X\). Exact inverse image makes \(u_*I\) injective on \(Y\). After any base change the complex \(Ru'_*a^{-1}I\) has only degree zero, equal to \(b^{-1}u_*I\), by the property for \(u\). Applying the property for \(v\) makes its positive higher image zero. Hence (BE.9) holds for \(vu\).

For completeness, the derived composition used in this step follows directly from resolutions. Direct image preserves injectives, being right adjoint to exact inverse image. Therefore a bounded-below injective resolution \(J^\bullet\) on the first source has injective terms after the first direct image, and applying the next direct image computes the derived composite. If the first pushed complex has cohomology only in degree zero, its augmentation from that degree-zero sheaf is a quasi-isomorphism and computes the second derived image. Resolution comparison gives the same map after replacement by an injective resolution of the degree-zero sheaf. Thus this deduction needs neither an unbounded totalization nor a separate convergence assumption.

There is a further descent step. Suppose \(u\) is proper and surjective, \(v\) is proper, and \(u\) and \(vu\) have \(P_\ell\). Then \(v\) has it. For an injective \(I\) on \(Y\), embed \(u^{-1}I\) in an injective \(J\) on \(X\). The adjoint map \(I\to u_*J\) is injective: after pullback, its composite with the counit is the chosen injection. Surjectivity of \(u\) makes its inverse image detect monomorphisms, since each geometric point downstairs has a geometric lift after choosing an algebraically closed field. The injection splits because \(I\) is injective. After base change, the property for \(u\) and the resolution calculation above identify

\[
R^q(v'u')_*a^{-1}J
 =R^qv'_*b^{-1}(u_*J).
\tag{BE.10}
\]

The left side vanishes for \(q>0\), by the property for \(vu\). Pullback retains the split inclusion of \(I\) in \(u_*J\), and additive derived direct image retains this retraction. Hence \(R^qv'_*b^{-1}I=0\). Criterion (BE.9) proves the asserted descent. This argument explains exactly where surjectivity is needed.

### BE.6. Projective space and proper modifications

There is a finite surjective morphism over every scheme \(S\),

\[
\rho:(\mathbb P^1_S)^n\longrightarrow\mathbb P^n_S,
\qquad
((a_i:b_i))_{i=1}^n\longmapsto
\left[\text{coefficients of }\prod_{i=1}^n(a_iT+b_iU)\right].
\tag{BE.11}
\]

The coefficients are sections of \(\mathcal O(1,\ldots,1)\). They have no common zero: in every geometric fibre a product of nonzero binary linear forms is nonzero. They therefore define a morphism on the opens where a coefficient generates that line bundle, and the coordinate ratios agree on overlaps. Every nonzero binary degree-\(n\) form over an algebraically closed field factors into linear forms. Such a factorization determines its unordered multiset of projective linear factors, so there are at most \(n!\) ordered points in each geometric fibre. Thus \(\rho\) is surjective with finite geometric fibres. It is proper by its closed graph and the properness of the product over \(S\). Its finite-type geometric fibres are zero-dimensional, hence have isolated points by the field-algebra argument in AW.1; thus it is quasi-finite. The proper quasi-finite consequence of AW.5 proves finiteness over an arbitrary base. Neither the construction nor the argument divides by \(n!\); repeated factors and characteristics dividing \(n!\) are allowed. For \(n=0\) use the identity of \(S\).

By BE.4 and composition, the projection \((\mathbb P^1_S)^n\to S\) has \(P_\ell\). The map \(\rho\) has it because it is finite. The proper-surjective descent step BE.5 now gives \(P_\ell\) for \(\mathbb P^n_S\to S\).

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be any proper morphism of schemes. Work over an affine open of \(Y\), permitted by locality. The arbitrary-base Chow construction AV.3 gives a proper surjection \(\pi:T\to X\) and an immersion \(h:T\to\mathbb P^n_Y\). The composite \(T\to Y\) is proper. The graph argument AU.1 therefore makes \(h\) proper, and a proper immersion is a closed immersion, with its local defining ideals glued as in AU.1. The map

\[
(\pi,h):T\longrightarrow X\times_Y\mathbb P^n_Y=\mathbb P^n_X
\tag{BE.12}
\]

is also a closed immersion: factor it through the closed graph of \(\pi\), using separatedness of \(X/Y\), and the base change of the closed immersion \(h\). Thus both \(\pi\) and \(f\pi\) factor as a closed immersion followed by a projective-space projection. Closed immersions are finite, so composition gives \(P_\ell\) for both maps. The surjectivity of \(\pi\) and BE.5 give \(P_\ell\) for \(f\). This uses the proper morphism itself, not an unproved finite-presentation assumption on it; AV.1–AV.3 supplied the necessary proper thickenings before the Chow reduction.

### BE.7. The torsion and bounded-below theorems

For every proper \(f:X\to Y\), every \(g:Y'\to Y\), and their Cartesian square with projections \(f',a\), the canonical map is an isomorphism

\[
g^{-1}R^qf_*F\xrightarrow{\sim}R^qf'_*a^{-1}F
\quad(q\geq0)
\tag{BE.13}
\]

for every torsion abelian sheaf \(F\). BE.6 proves this for all sheaves killed by a prime \(\ell\), without constructibility. If \(\ell^mF=0\), use the exact sequence with kernel \(F[\ell]\) and quotient \(F/F[\ell]\). The latter is killed by \(\ell^{m-1}\); induction and the natural long exact sequences prove the assertion. A sheaf killed by an integer is the finite direct sum of its primary parts, using the integer Chinese remainder idempotents acting on it. For an arbitrary torsion sheaf, use \(F=\varinjlim_n F[n]\).

Here the required continuity of higher direct images follows from the proved cohomology continuity BA.5: restrict the target to an affine open and use affine étale test objects in (AB.8). Their inverse images under a proper map are qcqs, so their cohomology commutes with the filtered coefficient colimit. Filtered colimits and exact sheafification preserve kernels and cokernels, giving the sheaf statement. Exact inverse image commutes with these colimits too. This proves (BE.13) at the stated arbitrary-base scope. It also shows that each \(R^qf_*F\) is torsion: for \(F[n]\) it is killed by \(n\), and the filtered colimit is torsion on every stalk.

More generally, if \(E\in D^+(X_{\rm ét},\mathbf Z)\) has torsion cohomology sheaves, then

\[
g^{-1}Rf_*E\xrightarrow{\sim}Rf'_*a^{-1}E.
\tag{BE.14}
\]

One can prove this without an infinite-filtration assertion. For a complex with cohomology in a finite interval, induction using the truncation triangle with successive quotient \(\mathcal H^r(E)[-r]\) reduces (BE.14) to (BE.13). Exact inverse images preserve these triangles; derived direct images preserve them by the mapping-cone construction on injective resolutions. In the general bounded-below case, fix a degree \(d\) and replace \(E\) by \(\tau_{\leq d}E\). The discarded complex belongs to \(D^{\geq d+1}\). A bounded-below injective resolution beginning in that degree shows that its derived direct image also belongs to \(D^{\geq d+1}\). This holds on both sides of the square, since inverse image is exact. The replacement therefore changes neither side's cohomology through degree \(d\). The finite-interval case proves the comparison there. As \(d\) was arbitrary, (BE.14) is a quasi-isomorphism. The map throughout is the derived adjoint of the pulled-back counit, so this verifies the canonical comparison.

### BE.8. Stalks, henselian fibres and the scope of the result

Take \(Y'=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\) at a geometric point \(\bar y\) in (BE.13). The étale topos of an algebraically closed field has exact global sections by AB.1–AB.2. Applying sections to the comparison gives

\[
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar y}\xrightarrow{\sim}H^q(X_{\bar y},F_{\bar y}).
\tag{BE.15}
\]

It is restriction from a neighbourhood representative to the geometric fibre. In particular, if the base is strictly henselian local, its sections functor is the closed stalk functor by (AX.11), and hence exact. Applying it to an injective resolution and to its pushed complex identifies global cohomology of the proper source with that of its closed fibre, for torsion coefficients. This includes all degrees and coefficients in the residue characteristic.

The arbitrary-base theorem (BE.13), its bounded-below form (BE.14), and the fibre formula (BE.15) supply the general proper-comparison input of Section 3.
