The proof has retained arbitrary torsion sheaves and arbitrary changes of base throughout. It does not construct the unbounded enhanced operations, normalized adic categories or their rationalization comparisons; those require their separate arguments.

## Appendix BF. Unbounded derived categories and sheaf representability

The adjoint construction in Proposition 3.3 takes place in an unbounded derived category. We construct that category and its sums before applying representability. Throughout, sets and smallness refer to one fixed universe, with the axiom of choice. A Grothendieck abelian category here is locally small, has small coproducts and exact filtered colimits, and has a generator. The assertions below apply to constant modules on a small étale site; no bound on the field's cohomological dimension is imposed.

### BF.1. The resolution input and comparison of maps

Let \(\mathcal B\) be a Grothendieck abelian category. For every complex \(M\), choose a monic quasi-isomorphism
\[
q_M:M\longrightarrow I_M
\tag{BF.1}
\]
with \(I_M\) K-injective. The existence used here is the construction for a general Grothendieck category in [Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Theorem 7.2 and Lemmas 7.2.1–7.2.5](course:derived-categories-and-sheaf-operations/sheaves-of-modules-and-their-derived-categories#7-k-injective-resolutions-of-unbounded-complexes). That construction precedes the derived category: it uses subobject sets, small acyclic complexes, monic pushouts and exact filtered unions. In particular its resolution assertion does not use the localization that we are about to define. We need its existence and K-injectivity assertions, rather than any assertion that its chosen resolution functor is additive.

Use the Hom complex and cone conventions of B.1. A complex \(J\) is K-injective precisely when \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,J)\) is acyclic for every acyclic \(A\): its degree-\(r\) cohomology consists of chain maps into a shift of \(J\), modulo homotopy, and shifts of acyclic complexes are acyclic. If \(s:M\to N\) is a quasi-isomorphism, its cone is acyclic. The Hom complex of its cone, by its two component summands, is the shifted cone of
\(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(N,J)\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(M,J)\), with the signs from B.1. Consequently
\[
s^*:\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal B)}(N,J)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal B)}(M,J).
\tag{BF.2}
\]
Here \(K(\mathcal B)\) means complexes and chain maps modulo homotopy, already defined directly by the Hom complex. This proves (BF.2) before a derived category exists.

Shifts and cones of K-injective complexes are K-injective, by the same Hom-complex calculation. An acyclic K-injective complex is contractible, since its identity is null-homotopic. A quasi-isomorphism between K-injective complexes is a homotopy equivalence: its cone is both acyclic and K-injective, and the contraction gives the homotopy inverse as in B.1. These statements do not require a first nonzero degree.

### BF.2. A locally small localization

Define a category \(D(\mathcal B)\) whose objects are complexes and whose morphism groups are
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal B)}(M,N)
 =\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal B)}(I_M,I_N).
\tag{BF.3}
\]
Composition is composition of homotopy classes. These groups are sets: the set of component maps is a countable product of Hom sets, chain maps form a subset, and homotopy is an equivalence relation on that subset.

For a chain map \(u:M\to N\), (BF.2) gives a unique homotopy class \(Qu:I_M\to I_N\) satisfying
\[
(Qu)q_M=q_Nu\quad\text{in }K(\mathcal B).
\tag{BF.4}
\]
Uniqueness proves additivity, compatibility with compositions and invariance under homotopy. Thus \(Q:K(\mathcal B)\to D(\mathcal B)\) is an additive functor. It inverts quasi-isomorphisms: (BF.4) makes \(Qu\) a quasi-isomorphism when \(u\) is one, and the preceding paragraph makes it a homotopy equivalence.

We verify the universal property. Write \(\mathcal I\) for the full subcategory of \(K(\mathcal B)\) on K-injective complexes. The functor \(M\mapsto I_M\) identifies (BF.3) fully faithfully with \(\mathcal I\), and is essentially surjective because \(q_J:J\to I_J\) is a homotopy equivalence for \(J\in\mathcal I\). For a functor \(F:K(\mathcal B)\to\mathcal E\) which inverts quasi-isomorphisms, define its factor on (BF.3) by applying \(F\) to maps between the \(I_M\)'s. The isomorphisms \(F(q_M)\) give a natural identification of its composite with \(F\), using (BF.4). Conversely, restriction to \(\mathcal I\) and those same isomorphisms determine every such factor, including its natural transformations. This proves localization at quasi-isomorphisms, up to the usual unique natural isomorphism, and independence of the choices in (BF.1).

It also gives localization from the category of complexes, without first imposing homotopy. To see why any functor inverting quasi-isomorphisms identifies homotopic maps \(f,g:M\to N\), let \(f-g=dh+hd\). The complex \(M\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(1_M)\) projects quasi-isomorphically to \(M\). Its two chain-map sections are
\(x\mapsto(x,0,0)\) and \(x\mapsto(x,x,0)\). They become equal after that projection is inverted. The chain map
\[
(x,y,z)\longmapsto g(x)+(f-g)(y)+h(z)
\tag{BF.5}
\]
has composites \(g,f\) with these sections: its chain identity is exactly \(f-g=dh+hd\). Thus those maps become equal in any such target category, even when the target functor was not assumed additive.

For a K-injective \(J\), this construction and (BF.2) give the useful natural formula
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal B)}(M,J)
 =\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal B)}(M,J).
\tag{BF.6}
\]
More precisely the equality denotes the canonical bijection obtained by replacing \(J\) and then using \(q_M\); it is independent of a representative of a homotopy class.

### BF.3. Triangles and arbitrary coproducts

The full category \(\mathcal I\) is closed under shifts and mapping cones. The cone, rotation, homotopy-square and octahedron matrices in B.1 therefore give a triangulated structure on it. Those matrix identities hold for arbitrary complexes; the bounded-below hypothesis in B.1 was used to obtain its earlier resolutions, not in any matrix identity. A cone of an identity is contractible; every chain map has its cone; cone triangles are taken together with all their isomorphic triangles. These observations, rotation and the two explicit cone-map constructions verify the triangle axioms. Transfer this structure along the equivalence (BF.3).

The functor \(Q\) carries each chain-level cone triangle to a distinguished triangle. Indeed (BF.4), represented by chain maps and a homotopy of its square, gives the cone comparison from B.1. Its first two component maps are quasi-isomorphisms, so its third map is a quasi-isomorphism by the long exact cohomology sequences. Those sequences follow directly from the degreewise split sequence defining a cone. Consequently the third map becomes invertible in (BF.3). The same comparison for shifts supplies the shift isomorphism. Long exact Hom sequences in either variable follow by applying the Hom complex to a cone and taking cohomology; hence all the cohomological exact sequences used here hold for unbounded objects.

Small coproducts in \(\mathcal B\) are exact. They are filtered colimits of finite sums, so this follows from the Grothendieck axioms. Thus the termwise sum of a family of acyclic complexes is acyclic, and termwise sums preserve quasi-isomorphisms. Moreover the termwise sum is the coproduct in (BF.3). For any K-injective \(J\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal B)}
 \left(\bigoplus_t M_t,J\right)
&=H^0\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet
 \left(\bigoplus_t M_t,J\right)\\
&=H^0\prod_t\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(M_t,J)\\
&=\prod_t\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal B)}(M_t,J).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BF.7}
\]
The second equality rearranges products of sets of component maps. The third uses exactness of products of abelian groups: kernels are componentwise, and a tuple in the image has a tuple of preimages by choice. Every target is represented by such a \(J\), so (BF.7) is the required universal property. We have not asserted that a sum of K-injective complexes remains K-injective. A sum of distinguished triangles is distinguished, since sums commute with the two-summand cone formula and carry componentwise quasi-isomorphisms to quasi-isomorphisms.

### BF.4. Derived functors without an additive resolution choice

Let \(\Phi:\mathcal B\to\mathcal D\) be an additive functor between Grothendieck abelian categories. On \(\mathcal I\), apply \(\Phi\) term by term and pass to \(D(\mathcal D)\). Additivity makes this preserve chain homotopies, shifts and cones: only sums of component maps and finite biproducts occur in these formulas. The equivalence (BF.3) consequently defines an exact functor
\[
R\Phi(M)=\Phi(I_M).
\tag{BF.8}
\]
Different choices in (BF.1) give the canonical comparison isomorphisms from (BF.2). This argument uses additivity of \(\Phi\), not additivity of a functorial choice of \(I_M\).

For completeness, (BF.8) has the right-derived universal property. Its natural map from \(Q\Phi\) on complexes is \(\Phi(q_M)\). Given a natural transformation from \(Q\Phi\) to a functor \(T\) on \(D(\mathcal B)\), its factor at \(M\) is the composite from \(\Phi(I_M)\) to \(T(I_M)\) followed by \(T(q_M)^{-1}\). Naturality follows from (BF.4), and the same equality forces uniqueness. If \(\Phi\) is exact, it already preserves quasi-isomorphisms and \(\Phi(q_M)\) is a quasi-isomorphism, so its derived functor is its ordinary termwise functor.

Suppose \(v:\mathcal D\to\mathcal B\) is exact and left adjoint to \(u:\mathcal B\to\mathcal D\). Component adjunction respects the Hom-complex differentials. For acyclic \(A\) and K-injective \(J\), it identifies \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,uJ)\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(vA,J)\), which is acyclic. Thus \(uJ\) is K-injective. Applying (BF.6) proves
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal B)}(vM,N)
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal D)}(M,RuN).
\tag{BF.9}
\]
This constructs the derived adjunction, its units and its counits directly from the original adjunction, for arbitrary complexes.

### BF.5. Presheaves, sheafification and compact generators

Take a small site \(\mathcal C\) and a constant ring \(\Lambda\). Write \(\mathcal P\) for presheaves of left \(\Lambda\)-modules and \(\mathcal A\) for sheaves. The matching-family proof in [Sites and sheaves, Sections 1–4](course:ag-etale-cohomology/sites-and-sheaves#1-local-data-and-their-agreement) gives exact sheafification \(a\dashv i\), with \(ai=1\). Its constructions preserve the module action: matching families, local equality and glued sections have that action componentwise. Presheaf kernels, cokernels and colimits are pointwise; sheaf kernels are pointwise and sheaf colimits are sheafifications. Since filtered module colimits are exact, exactness of \(a\) proves exact filtered colimits in \(\mathcal A\) as well.

For \(U\in\mathcal C\), let \(P_U(V)\) be the free left \(\Lambda\)-module on the set of arrows \(V\to U\). A map from \(P_U\) is determined by the image of \(1_U\); conversely a section over \(U\) defines its images by restriction and linear extension. Hence
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal P}(P_U,M)=M(U),
\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(aP_U,F)=F(U).
\tag{BF.10}
\]
The sums of these presheaves and of their sheafifications are generators in their respective categories. To verify the latter assertion, a nonzero map of sheaves is nonzero on some section over some site object; the corresponding map in (BF.10) detects it. Local smallness holds because a natural transformation is a subset of the product of the sets of section maps. These facts verify all the Grothendieck hypotheses required in BF.1 for both categories.

Apply BF.4 to \(a\dashv i\). If \(I\) is a K-injective sheaf complex, \(iI\) is K-injective as a presheaf complex and \(aiI=I\). Therefore
\[
a:D(\mathcal P)\rightleftarrows D(\mathcal A):Ri,
\qquad aRi\simeq1.
\tag{BF.11}
\]
The second assertion is the counit isomorphism, and implies full faithfulness of \(Ri\): adjunction identifies maps \(RiK\to RiL\) with maps \(aRiK\to L\), hence with maps \(K\to L\). By BF.3, \(a\) preserves derived coproducts, because it preserves termwise coproducts.

Finally (BF.6) and pointwise exactness of evaluation give, for any presheaf complex \(M\),
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal P)}(P_U[r],M)
 =H^{-r}(M(U)).
\tag{BF.12}
\]
Indeed replace \(M\) by \(I_M\); its evaluation remains a quasi-isomorphism and the Hom complex from \(P_U\) is the evaluation complex itself. Evaluation and module cohomology commute with sums, so the set of all \(P_U[r]\) consists of compact objects. It detects zero objects: the vanishing of (BF.12) for every \(U,r\) says exactly that every cohomology presheaf is zero. The map of that complex to zero is then a quasi-isomorphism, hence an isomorphism in BF.2. Thus every hypothesis of [The right adjoint of derived pushforward, Lemma 1.F and Theorem 1.G](course:AG-QC/the-right-adjoint-of-derived-pushforward#the-representability-argument) is verified. Those earlier proofs construct the compact-generator telescope and its representing object; they use only the triangulated structure, local smallness, coproducts and compact detection established here.

### BF.6. Representability on the sheaf category

Let \(H:D(\mathcal A)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Ab}\) be cohomological and carry coproducts to products. BF.5 and the cited compact-generator theorem give a presheaf complex \(L\) and a natural identification \(H(aM)=\operatorname{Hom}(M,L)\). Complete the adjunction unit to a triangle
\[
N\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow Ri(aL)\longrightarrow N[1].
\tag{BF.13}
\]
The adjunction identity and invertibility of the counit imply that applying \(a\) to its middle map gives an isomorphism. Thus \(aN=0\). In the long exact sequence obtained by applying \(\operatorname{Hom}(N,-)\), the term \(\operatorname{Hom}(N,N)\) lies between
\(\operatorname{Hom}(N,Ri(aL)[-1])=0\), by adjunction, and
\(\operatorname{Hom}(N,L)=H(aN)=0\), by representation. Its identity therefore vanishes, which means \(N\) is a zero object. We obtain \(L\simeq Ri(aL)\), and full faithfulness gives
\[
H(K)\simeq H(aRiK)
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}(RiK,L)
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}(K,aL).
\tag{BF.14}
\]
This proves representability on \(D(\mathcal A)\) without assuming that its sheafified generators are compact or splitting an unspecified idempotent.

In particular, any exact coproduct-preserving functor \(F:D(\mathcal A)\to\mathcal T\), with \(\mathcal T\) locally small and triangulated, has a right adjoint. Apply (BF.14) to \(K\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T}(FK,B)\) for each \(B\). A map \(B\to B'\) gives a unique map of representing objects: a natural transformation between representable Hom functors is determined by its value on the identity of the representing object. This also proves identity and composition compatibility and gives the adjunction in both variables.

The right adjoint is exact. Adjunction and the shift isomorphism of \(F\) first give the shift isomorphism for the right adjoint. For a triangle \(B_0\to B_1\to B_2\to B_0[1]\), complete its first adjoint map to a triangle \(RB_0\to RB_1\to C\to RB_0[1]\). Apply \(F\) and the two counits; the triangle-map axiom supplies \(FC\to B_2\), hence \(C\to RB_2\). For every \(K\), the resulting comparison from the long exact Hom sequence of the completed triangle to \(\operatorname{Hom}(FK,B_\bullet)\) has isomorphisms on the terms involving \(B_0,B_1\) and all their shifts, by adjunction. Exactness gives an isomorphism on the remaining terms: to lift an element, lift its boundary through the adjacent isomorphism, subtract a lift, and then use the preceding term; the same subtraction shows injectivity. Thus \(\operatorname{Hom}(K,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}(K,RB_2)\) is an isomorphism for every \(K\). Taking identities gives an inverse to \(C\to RB_2\), proving exactness.

For Proposition 3.3 this proves the categorical implication from an exact, coproduct-preserving \(Rf_!\) to \(f^!\). BG.1–BG.6 construct that geometric functor, prove its coproduct property and compactification independence, and apply the implication. The subsequent trace and Gysin comparisons retain their own proofs. These arguments apply to unbounded ordinary complexes; they supply no adic normalization or rationalization by themselves.

## Appendix BG. Proper support on arbitrary ordinary complexes

Let \(\Lambda\) be a constant commutative ring killed by a positive integer. We construct the exact, coproduct-preserving \(Rf_!\) needed in Proposition 3.3 for separated finite-type morphisms of finite-type schemes over a field. No invertibility of that integer is needed in this appendix. The source complex may be unbounded. Proper comparison itself will be used over arbitrary bases.

### BG.1. Geometric inputs for the cohomological bound

The normalization facts needed for the dimension argument are already proved with arbitrary field coefficients in AG.1–AG.3. They include finite normalization of a reduced finite-type scheme, localization and gluing of integral closures, and preservation of the generic fields. Normalization is an isomorphism on an open containing every generic point: on a reduced affine chart, write its finitely many integral-closure generators as fractions in the total ring of fractions and invert the product of their nonzerodivisor denominators. The two rings then coincide. That product avoids every minimal prime, so the chosen open contains the generic points. These chart opens give the assertion for a scheme.

For an integral normal Noetherian scheme, the local ring at a height-one point is a one-dimensional normal Noetherian local domain. The algebraic DVR proof in L.1 applies to exactly that ring; it does not require the ambient scheme to be a curve. Thus a rational function \(t\) defines a map to \(\mathbf P^1\) near every height-one point: in the valuation ring either \(t\) or \(t^{-1}\) is regular, and that membership holds on a neighbourhood. The union of these domains, together with the generic point, is an open domain of definition. Its closed complement has no point of height zero or one.

Here are the dimension deductions, including the generic fibre. If \(T\) is integral of finite type over a field and has dimension \(d\), a proper closed subset has dimension at most \(d-1\). For a prime chain in an irreducible component of that subset, append the strictly smaller generic prime of \(T\). If the component has height at least two, append a chain of length two below its generic prime instead. The resulting bounds are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dim Z&\leq d-1,\\
\dim Z&\leq d-2\quad(\text{all component heights}\geq2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BG.1}
\]
These statements are local on affine charts and hence give the scheme dimensions. If \(T\to\mathbf P^1_k\) is dominant, every closed fibre is a proper closed subset and satisfies the first bound. The generic fibre is integral of finite type over \(k(t)\); its function field has transcendence degree \(d-1\) over \(k(t)\), so its dimension is \(d-1\). The equality between dimension and transcendence degree follows from polynomial normalization in Y.5: finite integral extensions preserve dimension by lying over, going up and incomparability, as proved in K.1 and AF.1. The same polynomial normalization after any field extension is still finite and injective, because extension of fields is faithfully flat. Thus extension of the fibre field preserves its dimension, including when the resulting algebra is not a domain. These bounds consequently hold on the geometric fibres as well.

For proper curves over an algebraically closed field the cohomological bound is
\[
H^q(C,F)=0\qquad(q>2)
\tag{BG.2}
\]
for every torsion sheaf. To specify the inputs in all characteristics, AK.5 and AL.3 give the prime-to-characteristic calculation on a smooth curve and its finite-monodromy devissage; BE.2–BE.3 supply the characteristic-primary case. Finite direct image is exact by AX.5, and the finite normalization in AG.3 reduces any reduced proper curve to its normal components, with a cokernel supported on finitely many points. Such normal proper curves are smooth over the algebraically closed field by AG.4, and the proper-curve case of P.3 proves that they are projective. The finite point terms have no positive cohomology. Nilpotents do not change the étale topos, by the purely inseparable argument of BE.4. Finally BA's coefficient continuity passes the bound from finite constructible primary coefficients to an arbitrary torsion sheaf. Thus (BG.2) includes nonreduced curves, arbitrary torsion coefficients and the residue characteristic.

### BG.2. The proper cohomological bound

For a proper morphism \(p:T\to S\) with geometric fibres of dimension at most \(d\), we prove
\[
R^qp_*F=0\qquad(q>2d)
\tag{BG.3}
\]
for every torsion sheaf. The argument is an induction on \(d\) over all proper morphisms. If \(d=0\), AW.5 makes the proper quasi-finite map finite, and AX.5 gives exactness. If \(d=1\), the geometric-fibre formula BE.8 and (BG.2) give the assertion.

Assume the result in lower dimensions. BE.8 reduces (BG.3) to a proper scheme over an algebraically closed field. Replace it by its reduction and take the finite normalization \(\nu\). The map \(F\to\nu_*\nu^{-1}F\) is injective: its pullback to a geometric point is the diagonal map into the nonempty finite collection of lifted stalks. Its cokernel is supported on a proper closed subset, because BG.1 gives a dense isomorphism locus. Exact finite direct image and induction on that subset reduce the bound to an integral normal proper scheme \(T\) of dimension \(d>1\).

Choose a nonconstant rational function and take its graph closure \(T'\subset T\times\mathbf P^1\), with projections \(b:T'\to T\) and \(r:T'\to\mathbf P^1\). Both are proper; the graph closure is integral. The first is an isomorphism on the domain in BG.1 and has fibres of dimension at most one, since its fibres are closed subschemes of \(\mathbf P^1\). Put
\[
Q=\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(F\longrightarrow Rb_*b^{-1}F\bigr).
\tag{BG.4}
\]
Surjectivity of \(b\) makes the degree-zero unit injective, and the already established one-dimensional case bounds its higher direct image by two. Thus \(Q\) has cohomology only in degrees \(0,1,2\), supported on a closed subset of dimension at most \(d-2\). Its cohomology sheaves are torsion: write coefficients as their filtered union of annihilator subsheaves and use BA's continuity. Closed extension and its exactness are AX.5. Induction and the three finite truncation triangles therefore give
\[
H^m(T,Q)=0\qquad(m>2d-2).
\tag{BG.5}
\]
This use of truncation involves three terms, not an unbounded convergence assertion.

The fibres of \(r\) have dimension at most \(d-1\), by BG.1. Hence \(Rr_*b^{-1}F\) has cohomology only in degrees \(0\) through \(2d-2\). Applying the proper curve bound to those finitely many sheaves and using their finite truncation triangles bounds its derived global sections by \(2d\). Derived composition holds because direct image preserves K-injectives, its inverse-image left adjoint being exact by BF.4. It follows that \(H^q(T',b^{-1}F)=0\) above \(2d\). The triangle (BG.4) and (BG.5) imply the same vanishing for \(F\), completing the induction. This supplies the geometry and finite-truncation proof behind [Cohomology with compact support, Theorem 4.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#4-the-proper-dimension-bound).

Locally on a quasi-compact base, a proper finite-type morphism has some uniform finite fibre-dimension bound: take finitely many affine charts over an affine base and finite algebra generators on each; their numbers bound the dimensions of the fibres of those charts. Thus (BG.3) supplies a uniform finite bound wherever the following local arguments are applied. BB.3 identifies sheaf-of-\(\Lambda\)-module cohomology with the corresponding abelian-sheaf cohomology, so the same bound applies to \(\Lambda\)-modules.

### BG.3. A finite bound controls unbounded complexes

We give the homological argument for a left exact additive functor \(F\) between the Grothendieck categories used here. Assume \(R^qF=0\) on objects for \(q>N\). A complex of \(F\)-acyclic objects computes \(RF\), without a boundedness hypothesis.

Indeed, let \(L\) be an acyclic complex whose terms are \(F\)-acyclic, and write \(Z^a=\ker(d:L^a\to L^{a+1})\). The short exact cycle sequences give
\[
R^qF(Z^{a+1})\simeq R^{q+1}F(Z^a)\quad(q\geq1).
\tag{BG.6}
\]
Repeatedly shifting to smaller indices makes each positive derived functor of a cycle vanish, since its degree eventually exceeds \(N\). Consequently applying \(F\) preserves exactness of every cycle sequence, and \(F(L)\) is acyclic. For an arbitrary complex of \(F\)-acyclic objects, compare it with a termwise injective K-injective resolution from BF.1. Its comparison cone has \(F\)-acyclic terms and is acyclic; the argument just given proves that applying \(F\) to the comparison remains a quasi-isomorphism. This proves the computation statement.

There is also an actual cohomological window:
\[
RF(D^{\geq a})\subset D^{\geq a},
\qquad RF(D^{\leq b})\subset D^{\leq b+N}.
\tag{BG.7}
\]
For the first inclusion, replace a lower truncation by its bounded-below injective resolution; the construction is T.4 and the homotopy argument is B.1. For the second take a termwise injective K-injective resolution \(I\) of an object with no cohomology above \(b\). If \(i>b+N\), the cycle sequences in the exact tail give
\[
H^i(FI)=R^1F(Z^{i-1})
 \simeq R^{N+1}F(Z^{i-N-1})=0.
\tag{BG.8}
\]
The last surjection used is \(I^b\to Z^{b+1}\) when \(i=b+N+1\), which is surjective because \(H^{b+1}(I)=0\). For \(N=0\), the functor is exact and the assertion follows directly. The truncation triangles and (BG.7) show that \(H^i(RFE)\) depends only on \(\tau_{\geq i-N}\tau_{\leq i}E\): the omitted upper part has no image cohomology through degree \(i\), and the omitted lower part has none from degree \(i\) onward. This argument neither assumes left completeness of a derived category nor exchanges cohomology with an infinite product.

### BG.4. Unbounded proper comparison and coproducts

Let \(p:T\to S\) be proper, and consider any change of base with projections \(a:T'\to T\), \(g:S'\to S\) and proper map \(p':T'\to S'\). For \(E\in D(T,\Lambda)\), choose a termwise injective K-injective resolution \(I\). The proper comparison theorem BE.7, applied to each individual term, gives
\[
R^qp'_*a^{-1}I^m=0\quad(q>0),
\qquad
g^{-1}p_*I^m\xrightarrow{\sim}p'_*a^{-1}I^m.
\tag{BG.9}
\]
All those sheaves are torsion because \(\Lambda\) is killed by an integer. The local finite bound (BG.3) and BG.3 make the unbounded complex \(a^{-1}I\) compute its derived direct image. Thus the termwise maps in (BG.9) give the canonical isomorphism
\[
g^{-1}Rp_*E\xrightarrow{\sim}Rp'_*a^{-1}E
\tag{BG.10}
\]
for arbitrary \(E\). They are the usual adjunction base-change maps: after comparing with a K-injective target resolution, the termwise direct-image adjunction defines the same morphism. Naturality of that adjunction proves compatibility with successive base changes and with compositions of proper maps. This identifies the comparison morphism itself, not only its source and target.

The same finite bound proves preservation of coproducts. Choose resolutions \(I_t\) for a family \(E_t\). BA's higher-direct-image continuity on quasi-compact, quasi-separated schemes, together with BB.3, implies that each term \(\bigoplus_t I_t^m\) is \(p_*\)-acyclic: a sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums, whose positive derived images vanish. Direct image also commutes with these sums in degree zero. BG.3 therefore computes both sides of
\[
\bigoplus_t Rp_*E_t\longrightarrow Rp_*\left(\bigoplus_tE_t\right)
\tag{BG.11}
\]
by the identical termwise image complex. BF.3 identifies the termwise sums with the derived coproducts. This proves (BG.11), without asserting that a sum of injective or K-injective objects is injective. Both statements are local on the base; a single global finite bound is unnecessary when the base is not quasi-compact.

### BG.5. Compactification at the required field scope

For a separated finite-type map of finite-type schemes over a field, the needed existence theorem is [The right adjoint of derived pushforward, Appendix N, Theorem N.E.1](course:AG-QC/the-right-adjoint-of-derived-pushforward#appendix-n-nagata-compactification-over-a-noetherian-base). Its N.A–N.E prove Nagata compactification for Noetherian schemes, preserving nilpotents and the entire open source. This hypothesis holds here. The theorem gives
\[
X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{p}Y,
\qquad j\text{ open},\quad p\text{ proper}.
\tag{BG.12}
\]

We specify the complete geometric inputs for that proof in the present use. AU.1 gives the finite affine equalizer, its localization and flat-base-change identities, and properness of maps from proper schemes to separated schemes. AU.2 gives scheme-theoretic closure and the Noetherian Chow modification. For a nonaffine Noetherian base the needed Chow statement is [Projective morphisms and Chow's lemma, Theorem 4.1](course:AG-MO/projective-morphisms-and-chows-lemma#4-chow-s-lemma-over-a-noetherian-base): its finite affine-cover construction and gluing retain the base and the schematically dense source. The relative immersion of each affine piece used there is constructed explicitly in N.E.1: finitely many distinguished opens over affine base charts supply algebra generators; their numerators and denominators are global coordinates, and on the corresponding target opens the coordinate-ring maps are surjective. This proves the relative immersion even when the base is not affine. The valuation domination and specialization witnesses are proved in [Valuation rings and separatedness, Theorems 2.1 and 4.1](course:AG-MO/valuation-rings-and-separatedness#2-a-valuation-ring-over-every-local-subring); AW.1 identifies their algebraic use. [Proper morphisms and valuative criteria, Sections 1–4](course:AG-MO/proper-morphisms-and-valuative-criteria#1-closedness-after-changing-the-base) gives the all-valuation properness criterion and properness of projective space. Its quasi-compact image criterion is the elementary localization argument in [Finiteness of morphisms, Theorem 1.2](course:AG-MO/finiteness-of-morphisms#1-finite-covers-over-the-base), and its graph and projective-chart inputs are [The diagonal and separated morphisms, Sections 1–2 and 4–6](course:AG-MO/the-diagonal-and-separated-morphisms#1-comparing-two-positions-in-a-family).

There is a useful direct replacement for the auxiliary quasi-affineness assertion N.A.4. AW.5 factors every separated quasi-finite finite-type map occurring there as an open immersion into a finite scheme over the target. That finite scheme is affine over the target, so the original map is quasi-affine. This proves the required assertion directly from AW.1–AW.5, with their conductor, regular-local and slicing arguments.

The rest of Appendix N consists of its written blowup-chart and strict-transform calculations, the protected elimination construction N.B.1, the three assembly lemmas N.C.1–N.C.3, and the two-open construction N.D.1. The blowup charts embed in localizations, so their protected opens stay schematically dense. The elimination construction uses finitely generated conductor ideals to extend rational coordinate maps and then separates the protected boundary. The two-open construction keeps a closed gluing graph, checks all valuation limits from a dense open and applies the proved Chow modification. Finally N.E.1 compactifies the finite affine cover. These arguments establish (BG.12) with the original possibly singular and nonreduced schemes; smoothness or quasi-projectivity of \(X\) is not added.

### BG.6. Construction, independence and the right adjoint

Define, using (BG.12),
\[
Rf_!E=Rp_*j_!E.
\tag{BG.13}
\]
Open extension by zero is exact and preserves coproducts, by its stalk description in [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#1-extension-by-zero-for-an-étale-morphism). BF.4 constructs \(Rp_*\) as an exact functor of derived categories, and (BG.11) proves that it preserves coproducts. Therefore (BG.13) is exact and coproduct-preserving on all of \(D(X,\Lambda)\).

The definition is canonical. Here is the comparison mechanism, with its full earlier proof locator. In a commuting square with open horizontal maps \(j:U\to T\), \(i:V\to S\) and proper vertical maps \(p':U\to V\), \(p:T\to S\), the induced open map \(U\to T\times_SV\) is proper, by the closed graph and proper projection argument. It is consequently clopen. Restriction to \(V\) thus identifies \(Rp_*j_!E\) with \(Rp'_*E\), and the open adjunction defines
\[
i_!Rp'_*E\longrightarrow Rp_*j_!E.
\tag{BG.14}
\]
It is an isomorphism over \(V\). On its complement the right side is zero by (BG.10), because the pulled-back support open is empty. The left side is zero by definition. Geometric stalks detect the resulting isomorphism. The square need not be cartesian.

A refinement \(h:\overline X_1\to\overline X_2\) gives (BG.14) in the form \(j_{2,!}\simeq Rh_*j_{1,!}\), hence an isomorphism between the two definitions (BG.13). Common refinements exist by taking the scheme-theoretic closure of the diagonal \(X\) in the product of two compactifications. Above the open \(X\) in either factor its graph is already closed, so the same copy of \(X\) is open in that closure. Parallel refinement maps are equalized by their closed equalizer, which still contains that open. The quasi-coherent closure ideal is the kernel of restriction; AU.1's finite affine equalizer gives its localization, also over a non-Noetherian base. These facts prove the cofiltered refinement assertion used here.

The identities and coherence of these particular maps are proved in [Cohomology with compact support, Lemma 6.1 and Theorems 7.1–9.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#6-the-proper-open-exchange-and-its-coherence). The inputs to those proofs are now (BG.10), exact open extension, proper composition from BF.4 and the preceding refinement construction. For precision, their pasting argument restricts an exchange to its source open, where it is the clopen pushforward identity; the open adjunction determines the entire map from that restriction. Stacking squares consequently agrees with composing the adjunction units. A common refinement then makes comparisons between any choices identical and proves their cocycle rule. For three composable maps, successive compactifications give a single array of opens and proper maps, and the two parenthesizations are the two pastings of that same array. Arbitrary base change pulls back (BG.12), and (BG.10) with exact open base change gives its comparison; the same pasting argument proves compatibility with refinements and composition. Thus these are canonical and associative functor isomorphisms, not choices of unrelated isomorphisms.

Finally apply BF.6 to (BG.13). This supplies an exact right adjoint \(f^!\) on arbitrary ordinary \(\Lambda\)-complexes, with the adjunction unit and counit. It completes the existence and coproduct-preservation prerequisite in Proposition 3.3. The smooth trace normalization, the ensuing Gysin comparisons, enhanced operation compatibilities and passage to normalized adic coefficients retain their own arguments; none follows solely from the existence of this right adjoint.

## Appendix BH. Tensor products and the proper-support projection formula

Fix a constant commutative coefficient ring \(\Lambda\). Sections BH.1–BH.4 work on the small étale site of a scheme, with a small basis fixed as in BF.5. Sections BH.5–BH.7 use a ring killed by an integer and the proper-support scope of BG. Every complex below may be unbounded; tensor totalization uses direct sums.

### BH.1. Flat resolutions on the étale site

For a basis object \(u:U\to X\), put \(B_U=u_!\Lambda_U\). The explicit construction and adjunction in [Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, Proposition 1.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/constructible-sheaves-and-extension-by-zero#1-extension-by-zero-for-an-étale-morphism) give
\[
\operatorname{Hom}(B_U,F)=F(U),\qquad
(B_U)_{\bar x}=\bigoplus_{\bar u\mapsto\bar x}\Lambda.
\tag{BH.1}
\]
In particular these stalks are free. Tensor sheaves have stalks equal to the tensors of their stalks: each tensor and each relation expressing its vanishing involve finitely many factors and balancing relations, which can all be represented on one pointed étale refinement. Sheafification leaves these germs unchanged. Exactness is detected on geometric stalks, so every \(B_U\) is flat. The sum
\[
L(F)=\bigoplus_{U}\ \bigoplus_{s\in F(U)}B_U\longrightarrow F
\tag{BH.2}
\]
is an epimorphism: its summand indexed by \(s\) represents that section, and every germ has such a representative. All indices form a set. Direct sums and filtered colimits of flat sheaves are flat, by their stalk tensor functors and exactness of these operations on modules.

A complex \(P\) is K-flat if \(A\otimes P\) is acyclic for every acyclic complex \(A\). A flat sheaf in one degree is K-flat: tensor its exact cycle sequences with that sheaf. Sums and filtered colimits of K-flat complexes are K-flat, since tensor commutes with them and filtered colimits are exact. A degreewise split extension of two K-flat complexes is K-flat: after tensoring, it remains degreewise split, and its long exact cohomology sequence applies. In particular a bounded complex of flats is K-flat by finite induction; a bounded-above complex of flats is the filtered union of its bounded brutal lower truncations and is K-flat as well. None of these assertions says that an arbitrary complex of flat terms is K-flat.

Here is a resolution for an arbitrary \(G\). Let \(D_n(F)\) have \(F\) in degrees \(n,n+1\) and identity differential. Start with
\[
P_0=\bigoplus_nD_n(L(G^n))\longrightarrow G.
\tag{BH.3}
\]
The lower term maps by (BH.2), and the upper term by its composite with \(d_G\). This is a termwise epimorphism. Each disk is contractible; tensoring its contraction \(h\) with an element of degree \(a\) uses the sign \((-1)^a h\). Thus \(P_0\) is K-flat and has flat terms.

Given a termwise epimorphism \(P_s\to G\), take its kernel \(K_s\). For every \(z\in Z^q(K_s)(U)\), attach one \(B_U\) in degree \(q-1\), with differential equal to the map represented by \(z\), and with zero image in \(G\). Explicitly, writing \(V_s\) for the graded sum of the added terms, set
\[
P_{s+1}=P_s\oplus V_s,\qquad
d(p,v)=(d p+\alpha(v),0).
\tag{BH.4}
\]
Here \(d\alpha=0\) and the composite of \(\alpha\) with \(P_s\to G\) is zero. Therefore (BH.4) is a complex over \(G\). Its quotient by \(P_s\) is a sum of shifts of flat sheaves, with zero differential. The degreewise splitting proves K-flatness by induction and preserves flat terms.

Set \(P(G)=\varinjlim_sP_s\). Filtered-colimit exactness gives
\[
H^q(\ker(P(G)\to G))
=\varinjlim_sH^q(K_s)=0.
\tag{BH.5}
\]
For the last equality, a germ of a kernel class is represented on some \(U\) by a cycle at stage \(s\); the cell attached at stage \(s+1\) kills it. Hence every transition map on these cohomology sheaves is zero. The long exact sequence of the termwise epimorphism proves that \(P(G)\to G\) is a quasi-isomorphism. This proves the resolution theorem on the actual étale site. It is the disk-and-cycle construction of [Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Sections 8–9](course:derived-categories-and-sheaf-operations/sheaves-of-modules-and-their-derived-categories#8-k-flat-resolutions), with (BH.1) supplying the required étale generators in place of topological open sets.

The construction can be made functorial on chain maps: send a generator indexed by a section to the generator indexed by its image, and do the same for each kernel cycle at each stage. These maps commute with the differentials in (BH.4), with identities and with composition. The resolution functor need not be additive; the derived functor constructed next will be additive.

### BH.2. Derived tensor, morphisms and coherence

Use the total differential
\[
d(a\otimes b)=d a\otimes b+(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes d b.
\tag{BH.6}
\]
Tensoring a quasi-isomorphism with a K-flat complex preserves quasi-isomorphisms: tensor its acyclic cone, and distribute the two cone summands, using (BH.6). If \(P\to P'\) is a quasi-isomorphism between K-flat complexes, tensoring it with **any** \(G\) also preserves quasi-isomorphisms. Indeed, resolve \(G\) by \(Q\). In the square with rows \(Q\otimes P\to Q\otimes P'\) and \(G\otimes P\to G\otimes P'\), both vertical maps and the top map are quasi-isomorphisms by K-flatness. The induced cohomology square makes the bottom map one too.

Consequently the functor on pairs of complexes
\[
(E,F)\longmapsto P(E)\otimes P(F)
\tag{BH.7}
\]
inverts quasi-isomorphisms in each variable. BF.2's localization property, including its property for natural transformations, lets (BH.7) descend in the two variables successively. This constructs \(E\otimes^LF\) as a bifunctor on the actual derived categories. For fixed \(F\), the natural quasi-isomorphism \(P(E)\otimes P(F)\to E\otimes P(F)\) identifies it with tensoring by \(P(F)\). The latter respects homotopies, addition, shifts and cones, by the formula (BH.6). Thus the derived functor is additive and exact in each variable despite the resolution functor's possible nonadditivity.

For completeness, two termwise-surjective K-flat resolutions of \(F\) have a common comparison: resolve their ordinary fibre product over \(F\). Each projection is a surjective quasi-isomorphism, with kernel the acyclic kernel of the other resolution. The resulting maps between K-flat complexes remain quasi-isomorphisms after tensoring with any \(G\). Resolving a triple fibre product proves the cocycle rule. Resolving the fibre product of two comparison resolutions proves independence of that choice. An arbitrary K-flat resolution becomes surjective by adding the contractible disk complex (BH.3). This establishes the same comparison for arbitrary choices, without assuming a direct map between them.

Tensor products of K-flat complexes are K-flat, because tensoring an acyclic complex first with one factor and then the other remains acyclic. The usual chain maps
\[
(a\otimes b)\otimes c\longmapsto a\otimes(b\otimes c),
\qquad
a\otimes b\longmapsto(-1)^{|a||b|}b\otimes a
\tag{BH.8}
\]
therefore give associativity and symmetry on simultaneous K-flat models. The three differential signs for associativity are \(1,(-1)^{|a|},(-1)^{|a|+|b|}\) on both sides. Every route through four-factor associativity gives the same ordered tensor. Moving a degree \(a\) past degrees \(b,c\) gives \((-1)^{a(b+c)}=(-1)^{ab}(-1)^{ac}\), proving symmetry coherence. Multiplication by the degree-zero flat unit \(\Lambda\) proves the unit identities. These calculations survive the canonical model comparisons. Tensoring preserves arbitrary coproducts: use the sum of the K-flat models and distribute the direct-sum totalization. Exactness of sums makes that sum a resolution of the corresponding derived coproduct.

### BH.3. Stalks and inverse image preserve K-flat models

For constant \(\Lambda\), a complex \(P\) is K-flat if and only if every \(P_{\bar x}\) is K-flat over \(\Lambda\). First assume sheafwise K-flatness and let \(N\) be any acyclic complex of \(\Lambda\)-modules and take its constant sheaf complex \(\underline N\). Its stalks are \(N\), so it is acyclic. Hence \(\underline N\otimes P\) is acyclic, and its stalk is \(N\otimes P_{\bar x}\). This is the defining test for \(P_{\bar x}\). In the other direction all stalk tests make \(A\otimes P\) acyclic for every acyclic sheaf complex \(A\).

For a scheme map \(g:Y\to X\), exact inverse image has stalk \((g^{-1}P)_{\bar y}=P_{g\bar y}\). The preceding test shows that \(g^{-1}P\) is K-flat whenever \(P\) is. Inverse image also preserves tensor sheaves and sums: this follows on stalks from the finite tensor presentation used in BH.1, and from the inverse-image stalk formula. We obtain the natural isomorphism
\[
g^{-1}(E\otimes^LF)
\simeq g^{-1}E\otimes^Lg^{-1}F.
\tag{BH.9}
\]
On K-flat models it is the ordinary inverse-image tensor map. Its compatibility with (BH.8), units and successive inverse images follows by applying the same maps to elementary tensors. Exact inverse image of a complex of flat terms alone would not have established this assertion; K-flatness itself has now been checked.

### BH.4. The derived tensor–Hom adjunction on the same site

For sheaf complexes write
\[
\mathcal H^r(B,I)=\prod_{a\in\mathbb Z}
\mathcal Hom(B^a,I^{a+r}),\qquad
d h=d_Ih-(-1)^r h d_B.
\tag{BH.10}
\]
The internal sheaf Hom is characterized on an étale object \(U\) by morphisms between the restrictions to \(U\); the usual sheaf gluing of module morphisms proves this description. In (BH.10) the products are products of sheaves. No exactness of products is assumed. The two middle terms cancel in \(d^2\), and the other two contain a squared differential.

A K-injective \(I\) remains K-injective after restriction to any étale \(u:U\to X\). Indeed, the exact left adjoint \(u_!\) in (BH.1) sends acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes, and
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{K(U)}(A,u^{-1}I[r])
=\operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(u_!A,I[r])=0
\tag{BH.11}
\]
for every acyclic \(A\) and integer \(r\). If \(B\) is acyclic, sections on every \(U\) of \(\mathcal H(B,I)\) consequently form an acyclic complex. Sheafification of these cohomology presheaves proves acyclicity of \(\mathcal H(B,I)\). Thus a quasi-isomorphism in the first variable induces a quasi-isomorphism of these internal Hom complexes. A quasi-isomorphism between K-injective second variables is a homotopy equivalence by BF.1, and internal Hom preserves that equivalence. We may therefore define
\[
R\mathcal Hom(B,C)=\mathcal H(B,I_C)
\tag{BH.12}
\]
independently of choices, with natural maps in both variables.

Take a K-flat \(P\to B\) and K-injective \(C\to I\). Currying sends \(\alpha(a)(p)\) to the same expression viewed as a function of \(a\otimes p\). For a degree-\(r\) homogeneous \(\alpha\), the differential on either side is
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_I\bigl(\alpha(a)(p)\bigr)
&-(-1)^r\alpha(d_Aa)(p)\\
&-(-1)^{r+|a|}\alpha(a)(d_Pp).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BH.13}
\]
Hom out of direct sums and into products proves that this is a bijection of all components, even when unbounded. It is a natural chain isomorphism. For acyclic \(A\), the complex \(A\otimes P\) is acyclic, so this adjunction makes \(\mathcal H(P,I)\) K-injective. It computes (BH.12), by the first-variable invariance. BF.1 now gives
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,R\mathcal Hom(B,C))
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_D(A\otimes^LB,C).
\tag{BH.14}
\]
This is the unbounded tensor–Hom adjunction actually used here. The same calculation on the localized étale site gives the étale restriction isomorphism for (BH.12), since the chosen K-injective remains K-injective there and internal Hom restricts by its just-given description. It does not claim an internal-Hom isomorphism for arbitrary inverse image. Evaluation is the transpose of the identity under (BH.14); composition is the transpose of two successive evaluations. Their associativity and unit identities follow by evaluating on a third factor and using the unique transpose. The corresponding topological computations are also given in [Supporting verifications for open prerequisites, DF-A–DF-F](course:sheaf-proof-readings/SH02-open-prerequisite-proofs#sh02-prp-df-a-coefficients-models-and-unbounded-totalization); (BH.1) and (BH.11) establish the étale-site inputs here.

### BH.5. A coefficient complex can be tested using free modules

Let \(T\) be qcqs with finite cohomological dimension for \(\Lambda\)-modules. For \(E\in D(T,\Lambda)\) and \(M\in D(\Lambda)\), there is a natural comparison
\[
R\Gamma(T,E)\otimes^LM
\longrightarrow R\Gamma(T,E\otimes^L\underline M).
\tag{BH.15}
\]
It is adjoint to evaluation from the constant complex \(\underline{R\Gamma(T,E)}\) to \(E\), tensored with \(\underline M\). BF.4 supplies that derived adjunction. Both sides are exact functors of \(M\) and preserve sums: for tensor this is BH.2; for global sections use BA's filtered-cohomology continuity and the finite-bound acyclic-complex argument of BG.3–BG.4. The map is the unit identification when \(M=\Lambda\), and likewise for shifts and sums of that object.

Here is the complete generation argument. For a sequence of complexes \(M_0\to M_1\to\cdots\), the map \(1-s\) on \(\bigoplus_iM_i\), where \(s\) moves each summand along its transition to the next, is termwise injective. A vector in its kernel has finite support; its zeroth component is zero, then its first component is zero, and induction kills them all. Its cokernel is the termwise colimit, by the defining relations of a direct limit. Hence
\[
\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)\simeq\varinjlim_iM_i.
\tag{BH.16}
\]
The quasi-isomorphism is the projection from the target sum to its cokernel; the long exact sequence of the termwise short exact sequence proves it.

Every module has a free resolution in nonpositive degrees: successively take the free module on the underlying elements and the kernel of its surjection. Every bounded brutal truncation of this resolution is obtained by finitely many cones from sums of shifts of \(\Lambda\). Its longer lower truncations have union the resolution, so (BH.16) and preservation of sums and cones prove (BH.15) for a module. A bounded-above complex is similarly the union of its bounded brutal lower truncations, now assembled from modules. Finally an arbitrary complex is the union of its good upper truncations \(\tau_{\leq b}M\) as \(b\) increases: at any fixed degree its terms and differential eventually agree with those of \(M\). Each truncation is bounded above. Applying (BH.16) a final time proves (BH.15) for every \(M\). This argument uses neither a finite free resolution nor finite Tor dimension.

### BH.6. Proper projection and its actual comparison map

For proper \(p:T\to S\), define
\[
\gamma_{p,E,M}:Rp_*E\otimes^LM
\longrightarrow Rp_*(E\otimes^Lp^{-1}M)
\tag{BH.17}
\]
by transposing the counit \(p^{-1}Rp_*E\to E\) tensored with \(p^{-1}M\), using (BH.9) and BF.4. Take a geometric stalk \(\bar s\). By (BH.9) and unbounded proper comparison BG.4, (BH.17) becomes (BH.15) on the proper geometric fibre \(T_{\bar s}\). This identification respects the map: both are adjoint to the pulled-back direct-image counit. The fibre has finite dimension, and BG.2 gives the required finite cohomological bound. Thus every stalk map is an isomorphism; geometric points detect quasi-isomorphisms, so (BH.17) is an isomorphism for arbitrary \(E,M\) over the torsion ring.

The maps retain composition and tensor coherence. For composable proper maps \(p,q\), the projection map for \(qp\) is the composite of the one for \(q\), with coefficient \(M\), and \(Rq_*\) of the one for \(p\), with coefficient \(q^{-1}M\). Transpose both maps through \((qp)^{-1}\dashv R(qp)_*\): each is the tensor of \(p^{-1}\) of the \(q\)-counit followed by the \(p\)-counit. Uniqueness of transpose proves equality. Applying this twice proves the three-map identity. With two coefficient factors, both orders of projection transpose to the same counit tensored with both factors, so (BH.8) proves compatibility with their associator and unit. Arbitrary base-change compatibility follows in the same way from BG.4's compatibility of the actual base-change map with counits and from (BH.9). These verifications identify the canonical maps, rather than just their isomorphism classes.

### BH.7. Proper supports and invertible twists

For an open \(j:U\hookrightarrow T\), extending a K-flat complex by zero preserves K-flatness: its stalk is the old K-flat stalk on \(U\) and zero elsewhere. The stalkwise tensor construction gives
\[
j_!E\otimes^LN\simeq j_!(E\otimes^Lj^{-1}N).
\tag{BH.18}
\]
Combine this with (BH.17) for a compactification \(f=pj\). We obtain
\[
Rf_!E\otimes^LM
\xrightarrow{\sim}Rf_!(E\otimes^Lf^{-1}M).
\tag{BH.19}
\]
It is independent of compactification. Indeed, a refinement comparison is BG.6's proper–open exchange. After restriction to its support open, compatibility with (BH.18) and (BH.17) is the identity on the open tensor factors and the naturality of the proper counit. Its source is an extension by zero, so the open adjunction determines the whole map from that restriction. This proves compatibility with a single refinement; a common refinement proves independence. The same square argument and the proper composition calculation in BH.6 prove composition compatibility. Pulling back the squares proves compatibility with arbitrary base change. These are the exact comparisons used in [Cohomology with compact support, Section 10](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#10-projection-formula-for-arbitrary-complexes), now with the tensor and étale-site prerequisites proved.

Transposing (BH.19) followed by the counit produces a canonical map
\[
f^!A\otimes^Lf^{-1}M\longrightarrow f^!(A\otimes^LM).
\tag{BH.20}
\]
For an invertible locally constant rank-one sheaf \(L\), it is an isomorphism. Its inverse tensor is \(L^\vee\); the evaluation isomorphisms hold on trivializing étale covers and therefore globally. For every \(T\), the following natural chain of adjunctions proves the assertion:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}(T,f^!A\otimes f^{-1}L)
&=\operatorname{Hom}(T\otimes f^{-1}L^\vee,f^!A)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!(T\otimes f^{-1}L^\vee),A)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!T\otimes L^\vee,A)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!T,A\otimes L)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(T,f^!(A\otimes L)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BH.21}
\]
The tensor functors here are exact because these lines and their inverses are locally free. Evaluating the chain on the identity gives precisely the counit-and-projection transpose (BH.20); evaluation with the inverse line gives its inverse. Shift compatibility follows from exactness of the functors. This establishes the invertible Tate-line cancellation used in Proposition 3.3. It makes no invertibility claim for (BH.20) with arbitrary \(M\), and does not by itself prove the smooth orientation or any adic comparison.

## Appendix BI. The affine-line trace and its local comparison

Fix a field \(k\), an integer \(n\geq2\) invertible in \(k\), and \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\). The schemes in this appendix are separated of finite type over \(k\), unless a selected strict localization is specified. We use the ordinary unbounded derived categories constructed in BF, proper support from BG, and tensor and internal Hom from BH.

### BI.1. The local adjunction and its actual maps

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated of finite type and let \(j:U\to X\) be a separated affine étale neighbourhood. The adjunctions of BG.6 and BH.1 give, for every complex \(A\) and integer \(r\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_S(R(fj)_!\Lambda,A[r])
&=\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\Lambda,f^!A[r])\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}_U(\Lambda,j^{-1}f^!A[r]).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BI.1}
\]
These are adjunction bijections, so their transitions under a refinement are the étale counits on the left and restrictions on the right. To identify the last group, take a K-injective representative \(I\) of \(f^!A\). Its restriction is K-injective by (BH.11); the group is \(H^r(\Gamma(U,I))\). Exact filtered colimits over pointed étale neighbourhoods commute with kernels and images in the section complexes. Their termwise colimit is the stalk complex \(I_{\bar x}\). Consequently
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_{(U,\bar u)}
\operatorname{Hom}_S(R(fj)_!\Lambda,A[r])
=H^r(f^!A)_{\bar x}.
\tag{BI.2}
\]
This proves the local test for unbounded \(A\).

There is also the internal adjunction
\[
Rf_*R\mathcal Hom(E,f^!A)
\simeq R\mathcal Hom(Rf_!E,A).
\tag{BI.3}
\]
Indeed Hom from any complex \(M\) into its left side is successively
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}M\otimes^LE,f^!A)
&=\operatorname{Hom}_S(Rf_!(f^{-1}M\otimes^LE),A)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}_S(M\otimes^LRf_!E,A).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BI.4}
\]
The first derived adjunction uses exact inverse image and BF.4. BH.4 supplies the tensor–Hom bijections, and BH.7 supplies the middle projection isomorphism. The last group is Hom into the right side of (BI.3). Naturality and the representing property prove (BI.3). Its map is evaluation followed by the counit: transposing that composite through these same bijections returns the identity. Thus this comparison includes its normalization and its compatibility with composition.

### BI.2. The projective-line splitting specifies the trace

Write \(p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S\), \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\), and let \(i\) be the infinity section. The unit and the Kummer class \(c=c_1^{(n)}(\mathcal O(1))\) define
\[
\alpha:\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-2]
\longrightarrow Rp_*\Lambda.
\tag{BI.5}
\]
For the second summand this means the adjoint of the class viewed as a morphism \(p^{-1}\Lambda(-1)[-2]\to\Lambda\). This uses the invertible twist, not a choice of a primitive root on \(S\).

Here is the full geometric-fibre check. Over an algebraically closed field \(\Omega\), the divisor presentation from AD.3 identifies \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1_\Omega)\) with \(\mathbf Z\) by degree. Every finite closed point is \(a\in\Omega\), and \(\operatorname{div}(t-a)=[a]-[\infty]\), so each divisor is equivalent to its degree times \([\infty]\). A rational function has divisor of degree zero: write it as a quotient of split polynomials and include its order at infinity. These observations prove both surjectivity and injectivity of the degree presentation. Global units are \(\Omega^\times\), on which the \(n\)-th power map is onto. Kummer therefore makes \(H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mu_n)=0\). The Kummer calculation (P.7), using the rational-unit vanishing (P.5), and the curve bounds of AL identify \(H^2(\mathbf P^1,\mu_n)=\Lambda\), with \(c\) mapping to \(1\), and give zero in higher degrees. The connected projective line has constant sections \(\Lambda\). Thus (BI.5) is a quasi-isomorphism on every geometric fibre. Proper comparison in BG.4 identifies these with its geometric stalks, which detect isomorphisms.

Under \(\alpha\), restriction \(Rp_*\Lambda\to\Lambda\) along \(i\) is projection onto the first summand. Its composite with the unit is the identity. Its composite with the other summand is zero because \(i^*\mathcal O(1)\) is the trivial line bundle and its Kummer class is zero. Apply proper pushforward to the open–closed triangle for \(\mathbf A^1_S\subset\mathbf P^1_S\). The map
\[
Rq_!\Lambda\longrightarrow Rp_*\Lambda
\xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}}\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-2]
\longrightarrow\Lambda(-1)[-2]
\tag{BI.6}
\]
is an isomorphism, as its long cohomology sequence shows. Formula (BI.6) specifies the map itself. Tensor with the Tate line and shift to obtain \(\operatorname{Tr}_q:Rq_!\Lambda(1)[2]\to\Lambda\). Proper-support base change, the unit, open extension and Kummer classes all commute with inverse image. Applying their maps to (BI.6) proves base-change compatibility of this trace. On each fibre it is the degree-normalized compact curve trace.

### BI.3. Étale transfer is transpose to restriction

For a separated étale map \(u:V\to U\) of smooth curves over an algebraically closed field, its transfer on compact cohomology is induced by the counit \(u_!u^{-1}\Lambda\to\Lambda\). Its stalk formula sums the values at the finitely many lifts, as proved in BH.1's extension-by-zero provider. This transfer preserves the degree-normalized curve trace.

To check the last assertion at the needed generality, complete the target to a smooth projective curve. For each component of \(V\), its nonconstant map gives a finite separable extension of the target function field. Normalize the completion in that extension. AG.1–AG.4 give a smooth proper curve finite over the target completion, and P.3 makes it projective. Its function field is the chosen component field of \(V\). The DVR-extension and normal-target open-immersion argument in P.3 therefore identifies that component of \(V\) with an open in this normalization. The map to the target completion agrees with the original map on their common dense open, hence everywhere on \(V\) by separatedness. On this open the finite-map trace restricts to the étale summation counit. More explicitly, over the dense unramified locus both maps sum the same sheets; maps from \(u_!\Lambda\) into the constant sheaf are determined by adjunction on \(V\), where they are the constant value \(1\) on each sheet. Thus they agree everywhere. The determinant and divisor calculation in AJ.5 proves the finite-trace and open-completion compatibility used in [Poincaré duality for curves, Proposition 2.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/poincare-duality-for-curves#2-the-trace-and-its-normalization). Their composite proves the assertion for \(u\).

For classes \(a\in H^r_c(V,\Lambda(1))\) and \(b\in H^{2-r}(U,\Lambda)\), the projection formula and the counit give
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_U\bigl(u_!a\mathbin\cup b\bigr)
=\operatorname{Tr}_V\bigl(a\mathbin\cup u^{-1}b\bigr).
\tag{BI.7}
\]
This is an equality of the actual pairings. To verify it, apply BH.7's projection map to \(u_!(\Lambda(1))\otimes^L\Lambda\), then evaluation. Its transpose under \(u_!\dashv u^{-1}\) is the identity coefficient pairing on \(V\). Composing with compact pushforward and the trace identity just proved gives (BI.7). The compact class remains first, so no interchange sign is introduced.

The finite and mutually perfect curve pairings are proved by the full argument in Sections 4–11 of that companion: AJ.1–AJ.3 supply the ramified-coefficient calculation, and AJ.4 supplies the finite counting and effacement inputs without a Jacobian pairing assumption. AK and AL supply their cohomological finiteness and degree bounds. Formula (BI.7) proves that compact transitions in AI.3 are exactly the duals of ordinary restrictions. It also proves the same assertion after passing from a separably closed geometric field to its algebraic closure, using the topological invariance in BE.4. This step concerns these curve pairings, without assuming the higher-dimensional smooth duality being proved.

### BI.4. Finite chains of triangles suffice

The trace arrows form an inverse system of arrows. A cone for each arrow need not come with a chosen functor on all arrows. We now state the precise finite construction used in AI.3–AI.4.

On a fixed base, write a trace triangle as
\[
K_i\xrightarrow{t_i}T_i\longrightarrow C_i\longrightarrow K_i[1],
\qquad K_i\in D^{[0,2]},\quad T_i\in D^{[2,2]},
\tag{BI.8}
\]
and suppose \(H^2(t_i)\) is surjective. In the relative-curve case, \(T_i=\Lambda(-1)[-2]\). After extension along a base neighbourhood it is its exact étale extension by zero; the same degree statements hold. The long exact sequence gives canonical identifications
\[
\begin{aligned}
H^{-1}(C_i)&=H^0(K_i),\\
H^0(C_i)&=H^1(K_i),\\
H^1(C_i)&=\ker\bigl(H^2(K_i)\to H^2(T_i)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\tag{BI.9}
\]
and all other cohomology is zero. For every commuting square between trace arrows, the triangle-map axiom gives a map between chosen cones. Its induced maps in (BI.9) are forced by the square, regardless of the chosen completion. The explicit cone formula in B.1 proves that axiom in the complexes used by BF; here no functorial choice of completions is needed. The terminology agrees with [Stacks, Tag 05QK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05QK).

Suppose a refinement kills the three maps in (BI.9). Every completion of its square is then a ghost. For completeness, let a finite chain of ghosts have all its objects in \(D^{[a,b]}\). After \(m\) steps its composite factors through the truncation \(\tau_{\leq b-m}\) of its target. This is an induction. Given the factorization after \(m\) steps, compose its last truncation with the next ghost \(v\). Its composite with \(\tau_{\geq b-m}\) of the new target is zero: by t-structure orthogonality the map into that truncation is determined by the map on \(H^{b-m}\), which \(v\) kills. The truncation triangle therefore factors it through \(\tau_{\leq b-m-1}\). For \(m=b-a+1\) this target truncation is zero, proving the assertion. Four steps suffice in the interval \([-1,2]\) used in AI.3; (BI.9) even permits the smaller interval \([-1,1]\).

For any fixed trace arrow, perform the constructible compactness refinement of AI.3, then repeat it three more times, descending the finitely many schemes and zero sheaf maps as in AI.4. At that finite stage, shrink the base to a pointed affine open in the intersection of the images of its finitely many smooth curve maps. Each image is open and contains the selected point, so this is an allowed refinement and makes every fibre nonempty. The top trace maps are then surjective on that actual base, so (BI.9) applies there. On that one final base neighbourhood, choose triangle completions for these four consecutive squares. Their composite is zero by the ghost argument. It is still a morphism of triangles, over the composite of the prescribed trace-arrow squares. Exact étale extension by zero carries it to a zero cone map on the original base. Thus every target trace triangle admits a later trace triangle and a morphism to it whose cone component is zero. This finite assertion is all that is required; no globally coherent cone system has been assumed.

### BI.5. Direct proof of the filtered Hom comparison

Let \(K_i\to T_i\) be the actual inverse system of trace arrows on \(S\). Assume the finite zero-cone assertion just proved. For any complex \(A\), composition gives
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_i\operatorname{Hom}(T_i,A[r])
\longrightarrow
\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_i\operatorname{Hom}(K_i,A[r]).
\tag{BI.10}
\]
Here the two Hom systems are defined by the actual transitions of \(K\) and \(T\), so their colimits need no choice of cone transitions.

To prove surjectivity, represent a class by \(a:K_i\to A[r]\). Choose a later triangle mapping to the triangle at \(i\) with zero cone map \(C_j\to C_i\). The obstruction to extending \(a\) from \(K_i\) to \(T_i\) is its composite with the boundary \(C_i[-1]\to K_i\). At stage \(j\) this obstruction factors through the zero map \(C_j[-1]\to C_i[-1]\). Exactness of Hom applied to the triangle at \(j\) therefore extends the restricted \(a\) to \(T_j\).

For injectivity, represent a class by \(b:T_i\to A[r]\) whose restriction becomes zero in the right colimit. At a later stage it restricts to zero on \(K\). Replace \(i\) by that stage. Exactness of Hom now factors \(b\) through \(T_i\to C_i\). Choose a further triangle with zero cone map into this one. The restriction of \(b\) to its \(T_j\) factors through that zero map and is zero. This proves injectivity and hence (BI.10) for every integer \(r\), with no boundedness imposed on \(A\).

For \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\), take the pointed pairs \((U,V)\) and selected strict base maps of AT.4. Put
\[
K_{U,V}=R(qj_U)_!\Lambda,
\qquad T_{U,V}=j_{V,!}\Lambda(-1)[-2].
\tag{BI.11}
\]
We may restrict to pairs whose smooth map \(U\to V\) is surjective: its open image contains the selected base point, and shrinking \(V\) to a pointed affine open in that image is a cofinal refinement. Define the trace arrow by (BI.6), the étale counit for \(U\to\mathbf A^1_V\), and extension along \(j_V\). Transitivity of those counits makes its refinement squares commute. BI.3 identifies its fibre pairings and transitions. AT.4 supplies the ordinary fibre colimit; finiteness kills the unwanted compact cohomology and the top trace kernel. Nonempty fibres make the top trace surjective. Constructible compactness and finite descent in AI.3–AI.4 give exactly the hypothesis of BI.4, so (BI.10) applies.

The projection from pointed pairs to either their source or base neighbourhoods is cofinal: a prescribed finite list is refined by fibre products and then a pointed affine chart, and parallel maps agree after a pointed étale refinement. The selected base map is retained throughout, as in (AT.9). The left colimit in (BI.10) is therefore \(H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s}\), by the exact étale adjunction and the same K-injective stalk calculation as BI.1. The right colimit is \(H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}\) by (BI.2). Consequently
\[
H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s}
\xrightarrow{\sim}H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}.
\tag{BI.12}
\]
Finally this is the stalk map of the specified comparison \(q^{-1}A(1)[2]\to q^!A\). Define that comparison by transposing the projection formula followed by \(A\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_q\). Test it by \(j_{U,!}\Lambda[-r]\) in (BI.1). Adjunction, BH.7's counit compatibility, and the definition of the neighbourhood trace turn that test into precomposition by \(K_{U,V}\to T_{U,V}\), which is precisely (BI.10). This proves the assertion about the map, including its orientation. Since exact geometric stalks detect quasi-isomorphisms, it proves the arbitrary-complex affine-line formula used in Proposition 3.3.

## Appendix BJ. Coordinate independence and the smooth trace

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated and smooth of constant relative dimension \(d\), between finite-type schemes over a field \(k\). Fix \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\), with \(n\geq2\) invertible in \(k\). The trace will first be constructed as a map of cohomology sheaves. This lets us compare coordinates on geometric fibres before transposing the trace to an exceptional inverse image. BF–BI supply the ordinary unbounded operations and the affine-line comparison used below.

### BJ.1. Top cohomology and descent on the source

For a separated finite-type map \(h:Y\to S\) with fibres of dimension at most \(e\),
\[
R^rh_!F=0\quad(r>2e)
\tag{BJ.1}
\]
for every \(\Lambda\)-sheaf \(F\). To see the precise dimension used here, compactify \(h\) and apply the geometric-fibre formula of BG. At a geometric fibre let \(Z\) be the reduced closure of \(Y_{\bar s}\) in that proper fibre. Its dimension is at most \(e\): its finitely many components meet the dense open \(Y_{\bar s}\), and a finite-type integral scheme over a field and a dense open have the same function field and dimension. The extended coefficient sheaf is zero off \(Z\), so it is the exact closed direct image of its restriction to \(Z\), as the stalk formula verifies. BG.2's proper bound on \(Z\) gives (BJ.1). Thus a compactification with larger boundary fibres causes no change to the bound.

It follows that \(Q_h=R^{2e}h_!\) is right exact on sheaves. In the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence, the obstruction to surjectivity is \(R^{2e+1}h_!\), which is zero. It also preserves finite direct sums. For a finite jointly surjective family of separated étale maps \(u_i:U_i\to Y\), the sequence
\[
\bigoplus_{i,j}u_{ij,!}u_{ij}^{-1}F
\longrightarrow\bigoplus_i u_{i,!}u_i^{-1}F
\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow0,
\qquad U_{ij}=U_i\times_YU_j,
\tag{BJ.2}
\]
is exact. The first map is the difference of the projection counits. At a geometric stalk the middle term is the direct sum of copies of \(F_{\bar y}\) indexed by all lifts, and the first map imposes all relations \(e_a m-e_b m\). The set of lifts is nonempty, so summation identifies the quotient with \(F_{\bar y}\). Exact stalks prove (BJ.2). Applying \(Q_h\) gives the corresponding right exact sequence of top compact direct images. A map out of \(Q_h(F)\) is therefore determined by compatible maps on the cover.

For maps \(g:Z\to Y\), \(h:Y\to S\) of fibre dimensions at most \(b,a\), respectively, truncation gives the natural isomorphism
\[
R^{2(a+b)}(hg)_!F
\simeq R^{2a}h_!R^{2b}g_!F.
\tag{BJ.3}
\]
Indeed \(Rg_!F\) has cohomology in \([0,2b]\). Apply \(Rh_!\) to its triangle with top quotient \(R^{2b}g_!F[-2b]\). The remaining term has finitely many cohomology sheaves in degrees at most \(2b-1\); successive good-truncation triangles and (BJ.1) place its image in degrees at most \(2(a+b)-1\). Taking the next degree proves (BJ.3). This argument uses only a finite interval, even though the operation itself is defined on unbounded complexes.

We compose top trace maps by (BJ.3) and the invertible-twist projection formula. This composition is associative: for three maps, the two orders are the two routes through the naturality square of the middle truncation map after truncating the innermost complex. Applying the outer direct image and taking top cohomology identifies the routes. The same square permits coefficient maps at each stage. Exact pullback commutes with these truncations; BG's base-change and composition comparisons therefore make (BJ.3) compatible with base change.

### BJ.2. Coordinate maps and a change in one coordinate

The local presentation from AE.1 writes a smooth affine algebra, after shrinking, as
\[
B=\bigl(A[x_1,\ldots,x_m]/(F_1,\ldots,F_c)\bigr)_h
\tag{BJ.4}
\]
with an invertible \(c\)-column Jacobian minor. Its differential module has rank \(m-c=d\), and the remaining \(d\) variables define an étale map to \(\mathbf A^d_A\). The square-zero lifting check solves the \(c\) error equations uniquely using that minor; AE.1 supplies flatness of the presentation. This is the coordinate construction also described in [Stacks, Tag 054L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054L).

More generally, if functions \(z_1,\ldots,z_d\) have differential classes forming a basis at a point of a smooth \(A\)-scheme, they are étale coordinates near that point. Lift them to the localized polynomial ring in (BJ.4) and adjoin the equations \(z_i-Z_i\) over \(A[Z_1,\ldots,Z_d]\). Their rows, together with the rows of the \(F_j\), form an invertible square Jacobian precisely when the \(dz_i\) give the stated basis modulo the original relations. Clearing the finitely many denominators and inverting that determinant gives the unique square-zero correction and the flat presentation just used. This proves the criterion without treating a tangent-space calculation alone as étaleness.

Over an algebraically closed field \(\Omega\), two coordinate maps \(u,v:W\to\mathbf A^d_\Omega\) can be joined locally by a finite sequence in which only one coordinate changes at each step. At a closed point, their differential bases differ by a matrix in \(\mathrm{GL}_d(\Omega)\). Gaussian elimination expresses it by row additions and nonzero row scalings: choose a nonzero pivot, move it to the diagonal, scale it, eliminate its column and continue on the smaller square matrix. A row interchange itself is a sequence of single-row changes,
\[
(a,b)\mapsto(a+b,b)\mapsto(a+b,-a)
\mapsto(b,-a)\mapsto(b,a).
\tag{BJ.5}
\]
Each intermediate basis is invertible, including in characteristic two. Apply these operations to the functions \(u_i\). The resulting tuple \(z\) has \(dz_i=dv_i\) at the chosen point. Replacing its functions successively by the \(v_i\) keeps a differential basis there. The preceding criterion makes every intermediate tuple étale on one common open neighbourhood. These opens cover \(W\): a nonempty closed complement in a finite-type \(\Omega\)-scheme would have a closed point, by Y.5. Quasi-compactness gives a finite subcover.

### BJ.3. Relative curves and products of affine lines

For a relative affine line use exactly the trace of (BI.6). For a smooth relative curve \(h:C\to S\), cover the source by finitely many coordinate opens \(u_i:C_i\to\mathbf A^1_S\). Compose the étale counit with the affine-line trace to obtain
\[
t_i:R^2(hu_i')_!\Lambda(1)\longrightarrow\Lambda,
\tag{BJ.6}
\]
where \(u_i':C_i\hookrightarrow C\) denotes the open inclusion. At each geometric base point this is the degree-normalized trace of the smooth fibre curve, by BI.3. On each overlap the two maps therefore agree as sheaf maps, since their geometric stalks agree. Sequence (BJ.2), after applying top direct image, glues them uniquely to \(t_h:R^2h_!\Lambda(1)\to\Lambda\). Its fibre description proves independence of the cover and compatibility with arbitrary étale refinement. Base change follows by pulling back (BJ.2), using exact inverse image and BG's compact-support comparison; every coordinate trace pulls back to the same coordinate trace. None of this construction uses a higher-dimensional orientation.

For \(p_{d,S}:\mathbf A^d_S\to S\), compose \(d\) copies of the affine-line trace using (BJ.3). Denote the result by \(t_{d,S}\). It commutes with base change and is unaffected by grouping consecutive coordinates. It is also invariant under coordinate permutations. Here are the product and sign checks. For structural maps \(a:V\to S\), \(b:W\to S\), first push the external tensor product along \(V\times_SW\to V\). Proper-support base change and the projection formula identify that pushforward with \(F\otimes^La^{-1}Rb_!G\); the outer projection formula then gives
\[
R(a\pi_V)_!(F\boxtimes G)
\simeq Ra_!F\otimes^LRb_!G.
\tag{BJ.7}
\]
The external product comparison is induced by the two counits and tensor evaluation, so reversing the factors reverses those two counits and applies the graded tensor symmetry of (BH.8). Equivalently, compactify the two maps: extension by zero commutes with external tensor on stalks, and the proper comparison is the transpose of the tensor of the two proper counits. This identifies (BJ.7) and its symmetry with the specified maps, rather than an arbitrary isomorphism.

On each geometric fibre, the tensor of the \(d\) positive degree-two affine-line classes generates \(H_c^{2d}(\mathbf A^d,\Lambda(d))\), by (BJ.7) and BI.2. Its iterated trace is \(1\). An adjacent permutation exchanges two degree-two factors and hence multiplies by \((-1)^4=1\). It fixes that generator and the trace. All permutations are products of adjacent ones; geometric stalks now prove invariance of \(t_{d,S}\). The dimension-zero case is the étale summation counit and satisfies the same composition rule directly by summing lifts.

### BJ.4. Independence of coordinates

For an étale chart \(u:X\to\mathbf A^d_S\), let
\[
t(f,u)=t_{d,S}\circ R^{2d}p_{d,S!}\bigl(\varepsilon_u(d)\bigr).
\tag{BJ.8}
\]
Composition of lower shrieks identifies its source with \(R^{2d}f_!\Lambda(d)\). For an étale refinement \(v:V\to X\), the composite counit is summation over successive lifts, and is the counit for \(uv\). Thus restricting (BJ.8) by transfer from \(V\) gives \(t(fv,uv)\).

Compare two charts of the same \(f\). Their candidate maps are sheaf maps and commute with base change, so it suffices to compare them over algebraically closed geometric fields. BJ.2 and the source-cover descent (BJ.2) reduce the problem to charts differing in one coordinate on a common open. By permutation invariance, place that coordinate last. Their first \(d-1\) functions give the same smooth relative curve map
\[
h:W\longrightarrow\mathbf A^{d-1}_\Omega.
\tag{BJ.9}
\]
Both last coordinates are étale maps from that relative curve to its relative affine line. BJ.3 says their inner traces are the same map \(t_h\). Composing with \(t_{d-1,\Omega}\), using the associativity proved after (BJ.3), makes the two maps (BJ.8) equal. For \(d=1\) this is already the curve comparison; for \(d=0\) it is summation. Thus (BJ.8) is independent of coordinates in every dimension.

For a general \(f\), choose a finite coordinate cover, locally on \(S\) if necessary. On overlaps its traces now agree, so the right exact sequence from (BJ.2) gives a unique
\[
t_f:R^{2d}f_!\Lambda(d)\longrightarrow\Lambda_S.
\tag{BJ.10}
\]
Refining two covers to their intersections proves independence of the cover. It also proves compatibility with étale localization on the source.
