These are equalities of actual morphisms of sheaves, not an inference from dimensions of cohomology groups. Over overlapping base opens the same construction agrees, so ordinary sheaf descent defines (BJ.10) on all of \(S\).

### BJ.5. From the trace to the unbounded smooth adjunction

The bound (BJ.1) puts \(Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\) in \(D^{\leq0}\). For \(K\in D^{\leq0}\) and a degree-zero sheaf \(B\), the truncation triangle gives
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_D(K,B)=\operatorname{Hom}(H^0K,B).
\tag{BJ.11}
\]
Both adjoining Hom groups vanish by t-structure orthogonality: they have source \(\tau_{\leq-1}K\) or its shift by \(1\), and target in \(D^{\geq0}\). Therefore (BJ.10) specifies a unique derived trace \(T_f:Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\to\Lambda\). Transpose, for every complex \(A\), the map
\[
Rf_!\bigl(f^{-1}A(d)[2d]\bigr)
\simeq A\otimes^LRf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]
\xrightarrow{1\otimes T_f}A
\tag{BJ.12}
\]
to obtain \(\theta_{f,A}:f^{-1}A(d)[2d]\to f^!A\). BH.7 proves the arbitrary-complex projection formula and its counit compatibility, so this is defined without a finite Tor-dimension assumption.

On a coordinate open it is the composite of the affine-line isomorphisms (BI.12) and exact étale inverse image. Indeed its transposed counit is the composed coordinate trace by (BJ.8) and (BJ.11). Uniqueness of the adjunction transpose identifies the maps. Exact étale restriction and BI.1's local adjunction therefore show that \(\theta_{f,A}\) is an isomorphism on every source neighbourhood and hence on every geometric stalk. It is an isomorphism in the unbounded derived category. This proves (3.7) with the coordinate-independent orientation just constructed.

### BJ.6. Composition, base change and the parameter section

There is one interchange needed for composition. For étale \(u:X\to A\), form \(u':\mathbf A^e_X\to\mathbf A^e_A\), with vertical projections \(q,r\). Under the canonical composition comparison, the two maps
\[
\varepsilon_u\circ u_!t_{e,X}
\quad\text{and}\quad
t_{e,A}\circ R^{2e}r_!\bigl(\varepsilon_{u'}(e)\bigr)
\tag{BJ.13}
\]
agree. At a geometric point of \(A\), each sends a finite family of top affine-space classes indexed by the lifts in \(X\) to the sum of their traces. BG's fibre and composition comparisons and the étale stalk formula identify these as the stalks of the displayed maps. Stalks detect equality, proving (BJ.13).

For smooth maps \(g:Y\to X\) and \(f:X\to S\) of dimensions \(e,d\), choose successive coordinate opens. Their concatenation is an étale chart into \(\mathbf A^{d+e}_S\). Formula (BJ.13) moves the intermediate étale counit past the affine-space trace; associativity after (BJ.3) then identifies its trace with \(t_f\) composed with \(t_g\). Sequence (BJ.2) extends this equality from the source cover to the entire map. Equation (BJ.11) makes it the equality of derived traces. Applying the projection formula and transposing (BJ.12) proves the corresponding composition of the \(\theta_{f,A}\). All orientation shifts are even, so no additional sign occurs.

Base change pulls a coordinate cover to a coordinate cover, preserves the right exact sequence (BJ.2), and preserves each coordinate trace by BI.2, (BJ.3) and (BJ.7). It therefore preserves (BJ.10) and (BJ.12). In a cartesian square with base map \(b:S'\to S\) and source map \(b_X\), the usual exceptional comparison is the transpose of
\[
Rf'_!b_X^{-1}f^!A
\simeq b^{-1}Rf_!f^!A\longrightarrow b^{-1}A.
\tag{BJ.14}
\]
Under the two smooth isomorphisms, both sides of its transpose identify with \(f'^{-1}b^{-1}A(d)[2d]\), and trace compatibility makes the map the identity. Thus it is the canonical base-change isomorphism, including its counit. These assertions apply to the changes of base in the stated field scope; the same coordinate traces and top-degree comparisons pull back along arbitrary base maps for which the compact-support construction is used.

In particular take the parameter-line projection \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\). The base-change isomorphism just proved gives (3.8). If \(s:S\to\mathbf A^1_S\) is a parameter section, transitivity for \(qs=\mathrm{id}\) and the affine-line formula give, for every \(B\),
\[
s^!q^{-1}B=B(-1)[-2].
\tag{BJ.15}
\]
This follows by canceling the pulled-back invertible Tate line in \(s^!q^!B=B\), using (BH.21). Its coefficient orientation is the positive point class. The two-open Kummer calculation of AI.2 applies to the standard charts of \(\mathbf P^1_S\): it uses their transition function and the exact coefficient sequences, and gives the image of \(-\lambda\kappa(t-t_0)\) as \(c_1^{(n)}(\mathcal O(s))\). The section divisor has line bundle \(\mathcal O(1)\), so (BI.6) sends this class to \(1\). Transitivity says that the composite section counit followed by the affine-line trace is the identity. Hence its generator is precisely that negative boundary, fixing the sign in (BJ.15) without a closed-base-change assumption for a general exceptional inverse image.

Finally, if \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) is a closed immersion of smooth \(S\)-schemes of relative dimensions \(d-c,d\), write \(g=fi\). Transitivity gives \(i^!f^!A=g^!A\). Substituting the proved smooth formulas and canceling the invertible twist gives
\[
i^!f^{-1}A\simeq g^{-1}A(-c)[-2c].
\tag{BJ.16}
\]
For \(A=\Lambda\) this is the smooth-pair purity identification in (3.9). Its counit defines the corresponding Gysin map; composition of such maps is composition of adjunction counits, by the triangle identities. This conclusion concerns these smooth pairs. It introduces no assertion of absolute purity for arbitrary regular schemes or a normalized adic comparison.

## Classical and arithmetic scope

The arithmetic constructions distinguish finite coefficients, complete integral coefficients and rational coefficients. Their geometric and categorical hypotheses enter at different stages. Appendix M gives the ordinary-image finiteness and singular biduality arguments over fields. M.5 proves the bounded-below internal-Hom restriction, closed-support comparison, nonfree lisse calculation and dimension-corrected generic evaluation; M.6 identifies double evaluation after proper global sections, and M.7 specifies the dual exchanges by their adjunction tests. These arguments retain their exact prerequisite and coefficient hypotheses. Propositions 3.2–3.3 prove the stated finite-coefficient proper finiteness and smooth trace/duality/smooth-pair purity from their identified programme foundations. The geometric ingredients are organized as follows. AU.1–AU.6 prove the locally Noetherian proper geometry, coherent finiteness and formal-functions chain. AV.1–AV.6 prove the arbitrary-base approximation, Chow modification and Stein factorization. AW.1–AW.6 prove the arbitrary-base separated quasi-finite factorization and finite-cover refinement. AX.1–AX.7 prove henselian-pair idempotent lifting, arbitrary-sheaf degree-zero restriction, arbitrary-base finite direct image and full faithfulness for finite étale covers. AY.1–AY.6 complete arbitrary-sheaf proper degree-zero comparison, including faithfully flat section descent and the exact geometric-fibre identification. AZ.1–AZ.6 prove compactness, finite-stage descent and the finite-direct-image embedding for constructible coefficients over arbitrary qcqs schemes. BA.1–BA.7 prove affine closed-subscheme effacement for torsion sheaves and arbitrary-base higher continuity. BB.1–BB.4 prove henselization along arbitrary ideals, affine henselian comparison and restricted-injective vanishing, with module cohomology justified. BC.1–BC.6 prove coherent algebraization and proper finite-torsor lifting over complete Noetherian pairs, and projective-line comparison over complete Noetherian local rings. BD.1–BD.6 prove finite-cover descent and pointed approximation on local integer models, then finite-cover and torsor lifting for proper schemes over arbitrary henselian local rings and projective-line comparison there. BE.1–BE.8 prove general higher proper comparison for arbitrary torsion sheaves, bounded-below complexes with torsion cohomology, and arbitrary changes of base, with the actual geometric-fibre map. BF.1–BF.6 construct the unbounded ordinary derived categories, their triangles and coproducts, derived adjunction, and sheaf representability. BG.1–BG.6 prove finite relative cohomological bounds, unbounded proper comparison and coproduct preservation, and construct compactification-independent proper support and its right adjoint at the stated field scope. BH.1–BH.7 construct étale K-flat models, the unbounded derived tensor–Hom adjunction, arbitrary-complex projection formulas and the canonical invertible-twist comparison. BI.1–BI.5 give the local and internal adjunctions, the specified affine-line trace, its transfer pairings and the arbitrary-complex stalk comparison using finite chains of triangles. BJ.1–BJ.6 construct the coordinate-independent top trace by single-coordinate changes and curve traces, and prove the unbounded smooth adjunction, composition, base change and smooth-pair Gysin counit. Specialization comparisons and enhanced operation compatibilities require their specified geometric inputs. The field-scope argument does not assert general absolute purity. The algebraic and completed-local node criterion, the two actual normalization points and their analytic comparison are proved in L.1–L.4. L.3–L.5 also prove finite normalization of complex curves and the smooth-branch comparison used in Exercise 3.

Appendices A–E prove the classical resolutions, localization, puncture, branch, cone, orientation, Thom–Gysin and plane-curve calculations. Appendices F–H construct the structural and general classical proper-support operations, their bounds, pairings, adjoints and the identities before biduality. Appendices I–J prove normal local triviality, coefficient comparison, canonical biduality, compact-link finiteness, both point dual exchanges and fixed-stratification duality. Appendix K proves algebraic Whitney refinements and compatible map stratifications, followed by constructibility of all six classical operations and internal Hom. Its algebraic and analytic curve-selection prerequisites are proved in K.1–K.4. Appendix L gives the node and smooth-branch normalization arguments, including completion and discrete-valuation algebra.

The classical topological link calculations apply over the complex numbers. The finite-coefficient singular étale argument is given separately in Appendix M. Appendix N supplies finite-cover monodromy, effective descent, compatible lisse systems, stable lattices and the congruence-cover construction. AJ.1–AJ.3 prove the wild-inertia and ramified-coefficient calculations at strict smooth curve points. Smooth-pair Gysin comparisons use the positive trace and negative Kummer-boundary convention of BI–BJ. BK–BX treat completion, integral operations and rationalization. These étale constructions do not identify a positive-characteristic neighbourhood with a classical topological link.

## Appendix BK. Derived reductions and completed comparison maps

Let \(O\) be a complete discrete valuation ring, with uniformizer \(\pi\) and residue characteristic \(\ell\), and put \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). Work with the constant coefficient ring \(\underline O\) on a pro-étale site. The completed constant sheaf \(\widehat O=\varprojlim\underline{O_n}\) need not be \(\underline O\). Completion below is a construction on complexes of \(\underline O\)-modules; restricting scalars also lets us apply it to complexes already carrying a \(\widehat O\)-action. We do not identify these two coefficient sheaves.

### BK.1. The site properties used in the limit

[The pro-étale site and ℓ-adic complexes, §1](course:AG-LTF/the-pro-etale-site-and-l-adic-complexes#1-enlarging-the-covers) proves two covering constructions over arbitrary rings. Theorem 1.1d refines a weakly étale affine object by a faithfully flat ind-étale cover whose composite to the base is ind-étale. Theorem 1.1f gives covers by w-contractible affines. Its proof first constructs w-local rings with strictly henselian maximal local rings, then replaces the profinite component space by an extremally disconnected cover. The retraction argument uses the local rigidity proof in Lemma 1.1a and the component-space constructions in Lemmas 1.1b–1.1e. These are the covering results used here; weakly étale does not mean ind-étale without refinement.

Evaluation on a w-contractible affine \(W\) takes sheaf epimorphisms to surjections: a lift exists on a finite affine cover, its disjoint union has a retraction to \(W\), and pulling the lift along that section gives a lift on \(W\). Successively lifting over such a cover proves repleteness, the assertion that the limit of a tower of epimorphisms surjects onto its first term locally. It also proves exactness of countable products of abelian sheaves. Given sections in the targets of countably many epimorphisms, the sheaves of lifts of the first \(r\) sections form a tower of epimorphisms; a compatible limit supplies all lifts at once. Kernels and finite products already commute with products, so the product functor is exact.

For a tower of complexes with actual transition maps, its homotopy limit is consequently
\[
\operatorname{holim}_n A_n
=\operatorname{Cone}\left(\prod_n A_n
 \xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_n A_n\right)[-1],
\qquad s(a)_n=u_n(a_{n+1}).
\tag{BK.1}
\]
This computes the derived inverse limit, including for unbounded complexes. Here is a resolution description. At level \(n\), embed a sheaf tower into \(B_n=\prod_{j\leq n}A_j\) by its maps to earlier levels. The quotient map takes successive differences \(x_j-u_jx_{j+1}\), and has target \(C_n=\prod_{j<n}A_j\). It is surjective by finite backward substitution. Both new towers are products of towers that are zero before a specified index and constant afterwards. The latter are the exact right adjoints to evaluation at that index. Injective resolutions and exact countable products show that \(B,C\) are limit-acyclic and give the two-term limit resolution (BK.1). On complexes this same finite resolution gives the displayed cone. Products preserve quasi-isomorphisms because they preserve cycle, boundary and cohomology sequences, so the formula also applies to unbounded complexes. All tower maps below will be specified; no inverse limit of mere isomorphism classes is taken.

### BK.2. Classical coefficients on the enlarged site

Write \(\nu:X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\to X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\). We give the particular comparison needed for reductions. On an affine ind-étale object \(U=\varprojlim U_i\) over an affine part of \(X\), define the pullback of an étale sheaf \(F\) by
\[
(\nu^*F)(U)=\varinjlim_i F(U_i).
\tag{BK.2}
\]
This description is independent of the presentation: maps between finite-presentation étale objects and their equalities descend to a common stage. It is a sheaf on the ind-étale basis. Indeed a finite family of ind-étale maps covering \(U\) can first be expressed through finite families of finitely presented étale maps over \(U\); each such family covers, since its images contain those of the limiting cover. These are finite families, not assertions that the individual morphisms are finite. A finite-presentation family and its covering property then descend to a stage of \(U\). The sheaf equalizer there passes to the filtered colimit, which commutes with the finite products and equalizer. Affine refinement from BK.1 makes this a basis for the whole site. The definitions agree on overlapping affine parts of \(X\), so they glue.

On an étale object (BK.2) is \(F(U)\). Conversely, sections of a pro-étale sheaf on the finite stages restrict to its sections on \(U\). These maps give the adjunction counit; on represented sections both triangle identities are identities. Thus the construction is \(\nu^*\) and satisfies \(\nu_*\nu^*F=F\). It preserves finite limits by the filtered-colimit formula, and preserves cokernels by its left adjunction. It is therefore exact on module sheaves.

If \(I\) is an injective étale module sheaf, the positive Čech cohomology of \(\nu^*I\) for any finite basis cover vanishes. Express the cover and its finite fibre products by the two stage systems just used. Each degree of its Čech complex is a filtered colimit of the corresponding degree on an étale cover of an étale object. Those augmented complexes are acyclic: the augmented free-sheaf Čech resolution is locally contracted by a section of the cover, and Hom into the restricted injective is exact. Exact filtered colimits preserve this acyclicity.

This Čech assertion implies derived acyclicity on every basis object. Embed a sheaf with those vanishings into an injective. A quotient section lifts on a cover; the differences of its lifts form a Čech 1-cocycle, whose coboundary expression corrects the lifts so that they glue. The quotient map is therefore surjective on sections of each basis object. Its quotient has the same positive Čech vanishings by the short exact sequences of Čech complexes. Iterating gives all higher derived vanishings. Applying this argument to \(\nu^*I\), and then to a bounded-below injective resolution, proves
\[
L\simeq R\nu_*\nu^*L\qquad(L\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)).
\tag{BK.3}
\]
Restriction of injectives to an étale object is justified by its exact extension-by-zero left adjoint, as in M.5. Thus the calculation is local on the base and applies to module sheaves, not just sets.

For a qcqs map \(f:X\to Y\), evaluate on an affine ind-étale \(V=\varprojlim V_i\) over \(Y\). The cohomology of the left side below is computed on \(X\times_YV\). Formula (BK.3) and qcqs étale cohomological continuity identify it with the colimit of the cohomologies on \(X\times_YV_i\). Sheafifying and using the bounded-below cohomology spectral sequence gives
\[
Rf_{\mathrm{pro\acute et},*}\nu_X^*L
 \simeq\nu_Y^*Rf_{\mathrm{\acute et},*}L.
\tag{BK.4}
\]
The continuity and finite-stage descent here are the actual statements proved in AH, AK and BA, and in §§1–3 of the cited pro-étale lesson. The maps in (BK.2) are restriction maps, so (BK.4) identifies the adjunction comparison itself. Pullback commutes with \(\nu^*\) on those same represented sections. This will identify the finite-level base-change arrows, not merely their objects.

### BK.3. The reduction complexes and their arrows

Put
\[
P_n=[\underline O\xrightarrow{\pi^n}\underline O],
\qquad \deg P_n=(-1,0).
\tag{BK.5}
\]
The augmentation \(P_n\to\underline{O_n}\) is a quasi-isomorphism, since multiplication by \(\pi^n\) is injective on \(O\). Both terms are free, so \(P_n\otimes K\) computes \(K_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n\) for every complex \(K\), without a boundedness or flatness assumption on \(K\). The finite cone of free tensor functors preserves quasi-isomorphisms.

For \(m\geq n\), use the chain map \(P_m\to P_n\) whose degree-zero component is the identity and whose degree-minus-one component is \(\pi^{m-n}\). Its two composites with the differentials are both \(\pi^m\). The maps compose exactly. They induce the quotient maps \(O_m\to O_n\), and give an actual tower of reductions, with the commuting triangles
\[
K\xrightarrow{\pi^n}K\longrightarrow K_n,
\qquad (K\to K)\text{ transitions }(\pi,1).
\tag{BK.6}
\]
Multiplication by \(\pi^n\) on \(P_n\) is null-homotopic: the degree-zero to degree-minus-one component of the homotopy is the identity. Tensoring this homotopy with \(K\), with the usual tensor differential, gives the same assertion on \(K_n\).

### BK.4. Completion and unchanged derived reductions

Define
\[
C(K)=\operatorname{holim}_n K_n,
\qquad L_\pi(K)=\operatorname{holim}(\cdots\xrightarrow{\pi}K).
\tag{BK.7}
\]
The telescope resolution of \(\underline{O[1/\pi]}\) is the two-term complex of countable free sums with differential \(1-\pi s\). Its cokernel is the localization and its kernel is zero: a finite-support element in the kernel has zero first coordinate, and induction kills every coordinate. Internal Hom from those free sums is an exact countable product. This finite resolution therefore identifies \(L_\pi(K)\) with \(R\mathcal Hom(\underline{O[1/\pi]},K)\), even for unbounded \(K\).

Take the homotopy limits of the actual cone triangles (BK.6). Finite cones commute with the products in (BK.1), including their differentials. The limit of the middle constant tower is \(K\): \(1-s\) has kernel the diagonal copy of \(K\), and a chain-level right inverse obtained by the recursion \(x_1=0\), \(x_{n+1}=x_n-b_n\). We obtain the natural triangle
\[
L_\pi(K)\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow C(K).
\tag{BK.8}
\]
Multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on \(L_\pi(K)\), since precomposition by that invertible map of \(O[1/\pi]\) induces its multiplication map.

Call \(E\) derived complete when \(L_\pi(E)=0\). Each \(K_n\) is complete. In its \(\pi\)-tower, the shift operator \(\pi s\) has its \(n\)-th power null-homotopic by BK.3; hence \(1-\pi s\) has inverse \(1+\pi s+\cdots+(\pi s)^{n-1}\) in the derived category. Derived internal Hom from \(O[1/\pi]\) preserves products and fibres, being right adjoint to tensor with that flat localization. Complete objects are consequently closed under homotopy limits and fibres. Thus \(C(K)\) is complete, and (BK.8) proves that \(K\) is complete precisely when \(K\to C(K)\) is an isomorphism.

There are no maps in any degree from a complex on which \(\pi\) is invertible to a complete complex. To verify this, such a source \(A\) satisfies \(O[1/\pi]\otimes_O^LA\simeq A\): localization is exact, and its action on cohomology inverts an already invertible map. Tensor-Hom adjunction then identifies its derived Hom into \(E\) with Hom from \(A\) into \(L_\pi(E)=0\). Applying this to (BK.8) proves that \(C\) is left adjoint to inclusion of the complete objects, with the displayed unit.

Most importantly, tensoring (BK.8) with \(P_n\) kills its first term, since \(\pi^n\) is invertible there. Hence the unit gives the canonical isomorphism
\[
K\otimes_O^LO_n\xrightarrow{\sim}C(K)\otimes_O^LO_n.
\tag{BK.9}
\]
Thus completion does not alter a derived reduction. A map between complete complexes is an isomorphism if all its derived reductions are isomorphisms: its complete cone has zero reductions, so its expression (BK.7) is zero. This detection statement needs neither finite generation nor a uniform cohomological bound.

In fact the first derived reduction alone detects an isomorphism between complete complexes. Let \(E\) be its complete cone and suppose \(E\otimes_O^LO_1=0\). The triangle \(E\xrightarrow{\pi}E\to E\otimes_O^LO_1\) shows that multiplication by \(\pi\) is an isomorphism on \(E\). Every power \(\pi^n\) is then invertible, so the corresponding triangle gives \(E\otimes_O^LO_n=0\) for every \(n\). Completeness identifies \(E\) with the homotopy limit of these zero reductions, hence \(E=0\). This is a criterion for invertibility of a map; it does not assert that reduction is faithful on morphisms.

### BK.5. Direct image preserves this completion

For the map of pro-étale topoi induced by \(f\), exact inverse image on constant \(O\)-modules has derived right adjoint \(Rf_*\). The injective and K-injective construction of BF applies to this sheaf category as well: it is a Grothendieck category, with exact sheafification, exact filtered colimits and a set of site generators. A right adjoint preserves derived products and homotopy limits. Its \(O\)-linearity and exactness also give
\[
Rf_*(K\otimes_O^LO_n)\simeq (Rf_*K)\otimes_O^LO_n,
\qquad Rf_*C(K)\simeq C(Rf_*K).
\tag{BK.10}
\]
For the first map, apply \(Rf_*\) to the two-term free complex (BK.5), or to its cone triangle. A finite cone of K-injectives is K-injective, so the computation uses the same multiplication and transition maps as BK.3. The second map follows by taking their homotopy limits. This verifies the maps and their compatibility with the unit in (BK.8). It is a perfect-coefficient calculation, and does not require a general projection formula for arbitrary \(O\)-complexes. In particular direct image takes complete complexes to complete complexes.

### BK.6. The completed base-change arrow

For any Cartesian square as in Proposition 3.1, write \(g^*_{\mathrm{comp}}=Cg^*\). Start with the ordinary adjunction comparison \(\beta_K:g^*Rf_*K\to Rf'_*g'^*K\). Apply \(C\), and use (BK.10) on the target. This defines its completed comparison. If \(K\) is complete, the two objects identify canonically with
\[
\operatorname{holim}_n g^*Rf_*K_n,
\qquad
\operatorname{holim}_n Rf'_*g'^*K_n.
\tag{BK.11}
\]
Indeed exact pullback commutes with (BK.5), (BK.9) identifies the reductions after completion, and (BK.10) moves direct image past those reductions and limits. Under these identifications the completed arrow is \(\operatorname{holim}_n\beta_{K_n}\). The adjunction unit and counit are \(O\)-linear and commute with the two free terms and their multiplication maps; they therefore give exactly these compatible finite-level arrows. This also proves compatibility with composition of base changes.

Suppose each \(K_n\) comes from a bounded-below étale \(O_n\)-complex. Formula (BK.4) and its pullback compatibility identify \(\beta_{K_n}\) with the pullback of the bounded-below torsion comparison on the étale site. A power of \(\ell\) kills \(O_n\), because \(\ell\in(\pi)\); thus its coefficient condition is satisfied wherever \(\ell\) is invertible. When those torsion comparisons are isomorphisms, (BK.11) proves that the completed arrow is an isomorphism. The lower bound may depend on \(n\): comparison is applied separately at each level, and a derived limit preserves isomorphisms. A uniform bound or a constructibility theorem would be an additional input for a finiteness assertion.

For smooth changes of base, including the affine inverse limits in Proposition 3.1, AS.1–AS.7 now prove the required torsion comparison over arbitrary bases, with the qcqs direct-image hypothesis and each invertible modulus. The general geometric proof uses AM–AN, AR and arithmetic normalization AG.5. Applying it at every finite reduction in (BK.11) proves the completed comparison with those hypotheses. This geometric input and the formal completion argument have different roles: neither their conjunction nor a derived limit asserts constructibility or supplies the remaining normalized adic operations.

### BK.7. A torsion example of the transition maps

Take \(K=\underline{O/\pi}\) in degree zero. Then
\[
K\otimes_O^LO_n=[K\xrightarrow{0}K]
\quad\text{in degrees }-1,0.
\tag{BK.12}
\]
The transition from level \(n+1\) to \(n\) is zero in degree \(-1\), and the identity in degree zero, by BK.3. The first tower has zero homotopy limit: its shift is zero, so \(1-s\) is the identity. The second tower has limit \(K\). Thus \(C(K)=K\), while every derived reduction still has the additional degree-minus-one term. Ordinary quotients alone would discard it.

These arguments establish completion, its unit and reduction maps, and the passage of the specified torsion comparison to completed direct image. BL constructs the completed tensor, its internal Hom and the inverse-image adjunction, including composition and finite-reduction maps. Normalized \(f_!\), \(f^!\), adic duality, rationalization and equivalence with the relevant strict systems retain their separate coherence, coefficient and finiteness requirements.

## Appendix BL. Tensor, internal Hom and inverse image after completion

Keep the coefficient ring and the pro-étale sites of BK. Write \(D_X=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},\underline O)\), and let \(D_X^c\) be its full subcategory of derived-complete objects. The superscript here means **complete**, not constructible. All complexes in this appendix may be unbounded. Put \(Q=O[1/\pi]\). We construct the operations in \(D_X^c\) and their comparison maps before imposing constructibility.

### BL.1. Tensor models on the enlarged site

The tensor constructions of BH extend to this site without a claim that ordinary étale geometric points detect every pro-étale sheaf. Here is the replacement for that use of stalks. For an object \(U\) of a site presenting the topos, let \(B_U\) be the sheafification of the free \(\underline O\)-module presheaf on its represented sheaf. For a sheaf \(M\), \(B_U\otimes M\) is the sheafification of the presheaf whose sections over \(V\) are finite sums of elements of \(M(V)\), labelled by sections of \(U\) over \(V\).

This tensor functor is exact. A section in its target has locally a finite-sum representative. An epimorphism of sheaves lifts each of its finitely many coefficients after a covering refinement. For a kernel, a finite-sum representative mapping to zero becomes zero in the presheaf after another refinement, by the definition of sheafification. Collecting equal labels expresses this as finitely many zero coefficient sums. Exactness of the original sequence on sections at its first two terms lifts those sums to the kernel. This proves exactness locally and hence for the sheaf. Thus \(B_U\) is flat. The sums indexed by sections in (BH.2) still surject onto every sheaf: every local section is one of their generators.

Apply the disk-and-cycle construction (BH.3)–(BH.5) to these generators. Each stage is a degreewise split extension by shifts of flat sheaves. Every local kernel cycle is killed at the next stage; exact filtered colimits therefore make the final kernel acyclic. The same tensor tests prove K-flatness at each stage and at the limit. This gives K-flat resolutions on the pro-étale site, with the functorial model comparisons, signs and coherence of BH.2.

A topos inverse image is exact, preserves colimits and preserves the free-module construction on a sheaf of sets. It therefore takes these particular filtered cell resolutions to K-flat resolutions: their flat generators remain flat by the same finite-sum argument. This proves the derived tensor comparison for inverse image using the chosen models. It does not assume that an arbitrary complex with flat terms is K-flat.

For internal Hom, use a K-flat resolution in the first variable and a K-injective resolution in the second, as in BH.4. The local verification there applies too. Indeed restriction to a slice topos has an exact extension-by-zero left adjoint: its finite-sum description has the same lifting and kernel argument as above. Restriction consequently preserves K-injectives, by adjunction on complexes, and preserves the chosen K-flat cell models. The tensor–Hom identity on each slice then proves both local independence of models and the derived internal adjunction. In particular \(D_X\) is a closed symmetric monoidal derived category, with the associativity and Koszul symmetry maps already checked in (BH.8).

### BL.2. Which changes disappear under completion

Call \(T\in D_X\) localized if multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(T\) is an isomorphism. Localization of modules is exact, so this is equivalent to \(\underline Q\otimes_O^LT\simeq T\). Equation (BK.8) says that the cone of the completion unit \(\eta_A:A\to C_XA\) is localized. Conversely, if \(C_XT=0\), (BK.8) identifies \(T\) with \(L_\pi(T)\), which is localized. Hence
\[
C_XT=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ is localized}.
\tag{BL.1}
\]
Completion is exact: its expression in (BK.7) uses exact finite coefficient cones and a derived limit, which preserves triangles by the product-and-cone formula (BK.1).

Localized objects form a tensor ideal. If \(\pi:T\to T\) has an inverse, tensoring that inverse with the identity of \(A\) inverts multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(T\otimes_O^LA\). They are also preserved by inverse image, which carries that inverse to an inverse. Tensoring a completion unit with any object, or taking its inverse image, therefore gives a map with localized cone. Completing such a map makes it an isomorphism. In particular the unit supplies natural isomorphisms
\[
C_X(A\otimes_O^LB)\xrightarrow{\sim}
C_X(C_XA\otimes_O^LB),\qquad
C_Xf^*A\xrightarrow{\sim}C_Xf^*C_YA.
\tag{BL.2}
\]
The second formula is for \(f:X\to Y\). The same assertions apply to the other tensor factor. These are maps induced by \(\eta\), not choices of isomorphisms between objects.

### BL.3. The completed tensor and its unit

For \(A,B\in D_X^c\), set
\[
A\widehat\otimes_OB=C_X(A\otimes_O^LB),\qquad
\mathbf1_X=C_X\underline O.
\tag{BL.3}
\]
The unit is the completed coefficient sheaf \(\widehat O\) in degree zero. Indeed \(\underline O\otimes_O^LO_n=\underline{O_n}\), and the transition maps are epimorphisms. Their derived limit has no positive cohomology: for a section \((b_n)\) of the product, the equations \(a_n-u_na_{n+1}=b_n\) can be solved for each finite initial segment by successive lifting; their sheaves of solutions have epimorphic transitions. Repleteness in BK.1 supplies a local compatible infinite solution. Thus \(1-s\) on the product is surjective, its kernel is the ordinary limit, and (BK.1) gives the assertion. This need not identify \(\widehat O\) with \(\underline O\).

Both iterated tensors in the associativity constraint identify by (BL.2) with
\[
C_X(A\otimes_O^LB\otimes_O^LD).
\tag{BL.4}
\]
Transport the associativity map of BL.1 through these unit-induced identifications. Similarly transport its signed interchange for symmetry. The unit constraints come from \(\underline O\otimes_O^LA\simeq A\), (BL.2), and \(C_XA\simeq A\).

These constraints satisfy their coherence identities. For example every map from the raw four-factor tensor to a complete target has a unique factorization through its completion, by BK.4. Precomposing either route in the completed pentagon with the raw tensor and its units gives the same ordinary reassociation map. The bijection on Hom sets makes the two completed routes equal. The triangle and symmetry hexagon follow in the same way from the ordinary unit and signed-interchange calculations of BH.2. This also identifies the multiplication of \(\mathbf1_X=\widehat O\) with its usual pointwise multiplication: both maps restrict to multiplication on \(\underline O\), and the tensor-unit comparison in (BL.2) gives the same uniqueness.

This argument uses the universal property of completion to compare maps. Reduction modulo every \(\pi^n\) detects isomorphisms between complete objects by BK.4; it is not being asserted to be faithful on all morphisms.

### BL.4. Internal Hom is already complete in its target

Let \(E\in D_X^c\) and \(A\in D_X\). The ordinary derived internal Hom \(H=R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\) is complete. Tensor–Hom adjunction and the symmetry from BL.1 give
\[
R\mathcal Hom_O(\underline Q,H)
\simeq R\mathcal Hom_O(A,R\mathcal Hom_O(\underline Q,E))=0.
\tag{BL.5}
\]
For clarity, the isomorphism is checked by applying Hom from any \(T\): the two sides both represent maps from \(T\otimes_O^LA\otimes_O^L\underline Q\) to \(E\), with the specified reassociation and interchange. Yoneda therefore proves the internal identity and its naturality. The last equality is the definition of completeness in BK.4.

For complete \(A,B,E\), the two adjunctions now give
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(A\widehat\otimes_OB,E)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X}(A\otimes_O^LB,E)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(A,R\mathcal Hom_O(B,E)).
\tag{BL.6}
\]
Thus (BL.3) is a **closed** symmetric monoidal structure. Its evaluation is the unique extension to the completed tensor of the ordinary evaluation map; its adjunction unit is defined by the corresponding identity. Their triangle identities hold because the displayed bijections are natural inverses.

### BL.5. Finite reductions of these operations

Write \(A_n=A\otimes_O^LO_n\). The units and the coefficient extension maps give
\[
(A\widehat\otimes_OB)_n\simeq
A_n\otimes_{O_n}^LB_n,
\qquad (\mathbf1_X)_n\simeq\underline{O_n}.
\tag{BL.7}
\]
The first comparison first uses (BK.9), then ordinary scalar extension of a tensor. On the cell models \(P_A,P_B\) of BL.1, its latter step is the equality
\((P_A\otimes_OP_B)\otimes_OO_n=(P_A\otimes_OO_n)\otimes_{O_n}(P_B\otimes_OO_n)\).
The reduced models are K-flat over \(O_n\): tensoring an acyclic \(O_n\)-complex with one is the same as tensoring its restricted \(O\)-complex with the original K-flat model. This proves the formula for unbounded complexes too.

There is also the canonical internal-Hom comparison
\[
R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\otimes_O^LO_n
\xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom_{O_n}(A_n,E_n).
\tag{BL.8}
\]
It is the adjoint of the reduced evaluation map. To prove it, restrict the target to \(O\)-modules. Derived extension/restriction adjunction identifies it with \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E_n)\). For this adjunction, resolve the source by a K-flat model and the target by a K-injective \(O_n\)-model. A quasi-isomorphism between the K-flat source models stays a quasi-isomorphism after coefficient extension, and Hom into the latter injective model preserves it. The ordinary scalar-extension adjunction therefore descends to the derived categories. Applying the same construction on each slice gives the internal adjunction. This uses no flatness of \(O_n\) over \(O\) and makes no assertion that restriction of an arbitrary K-injective \(O_n\)-complex is K-injective over \(O\).

Now \(E_n\) is the cone of \(\pi^n:E\to E\). The exact \(O\)-linear functor \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,-)\) takes this to the cone of multiplication by \(\pi^n\) on \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\), which is the left side of (BL.8). The natural map just computed is its evaluation-defined comparison, since this holds on the two free terms of (BK.5). Restriction of scalars detects quasi-isomorphisms, proving (BL.8) as an \(O_n\)-comparison. These formulas commute with successive coefficient reduction: the tensor maps are scalar-extension maps, and the Hom maps are their evaluation adjoints. The transition maps are those of (BK.5), including their degree-minus-one factors.

### BL.6. Inverse image, its adjunction and composition

Define
\[
f_c^*=C_Xf^*:D_Y^c\longrightarrow D_X^c.
\tag{BL.9}
\]
BK.5 proves that \(Rf_*\) takes complete objects to complete objects. For complete \(A,E\), completion and the ordinary derived adjunction give
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(f_c^*A,E)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X}(f^*A,E)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_Y^c}(A,Rf_*E).
\tag{BL.10}
\]
Its counit is the unique map \(C_Xf^*Rf_*E\to E\) extending the ordinary counit. Its unit is the ordinary unit \(A\to Rf_*f^*A\) followed by \(Rf_*\eta_{f^*A}\). These descriptions are the maps corresponding to the identity under (BL.10), so they satisfy both triangle identities.

For composable maps \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\), (BL.2) and ordinary inverse-image composition give
\[
f_c^*g_c^*\simeq(gf)_c^*.
\tag{BL.11}
\]
All parenthesizations are coherent: after inserting the raw inverse-image object, each comparison is uniquely determined by its ordinary composition map and the completion unit. Applying the same argument to tensor and its unit gives
\[
f_c^*(A\widehat\otimes_OB)\simeq
f_c^*A\widehat\otimes_Of_c^*B,
\qquad f_c^*\mathbf1_Y\simeq\mathbf1_X.
\tag{BL.12}
\]
The associativity, symmetry and unit diagrams reduce by the bijections of BK.4 to the corresponding ordinary diagrams in BL.1. Thus completed inverse image is a strong symmetric monoidal functor, with the stated right adjoint.

Finally \((f_c^*A)_n\simeq f^*A_n\), by (BK.9) and the inverse-image models of BL.1. Together with (BK.10) this identifies the reductions of its unit and counit with the ordinary coefficient-level adjunction maps. In a Cartesian square, the mate made from these units and counits is exactly the completed comparison of BK.6: precomposition with the raw pullback gives the ordinary base-change map followed by completion, and the same uniqueness determines its extension. This verifies the operation map, in addition to its objectwise finite-level formula.

The free general comparisons for the last construction are [derived-complete inverse image, Tag 099K](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099K) and [constant Noetherian coefficients, Tag 099N](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099N). Here the proof uses the explicit one-parameter completion and its unit from BK. BM uses these categorical operations to construct completed proper support, with its reduction-defined constructibility and comparisons. BP–BS supply the strict-system and derived-diagram comparisons; BV constructs exceptional inverse image and proves adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. General heart realization remains a distinct requirement.

## Appendix BM. Proper support for completed coefficients

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic different from \(\ell\), and initially let all schemes be separated and of finite type over \(k\). Keep \(O,\pi,O_n\) and \(C_X\) from BK. For the constructibility assertions below assume that the residue field of \(O\) is finite; in particular they apply to the valuation ring of every finite extension of \(\mathbf Q_\ell\).

Write \(\mathscr A_X\) for the full subcategory of complete pro-étale \(O\)-complexes \(K\) such that every \(K_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n\) is the pullback of a bounded-below étale \(O_n\)-complex. The bound may depend on \(n\). The categories and coefficient actions are specified: “comes from étale” refers to \(\nu_X^*:D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\to D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},O_n)\). BK.2 proves this functor fully faithful, by its derived unit. Its image is closed under triangles, since maps lift uniquely and its exact functor takes their cones to the corresponding cones. Thus \(\mathscr A_X\) is triangulated. We will construct proper support on this category, then prove a constructible subcategory is preserved.

### BM.1. Complete extension by zero

For a quasi-compact open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\), restriction \(j^*\) is exact and is right adjoint to exact extension by zero \(j_!\). Exactness here can be checked directly from the open-subtopos construction: sections of an extension by zero are locally sections on the specified open, with zero extension wherever the support is absent; lifting and kernel equations are checked on those local representatives. This is the same finite local lifting argument as BL.1. The termwise adjunction therefore descends to derived categories.

As a right adjoint, \(j^*\) preserves products. Exactness makes it preserve the product-and-cone homotopy limits in BK.1. It commutes with the two free terms of \(P_n\), and hence with completion. In particular it preserves complete objects and \(j_c^*=j^*\). Define
\[
j_{!,c}K=C_Xj_!K.
\tag{BM.1}
\]
The completion adjunction proves \(j_{!,c}\dashv j^*\) on complete categories. Its unit and counit are obtained from the ordinary open adjunction and the completion unit, as in BL.6. Since \(j_!\) is exact and \(O\)-linear, it preserves localized complexes. Therefore inserting or deleting an intermediate completion inside \(C_Xj_!\) gives an isomorphism by (BL.1). This proves the composition law for complete extension by zero along two opens, with its ordinary composition map.

We will use
\[
(j_{!,c}K)_n\simeq j_!K_n,
\qquad j_{\mathrm{pro\acute et},!}\nu_U^*L
\simeq\nu_X^*j_{\mathrm{\acute et},!}L.
\tag{BM.2}
\]
The first follows from (BK.9) and the two-term coefficient cone. For the second, restriction and \(\nu_*\) commute on étale objects, because both are evaluation on those same objects. The two proposed functors are consequently left adjoint to the same functor, by the open and site adjunctions. Their identification is the one given by extension of the same local sections by zero. All these functors are exact, so the assertion applies to complexes and to their actual maps. It follows that \(j_{!,c}\) takes \(\mathscr A_U\) into \(\mathscr A_X\).

### BM.2. A compactification and its finite reductions

For \(f:X\to Y\), choose the compactification established in BG.5,
\(X\xrightarrow j\overline X\xrightarrow pY\), with \(j\) open and \(p\) proper. Define
\[
F_{p,j}(K)=Rp_*j_{!,c}K
\simeq C_YRp_*j_!K.
\tag{BM.3}
\]
The isomorphism is (BK.10). The first expression is complete. Its canonical reductions are
\[
F_{p,j}(K)_n\simeq Rp_*j_!K_n
\simeq\nu_Y^*R p_{\mathrm{\acute et},*}
 j_{\mathrm{\acute et},!}L_n,
\quad K_n\simeq\nu_X^*L_n.
\tag{BM.4}
\]
Indeed \(Rp_*\) commutes with the finite free coefficient cone, (BM.2) handles extension by zero, and (BK.4) identifies the proper direct image. The étale complex on the right is bounded below. Thus (BM.3) takes \(\mathscr A_X\) into \(\mathscr A_Y\). It is exact, since each of its functors is exact on the derived categories.

The construction has a specified inverse-limit description:
\[
F_{p,j}(K)\simeq
\operatorname{holim}_n Rp_*j_!K_n.
\tag{BM.5}
\]
These are the reductions of the single functor (BM.3), with the transitions of \(P_n\). Formula (BM.5) is not a choice of an inverse limit of isomorphism classes of étale complexes. This distinction retains the comparison maps when we change compactification.

### BM.3. The completed proper–open exchange

Consider a commuting square \((U,T;V,S)\) with opens \(j:U\to T\), \(i:V\to S\) and proper maps \(p':U\to V\), \(p:T\to S\). It need not be cartesian. The induced map \(a:U\to T_V=T\times_SV\) is an open-and-closed immersion: it is open, and is proper by the closed graph into a separated \(V\)-scheme followed by proper projection. Thus \(a_!=a_*\) is exact, and preserves completion by the decomposition into the two open-and-closed topoi.

Restriction of a derived direct image to an open is its direct image on that open. One can check this without a proper base-change theorem: restriction preserves K-injectives because its extension-by-zero left adjoint is exact, and the section formula for direct image already has that equality. Hence
\[
i^*Rp_*j_{!,c}E\simeq Rp'_*E.
\tag{BM.6}
\]
The inverse of this identification and the complete open adjunction define a particular map
\[
\epsilon_c:i_{!,c}Rp'_*E\longrightarrow Rp_*j_{!,c}E.
\tag{BM.7}
\]
If \(E\in\mathscr A_U\), this map is an isomorphism. Reduce it modulo \(\pi^n\). The reduction rules in BK and (BM.2) identify its adjunction construction with the étale proper–open exchange (BG.14) on \(E_n\). That exchange is an isomorphism by its earlier proof: over \(V\) it is the clopen identity, and on the complement proper base change gives zero because the support open has empty fibre. The coefficients are torsion and bounded below, as required. Both sides of (BM.7) are complete. The complete cone has zero reductions, so it is zero by BK.4.

The maps (BM.7) obey pasting before any appeal to reduction. Restrict a vertically stacked exchange to its bottom open. The two candidates are the same proper pushforward of the same clopen-supported complex, with the composite direct-image adjunction unit. The identity for that composite unit makes the restrictions equal. The bijection for \(i_{!,c}\dashv i^*\) makes the maps themselves equal. Horizontal pasting uses the composition law of complete open extension from BM.1 and the same argument on the smallest open. Exchanges in separate positions commute by naturality. The argument is the explicit one in [Cohomology with compact support, Lemma 6.1](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#6-the-proper-open-exchange-and-its-coherence), now with the complete adjunction. Reduction was used to prove invertibility, not faithfulness on morphisms.

### BM.4. Independence and associative composition

A refinement \(h:\overline X_1\to\overline X_2\) of compactifications is proper and restricts to the identity on \(X\). Apply (BM.7) with \(p'=\mathrm{id}_X\). It gives
\[
j_{2,!,c}K\xrightarrow{\sim}Rh_*j_{1,!,c}K,
\tag{BM.8}
\]
and hence a comparison from the second functor (BM.3) to the first. The comparison for two refinements is their composite by vertical pasting; the identity refinement gives the identity.

BG.6 supplies the necessary common refinements without deleting any part of \(X\): take its schematic closure in the product of two compactifications. Its graph is closed over either copy of the open \(X\), so the same \(X\) remains open in the closure. Parallel maps are equalized by their closed equalizer containing that open. To compare arbitrary compactifications, map each to a common refinement using (BM.8). A further common refinement makes comparisons through two different choices equal, by pasting and cancellation of isomorphisms. A common refinement of three choices proves the cocycle identity. Thus (BM.3) defines a canonical functor
\[
Rf_{!,c}:\mathscr A_X\longrightarrow\mathscr A_Y.
\tag{BM.9}
\]
For a proper map it is \(Rf_*\), and for an open immersion it is (BM.1), by choosing the identity part of the compactification.

Here is the composition map explicitly. For \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\), compactify \(g\) as \(Y\xrightarrow iD\xrightarrow qZ\), then compactify \(if\) as \(X\hookrightarrow T\xrightarrow pD\). Put \(V=p^{-1}Y\), with \(j:X\hookrightarrow V\), \(a:V\hookrightarrow T\) and \(h:V\to Y\). The proper–open exchange gives
\[
Rq_*i_{!,c}Rh_*j_{!,c}
\xrightarrow{Rq_*\epsilon_cj_{!,c}}
Rq_*Rp_*a_{!,c}j_{!,c}
\simeq R(qp)_*(aj)_{!,c}.
\tag{BM.10}
\]
It is \(Rg_{!,c}Rf_{!,c}\simeq R(gf)_{!,c}\).

For completeness, compatible systems of this kind have common refinements too. First refine their compactifications \(D_1,D_2\) of \(Y\). In the product of their \(T_i\) with that refinement impose the closed equations equating the maps to \(D_1,D_2\), and take the closure of the diagonal \(X\). Properness and the closed-graph argument retain the required open and give a refinement at every vertex. Comparing (BM.10) in this diagram gives a grid of exchanges. Adjacent exchanges paste to the outer exchange by BM.3, and exchanges in disjoint positions commute. Thus its composition map is independent of choices. For three maps, successive compactifications give a single triangular grid; its two parenthesizations perform the same exchanges. The same two pasting rules make them equal. Identity maps use identity exchanges. This proves associative, unital composition, including its actual maps.

### BM.5. Base change and the coefficient comparison

Given any change of base \(g:Y'\to Y\), pull back the chosen compactification to obtain \(X'\xrightarrow{j'}\overline X'\xrightarrow{p'}Y'\); write \(g_X,g_{\overline X}\) for the other projections. Use the completed proper comparison of BK.6 and complete open base change to form
\[
g_c^*Rp_*j_{!,c}K
\longrightarrow Rp'_*g_{\overline X,c}^*j_{!,c}K
\xrightarrow{\sim}Rp'_*j'_{!,c}g_{X,c}^*K.
\tag{BM.11}
\]
The open comparison follows from exact ordinary open base change and the localized-cone rule (BL.2); \(j_!\) also preserves localized cones by its exact \(O\)-linearity. For the proper comparison, each reduction of \(j_{!,c}K\) is a bounded-below classical torsion complex by (BM.2). BE.1–BE.8 prove its arbitrary-base proper comparison, and BK.6 identifies the completed map with the corresponding limit. Thus (BM.11) is an isomorphism. This construction and proof also work for the pulled-back compactifiable map even when \(Y'\) is not of finite type over \(k\); properness and quasi-compactness of the open are preserved by base change, and the comparison statements used above are local on \(Y'\).

This map commutes with refinement and composition. Indeed (BM.7) is defined by its restriction to the source open. After base change its two candidate restrictions are the same composition-compatible proper comparison and the same clopen identity. The complete open adjunction proves their equality. Expanding a refinement or composition comparison into its exchanges, as in (BM.8)–(BM.10), now gives a commuting grid. Consecutive base changes likewise paste, by BK.6 and exact open base change. Consequently (BM.11) is the canonical isomorphism
\[
g_c^*Rf_{!,c}K\simeq Rf'_{!,c}g_{X,c}^*K
\tag{BM.12}
\]
for the choice-independent functor. Its coefficient-level maps are the ordinary proper-support base-change maps, by (BM.4) and the definitions of the completed units and counits.

### BM.6. Constructibility and bounds from the first reduction

Define \(\mathscr C_X\) to consist of complete \(K\) whose first derived reduction comes from a bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complex. This is a definition by derived reduction; the comparison with strict adic systems and their hearts is a further assertion, not part of this definition.

Every such \(K\) belongs to \(\mathscr A_X\). Suppose \(K_1\) has cohomology in \([a,b]\). Tensor the exact coefficient sequence \(0\to O_{n-1}\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n\to O_1\to0\) with \(K\). It gives a triangle
\[
K_{n-1}\longrightarrow K_n\longrightarrow K_1.
\tag{BM.13}
\]
View its outer terms as \(O_n\)-complexes by restriction along the quotient maps. The fully faithful image of bounded-below étale complexes is triangulated, as observed at the start. Induction therefore proves that \(K_n\) is classical as an \(O_n\)-complex. Its long cohomology sequence gives the same bound \([a,b]\) for every \(n\). Finite local constancy on a common refinement is closed under kernels and cokernels: after trivialization, the map is locally a fixed map of finite modules. It is also closed under extensions. In \(0\to A\to B\to D\to0\), trivialize finite \(A,D\), then lift every element of \(D\) on one étale refinement. Differences between sums of these lifts and the chosen lift of their sum lie in \(A\), as do the differences for scalar multiplication. There are finitely many such differences, because \(O_n,A,D\) are finite. Refine again until they are constant. They define one finite module extension, whose constant sheaf maps to \(B\); every section is locally a chosen lift plus an element of \(A\), and its kernel is zero. This is the required local trivialization. The same induction therefore proves constructibility at each level. No uniform stratification for all levels is asserted here.

If the fibres of \(f\) have dimension at most \(d\), Proposition 3.2 and (BM.4) show that every reduction of \(Rf_{!,c}K\) is constructible with cohomology in \([a,b+2d]\). In particular its first reduction is bounded constructible, so
\[
Rf_{!,c}(\mathscr C_X)\subset\mathscr C_Y.
\tag{BM.14}
\]
The complete complex itself also has cohomology in this range. Here are the inverse-limit details, which apply to \(K\) with \([a,b]\) as well. Exact products and (BK.1) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&\to\operatorname{coker}(1-s:\prod H^{q-1}B_n\to\prod H^{q-1}B_n)\\
 &\to H^q(\operatorname{holim}B_n)\\
 &\to\ker(1-s:\prod H^qB_n\to\prod H^qB_n)\to0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BM.15}
\]
Take \(B_n=Rp_*j_!K_n\), all in \([a,t]\), with \(t=b+2d\). Only a possible degree \(t+1\) remains outside that range. The coefficient sequence \(0\to O_1\xrightarrow{\pi^n}O_{n+1}\to O_n\to0\), followed by the exact functor \(Rp_*j_!\), gives \(B_1\to B_{n+1}\to B_n\). Since \(H^{t+1}(B_1)=0\), the transitions on \(H^t(B_n)\) are epimorphisms. Repleteness solves the successive lifting equations for their product, exactly as in BL.3, so the cokernel in degree \(t+1\) is zero. This proves the claimed bound. The indices and maps in this argument are the quotient transitions, not ordinary quotients substituted for derived reductions.

The construction has proved proper support, its composition and arbitrary base change on \(\mathscr A\), and bounded constructibility in the precise reduction-defined sense of (BM.14). BV constructs the exceptional right adjoint and proves biduality on this complete bounded constructible category. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves and the ordinary operations. The strict-system comparison and its lisse subcategory are proved in BP; BQ proves constructible cohomology and identifies the heart of the restricted standard t-structure. BR constructs the derived-cartesian pro-étale diagram comparison, with its actual adjunction and higher morphisms; BS proves its étale-site presentation with the same coefficient transitions. BT proves finite-coefficient realization and constructs the adic heart realization functor. BU proves its equivalence in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields; the general positive-dimensional effacement condition stated precisely in BT.5 remains required.

Free comparisons for the exchange and compactification construction are [Tag 0F7A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F7A) and [Tag 0F7H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F7H). The completed maps above are derived from BK–BL and the stated finite-coefficient proofs, with the open adjunction supplying their coherence.

## Appendix BN. Uniform coefficient bounds and completed projection

Keep the field, schemes and complete discrete valuation ring of BM, including its finite residue field. Write \(\kappa=O_1\). We use the category \(\mathscr C_X\) defined in BM.6 by complete complexes with bounded constructible first derived reduction. The tensor and inverse image in this appendix are the completed operations of BL. The result will identify the projection map itself and its compatibility with the proper-support comparisons of BM.

### BN.1. Tor bounds at every finite coefficient level

Let \(K\in\mathscr C_X\), with \(K_1\) having cohomology in \([a,b]\). Every sheaf of modules over the constant field \(\kappa\) is flat, on either of the sites used here. Indeed sheaf tensor is obtained by sheafifying the sectionwise tensor over \(\kappa\): the additional relations over the constant ring sheaf are already locally relations over \(\kappa\), since each of the finitely many coefficients in a relation becomes constant on a cover. A monomorphism of sheaves is injective on sections. Tensoring an injective map of \(\kappa\)-vector spaces is injective: write a putative kernel element using a basis of the finite-dimensional span of its second factors; the coefficient of each basis vector must vanish. Sheafification preserves the resulting exact sequence. This proves the assertion without using ordinary étale points to detect arbitrary pro-étale sheaves.

Good truncation therefore represents \(K_1\) by a bounded complex of flat \(\kappa\)-sheaves in degrees \([a,b]\). Such a complex is K-flat: a single flat sheaf preserves exact complexes, and induction on the number of terms, using its termwise split truncation triangles, proves the claim. Consequently \(K_1\) has Tor amplitude in \([a,b]\), meaning that its derived tensor with any sheaf placed in degree zero has cohomology only in that interval.

In fact the same interval is a Tor bound for \(K_n\) over \(O_n\), for every \(n\). If \(M\) is an \(O_n\)-sheaf killed by \(\pi\), scalar-extension associativity gives
\[
K_n\otimes_{O_n}^LM
\simeq K\otimes_O^LM
\simeq K_1\otimes_\kappa^LM.
\tag{BN.1}
\]
These are derived identities: take a K-flat \(O\)-model of \(K\); its reduction is K-flat over each quotient by the tensor test in BL.5. For arbitrary \(M\), the finite filtration
\(M\supset\pi M\supset\cdots\supset\pi^nM=0\)
has layers killed by \(\pi\). Apply the exact derived tensor functor to each of its short exact sequences. The long cohomology sequences and (BN.1), by induction on the layers, give the same interval \([a,b]\). The argument applies to arbitrary sheaves \(M\), not just constructible ones.

BM.6 already proves that \(K_n\) is classical and bounded constructible. Its étale model also has this Tor bound. To see the descent of the bound, tensor that model with any étale \(O_n\)-sheaf and pull back by \(\nu_X^*\). The tensor comparison of BL.1 identifies the result with the tensor just bounded. Exact \(\nu_X^*\) detects zero étale sheaves by the unit comparison in BK.2, so the étale tensor has the same vanishing. This is an assertion about Tor amplitude, not a claim that every cohomology sheaf is flat. For example the complete torsion object \(\underline\kappa\) has derived reductions in degrees \(-1,0\), as BK.7 computes; ordinary quotients alone do not satisfy this calculation.

### BN.2. Tensor and inverse image preserve the constructible category

Take \(K,A\in\mathscr C_X\), with first-reduction bounds \([a,b]\), \([c,e]\). The specified comparison (BL.7) reads
\[
(K\widehat\otimes_OA)_1
\simeq K_1\otimes_\kappa^LA_1.
\tag{BN.2}
\]
This is a classical complex: choose the bounded flat representatives from BN.1 on the étale site and apply exact inverse image. Its cohomology lies in \([a+c,b+e]\). It is constructible too, without assuming that a complex with locally constant cohomology has already been trivialized as a constant complex. Apply the finite cohomology truncation triangles to the two factors. They reduce the assertion to tensor products of two constructible \(\kappa\)-sheaves and to finite extensions of their cohomology sheaves. On a common finite locally closed partition the two sheaves are finite locally constant; their tensor is so as well, by tensoring their finite trivializations. Closure under kernels, cokernels and extensions was proved in BM.6. Induction through the triangles gives the assertion.

Thus \(K\widehat\otimes_OA\in\mathscr C_X\), and the completed object itself has cohomology in \([a+c,b+e]\) by the inverse-limit proof (BM.15). BN.1 gives this same Tor interval for all its reductions. The tensor unit belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\), since its first reduction is \(\underline\kappa\). The associativity, unit and symmetry constraints of BL therefore restrict to this category.

For \(f:X\to Y\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_Y\), the formula
\[
(f_c^*A)_1\simeq f^*A_1
\tag{BN.3}
\]
shows that \(f_c^*A\in\mathscr C_X\). Exact inverse image preserves the cohomological interval. Inverse images of the finitely many locally closed strata form a finite partition, and pulling back their trivializing étale covers proves constructibility on that partition. BL.6 supplies the strong symmetric monoidal comparison and its actual maps. Together with BM.6, we now have all the objects needed in the completed projection formula inside \(\mathscr C\).

### BN.3. The proper projection map

For a proper map \(p:T\to S\), \(E\in\mathscr C_T\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_S\), use the strong monoidal inverse image and its counit to form
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_c^*(Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_OA)
&\simeq p_c^*Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A\\
&\longrightarrow E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BN.4}
\]
Transpose under \(p_c^*\dashv Rp_*\). This defines a canonical map
\[
\gamma^c_{p,E,A}:Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_OA
\longrightarrow Rp_*(E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A).
\tag{BN.5}
\]
Both objects belong to \(\mathscr C_S\), by BM.6 and BN.2.

Reduce this particular map modulo \(\pi^n\). BK.5, BL.5 and BL.6 identify its transpose with the ordinary finite-coefficient counit tensored with \(p^*A_n\). BK.2 identifies the classical direct images and the adjunction maps with those on the étale site. Thus its reduction is exactly
\[
Rp_*E_n\otimes_{O_n}^LA_n
\longrightarrow Rp_*(E_n\otimes_{O_n}^Lp^*A_n),
\tag{BN.6}
\]
the map proved invertible in BH.6. In particular the reduction for \(n=1\) is an isomorphism. Its complete cone is zero: the coefficient triangles (BM.13) give zero at all levels from zero at level one, and BK.4 then gives zero for the complete cone itself. This proves that (BN.5) is an isomorphism. The argument uses the actual counit-defined arrow, not an isomorphism selected from a comparison of objects.

The proper maps compose compatibly with (BN.5). For \(T\xrightarrow pS\xrightarrow qZ\), transpose the two proposed projection maps under \((qp)_c^*\dashv R(qp)_*\). Both are the \(q\)-counit pulled back by \(p_c^*\), followed by the \(p\)-counit, tensored with \((qp)_c^*A\). The composite-adjunction identity in BL.6 makes them equal. With two coefficient factors, their two orders similarly transpose to the same counit tensored with those factors; BL.3's associativity proves the tensor compatibility, and its unit constraint proves the unit compatibility. In a cartesian proper square the base-change map is the mate of the same units and counits by BK.6. Substituting (BN.4) on both sides therefore gives the same pulled-back counit and the same tensor reassociation. This proves base-change compatibility of the maps, not merely of their reductions.

### BN.4. Extension by zero and projection

For an open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow T\), the ordinary sheaf identity is
\[
j_!M\otimes_ON\simeq j_!(M\otimes_Oj^*N).
\tag{BN.7}
\]
One can verify it on the local representatives in BM.1: a section supported on the open is tensored with the restriction of the second section; wherever its first factor is extended by zero the tensor is zero. Finite sums and the bilinear relations give mutually inverse maps after sheafification. This proof works on the pro-étale site and does not use ordinary geometric stalks there.

The identity descends to derived tensors. If \(P\) is a K-flat complex on \(U\), then \(j_!P\) is K-flat: for any acyclic complex \(N\), the termwise identity (BN.7) identifies its tensor with \(j_!(P\otimes_Oj^*N)\), which is acyclic since \(j^*\) and \(j_!\) are exact. Direct sums in the total tensor commute with \(j_!\), by its left adjunction. Choose these resolutions for the first factor to obtain the derived form of (BN.7).

For complete \(E,A\), apply completion and the unit comparisons (BL.2) to this derived identity. Exact \(O\)-linear \(j_!\) preserves localized cones, as BM.1 proves, so an intermediate completion inside \(C_Tj_!\) may also be removed. Since \(j^*\) preserves completeness, the result is
\[
j_{!,c}E\widehat\otimes_OA
\xrightarrow{\sim}j_{!,c}(E\widehat\otimes_Oj^*A).
\tag{BN.8}
\]
It restricts to the identity on the open tensor. This description fixes its compatibility with successive open immersions, tensor associativity and base change: the ordinary section maps have these properties, and completion factors them uniquely through the units. Equivalently the complete open adjunction determines each resulting map from that restriction.

### BN.5. Proper support, refinements and composition

Let \(f:X\to Y\), \(K\in\mathscr C_X\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_Y\). Choose \(f=pj\) as in BM.2. Apply (BN.5) followed by (BN.8) and inverse-image composition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Rf_{!,c}K\widehat\otimes_OA
&\longrightarrow Rp_*(j_{!,c}K\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A)\\
&\xrightarrow{\sim}Rf_{!,c}(K\widehat\otimes_Of_c^*A).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BN.9}
\]
Both arrows are isomorphisms. This proves the completed proper-support projection formula at the full field and finite-type scope of BM, for every pair of objects in its reduction-defined constructible categories.

We verify independence of the compactification. In the proper–open square of BM.3, compare projection before and after the exchange (BM.7). By (BN.8) its common source can be written as a complete extension from the bottom open \(V\). Maps from this source are determined by their restrictions to \(V\), using \(i_{!,c}\dashv i^*\). On \(V\), (BM.6) identifies the exchange with the clopen identity and the direct image by \(p'\). The two projection routes are now (BN.5) for \(p'\): transposition gives the same proper counit tensored with the restricted coefficient. Their equality follows from the ordinary direct-image restriction identity and the counit description (BN.4). The complete open adjunction proves equality before restriction. This establishes tensor compatibility with a single proper–open exchange.

A refinement (BM.8) is such an exchange; hence it commutes with (BN.9). Passing to a common refinement proves independence. The composition map (BM.10) is a proper–open exchange between composites of proper and open functors. Its compatibility follows from the exchange calculation just given, proper composition in BN.3 and open composition in BN.4. For three morphisms the common grid in BM.4 gives the same equality under either parenthesization. The tensor associativity and unit identities follow from the corresponding proper and open identities. Thus (BN.9) is a coherent natural comparison for the functor constructed in BM, not only for a chosen compactification.

Finally pull back that compactification in a cartesian square. The base-change comparison (BM.11) is a proper comparison followed by open base change. These commute with projection by BN.3 and BN.4. The resulting square for (BN.9) commutes; common refinements and BM.5 make it the comparison for the choice-independent functor. This argument also applies to arbitrary changes of base using BM.5's pulled-back compactification and bounded classical finite reductions. Every reduction of (BN.9) is the finite-coefficient projection map (BH.19), and its transition compatibility is inherited from the reduction maps in BL.5–BL.6.

We have proved tensor and inverse-image closure, uniform finite-level Tor bounds and completed proper-support projection with its operation maps. None of these proofs uses a simultaneous local trivialization of all coefficient complexes. BO proves that local trivialization, including its finite-coefficient theorem and actual compatible lifting map. BP identifies the strict coefficient systems in degree zero, and BQ proves constructible cohomology and standard truncations. BR supplies the derived-cartesian coefficient-diagram comparison. BV constructs the exceptional right adjoint and proves singular adic biduality. BW constructs the completed-ring equivalence and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. General bounded-derived realization of the strict heart remains a separate requirement. The free comparison for the uniform bound is [Tag 09C2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C2); BN.1 supplies the coefficient-filtration and étale-descent details used here. The finite projection comparison and its prerequisites are the proved BH.5–BH.7, also explained in [Cohomology with compact support, Section 10](course:ag-etale-cohomology/cohomology-with-compact-support#10-projection-formula-for-arbitrary-complexes).


## Appendix BO. Local finite-free models and their compatible adic limit

Retain \(O,\pi,O_n\) from BM–BN, with finite residue field \(\kappa\). We prove the local model assertion needed for the adic coefficient comparison. If \(X\) is connected and \(K\in\mathscr C_X\) has locally constant first-reduction cohomology, there is one bounded finite free \(O\)-complex \(P\) such that, on a pro-étale covering, \(K\) is isomorphic to the completed constant complex associated to \(P\). The differential matrices of this model are constant matrices over \(O\). The proof will construct a morphism of complete objects; it will not take a homotopy limit of an unspecified family of morphism classes.

### BO.1. A finite-coefficient complex can be made finite free locally

Put \(R=O_n\). Let \(L\) be an étale complex with finite locally constant cohomology and Tor amplitude \([a,b]\). We claim that étale locally it is represented by a constant complex of finite free \(R\)-modules in exactly that degree interval.

We first record the top-degree tensor calculation. A sheaf has a flat resolution in nonpositive degrees by repeatedly taking the epimorphism (BH.2) and its kernel. BH.1 proves such a bounded-above flat complex K-flat. Thus, for sheaves \(F,M\), \(F\otimes_R^LM\) has no positive cohomology and has degree-zero cohomology \(F\otimes_RM\). Applying the finite cohomology truncation triangles to a bounded complex \(B\) gives
\[
H^b(B\otimes_R^LM)=H^b(B)\otimes_RM
\quad\text{if }H^{>b}(B)=0.
\tag{BO.1}
\]
Indeed the tensor of \(\tau_{\leq b-1}B\) has no cohomology above \(b-1\), by induction through its finitely many cohomology sheaves; the top truncation triangle then gives the equality. This also proves the asserted naturality of (BO.1).

Proceed by induction on \(b-a\). If \(a=b\), write \(L=F[-a]\). Trivialize \(F\) as a constant finite module \(M\). The Tor condition gives \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,\kappa)=0\), by testing the constant coefficient sheaf and a geometric stalk. Lift a basis of \(M/\pi M\) to obtain \(R^r\to M\). Its cokernel \(Q\) satisfies \(Q=\pi Q\), hence \(Q=\pi^nQ=0\). For its kernel \(J\), the Tor sequence gives an injection \(J/\pi J\to\kappa^r\), whose image is the kernel of the chosen basis isomorphism to \(M/\pi M\). It is zero. Therefore \(J=\pi^nJ=0\) too. We have proved \(M\simeq R^r\), including the algebra needed at the bottom of the induction.

Suppose \(a<b\). Trivialize \(H^b(L)\) and choose finitely many module generators. For any complex representing \(L\), its cycle sheaf surjects onto its cohomology sheaf. After an étale refinement the chosen generators lift to actual cycles. These define a map \(\underline{R^r}[-b]\to L\). Complete it to a triangle
\[
\underline{R^r}[-b]\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow B
\longrightarrow\underline{R^r}[-b+1].
\tag{BO.2}
\]
Its tensor with any sheaf \(M\) has zero cohomology outside \([a,b-1]\): below \(a\) this follows from the outer bounds and \(b-1\geq a\); in degree \(b\), (BO.1) makes the first map surjective. Hence \(B\) has Tor amplitude \([a,b-1]\). Its cohomology is still finite locally constant. The only new piece is an extension of \(H^{b-1}(L)\) by the kernel of \(\underline{R^r}\to H^b(L)\); the finite-module kernel and extension arguments are those proved in BM.6.

By induction, after another refinement \(B\) has a constant finite free model \(P^a\to\cdots\to P^{b-1}\). The last arrow in (BO.2) is determined by a sheaf map \(H^{b-1}(B)\to\underline{R^r}\): the lower truncation has cohomology at most \(b-2\), so the derived truncation orthogonality and its shift give this factorization and its uniqueness. Compose with the quotient from \(\underline{P^{b-1}}\). This is a map of finite free constant sheaves, so its finitely many matrix entries become constant after a common étale refinement. It kills the preceding differential. Append that matrix as the last differential of the model, with the cone sign convention of Appendix B. Rotating its cone triangle gives (BO.2), and the induced map of triangles is an isomorphism on the other two objects, hence on \(L\). This proves the claim. In particular no local-structure theorem has been substituted for a proof.

### BO.2. One coefficient type on a connected scheme

If \(X\) is connected, all the coefficient complexes in these local models have the same isomorphism class in \(D(R)\). Where two covering opens have intersecting images, choose a geometric point in their fibre product. The two stalk complexes there are both the stalk of \(L\); hence their coefficient complexes are isomorphic. The union of the images carrying a fixed isomorphism class is open, because étale maps are open. Distinct such unions are disjoint and cover \(X\). Connectedness leaves one nonempty union. This gives one finite free coefficient complex \(M_n\), which may require many local trivializations. It does not give a global trivialization of \(L\).

Apply this to the classical models of \(K_n\). Their uniform Tor bounds are BN.1. If \(K_1\) has finite locally constant cohomology, the coefficient triangles (BM.13) and the local extension argument in BM.6 prove the same property for every \(K_n\), on this same scheme. Thus BO.1 applies at every level. Fix a geometric point of \(X\). Taking the stalks of the classical models and their transition maps selects the coefficient objects \(M_n\) and maps with
\[
M_{n+1}\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LO_n\simeq M_n.
\tag{BO.3}
\]
The classical models and maps here can be obtained using the derived site adjunction of BK.2; its unit identifies them with the given reductions, and exact stalks commute with derived scalar extension. Consequently these are the reductions of the specified maps, not arbitrary maps between equal isomorphism classes.

### BO.3. Compatible matrices over the complete ring

We give the coefficient lifting argument in this setting. In a bounded finite free complex over \(O_n\), a unit entry of a differential can be made into an isolated \(1\) by row and column operations. The equation \(d^2=0\) makes the neighbouring maps zero on that summand. It is the contractible direct summand \(O_n\xrightarrow{1}O_n\). Removing such summands terminates, and leaves a minimal complex: every differential entry is in \((\pi)\).

A bounded projective complex computes its derived maps by its ordinary Hom complex. Indeed Hom from a projective module preserves exact sequences, and finite truncation of the source shows that Hom from the complex takes acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes. The same observation shows that a quasi-isomorphism between bounded projective complexes is a homotopy equivalence. More explicitly, its bounded acyclic projective cone contracts by successively splitting the surjection onto its last nonzero term and removing the resulting two-term identity summand.

A homotopy equivalence between minimal complexes is an actual complex isomorphism. After reduction modulo \(\pi\), both differentials vanish, so the inverse homotopies say that its degree maps are mutually inverse. Lift their matrix inverses; the error matrices lie in the nilpotent ideal \((\pi)\), and the finite geometric series in that error corrects each to an inverse over \(O_n\).

Choose a minimal representative \(P_1\). Inductively choose a minimal representative at level \(n+1\). Its reduction is minimal, and (BO.3) gives a homotopy equivalence to \(P_n\), hence an actual isomorphism by the preceding paragraph. Change bases at level \(n+1\) to lift this isomorphism. Such a lift is invertible by the same nilpotent-ideal argument. Its reduced differential matrices are now exactly those of \(P_n\). At every level the term ranks are the dimensions of \(H^i(M_1)\), because minimal differentials reduce to zero. They vanish outside \([a,b]\). Taking inverse limits of these fixed-size matrices gives a bounded finite free \(O\)-complex \(P\) with
\[
P/\pi^nP=P_n,\qquad P_n\simeq M_n.
\tag{BO.4}
\]
Completeness identifies each matrix entry with its compatible residue sequence. The square of the limiting differential has zero image in every quotient and is zero since \(\bigcap_n\pi^nO=0\). The coefficient transitions in (BO.4) are the prescribed derived transitions. This matrix argument, also given in [ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Theorem 6.1](course:AG-LTF/l-adic-sheaves-and-their-cohomology#6-recovering-a-finite-complex-over-the-complete-ring), uses the uniformizer \(\pi\); it includes ramified coefficient rings.

### BO.4. A uniform stabilization argument on a contractible cover

Choose the weakly contractible affine pro-étale cover from BK.1 and work on one member \(W\). Restriction to this site object is the slice functor of BL.1. Its exact left adjoint makes restriction preserve products and homotopy limits, so it preserves completion as well. Write \(K_W\) for the resulting complete object. Let
\[
\mathcal P=C_W\underline P,
\qquad H=R\mathcal Hom_O(\mathcal P,K_W).
\tag{BO.5}
\]
BL.4 proves \(H\) complete, and BL.5 identifies its actual reductions and their maps as
\[
H_n=R\mathcal Hom_{O_n}(\underline{P_n},K_n|_W).
\tag{BO.6}
\]
Here \(\mathcal P_n=\underline{P_n}\) by the completion unit. Since \(P_n\) is bounded finite free, the internal Hom in (BO.6) is computed by its finite Hom complex, or equivalently by its finite dual tensored with \(K_n|_W\).

For each \(n\) there is an isomorphism \(K_n|_W\simeq\underline{P_n}|_W\). To justify a global isomorphism on \(W\) at this single level, pull the étale trivializing cover of BO.2 back to \(W\). The weakly contractible covering property in BK.1 splits a finite affine refinement of that cover. Pulling its local isomorphism along the section gives the stated isomorphism. These choices need not commute as \(n\) varies.

Nevertheless the groups
\[
A_n=H^0(W,H_n)
