=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(W,O_n)}(\underline{P_n},K_n|_W)
\tag{BO.7}
\]
form a Mittag–Leffler tower, as follows. Put \(E_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{O_n}^{\bullet}(P_n,P_n)\). The groups \(G_n=H^0(E_n)\) are finite: \(O_n\) is finite, by its length-\(n\) filtration with finite residue-field layers, and every term of \(E_n\) is finite. For fixed \(n\), the descending images of \(G_m\to G_n\) consequently stabilize at some \(N(n)\).

For any finite segment \(q\geq m\geq n\), choose the single isomorphism \(K_q|_W\simeq\underline{P_q}\) at its highest level and reduce it to the other two levels. Derived reduction and the finite-free Hom calculation identify the whole segment \(H_q\to H_m\to H_n\) with \(\underline{E_q}\to\underline{E_m}\to\underline{E_n}\). The cohomology sheaves of this constant complex are the constant groups \(G_i\), because the constant-sheaf functor is exact. Thus, if \(q\geq m\geq N(n)\), the images from both higher levels into \(H^0(H_n)\) agree: under this one identification they are the equal coefficient-group images. This proves uniform stabilization as sheaves. Evaluation on \(W\) is exact by BK.1, so it preserves these images and identifies sheaf cohomology sections with \(H^0(W,H_i)\). The images in \(A_n\) therefore stabilize too. The section groups \(A_n\) themselves were not assumed finite, and no simultaneous choice of the preceding isomorphisms was used.

### BO.5. Producing one actual isomorphism of complete objects

Let \(I_n\subset A_n\) be the eventual image. Its transition \(I_{n+1}\to I_n\) is surjective. Given an element of \(I_n\), choose a level beyond both stabilization indices, lift it from that level, and then map to level \(n+1\); the resulting element lies in \(I_{n+1}\). Moreover \(I_1\) contains an isomorphism \(\underline{P_1}\to K_1|_W\): take any single-level isomorphism at a level beyond \(N(1)\), and reduce it. Starting with this element and successively using the surjections gives
\[
(\varphi_n)_n\in\varprojlim A_n,
\qquad \varphi_1\text{ an isomorphism}.
\tag{BO.8}
\]

We now lift this compatible family of classes to a morphism. Because \(H\) in (BO.5) is complete, BK.4 identifies it with the homotopy limit of its actual reductions (BO.6). Apply derived sections on \(W\) to the product-and-cone formula (BK.1). Sections commute with products and are exact on this object by BK.1. The cohomology sequence therefore gives a surjection
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(W,O)}(\mathcal P,K_W)
&=H^0(W,H)\\
&\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n H^0(W,H_n)
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BO.9}
\]
Explicitly the last group is the kernel of \(1-s\) on \(\prod_nH^0(W,H_n)\); the product-cone long exact sequence maps onto precisely this kernel. A possible preceding cokernel from degree \(-1\) affects uniqueness, not this surjectivity.

Choose a preimage \(\Phi:\mathcal P\to K_W\) of (BO.8). BL.5's evaluation-defined Hom comparison ensures that its reduction is the specified class \(\varphi_n\) at every level. In particular its first reduction is an isomorphism. Its cone is complete; the coefficient triangles give zero at all finite levels from zero at level one, and BK.4 then makes the cone zero. Thus \(\Phi\) is the required isomorphism. This construction supplies an actual map through the internal-Hom limit and its cohomology sequence. It does not assume that compatible classes automatically specify compatible chain representatives.

### BO.6. The resulting local description and its scope

We have proved that on a connected scheme where the cohomology of \(K_1\) is finite locally constant, a single bounded finite free coefficient complex \(P\) gives the pro-étale local model of \(K\). The object \(C\underline P\) is the finite complex of completed constant finite free modules with the constant differential matrices of \(P\): completion is exact and the finite sums and successive cones constructing this complex are preserved by it. Its reductions are the actual complexes \(P_n\) of (BO.4).

For a Noetherian \(X\) in BM, choose the finite locally closed partition making the finitely many cohomology sheaves of \(K_1\) locally constant. Each piece has finitely many connected components, which are open and closed: its finitely many irreducible components group into finitely many connected intersection classes. Refining by those components and applying the theorem to the completed restriction to each piece gives a finite stratification on which \(K\) has the local description just proved. Completed restriction has the indicated first reduction by BL.6, so this use of the theorem meets its hypotheses.

This proves the forward local-model assertion for every object of \(\mathscr C_X\). It does not identify a category of unspecified inverse systems with the derived category, or assert that all pro-étale local models descend to a prescribed strict-system heart. BP proves the precise degree-zero equivalence and its sheaf morphisms. BQ proves standard truncation closure and identifies the strict-system heart. BR supplies a precise derived diagram category and proves its equivalence with complete objects, including all higher morphisms; BS proves the étale-diagram comparison. BT constructs realization from the bounded derived category of the strict heart and proves its low-degree Ext comparisons; the general higher-effacement condition remains to establish equivalence. BV constructs exceptional right adjoints and proves adic biduality at this bounded constructible scope. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX supplies the full rational-sheaf comparison, including its integral models and higher morphisms. The free comparisons are [finite-coefficient local structure, Tag 09BI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BI), [stabilization, Tag 09C5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C5), and [adic local structure, Tag 09C6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C6). The proof above uses finite Tor induction, finite coefficient groups and the internal-Hom product-cone map to establish the assertions at the stated complete-DVR scope.


## Appendix BP. Strict systems and complete sheaves in degree zero

Keep the Noetherian schemes and the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\) with finite residue field from BM. A **strict constructible system** is a sequence \(F_n\) of constructible étale \(O_n\)-sheaves whose specified transitions induce \(F_{n+1}/\pi^nF_{n+1}\simeq F_n\). A morphism is a compatible sequence of sheaf maps. Quotients in this definition are ordinary quotients. We prove an equivalence between this category and the full subcategory of \(\mathscr C_X\) consisting of objects concentrated in degree zero. No derived equivalence is included in the statement.

### BP.1. One stratification and a uniform torsion exponent

A constructible finite étale sheaf of sets on a Noetherian scheme satisfies the ascending chain condition on subsheaves. To prove it, restrict to a finite locally closed stratification on which it is finite locally constant. By N.1 its restriction is represented by a finite étale scheme \(Y\), which is Noetherian. A subsheaf of the represented sheaf is represented by an open subset of \(Y\). Indeed take the union of the images of all étale local sections belonging to the subsheaf. These images are open. A section factoring through this union belongs locally to the subsheaf, and hence belongs to it by the sheaf axiom; the reverse inclusion follows from the definition of the union. Increasing chains of such opens stabilize on Noetherian \(Y\). The finitely many strata give one stabilization index, and equality on their geometric stalks gives equality on the original scheme.

For a strict system form
\[
D_j=\pi^jF_m/\pi^{j+1}F_m\quad(m>j).
\tag{BP.1}
\]
Strictness identifies this independently of \(m\): first quotient \(F_m\) by \(\pi^{j+1}\), then take the indicated image. Lifting a section of \(F_1\) and multiplying by \(\pi^j\) defines a surjection \(F_1\to D_j\), independent of its lift. Multiplication by \(\pi\) gives compatible surjections \(D_j\to D_{j+1}\). Their kernels in \(F_1\) therefore form an increasing chain, which stabilizes by the preceding paragraph. All \(D_j\) after some index are the same quotient of \(F_1\).

The finitely many earlier \(D_j\) are constructible, being images and quotients of constructible finite-coefficient sheaves. Choose one finite partition making these and the stable quotient locally constant. The power filtration of every \(F_m\) has these locally constant graded pieces. The finite extension proof in BM.6 then makes every \(F_m\) locally constant on this same partition. Refine into finitely many connected pieces as in BO.6. On each piece N.4, with its complete discrete valuation ring and finite residue-field hypotheses, identifies the strict lisse system with the quotients of one finite \(O\)-module \(M\).

Such a module is \(O^r\oplus T\), where \(T\) is killed by some \(\pi^c\). Here is the needed algebra: N.4's submodule argument makes the torsion submodule finite; its finitely many generators have a common annihilating power. The quotient is finite torsion-free, hence free by that same argument, and lifting a basis splits the quotient map. Take the maximum exponent over the finitely many pieces. This gives one \(c\) valid on all of \(X\). The stratification concerns the whole system, rather than a separate choice at each level.

### BP.2. Limits, quotients and the torsion kernel

We use the following consequence of BK.1. A sheaf tower with stabilizing images at every target index has zero degree-one derived limit on the pro-étale site. Let \(I_n\) be its eventual images. Their transitions are epimorphisms: lift an element from an index beyond the two stabilization indices and then project to the next level. The quotient tower has eventually zero transitions into each fixed index. On its product, the inverse of \(1-s\) is the sum \(1+s+s^2+\cdots\), which is finite in each coordinate. For the tower \(I_n\), repleteness solves the successive lifting equations, so \(1-s\) is surjective. Exact products applied to the short exact sequence of towers now make \(1-s\) surjective for the original tower. The product-cone formula proves the assertion. The same argument for an epimorphic tower gives its derived limit in degree zero.

Put
\[
F=\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*F_n.
\tag{BP.2}
\]
The transitions are epimorphisms. Thus this is also the derived limit and is a sheaf in degree zero. Each term is killed by a power of \(\pi\), hence complete by BK.4; closure under derived limits makes \(F\) complete.

Fix \(n\). For \(m\geq n\), the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow\pi^nF_m\longrightarrow F_m
\longrightarrow F_n\longrightarrow0
\tag{BP.3}
\]
has epimorphic transitions in its first terms. After exact pullback and passage to limits, it identifies the kernel of \(F\to\nu_X^*F_n\) with \(\varprojlim_m\nu_X^*(\pi^nF_m)\). To identify that limit as \(\pi^nF\), consider the kernels \(B_m=F_m[\pi^n]\). They have uniformly stabilizing images into each fixed level. On each piece of BP.1, for \(m\geq\max(n,c)\), their module is
\[
\bigl(\pi^{m-n}O^r/\pi^mO^r\bigr)\oplus T[\pi^n].
\tag{BP.4}
\]
Its free-part image in level \(a\) is zero for \(m\geq a+n\), and its torsion-part image is constant for \(m\geq c\). The common \(c\) gives a uniform stabilization index. Equality of these finite constructible image sheaves is detected on étale geometric stalks. Exact \(\nu_X^*\) preserves the images. The preceding tower argument and the exact sequence with terms \(B_m,F_m,\pi^nF_m\) prove surjectivity of
\(F\xrightarrow{\pi^n}\varprojlim_m\nu_X^*(\pi^nF_m)\).
Consequently the canonical maps give
\[
F/\pi^nF\simeq\nu_X^*F_n.
\tag{BP.5}
\]

There is also finite control of \(F[\pi^n]\). Limits preserve kernels, so this sheaf is the limit of the \(B_m\). Replace that tower by its eventual image sheaves. At every level \(a\geq c\), their geometric stalks are \(T[\pi^n]\), by (BP.4), and their subsequent transition maps are isomorphisms. Thus the eventual-image tower is eventually a constant tower of constructible étale sheaves. Its limit, pulled back by \(\nu_X^*\), is \(F[\pi^n]\). In particular this kernel is classical and constructible and is killed by \(\pi^c\), with the same \(c\) for all \(n\).

The two-term coefficient resolution therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H^{-1}(F\otimes_O^LO_n)&=F[\pi^n],\\
H^0(F\otimes_O^LO_n)&=\nu_X^*F_n,
\end{aligned}
\tag{BP.6}
\]
with no other cohomology. Both sheaves are bounded constructible classical coefficients. BK.2's fully faithful triangulated image, applied to the truncation triangle between these two sheaves, makes the complex classical too. Hence \(F\in\mathscr C_X\). This proves the forward functor, including the torsion information omitted by ordinary quotients.

### BP.3. Recovering every morphism

An \(O\)-linear sheaf map \(F\to G\) preserves every power of \(\pi\), so (BP.5) gives maps between their finite quotient sheaves. Full faithfulness of \(\nu_X^*\) on étale sheaves in BK.2 recovers unique maps \(F_n\to G_n\). They commute with the transitions because the original quotient maps do. Conversely a compatible system of such maps has a limit map (BP.2). Taking its quotients returns the original maps, and taking the limit of the quotients of a map returns that map. Thus
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{strict}}((F_n),(G_n))
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{O,X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}}(F,G).
\tag{BP.7}
\]
For objects concentrated in degree zero, this is also the Hom set in the derived category, by its ordinary truncation embedding. It is a statement about these Hom sets, not about all higher Ext groups or a derived equivalence.

### BP.4. Every degree-zero constructible complete object is recovered

Now let \(F\in\mathscr C_X\) be concentrated in degree zero. BM.6 makes every derived reduction classical and bounded constructible. Its degree-zero cohomology is the ordinary quotient \(F/\pi^nF\). Let \(F_n\) be the corresponding étale sheaf. Ordinary successive quotient identities, exact pullback and its full faithfulness show that these form a strict constructible system. BP.2 constructs
\(G=\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*F_n\in\mathscr C_X\)
and a natural map \(u:F\to G\), whose ordinary quotient maps are all identities under (BP.5).

We prove that \(u\) is an isomorphism; derived completeness alone should not be silently replaced by ordinary completeness. Let \(C\) be its cone. Both objects are complete and in \(\mathscr C_X\), so the same is true of \(C\). The first reductions of \(F\) and \(G\) have cohomology only in \([-1,0]\), and their degree-zero map is an isomorphism. Hence \(C_1\) has cohomology in \([-2,-1]\). The actual complete-object bound proved in BM.6 makes \(C\) have cohomology in that interval. But the cone of a map of sheaves has cohomology only in \([-1,0]\). Its degree-zero cohomology is therefore zero: \(u\) is surjective. Its kernel \(T=C[-1]\) is a sheaf in \(\mathscr C_X\).

Tensor the resulting short exact sequence \(0\to T\to F\to G\to0\) with the specified two-term resolution of \(O_n\). Since the ordinary quotient map from \(F\) to \(G\) is an isomorphism, the cohomology sequence gives a surjection
\[
G[\pi^n]\longrightarrow T/\pi^nT.
\tag{BP.8}
\]
For \(m\geq n\), naturality in the resolution (BK.5) makes the transition on its left multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\), and the transition on its right the ordinary quotient map. BP.2 gives one \(c\) killing all \(G[\pi^m]\). Taking \(m\geq n+c\) makes the left transition zero. Surjectivity in (BP.8) makes the right transition zero as well. It is also a surjective quotient map. Thus \(T/\pi^nT=0\) for every \(n\).

In particular the first derived reduction of \(T\) has cohomology only in degree \(-1\). Since \(T\in\mathscr C_X\), BM.6 forces \(T\) itself into degree \(-1\). It is already a degree-zero sheaf, so it is zero. This proves \(F\simeq G\), establishing essential surjectivity together with the explicit inverse functor. The degree-zero comparison, on both objects and morphisms, is proved.

### BP.5. Lisse objects, torsion and the next categorical distinction

The lisse subcategory in N.4 has the following compatible description. On a connected scheme, let a strict lisse system correspond to a finite \(O\)-module \(M\) with continuous fundamental-group action. On each affine open, take the tower of finite étale covers given by the kernels of its actions on \(M/\pi^nM\). Refinement and the tautological points make the trivializations compatible. The affine inverse limit is an ind-étale faithfully flat cover: its algebra is a filtered colimit of flat algebras, and each geometric fibre is the nonempty inverse limit of finite surjective fibres. On that cover (BP.2) becomes
\[
\widehat{\underline M}
=\varprojlim_n\underline{M/\pi^nM}
\simeq\widehat O^{\,r}\oplus\underline T
\quad(M\simeq O^r\oplus T).
\tag{BP.9}
\]
The last identification follows from the module decomposition in BP.1; the finite torsion system is eventually constant. This is also \(C\underline M\), by exact completion, BL.3 and completeness of torsion objects. It is locally free precisely when the finite module is torsion-free.

Conversely, suppose a sheaf in the degree-zero category of BP.4 is pro-étale locally a completed constant finite module. Its quotients (BP.5) are then locally constant finite module sheaves in that topology. They are finite locally constant étale sheaves as well. Here is the finite descent step. On an affine base refine a trivializing cover to a faithfully flat affine ind-étale cover using BK.1. Each finite quotient there is represented by a finite disjoint union of copies of that cover. Its overlap maps are maps of represented sheaves, hence maps of their finite étale algebras, by the sheaf Yoneda property. The faithfully flat finite-algebra descent calculation N.1 descends them to a finite étale scheme over the base, along with their module operations. Its sheaf is the quotient by the same descent equalizer. This proves the assertion and gives the strict lisse system. BP.7 identifies all of its maps; N.4 then identifies its finite-module representation.

For example, the strict constant system \(F_n=\kappa\) has limit \(\underline\kappa\). Its ordinary quotients are still \(\underline\kappa\), whereas its first derived reduction is \([\underline\kappa\xrightarrow0\underline\kappa]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). For the torsion-free constant system \(F_n=O_n\), multiplication by \(\pi\) on its limit \(\widehat O\) is injective even though every finite-level kernel is nonzero: those kernels have zero transition maps. These examples identify exactly why neither levelwise kernels nor ordinary quotients can replace the required derived coefficient data.

This appendix proves the comparison for sheaves in degree zero, and its lisse subcategory. BQ proves that its cohomology sheaves and truncations stay constructible, and thus identifies this subcategory as the heart of the restricted standard t-structure on all of \(\mathscr C_X\). To identify a bounded derived category of strict systems with the full constructible derived category, one must additionally prove the higher-morphism and realization assertions. BR proves the higher-morphism comparison for the specified cartesian derived diagrams, and BS proves its étale presentation. BT constructs bounded-derived realization from this strict heart, proves the degree-one comparison and degree-two injection, and identifies the exact higher-effacement condition still needed for equivalence. The exceptional, duality and rationalization comparisons also remain separate from (BP.7). The free strict-system comparison material is [ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Sections 1–3](course:AG-LTF/l-adic-sheaves-and-their-cohomology#1-what-a-compatible-system-remembers), [the pro-étale lesson, Proposition 4.2](course:AG-LTF/the-pro-etale-site-and-l-adic-complexes#4-completion-remembers-a-complex), and [Tags 03UN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03UN) and [03UP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03UP). The common-stratification, division and complete-sheaf recovery proofs needed here have been given above.


## Appendix BQ. Normalized cohomology and the constructible heart

Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), uniformizer \(\pi\), finite residue field and Noetherian scheme of BM–BP. For \(K\in\mathscr C_X\), we prove that every ordinary cohomology sheaf \(H^i(K)\) belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\). This will give the restricted standard t-structure and identify its heart with strict constructible coefficient systems. The finite-level cohomology sheaves themselves generally do not form a strict system; the proof identifies exactly which images do.

### BQ.1. The coefficient calculation and its transition maps

Let \(P\) be a bounded finite free \(O\)-complex, and put \(M^i=H^i(P)\). These are finite modules: kernels and images of maps of finite modules over the Noetherian ring \(O\) are finite. Choose \(c\geq0\) which kills the torsion of every \(M^i\). There are only finitely many nonzero modules, and BP.1 supplies such an exponent for each.

The termwise exact sequence of complexes \(0\to P\xrightarrow{\pi^n}P\to P/\pi^nP\to0\) gives
\[
0\longrightarrow M^i/\pi^nM^i
\longrightarrow H^i(P/\pi^nP)
\longrightarrow M^{i+1}[\pi^n]
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BQ.1}
\]
For \(m\geq n\), compare this sequence at the two indices using multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\) on its first copy of \(P\), the identity on its second copy, and the quotient on its last complex. The square of the first arrows commutes because \(\pi^n\pi^{m-n}=\pi^m\). The resulting map on the left of (BQ.1) is the ordinary quotient; on the right it is multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\).

Consequently, for \(m\geq n+c\), the image of
\(H^i(P/\pi^mP)\to H^i(P/\pi^nP)\)
is precisely the embedded module \(M^i/\pi^nM^i\). Indeed its image in the right term is zero, while the quotient map on the left terms is surjective. This proves both inclusions, with one exponent valid for every degree. It also proves that the maps between these stabilized images are the quotient maps of the modules \(M^i\). No choice of a splitting of (BQ.1) has entered the calculation.

### BQ.2. Uniform stabilization on the scheme

Write \(A_n^i\) for the constructible étale sheaf whose pullback is \(H^i(K_n)\). These sheaves and their transition maps exist by BM.6 and the exact, fully faithful classical comparison in BK.2. Choose the finite connected stratification of BO.6. On a piece \(S\), the completed restriction \(K_S=C_Si^*K\) has the actual compatible local model \(C_S\underline{P_S}\) of BO.5. BL.6 identifies its finite reductions, with their maps, with \(i^*K_n\). Thus on a pro-étale cover of \(S\) the entire cohomology tower is that of the reductions of one bounded finite free complex \(P_S\).

Take the maximum of the exponents of BQ.1 for the finitely many \(P_S\). Call it \(c\). Exact inverse image commutes with the finite images and quotients under consideration. On the indicated cover of each stratum, BQ.1 therefore proves equality of the image sheaves from any two indices \(m,q\geq n+c\) into \(A_n^i\). Equality can be checked on a covering after the faithful classical pullback, and then on the étale geometric stalks of all the strata. Hence it holds on \(X\).

Define the constructible étale sheaf
\[
I_n^i=\operatorname{im}(A_{n+c}^i\longrightarrow A_n^i).
\tag{BQ.2}
\]
It is the image from every sufficiently late level, so the definition is independent of any larger choice of \(c\). The transitions take \(I_{n+1}^i\) onto \(I_n^i\), and the induced map
\[
I_{n+1}^i/\pi^nI_{n+1}^i
\xrightarrow{\sim} I_n^i
\tag{BQ.3}
\]
is an isomorphism. To verify this, restrict the map to a stratum and the cover just used. Under the compatible local model, its source and target are respectively
\((M_S^i/\pi^{n+1}M_S^i)/\pi^n\) and \(M_S^i/\pi^nM_S^i\), and the map is their quotient isomorphism. The kernel and cokernel of the global finite constructible map are therefore zero on every geometric stalk. This proves (BQ.3), including its actual transition map.

This argument used restrictions only at finite coefficient levels. It did not commute an arbitrary inverse image with an infinite limit, or assume that restricting \(H^i(K)\) agrees with taking cohomology after completed restriction. Those assertions are unnecessary for the construction of \(I_n^i\).

### BQ.3. Recovering the cohomology sheaf

All the towers \(A_n^i\) have stabilizing images by BQ.2. The Mittag–Leffler argument of BP.2 makes the degree-one derived limit of \(\nu_X^*A_n^i\) vanish. Completeness of \(K\) and the exact-product cohomology sequence (BM.15) now give the natural identification
\[
H^i(K)\simeq\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*A_n^i
\simeq\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*I_n^i.
\tag{BQ.4}
\]
For the second identification, the quotient tower \(A_n^i/I_n^i\) has zero transitions from index \(n+c\) to \(n\). Its product operator \(1-s\) is invertible by the coordinatewise finite geometric sum in BP.2, so its derived limit is zero. The short exact sequence of towers, followed by exact products and their cones, identifies the derived limits of \(I_n^i\) and \(A_n^i\). Both are ordinary limits, because their image towers stabilize.

Equations (BQ.2)–(BQ.3) make \((I_n^i)_n\) a strict constructible system. BP.2 therefore proves that its limit is a degree-zero object of \(\mathscr C_X\), and identifies its ordinary quotients. Thus
\[
H^i(K)\in\mathscr C_X,\qquad
H^i(K)/\pi^nH^i(K)\simeq\nu_X^*I_n^i.
\tag{BQ.5}
\]
These isomorphisms are natural in \(K\). A map of complexes induces maps on all finite cohomology towers; taking a common stabilization index for source and target makes these preserve the images in (BQ.2). The maps are independent of that index, and (BM.15) and the quotient maps in BP.2 are natural.

There is a useful intrinsic check on the inclusion of these images. The actual coefficient cone triangle for \(K\) gives
\[
0\longrightarrow H^i(K)/\pi^nH^i(K)
\longrightarrow H^i(K_n)
\longrightarrow H^{i+1}(K)[\pi^n]
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BQ.6}
\]
The first map is the map from (BQ.4) to its level \(n\), factored through the ordinary quotient. Under (BQ.5) it is exactly the image inclusion from (BQ.2). The transition on the last term is multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\), by the same comparison of coefficient cones as in BQ.1. BP.2, applied to each \(H^{i+1}(K)\), also proves directly that its torsion kernels have a common annihilating power. Thus the disappearance of the last term agrees with the finite-model calculation; it is not a claim that it is zero at every level.

### BQ.4. Truncations, the heart and its kernels

BM.6 proves that \(K\) has cohomology in a finite interval. The subcategory \(\mathscr C_X\) is triangulated: complete objects are closed under shifts and cones by BK.4, and taking a first derived reduction is exact; the classical bounded constructible category is triangulated by BK.2 and the finite constructible kernel, cokernel and extension argument in BM.6.

Starting at the lowest nonzero cohomology degree, apply the ordinary truncation triangles
\[
\tau_{\leq q-1}K\longrightarrow\tau_{\leq q}K
\longrightarrow H^q(K)[-q].
\tag{BQ.7}
\]
The initial lower truncation is zero. Equation (BQ.5), induction and triangulated closure prove that every \(\tau_{\leq q}K\) lies in \(\mathscr C_X\). Its complementary truncation \(\tau_{\geq q+1}K\) lies there by the triangle with \(K\). Therefore intersection with the ambient standard subcategories \(D^{\leq0}\) and \(D^{\geq0}\) gives a bounded t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\). Shift closure and orthogonality are inherited from the ambient derived category; (BQ.7) supplies its truncation triangles, and BM.6 supplies boundedness.

Its heart is precisely the degree-zero category compared with strict constructible systems in BP. Consequently BP.2–BP.4 give an equivalence of that heart with the category of strict systems and their compatible sheaf maps. This category is abelian. More concretely, if \(u:F\to G\) is a map of heart objects, its ordinary sheaf kernel and cokernel are \(H^{-1}(\operatorname{Cone}u)\) and \(H^0(\operatorname{Cone}u)\). They belong to the heart by (BQ.5). Images and coimages are obtained by applying the same assertion again. Their canonical comparison is the ordinary sheaf isomorphism, which lies in this full subcategory; finite sums also remain there. This proves the abelian assertions without assuming that termwise kernels are strict.

The cokernel strict system is the termwise cokernel system, because
\((\operatorname{coker}u)/\pi^n\) is the cokernel of \(F/\pi^nF\to G/\pi^nG\). For the kernel, first take \(\ker u\), then its ordinary quotients as in BP.4. Taking the termwise kernels instead can give a different tower. For example, multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(\widehat O\) has zero kernel, while the kernels of \(O_n\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n\) are nonzero. Their transitions are zero. The cohomology normalization (BQ.2) is applied to the derived reductions of the cone when recovering this kernel; it is not an assertion that arbitrary termwise kernel towers are strict.

### BQ.5. Exactness of the completed inverse image and open extension

Let \(f:Y\to X\) be a morphism in the Noetherian scope above. BN proves \(f_c^*K\in\mathscr C_Y\), and BL.6 identifies its reductions with \(f^*K_n\). Ordinary inverse image on the finite coefficient sheaves is exact. It therefore commutes with their cohomology sheaves, the images (BQ.2) and the quotient maps (BQ.3). The same exponent \(c\) proves stabilization after pullback, and the normalized cohomology system is exactly
\[
\bigl(f_{\acute et}^*I_n^i\bigr)_n.
\tag{BQ.8}
\]
To apply this also to a heart object \(F\), use (BQ.5): its normalized systems vanish outside degree zero and in degree zero are \(F/\pi^nF\). Equation (BQ.8) implies that \(f_c^*F\) is a heart object with the pulled-back strict system. Applied first to \(K\) and then to \(H^i(K)\), this proves natural isomorphisms
\[
H^i(f_c^*K)\simeq f_c^*H^i(K).
\tag{BQ.9}
\]
Hence completed inverse image is t-exact and commutes with standard truncations. Explicitly, apply it to a truncation triangle: its two outer objects have the required cohomological bounds by (BQ.9), so truncation uniqueness identifies the resulting triangle. This statement concerns completed inverse image, with its specified coefficient comparisons.

For an open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\), the same argument uses BM.1's reduction comparison for \(j_{!,c}\). At each finite level, extension by zero is exact and sends a constructible sheaf to a constructible sheaf: extend its finite strata on \(U\) by the closed complement, on which the sheaf is zero. It preserves the image and quotient diagrams. Thus the normalized cohomology system of \(j_{!,c}K\) is \((j_!I_n^i)_n\). Membership in \(\mathscr C_X\) follows either from BM.14 or directly from its first reduction. As before,
\[
H^i(j_{!,c}K)\simeq j_{!,c}H^i(K),
\tag{BQ.10}
\]
and \(j_{!,c}\) is t-exact. This includes the exact extension functor on the strict-system heart, with the finite-level extension-by-zero maps.

The proof establishes normalized cohomology, bounded standard truncations, the strict-system heart and these two exact functors. BR proves a full comparison with the specified cartesian derived diagrams and a limit formula for their higher morphisms; BS proves the same comparison on the étale diagram site. BT proves the finite-coefficient heart realization, constructs the strict adic heart realization functor and gives its low-degree Ext comparison. Its general higher-effacement condition remains a separate obligation. BV supplies the exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality with their specified comparisons. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX completes its comparison with constructible rational sheaves and their operations. The free coefficient calculation is also explained in [ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Theorem 7.3](course:AG-LTF/l-adic-sheaves-and-their-cohomology#7-cohomology-and-its-torsion-correction); [Tag 09C5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C5) provides a general stabilization comparison. BQ.1–BQ.3 prove the uniform complete-DVR estimate and the sheaf normalization actually used here.

## Appendix BR. Derived coefficient systems and all their morphisms

Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), and \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). We now specify a category of coefficient diagrams and prove its equivalence with complete complexes on the pro-étale site. Its morphisms are derived morphisms of whole diagrams. A family of morphism classes at the individual levels carries less information; BR.5 gives the exact difference.

### BR.1. The category in which a coefficient diagram lives

Let \(\mathcal T=X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\), presented by the site used in BK. Form the site whose objects are pairs \((U,n)\), with a map \((U,n)\to(V,m)\) when \(n\leq m\) and a site map \(U\to V\). Coverings at fixed index are the original coverings. A sheaf on this site is exactly an inverse system of sheaves on \(\mathcal T\): the maps of pairs give its transitions, and the covering condition is the sheaf condition at each index.

There are two ring sheaves on this diagram site. Write \(B\) for the constant system \(\underline O\), and \(A\) for the system \((\underline{O_n})_n\) with quotient transitions. An \(A\)-module is an actual system \((M_n,u_n)\), where \(M_n\) is an \(O_n\)-sheaf and \(u_n:M_{n+1}\to M_n\) is linear over \(O_{n+1}\). Kernels, cokernels and exactness are evaluated at each index. Colimits are computed at each index, using sheafification, so filtered colimits are exact.

These module categories are Grothendieck categories. To check the generator condition explicitly, for each \((U,n)\) use the free module on its represented sheaf. At index \(j\leq n\) its value is the free \(A_j\)-module on the sheaf represented by \(U\), and at larger indices it is zero. A map from it to \(M\) is a section of \(M_n\) on \(U\). The sum over this set of objects is therefore a generator. For \(B\) use the same construction with \(O\) at every level. Thus BF.1–BF.4 apply, including the general Grothendieck-category resolution proved in [Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Theorem 7.2](course:derived-categories-and-sheaf-operations/sheaves-of-modules-and-their-derived-categories#7-k-injective-resolutions-of-unbounded-complexes). We obtain the locally small derived categories \(D(A)\) and \(D(B)\), by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms of actual diagram complexes.

There are also simultaneous K-flat resolutions. The displayed free generators are flat at each index by BL.1's finite-label sheafification argument. Tensor of diagram modules is evaluated at each index, so they are flat as diagram modules. Apply the disk-and-cycle construction of BL.1 to this set of generators. Its degreewise split attachments and exact filtered union give a quasi-isomorphism from a K-flat diagram complex; at each index the same filtration proves K-flatness and flatness of its individual terms. In particular, coefficient extension at a chosen index is computed by the same resolution of the whole diagram. Chain maps, cones and the comparisons of different resolutions retain the diagram maps throughout.

Call \(M\in D(A)\) **derived cartesian** if every transition induces an isomorphism
\[
O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^L M_{n+1}\xrightarrow{\sim}M_n.
\tag{BR.1}
\]
Evaluation is exact, so \(M_n\) is unambiguously an object of \(D(\mathcal T,O_n)\). The map in (BR.1) is the adjoint of the specified transition. By composition and derived tensor associativity it is an isomorphism for any pair of indices \(m\geq n\). Let \(D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A)\) be the full subcategory with this property. It is triangulated, since derived extension is exact and the cone comparison at each index is an isomorphism whenever the first two comparisons are. This definition includes the morphisms in \(D(A)\), rather than replacing them by a termwise limit of Hom sets.

### BR.2. Reduction and limit form a derived adjunction

First keep the constant coefficient ring \(O\). The constant-system functor \(c\) is exact and left adjoint to ordinary inverse limit on \(B\)-modules. Consequently its derived right adjoint is computed by taking a K-injective resolution \(J\) in the diagram category and then \(\varprojlim J_n\). Indeed inverse limit sends K-injectives to K-injectives: the Hom-complex adjunction tests it against the exact functor \(c\). Applying BF.6 proves the derived adjunction on all shifts and all morphisms.

Here this derived limit is the product-cone limit of BK.1. Choose \(J\) with injective terms, as supplied by the stated resolution theorem. For an injective \(B\)-diagram \(E\), the maps \(E_{n+1}(U)\to E_n(U)\) are surjective. To see this, the inclusion of the free diagram generated at \((U,n)\) into the one generated at \((U,n+1)\) is monic; extension of maps into \(E\) gives the asserted surjection on sections. The recursion for \(1-s\) can therefore be solved on sections. It follows that
\[
0\longrightarrow\varprojlim J_n
\longrightarrow\prod_nJ_n\xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_nJ_n
\longrightarrow0
\tag{BR.2}
\]
is an exact sequence of complexes. Countable products of \(O\)-sheaves on \(\mathcal T\) are exact by BK.1, so they preserve quasi-isomorphisms of arbitrary complexes. Hence the product-cone complex in (BR.2) computes the same functor on any representative of the original diagram. This proves the formula and its naturality as a functor of actual diagrams, without selecting nonfunctorial cones of morphism classes.

Factor coefficient reduction through the ring map \(B\to A\). Derived extension of scalars on the diagram site is left adjoint to exact restriction of scalars. The construction and verification are the scalar-extension argument of BL.5 on this site: use a K-flat diagram resolution in the source and a K-injective \(A\)-resolution in the target, and apply the ordinary tensor–Hom adjunction on complexes. If a K-flat source complex is acyclic, its extension is acyclic, so Hom into the latter K-injective resolution is acyclic. Replacing the middle object of a quasi-isomorphism roof by a K-flat resolution reduces the comparison to cones of quasi-isomorphisms between K-flat complexes. The preceding acyclicity makes precomposition by each such comparison an isomorphism on Hom groups in every degree. Thus the ordinary adjunction computes the localized Hom groups and descends through BF.2. This does not require restriction of that target resolution to be K-injective over \(B\).

Compose this adjunction with the constant-system adjunction. The result is
\[
F:D(\mathcal T,O)\rightleftarrows D(A):G,
\qquad
F(K)_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n,\quad
G(M)=\operatorname{holim}_n M_n.
\tag{BR.3}
\]
For the displayed formula for \(F\), choose a K-flat \(O\)-resolution \(P\) of \(K\). Its constant diagram is K-flat over \(B\), since every tensor test is evaluated at an index. Extension gives the actual diagram \((P\otimes_OO_n)_n\). For \(G\), first forget the coefficient structures to a \(B\)-diagram and then apply (BR.2). Both formulas therefore describe the composed adjunction, including its unit and counit. The triangle identities follow from those of the two adjunctions.

Derived scalar associativity shows \(F(K)\) is cartesian. Every term \(M_n\), viewed as an \(O\)-complex, is complete: multiplication by \(\pi^n\) is zero, so the finite geometric inverse to its multiplication-tower operator is the one in BK.4. Complete objects are closed under homotopy limits. Thus \(G(M)\) is complete, even without assuming that \(M\) is cartesian. Finally,
\[
GF(K)=C(K),
\tag{BR.4}
\]
with the actual completion unit of BK.4. This follows on the displayed K-flat representative from exactly its reduction tower. In particular the adjunction unit is an isomorphism whenever \(K\) is complete.

### BR.3. A cartesian diagram with zero limit is zero

We prove that \(G\) detects zero objects on \(D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A)\). Fix \(n\), and represent \(M\) by the simultaneous K-flat diagram \(P\) of BR.1. For \(m>n\), tensor the short exact coefficient sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow O_{m-n}\xrightarrow{\pi^n}O_m
\longrightarrow O_n\longrightarrow0
\tag{BR.5}
\]
with \(P_m\) over \(O_m\). Its terms are flat, so we obtain an actual short exact sequence of complexes, hence the natural cone triangle. These sequences commute as \(m\) varies: both outer coefficient maps are quotient maps and the middle one is the quotient transition, and the two multiplication squares commute.

The left complexes \(P_m\otimes_{O_m}O_{m-n}\) map to \(P_{m-n}\), and the right complexes \(P_m\otimes_{O_m}O_n\) map to \(P_n\). These are actual chain maps induced by the transitions of \(P\). They are quasi-isomorphisms by (BR.1) and the levelwise K-flat property. The right maps form a map to the constant diagram \(P_n\); the left maps form a map to the shifted-index diagram \((P_{m-n})_{m>n}\). Thus the coherent triangle of diagrams has the form
\[
(M_{m-n})_{m>n}\longrightarrow(M_m)_{m>n}
\longrightarrow(M_n)_{m>n}.
\tag{BR.6}
\]
This notation denotes the triangle just constructed from complexes and quasi-isomorphisms, not independently chosen triangle isomorphisms at each level.

Taking its product-cone limit is exact: finite cones commute with the products in (BR.2). Removing finitely many initial terms does not change that limit. For completeness, the forgotten initial coordinates form a finite complex of coordinate equations in \(1-s\); solving these successively eliminates them and gives a quasi-isomorphism with the tail product-cone complex. The left limit in (BR.6) is also \(G(M)\), by reindexing, and the right limit is \(M_n\): the diagonal and the successive-difference recursion identify the limit of a constant diagram, as in BK.4.

If \(G(M)=0\), the first two limits are therefore zero, so the triangle makes \(M_n=0\). This holds for every \(n\). A diagram complex is acyclic exactly when all its evaluations are acyclic, proving \(M=0\) in \(D(A)\). This argument uses the exact sequence (BR.5), available for the uniformizer in a discrete valuation ring; it asserts no such short exact sequence for arbitrary ideals in arbitrary rings.

### BR.4. Equivalence, coefficients and the constructible restriction

Restrict (BR.3) to complete objects on the left and cartesian objects on the right. The unit is an isomorphism by (BR.4). For a cartesian \(M\), let
\(\varepsilon_M:FG(M)\to M\)
be the adjunction counit. Both objects are cartesian, so its cone is cartesian. The triangle identity says
\(G(\varepsilon_M)\eta_{G(M)}=1\).
Since \(G(M)\) is complete, \(\eta_{G(M)}\) is an isomorphism; hence \(G(\varepsilon_M)\) is an isomorphism. BR.3 makes its cartesian cone zero. Therefore \(\varepsilon_M\) is an isomorphism. We have proved inverse equivalences
\[
D_X^c\simeq D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A).
\tag{BR.7}
\]
In particular, evaluating this actual counit gives
\[
G(M)\otimes_O^LO_n\xrightarrow{\sim}M_n
\tag{BR.8}
\]
as \(O_n\)-complexes, with their coefficient transition maps. Using the counit proves its module structure and naturality; an isomorphism merely after forgetting the coefficient structure would not supply those assertions.

Let \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A)\) be the full subcategory for which \(M_1\) is the pullback of a bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complex. By (BR.8) and the definition in BM.6, (BR.7) restricts to
\[
\mathscr C_X\simeq D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A).
\tag{BR.9}
\]
Every finite reduction on the right is consequently classical and bounded constructible, with the common bounds of BM.6. Its inverse-limit object has normalized cohomology and the bounded standard t-structure proved in BQ. The transported heart is BP's strict constructible coefficient category.

The last sentence does not place a strict system into \(D(A)\) simply as a degree-zero diagram. For a strict system \((F_n)\), form its complete sheaf \(\mathcal F=\varprojlim\nu_X^*F_n\) and then its derived diagram \(F(\mathcal F)\) using the reduction functor in (BR.3). Its terms have the torsion correction (BP.6). For example, the strict constant system \(F_n=\kappa\) has limit \(\underline\kappa\); its derived reductions are represented by \([O_n\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). In this model the transition is the quotient map in both terms. Its induced map on degree-minus-one cohomology is zero: the generator \(\pi^n\) of the kernel at level \(n+1\) becomes zero at level \(n\). This agrees with the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) transition on \(\kappa[\pi^n]\) obtained from the coefficient resolution in BK.3. The underived constant diagram \((\kappa)_n\) is not cartesian: already \(\kappa\otimes_{O_2}^L\kappa\) has nonzero negative cohomology. Indeed the free resolution over \(O_2\) with every differential multiplication by \(\pi\) is exact away from its last term, because kernel and image are both \(\pi O_2\); tensoring with \(\kappa\) makes all those differentials zero. This explains the required distinction between the strict heart and its derived coefficient diagram.

### BR.5. The higher-morphism formula and its degree-one-limit term

For \(K,L\in D_X^c\), let
\[
E_n=R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O_n}(K_n,L_n)
\quad\text{in }D(\mathbf{Ab}).
\tag{BR.10}
\]
One explicit way to retain this diagram is to resolve the fixed-\(O\) target tower by a K-injective \(B\)-diagram \(J\). Each \(J_n\) is K-injective over \(O\): evaluation at \(n\) has the exact left adjoint which repeats an \(O\)-sheaf at indices at most \(n\) and is zero afterwards. The Hom-complex adjunction therefore tests K-injectivity after evaluation. The actual complexes \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,J_n)\) now retain every transition.

The coefficient extension adjunction identifies \(E_n\) with
\(R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,L_n)\).
Use this identification to specify the transition maps: they are induced by \(L_{n+1}\to L_n\). Equivalently they reduce both source and target at once; associativity and the adjunction unit verify that description. Thus \((E_n)\) is the actual derived diagram obtained from the target reduction diagram by the fixed-source derived Hom functor.

Derived Hom in its second argument commutes with the products and the cones defining a homotopy limit. One can check the product assertion with K-injectives: a product of them is K-injective, since its Hom complex from any acyclic object is a product of acyclic complexes of abelian groups, and those products are exact. Ordinary Hom into the product is the product of the Hom complexes. The cone assertion follows from the two-summand cone formula. Since \(L\) is complete, this proves the natural isomorphism
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,L)
\simeq\operatorname{holim}_n E_n.
\tag{BR.11}
\]
These are derived Hom complexes of abelian groups, rather than sheaf Hom followed by an unproved interchange of ordinary sections and limits.

Taking cohomology of the product-cone complex gives, for every integer \(r\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&\longrightarrow
\varprojlim{}^{1}_n
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal T,O_n)}(K_n,L_n[r-1])\\
&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(K,L[r])\\
&\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal T,O_n)}(K_n,L_n[r])
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BR.12}
\]
Here \(\varprojlim{}^1\) means the cokernel of \(1-s\) on the product of the indicated groups. The kernel is the ordinary limit. Exactness of products of abelian groups gives precisely these two terms in the cone's long cohomology sequence; no finite-level Mittag–Leffler assertion has been assumed.

The right arrow takes a morphism to its actual reductions. Thus every compatible family of these morphism classes lifts, but its possible nonuniqueness is the left term. Replacing the middle group by the right group without proving that term zero would lose morphisms. When the preceding Hom groups are finite, their descending images stabilize, and the eventual-image and finite-geometric-sum proof of BP.2 for abelian groups makes this cokernel zero. As an elementary coefficient example, for two bounded finite free \(O\)-complexes the finite-level Hom complexes have finite terms, so this finiteness condition holds in each degree. No analogous global finiteness claim on an arbitrary base is needed for (BR.12).

The adjunction in BR.2 gives the same morphisms in the diagram category under (BR.7), for all shifts. Its unit and counit make the identification compatible with identities and composition. The transition maps in (BR.10) are evaluation adjoints as in BL.5, so (BR.11) uses the same coefficient maps. This establishes the full derived-diagram comparison, not just a bijection on isomorphism classes of objects.

BT constructs the realization functor from the bounded derived category of the strict-system heart to \(\mathscr C_X\), proves its degree-one comparison and degree-two injection, and reduces equivalence to the specified higher-effacement condition. Neither (BR.9) nor (BR.12) establishes that condition: its extension classes are computed inside the heart. BS proves the presentation on the étale diagram site, including its comparison functors and all transition maps. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX completes the full rational-sheaf comparison. Free comparisons for the constructions above are [derived limits, Tag 0940](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0940), [ringed-site adjunction, Tag 03D5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03D5), and [derived coefficient systems, Tag 0GZG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GZG); the uniformizer-sequence and counit proof above establishes the precise pro-étale complete-DVR statement used here.

## Appendix BS. Étale coefficient diagrams and their comparison maps

The coefficient diagrams of BR can also be formed on the étale site. We prove the comparison in the derived category of whole diagrams, including its arrows. Continue to write \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). Put \(A_{\mathrm e}=(\underline{O_n})_n\) on the diagram site of \(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\), and \(A_{\mathrm p}=(\underline{O_n})_n\) on the diagram site of \(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\). Thus \(A_{\mathrm p}\) is BR's \(A\). The generators, exact filtered colimits and resolutions of BR.1 work on either site.

### BS.1. Evaluation and its derived left adjoint

Let \(e_n\) denote evaluation at index \(n\). This is exact. Its ordinary left adjoint sends an \(O_n\)-sheaf \(H\) to the diagram
\[
(e_{n,!}H)_j=
\begin{cases}
O_j\otimes_{O_n}H,&j\leq n,\\
0,&j>n.
\end{cases}
\tag{BS.1}
\]
The transitions are the quotient maps on coefficients. A map from this diagram to \(M\) is determined by its component \(H\to M_n\); its other components are precisely the composites with the transitions of \(M\). This proves the adjunction. The functor in (BS.1) need not be exact: already \(O_1\) need not be flat over \(O_2\). Consequently evaluation of an injective coefficient diagram cannot be treated as injective by an exact-left-adjoint argument.

Resolve \(H\) by the K-flat cell complex of BL.1. Applying (BS.1) gives a derived functor with components
\[
(Le_{n,!}H)_j=
\begin{cases}
O_j\otimes_{O_n}^LH,&j\leq n,\\
0,&j>n.
\end{cases}
\qquad Le_{n,!}\dashv e_n.
\tag{BS.2}
\]
Here is a verification of the last assertion that also explains its unbounded meaning. Formula (BS.1) sends a free sheaf generator \(O_n[U]\) to the free diagram generator at \((U,n)\). It therefore sends the chosen cell filtration to a diagram cell filtration. An acyclic K-flat source complex is sent to an acyclic diagram, since every component is a tensor of that complex. Choose a K-injective target diagram \(I\). The ordinary complex adjunction identifies
\(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(e_{n,!}P,I)\)
with \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(P,I_n)\).
For an acyclic K-flat \(P\) the first complex is acyclic. To calculate a derived morphism to \(I_n\), replace the source and the middle object of each quasi-isomorphism roof by K-flat resolutions. The cone of the resulting quasi-isomorphism between K-flat complexes is acyclic and K-flat, so the preceding acyclicity makes precomposition an isomorphism on these Hom groups. The ordinary adjunction therefore descends to the localized Hom groups, exactly as in BR.2. Since \(I_n\) represents evaluation of the target, this proves (BS.2) without assuming it is K-injective.

The exact functor \(\nu^*\) of BK.2 acts on all components and transitions. Denote this diagram functor by \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\). Its right adjoint \(\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\) is ordinary componentwise \(\nu_*\): the component adjunction bijections take a commuting transition square to its adjoint commuting square. Exactness of \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) makes \(\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\) preserve K-injectives, by the Hom-complex test. Thus
\[
\nu_{\mathrm s}^*:D(A_{\mathrm e})
\rightleftarrows D(A_{\mathrm p}):R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}
\tag{BS.3}
\]
is a derived adjunction.

Pullback commutes with coefficient extension and the prefixes (BS.2). Indeed inverse image preserves tensor products by their free-module and relation presentation. It pulls each flat free-sheaf cell to a flat free-sheaf cell; the degreewise split filtration therefore remains K-flat. Applying this to a chosen resolution gives the natural isomorphism
\[
\nu_{\mathrm s}^*Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e}
\simeq Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm p}\nu_n^*.
\tag{BS.4}
\]
The same argument gives the coefficient-extension comparison at any two indices. These are comparisons of the chosen complexes and their quotient maps, so associativity agrees for three or more indices.

### BS.2. Deriving direct image retains every transition

For \(E\in D(A_{\mathrm p})\), (BS.2)–(BS.4) give, naturally in every \(H\in D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}(H,e_nR\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E)
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e}H,R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e}H,E)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm p}\nu_n^*H,E)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(\nu_n^*H,E_n)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(H,R\nu_{n,*}E_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BS.5}
\]
Yoneda consequently identifies
\[
e_nR\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E\simeq R\nu_{n,*}E_n.
\tag{BS.6}
\]
The notation on the right means derived direct image of \(O_n\)-modules. In particular (BS.6) has been proved, rather than inferred by evaluating a diagram resolution and declaring it a resolution at each index.

We check transition compatibility. For an \(O_{n+1}\)-complex \(H\), there is a natural map
\[
Le_{n,!}(O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LH)
\longrightarrow Le_{n+1,!}H.
\tag{BS.7}
\]
At indices at most \(n\) this is the tensor-associativity identification; at \(n+1\) it is the map from zero, and above that both sides are zero. Choose one K-flat resolution of \(H\) to construct all these components. Under the two evaluation adjunctions, precomposition with (BS.7) is exactly the transition from component \(n+1\) to component \(n\), with restriction of coefficients understood. Pullback respects (BS.7). Every bijection in (BS.5) therefore respects this precomposition, which proves compatibility of (BS.6) with the transitions. The same argument with the adjunction identity maps shows that the unit and counit of (BS.3), evaluated at \(n\), are the ordinary derived \(\nu_n\) unit and counit. There is no independent choice of an isomorphism at each level.

### BS.3. Bounded-below descent and the constructible restriction

We recall the exact finite-coefficient input and its essential-image argument. By (BK.3), \(\nu_n^*\) is fully faithful on \(D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\). Call an \(O_n\)-sheaf on the enlarged site classical if it is a pullback from the étale site. A bounded complex whose cohomology sheaves are classical is in the image: induct on its finite cohomology interval. Its truncation triangle is glued from the previous truncation and a shifted classical sheaf. Full faithfulness lifts the connecting morphism, and its cone gives the required étale object.

For a bounded-below complex \(E\) with classical cohomology, apply this argument to \(\tau^{\leq r}E\). The functor \(R\nu_{n,*}\) preserves lower bounds. To verify this, represent any complex in degrees at least \(a\) by a bounded-below injective resolution starting in degree \(a\); ordinary direct image does not introduce lower terms. Hence \(R\nu_{n,*}(\tau^{>r}E)\) has cohomology only above \(r\). Exactness of \(\nu_n^*\) has the same property. Naturality of the counit triangle now identifies the counit for \(E\), through degree \(r\), with that for \(\tau^{\leq r}E\), which is an isomorphism. Letting \(r\) vary proves
\(\nu_n^*R\nu_{n,*}E\simeq E\).
This proves the bounded-below essential-image assertion using finite truncations; it assumes no preservation of arbitrary inverse limits by étale inverse image.

For \(L\in D^+(A_{\mathrm e})\), (BS.6) identifies every component of its unit with (BK.3), so the unit is an isomorphism. Evaluations detect acyclicity of diagram complexes. It follows that \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) is fully faithful on \(D^+(A_{\mathrm e})\).

Conversely let \(E\in D^+(A_{\mathrm p})\) have classical cohomology at every index. Apply (BS.6) and the preceding finite-coefficient argument to its counit: every component is an isomorphism, hence so is the diagram counit. Its preimage is bounded below as a diagram. In fact \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\), being a right derived functor of a left exact functor, preserves the common lower bound by the same bounded-below injective-resolution argument. We have proved an equivalence between bounded-below étale diagrams and bounded-below pro-étale diagrams with componentwise classical cohomology. It includes all derived morphisms, because it is the restriction of (BS.3).

Define \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm e})\) to be the full subcategory of \(D(A_{\mathrm e})\) satisfying the cartesian transition condition (BR.1) and having bounded constructible first component. No separate bound on all components is imposed in this definition. Applying \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) gives an object of \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm p})\), by the tensor comparison proved in BS.1. BR.4 and BM.6 show that all its components have classical constructible cohomology with one common finite interval of degrees. The original étale components have those same bounds: exact \(\nu_n^*\) is conservative, since \(\nu_{n,*}\nu_n^*\) is the identity on sheaves by BK.2. Thus the étale diagram itself is bounded.

In the other direction a pro-étale cartesian constructible diagram is bounded with classical components by BR.4, so it descends by the bounded-below equivalence just proved. Its descended transitions are cartesian: their derived scalar-extension maps become isomorphisms after \(\nu_n^*\), by BS.1–BS.2, and conservativity makes them isomorphisms already on the étale site. Its first component is bounded constructible by the finite-level comparison and the definition in BR.4. Consequently
\[
D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm e})
\xrightarrow[\ \nu_{\mathrm s}^*\ ]{\ \sim\ }
D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm p})
\simeq\mathscr C_X.
\tag{BS.8}
\]
The inverse to the first arrow is \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\). The inverse from \(\mathscr C_X\) to the left is \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}F\), with BR's reduction functor \(F\). All components, transitions, units and counits are those established above.

### BS.4. Higher morphisms on the étale site

For \(K,L\in\mathscr C_X\), denote the components of their étale diagrams in (BS.8) by \(K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}\). Their pullbacks are their actual derived reductions \(K_n,L_n\), with the transitions of BR. Thus full faithfulness of the bounded-below finite-level comparison identifies the groups and the transition maps in (BR.12). We obtain, for every integer \(r\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&\longrightarrow\varprojlim{}^1_n
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)}
(K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}[r-1])\\
&\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(K,L[r])\\
&\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)}
(K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}[r])
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BS.9}
\]
The transition maps reduce both arguments along the specified cartesian arrows, or equivalently use BR.5's fixed-source adjunction. Their agreement follows from the tensor and transition compatibilities in BS.1–BS.2. The middle term is equally the Hom group of the two actual étale diagrams under (BS.8). Identities and composition agree by the adjunction triangle identities. No finiteness hypothesis has been added to discard the degree-one-limit term.

The standard t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\) transports through (BS.8). Its heart is BP's strict constructible systems, represented by the derived reductions of their complete sheaves. It is not identified by declaring their underived systems to be cartesian: BR.4's constant torsion example still has its negative-degree correction. BT constructs the realization functor from the bounded derived category of this heart, proves its low-degree extension comparisons and gives the exact remaining effacement condition for equivalence. That condition is not deduced from the existence of a bounded t-structure. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality on these categories. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX supplies the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves, all higher morphisms and the ordinary operations.

The free finite-level comparison is discussed in [the Stacks Project, Section 61.19](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099R), especially Lemmas 61.19.4, 61.19.5 and 61.19.8. BK.2 proves the acyclicity and unit used here; BS.1–BS.3 supply the derived-prefix, transition and whole-diagram arguments needed to pass from that input to (BS.8).

## Appendix BT. Finite-coefficient realization and the adic extension problem

The equivalence in BS concerns derived categories of coefficient diagrams. A different functor starts with bounded complexes in the abelian category of constructible sheaves. We construct this functor, prove the finite-coefficient equivalence, and state and prove the exact additional condition needed for its adic counterpart. Throughout, \(X\) has the arithmetic hypotheses of this lesson and \(R=O_n\) for a fixed \(n\geq1\).

### BT.1. Constructible subsheaves and finite generation

Write \(\mathcal A_R=\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},R)\), and let \(\mathcal B_R\) be its full subcategory of constructible sheaves. Kernels, cokernels and extensions of its objects are constructible by the finite-module argument in BM.6. We need the stronger assertion that every ambient subsheaf of a constructible sheaf is constructible and that these sheaves are Noetherian objects of \(\mathcal A_R\).

Here is a local description of an arbitrary subsheaf \(Q\subset\underline M\), where \(M\) is a finite \(R\)-module on a Noetherian scheme \(V\). For \(m\in M\), the points where the constant germ \(m\) belongs to \(Q\) form an open subset \(V_m\). A germ belonging to \(Q\) lifts on an étale neighbourhood; equality of its image with the constant section holds after shrinking that neighbourhood. Its image in \(V\) is open. On overlaps the lifts agree, because \(Q\to\underline M\) is monic, so they descend to a section on this image. Taking their union proves both openness and the existence of the section \(m\in Q(V_m)\). Thus \(Q\) is determined by the finitely many membership opens \(V_m\). A partition refining these opens and their complements makes its stalk submodules constant, and hence makes \(Q\) locally constant on each part.

Apply this description on étale trivializing neighbourhoods of each stratum of a constructible sheaf \(F\). For clarity, constructibility descends here without assuming a stratification has already descended. On an irreducible stratum choose a trivializing étale neighbourhood of its generic point. Choose an irreducible component containing a point over that generic point, and remove the other components; this gives a nonempty irreducible open still mapping onto an open containing the generic point. In this irreducible neighbourhood, intersect the finitely many nonempty membership opens. The resulting nonempty open has \(Q\) constant; its open image contains the generic point, and \(Q\) is locally constant there by this étale cover. Separate the finitely many generic points first and repeat on the remaining closed subset. Noetherian induction gives a finite constructible partition. This proves that \(Q\subset F\) is constructible. A quotient of \(F\) is then constructible by the cokernel assertion already proved.

For an ascending sequence of subsheaves of \(F\), use one finite collection of quasi-compact étale neighbourhoods trivializing \(F\) on its finitely many strata. Each membership open is now an ascending sequence of opens in a Noetherian scheme, so it stabilizes. There are finitely many neighbourhoods and finitely many elements of their finite modules. One index therefore works for all of them. Equality on these neighbourhoods implies equality on all geometric stalks, hence equality of sheaves. Thus \(F\) is Noetherian even with respect to arbitrary ambient subsheaves.

The category \(\mathcal A_R\) is generated by such objects. Take affine étale maps \(u:U\to X\) of finite presentation, with image in an affine open of \(X\). The free sheaf \(R[U]\) represents sections on \(U\). It is also \(u_!\underline R_U\): by the exact étale adjunction of M.5, maps from either sheaf to \(H\) are \(H(U)\). Proposition 3.2 makes this sheaf constructible. The maps from these generators indexed by all local sections surject onto any \(H\in\mathcal A_R\), as is checked on stalks. Images of their finite sums are constructible quotients. Consequently
\[
H=\bigcup_{H'\subset H,\ H'\in\mathcal B_R}H'.
\tag{BT.1}
\]
The union is directed by sums. In particular, an epimorphism \(H\twoheadrightarrow F\) with constructible target has a constructible subobject of \(H\) still surjecting onto \(F\). Indeed the images in \(F\) form a directed union of subobjects; the ascending chain condition makes that union attained. If it were not attained, repeatedly choosing an image not contained in the previous one and taking sums would give a strictly ascending sequence.

### BT.2. Extension classes as actual derived morphisms

For an abelian category \(\mathcal A\), write \(D^b(\mathcal A)\) for the localization of bounded complexes up to chain homotopy at quasi-isomorphisms. The construction by roofs, including common refinements, cancellation and composition, is proved in [Complexes, cones and localization, §4](course:derived-categories-and-sheaf-operations/complexes-cones-and-localization#4-fractions-at-quasi-isomorphisms). Its fraction squares and cancellation witnesses use finite sums, shifts and cones, so bounded inputs give bounded witnesses. This construction does not require injectives in \(\mathcal A\). We retain the shift \(K[r]^n=K^{n+r}\), with differential \((-1)^r d_K\), and the cone triangle with positive projection fixed in B.1.

The [bounded-roof lemma](course:sheaf-proof-readings/SH03-derived-constructibility-through-common-triangulations#bounded-roofs-and-their-homotopy-witnesses) proves that this localization embeds fully faithfully into the localization of all complexes, with essential image the objects of bounded cohomology. The actual comparison is useful here. For a roof \(F\leftarrow Q\to G\) with bounded ends, choose \(a<b\) strictly outside their term supports and put \(U=\tau_{\le b}Q\), \(L=\tau_{\ge a}U\). The upper cut uses \(\ker d_Q^b\); the lower cut uses \(U^a/\operatorname{im}d_U^{a-1}\). Both arrows \(Q\leftarrow U\to L\) are quasi-isomorphisms. The maps to \(F,G\) restrict to \(U\) and factor through \(L\), by their chain-map equations. A specified homotopy into a bounded target also descends after taking \(a\) below that target's support: its degree-\(a\) target is zero, and its equation descends along the termwise epimorphism \(U\to L\). Thus a common refinement or a nullhomotopy witnessing equality of bounded roofs has a bounded witness. This supplies both fullness and faithfulness; the same two cuts give the essential-image assertion. These arguments apply to the constructible and strict adic hearts below, independently of the ambient injective resolutions.

We will use the following elementary description in an abelian category \(\mathcal A\). For \(F,G\in\mathcal A\) and \(r>0\), an \(r\)-extension is an exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow E_{r-1}\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow E_0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BT.2}
\]
Two such sequences represent the same Yoneda class if they are joined by a finite zigzag of maps of exact sequences that are the identity on \(F,G\). The Baer operation uses direct sum followed by pullback along the diagonal of \(F\) and pushout along addition on \(G\).

Let \(Q_E=[G\to E_{r-1}\to\cdots\to E_0]\) in degrees \(-r,\ldots,0\), with the differentials displayed in (BT.2). Its augmentation \(s_E:Q_E\to F\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Write \(p_E:Q_E\to G[r]\) for the projection that is the identity in degree \(-r\). Set
\[
\varepsilon_r=(-1)^{r(r-1)/2},\qquad
\Theta_r(E)=(\varepsilon_r p_E)s_E^{-1}.
\tag{BT.3a}
\]
For \(r=0\), \(\Theta_0\) is the ordinary inclusion of morphisms. The scalar in (BT.3a) makes extension splicing agree with shifted composition, as verified below. For \(r>0\) this construction gives the natural map
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal A}(F,G)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal A)}(F,G[r]).
\tag{BT.3}
\]
It is a bijection, as the following inverse construction shows. Represent a morphism by \(F\xleftarrow{\sim}Q\to G[r]\). Good truncation above zero, and then quotient truncation below \(-r\), preserve both arrows and the quasi-isomorphism to \(F\). We may therefore take \(Q\) in degrees \([-r,0]\), exact in all negative degrees. Its first differential \(Q^{-r}\to Q^{-r+1}\) is monic. If \(f:Q\to G[r]\) is the numerator, push this monomorphism out along \(\varepsilon_r f^{-r}:Q^{-r}\to G\). Appending \(Q^{-r+2},\ldots,Q^0,F\) gives (BT.2). For \(r=1\) the pushout is simply an extension of \(F\) by \(G\).

A common refinement of roofs gives maps between the pushed-out sequences. For the homotopy check, suppose two numerators satisfy \(f-g=hd_Q\) in degree \(-r\), where \(h:Q^{-r+1}\to G\). Write the pushout for \(f\) as the quotient of \(Q^{-r+1}\oplus G\) by the image of \(x\mapsto(d_Qx,-\varepsilon_r f x)\). The map \((e,y)\mapsto(e,y+\varepsilon_r h e)\) carries this relation to the relation for \(g\), so it gives an isomorphism of extensions fixing both endpoints. Its inverse uses the negative of the same added term. The augmentation to \(F[0]\) cannot change under a homotopy once the middle complex has been cut above zero: every possibly contributing homotopy term has zero source or target. Thus common refinements and their homotopies give a finite zigzag of actual extension maps.

Conversely the pushed-out extension receives a map from \(Q\), whose degree-\(-r\) component is \(\varepsilon_r f^{-r}\). Its normalized roof numerator is therefore \(\varepsilon_r^2 f=f\). Starting from an extension, the inverse construction pushes out along \(\varepsilon_r^2 1_G=1_G\), so it returns that extension. This proves the bijection and the zigzag criterion. Direct sums, diagonal pullbacks and addition pushouts give precisely addition of roofs; the same constructions show naturality in both endpoints.

Here is the sign computation for splicing. Let \(E\) be a \(p\)-extension of \(F\) by \(K\), let \(D\) be a \(q\)-extension of \(K\) by \(G\), and write \(C=Q_{D\#E}\) for their ordinary splice complex. There is a quasi-isomorphism \(v:C\to Q_E\): it is the identity in degrees greater than \(-p\), the augmentation \(D_0\to K\) in degree \(-p\), and zero below. It commutes with augmentation to \(F\). Define \(a:C\to Q_D[p]\) to be zero above \(-p\) and multiplication by \((-1)^{pj}\) in degree \(-p-j\), for \(0\le j\le q\). The successive factors satisfy \((-1)^p(-1)^{pj}=(-1)^{p(j-1)}\), exactly the chain-map equation for the shifted differential. At the joining degree both outgoing composites are zero. Moreover \(s_D[p]a=p_Ev\), whereas \(p_D[p]a=(-1)^{pq}p_{D\#E}\). These maps give the square for the unsigned roofs; replacing \(a\) by \(\varepsilon_p a\) gives the square for the normalized first numerator. Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta_q(D)[p]\,\Theta_p(E)
 &=\varepsilon_q\varepsilon_p(-1)^{pq}
       p_{D\#E}s_{D\#E}^{-1}\\
 &=\Theta_{p+q}(D\#E),\\
\varepsilon_{p+q}&=(-1)^{pq}\varepsilon_p\varepsilon_q.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BT.3b}
\]
For \(p=q=1\), the map \(a\) is the identity on \(D_0\) and minus the identity on \(G\); the unsigned roof composite is therefore the negative of the splice projection. In degree one, \(\varepsilon_1=1\) and \(Q_E\) is the cone of \(G\to E_0\), so \(\Theta_1\) is exactly the connecting morphism with B.1's positive cone projection. Formula (BT.3b) therefore proves the compatibility with connecting morphisms used in BT.4–BT.5. No injective objects in the heart are needed.

### BT.3. Finite subextensions give every higher comparison

Consider an \(r\)-extension (BT.2) in \(\mathcal A_R\), with \(F,G\in\mathcal B_R\). Choose a constructible \(E'_0\subset E_0\) surjecting onto \(F\), using (BT.1). Its kernel \(K_1\) is constructible. The inverse image of \(K_1\) in \(E_1\) surjects onto \(K_1\), so choose a constructible \(E'_1\) in that inverse image still surjecting onto \(K_1\). Continue towards \(G\). At the last step include the entire given \(G\) in \(E'_{r-1}\). The latter remains constructible, because finite sums and images are constructible. Its kernel is now exactly \(G\). This gives a subextension all of whose terms belong to \(\mathcal B_R\), with the original endpoints.

There is a useful relative version. Suppose finitely many constructible subcomplexes in the middle terms have already been specified. At degree zero include their sum when choosing \(E'_0\). At each next step their degree-\(i\) sum already maps into the chosen kernel, because they are subcomplexes. Include that sum in the chosen preimage and add the finitely many further generators needed to cover the kernel. This constructs a subextension containing every specified subcomplex.

It follows that all ambient extension classes lift to \(\mathcal B_R\). They have the same equivalence relation there. To prove this last point, take a finite zigzag relating two extensions already in \(\mathcal B_R\). Regard its nodes as extensions and orient each edge by its actual map. A finite path with these orientations has no directed cycles. Process the nodes in an order consistent with the arrows. At each nonfixed node choose a constructible subextension containing the images of all previously chosen incoming extensions, using the relative version. The two original endpoints are kept in their entirety. An arrow into such a fixed endpoint automatically lands in it. Every arrow now restricts to the chosen subextensions. This is a zigzag wholly inside \(\mathcal B_R\) with the same fixed ends.

Using (BT.3), we have proved for every \(r\geq0\)
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal B_R)}(F,G[r])
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},R)}(F,G[r]).
\tag{BT.4}
\]
For \(r=0\), a roof into \(G[0]\) can first be cut above zero; its numerator factors through its degree-zero cohomology, identified with \(F\) by the denominator. This identifies the derived Hom group with ordinary \(\operatorname{Hom}(F,G)\), in either category. For \(r<0\), the same upper cut has no term in the positive degree supporting \(G[r]\), so the group is zero. The bounded-comparison proof in BT.2 embeds the ambient bounded localization fully in the unbounded derived category constructed in BF. Thus (BT.3) computes exactly the groups in (BT.4).

Exact inclusion defines a functor on bounded complexes and takes acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes. Its derived functor lands in complexes with constructible cohomology. It is fully faithful on all bounded complexes: first fix a shifted heart object as source and induct on the target's finite cohomology interval, using its truncation triangle and the long exact Hom sequences; then induct on the source interval in the same way. At each step the five-term exact-sequence argument uses the already known outer comparisons and proves the middle one. For essential surjectivity, truncate a bounded constructible ambient complex. Inductively realize its lower truncation and its top cohomology sheaf; full faithfulness lifts the connecting map, and its cone realizes the original complex. We have proved
\[
D^b(\mathcal B_{O_n})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n).
\tag{BT.5}
\]
This is an assertion for the category allowing all finite constructible stratifications. It does not assert realization for an arbitrarily prescribed fixed stratification or for the lisse subcategory alone. The construction in BT.1 may refine the stratification when it takes a subsheaf.

### BT.4. The realization functor for the strict adic heart

Let \(\mathcal H_X=\mathscr C_X\cap D^{[0,0]}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},O)\). BQ proves that this is an abelian category with exact inclusion into ambient \(O\)-sheaves, and BP identifies it with strict constructible systems. It is closed under ambient extensions: a short exact sequence with endpoints in \(\mathcal H_X\) gives a triangle in which the middle sheaf is complete and has constructible first derived reduction. Thus it belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\) and is in degree zero.

Applying exact inclusion to a bounded complex in \(\mathcal H_X\) gives an object of \(\mathscr C_X\). This follows also by its finite sequence of brutal-truncation triangles, whose individual terms are shifts of heart objects. Acyclic complexes remain acyclic. Localization therefore gives the specified functor
\[
\operatorname{real}_X:D^b(\mathcal H_X)\longrightarrow\mathscr C_X.
\tag{BT.6}
\]
It preserves standard cohomology, since inclusion preserves kernels, images and cokernels. Through BP this is also a realization functor from the strict-system heart. It is not the functor sending an underived strict tower directly to the cartesian diagram category; its image is first a complex of complete sheaves, whose diagram is then given by BR–BS.

For \(F,G\in\mathcal H_X\), write
\[
\theta_r:\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_X}(F,G)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(F,G[r]).
\tag{BT.7}
\]
The map \(\theta_0\) is an isomorphism. So is \(\theta_1\): (BT.3) identifies the ambient morphisms with short exact extensions, and their middle sheaves belong to \(\mathcal H_X\) by extension closure. Maps and equivalences of these extensions are maps in the same full subcategory.

The map \(\theta_2\) is injective. Represent a two-extension as the splice of \(0\to K\to E_0\to F\to0\) with a one-extension of \(K\) by \(G\), whose class is \(\beta\). If its ambient class is zero, the exact Hom sequence of the first triangle says that the ambient class of \(\beta\) is the restriction of a morphism \(E_0\to G[1]\). By \(\theta_1\), this morphism is a heart one-extension. Injectivity of \(\theta_1\) makes its restriction equal to \(\beta\) already in the heart. The connecting homomorphism inside \(D^b(\mathcal H_X)\) kills that restriction, so the original two-extension is zero. This argument proves injectivity; it does not supply surjectivity in degree two.

### BT.5. The precise remaining effacement condition
