For this specified functor, the following condition is necessary and sufficient for equivalence:

For every \(F,G\in\mathcal H_X\), every integer \(r>0\), and every \(\alpha:F\to G[r]\) in \(\mathscr C_X\), there exists an epimorphism \(E\twoheadrightarrow F\) in \(\mathcal H_X\) such that the composite \(E\to F\xrightarrow\alpha G[r]\) is zero.
\[
\text{This condition will be denoted }(\mathrm E_X).
\tag{BT.8}
\]
Only the given morphism is required to be killed; a single epimorphism killing all positive morphisms is not asserted.

Suppose \((\mathrm E_X)\) holds. We prove all \(\theta_r\) are isomorphisms by induction. Degrees zero and one are established above. Given an ambient class \(\alpha\) in degree \(r>1\), choose the indicated epimorphism and let \(K\) be its heart kernel. Exactness of Hom for \(K\to E\to F\) lifts \(\alpha\) to a morphism \(K\to G[r-1]\). Induction realizes that morphism by a heart extension. Splicing it with \(0\to K\to E\to F\to0\) proves surjectivity of \(\theta_r\).

For injectivity, represent a heart \(r\)-extension as the same kind of splice, with an \((r-1)\)-extension class \(\beta\) on \(K\). If its ambient image is zero, the ambient exact sequence expresses the image of \(\beta\) as the restriction of a morphism \(E\to G[r-1]\). Surjectivity in degree \(r-1\) lifts that morphism to a heart class; injectivity in degree \(r-1\) identifies its restriction with \(\beta\). The heart connecting homomorphism therefore kills \(\beta\), proving the original class zero. The finite-truncation argument of BT.3 now proves full faithfulness and essential surjectivity of (BT.6), since BQ supplies the bounded t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\).

Conversely, if (BT.6) is an equivalence, any \(\alpha\) comes from a Yoneda extension by (BT.3). Take its final epimorphism \(E_0\twoheadrightarrow F\). Pullback along this epimorphism splits the last short exact sequence, so it kills the spliced extension, and therefore kills \(\alpha\). This proves \((\mathrm E_X)\).

The finite-coefficient result (BT.5) proves the corresponding condition separately at each fixed \(O_n\). It does not produce a compatible family of heart epimorphisms as \(n\) varies. Moreover, derived reduction of an adic heart object may have degree-minus-one cohomology, as BR.4 explicitly calculates for torsion. Ordinary quotient maps cannot simply replace these derived reductions in the effacement problem. Thus (BT.6), the degree-zero and degree-one isomorphisms, the degree-two injection and criterion (BT.8) are proved. BU establishes this condition and full equivalence in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields. BY proves full integral and rational realization for curves over those fields, and proves the formal implication from a specified higher-dimensional projection theorem. The higher-dimensional projection and realization arguments are treated separately in BZ–CB. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX proves the full rational-sheaf comparison with integral models and operations.

Free comparisons are [constructible sheaves on Noetherian schemes, Tag 03RY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RY), [constructible closure, Tag 03RZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RZ), [derived subcategories, Tag 06UP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06UP), and [Yoneda extensions, Stacks Project §13.27](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06XP). The sign distinction between ordinary splicing and unsigned roof composition is also discussed by Volkov and Witherspoon, [*Graded Lie Structure on Cohomology of Some Exact Monoidal Categories*, §2, pp.82–83, free author-hosted copy](https://people.tamu.edu/~sjw/pub/HHA-2024-26-2-a04.pdf). The membership-open, finite-subextension, roof and effacement arguments above give the particular realization statements used here, with the shift signs explicitly computed in (BT.3a)–(BT.3b).

## Appendix BU. Adic realization in dimension zero

We prove the full realization assertion of BT over a finite field, over an algebraically closed field, and over every zero-dimensional scheme of finite type over either field. We retain the coefficient ring \(O\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), and \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). The residue characteristic of \(O\) is invertible on the scheme. Write \(\mathcal H_X\) for the strict adic heart of BP–BQ and \(\mathscr C_X\) for the complete constructible category.

### BU.1. A natural two-term complex for finite-field coefficients

Let \(s=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q\), choose an algebraic closure, and put \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbf F}_q/\mathbf F_q)\). Here \(\phi(a)=a^q\) is **arithmetic** Frobenius. The field and sheaf arguments in [Galois cohomology and the étale cohomology of a field, Sections 1–3 and 6](course:ag-etale-cohomology/galois-cohomology-and-the-etale-cohomology-of-a-field#1-reconstructing-a-sheaf-from-its-geometric-stalk) prove the following facts with their actual maps. The group \(G\) is \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\), generated topologically by \(\phi\); discrete continuous \(G\)-modules are equivalent to étale module sheaves; and derived sections are computed by the continuous inhomogeneous cochain complex \(C^\bullet(G,N)\). The finite-étale field classification and exact sheaf equivalence required by those arguments are also proved in AB.1–AB.2; AA.1–AA.2 supply their compactness, continuous-cochain and injective-comparison prerequisites.

For a finite \(O_n\)-module \(N\), write \(T\) for the action of \(\phi\). Define
\[
B_\phi(N)=[N\xrightarrow{T-1}N]
\quad\text{in degrees }0,1.
\tag{BU.1}
\]
There is a natural chain map
\[
C^\bullet(G,N)\longrightarrow B_\phi(N)
\tag{BU.2}
\]
which is the identity in degree zero, sends a degree-one cochain \(c\) to \(c(\phi)\), and is zero in higher degrees. The only nonzero differential to check is degree zero: \((dm)(\phi)=Tm-m\). Thus it is a chain map on all cochains, not merely a correspondence between cocycles.

It is a quasi-isomorphism. Here is the precise finite-quotient calculation supplying this conclusion. Section 6 of the cited lesson proves the cyclic resolution with alternating maps \(t-1\) and \(1+t+\cdots+t^{d-1}\). For inflation from the cyclic quotient of order \(d\) to the one of order \(ed\), its comparison map multiplies degree-\(r\) cochain representatives by \(e^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}\). Its proof checks the chain equations and the resolution comparison homotopy. Once \(e\) kills \(N\), all classes in degree at least two die under this inflation. In degree one the map on representatives is the identity, and the norm condition becomes zero after this enlargement. Passing to the continuous cochains, which are the filtered union of these finite-quotient cochains by AA.1–AA.2, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H^0(G,N)&=\ker(T-1),\\
H^1(G,N)&=\operatorname{coker}(T-1),\\
H^{r}(G,N)&=0\qquad(r\geq2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BU.3}
\]
The degree-one identification is evaluation at \(\phi\): a crossed homomorphism on a cyclic quotient is determined by its value at the generator, and its relation is exactly the norm condition. Hence (BU.2) induces these identifications. Every map in (BU.2) commutes with coefficient homomorphisms. In particular it compares an entire quotient tower of coefficients.

### BU.2. Completed sections of a heart object

At \(s\), every constructible finite sheaf is lisse. BP and N.4 therefore identify \(\mathcal H_s\) with the abelian category of finite \(O\)-modules \(M\) with continuous \(G\)-action. Such an action is equivalent to an automorphism \(T\) of \(M\). Indeed \(T\) acts on each finite quotient \(M/\pi^nM\) with finite order, so the homomorphism from \(\mathbf Z\) extends to \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\) on that quotient. Uniqueness makes these extensions compatible, and N.4 recovers a continuous action on \(M\). Conversely continuity and density determine the action from \(T\). An intertwining \(O\)-linear map is automatically continuous by preservation of the \(\pi\)-adic filtration. This proves the assertion also on morphisms.

Let \(H\) be the complete sheaf corresponding to \((M,T)\), and let \(H_n\) be its ordinary quotient sheaf. BP.2–BP.4 give the actual identification
\[
H=\operatorname{holim}_n\nu_s^*H_n,\qquad (H_n)_{\bar s}=M/\pi^nM.
\tag{BU.4}
\]
These are ordinary quotients of a heart object; their limit is justified by BP. This does not replace the derived reductions in BR–BS.

Derived sections commute with this homotopy limit. One can check the assertion on the product-and-cone model: use the diagram injective replacements of BR.5, apply sections to the products, and retain the actual \(1-s\) map. The finite-coefficient comparison BK.2 and the natural maps (BU.2) consequently give
\[
R\Gamma(s_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},H)
\simeq\operatorname{holim}_n B_\phi(M/\pi^nM)
\simeq [M\xrightarrow{T-1}M].
\tag{BU.5}
\]
For the second isomorphism, both terms of the tower in (BU.1) have surjective quotient transitions. On their products the equations \(a_n-u_na_{n+1}=b_n\) are solved successively: choose \(a_1\), then lift \(a_n-b_n\) to choose \(a_{n+1}\). Thus \(1-s\) is surjective in each degree and its kernel is the degreewise inverse limit. The short exact sequence of complexes identifies the homotopy limit with that kernel. N.4 identifies its two terms with \(M\). This also proves naturality of (BU.5), including for modules with torsion.

For a geometric point \(\bar s=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\), with \(\Omega\) algebraically closed, the étale site has the one-point module category: every finite separable field extension is \(\Omega\). The same sheaf reconstruction proves exactness of sections. The corresponding argument yields
\[
\mathcal H_{\bar s}\simeq\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathrm{fin}}(O),
\qquad R\Gamma(\bar s_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},H)\simeq M[0].
\tag{BU.6}
\]

### BU.3. Derived Hom with a free source

Suppose \(F,G\in\mathcal H_s\), and the module \(M_F\) is finite free over \(O\). Its ordinary dual with action
\[
(T_F^\vee\lambda)(x)=\lambda(T_F^{-1}x)
\tag{BU.7}
\]
defines another heart object \(F^\vee\). Evaluation and the dual-basis coevaluation descend, since these actions make them equivariant. They exhibit \(F^\vee\) as the dual of \(F\) for the completed tensor of BL.3. Indeed BP.5 supplies a pro-étale cover on which the finite free module and its dual are powers of \(\widehat O\); there the two duality identities are the finite-basis identities. Equality of sheaf maps descends from that cover. The completed tensor and internal-Hom adjunction of BL.4 then give
\[
R\mathcal Hom_O(F,G)\simeq F^\vee\widehat\otimes_O G.
\tag{BU.8}
\]
The right side is a heart object. On the same cover tensoring by a finite power of the completed unit is a finite direct sum, hence has no additional cohomology. Its quotient modules descend to those of
\[
P=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M_F,M_G),\qquad
S(h)=T_GhT_F^{-1}.
\tag{BU.9}
\]
Equivalently, this follows by reduction and BP's full faithfulness; freeness of \(M_F\) makes formation of this Hom module commute with the ordinary quotients. Applying (BU.5) proves
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G)
\simeq[P\xrightarrow{S-1}P].
\tag{BU.10}
\]
Here the left side is the ambient derived Hom complex between these objects. In particular \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G[r])=0\) for \(r\geq2\). At a geometric point, (BU.6) makes this Hom complex \(P[0]\), so it vanishes in every positive degree. Freeness is imposed on the source only; \(G\) may have torsion.

### BU.4. Free covers and comparison in every degree

Every \((M,T)\) admits an exact sequence in the heart
\[
0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0,
\qquad N,L\text{ finite free over }O.
\tag{BU.11}
\]
To construct it, choose lifts \(m_1,\ldots,m_a\) of a basis of \(M/\pi M\). These generate \(M\), by the successive approximation argument of N.4. Express each \(T(m_j)\) in these generators, giving a matrix \(A\) on \(L=O^a\). Modulo \(\pi\) it is the invertible matrix induced by \(T\), so its determinant is a unit and \(A\) is invertible. With \(A\) as its automorphism, \(L\to M\) intertwines the actions. The kernel \(N\) is finite free by the submodule proof in N.4. It is stable under \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\), since the surjection intertwines both inverse automorphisms as well. BU.2 makes all these actions continuous. The equivalence of abelian categories there transports (BU.11) to the claimed heart sequence. The zero module permits \(a=0\). At a geometric point the same construction omits the automorphisms.

Let \(\theta_r\) be the realization comparison (BT.7). If its source \(L\) is finite free, (BU.10) and injectivity of \(\theta_2\) give
\(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)=0\) for every \(G\). Every longer Yoneda extension starting at \(L\) factors through a two-extension starting at \(L\): take the last two middle terms and their left kernel, then splice the remaining extension. The two-extension vanishes, so
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)=0
\quad(r\geq2).
\tag{BU.12}
\]
Together with BT.4 this proves all comparison maps for a free source.

For arbitrary \(F,G\), use (BU.11) with \(M=F\), and apply Hom into \(G\) both in \(D^b(\mathcal H_s)\) and in \(\mathscr C_s\). The realization functor gives a map between the long exact sequences. The two adjacent degree-one comparisons for \(L,N\) are isomorphisms, and the degree-two groups with source \(L\) vanish on both sides. Thus both degree-two groups with source \(F\) are the corresponding cokernel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal H_s}(F,G)
&=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)\to
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal H_s}(N,G)\bigr),\\
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G[2])
&=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(L,G[1])\to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(N,G[1])\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BU.13}
\]
The natural map is an isomorphism. For \(r\geq3\), the same sequences and the free-source vanishing make both groups zero. Degrees zero and one are BT.4, and negative degrees vanish by the t-structure. The finite truncation and connecting-map induction of BT.3 therefore proves
\[
\operatorname{real}_s:D^b(\mathcal H_s)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathscr C_s.
\tag{BU.14}
\]
At a geometric point the same proof applies, with the stronger free-source vanishing from BU.3. In that case the groups with arbitrary heart source vanish for \(r\geq2\). In particular (BU.14) also holds for \(\bar s\). By BT.5 these equivalences prove the required heart-epimorphism effacement at both kinds of point.

### BU.5. Nilpotents and finite unions of points

The assertion extends to a zero-dimensional finite-type scheme \(X\) over \(\mathbf F_q\) or an algebraically closed field. We give the algebra and site reductions, including nilpotents.

A zero-dimensional Noetherian affine scheme has finitely many points: its primes are all maximal and minimal, and there are finitely many minimal primes. Its nilradical is nilpotent, since it is generated by finitely many nilpotent elements. Chinese remainders for sufficiently high powers of its distinct maximal ideals express its ring as a finite product of local rings with nilpotent maximal ideals. A finite affine cover gives the same conclusion for \(X\): every point is open, so its singleton neighbourhood is affine, and \(X\) is the finite disjoint union of these local spectra.

Their residue fields are finite extensions of the base. For completeness, the finite-type field argument works over either base field. Choose a maximal algebraically independent sublist of algebra generators of such a field \(K\). Clearing the finitely many denominators in their remaining algebraic equations makes \(K\) integral over \(k[t_1,\ldots,t_d,1/f]\). A subring over which a field is integral is itself a field: apply a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element and multiply by the appropriate power of that element. If \(d>0\), choose an irreducible polynomial in \(k[t_1]\) not dividing \(f\); there are infinitely many by the usual product-plus-one argument, whereas \(f\) has only finitely many such divisors. That polynomial remains a nonunit after inverting \(f\), a contradiction. Hence \(d=0\) and \(K/k\) is finite. The nilpotent maximal-ideal filtration has finite-dimensional residue-field quotients, since each ideal power is finitely generated. The local rings in question are consequently Artinian and finite over \(k\).

For an Artinian local ring \(A\) with residue field \(k'\), BC.4 proves that finite étale algebras over \(A\) and \(k'\) are equivalent, including every morphism. These objects form a basis of both small étale sites. To check this on the \(A\)-side, an affine étale algebra \(B\) of finite presentation has finite-dimensional reduction \(B/\mathfrak m_AB\), by the field-fibre description. Lift a finite module-generating list of this reduction to \(B\), and denote its \(A\)-span by \(V\). Then \(B/V=\mathfrak m_A(B/V)\); nilpotence implies \(B=V\), proving finiteness without a prior finite-module assumption. Covers are preserved and reflected, because nilpotent reduction changes no points and finite étale surjectivity is checked on residue-field fibres. Thus the equivalent bases, with their coverings, give equivalent sheaf categories.

This equivalence preserves the constant coefficient rings \(O_n\), their quotient maps and all module operations. Applying it to the diagram categories of BS preserves derived tensor, evaluation and cartesianness. It preserves constructibility and the coefficient bounds, since each local spectrum has one point. BS and BP therefore transport both \(\mathscr C_X\) and its heart to their counterparts on \(X_{\mathrm{red}}\), compatibly with realization. Finally sheaves and all these categories on a finite disjoint union are finite products of the categories on its parts. Kernels, complexes, quasi-isomorphisms and truncations are componentwise. Applying (BU.14) in each factor proves
\[
\operatorname{real}_X:D^b(\mathcal H_X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathscr C_X
\quad(\dim X=0)
\tag{BU.15}
\]
under the stated finite-type and base-field hypotheses.

### BU.6. Frobenius conventions and the remaining geometric step

If the same representation is described using geometric Frobenius, its operator is \(T^{-1}\). The complexes \([M\xrightarrow{T-1}M]\) and \([M\xrightarrow{T^{-1}-1}M]\) are naturally isomorphic by the identity in degree zero and \(-T^{-1}\) in degree one. Indeed \(-T^{-1}(T-1)=T^{-1}-1\). Thus the convention change is explicit in (BU.5) and (BU.10).

The zero-dimensional theorem proves all higher extension comparisons for the strict adic heart, with no freeness assumption on its objects. Its proof does not supply an effacing heart epimorphism on a positive-dimensional scheme. In particular, neither separate finite-level covers nor a geometric stalk calculation establishes \((\mathrm E_X)\) for such a scheme. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. BY proves the curve case by constructible effacement; its general higher-dimensional projection input remains an additional assertion.

Free comparisons for the finite-field calculation and convention are [Milne's freely available lecture notes, Section 14, pp. 98–99](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/LEC.pdf), and [Frobenii, Definition 64.3.10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SL). The earlier programme proof cited in BU.1 supplies the finite-group resolutions and continuous-cochain comparison; the completed passage and the realization argument are proved above.

## Appendix BV. Exceptional inverse image and duality for complete coefficients

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a separated morphism of finite-type schemes over a field \(k\), and let \(\ell\) be invertible in \(k\). Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\) with finite residue field of characteristic \(\ell\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), the rings \(O_n=O/\pi^n\), and the category \(\mathcal C_X\) of BM–BS. Thus an object of \(\mathcal C_X\) is derived complete on the pro-étale site and has bounded constructible classical first derived reduction. This is the already constructed category, without assuming its realization from the derived category of its heart.

We construct a right adjoint \(f_c^!\) to the proper-support functor of BM and prove singular biduality in \(\mathcal C_X\). The construction uses the derived category of whole coefficient diagrams. In particular its adjunction retains the higher morphisms and the degree-one inverse-limit term of BR–BS.

### BV.1. Coefficient change for ordinary and proper images

First use a finite commutative coefficient ring \(R\), killed by an integer invertible in \(k\). The bounds of M.1 and BG.2 apply to arbitrary \(R\)-module sheaves. Their comparison with underlying torsion-sheaf cohomology follows from the argument in AS.1 and BB.3: use free \(R\)-module sheaves on the hypercover terms; the local augmented contraction is \(R\)-linear, and Hom into an \(R\)-module injective makes the augmented complex exact. This proves the section-cohomology comparison on every étale test object. The finite cohomological windows of BG.3 extend the comparison to unbounded complexes. It also proves compatibility with exact restriction of coefficient rings.

Ordinary direct image \(Rf_*\) preserves coproducts at this scope. On individual sheaves, higher continuity from BA and M.1 identifies the image of a sum with the sum of its images: a sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums. A sum of injective resolutions consequently has direct-image-acyclic terms. The proof of BG.3, applied with M.1's ordinary-image bound, shows that this complex computes its unbounded derived image. The resulting comparison is the termwise coproduct comparison. This repeats BG.4's argument with the ordinary-image bound; it does not use a nonproper geometric-fibre formula. Proper support preserves coproducts by BG.4–BG.6.

Let \(P\in D(R)\) be a complex of coefficient modules, regarded as a constant complex on the schemes. For either \(T=Rf_*\) or \(T=Rf_!\), the projection map gives
\[
P\otimes_R^L T(K)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\
T(P\otimes_R^L K).
\tag{BV.1}
\]
Here the copy of \(P\) on the source is its inverse image. Fix \(K\). Both sides are exact functors of \(P\) preserving coproducts, by the preceding paragraph and BH. The map is an isomorphism for \(P=R\), hence for its shifts, sums and cones. These objects generate \(D(R)\): the free-module cell resolution of BH.1 expresses any complex by successive additions of shifted free modules, and its union is the cone of \(1-s\) on the sum of the stages. Exactness of filtered module colimits identifies that cone with the union. The same cone argument proves that the class on which (BV.1) is invertible contains this union. This proves (BV.1) even when \(P\) has infinite projective dimension.

For a homomorphism \(R\to R'\) of such rings, extension of coefficients is \(T_R^{R'}=R'\otimes_R^L-\). Forgetting the \(R'\)-action is exact and conservative. The underlying-cohomology comparison above and (BV.1) therefore give the actual scalar-extension comparisons
\[
T_R^{R'}Rf_{*,R}\simeq Rf_{*,R'}T_R^{R'},
\qquad
T_R^{R'}Rf_{!,R}\simeq Rf_{!,R'}T_R^{R'}.
\tag{BV.2}
\]
These are projection maps, rather than isomorphisms selected from the equality of cohomology groups. On K-flat coefficient resolutions their composites for \(R\to R'\to R''\) are the same tensor-associativity map followed by the same projection map. Thus successive coefficient changes, geometric compositions and the adjunction units agree.

For \(K\in\mathcal C_X\), BK.5 already shows that the pro-étale \(Rf_*K\) is complete and that
\[
(Rf_*K)_n\simeq Rf_{*,O_n}(K_n).
\tag{BV.3}
\]
The comparison with the classical étale image is the bounded-below comparison in BK.2 and BK.5. M.4 makes the right side bounded constructible at \(n=1\), so \(Rf_*K\in\mathcal C_Y\). Consequently the adjunction \(f_c^*\dashv Rf_*\) of BL.6 restricts to these constructible categories. The common cohomological bound from M.1 also bounds all finite reductions together.

### BV.2. Finite-coefficient exceptional adjoints and their bounds

BF.1–BF.6 apply to sheaves of \(R\)-modules: their presheaf generators, exact sheafification and representability proof do not require \(R\) to be a field or self-injective. Since \(Rf_{!,R}\) preserves coproducts, they construct its right adjoint \(f_R^!\), with its specified counit. Composition of proper supports gives composition of these right adjoints.

The smooth formula of Proposition 3.3 holds with these \(R\)-coefficients too. We justify this coefficient extension without assuming the desired formula. Choose \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/m\) mapping to \(R\), with \(m\) invertible in \(k\). Write \(T=R\otimes_\Lambda^L-\) and \(U\) for coefficient restriction. Equation (BV.2) and the two adjunctions give, for \(E\in D(X,\Lambda)\) and \(B\in D(Y,R)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}(E,Uf_R^!B)
&=\operatorname{Hom}(TE,f_R^!B)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(T Rf_{!,\Lambda}E,B)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(E,f_\Lambda^!UB).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BV.4}
\]
Thus \(Uf_R^!B=f_\Lambda^!UB\), naturally with respect to the coefficient action and the counit. No preservation of injectives by \(U\) was used.

For a smooth \(p\) of relative dimension \(d\), extend the trace of Proposition 3.3 from \(\Lambda\) to \(R\) using (BV.2). The resulting \(R\)-linear trace and projection map define
\(p^*B(d)[2d]\to p_R^!B\).
Under (BV.4), its underlying map is exactly Proposition 3.3 applied to \(UB\): reassociating \(UB\otimes_\Lambda^L Rp_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\) gives its trace pairing. Hence the map is an isomorphism, since \(U\) is conservative. In particular
\[
p_R^!B\simeq p^*B(d)[2d].
\tag{BV.5}
\]
Its orientation is the positive Kummer orientation already fixed in BI–BJ. Extending that trace twice is extending it once through the composite ring map, so (BV.5) respects further coefficient change.

For a closed immersion \(i:Z\hookrightarrow W\), with complementary open immersion \(j\), the closed-support triangle is
\[
i_*i_R^!B\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*B
\longrightarrow i_*i_R^!B[1].
\tag{BV.6}
\]
It is the counit triangle of M.5, with the same proof over \(R\). Formula (BV.1) for \(j\) shows that its scalar extension is the corresponding triangle over \(R'\). Exact closed image commutes with coefficient extension, as can be checked on its zero and unchanged geometric stalks. Thus scalar extension commutes with \(i^!\). This is the map obtained by extending the counit and transposing, not a choice of a cone isomorphism.

More generally that construction defines
\[
R'\otimes_R^L f_R^!B
\longrightarrow f_{R'}^!(R'\otimes_R^L B).
\tag{BV.7}
\]
To define it, apply \(Rf_{!,R'}\) to its proposed source, use (BV.2), extend the \(R\)-counit, and transpose. It is an isomorphism. The assertion is local on the source and target. Indeed restriction of \(f^!B\) to an open source is the right adjoint for the restricted map, because open extension by zero composes with \(f_!\). For an open target, the same Hom calculation with its inverse-image open proves the target restriction formula. Both identifications preserve the counit.

On affine pieces of source and target, write
\[
X_0\xrightarrow{i}\mathbf A^N_{Y_0}\xrightarrow{p}Y_0
\tag{BV.8}
\]
with \(i\) closed and \(p\) the projection: finitely many algebra generators give the closed embedding. Here \(f_R^!=i_R^!p_R^!\). The smooth and closed calculations prove (BV.7) on this piece. These pieces cover \(X\), so their conservative restrictions prove it globally. The defining counit computation also proves that the comparison for a composite is the composite comparison: transpose either map and cancel the same successive adjunction units. This proves coherence for every sequence of coefficient changes.

This argument gives bounds independent of \(R\). If the input has cohomology in \([a,b]\), the smooth step has cohomology in \([a-2N,b-2N]\). If \(Rj_*\) has cohomological dimension at most \(c\), (BV.6) places its closed-support fibre in
\([a-2N,b-2N+c+1]\).
This deliberately sufficient bound follows from the long exact sequence. Finitely many choices of (BV.8) give one finite interval for \(f_R^!B\), depending on the geometry and \([a,b]\), not the coefficient modulus. M.4 over finite rings, exact pullback, (BV.5) and (BV.6) also prove that \(f_R^!\) preserves bounded constructibility. Neither assertion uses singular biduality or a finite projective resolution of \(R'\) over \(R\).

### BV.3. The adjoint on whole coefficient diagrams

Let \(\mathcal A_X\) be the abelian category of étale sheaves of modules over the diagram \((O_n)_n\), as in BS. Fix one compactification \(X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{p}Y\), supplied by BG.5, and define
\[
F_f=Rp_{\mathrm s,*}j_{\mathrm s,!}:
D(\mathcal A_X)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A_Y).
\tag{BV.9}
\]
The subscript denotes the functor on entire diagrams. Extension by zero is componentwise exact. Direct image is right adjoint to componentwise exact inverse image. The proof of BS.2 applies with \(p\) in place of \(\nu\): inverse image commutes with the derived prefixes \(Le_{n,!}\), so their adjunction gives
\[
e_nF_fK\simeq Rf_{!,O_n}K_n.
\tag{BV.10}
\]
Precomposition with (BS.7) proves compatibility with transitions. This does not assume that evaluation of an injective diagram is injective.

Evaluations jointly detect zero objects and isomorphisms. The common proper-image bound of BG.2 and preservation of coproducts at every level therefore show that \(F_f\) is exact and preserves coproducts. The compactification comparisons of BG.6 give comparisons of (BV.9): use the same proper-image and open-extension adjunction maps on diagrams. Their evaluated maps are the finite-coefficient comparisons, so they are isomorphisms. Their composition identities are the adjunction identities before evaluation. Thus (BV.9) is independent of compactification with the specified composition maps.

We spell out why BF's representability proof applies to this diagram category. A presheaf diagram has a free generator at each pair \((U,n)\); Hom from it is \(M_n(U)\). Those functors are exact on presheaves and preserve sums, so the generators and their shifts are compact projective generators in the derived presheaf category, by BF.5. Their sheafifications generate the sheaf category. Sheafification is exact componentwise and preserves the coefficient action and transitions. The inclusion of sheaves has the fully faithful derived right adjoint of (BF.11). Hence the representability argument of BF.6 applies word for word to this explicit set of generators and this exact sheafification. The Grothendieck resolution hypotheses are those verified in BR.1. It follows that \(F_f\) has a right adjoint \(\Psi_f\) on \(D(\mathcal A)\).

Its components are the desired exceptional images. By (BV.2), proper support commutes with the derived prefixes:
\[
F_fLe_{n,!}\simeq Le_{n,!}Rf_{!,O_n}.
\tag{BV.11}
\]
At an index \(m\leq n\), this is precisely coefficient extension from \(O_n\) to \(O_m\) followed by proper support; above \(n\) both objects are zero. The projection maps of BV.1 respect all prefix transitions. For every test complex \(H\) at index \(n\), adjunction now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}(H,e_n\Psi_fG)
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}H,\Psi_fG)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}Rf_{!,O_n}H,G)\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}(H,f_{O_n}^!G_n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BV.12}
\]
These natural bijections identify \(e_n\Psi_fG=f_{O_n}^!G_n\).

To identify the transitions, precompose (BV.12) with the map (BS.7) between prefixes. Equation (BV.11) takes that map to its proper-support counterpart. Transposing then gives the exceptional coefficient-change map (BV.7), followed by \(f_{O_n}^!\) of the transition of \(G\). In particular, if \(G\) is derived cartesian, then
\[
O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^L(\Psi_fG)_{n+1}
\simeq f_{O_n}^!(O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LG_{n+1})
\simeq(\Psi_fG)_n.
\tag{BV.13}
\]
All these maps belong to the one object \(\Psi_fG\) in the derived category of diagrams. The construction does not replace such an object by a sequence of objects in separately formed derived categories.

### BV.4. The complete exceptional inverse image

If \(G\) belongs to the cartesian constructible subcategory of BS.3, its components have one common bounded interval. BV.2 proves bounded constructibility of \((\Psi_fG)_n\), with one bound for all \(n\), and (BV.13) proves that this diagram is cartesian. Thus \(\Psi_f\) preserves exactly the subcategory corresponding to \(\mathcal C_Y\) and \(\mathcal C_X\).

Transport this restricted functor through BR–BS and call it \(f_c^!\). The identification of the restricted \(F_f\) with BM's \(Rf_!^c\) comes from actual diagram maps: extension by zero commutes with \(\nu^*\) by (BM.2), and the proper-image comparison is the diagram adjunction map of BS.2. Its evaluated maps are BK's proper comparisons, so it is an isomorphism. Applying BR's inverse equivalence, namely the derived limit, gives exactly (BM.5), with the reductions of the single functor (BM.3). Thus the identification preserves the whole diagram, rather than just its component isomorphism classes. The diagram adjunction consequently gives the full adjunction
\[
Rf_!^c:\mathcal C_X\rightleftarrows\mathcal C_Y:f_c^!,
\qquad (f_c^!G)_n\simeq f_{O_n}^!G_n.
\tag{BV.14}
\]
Its unit and counit are the transported diagram unit and counit. They satisfy both triangle identities before restriction. The adjunction holds for every shift and every morphism in these categories; it was not obtained by replacing a derived inverse limit of Hom complexes with an ordinary inverse limit of Hom groups.

Composition of right adjoints, with the counits specified by (BV.14), gives
\((gf)_c^!\simeq f_c^!g_c^!\).
The identities for three composable maps follow by transposing to the same composite counit. Smooth orientation and closed supports likewise pass from the diagram maps to give
\[
p_c^!G\simeq p_c^*G(d)[2d],
\qquad
i_*i_c^!G\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow Rj_*j_c^*G
\longrightarrow i_*i_c^!G[1].
\tag{BV.15}
\]
The first formula is for smooth relative dimension \(d\), and the second for a closed immersion with open complement. The Tate object here is the compatible completed rank-one system; BN supplies its invertible completed tensor. The positive trace and its composition are inherited from the coefficient-compatible maps of BV.2.

### BV.5. Finite internal Hom across the two sites

One comparison is needed before reducing duality. For bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complexes \(A,B\), the evaluation-defined map is
\[
\nu^*R\mathcal Hom_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A,B)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
R\mathcal Hom_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}(\nu^*A,\nu^*B).
\tag{BV.16}
\]
Here and below the internal Hom has coefficients \(O_1\).

To prove it, first let \(A\) be a constructible sheaf. BT.1 and M.5 give a resolution of \(A\) in nonpositive degrees by finite sums of \(u_!O_1\), for affine étale maps \(u\) of finite presentation. Pullback by \(\nu\) preserves the resolution and these extension-by-zero sheaves. On either site, internal derived Hom from \(u_!O_1\) is \(Ru_*u^*B\), by the local adjunction of M.5 and BL.1. The bounded-below comparison of BK.2 and BK.5 identifies these terms across \(\nu\). All have the same lower bound as \(B\).

Resolve the target in bounded-below injectives. If its lower bound is \(b\), the Hom resolution has bidegrees \((r,s)\) with \(r\geq0\), \(s\geq b\), and total degree \(r+s\). Every diagonal is finite. Thus the termwise comparisons and exact pullback compare the resulting filtration degree by degree and prove (BV.16). They compare the evaluation map itself, because each generator comparison is its adjunction map. The finite cohomology filtration of a bounded \(A\) extends the assertion to complexes. This is not an assertion that a topos inverse image preserves internal Hom for arbitrary unbounded objects.

Since \(O_1\) is a finite field, M.7 proves that its bounded constructible category is closed under tensor and internal Hom. Thus the right side of (BV.16) is again bounded constructible classical. For any \(K,L\in\mathcal C_X\), BL.4 proves completeness of \(R\mathcal Hom_O(K,L)\), while BL.5 identifies its first reduction with
\(R\mathcal Hom_{O_1}(K_1,L_1)\).
Equation (BV.16) and M.7 make that reduction bounded constructible classical. Therefore
\[
R\mathcal Hom_O(K,L)\in\mathcal C_X.
\tag{BV.17}
\]
Together with BN, this gives a closed completed tensor structure on the bounded constructible category itself.

### BV.6. Singular biduality with the canonical evaluation

For \(a_X:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\), put
\[
\Omega_X=a_{X,c}^!\mathbf1_k,\qquad
\mathbb D_XK=R\mathcal Hom_O(K,\Omega_X).
\tag{BV.18}
\]
BV.4 puts \(\Omega_X\) in \(\mathcal C_X\), and BV.5 puts \(\mathbb D_XK\) there. The exceptional coefficient comparison identifies
\((\Omega_X)_1=a_{X,O_1}^!O_1\), the structural finite-field dualizing complex used in M.5–M.7.

The evaluation of the closed completed tensor category defines
\[
\eta_K:K\longrightarrow\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK.
\tag{BV.19}
\]
Explicitly, it is adjoint to the evaluation of \(K\) against its dual after tensor symmetry. This fixes the Koszul signs. By BL.5, both reductions of internal Hom are adjoints of reduced evaluation. Equation (BV.16) also preserves evaluation. Consequently reduction of (BV.19) modulo \(\pi\) is the canonical finite-field biduality map of M.6, not just a map between objects abstractly isomorphic to its domain and codomain. M.6–M.7 prove that map invertible on every bounded constructible complex, including singular and nonreduced schemes.

Both objects in (BV.19) are complete. Its cone is therefore complete; its first derived reduction vanishes. BK.4's complete-object conservativity makes the cone zero. This proves that (BV.19) is an isomorphism. Naturality follows from evaluation, and the two evaluation triangle identities identify \(\mathbb D_X\eta_K\) with the inverse of \(\eta_{\mathbb D_XK}\). Hence \(\mathbb D_X\) is an involutive contravariant equivalence of \(\mathcal C_X\).

This proof includes torsion \(O\)-coefficients. Their first derived reduction can have two adjacent cohomology degrees; the argument applies M.6 to that whole complex. It never replaces derived reduction by the ordinary quotient of cohomology or assumes a torsion sheaf is \(O\)-flat.

### BV.7. The dual exchanges and coefficient comparisons

Transitivity gives \(f_c^!\Omega_Y=\Omega_X\). Tensor–Hom adjunction, BN's proper-support projection formula and (BV.14) now give
\[
\mathbb D_YRf_!^cK\simeq Rf_*\mathbb D_XK,
\qquad
\mathbb D_Xf_c^*G\simeq f_c^!\mathbb D_YG.
\tag{BV.20}
\]
Here are the representing Hom calculations. Testing the first object against \(E\in\mathcal C_Y\) gives maps from
\(E\widehat\otimes Rf_!^cK\) to \(\Omega_Y\). Projection and exceptional adjunction turn these into maps from
\(f_c^*E\widehat\otimes K\) to \(\Omega_X\). Internal Hom and \(f_c^*\dashv Rf_*\) identify these with maps from \(E\) to the first right-hand side. For the second identity, test \(f_c^!\mathbb D_YG\) against \(E\in\mathcal C_X\). Successively applying exceptional adjunction, internal Hom and projection gives maps from
\(E\widehat\otimes f_c^*G\) to \(\Omega_X\). This represents the second left-hand side. Every object in these calculations belongs to the stated constructible category by BV.1, BV.4, BV.5 and BN.

Both calculations transpose evaluation through the specified counit. Their naturality therefore makes (BV.20) compatible with double evaluation. Applying (BV.19) gives
\[
\mathbb D_YRf_*K\simeq Rf_!^c\mathbb D_XK,
\qquad
f_c^!G\simeq\mathbb D_Xf_c^*\mathbb D_YG.
\tag{BV.21}
\]
The same test, with an arbitrary \(G\) in place of \(\Omega_Y\), gives the internal exceptional adjunction
\[
Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_O(K,f_c^!G)
\simeq R\mathcal Hom_O(Rf_!^cK,G).
\tag{BV.22}
\]
Indeed maps from \(E\) to either side become maps from
\(Rf_!^c(f_c^*E\widehat\otimes K)\) to \(G\). This proves the comparison with its pairing and counit.

Thus ordinary image, exceptional inverse image, the structural dualizing complex and singular biduality are established in the complete bounded constructible category over the stated field. The construction supplies the duality prerequisite for the positive-dimensional realization problem. BY proves realization on curves and the precise remaining geometric reduction in higher dimension; realization is not a consequence of biduality alone. BW–BX prove the rational coefficient passage with its lattice and higher-morphism comparisons. The complete finite-coefficient arguments used above are M, BF–BJ and BK–BS, with their precise earlier-programme prerequisites. The free comparison text [Laszlo–Olsson, II], §§4 and 7–9, treats adic internal Hom, duality and these operations.

## Appendix BW. The coefficient ring and central rationalization

The complete category constructed in BK–BV lives initially in the derived category of sheaves over the constant ring \(\underline O\). Its tensor unit is the different sheaf \(\widehat O=\varprojlim_n\underline{O_n}\). We now construct the comparison with actual complexes of \(\widehat O\)-modules. This must be an equivalence on derived morphisms, not just an identification of quotient sheaves. We then invert the uniformizer in the resulting constructible category, keeping track of its heart, torsion kernel and operations.

Use the hypotheses and notation of BV. Write
\[
\begin{gathered}
A_X=\underline O,\qquad R_X=\widehat O,\qquad E_X=R_X[1/\pi],\\
D_A=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},A_X),\qquad
D_R=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},R_X).
\end{gathered}
\tag{BW.1}
\]
The map \(A_X\to R_X\) is the completion unit with its ring multiplication. Subscripts \(A,R\) on completion distinguish the two module categories. A superscript \(c\) means derived complete; \(\mathcal C_X\subset D_A^c\) is the bounded constructible category of BM–BV.

### BW.1. Derived completion for the completed ring itself

BP.2, applied to the strict constant system \(O_n\), gives
\[
R_X/\pi^nR_X=\underline{O_n},\qquad R_X[\pi]=0.
\tag{BW.2}
\]
The second equality also follows directly: in the tower of kernels of multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(O_n\), every transition is zero. Thus
\([R_X\xrightarrow{\pi^n}R_X]\), in degrees \(-1,0\), is a free resolution of \(\underline{O_n}\) as an \(R_X\)-module. Its transition from \(n+1\) to \(n\) is \((\pi,1)\), exactly as in BK.3.

The module categories over \(A_X\) and over \(R_X\) have exact countable products. Products and kernels are computed in the underlying sheaves of abelian groups, where BK.1 proves exactness; their compatible coefficient actions are defined componentwise. The cell and injective constructions of BL.1 work for either sheaf of rings: replace its free module on each represented sheaf by the corresponding free \(R_X\)-module. The finite-sum lifting proof of flatness, the filtered cell construction and the slice adjunction remain the same.

Consequently the proof of BK.3–BK.4 applies to \(R_X\) with the free complexes just specified. Explicitly put
\[
C_R P=\operatorname{holim}_n
  (P\otimes_{R_X}^L\underline{O_n}),\qquad
L_{\pi,R}P=\operatorname{holim}(\cdots\xrightarrow{\pi}P).
\tag{BW.3}
\]
The free telescope of \(R_X[1/\pi]\) identifies the second expression with \(R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(R_X[1/\pi],P)\). Taking the product-cone limits of the coefficient triangles gives
\[
L_{\pi,R}P\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow C_RP.
\tag{BW.4}
\]
Multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on the first term. Each finite reduction is complete: in its \(\pi\)-tower the \(n\)-th power of the shift is null-homotopic, and the finite geometric series in that shift inverts \(1-s\). Complete objects are closed under products and fibres, so \(C_RP\) is complete. Tensoring (BW.4) with the finite free coefficient complex kills its first term. The completion unit therefore induces the identity comparison on every derived reduction.

If \(Q\) is complete, maps in every degree from a \(\pi\)-invertible object to \(Q\) vanish by tensor–Hom adjunction with \(R_X[1/\pi]\). Equation (BW.4) then proves that \(C_R\) is left adjoint to the inclusion of complete objects. It also proves detection of isomorphisms by all derived reductions. A zero first reduction suffices: its cone says that multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible, while a complete object with that property is zero by (BW.4). These arguments use the actual \((\pi,1)\) transitions and apply to unbounded complexes.

### BW.2. Extension and restriction of the coefficient ring

Let \(U:D_R\to D_A\) forget the \(R_X\)-action, and let
\(S=R_X\otimes_{A_X}^L-\) be its derived left adjoint. The adjunction follows on the cell and injective models of BL.1, also on every slice; it does not require that \(R_X\) be a finite \(O\)-module. Restriction is exact and conservative and preserves products and the finite coefficient cones. Hence
\[
UC_RP=C_AUP,\qquad
P\in D_R^c\ \Longleftrightarrow\ UP\in D_A^c.
\tag{BW.5}
\]
These identifications preserve completion units and all transition maps.

For later use \(R_X\) is flat over \(A_X\). Here is the local algebra check. For each site object, the \(O\)-module of sections of \(R_X\) is torsion-free, by (BW.2). A torsion-free \(O\)-module is flat: each finitely generated submodule is free by the DVR submodule argument in N.4, it is the filtered union of those submodules, and tensor and exactness pass to filtered unions. This sectionwise argument gives the sheaf assertion by the finite-relation criterion. A finite list of coefficients from the constant sheaf is constant after a covering refinement; a relation in a tensor sheaf has a finite local representative. The preceding flat-module calculation resolves that relation on this refinement, and sheafification is exact. In particular \(S\) is also represented by the exact ordinary extension functor, though the derived notation will retain the coefficient comparisons. Its exactness implies that \(U\) takes K-injectives to K-injectives: Hom from an acyclic \(A_X\)-complex is Hom from its acyclic scalar extension.

Define
\[
T:D_A^c\longrightarrow D_R^c,\qquad
T(K)=C_R(SK).
\tag{BW.6}
\]
Completion and scalar adjunction give \(T\dashv U\) on the complete categories. On the source side of this adjunction \(U\) means its restriction in (BW.5).

We verify its unit, rather than deducing full faithfulness from a list of matching objects. Equations (BW.2) and the two free resolutions give, naturally in \(K\),
\[
U(TK)\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n}
\simeq U\bigl(TK\otimes_{R_X}^L\underline{O_n}\bigr)
\simeq K\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n}.
\tag{BW.7}
\]
For the second comparison first discard \(C_R\) using its unit, then use associativity of scalar extension and
\(R_X\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n}=\underline{O_n}\).
The latter equality is the two-term multiplication complex with (BW.2); no underived quotient of \(K\) is used. Under (BW.7) the unit \(K\to UTK\) is the identity of the displayed reduction: both are induced by \(A_X\to R_X\) and the same augmentation to \(O_n\). Its cone is complete with zero first reduction. Thus the unit is an isomorphism.

For complete \(P\in D_R\), the triangle identity is
\[
U(\epsilon_P)\circ\eta_{UP}=1_{UP}.
\]
Since \(\eta_{UP}\) is invertible, \(U(\epsilon_P)\) is its inverse. Conservativity of restriction makes the counit invertible as well. We have proved
\[
D_A^c\ \simeq\ D_R^c
\tag{BW.8}
\]
by a specified adjunction. In particular the comparison includes every higher morphism. Equality of maps has been obtained from the adjunction identities, not from an assertion that reduction is faithful on maps.

### BW.3. Constructibility, strict systems and the standard heart

Let \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) consist of the complete \(R_X\)-complexes whose first derived reduction is a bounded constructible classical \(\kappa\)-complex. Equations (BW.5)–(BW.7) restrict (BW.8) to
\[
T:\mathcal C_X\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{\mathcal C}_X,
\qquad U\text{ its inverse}.
\tag{BW.9}
\]
The boundedness assertions of BM and BQ carry over because restriction is exact. In particular \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) is closed under standard truncations, and (BW.9) is t-exact for these bounded t-structures.

In degree zero this is especially concrete. The strict system \((F_n)\) of BP has limit
\(F=\varprojlim_n\nu^*F_n\), and \(R_X=\varprojlim_n\underline{O_n}\) acts on it component by component. Its underlying \(A_X\)-sheaf is exactly BP.2's limit. Equation (BW.9) identifies that module sheaf with \(TF\). Every \(A_X\)-linear map between two such complete sheaves is therefore \(R_X\)-linear, by full faithfulness of \(U\); BP.3 identifies it with the compatible maps on the ordinary quotients.

The same equivalence for complexes cannot be constructed by arbitrarily adding coefficient actions to their cohomology sheaves. It is supplied by the actual complex \(C_R(SK)\) and its counit. Reduction of this complex produces the specified whole diagram of BR–BS: its augmentation maps and the coefficient transitions in (BW.7) are the same \((\pi,1)\) maps. Thus their diagram adjunctions and the degree-one inverse-limit term in BR.5 remain in force. Neither replacing derived reductions by ordinary quotients nor deleting that term is part of the comparison.

### BW.4. Tensor, internal Hom and evaluation

Equip \(D_R^c\) with completed tensor
\[
P\widehat\otimes_{R_X}Q=C_R(P\otimes_{R_X}^LQ).
\tag{BW.10}
\]
Its unit is \(R_X\): the epimorphic tower \(O_n\) has derived limit equal to its ordinary limit by BK.1, so \(R_X\) is complete.

The equivalence \(T\) is symmetric monoidal for these completed tensors. To prove this with the specified maps, scalar extension has its ordinary associative isomorphism
\[
S(K\otimes_{A_X}^LL)
 \simeq SK\otimes_{R_X}^LSL.
\]
The cone of each completion unit is \(\pi\)-invertible, by (BW.4) or BK.4. Scalar extension and tensor carry such a cone to another \(\pi\)-invertible cone. Completing therefore identifies both sides, with any of their factors first completed, and gives
\[
T(K\widehat\otimes_OL)
 \simeq TK\widehat\otimes_{R_X}TL.
\tag{BW.11}
\]
The unit comparison \(T(\mathbf1_X)\simeq R_X\) is the counit of (BW.8) at \(R_X\). Associativity, symmetry and the unit identities follow by precomposing with the uncompleted scalar-extension maps: maps into a complete object factor uniquely through completion, and the ordinary tensor identities already agree before that factorization. This is the coherence argument of BL.3 applied to the present scalar adjunction.

If \(Q\) is complete, \(R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q)\) is complete. Indeed internal Hom carries the \(\pi\)-tower of \(Q\) and its product-cone limit to the \(\pi\)-tower of this internal Hom; tensor–Hom adjunction makes its localization Hom vanish just as in BL.4. Restriction of coefficients gives the natural comparison
\[
U R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}
R\mathcal Hom_{A_X}(UP,UQ)
\qquad(P,Q\in D_R^c).
\tag{BW.12}
\]
Here is also a check of this arrow. On every slice, scalar adjunction identifies the right side with the internal Hom from \(S(UP)\) into \(Q\). Replacing \(S(UP)\) by its completion changes no maps into the complete \(Q\). The counit \(TUP\to P\) then identifies this with the left side. Slice restriction preserves products and completion, by its exact extension-by-zero left adjoint in BL.1, so this is a sheafwise derived comparison. It is precisely the restriction map on evaluation and is compatible with (BW.11).

Consequently the evaluation maps, dualizing object and double-evaluation isomorphism of BV transport to \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\). Constructibility of internal Hom and completed tensor is preserved by (BW.9). These assertions concern completed tensor. BX.3 proves that ordinary tensor over \(R_X\) already agrees with it on the bounded constructible category.

### BW.5. Geometric operations with their coefficient maps

For \(f:X\to Y\), the quotient-ring maps define a natural ring map
\(f^{-1}R_Y\to R_X\). Set
\[
\widehat f^{\,*}P
 =R_X\otimes_{f^{-1}R_Y}^Lf^{-1}P,\qquad
\widehat f_c^{\,*}P=C_{R_X}\widehat f^{\,*}P.
\tag{BW.13}
\]
The tensor associativity map before completion gives
\(\widehat f^{\,*}S_YK=S_Xf^{-1}K\).
Completing and using the \(\pi\)-invertible cones of the units as in BW.4 proves
\[
\widehat f_c^{\,*}T_YK\simeq T_X f_c^*K.
\tag{BW.14}
\]
The formula uses scalar extension along the displayed ring map. It makes no assumption that a general naive inverse image already preserves the completed coefficient ring.

Ordinary derived image for these ringed topoi satisfies
\[
U_YR\widehat f_*P=Rf_*U_XP.
\tag{BW.15}
\]
Resolve \(P\) by a K-injective \(R_X\)-complex. BW.2 makes its restriction K-injective over \(A_X\); both sides of (BW.15) are its same sectionwise image with the same underlying \(O\)-action. BK.5 and BV.1 now show that \(R\widehat f_*\) preserves completeness and constructibility. Scalar and geometric adjunction identify it as the right adjoint of (BW.13) on complete objects. Formulas (BW.14)–(BW.15) preserve the actual units and counits.

For an open immersion \(j\), restriction is a slice functor and \(j^{-1}R_X=R_U\). Extension by zero has the same underlying \(O\)-sheaf extension by zero, with its unique extended ring action. Applying completion gives the transported functor of BM.1, by (BW.5). A compactification \(f=pj\) therefore transports BM's \(Rp_*j_{c,!}\), together with its refinement comparisons, to \(\widehat{\mathcal C}\). BV's exceptional right adjoint transports through (BW.9), since the adjunction is a natural bijection on all morphisms in these categories. The completed projection formula, base change, composition, duality and their exchange maps transport through the same units and counits. Thus the change of coefficient-ring presentation preserves these operations. Equivalence with the bounded derived category of the heart is the separate realization assertion of BT, BU and BY–CB.

### BW.6. Inverting the uniformizer as a triangulated localization

Define \(\mathcal C_X[1/\pi]\) to have the objects of \(\mathcal C_X\) and morphisms
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C_X[1/\pi]}(K,L)
 =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C_X}(K,L)\otimes_O O[1/\pi].
\tag{BW.16}
\]
Composition multiplies fractions. The same construction for \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) is identified with it by (BW.9). A fraction \(u/\pi^a\) vanishes exactly when some \(\pi^b u\) vanishes in the original Hom module.

Declare a triangle distinguished if it is isomorphic to the image of a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal C_X\). We verify that this is a triangulated structure. Shifts commute with fractions. Every morphism \(u/\pi^a\) has a cone triangle: use the original triangle of \(u\) and rescale its source by the invertible \(\pi^a\). Identity and rotation axioms follow immediately. Hom sequences of these triangles are exact because localization of \(O\)-modules is exact: an element or equality involves only finitely many denominators, which can be cleared.

For the morphism-of-triangles axiom, first replace the two given triangles by images of original triangles. Multiply both vertical maps of a commuting square by a common denominator. Their commutativity defect is zero after localization, so another common power of \(\pi\) kills it in the original Hom module. The original axiom supplies a third vertical map for this now commuting square. Divide all three vertical maps by the common power used. This gives exactly the requested map of triangles.

For the octahedron, write the two composable maps as \(a/\pi^r\) and \(b/\pi^s\). The diagram of the original maps \(a,b\) is isomorphic after localization to this diagram: the maps on its three objects are respectively \(\pi^{r+s},\pi^s,1\), and the two squares commute. Apply the original octahedral axiom to \(a,b\) and transport the result. Any prescribed cone triangles can be substituted: the preceding morphism-of-triangles axiom supplies their comparison, and exact localized Hom sequences show that a map of triangles invertible on two objects is invertible on the third. This proves the remaining axiom.

The functor to (BW.16) is exact and universal among \(O\)-linear exact functors making \(\pi\) invertible: its value on \(u/\pi^a\) must be the value on \(u\) followed by the inverse of multiplication by \(\pi^a\). This prescription is well defined by the zero-fraction criterion, respects composition and is unique.

Its zero objects are exactly those \(K\) for which \(\pi^N1_K=0\) for some \(N\). They are also exactly the objects all of whose cohomology sheaves are killed by some power of \(\pi\). One direction follows by applying cohomology. For the converse only finitely many cohomology sheaves occur, by BM.6 and BQ. In a triangle \(A\to B\to C\), if \(\pi^a1_A=0\) and \(\pi^b1_C=0\), exactness of \(\operatorname{Hom}(B,-)\) makes \(\pi^b1_B\) factor through \(A\). Multiplication by \(\pi^a\) kills that factorization. Induction through the finite truncation tower kills \(K\) by the product of the powers killing its cohomology. This also proves directly that the zero objects form a thick triangulated subcategory.

### BW.7. The rational heart, adjunctions and duality

The images of the standard nonpositive and nonnegative subcategories, closed under isomorphism, define a bounded t-structure on (BW.16). Orthogonality follows by localizing its zero Hom groups; every original truncation triangle gives the required triangle after localization. The shift inclusions and boundedness persist. Uniqueness of the truncation triangle follows from the same orthogonality argument as before localization, so these really are the induced truncation functors.

Its heart is the localization of the strict constructible heart in BP–BQ. Indeed this heart embeds fully faithfully by (BW.16). If an object of the localized category lies in the heart, its cohomology in every other degree is zero in that category. Each such cohomology sheaf is therefore killed by a power of \(\pi\). The finite-truncation argument in BW.6 makes both outer truncations zero, identifying the object with its degree-zero cohomology. For a morphism between heart objects, choose a numerator; its kernel and cokernel are the localized kernel and cokernel of that numerator, since multiplication by its denominator is an isomorphism. The explicit BP quotient and torsion constructions therefore also describe this rational heart.

Every operation constructed in BL, BM, BN and BV is \(O\)-linear, including the internal Hom contravariantly in its first variable. They consequently descend to this localization. Their adjunctions continue to hold: tensor each of their natural \(O\)-linear Hom bijections with \(O[1/\pi]\). For example
\[
\operatorname{Hom}(f_!K,L)
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}(K,f_c^!L)
\tag{BW.17}
\]
in the localized categories is exactly the localization of BV's bijection. The completed tensor and its internal Hom remain adjoint for the same reason. All units, counits, projection and base-change maps, positive Tate orientations and the canonical biduality map are the images of those already constructed. Their identities and invertibility are preserved by the exact localization functor. In particular this gives the rational six-operation formalism on the localized complete category.

This statement is independent of whether the general realization functor of BT is an equivalence. No higher Ext comparison for that heart has been inferred just from constructing its localization.

### BW.8. The canonical comparison with actual rational sheaves

There is a canonical exact functor
\[
\Phi_X:\widehat{\mathcal C}_X[1/\pi]
 \longrightarrow D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X),\qquad
P\longmapsto E_X\otimes_{R_X}^LP.
\tag{BW.18}
\]
Localization of module sheaves is exact: it is the filtered colimit of the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) sequence. Thus the formula is also \(P[1/\pi]\), and multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on its target. BW.6 gives the displayed factorization on all fractions.

This functor is conservative. To check its kernel on objects, suppose \(P[1/\pi]=0\). Each cohomology sheaf \(F\) of \(UP\) then consists locally of sections killed by powers of \(\pi\). BP.1–BP.2 give a single exponent \(c_F\) killing all its torsion kernels \(F[\pi^n]\), simultaneously for every \(n\). Their filtered union is \(F\), so \(\pi^{c_F}F=0\). Only finitely many \(F\) occur, and BW.6 now makes \(P\) zero in the localized category. Conversely any zero object there plainly has zero image. Applying this to cones proves detection of isomorphisms.

BX proves full faithfulness on every higher Hom and constructs integral models for every bounded complex with constructible \(E_X\)-cohomology. It also identifies the ordinary tensor and geometric operations. These assertions require more than the conservativity just proved. A global lisse integral lattice can fail on a singular scheme, as [the pro-étale lesson, Proposition 7.2](course:AG-LTF/the-pro-etale-site-and-l-adic-complexes#integral-lattices-are-a-local-condition) proves by its nodal example; BX.6 constructs the appropriate constructible integral models without assuming a global lisse lattice.

The coefficient categories and these rational comparisons are discussed in the freely accessible [Bhatt–Scholze, §§6.5 and 6.8, version 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1198v2). The adjunction, localization and conservativity above are completed by the full comparison (BX.20). Heart realization is a separate assertion, treated in BT, BU and BY–CB.

## Appendix BX. Strata, integral models and the rational sheaf category

Keep the finite-type schemes, complete DVR \(O\), finite residue field, uniformizer \(\pi\), and coefficient sheaves \(R_X=\widehat O\) and \(E_X=R_X[1/\pi]\) of BW. Write \(E=O[1/\pi]\). A constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf means one which is locally finite free in the pro-étale topology on each member of a finite algebraic stratification. Let \(D_{\mathrm{cons}}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X)\) be the full subcategory of complexes with bounded constructible cohomology. We will prove that (BW.18) is an equivalence with this category, including all higher morphisms. The proof also identifies the ordinary tensor and geometric operations. It does not assume the separate realization theorem for the derived category of the constructible heart.

### BX.1. Lifting a closed-stratum neighbourhood

We first give the site calculation needed for restriction to a stratum. Let \(A\) be a ring, \(I\) an ideal, and \(B_0\) an ind-étale \(A/I\)-algebra. Consider all factorizations \(A\to C\to B_0\) with \(C\) étale over \(A\), and put
\[
H_A(B_0)=\varinjlim_{(C\to B_0)}C.
\tag{BX.1}
\]
This indexing category is filtered. Tensor products give common successors. To equalize two parallel maps \(C\rightrightarrows D\), take their equality locus in \(\operatorname{Spec}D\). The diagonal of the affine étale \(A\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}C\) is both open and closed, so this locus is a clopen affine subscheme, still étale over \(A\). The map \(\operatorname{Spec}B_0\to\operatorname{Spec}D\) factors through it. Its coordinate algebra gives the required equalizer in the indexing category.

We use the following elementary lifting fact at its arbitrary-ideal scope. An étale \(A/I\)-algebra has a presentation by a square system with invertible Jacobian. Lift the coefficients to \(A\) and invert the lifted Jacobian determinant. The resulting algebra is étale over \(A\) and reduces to the given algebra. The square presentation and its determinant-trick proof are in [Infinitesimal lifting, Lemma 6.1](course:AG-FSE/infinitesimal-lifting-and-invariance-under-thickenings#6-keeping-the-lift-finite); the lifting calculation is [Étale neighbourhoods, Lemma 5.4](course:AG-FSE/etale-neighbourhoods-henselization-and-quasi-finite-morphisms#henselian-pairs-and-finite-étale-algebras). In particular this assertion does not require \(I\) to be nilpotent.

The natural map
\[
H_A(B_0)/IH_A(B_0)\longrightarrow B_0
\tag{BX.2}
\]
is an isomorphism. It is surjective because every element of \(B_0\) occurs at a finitely presented étale \(A/I\)-stage, and that stage has the preceding lift. For injectivity, represent an element in its kernel by \(c\in C\). The map \(C/IC\to B_0\) is ind-étale. To see the assertion about this map, descend the finitely presented algebra \(C/IC\) and its map to a stage of an étale presentation of \(B_0\). A map between two étale algebras over the same base is étale: its scheme map factors as its open graph into the fibre product followed by the étale projection. The tail is therefore an étale presentation over \(C/IC\). At some such stage \(D_0\), the image of \(c\) is zero. Lift \(D_0\) to an étale \(C\)-algebra \(D\). Then \(c\in ID\), and \(D\to D/ID=D_0\to B_0\) is a later object of (BX.1). Thus \(c\) is zero in the left side of (BX.2).

For every ind-étale \(A\)-algebra \(T\) there is a natural bijection
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_A(T,H_A(B_0))
 =\operatorname{Hom}_{A/I}(T/IT,B_0).
\tag{BX.3}
\]
A map on the right makes each étale stage of \(T\) an object of (BX.1), giving its lift. For uniqueness, a map from a finitely presented stage factors through some \(C\) in (BX.1). Its composite to \(B_0\) fixes that stage's object in the indexing category; its map into the colimit is consequently the specified one. Passing to the colimit of stages proves uniqueness for \(T\).

Set \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\). On the affine ind-étale bases let \(u(V)=V\times_XZ\) and
\[
v(\operatorname{Spec}B_0)=\operatorname{Spec}H_A(B_0).
\]
Equations (BX.2)–(BX.3) say that \(v\) is a fully faithful left adjoint to \(u\), and \(u v=1\). Every point of \(v(V)\) specializes into \(V\). Indeed, if \(b\in H_A(B_0)\) becomes invertible modulo \(I\), the localization at \(b\) is ind-étale over \(A\). Equation (BX.3) supplies a map from this localization back to \(H_A(B_0)\) whose composite with localization is the identity. Hence \(b\) was already a unit, so \(I H_A(B_0)\) lies in the Jacobson radical.

The functor \(v\) sends finite covers to covers. Their lifted maps are flat: maps between ind-étale algebras over \(A\) are ind-étale by the same finite-stage argument used above. Their images are stable under generalization, by flat going down. They cover the closed part \(V\), and every point of \(v(V)\) has a specialization there. They therefore cover \(v(V)\). Furthermore, any cover of \(v(V)\) pulls back to one of \(V\); applying \(v\) to that cover gives, by adjunction, a refinement of the original cover.

If \(V\) is weakly contractible, so is \(v(V)\). A finite affine covering of \(v(V)\), pulled back to \(V\), has a section from \(V\) to its disjoint union. Apply \(v\) and the preceding refinement maps. Since a left adjoint preserves finite disjoint unions, this gives a section of the original disjoint-union cover. Refinement by affine ind-étale objects, proved in the pro-étale lesson, tests all covers. Thus evaluation at \(v(V)\) is exact, just as evaluation at \(V\) is.

### BX.2. The ordinary localization sequence on the pro-étale site

Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) be closed with quasi-compact open complement \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\). All closed immersions between the Noetherian schemes used here satisfy this condition. The formula for inverse image on the preceding affine bases is sheafification of \(V\mapsto F(v(V))\). This follows directly from (BX.3): the neighbourhood colimit defining inverse image has the specified initial geometric neighbourhood. At a weakly contractible \(V\), sheafification leaves that value unchanged:
\[
(i^{-1}F)(V)=F(v(V)).
\tag{BX.4}
\]
For detail, the presheaf is separated since \(v\) sends covers to covers. It preserves finite disjoint unions as products. A finite cover of \(V\) can be replaced by its disjoint union and then split, so its matching family is already a section. This proves (BX.4), including its compatibility with maps of sheaves.

Limits of sheaves are computed on sections. Evaluating on the weakly contractible basis in (BX.4) proves that \(i^{-1}\) commutes with all small limits. As an inverse-image functor it is also exact and preserves colimits. In particular
\[
i^{-1}R_X=R_Z,\qquad i^{-1}E_X=E_Z.
\tag{BX.5}
\]
For an open immersion the same facts follow from restriction to the slice site.

The functor \(i_*\) is exact. Suppose \(F\to G\) is an epimorphism on \(Z\) and \(g\in G(V_Z)\) for an affine ind-étale \(V\to X\). Lift \(g\) on a finite affine ind-étale cover \(W\to V_Z\). Its lift \(v_V(W)\to V\), together with a finite affine cover of \(V_U\), is a pro-étale cover of \(V\). On its first piece \(g\) lifts by construction; on its other pieces the closed fibre is empty. This proves the required local surjectivity. The quasi-compactness of \(V_U\), and hence the hypothesis on \(U\), is used here. Equation (BX.4) also proves the counit \(i^{-1}i_*\to1\) is an isomorphism.

Open extension by zero \(j_!\) is exact, by the local finite-sum description in BL.1. We check its closed restriction. If \(V\) is weakly contractible over \(Z\), the affine \(v(V)\) is weakly contractible and each of its points specializes into \(V\). A section of \(j_!F\) is locally a finite collection of sections on pieces mapping into \(U\). Split such a finite cover of \(v(V)\). The splitting partitions \(v(V)\) into clopen pieces; any piece supporting one of those sections must lie in \(U\). It is empty: a nonempty clopen piece contains the specializations of its points, including one in \(V\). Consequently \(j_!F(v(V))=0\), so \(i^{-1}j_!=0\).

The exact functors \(i^{-1}\) and \(j^{-1}\) are jointly conservative. To verify this for a sheaf, cover the closed fibre of any affine object by weakly contractible affines, lift them by \(v\), and add its open complement. Zero on both restrictions gives zero sections locally on this cover. Applied to kernels and cokernels, this detects isomorphisms. We already have \(j^{-1}i_*=0\), \(j^{-1}j_!=1\), and \(i^{-1}i_*=1\). Applying the two restrictions therefore proves the functorial exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow j_!j^{-1}F\longrightarrow F
 \longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}F\longrightarrow0.
\tag{BX.6}
\]
This proves the sequence without assuming that ordinary geometric stalks form a conservative family for all pro-étale sheaves.

Everything just proved applies to modules over \(R_X\), using (BX.5), and to \(E_X\)-modules. Exactness gives the corresponding triangle on the unbounded derived categories. These categories have exact products by BK.1 and its ringed version in BW.1. Thus \(i^{-1}\), being exact and product-preserving, commutes with the product-cone formula for derived inverse limits. The exact right adjoint \(i_*\) also commutes with those limits. Applied to \(Rj_*K\), (BX.6) gives
\[
j_!K\longrightarrow Rj_*K
 \longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}Rj_*K.
\tag{BX.7}
\]
The other two functors commute with homotopy limits, since \(Rj_*\) is a right adjoint. Taking fibres proves the same assertion for \(j_!\). All these functors commute with the two-term coefficient cones. Therefore ordinary \(i^{-1},i_*,j^{-1},j_!\) preserve derived completeness whenever their inputs are complete.

Their first reductions are the corresponding finite-coefficient operations. For \(i_*\) and \(j_!\), compatibility with classical finite-coefficient sheaves follows either from the coefficient comparison of BK.2 or directly on affine ind-étale presentations: finite-presentation descent and the finite sheaf equalizer commute with the filtered limit of the presentation; extension by zero is then determined by (BX.6). Consequently these four ordinary functors preserve the bounded constructible categories in BW.3. Ordinary and completed restriction and extension by zero agree there.

For later use closed support has an explicit right adjoint even on the ambient derived category. Set
\[
i^!Q=i^{-1}\operatorname{Fib}
 \bigl(Q\longrightarrow Rj_*j^{-1}Q\bigr).
\tag{BX.8}
\]
The fibre restricts to zero on \(U\), so (BX.6) identifies it with \(i_*i^!Q\). Every map, in every degree, from \(i_*L\) to \(Rj_*j^{-1}Q\) is zero by open adjunction. Hence the fibre triangle and the full faithfulness of \(i_*\) give \(i_*\dashv i^!\). Both (BX.7) and (BX.8) use their actual adjunction maps.

### BX.3. Ordinary tensor and inverse image

For \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\), ordinary restriction to a stratum now equals its completed restriction. BO therefore supplies a pro-étale local finite perfect \(O\)-complex on each connected stratum. As an \(R\)-complex this is the corresponding finite free complex with those same constant matrices. In particular its ordinary tensor with a complete complex is complete: locally it is made from finitely many shifts, sums and cones of that complex. Completeness is local in the pro-étale topology, because slice restriction preserves products, coefficient cones and the completion unit.

Here are the support formulas used to assemble the strata. For an arbitrary \(R_X\)-complex \(Q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(j_!L)\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q
 &\simeq j_!\bigl(L\otimes_{R_U}^{L}j^{-1}Q\bigr),\\
(i_*L)\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q
 &\simeq i_*\bigl(L\otimes_{R_Z}^{L}i^{-1}Q\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{BX.9}
\]
These are the projection maps defined by adjunction. The first is the finite-sum extension-by-zero formula on the K-flat cell resolutions. For the second use the unit to the closed-support image. Applying \(i^{-1}\) makes this map the tensor identity, since (BX.5) makes restriction exact and monoidal. Applying \(j^{-1}\) makes both sides zero. Joint conservativity proves it is an isomorphism. Thus no flatness assertion about a closed-support module is being assumed to prove the formula.

Choose an open stratum where \(P\) has its local finite-perfect description and use (BX.6) for \(P\). Formula (BX.9) treats its open term. Induction on the finite closed-stratum filtration treats its closed term. BX.2 makes both ordinary extensions preserve completeness. We obtain
\[
P\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q
\ \xrightarrow{\sim}\
P\widehat\otimes_{R_X}Q
\qquad(P,Q\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X).
\tag{BX.10}
\]
Its first reduction is the constructible finite-coefficient tensor, so the ordinary tensor is constructible as well. Any finite stratification can be refined to the filtration used here: remove a dense open part of its finitely many generic strata, and repeat on the closed complement. Noetherian induction terminates; in the present finite-dimensional schemes the remaining dimension decreases after collecting all generic pieces.

The same argument identifies ordinary geometric inverse image. For \(f:X\to Y\) use the actual ringed inverse image
\[
Lf_R^*P=R_X\otimes_{f^{-1}R_Y}^{L}f^{-1}P.
\tag{BX.11}
\]
It takes a local finite perfect complex to the same finite complex over \(R_X\), after pulling back its trivializing cover. It commutes with extension by zero and with closed-support image in a cartesian square. For the closed formula, the pulled-back complex is zero on the complementary open, and its closed restriction is the claimed inverse image by associativity of scalar extension. Equation (BX.6) identifies the complex with that closed image. The open formula follows in the same way, or from the first cell formula in (BX.9). Devissage on strata now proves that (BX.11) is complete and constructible for \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_Y\). Its completion map is therefore an isomorphism, so it is the transported inverse image of BW.5. The coefficient map \(f^{-1}R_Y\to R_X\) remains part of the formula for general \(f\).

### BX.4. Bounded-below continuity

We need continuity in the target of derived Hom, including positive degrees. We give the site argument, so an unrestricted compactness assumption is unnecessary.

On the pro-étale site of a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme, evaluation at a quasi-compact quasi-separated object commutes with filtered colimits of sheaves. Indeed that site has a basis of quasi-compact objects, finite fibre products can be covered by finitely many basis objects, and coverings of a basis object have finite covering refinements. The sheaf equalizer for any such finite cover uses finite products and equalizers. Filtered colimits of modules commute with these finite limits. Thus the sectionwise filtered colimit is already a sheaf on the basis.

The derived statement is
\[
\varinjlim_\alpha R\Gamma(V,Q_\alpha)
 \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\
R\Gamma\bigl(V,\varinjlim_\alpha Q_\alpha\bigr)
\quad\text{if every }Q_\alpha\in D^{\ge b},
\tag{BX.12}
\]
for one common \(b\). Here and below filtered colimits are derived colimits, computed termwise on complexes because filtered colimits of sheaves are exact. To prove (BX.12), cover \(V\) by finitely many weakly contractible affine objects. Cover the successive matching objects in the same way. They are quasi-compact quasi-separated: at each finite stage only finite products, fibre products and finite covers of the preceding objects occur. This constructs a hypercover with a finite disjoint union of weakly contractible affines in every degree.

Its augmented alternating-face free-module complex resolves the free module represented by \(V\). The exactness can be checked locally in each degree: choose a local vertex and lift the finitely many cones on the faces of a finite chain successively along the matching covers. The alternating boundary formula for these cones is \(\partial h+h\partial=1\), with augmentation in degree zero. Thus a cycle becomes a boundary on a covering, which is exactly sheaf exactness. Each term of this resolution is a finite sum of modules represented freely by weakly contractible affines. Such a module is projective, since Hom from it is exact section evaluation, and that Hom commutes with filtered colimits by the preceding paragraph.

Use this bounded-above projective resolution to compute derived Hom into \(Q_\alpha\). Replace each target by its good truncation in degrees at least \(b\). In total degree \(n\), only resolution degrees \(0,\ldots,n-b\) occur. The resulting diagonal is finite. Filtered colimits therefore commute with every term on the diagonal and with its cohomology. This proves (BX.12). The proof works for any of the sheaves of rings under discussion, using free modules over that sheaf, and on every quasi-compact slice.

It follows that \(Rg_*\) commutes with uniformly bounded-below filtered colimits for every quasi-compact quasi-separated geometric map under consideration, with its indicated coefficient map. Indeed its value as derived sections on an affine target object is \(R\Gamma\) of the quasi-compact quasi-separated base change on the source. Such evaluations test the comparison. For an open \(j\), (BX.8) and exact restriction consequently give the same continuity for \(i^!\). This functor preserves a common lower bound: \(Rj_*\) is left t-exact, and the fibre of a map between objects in \(D^{\ge b}\) lies in \(D^{\ge b}\).

Now fix \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\). We claim
\[
\varinjlim_\alpha R\operatorname{Hom}_{R_X}(P,Q_\alpha)
 \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\
R\operatorname{Hom}_{R_X}
 \bigl(P,\varinjlim_\alpha Q_\alpha\bigr)
\qquad(Q_\alpha\in D^{\ge b}).
\tag{BX.13}
\]
There is also the analogous internal-Hom comparison on every slice. On a stratum where \(P\) is locally finite perfect, internal Hom is computed by a finite dual complex and tensor. It preserves these colimits locally, hence as sheaves.
