Its targets have a common lower bound: use the common finite amplitude from BO, or take the maximum over a finite quasi-compact trivializing cover.

For the closed term of a stratification use the derived adjunction
\[
R\mathcal Hom_X(i_*L,Q)
 =i_*R\mathcal Hom_Z(L,i^!Q).
\tag{BX.14}
\]
For the open term use \(Rj_*R\mathcal Hom_U(L,j^{-1}Q)\). These identities hold internally because the adjunctions just proved hold on every slice; the formula for \(i^!\) restricts to that slice by its fibre formula. The functors \(i_*\) and \(i^{-1}\) preserve filtered colimits, either by (BX.4) and finite-cover section evaluation or by the same evaluation proof on the closed fibre. The other functors have the bounded-below continuity just established. Inducting on the finite strata with the contravariant Hom triangle proves the internal comparison and a uniform lower bound for its targets. Finally apply (BX.12) to obtain (BX.13). This argument retains a fixed lower bound throughout. It makes no assertion about arbitrary families unbounded below.

### BX.5. Localization of every higher morphism

Take the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) sequence of a bounded constructible \(R_X\)-complex \(Q\). Its colimit is \(Q[1/\pi]\). Equation (BX.13), with no dependence of its lower bound on the transition index, gives for every integer \(m\)
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D_R}(P,Q[m])[1/\pi]
 \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\
\operatorname{Hom}_{D_R}(P,Q[1/\pi][m]).
\tag{BX.15}
\]
Localization is flat and left adjoint to restriction of \(E_X\)-modules. Its derived scalar adjunction identifies the right side with
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{D(E_X)}(P[1/\pi],Q[1/\pi][m])\).
The resulting map is precisely rationalization of a numerator followed by its scalar denominator. Thus (BW.18) is fully faithful, including all higher morphisms and their compositions. Applied on slices, the same proof gives the specified comparison
\[
R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q)[1/\pi]
 \simeq
R\mathcal Hom_{E_X}(P[1/\pi],Q[1/\pi]).
\tag{BX.16}
\]
It is compatible with evaluation, because both its adjunction and the filtered-colimit map are induced by evaluation.

The image has bounded constructible cohomology. BQ and BP express the cohomology of \(P\) on finitely many strata by finite \(O\)-modules. Localizing those modules gives finite-dimensional \(E\)-spaces, and localization is exact. This also shows that (BW.18) is t-exact.

### BX.6. Constructible integral models

We first establish lattices étale locally for a lisse \(E_X\)-sheaf \(L\), without a hypothesis that \(L\) comes from a global profinite representation. On an affine pro-étale object \(V\), sections of \(R_X\) are continuous functions from the profinite component space of \(V\) to \(O\): this is the inverse limit of the finite locally constant \(O_n\)-valued functions. Sections of \(E_X\) are the corresponding continuous \(E\)-valued functions. Their denominators are bounded by compactness, so this follows by localizing the first description and the finite-cover colimit calculation in BX.4.

On a trivialization \(L=E_X^r\), the sheaf of integral lattices in \(L\) is the constant discrete sheaf with value
\[
\operatorname{GL}_r(E)/\operatorname{GL}_r(O).
\tag{BX.17}
\]
A proposed lattice, trivialized together with \(L\), is described by a continuous invertible matrix. Its coset is locally constant because \(\operatorname{GL}_r(O)\) is open; conversely each coset supplies a lattice. This proves the assertion as sheaves, allowing different cosets on different clopen pieces. The classical-descent proof in [the pro-étale lesson, Lemma 7.1](course:AG-LTF/the-pro-etale-site-and-l-adic-complexes#integral-lattices-are-a-local-condition) then makes the lattice sheaf classical. It is locally inhabited on the pro-étale site, so its corresponding étale sheaf is locally inhabited: the fully faithful exact inverse image reflects the image subobject of its map to the terminal sheaf. Hence a lattice exists on an étale cover. This proof uses completeness, the finite residue quotients and the open subgroup in (BX.17); it works for the stated DVR \(O\), including equal characteristic.

There is a finite stratification on which that cover can be replaced by finite étale covers carrying lattices. Here are the algebraic details. A reduced irreducible affine stratum has an integral coordinate ring \(A\). Choose an affine piece of the étale cover meeting its generic point. Its coordinate algebra \(B\) is finitely presented and its generic fibre is a nonzero finite étale algebra over \(\operatorname{Frac}A\). Each of finitely many algebra generators satisfies a monic equation over that field. Clear all coefficient denominators. The equation evaluated in \(B\) is zero after passage to the generic fibre, so invert also the finitely many elements of \(A\) that kill these errors. On the resulting nonempty open, \(B\) is generated by finitely many integral elements and is therefore finite over \(A\). It remains étale; its positive generic rank is constant after taking a connected open part, so it is surjective there. Do this for the finitely many generic components and continue on the smaller closed complement. Finite dimension gives termination. Nonreduced strata cause no problem: reduction induces an equivalence of the pro-étale topoi, since (BX.6) for a nilpotent closed immersion has empty open complement and \(i^{-1}i_*=1\). We may perform the construction on the reduced strata.

Let \(W\to S\) be one of the resulting finite étale surjections, of constant degree \(d\), with a lattice on \(W\). The scheme \(T\) of orderings of its \(d\) geometric fibre points is a finite étale surjection: it is the clopen locus in \(W^d_S\) where all coordinates are distinct. Étale local splitting of \(W\), proved in N.1, identifies \(T\) with the permutations of \(d\) points. Thus \(T\to S\) is a torsor under the finite group \(G=\mathfrak S_d\). Pull the lattice to \(T\) through its first projection and call it \(N\subset L|_T\). Inside that same sheaf form
\[
N'=\sum_{g\in G}gN.
\tag{BX.18}
\]
This is again a lisse \(R_T\)-lattice. Locally trivialize \(L\) and the finitely many lattices. By (BX.17) refine into clopen pieces on which their relative lattice positions are fixed. On each piece their sum is the extension of a sum of finitely many \(O\)-lattices in \(E^r\). That sum is a finite torsion-free \(O\)-module of rank \(r\), hence free, and spans \(E^r\). Equation (BX.18) is invariant under \(G\). Its descent maps satisfy the cocycle condition as restrictions of those of \(L|_T\). Sheaf descent along the finite étale torsor therefore gives a lattice on \(S\). This argument uses a finite group of deck transformations, not a profinite classification on an arbitrary singular scheme.

A lisse integral lattice lies in the heart of \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_S\). Completeness is local on the trivializing pro-étale cover. Its first quotient is locally constant and finite over \(\kappa\); it is classical by the same descent lemma. Equivalently BP identifies its strict quotient system. BX.2 shows that its extension by zero from a locally closed stratum is still a constructible complete sheaf.

Every constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf \(F\) has a constructible integral model. Refine its stratification by the one just constructed. The exact sequence (BX.6), repeatedly applied, filters \(F\) by extensions of lisse stratum sheaves extended by zero, each with an integral model. Suppose two successive pieces have models \(N'\) and \(N''\). Equation (BX.15) in degree one identifies their extension class with
\[
e=u/\pi^a,\qquad
u\in\operatorname{Ext}^1_{R_X}(N'',N').
\tag{BX.19}
\]
The degree-one roof-to-extension construction in BT.2 supplies the \(R_X\)-module extension with class \(u\): its normalization is \(\epsilon_1=1\), so the pushout represents the given degree-one derived morphism. Its middle sheaf is constructible and complete: the associated triangle has endpoints \(N',N''\) in \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\), which is a full triangulated subcategory by BW.3, and the extension construction makes its middle term a sheaf. The exact completed-ring equivalence of BW.3 transports BT.4's degree-one comparison to this heart, so this is the required heart extension. After rationalization, rescale the identification of the first end term by \(\pi^{-a}\). The resulting extension class is \(e\), so the rationalized middle term is the desired extension. Induction constructs a model for \(F\). The result is a constructible model; no global lisse lattice has been asserted.

### BX.7. Equivalence and the geometric operations

The essential image of the fully faithful functor (BW.18) is closed under all cones of morphisms between its objects. By (BX.15) each such morphism is a fraction of an integral one. Its cone is isomorphic to the localization of that integral cone, by rescaling the source. It is closed under shifts as well. BX.6 places every constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf in the image. The finite cohomological truncation tower of any bounded complex with constructible cohomology therefore places that complex in the image. We have proved the t-exact equivalence
\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}_X[1/\pi]
 \ \xrightarrow[\ P\mapsto P[1/\pi]\ ]{\ \sim\ }\
D_{\mathrm{cons}}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X).
\tag{BX.20}
\]
This also proves that the indicated full subcategory on the right is triangulated and closed under standard truncations: it is the essential image of a triangulated functor and of its t-exact bounded truncations. Its heart is the category of constructible \(E_X\)-sheaves and is the rationalized strict heart of BW.7.

For clarity the operation comparisons use actual ambient functors. By (BX.10), ordinary derived tensor over \(R_X\), then localization, gives ordinary derived tensor over \(E_X\). Equation (BX.16) identifies the internal Homs with their evaluation. Ordinary ringed inverse image in (BX.11) already equals completed inverse image on the integral constructible category. Associativity of extension of scalars consequently gives
\[
(Lf_R^*P)[1/\pi]
 \simeq
E_X\otimes_{f^{-1}E_Y}^{L}f^{-1}(P[1/\pi]).
\tag{BX.21}
\]
For ordinary derived image apply (BX.12) to the multiplication tower on every quasi-compact target slice:
\[
(Rf_{R,*}P)[1/\pi]
 \simeq Rf_{E,*}(P[1/\pi]).
\tag{BX.22}
\]
The map is the natural scalar-localization comparison. Coefficient restriction preserves the resolutions used to calculate these images, as in BW.2; alternatively the sectionwise calculation in BX.4 proves the same map. BV's constructibility result and (BX.20) show that its right side is constructible at the geometric scope of BV.

Ordinary \(j_!\) is already complete by BX.2 and commutes with localization by its exact finite-sum description. For a compactification \(f=pj\), equations (BX.22) and this open comparison identify the localized proper-support functor with \(Rp_*j_!\) on actual rational sheaf complexes. The refinement maps are induced by the same adjunction maps before and after localization. Thus the compactification independence proved in BM carries over with those maps.

Finally transport BV's \(f_c^!\) through (BX.20). This identifies its Hom adjunction with the actual proper-support functor just identified, for every pair of constructible rational complexes and in every degree. It is therefore that functor's exceptional right adjoint on the constructible categories. For a closed immersion it also agrees with the ambient right adjoint (BX.8), since that formula commutes with the same localization comparisons. No right adjoint on every unbounded nonconstructible complex is needed for this statement.

All tensor adjunctions, operation adjunctions and comparisons used above are their scalar-extension, restriction or support maps. Their mates consequently identify the projection, base-change and composition maps with those of BW.7. In particular the localized dualizing object is the exceptional image of the rational unit, (BX.16) identifies its duality functor with ambient internal Hom, and its double-evaluation map is BV's isomorphism under (BX.20). This proves the rational comparison with its six operations and duality at the established constructible scope.

For pro-étale constructible coefficients, see [Bhatt–Scholze, version 2, §§2.2, 6.1 and 6.8](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1198v2). The neighbourhood calculation, finite-diagonal continuity, finite-group lattice descent and extension-class lifting above supply the proofs used here. Equivalence (BX.20) concerns the full constructible subcategory of the ambient derived category. Equivalence with the bounded derived category of its heart is a further assertion. BY proves it for curves over finite or algebraically closed fields. The higher-dimensional projection and effacement arguments are treated in BZ–CB.

## Appendix BY. Constructible effacement and realization on curves

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed or finite, and let \(X\) be separated and of finite type over \(k\). Retain the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), its finite residue field \(\kappa\), and its fraction field \(E\); the residue characteristic is invertible in \(k\). We prove realization in dimension at most one, including singular schemes, integral torsion and rational coefficients. The reduction in general dimension uses the precise projection assertion (BY.26). Appendix CB supplies its geometric argument from BZ–CA; the realization deduction retains the stated coefficient and foundational hypotheses of these appendices.

We use the equivalent actual completed-ring category of BW, with unit \(\mathbf1_X=R_X\), and write \(\mathcal H_X\) for its constructible heart. Thus
\[
H^q(X,F)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(\mathbf1_X,F[q])
\]
is ordinary derived cohomology of the corresponding \(R_X\)-module. BW's adjunction identifies this with the preceding complete-coefficient calculation. Inverse image on these hearts is exact by BQ and BX.3. The stratum support sequence is BX.2, constructibility of ordinary direct image is BV, and finite direct image is exact: proper comparison identifies its geometric restrictions with finite sums on zero-dimensional fibres. BU and finite-coefficient detection then give t-exactness. These assertions include nilpotent thickenings.

### BY.1. Moving a monomorphism through an adjunction

Here is an elementary construction we shall use several times. Suppose \(L : \mathcal A\rightleftarrows\mathcal B : R\) is an adjunction of abelian categories and \(L\) is exact. Given \(B\in\mathcal B\) and a monomorphism \(u:RB\to A\), form the pushout
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
LRB&\xrightarrow{Lu}&LA\\
\epsilon_B\downarrow&&\downarrow t\\
B&\xrightarrow{v}&B'.
\end{array}
\tag{BY.1}
\]
The map \(v\) is monic, because it is the pushout of the monomorphism \(Lu\). Under adjunction \(t\) corresponds to \(w:A\to RB'\), and naturality and the triangle identity give
\[
w u=Rv.
\tag{BY.2}
\]
For example, the adjoint of \(tLu=v\epsilon_B\) is respectively \(wu\) and \(Rv\). Thus any class killed after applying a functor to \(u\) is also killed after applying that functor to \(Rv\). The construction takes place inside the constructible hearts whenever both functors preserve them. No injective object of a constructible heart is required.

Call \(P\in\mathcal H_X\) **effaceable as a source** if, for every \(G\in\mathcal H_X\), \(q>0\), and
\(\xi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(P,G[q])\), there is a heart monomorphism \(G\to G'\) killing \(\xi\). This is a condition on individual classes. Finite lists of classes can be killed by successively applying the condition to their images and composing the resulting monomorphisms.

For an open immersion \(j:U\to X\), derived adjunction gives
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(j_!P,G[q])
=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_U}(P,j^*G[q]).
\tag{BY.3}
\]
If \(P\) is effaceable as a source on \(U\), kill the right-hand class by a monomorphism \(j^*G\to A\). Apply (BY.1) to \(j_!\dashv j^*\). Equation (BY.2) proves that \(j_!P\) is effaceable as a source on \(X\). Exactness of \(j_!\) and constructibility of the pushout follow from BX.2 and BQ.

We shall also use (BY.1) for \(f^*\dashv f_*\) when \(f\) is finite. In that case both heart functors are exact and
\[
H^q(X,F)=H^q(Y,f_*F).
\tag{BY.4}
\]
Consequently an embedding of \(f_*F\) on \(Y\) killing a specified cohomology class lifts to an embedding of \(F\) on \(X\) killing that class.

### BY.2. The obstruction in degree one and gluing over opens

For an open \(U\subset X\), put \(P[U]=j_!j^*P\). There is a useful way to extend maps out of \(P[U]\) after enlarging their target. For \(G\in\mathcal H_X\), set
\[
Q=j_*j^*G\oplus i_*i^*G,\qquad i:X\setminus U\to X.
\tag{BY.5}
\]
Here \(j_*\) means the degree-zero ordinary image. BV and BQ make \(Q\) a constructible heart object. The two adjunction units give a monomorphism \(G\to Q\): over \(U\) its first component is the identity, and on the complement its second component is the identity. Exact restriction and the joint conservativity of BX.2 detect the kernel.

Moreover
\[
\operatorname{Hom}(P[U],i_*i^*G)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}(P[U],j_*j^*G)
=\operatorname{Hom}(P,j_*j^*G).
\tag{BY.6}
\]
The first identity uses \(i^*P[U]=0\); the second uses \(j^*P[U]=j^*P\) and the ordinary adjunction. In particular every map \(P[U]\to G\) extends to a map \(P\to Q\) after the monomorphism \(G\to Q\).

We record the exact-sequence arguments involved. If \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) has \(A,C\) effaceable as sources, then so is \(B\). Given a class from \(B\), first kill its restriction from \(A\). Exactness lifts the resulting class to one from \(C\), which can then be killed. If \(A,B\) are effaceable as sources, the same long exact sequence proves the assertion for \(C\) in degrees \(q>1\): first kill the image from \(B\), then the lifting class from \(A\) in degree \(q-1\). In degree one the remaining obstruction is a map \(A\to G\) modulo maps extending to \(B\). Thus the same conclusion for \(C\) holds if those obstructions can be killed by enlarging \(G\). Finite sums, direct summands and finite extensions preserve source effaceability by these arguments.

Taking \(A=P[U]\), \(B=P\), equations (BY.5)–(BY.6) handle precisely this degree-one obstruction. Thus \(P/P[U]\) is effaceable as a source whenever \(P\) and \(P[U]\) are. For opens \(V,W\), the exact sequence
\[
0\to P[V\cap W]\xrightarrow{(1,-1)}
P[V]\oplus P[W]\xrightarrow{(1,1)}
P[V\cup W]\to0
\tag{BY.7}
\]
is checked after restriction to the four parts of the open cover and its complement. A map from \(P[V\cap W]\) extends after (BY.5), with \(U=V\cap W\), to \(P\), hence to \(P[V]\). This supplies its degree-one obstruction condition. Source effaceability of the first three open terms therefore implies that of the union.

It follows that cohomological effacement on affine open subsets implies it on every separated \(X\). Indeed \(\mathbf1_U\) being effaceable as a source is precisely cohomological effacement on \(U\). Transfer by (BY.3) gives \(\mathbf1_X[U]\). Induct over a finite affine cover, using (BY.7). Intersections of affine opens in a separated scheme are affine: the intersection is the inverse image of the closed diagonal in the affine product of the two opens over \(k\), hence is a closed subscheme of that product. At the induction step \(V\cap W\) is covered by the intersections of \(W\) with the previous affine opens. This proves the induction with the same finite-cover bound.

### BY.3. A diagonal kernel with zero ordinary image

For the affine-line projection \(\pi:T=S\times\mathbf A^1\to S\), the actual adjunction unit is an isomorphism
\[
K\xrightarrow{\sim}R\pi_*\pi^*K,\qquad K\in\mathscr C_S.
\tag{BY.8}
\]
Here is a deduction from the established trace, valid also for singular \(S\). BI.2 identifies \(R\pi_!\mathbf1_T\) with \(\mathbf1_S(-1)[-2]\), with its specified trace. BN's projection formula and BV.15 consequently identify
\[
R\pi_!\pi^!A
=R\pi_!\bigl(\pi^*A(1)[2]\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\epsilon}A
\]
with an isomorphism, for every \(A\in\mathscr C_S\). BV.20–BV.21 identify its Verdier dual with the unit in (BY.8), taking \(A=\mathbb D_SK\). These are the specified counit and unit, because those exchange maps transpose evaluation. Biduality proves (BY.8), not merely an unspecified isomorphism of its endpoints. The section of a projection therefore inverts this unit by the adjunction triangle identity.

Suppose now that \(S=\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\), that \(Y\subset T=\mathbf A^m_k\) is closed, finite and surjective over \(S\), and that \(F\in\mathcal H_T\) vanishes on \(Y\) and is lisse on its complement. Suppose in addition that the ordinary fibre-comparison maps
\[
s^*R\pi_*F\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(T_s,F|_{T_s})
\tag{BY.9}
\]
are isomorphisms at geometric points of \(S\), as complete complexes on the point. This is the extra hypothesis in this construction.

Then \(R\pi_*F\) is concentrated in degree one. To check the upper bound on a geometric fibre, use [Torsion sheaves on curves, Theorem 1.1 and Section 10](course:ag-etale-cohomology/torsion-sheaves-on-curves#1-the-assertions-and-their-coefficient-conventions): an affine curve has torsion cohomological dimension at most one. Its curve, normalization and finite-cover prerequisites are supplied by P–AG, AK and AL. The derived first reduction of a heart object has cohomology in degrees \(-1,0\). Finite-coefficient comparison and its two truncation triangles therefore give the upper bound one for the first reduction of its derived sections. These sections are bounded and have finite \(O\)-module cohomology by BV and BU. If their largest nonzero degree were \(a>1\), the coefficient cone would give
\[
H^a/\pi H^a=H^a(K\otimes_O^L\kappa)=0.
\]
Finite-module Nakayama contradicts its nonvanishing. This proves the adic upper bound without replacing derived reduction by an underived quotient.

Degree zero is zero as well. For each ordinary quotient of \(F|_{T_s}\), a section on the connected open \(\mathbf A^1_{\bar s}\setminus Y_s\) has open and closed zero locus. A nonzero section would thus be nonzero everywhere on that open, whereas extension by zero requires its support to avoid a neighbourhood of every point of the nonempty \(Y_s\). This is impossible. Sections of the adic sheaf are the inverse limit of those quotient sections by BP and BX.2, so they too vanish. Negative cohomology is zero for a sheaf. Finally inverse image to a geometric point is t-exact on these constructible categories, and those restrictions detect zero by first reduction and classical geometric stalks. Thus (BY.9) gives the asserted degree-one concentration on \(S\).

Write \(p_1,p_2:T\times_ST\to T\) for the projections and \(\Delta:T\to T\times_ST\) for the diagonal. Define the heart object \(B\) by
\[
0\to B\to p_1^*F\to\Delta_*F\to0.
\tag{BY.10}
\]
The last map is restriction to the diagonal. It is an epimorphism by the support sequence, since \(\Delta^*p_1^*F=F\). Smooth base change gives
\[
Rp_{2,*}p_1^*F\simeq\pi^*R\pi_*F.
\tag{BY.11}
\]
For complete coefficients this is the reduction-compatible finite-coefficient smooth comparison of AS and BV.1; completeness detects its cone. The right side is concentrated in degree one. Applying \(Rp_{2,*}\) to (BY.10) consequently gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\to F\xrightarrow{\delta}C\to\pi^*H^1(R\pi_*F)\to0,\\
C=H^1(Rp_{2,*}B),\qquad Rp_{2,*}B=C[-1].
\end{gathered}
\tag{BY.12}
\]
All terms are constructible by BV and BQ. If \(\Pi=\pi p_1=\pi p_2\), then
\[
R\pi_*C=
\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(R\Pi_*p_1^*F\to R\Pi_*\Delta_*F\bigr)=0.
\tag{BY.13}
\]
For the last equality, \(p_1\) is an affine-line projection. Under the unit (BY.8), the map
\(F\to Rp_{1,*}p_1^*F\to Rp_{1,*}\Delta_*F=F\)
is the identity because \(p_1\Delta=1\). Thus the second arrow is an isomorphism, and applying \(R\pi_*\) proves (BY.13). This verifies the actual arrow in the cone.

### BY.4. Effacing cohomology on the affine line and on curves

For \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\), hypothesis (BY.9) requires no higher-dimensional projection choice. Over algebraically closed \(k\) it is the identity at the chosen geometric point. Over a finite field, passage to its algebraic closure is the affine inverse limit of finite étale extensions. AS proves the finite-coefficient comparison for that inverse limit; the coefficient cone and completeness give the complete comparison. These chosen geometric points detect the required bounds.

Take any \(F\in\mathcal H_{\mathbf A^1_k}\). Choose a finite closed \(Y\) containing its nonlisse locus and the rational point zero. Put \(A=j_!j^*F\), and embed \(A\) into \(C\) by (BY.12). The pushout along \(A\to F\) gives a monomorphism \(F\to H\) and an exact sequence
\[
0\to C\to H\to D\to0,\qquad D=i_*i^*F.
\tag{BY.14}
\]
Finite-image exactness and (BY.13) imply
\[
R\pi_*H\simeq R\pi_*D=M[0],\qquad M=\pi_*H\in\mathcal H_k.
\tag{BY.15}
\]
The counit \(e:\pi^*M\to H\) becomes an isomorphism after \(R\pi_*\). Indeed the composite of the unit \(M\to R\pi_*\pi^*M\) with \(R\pi_*e\) is the identity of \(R\pi_*H=M\), and the unit is (BY.8).

Over an algebraically closed field every \(M\) already has zero higher cohomology. Over \(\mathbf F_q\), BU identifies a heart object with a finite \(O\)-module \(M\) and an invertible arithmetic-Frobenius operator \(T\), and computes its cohomology by \([M\xrightarrow{T-1}M]\). On \(J=M\oplus M\) use the automorphism
\[
T_J(x,y)=(Tx+y,y).
\tag{BY.16}
\]
It defines a continuous \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\)-action: on every finite quotient \(J/\pi^nJ\) its powers factor through a finite cyclic group, and these actions are compatible. The inclusion \(M\to J,\ x\mapsto(x,0)\), respects Frobenius and is monic. Since
\[
(T_J-1)(0,y)=(y,0),
\]
it kills the induced map in \(H^1\); higher cohomology vanishes by BU. The argument includes torsion \(M\).

Use this embedding \(u:M\to J\), or the identity \(J=M\) in the algebraically closed case, and push out \(e:\pi^*M\to H\) along the monomorphism \(\pi^*u:\pi^*M\to\pi^*J\). This yields a monomorphism \(H\to G\). In the derived category the pushout is the cone of the monomorphism
\((e,-\pi^*u):\pi^*M\to H\oplus\pi^*J\). Applying \(R\pi_*\), (BY.8) and (BY.15) identify this cone with the cone of
\[
M\xrightarrow{(1,-u)}M\oplus J,
\]
which is \(J\). Under this identification the map \(R\pi_*H\to R\pi_*G\) is \(u:M\to J\). Thus \(F\to H\to G\) kills every positive cohomology group. Over algebraically closed \(k\), \(G\) itself has zero positive cohomology. Over finite \(k\), only the induced maps are asserted to vanish.

This proves cohomological effacement on every affine curve. First consider an integral affine curve \(X\). Polynomial normalization in Y.5 and AG.1 gives a finite morphism \(f:X\to\mathbf A^1_k\). Apply the affine-line result to \(f_*F\) and then (BY.1)–(BY.4). For a general reduced affine curve, its finite normalization \(\nu:\widetilde X\to X\), proved in AG, is a finite union of integral affine curves and points. The unit \(F\to\nu_*\nu^*F\) is monic: on a geometric fibre it is the diagonal into a nonempty finite sum of copies of the stalk. Kill the image of a prescribed class on each component of \(\widetilde X\), and push the resulting embedding down by the exact \(\nu_*\). The composite embedding of \(F\) kills the original class. Points are covered by BU and (BY.16); nilpotents are removed by BX.2. Finally BY.2 proves cohomological effacement on every separated curve and on every open subset of it.

### BY.5. Elementary sources and a separating finite projection

We need the following geometric fact with its separability condition: for an integral affine scheme of dimension \(d\) over a perfect field there are algebraically independent functions \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) over whose polynomial ring its coordinate ring is finite, and whose function-field extension is separable.

In characteristic zero Y.5 gives the finite polynomial normalization and every finite field extension in characteristic zero is separable. Here is the extra argument in characteristic \(p>0\). For a finitely generated field \(K/k\) of transcendence degree \(d\), take any transcendence basis \(z\). Frobenius identifies the finite degrees
\([K:k(z)]=[K^p:k(z)^p]\). Since \(k\) is perfect,
\([k(z):k(z)^p]=p^d\), by the monomial basis with exponents from \(0\) to \(p-1\). Computing \([K:k(z)^p]\) in two ways gives
\[
[K:K^p]=p^d.
\tag{BY.17}
\]
Adjoin successively elements outside the field already generated over \(K^p\). Each adjunction has degree \(p\), so after \(d\) steps the corresponding monomials form a basis of \(K\) over \(K^p\). Differentiation in these variables, with \(K^p\) constant, is well defined on that basis and obeys the product rule; the relations \(b_i^p\in K^p\) have zero derivative. The universal differential module therefore has basis \(db_i\). In particular \(\dim_K\Omega_{K/k}=d\).

Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) generate the given domain, ordered so that \(dx_1,\ldots,dx_d\) are independent; the differentials of algebra generators span. If \(N>d\), choose a nonzero polynomial relation among them. Choose a sufficiently large power \(P\) of \(p\), larger than every exponent in that relation, and replace
\[
x_i\ \text{by}\ y_i=x_i-x_N^{P^i}\quad(1\leq i<N).
\tag{BY.18}
\]
After substitution, the terms involving only \(x_N\) have distinct exponents
\(a_N+\sum_{i<N}a_iP^i\). The unique largest one has a nonzero scalar coefficient. Thus the relation is, after scaling, monic in \(x_N\) over \(k[y_1,\ldots,y_{N-1}]\). The original algebra is finite over this smaller algebra. Meanwhile \(dy_i=dx_i\), so the first \(d\) differentials stay independent. Repeating gives a finite polynomial normalization \(k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\), with the \(dt_i\) independent. Algebraic independence also follows from integrality and equality of transcendence degree.

The finite extension \(K/k(t)\) is separable because its relative differential module is zero. To recall the finite-field criterion, separable algebraic generators have invertible polynomial derivative and contribute no relative differentials. After adjoining the maximal separable subextension, a remaining nontrivial purely inseparable finite extension \(L/M\) has \(L\ne L^pM\): otherwise iteration would give \(L=L^{p^r}M=M\) for sufficiently large \(r\). A monomial basis over \(L^pM\), as above, supplies a nonzero relative differential. Hence an inseparable finite extension cannot have zero relative differentials. This proves the criterion and the required separability.

Such a finite projection becomes finite étale over a nonempty principal open \(W\subset\mathbf A^d\). Indeed choose a primitive element of its separable function field, make it integral by clearing denominators, and then invert a nonzero polynomial so that it generates the whole finite algebra. Invert also its nonzero polynomial discriminant. The resulting monic polynomial \(g(T)\) has invertible derivative at its root. Here is the lifting calculation: over a square-zero ideal \(I\), a lift \(t\) of a root is corrected uniquely to \(t-g(t)/g'(t)\). Taylor expansion has no higher correction terms since \(I^2=0\), and the unit \(g'(t)\) gives uniqueness. Iterating along the powers of a nilpotent ideal gives formal étaleness; finite presentation gives an étale algebra. The primitive-element proof over the infinite field \(k(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\), for \(d>0\), is Z.3. In dimension zero perfectness already gives a finite separable, hence finite étale, map to the point.

We use this projection to extend a lisse sheaf from a stratum as a summand. For \(P\in\mathcal H_X\), choose an affine open \(U'\) meeting a generic point of its support closure such that \(Z=U'\cap\overline{\operatorname{supp}P}\) is integral, closed in \(U'\), and \(P|_Z\) is lisse, while \(P\) is zero off \(Z\) in \(U'\). Such an open exists by removing the other components, the boundary of a locally constant stratum and then taking a principal neighbourhood of that generic point. Reducing \(Z\) does not change its coefficient category.

Choose the separating finite projection of \(Z\) just proved. Its coordinate functions lift along the surjection of affine coordinate rings, giving \(h':U'\to\mathbf A^d\). Restrict to \(U=h'^{-1}(W)\) and rename \(Z\cap U\) as \(Z\), so \(f=h'|_Z:Z\to W\) is finite étale. For \(G=P|_Z\), let
\[
L=h^*f_*G,\qquad V=U\setminus Z,\qquad h=h'|_U.
\tag{BY.19}
\]
Finite étale pushforward and inverse image make \(L\) lisse on \(U\). The diagonal is an open and closed component of \(Z\times_W Z\). Finite base change therefore exhibits \(G\) as a direct summand of \(f^*f_*G=i^*L\). Pushing by \(i:Z\to U\) gives
\[
P|_U=i_*G\ \text{as a direct summand of}\
i_*i^*L=L/L[V].
\tag{BY.20}
\]
The last equality is the exact support sequence, not a claim that \(L\) itself extends \(G\).

Extend (BY.20) by zero to \(X\). The quotient \(P/P[U]\) has support closure a proper closed subset of the old support closure, missing the selected generic point. Noetherian induction yields a finite filtration of \(P\) whose successive quotients are summands of sheaves
\[
j_!\bigl(L/L[V]\bigr),\qquad V\subset U,\quad j:U\to X.
\tag{BY.21}
\]
For a finite-dimensional scheme termination can also be seen by ordering support dimension and the number of components of largest dimension. If \(P\) has torsion-free stalks on its strata, the same is true of its support quotients, and all the lisse \(L\) in this construction are finite free: their stalks are finite sums of stalks of \(P\), and a finite torsion-free module over a discrete valuation ring is free. This construction works over finite fields as well; (BY.18) did not require an infinite field.

### BY.6. From cohomological effacement to every higher extension

Suppose cohomological effacement is known on every open subset of \(X\). For an open \(U\subset X\) and a lisse finite free object \(L\) on \(U\), we have
\[
R\mathcal Hom(L,G)=L^\vee\otimes G,\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}(L,G[q])=H^q(U,L^\vee\otimes G).
\tag{BY.22}
\]
Locally this is the finite-free matrix calculation of BO and BW, so it is an identity of derived internal Homs, not an assertion about arbitrary constructible \(L\). Both \(L\otimes-\) and \(L^\vee\otimes-\) are exact on the heart and are adjoint. Kill the right-hand class in (BY.22) and apply (BY.1) to this adjunction. It follows that \(L\) is effaceable as a source.

Apply the same argument on \(V\), use (BY.3) to extend by zero to \(U\), and then use (BY.5)–(BY.6) for the quotient \(L/L[V]\). Another application of (BY.3) proves source effaceability of (BY.21). Finite extensions and summands, together with BY.5, prove it for every constructible heart object with torsion-free stratum stalks.

For such a source \(P\), all maps
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_X}(P,G)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(P,G[r])
\tag{BY.23}
\]
are isomorphisms. Here is the target version of the induction in BT.5. Degrees zero and one are BT.4. For a class in degree \(r>1\), choose a monomorphism \(G\to G'\) killing it, with cokernel \(Q\). The triangle lifts the class to a morphism \(P\to Q[r-1]\). Realize that morphism by induction and splice its heart extension with \(0\to G\to G'\to Q\to0\). This proves surjectivity. For injectivity, write a heart \(r\)-extension as the splice of its first short exact sequence \(0\to G\to B\to Q\to0\) and an \((r-1)\)-extension from \(P\) to \(Q\). If its ambient class is zero, the latter class comes from \(\operatorname{Hom}(P,B[r-1])\). Inductive surjectivity lifts this class to the heart, and inductive injectivity identifies its image with the given \((r-1)\)-extension. The heart connecting map kills it, proving injectivity.

These torsion-free objects generate both categories needed for realization. BP gives a uniform torsion exponent for the torsion subobject of a constructible heart object, with torsion-free quotient. A torsion object has a finite support filtration with terms \(j_!M\), where \(M\) is lisse with finite underlying stalk on a locally closed stratum. N's finite-monodromy construction provides a finite étale cover \(p:T\to Z\) trivializing \(M\). Choose a surjection \(O^a\to M|_T\). The composite
\[
j_!p_*\mathbf1_T^{\,a}\longrightarrow
j_!p_*p^*M\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sum}}j_!M
\tag{BY.24}
\]
is an epimorphism. On each geometric fibre the last map adds the nonempty finite family of entries; it is onto even when the cover degree is divisible by the residue characteristic. The source is torsion-free, and its heart kernel is torsion-free as a subobject. Thus \(j_!M\) is the cone of a map between two torsion-free heart objects. Support filtrations, the torsion exact sequence and finite truncation triangles prove the generation assertion.

First use the target truncation triangles to extend (BY.23) to every bounded heart complex, keeping a torsion-free source. Then use the source generation just proved and long exact Hom sequences to obtain full faithfulness on all of \(D^b(\mathcal H_X)\). Every bounded constructible ambient complex is realized by induction on its cohomology interval: lift the connecting map by full faithfulness and take its cone, exactly as in BT.3. We have proved that cohomological effacement on all opens implies
\[
D^b(\mathcal H_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathscr C_X.
\tag{BY.25}
\]
BY.4 supplies its hypothesis for every \(X\) of dimension at most one. This establishes the asserted integral realization theorem on all separated finite-type curves over finite or algebraically closed fields.

The rational realization theorem follows with its actual functor. By BX.6 every rational heart object has an integral heart model, and BX.5 expresses every positive derived morphism between such models as \(\pi^{-a}\) times an integral derived morphism. Integral realization and BT.5 give a heart epimorphism killing that integral morphism. Its exact rationalization is an epimorphism killing the original rational morphism. The proof of the criterion in BT.5 applies verbatim to the full rational heart and its exact realization functor. Hence (BY.25) holds with the rational heart and the category in (BX.20) as well.

### BY.7. The geometric assertion and realization in higher dimension

The following geometric assertion, proved in Appendix CB, runs the preceding proof in every dimension. For \(m\geq2\):

For every bounded constructible \(\kappa\)-complex \(K\) on \(\mathbf A^m_k\), after an automorphism of affine space, there is a closed subset \(Y\), finite and surjective over \(\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\), such that the cohomology sheaves of \(K\) are lisse off \(Y\) and the open compactification
\(a:\mathbf A^m_k\to\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\times\mathbf P^1_k\)
satisfies
\[
s^*Ra_*K\xrightarrow{\sim}Ra_{s,*}s^*K
\tag{BY.26}
\]
at geometric fibres of \(\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\). Over finite \(k\), a finite extension of \(k\) may be made first.

Apply this assertion to the first derived reduction of an integral heart object \(F\). BO and BP then make \(F\) lisse off the same \(Y\). Every functor in the comparison for \(F\) commutes with that reduction, using the two-term free \(O\)-resolution of \(\kappa\), and its cone is bounded constructible and complete. Vanishing after first reduction forces vanishing by BK.4. Thus one coordinate change works for the integral object itself; choosing unrelated changes at every coefficient level would not prove this.

Replacing \(F\) by \(j_!j^*F\), for \(j:\mathbf A^m\setminus Y\to\mathbf A^m\), preserves (BY.26). Its quotient is supported on \(Y\), whose closure in the compactification stays away from infinity because \(Y\) is finite over the base. Proper comparison handles that quotient, and its triangle gives the claim. Proper comparison for \(\mathbf A^{m-1}\times\mathbf P^1\) then turns (BY.26) into (BY.9).

With this geometric input, the induction on affine dimension proceeds as follows. Construct \(C,H,D\) as in (BY.12)–(BY.14). Since \(Y\to S\) is finite, \(R\pi_*H=M[0]\) for a constructible heart object \(M\) on \(S=\mathbf A^{m-1}\). By induction choose \(M\to J\) killing positive cohomology. One embedding can kill all of it: those groups are finite \(O\)-modules, vanish outside finitely many degrees by BV and BU, and finitely many module generators can be killed successively. The counit and pushout calculation following (BY.15) then give \(F\to G\) killing all positive cohomology on \(\mathbf A^m\).

If the coordinate choice required a finite field extension, descend this conclusion without dividing by its degree. For \(q:X_{k'}\to X\), the unit \(F\to q_*q^*F\) is monic on geometric fibres. Compose it with the finite exact image of an embedding of \(q^*F\) killing the pulled-back class. Its cohomology map factors through the killed class on \(X_{k'}\), so the composite kills the original class. No trace splitting is needed.

For an arbitrary affine \(X\), choose a closed embedding \(i:X\to\mathbf A^N\). Apply the established affine-space effacement to \(i_*F\to G\). Exact \(i^*\) gives an embedding \(F\to i^*G\), and the natural diagram
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
H^q(\mathbf A^N,i_*F)&\longrightarrow&H^q(\mathbf A^N,G)\\
\Vert&&\downarrow\\
H^q(X,F)&\longrightarrow&H^q(X,i^*G)
\end{array}
\tag{BY.27}
\]
proves effacement on \(X\). BY.2 handles arbitrary separated \(X\), and BY.5–BY.6 then give full integral and rational realization. Appendix CB proves (BY.26), so this argument gives the higher-dimensional deduction with the same coefficient and foundational inputs as BY.1–BY.6.

The freely accessible comparison texts are [Nori, *Constructible Sheaves*, §§2–3, arXiv version 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.02417v1) and [Barrett, *The derived category of the abelian category of constructible sheaves*, §§2–3, arXiv version 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.10859v1). The proof here uses the established étale constructibility and duality arguments, the explicit target pushouts, and the separating projection (BY.18). It does not import a topological constructibility theorem from Nori's Proposition 3.4.

For \(m\geq2\), Barrett's geometric argument for (BY.26) uses a dimension bound for étale microsupport and a transversality comparison at infinity. BZ proves the Radon inversion triangle and projective incidence dimension estimate. CA proves that the resulting cone controls transverse tests, and proves the canonical exceptional inverse-image comparison for transverse maps. CB proves the quadratic coordinate change at infinity, the characteristic-two descent of the actual comparison map, and the finite-field choice. The realization deduction retains the recursive prerequisites of BY.1–BY.6; it does not supply the separate nearby-cycle, weight or other later lesson theorems.

## Appendix BZ. Projective incidence and the dimension of non-acyclic directions

Let \(k\) be a finite or algebraically closed field, and let \(\kappa\) be a finite coefficient field of characteristic \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\). All complexes in this appendix are bounded and constructible unless another description is given. We prove the projective incidence dimension estimate needed to construct a cotangent bound for BY.26. We also prove the Radon inversion triangle, including its coefficient maps. The subsequent passage from that bound to noncharacteristic exceptional inverse image is a separate assertion.

### BZ.1. Detecting failure of universal local acyclicity

For a finite-type map \(f:X\to Z\), a geometric point \(z\) of \(Z\), and a geometric point \(t\) of the strict localization \(Z_{(z)}\), put
\[
 X_z\xrightarrow{i}X\times_ZZ_{(z)}
 \xleftarrow{u}X_t,\qquad
 \Phi_f(K)_{z,t}
 =\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(K|_{X_z}\longrightarrow i^*Ru_*(K|_{X_t})\bigr).
\tag{BZ.1}
\]
The morphism is the adjunction unit followed by restriction. AT.1–AT.4 identify its stalk at \(x\) with the restriction map from \(K_x\) to cohomology on the selected local geometric fibre. Thus the vanishing of (BZ.1) for all \(z,t\) is precisely local acyclicity. Universal local acyclicity requires the same vanishing after every change of base.

Let \(E_f(K)\) be the closure in \(X\) of the union of the images of the supports of (BZ.1), allowing every change of base \(Z'\to Z\) before forming the pair \(z,t\). Here the support means the union of the nonzero cohomology stalks; the nearby-cycle complex need not be constructible. This definition gives the smallest closed subset outside which \(f\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\). Indeed vanishing of the restricted cone is equivalent to vanishing at all of its geometric stalks. A closed set contains the support images if and only if its complement has that property after every base change.

The construction is local for the étale topology of source and base. For an étale neighbourhood, strict localizations at compatible geometric points agree, and therefore the local fibre and the unit in (BZ.1) agree. Taking closures commutes with restriction to an open set. These observations also prove
\[
 E_{f|_V}(K|_V)=E_f(K)\cap V
\tag{BZ.2}
\]
for an open \(V\subset X\), and the corresponding inverse-image equality for étale changes of source or base. This argument uses the selected lift, as in AT.4; it does not identify an entire base-changed strict localization with one of its factors.

If \(f\) is smooth and \(K\) has locally constant cohomology on \(X\setminus D\), then
\[
 E_f(K)\subset D.
\tag{BZ.3}
\]
For one locally constant sheaf this is AT.2–AT.3, or [Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Lemma 9.2](course:ag-etale-cohomology/smooth-base-change-and-local-acyclicity#9-local-fibres-and-universal-local-acyclicity). For a bounded complex use its finitely many truncation triangles: (BZ.1) is exact in the coefficient complex, and two zero cones give the third. Local constancy and smoothness persist under every base change. No acyclicity of a whole smooth affine fibre is asserted.

### BZ.2. Proper transport and finite detection

Suppose \(r:X\to Y\) is proper, \(g:Y\to Z\), and \(f=gr\). Then
\[
 E_g(Rr_*K)\subset r(E_f(K)).
\tag{BZ.4}
\]
If \(r|_{E_f(K)}\) is finite, equality holds.

Here is the comparison that proves both assertions. Use the strict-local diagram of BZ.1 for \(f\) and \(g\). Proper base change identifies restriction of \(Rr_*K\) to either geometric fibre with proper image of the corresponding restriction of \(K\). On the strict-local total spaces, derived composition and the equality of the two maps from \(X_t\) to the total space over \(Y\) identify the ordinary direct images. A final proper base change along \(Y_z\) therefore gives
\[
 \Phi_g(Rr_*K)_{z,t}
 \simeq Rr_{z,*}\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}.
\tag{BZ.5}
\]
Naturality of the adjunction units gives this isomorphism on the cones themselves. The proper comparison applies to these bounded-below torsion complexes by BE.7–BE.8; constructibility of the nearby cycles is unnecessary.

The support of a proper direct image is contained in the image of the support. Consequently each support image on the left of (BZ.5) lies in the proper image of the corresponding support image on the right. Apply this after every \(Z'\to Z\) and take closures. Proper maps are closed, so (BZ.4) follows.

For the reverse inclusion under the finiteness hypothesis, give \(E_f(K)\) its reduced closed scheme structure. The cone in (BZ.5) is supported on its pullback to \(X_z\), since a point of nonzero cohomology would otherwise contribute to the defining support union outside \(E_f(K)\). The closed-support equivalence and finite direct-image formula of AL.1 and BE give, for every geometric \(y\in Y_z\),
\[
 \bigl(Rr_{z,*}\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}\bigr)_y
 \simeq
 \bigoplus_{x\in E_f(K)\times_Y y}
       \bigl(\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}\bigr)_x.
\tag{BZ.6}
\]
The sum is finite. It vanishes exactly when all its summands vanish, in each cohomological degree. Thus the support in (BZ.5) is exactly the image of the other support. This reasoning remains valid after every base change. Taking the union and then its closure proves equality in (BZ.4), because for a proper map \(r\) and any subset \(A\), continuity and closedness give \(r(\overline A)=\overline{r(A)}\). In particular, under this hypothesis,
\[
 \dim E_g(Rr_*K)=\dim E_f(K),
\tag{BZ.7}
\]
with empty sets omitted. Finiteness, rather than an Euler characteristic or an alternating sum, prevents cancellation in this argument.

### BZ.3. The projective-space calculation with its maps

For a projective bundle \(a:\mathbf P(V)\to S\) of relative dimension \(d\), the powers of the Kummer class \(c=c_1(\mathcal O(1))\) give
\[
 \bigoplus_{q=0}^{d}\kappa_S(-q)[-2q]
 \xrightarrow{(1,c,\ldots,c^d)}Ra_*\kappa_{\mathbf P(V)}
 \quad\text{as an isomorphism.}
\tag{BZ.8}
\]
We spell out the normalization. The finite-coefficient versions of BG, BH and BJ give proper support, projection and the smooth trace. Iterating the affine-line calculation BI.2 gives
\[
 R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^d_{\bar k},\kappa)
 =\kappa(-d)[-2d]
\tag{BZ.9}
\]
with the product trace; BJ.3–BJ.6 prove its independence of coordinates and its compatibility with smooth-pair Gysin maps.

The closed hyperplane \(\mathbf P^{d-1}\) and its affine complement, together with (BZ.9), prove by induction that geometric \(\mathbf P^d\) has one copy of \(\kappa(-q)\) in each degree \(2q\), \(0\le q\le d\), and no other cohomology. Explicitly, the localization triangle with \(j_!\kappa\) has a term concentrated in degree \(2d\), while the hyperplane has degrees at most \(2d-2\). Its long exact sequence is therefore an isomorphism to the hyperplane in smaller degrees and an isomorphism from compact affine cohomology in degree \(2d\).

The class \(c\) restricts to the hyperplane class. Its powers are the generators in degrees below \(2d\) by induction. The smooth-pair Gysin counit for a hyperplane sends \(1\) to \(c\): on a local coordinate chart this is the Kummer boundary calculation in BJ.6, and its line-bundle transition functions give \(\mathcal O(1)\). The projection formula then sends the hyperplane's \(c^{d-1}\) to \(c^d\). The iterated trace sends that class to \(1\), by compatibility of the Gysin counit and the smooth trace. Hence \(c^d\) is the normalized top generator too. The case \(d=0\) is the identity.

Over any finite-type \(S\), the same global Kummer powers define the map (BZ.8). Proper base change identifies its geometric stalks with the just-proved isomorphisms. Stalks detect an isomorphism, proving (BZ.8), also when \(S\) is singular. This proves the splitting by actual classes; it does not merely list the ranks of the direct images.

Write \(P=\mathbf P^n_k\), let \(P^\vee\) parametrize its hyperplanes, and let
\[
 Q=\{(x,H):x\in H\}\subset P\times P^\vee,
 \qquad p:Q\to P,\quad p^\vee:Q\to P^\vee.
\]
For \(n\ge1\) define
\[
 \mathcal R F=Rp^\vee_*p^*F[n-1],
 \qquad
 \mathcal R^\vee G=Rp_*p^{\vee *}G[n-1].
\tag{BZ.10}
\]
Proper constructibility from M and BV makes these bounded constructible complexes. They are not ordinary unshifted direct images.

Consider
\[
 W=\{(x,H,y):x,y\in H\}
 \xrightarrow{b}P\times P.
\]
The fibre is \(\mathbf P^{n-2}\) when \(x\ne y\), and \(\mathbf P^{n-1}\) when \(x=y\). For \(n=1\) the off-diagonal fibre is empty. Pull back the hyperplane class from \(P^\vee\). Its powers through \(n-2\) define a map
\[
 B:=\bigoplus_{q=0}^{n-2}\kappa_{P\times P}(-q)[-2q]
 \longrightarrow Rb_*\kappa_W.
\]
The sum is zero for \(n=1\). By (BZ.8) and proper base change its cone is supported on the diagonal \(\delta:P\to P\times P\). Restriction of the cone to that diagonal is
\(\kappa_P(-(n-1))[-2(n-1)]\): over the diagonal \(b\) is the projective bundle of hyperplanes through a point, and (BZ.8) identifies the displayed map with precisely the first \(n-1\) summands. The exact closed-support equivalence identifies the whole cone with its closed direct image. We have therefore proved the distinguished triangle
\[
 B\longrightarrow Rb_*\kappa_W
 \longrightarrow\delta_*\kappa_P(-(n-1))[-2(n-1)]
 \longrightarrow B[1].
\tag{BZ.11}
\]

Tensor (BZ.11) with the inverse image of \(F\) from the first factor, and take proper image to the second factor. The projection formula and proper base change identify the middle transform, shifted by \(2n-2\), with \(\mathcal R^\vee\mathcal R F\). The diagonal term is \(F(-(n-1))\). The first term is
\[
 L_F=
 \bigoplus_{q=0}^{n-2}
 a_P^*R\Gamma(P,F)(-q)[\,2n-2-2q\,],
\tag{BZ.12}
\]
where \(a_P:P\to\operatorname{Spec}k\). Thus
\[
 L_F\longrightarrow\mathcal R^\vee\mathcal R F
 \longrightarrow F(-(n-1))\longrightarrow L_F[1].
\tag{BZ.13}
\]
Over a finite field, \(R\Gamma(P,F)\) in (BZ.12) denotes the derived direct image to the étale topos of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), retaining its Galois action. It is not the complex obtained by subsequently taking Galois invariants. Consequently \(L_F\) has locally constant cohomology over either allowed base field. Interchanging \(P\) and \(P^\vee\) proves the other inversion triangle. The proof uses no perverse-sheaf decomposition, semisimplicity or characteristic-cycle formula.

### BZ.4. The incidence dimension estimate in families

Let \(S\) be an integral finite-type \(k\)-scheme, \(V\) a vector bundle of rank \(n+1\), \(P=\mathbf P(V)\), and \(P^\vee=\mathbf P(V^\vee)\). Denote the relative incidence projections by \(p:Q\to P\) and \(p^\vee:Q\to P^\vee\). For every \(G\in D_c^b(P,\kappa)\), there is a dense open \(S^\circ\subset S\) such that
\[
 \dim\bigl(E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)|_{S^\circ}\bigr)
 \le \dim S+n-1=\dim P-1.
\tag{BZ.14}
\]
The dimension is absolute, not relative to a fibre of \(P^\vee\).

Choose a proper closed \(D\subset P\) outside which all cohomology sheaves of \(G\) are locally constant. Such a \(D\) exists by constructibility at the generic point and the finite cohomological interval. Smoothness of \(p^\vee\) and (BZ.3) give
\[
 E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\subset p^{-1}(D).
\tag{BZ.15}
\]
For \(n=0\) the incidence scheme is empty. For \(n=1\) it is isomorphic to both projective bundles, so (BZ.15) proves the bound. Proceed by induction on \(n\).

Take a relative line \(T\subset P\) whose generic point is outside \(D\), and begin with \(T^\circ=T\setminus D\). A hyperplane not containing \(T\) meets it at one point. Let \(P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) be the open set of hyperplanes whose intersection point \(t\) lies in \(T^\circ\), and let \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\) be its inverse image in \(Q\). Over \(T^\circ\), let \(\bar P\) parametrize the lines \(L\subset P_s\) through \(t\); it is a projective bundle of relative dimension \(n-1\). Let \(\widetilde P\) parametrize \((t,x,L)\) with \(x,t\in L\), with maps
\[
 q:\widetilde P\to P,\qquad
 r_T:\widetilde P\to\bar P.
\]
The latter is a projective-line bundle. Let \(\bar Q\) parametrize \((t,L,H)\) with \(L\subset H\) and \(H\cap T=\{t\}\). Let \(\widetilde Q\) additionally parametrize \(x\in L\). Its maps fit into
\[
 \begin{matrix}
 \widetilde P&\xleftarrow{\widetilde p}&\widetilde Q
       &\xrightarrow{\widetilde q}&Q_{(T^\circ)}\\
 r_T\downarrow&&\downarrow r&&\downarrow p^\vee\\
 \bar P&\xleftarrow{\bar p}&\bar Q
       &\xrightarrow{\bar p^\vee}&P^\vee_{(T^\circ)} .
 \end{matrix}
\tag{BZ.16}
\]
The left square is cartesian, \(r\) is a projective-line bundle, and
\(p\widetilde q=q\widetilde p\). Write this common map as \(\pi\).

For clarity, these assertions can be checked in vector spaces. For a line \(kt\subset V_s\), lines \(L\) through \(t\) are one-dimensional subspaces of \(V_s/kt\). A hyperplane \(H\) through \(t\) is a hyperplane in this quotient; excluding those containing \(T_s\) is an open condition in its dual projective space. Hence the bottom row is an open restriction of the incidence correspondence of \(\bar P/T^\circ\). For fixed \((t,L,H)\), the possible \(x\)'s form \(L\simeq\mathbf P^1\). The maps \(\widetilde Q\to P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) and \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\to P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) are smooth: the first has fibres the projective-line bundle over the \(\mathbf P^{n-2}\) of lines through \(t\) in \(H\), and both descriptions are relative flag bundles on coordinate charts.

Off \(x=t\), \(\widetilde q\) is an isomorphism, since \(x\) and \(t\) determine the unique line \(L\). On \(x=t\) the point lies outside \(D\). By smoothness and (BZ.3), both non-acyclicity loci avoid that exceptional locus. Étale locality and (BZ.2) consequently identify
\[
 E_{p^\vee\widetilde q}(\pi^*G)
 \simeq E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\cap Q_{(T^\circ)}.
\tag{BZ.17}
\]
Moreover \(\pi^{-1}(D)\to\bar Q\) is finite. It is proper as a closed subscheme of the projective-line bundle \(r\). No geometric fibre is the whole line, because its point \(x=t\) is outside \(D\). A proper closed subset of a projective line has finitely many points, so the map is quasi-finite and hence finite by AU.6/AW. The same is true for the closed subset on the left of (BZ.17).

Set \(\bar G=Rr_{T,*}q^*G\). Proper base change in the left square of (BZ.16) gives \(Rr_*\pi^*G=\bar p^*\bar G\). Applying BZ.2, including its equality case, now yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dim\bigl(E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\cap Q_{(T^\circ)}\bigr)
 &=\dim E_{p^\vee\widetilde q}(\pi^*G)\\
 &=\dim E_{\bar p^\vee}(\bar p^*\bar G).
 \end{aligned}
\tag{BZ.18}
\]
The induction hypothesis applies to the projective bundle \(\bar P/T^\circ\). Shrinking \(T^\circ\) to a dense open gives a bound
\(\dim T^\circ+(n-1)-1=\dim S+n-1\) on the last line. We have proved (BZ.14) on \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\) for each such line \(T\).

We finish the covering argument. After an étale neighbourhood of the generic point of \(S\), and then shrinking \(S\), choose a projective coordinate frame \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\) outside \(D\). Indeed the choices form a nonempty open of the space of frames over the function field; over its separable closure this open has a point. Its finitely many coordinates lie in a finite separable extension, which spreads to an étale neighbourhood. A basis stays a basis after shrinking, and avoiding \(D\) is open. An estimate over this neighbourhood descends to its open image by the étale equality of BZ.1 and invariance of dimension under an étale map.

Each line \(T_{ij}\) joining \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) is good. Apply (BZ.18) to its dense open \(T_{ij}^\circ\). Shrink \(S\) so that every complement \(T_{ij}\setminus T_{ij}^\circ\) is finite over \(S\): it is a proper closed subset of a projective-line bundle with finite generic fibre; removing the closed locus of positive-dimensional fibres makes it proper and quasi-finite. In this particular bundle that locus is exactly the closed set where all coefficients of a finite collection of homogeneous defining equations vanish, so no fibre-dimension theorem is needed for this step.

There are only finitely many hyperplanes in any geometric fibre outside the union of the \(P^\vee_{(T_{ij}^\circ)}\). To see this, write a hyperplane as \(\sum a_iX_i=0\) and choose an index with \(a_i\ne0\). For each \(j\ne i\), the line \(T_{ij}\) is not contained in the hyperplane, and its intersection point determines \(a_j/a_i\). Every such intersection must belong to the specified finite complement. These finitely many choices determine the hyperplane, and there are only \(n+1\) choices for \(i\). The residual closed subset of \(P^\vee\) is therefore proper and quasi-finite over \(S\), hence finite.

The inverse image of this residual subset in \(Q\) is a projective bundle of relative dimension \(n-1\) over a finite \(S\)-scheme; its dimension is at most \(\dim S+n-1\). On the other finitely many open sets the same bound was proved in (BZ.18). Their union with that residual inverse image covers \(Q\), proving (BZ.14).

### BZ.5. A cotangent candidate and the next comparison

Over \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\), (BZ.14) requires no shrinking. Thus for every \(G\) on \(\mathbf P^n\),
\[
 \dim E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\le n-1.
\tag{BZ.19}
\]
Apply the version with \(P\) and \(P^\vee\) interchanged to \(G=\mathcal RF\). The incidence variety identifies with \(\mathbf P(T^*P)\): a pair \((x,H)\) gives the conormal line of \(H\) at \(x\), and a nonzero covector up to scale determines that hyperplane uniquely. This is an isomorphism on the usual affine coordinate charts. Form the cone over the closed subset \(E_p(p^{\vee *}\mathcal RF)\subset Q\) under this identification, and adjoin the zero section. It is a closed conical subset \(C_F\subset T^*P\) with
\[
 \dim C_F\le n.
\tag{BZ.20}
\]
The cone over a nonempty projective subset has dimension one larger, as is seen by trivializing the tautological line on its projective charts; adjoining the zero section adds a subset of dimension \(n\). This proves the bound also when the incidence subset is empty.

For \(F\) on affine space, extend it by zero to projective space and restrict this candidate cone back to the affine open. The same dimension bound holds. CA.1–CA.4 prove that every transverse test pair is universally locally acyclic, and CA.5–CA.6 prove the canonical exceptional inverse-image comparison for transverse maps. These comparisons turn the candidate into a microsupport bound. Appendix CB supplies the quadratic coordinate construction at infinity needed in (BY.26). Higher-dimensional realization uses that construction together with the coefficient comparisons and foundational hypotheses of BY–CA.

The freely accessible source for the incidence construction and its dimension induction is [Beilinson, *Constructible sheaves are holonomic*, version 7, §§1.6 and 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.06768v7). The arguments above supply the projective cohomology, kernel triangle, finite-support detection and covering steps used here.

## Appendix CA. Transverse tests and exceptional inverse image

We keep the finite field of coefficients \(\kappa\) and the base-field assumptions of BZ. The aim is to prove that the cone constructed there controls transverse tests, and to prove the exceptional inverse-image comparison those tests imply. We first supply the local-acyclicity composition argument used in passing through the incidence correspondence. All local fibres retain the selected geometric specialization.

### CA.1. A local comparison criterion

We need a criterion for a qcqs map \(r:V\to S\) and a bounded-below torsion complex \(K\). In its applications \(S\) and \(V\) are strict localizations or affine-transition limits of finite-type schemes, and \(K\) is pulled back from a bounded constructible complex. Cohomological continuity is therefore the one proved in AS.1 and BA.5.

For a geometric specialization \(t\to S_{(s)}\), let \(Z\) be the reduced closure of its underlying point in \(S_{(s)}\). Let \(N\) be the integral closure of \(Z\) in an algebraic closure of its function field. The selected map to \(s\) is understood. The following condition implies that \(Rr_*K\) commutes with finite, quasi-finite, and affine inverse limits of quasi-finite changes of base:
\[
 R\Gamma(V\times_SN,K)\longrightarrow
 R\Gamma(V_s,K)
 \quad\text{is an isomorphism for every such }N.
\tag{CA.1}
\]
For the statement on strict-local bases, the right side uses the closed geometric fibre of \(N\); its residue field is purely inseparable over the selected residue field at \(s\), which does not change that fibre's étale topos. Condition (CA.1) is imposed after étale localization of \(S\).

We give the algebra and descent proof. The ring of \(N\) is a filtered union of finite integral algebras over the local domain of \(Z\): adjoining finitely many integral elements is module finite. Each such algebra is a domain. A finite algebra over a henselian local ring is a product of local rings, by the idempotent lifting of AX.1–AX.3; a domain has only one factor. The union is consequently local, with purely inseparable residue extension of the separably closed residue field. In addition, every localization of the integral closure has algebraically closed fraction field and is integrally closed. Every monic polynomial splits into linear factors there: its roots in that fraction field are integral and therefore belong to the ring. This proves that the residue field is algebraically closed. A simple residue root of a monic polynomial lifts to one of its roots, and the factorization gives the usual simple-root uniqueness. Thus these localizations are strictly henselian.

Finite maps have exact direct image and proper base change by AX.5 and BE. The same statements for coefficients pulled back along an affine inverse limit of finite maps follow from AS.1/BA.5. A surjective map \(N\to Z\) of this form gives cohomological descent for its augmented Čech nerve. Here this can be proved without a general descent theorem. After taking a geometric stalk, the nerve is the nerve of a nonempty profinite set mapping to a point. Its cochains are locally constant functions with values in the stalk module. Choose a point in that profinite set. Inserting it as the first entry gives the contracting homotopy for the augmented alternating complex. The insertion preserves local constancy. Direct image is exact in the vertical direction, so this stalk calculation proves exactness of the augmented complex of sheaves.

To apply it to the comparison, let \(D(S',s')\) be the cone of
\[
 R\Gamma(V\times_SS',K)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(V_{s'},K)
\tag{CA.2}
\]
when \(S'\) is strictly local and is an inverse limit of quasi-finite schemes over an étale neighbourhood in \(S\). These cones have a common lower bound: if \(K\in D^{\ge a}\), then they are in \(D^{\ge a-1}\). We prove simultaneous vanishing of their cohomology by induction on degree.

The reductions used in this induction have finite models. Zariski Main factorization AW replaces a quasi-finite neighbourhood by an open in a finite scheme. At its selected strict-local point this is a local factor of that finite scheme; the open has become the whole local factor. Nilpotents may be discarded by étale invariance. A reduced Noetherian finite model is covered by the finite disjoint union of its integral components. The same Čech contraction, now for a finite closed surjection, reduces the degree induction to integral strict-local finite models. Passing to the affine inverse limit is legitimate degree by degree by AS.1. Thus no normalization is assumed finite.

For such an integral model \(S'\), take its integral closure \(N\) in an algebraic closure of its generic field. This is also the integral closure of the corresponding reduced image in the strictly localized original base: the two rings differ by an integral extension, and integrality is transitive. Its comparison cone is zero by (CA.1). Resolve \(S'\) by the Čech nerve \(N_\bullet/S'\). The column-zero comparison cone is zero. If all cones in (CA.2) have vanishing cohomology through degree \(q\), the cones of the positive Čech columns have that same vanishing. To check this for a column that is not local, take its geometric points over the selected closed point; the relevant comparison is stalkwise, and sections on their profinite fibre are exact by the preceding locally constant-function calculation. In the resulting first-quadrant horizontal totalization, a positive column contributes only above degree \(q+1\). Hence \(D(S',s')\) vanishes through degree \(q+1\). Starting below the common lower bound proves all degrees. Only finitely many columns contribute in any fixed degree.

We have proved (CA.2) for all the indicated local bases. Taking stalks gives finite base change for \(Rr_*K\). Open and étale localization commute with ordinary direct image by their slice adjunctions. Zariski Main factorization then gives quasi-finite base change, and the finite-data cohomology continuity gives the affine-limit assertion. This proves the criterion.

### CA.2. Locally acyclic maps composed with smooth maps

Local acyclicity is preserved by quasi-finite changes of base in the present setting. For a finite change, localize the original base strictly at the image \(s\), and select a local factor \(B\) of the finite base. Its residue extension is purely inseparable. For a selected point \(x\) upstairs, the finite scheme \(V_{(x)}\times_{S_{(s)}}B\) has one geometric closed point, since its closed fibre is local with a purely inseparable residue extension. It is the selected strict localization upstairs. Its fibre at a geometric point \(t'\) of \(B\) is precisely the original local fibre at the composite geometric point \(t'\to S_{(s)}\). The two restriction maps agree. Thus the original local-acyclicity isomorphism proves the new one. Open and étale changes are immediate from the same local-fibre description. AW factorization and AS continuity give the quasi-finite and affine-limit cases.

Suppose \(r:V\to S\) is locally acyclic relative to \(K\), and fix \(x\mapsto s\). Write \(r_x:V_{(x)}\to S_{(s)}\). We claim
\[
 Rr_{x,*}(K|_{V_{(x)}})\simeq\underline{K_x},
\tag{CA.3}
\]
and that this direct image commutes with every ind-quasi-finite base change. The underline denotes the constant complex on the strictly local base, with its actual evaluation map.

To apply CA.1, first consider a normalization \(N\) for a specialization \(t\to S_{(s)}\). Local acyclicity persists over \(N\) by the preceding paragraph. Its fraction field is algebraically closed, and each \(N_{(z)}\) has that same geometric generic point. The adjunction map from \(K|_{V_{(x)}\times N}\) to the ordinary image of its geometric generic restriction is therefore an isomorphism at every geometric point, by local acyclicity. Hence
\[
 R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_SN,K)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_St,K)
 \xleftarrow{\sim}K_x.
\tag{CA.4}
\]
The right arrow is the original local-acyclicity map. The closed fibre in (CA.4) is a closed subscheme of the strictly local \(V_{(x)}\), so its cohomology is \(K_x\), by AT.1. Naturality of restriction shows that the map from the first term to this closed-fibre cohomology is inverse to the same identification with \(K_x\). This proves (CA.1).

For completeness, the criterion must also be checked at a geometric point \(z\) of \(S_{(s)}\) other than its closed point. The construction (CA.4) defines a cospecialization between any two geometric fibres over a specialization: invert generic restriction over the corresponding normalization and then restrict to the closed fibre. These maps compose. To verify this, normalize the closure of the most generic point in its algebraic closure, select the prime corresponding to the intermediate geometric specialization, and use the localization at that prime and the quotient by it. The quotient is again an absolutely integrally closed domain: every monic polynomial lifts to the original ring and its linear factorization descends. Thus the quotient and the localization supply the two intermediate normalization diagrams, up to the purely inseparable and geometric-field identifications already proved in AS. Restriction through the localization and then its residue field agrees with restriction through the quotient and then its fraction field. Pasting the adjunction units, and inverting the generic-restriction units, proves the composition identity. Every fibre over \(S_{(s)}\) has a specialization to its closed point. Its cospecialization to that closed fibre is the inverse of \(K_x\to R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_St,K)\), hence is an isomorphism by local acyclicity at \(x\). Transitivity forces every intermediate cospecialization to be an isomorphism as well. Applying (CA.4) at \(z\) now proves (CA.1) there. Thus the criterion applies on the whole strict-local base.

It follows that the geometric stalks of \(Rr_{x,*}K\) are the cohomology of these geometric fibres: a geometric residue point is an affine inverse limit of quasi-finite neighbourhoods. The evaluation \(\underline{K_x}\to Rr_{x,*}K\) is obtained from the evaluation of sections on \(V_{(x)}\), whose derived sections are \(K_x\). On every geometric fibre it is exactly the local-acyclicity isomorphism at \(x\). This proves (CA.3) as a morphism of complexes.

We specify the two limit reductions used in composing maps. First let \(L'/L\) be an extension of separably closed fields, let \(Z/L\) be qcqs, and let \(A\in D^+(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\) have torsion cohomology of orders invertible in \(L\). The canonical pullback gives
\[
 R\Gamma(Z,A)\xrightarrow{\sim}
 R\Gamma(Z_{L'},A|_{Z_{L'}}).
\tag{CA.4a}
\]
To prove this, first suppose both fields are algebraically closed. They are then perfect. Every finitely generated \(L\)-subalgebra \(B\subset L'\) is a domain. The separating-normalization argument of M.1 supplies a nonzero \(b\in B\) for which \(B_b\) is smooth over \(L\); this localization is still a subalgebra of \(L'\). Given two such smooth subalgebras, form the subalgebra generated by their finite generating lists and localize it once more in this way. It contains both. Every element of \(L'\) belongs to one of them. Thus \(L'\) is the filtered union of smooth finitely generated \(L\)-subalgebras, and \(\operatorname{Spec}L'\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is an affine inverse limit of smooth morphisms.

Apply AS.7 to this change of base and the qcqs structural morphism \(Z\to\operatorname{Spec}L\). The étale topoi of the algebraically closed fields have exact sections by AB.1–AB.2, so the resulting ordinary direct-image comparison is exactly (CA.4a). This argument applies to the given bounded-below complex: AS.7 uses its common lower cohomological bound, rather than an unbounded totalization. No finite-type or properness assumption on \(Z\) has been introduced.

For merely separably closed fields, choose compatible algebraic closures \(\overline L\subset\overline {L'}\). Each vertical extension is purely inseparable: a finite separable subextension of a separably closed field is trivial, and the separable/purely-inseparable decomposition in AH.1 applies to every algebraic element. BE.4 identifies the two vertical cohomology pullbacks with isomorphisms, for the actual pulled-back complex. The algebraically closed case gives the isomorphism between the two upper fields. The square of pullback maps commutes, so its remaining edge is (CA.4a). Its construction is compatible with restrictions and successive field extensions because the AS.7 and BE.4 maps have those compatibilities. This is the cohomology-invariance statement of [Stacks, Lemma 59.90.2(1)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0B), with its deduction from the earlier comparisons given here.

Second, suppose \(\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) has image \(\mathfrak p\), and \(\Omega\) is algebraic over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak p)\). Then \(\eta\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) is an affine inverse limit of quasi-finite morphisms. Indeed choose finitely many elements \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a\) of \(\Omega\). Their monic algebraic equations have coefficients in \(\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak p)\). Invert a single nonzero \(u\in B/\mathfrak p\) containing all their denominators. The subalgebra
\[
 (B/\mathfrak p)_u[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a]\subset\Omega
\]
is finite over \((B/\mathfrak p)_u\), by the bounded-power argument of K.1. Its spectrum is therefore quasi-finite over \(\operatorname{Spec}B\): the composite is a finite morphism, followed by a principal open immersion and a closed immersion. These subalgebras form a directed system, since any two finite lists and their denominators fit in a third. Their union is \(\Omega\), as every element is algebraic. All transitions are affine, which proves the asserted inverse-limit presentation without requiring \(\Omega\) to be a finite extension.

Now let \(V\xrightarrow{r}S\xrightarrow{g}T\), where \(g\) is smooth and \(r\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\). Fix \(x\mapsto s\mapsto t\) and a geometric specialization \(\eta\to T_{(t)}\). It suffices to take the geometric field of \(\eta\) algebraic over the residue field of its image. To see this, pass to an algebraic closure of that geometric field using BE.4, take the algebraic closure of the image's residue field inside it, and apply (CA.4a) to the local fibres after this inclusion of algebraically closed fields. These local fibres are qcqs, since they are base changes of morphisms between the affine strict localizations. The comparison retains the chosen map to \(T_{(t)}\). The inverse-limit presentation just proved, followed by base change, makes
\(S_{(s)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta\to S_{(s)}\) ind-quasi-finite. Apply the base-change part of (CA.3):
\[
 R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta,K)
 \simeq
 R\Gamma(S_{(s)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta,\underline{K_x})
 \simeq K_x.
\tag{CA.5}
\]
The last map is AT's smooth local acyclicity, applied to the finitely many cohomology vector spaces of the perfect complex \(K_x\). All maps are restriction maps. After any base change \(T'\to T\), the map \(g\) stays smooth and \(r\) stays locally acyclic. Thus \(gr\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\).

We also use smooth change of source. If \(e:V'\to V\) is smooth and \(r\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\), then \(re\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(e^*K\). In the strict-local nearby-cycle diagram BZ.1, smooth base change AS identifies the pullback of \(Ru_*K\) with the corresponding image upstairs. Its unit is the pulled-back unit. The defect cone upstairs is consequently the smooth pullback of the cone downstairs. It vanishes, before and after every base change.

### CA.3. Universal local acyclicity over a field

We prove the generic statement used for the product projection. For \(r:V\to S\) separated of finite type over \(k\), \(S\) integral, and \(K\) bounded constructible, some dense open \(S^\circ\) makes \(r\) universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\).

Induct on the dimension \(d\) of the generic fibre. The empty generic fibre disappears after shrinking for a proper source. The question is local on the source, so one may cover by finitely many affines, take a projective closure of each over an affine base, and extend its coefficient complex by zero. The generic closure has the same dimension. It is therefore enough, at each induction stage, to handle \(r\) proper.

If \(d=0\), properness makes \(r\) finite after shrinking: its positive-dimensional fibre locus may be removed, or equivalently apply the generic quasi-finite locus and proper closedness of its complement. The finite-coefficient proper constructibility proved in Proposition 3.2 lets us shrink again so that every cohomology sheaf of \(Rr_*K\) is locally constant. BZ.2, applied with \(g=\mathrm{id}_S\), says that \(E_r(K)\) is empty: it is finite over \(S\), and its proper image equals the empty defect locus of the locally constant complex \(Rr_*K\). This proves the base case.

For \(d>0\), cover the proper \(V\) by affine opens \(V_\alpha\), and present each as a closed subscheme of \(\mathbf A^{N_\alpha}_S\). For every coordinate \(z_i\), consider
\[
 u_i:V_\alpha\longrightarrow\mathbf A^1_S,
 \qquad r|_{V_\alpha}=\operatorname{pr}_S u_i.
\]
The generic fibre of \(u_i\) over the integral base \(\mathbf A^1_S\) has dimension at most \(d-1\). A component on which \(z_i\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\) misses that generic point; on any remaining component adjoining the transcendental coordinate decreases the function-field transcendence degree by one. The induction hypothesis therefore gives a dense open \(U_i\subset\mathbf A^1_S\) over which \(u_i\) is universally locally acyclic. CA.2 makes \(r\) universally locally acyclic on \(u_i^{-1}U_i\).

After shrinking \(S\), the closed complement \(D_i=\mathbf A^1_S\setminus U_i\) is finite over \(S\). Its generic ideal contains a nonzero polynomial; clearing denominators and inverting its leading coefficient supplies a monic polynomial in its ideal, proving finiteness directly. Hence
\[
 E_r(K)\cap V_\alpha
 \subset T_\alpha:=
 V_\alpha\cap\prod_iD_i,
\tag{CA.6}
\]
which is finite over \(S\).
